name: LONE RUIN
detailed_description: MORE FROM US About the Game Lone Ruin is a spell-based roguelike twin-stick shooter with a focus on replayability. Play as an explorer who seeks a mysterious ancient power and venture in a ruined magical city, built atop a source of magic used by olden mages to power and transform themselves. Dive deeper and deeper, battling your way through twisted creatures, utilising your very own magic abilities to ultimately reach the center of the Lone Ruin. An ancient city enveloped by magic. What once was a buzzy civilisation and people living in harmony with the magic surrounding them has long since been driven mad and twisted beyond recognition by the very magic that used to help sustain them. What could have corrupted this city? Having heard the legends, you, a gifted spellcasting explorer, arrive at these hostile ruins a millenia later with the goal of seeking this ancient power and finally cleansing the city of the corruption it was consumed by all those years ago. The answer probably lies in the center of Lone Ruin… if you can make it there . Fight your way through blood-pumping battles and more than a whole host of enemies and multiple bosses in several distinct, hellishly vibrant areas. Don't let the horrifying creatures get the best of you! It’s dangerous to go ‘lone, so pick the spell that best fits your play style to survive the hazards of the Lone Ruin. Maximise your destructive magical setup combo through the many upgrades and customisation options available as you venture deeper into the ruins via your chosen path. Looking for a different challenge? Take on the Survival mode for a timed, wave-based game mode. How long can you survive against the rising difficulty and increasingly tougher foes?

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly really hate to say this, as I've been excited for this game since before it was even named Lone Ruin, back when it was a small arena shooter named Robes over on itch.io. That game was really fun.This game just... isn't that game.Sure, it's got some of the same/similar spells, but that's really where the similarities end. This game takes a very easy-to-dodge-but-highly-punishing approach to enemies which can be done very well (case in point: Scourgebringer) but unfortunately fails to lean into that approach in a meaningful manner. The best games to use this approach go about it by making difficult-to-dodge projectiles that are very easy to predict via signals from the enemies, such as an exclamation point. This game has somewhat slow projectiles that come about seemingly randomly as there isn't a lot of evident lead-up to attacks. The slow projectiles make dodging easy unless the enemy happens to be nearby, and the enemies (in Medium mode) pretty much get one-shot, though they can be pretty tanky in Hard Mode which is a welcome change for the game's structure.I had realized I wasn't enjoying the roguelike mode pretty quickly, so I slipped over to the Survival mode, hoping it would be the same or similar to Robes or the Lone Ruin demo. It bore the same fruits as the standard gamemode -- the enemies were too easy, and the action just wasn't there anymore.Hard Mode seeks to remedy this, and to an extent, it does -- I'll happily admit I had more fun with Hard Mode than Medium -- but ultimately it's got too much "hard" without enough "challenging". Hard Mode seeks to challenge the player by beefing up the enemies and giving the player less health, but ultimately the enemies weren't designed for that kind of game. They're very evidently designed to be swarm enemies, as they were used in the game's predecessors. Large, open maps with tons and tons of them scattered about, all trying to get a taste of the player's buns -- that's the environment where they thrived in Robes and the Lone Ruin demo. Instead, Lone Ruin utilizes relatively tight rooms with usually not many enemies. Beefing up the enemies but using them in an environment that doesn't use them the way they were designed to be used makes the game hard -- not challenging. The game is made more difficult, but the issues with the enemies and gameplay remain, they're just made to be more beefy and difficult.Admittedly, I was super disappointed. I've played Hell is Other Demons, I've played Robes, and I played this game's demo the moment it was available. I had fun with all of them, and I know very well that Kebabskal/Cuddle Monster Games is a VERY talented game developer. I don't know exactly what went wrong in the development of this game, especially when its demo and predecessor were both very, *very* fun, but this game just isn't.This game isn't Robes, which charmed players with intense action and good-looking visuals.This game isn't the Lone Ruin demo, which did everything that Robes did and cranked it up to 11.This game is Lone Ruin, and I honestly hate to say that it just doesn't live up to its predecessors.

_childDocuments_.review: After 38 minutes with the game and just two runs (on Medium difficulty) I'd seen the end Credits... I don't know how this game was playtested (or if it was even tested at all), but it's disturbingly easy to trivialise the game due to several poor design choices.As soon as I figured out you could damage things before they'd spawned in completely, I just focused on making boomerang and blizzard as strong as possible, and was able to kill the first boss in about 6 seconds after struggling with it on my first run using chain lightning.I think the game has a neat art-style, but the use of chromatic aberration and not making enemies visually distinct (or visible through indestructible scenery) are two visual elements that felt really lacking, when all other games in the genre do this so well. And mechanically the gameplay is too basic, again because there are so many other games that do it much better.I will say I expected more from the game when I saw the pricetag and artstyle, but I'm afraid that the budget for the game have been misplaced.Also, there's basically no variety thus far.This may seem overly harsh for an Early Access review, but look at the competitors, and you'll understand. We don't need more of this genre just for the sake of the quantity, we need more games in this genre with well-planned and designed elements to remind us why roguelites are worth buying. This one is not worth your time, and it would need major changes to become worthwhile in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool visuals, a decent soundtrack, and a nice overall base for a game. However in terms of gameplay this is just severely undercooked and underdeveloped. It is lacking in the content department massively. There are 3 very simplistic bosses, approximately 5-6 enemy types, 1 biome that is repeated 3 times, and a handful of upgrades you can get on a run that are either just basic spell upgrades or completely useless.You have 3 spell slots, however because of the way the spell cooldowns work, there is almost no reason to ever use anything other than your starting spell unless you get 1 of the other buff spells in which case you just press that button every 10 seconds or so to buff your damage.You can choose your starting spell, and some of them are just obviously better than others. There is an attempt at forcing diversity by having a random selection of spells being given a free upgrade at the start, however this can be bypassed by simply exiting to menu and re-entering the game until you get an upgrade on a spell you want. This, in conjunction with the severe lack of useful other upgrade options, makes every run feel identical in almost every way.------------Overall, the game is very much style over substance atm. The animations and spells and everything look pretty great, and the game feels fine to play, just none of it fits together all that well and there isn't enough here to justify the roguelike design. The game is a mishmash of mechanics from other roguelikes, and you would be much better off spending your time/money on any of those games. The closest comparison game would be Hades, and this game has probably 3% of the content of Hades at the absolute most, and that isn't an exaggeration. This feels very much like a vertical slice rather than a fully released game.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I have to agree with what many reviewers said about how short and lacking in content the game is.The combat is okay (the isometric view can be confusing and it doesn't really feel snappy or fluid) and the game is pretty (nice sprites, colors, etc), but there's so little variety in items, weapons, enemies and levels, it'll feel like you're playing the same run over and over again. The only 'replayability' comes from unlocking harder difficulty levels, but that's it - no new powers, weapons, enemies, nothing, even the landscapes are repeated ad nauseum.It's not terrible, but doesn't come even close to other similar roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay Video: EDIT: After the recent update, they removed the easy difficulty, so the game only has normal and hard for both the campaign and survival modes.LONE RUIN is a roguelike twin-stick shooter, where you kill various enemies in a room by casting different spells and move on to the next one. The campaign (which is basically a room-to-room roguelike) is about 30-50 minutes long, depending on the difficulty, and it features 3 bosses. Is the game too easy for you? well luckily there are 3 difficulty settingsIt also has a survival mode, which I liked more than the campaign. You have to stay alive in a room for a limited amount time, it gets harder after every minute, and you have to collect a certain amount of coins (enemies drop coins upon death) in order to upgrade, equip new weapons, regain health and so on to help you survive.There is a good variety of spells, upgrades and blessings (which are artifacts/game modifiers) that makes the game replayable. Other than that, no performance issues or bugs at all, the soundtrack is pretty sick, and it's great on the Steam Deck, so I highly recommend playing it there.

_childDocuments_.review: Lone Ruin is a super stylish action roguelite and one of the first great new indie games of 2023. The pixel-art and neon colour palette really pop on screen, with an isometric perspective akin to Hades and Dandy Ace. In fact, I'd say, due to the flexible spell system, combat in Lone Ruin plays a lot like the latter. With a number of short and ranged weapons, the player is able to choose a load-out to suit their play style.Gameplay is fast and fluid, with runs lasting from 5 - 20 mins. Like many roguelites, this is perfect for a quick go - and Steam deck owners will be pleased to know that everything runs beautifully out-of-the-box at a rock solid 60fps. Lone Ruin has an addictive gameplay loop, and a scoring system with leaderboards to keep things competitive. There are several modes and difficulties to keep things fresh - and plenty of accessibility/gameplay options to tweak.Whilst I think this is a really good game, one well worth your time, there are a couple of drawbacks. Firstly, maybe it's just me, but I couldn't warm to the game's music. It's a sort of discordant drum and bass/synth soundtrack that meanders in places. And, for all its beauty, the game lacks variety in level and enemy design. For anyone that enjoys roguelites and high score chasing arcade action, Lone Ruin is an easy recommendation. If you are looking for something new to play, post-Christmas, give this a try!

_childDocuments_.review: - The music is probably the best thing - A solid 9 in my opinion, really well made graphics, I like the pixelated aesthetic and low resolution textures, the contrast of pink and cyan colors are really well put together, so well done to that. - This game needs a lot of tweaking, but I trust the developer will continue updating the game with fixes, the main issue in my opinion is abilities are very unbalanced, there is one obvious spell that instantly kills enemies, making the other spells much less of use. Why would I choose to aim when I can just one shot anyone that comes close enough? Nerfing the lightning spell would be a mistake, so I would suggest to buff the other spells and make them easier to aim, maybe homing towards the enemy and reduce the cooldown. - Enemy projectiles are too fast and come out of nowhere, as soon as you get close enough to an enemy it shoots projectiles at you without any wind-up or warning, it's kind of a annoying. The camera makes it hard to spot an enemy if he is below the screen, making it more optimal to play having the enemy north, but forcing you against the wall so enemies don't spawn south. Some items are absolutely useless, I would say at least 60% of the items don't have any synergy or even a good use, like the root potion, why on Earth would any sane human being stay 1 second in the same place in this game, it just doesn't work and doesn't make any sense. The The power increasing and cooldown reducing items are probably the most relevant ones. The speed items are actually a debuff because if you are walking faster then it's HARDER to run away from enemy projectiles because your speed is inconsistent, making it easier to actually run into a projectile.I would say to anyone wanting to buy this game, do so, because it's fun enough as it is, but I wouldn't get it at 100% price at the current state. HOPEFULLY the Dev actually reads reviews and fixes all the wrong things with the balancing issues. So far the game has not a single bug that I found, except on Survival mode sometimes there is no music playing even if my music volume is 100%, only the SFX can be heard. I would say gameplay is fun enough for an Early access gamePeace.

It can be hard to make out enemy bullets at times and it will often feel like you're a bit too zoomed in though.Music is great honestly, overall sound design is solid.Gameplay is simple yet hectic, it works quite well. The spells all feel quite different and unique however they all have the same upgrade path and the cooldowns are often so short that you can't even cast them quick enough. It feels like we should be managing our cooldowns but it doesn't necessarily feel that way.As you can see, I've played for less than 2 hours. I have done 3 runs and won 2 of them. There is very little else for me to do in the game already besides try Hard mode and the Survival mode. If this was early access, I'd look past it but it's not. _childDocuments_.review: Lone Ruin is a spell-based roguelike twin-stick shooter that aesthetically looks great while offering a thrilling and challenging experience, albeit short. Explore the ruins of an ancient city consumed by magic, and fight through waves of corrupted enemies and bosses. Customize your magical arsenal with different spells, blessings, and upgrades to fit your play style and overpower the dangers that await you. An ancient city from long ago, surrounded by magic, has been driven mad and twisted by the magic that once helped its people thrive. You, a spellcasting explorer, arrive to investigate what caused this corruption, to find the source and purify the city. While an intriguing concept, it ultimately never gets properly explored aside from a few brief and vague cutscenes, which is a shame.In Lone Ruin, you engage in combat against waves of corrupted enemies using an arsenal of powerful and satisfying spells. you can equip up to four spells at a time, including a dash spell for quick movement and evasive maneuvers. Your various spells can be sold at any time for gold, upgraded given the right path, or synergized with a powerful blessing. As you journey toward the heart of the corrupted ancient city, you will encounter hazardous environments, shops, and formidable bosses, each offering unique challenges and rewards based on your chosen path. The combat is fast-paced and exhilarating while also incredibly snappy and entertaining. Despite its compelling gameplay and gratifying spell mechanics, the core game is limited in terms of content and replayability. With only a small selection of environments, enemies, and bosses, the campaign can be finished in less than 35 minutes with only three unique bosses to encounter.All of this results in replayability to a bare minimum, and at most try the three different difficulties in the two game modes. That being said, if you are looking for a fast-paced, fluid, fun roguelike and can look past the lack of content, Lone Ruin is nevertheless an entertaining experience if you want a mechanically polished but short roguelike. Lone Ruin's visual style is a beautiful mashup of 2D and 3D pixel art with great use of color and contrast. The dark and grim environment is blanketed by a fog setting the tone while various props, assets, spells, and enemies fill the screen with neon light hues that create a vibrant and eye-catching aesthetic that perfectly contrast with the gloomy setting.The sound effects are good, adding immersion and overall elevating the game's atmosphere while enhancing the gameplay experience. The spells have unique, impactful sounds, while the environment's distinctive and fitting ambient noises perfectly fit the different areas. However, the enemies' sound design leaves something to be desired, as they lack any characteristic or potent sounds for their attacks or deaths. The soundtrack of the game was a mixed experience for me. While some tracks had an engaging and upbeat sound that complemented the fast-paced gameplay, I felt it was primarily lackluster and not well-suited for the game. However, if you're a fan of synth techno music, you may appreciate it and find it more enjoyable than I did.Performance is excellent on the Deck. At 800p and default settings, it maintains a consistent 60 FPS. ~3.3 hours of continuous playing and drawing ~11.3W while sitting at ~60C degrees. You could tinker with other settings for maximum battery, but otherwise, the default is good without tinkering needed, especially considering you can finish the game before running out of battery. Altogether a pleasant experience on the Deck.Lone Ruin is a well-made twin-stick shooter that offers an exciting fast-paced gameplay experience. The game's stunning combination of 2D and 3D pixel art, coupled with its expert use of color and contrast, creates a visually impressive and immersive atmosphere that makes the game's art style and combat its two standout features. However, the game also has shortcomings, such as the limited amount of content, replayability, a vague story, and a hit-or-miss soundtrack.All in all, if you're looking for a mechanically fleshed-out roguelike with a unique art style and do not mind the short playtime, Lone Ruin is worth checking out. But If you're looking for a more content-rich experience, it may not be what you are looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into pure action, this game is for you.Lone Ruin mixes frenzied pacing, stylish audio and visuals, and twin-stick shooter gameplay into an addictive roguelite package. A pumping electronic soundtrack sets the pace as you tackle the titular ruin, and, while there's not a ton of lore or story, the style is intriguing enough to give the game a unique ambiance. Plus, that's not really the 'point' of Lone Ruin -- this game is all about collecting spells and items as you blast your way through hordes of eldritch monsters. The overall gameplay is simple in a good way, leaving you to focus on the action without getting bogged down in mechanics, and, like Hades, you'll clear waves of enemies before choosing one of two rooms you'd like to enter next based on which displayed reward you'd prefer. It's not groundbreaking, but it works.The clear highlight of Lone Ruin is, as you'd expect, the aforementioned spells -- and there are a TON. From your somewhat expected fireball and lightning spells, to lasers and ice barrages and more, each spell has a totally unique feel and purpose. You choose one spell from a selection of spells to start your run with (cleverly, some randomly come with free upgrades to incentivize you to mix up your choices), and you'll collect up to three total over the course of a run (plus your dash). The performance and feel of your loadout will evolve as you delve deeper into the ruins and, of course, will vary wildly from run to run as well. And, as mentioned, these spells are upgradeable with a wide variety of options -- additional projectiles, piercing, bouncing, mirrored shots, burning, chill, bigger explosions... there's pretty much everything you could want to make it easier (and more fun!) to rain destruction down upon upon baddies intent on ending your run. These upgrades all stack 'Isaac-style' as well, meaning your relatively simple attacks scale exponentially in effect -- exactly what I crave in an in-run progression system.You'll also collect a variety of passive relics (up to 5 per run), and these are upgradable, too. These vary in function, but there are clear sets of synergies, making it fun to decisively assemble a build over the course of a run. A recent favorite combination of mine was one relic that reduced damage taken at the cost of gold, paired with another relic that gave me gold every time I took damage -- this led to a positive feedback loop that gave me tons of defense without causing me to lose too much money, meaning I was free to spend as I pleased at various shops. There are a plethora of great combos like these, and your relics will support your spell choices as well. Got a spell that inflicts a chill status on enemies? You'll also want to pick up the relic that causes chilled enemies to explode on death. Neat stuff!All in all, Lone Ruin is a fantastic game with tons of variety to keep you hooked. With a unique visual style and a roster of spells and items to keep avid roguelite fans entertained, this game is a winner. An ascension-style difficulty progression system also means the game will continually challenge you as you die over and over again. A very easy recommend at a fair price!

_childDocuments_.review: Lone Ruin is a solid but stripped-down Hades clone wrapped in the look and feel of Hyper Light Drifter (from Heart Machine). "Ruin Run" seems to be the "main" game mode with branching path/upgrade choices and encounters (a la Hades,) and the "Survival" mode's arena is exactly what one may expect. The small selection of upgradeable spells/abilities are generally well-done and fun to use, though the contact damage, visual design, and restrictive view lead to combat feeling far less precise than the otherwise tight controls would suggest. While its simple coffee-break premise isn't a bad thing, the lack of persistent progression beyond unlockable cloaks (or build modifiers) means that there just aren't many compelling reasons to play beyond achieving arcade-style leaderboard ranks.

_childDocuments_.review: What I like:- Cool neon 9bit vibe- Great music- Casting spells sometimes feels impactful and satisfyingWhat I dislike:- Lack of spell balance - some of them are great from the get go, others need a bunch of upgrades before they even come close to being useful, let alone strong- No plot or any context at all- Unoriginal- Gameplay loop is too repetitive and boring- Small variety of enemies, spells and blessings- Barebones, basic level design with little to catch the eye at all- Camera isn't locked to character but floats around you which doesn't feel great at all- When low on HP the screen gets so oversaturated with some stupid effect you can barely see anything, and that's when you need to be the most focused and careful- Can't remap dodge to a different keybindOverall, it's just another roguelike, nothing new under the sun. I tried to like it, I really did. Has some cool things about it, but the boring nature of what little content it has make it so you're much better off playing something like Dead Cells or Hades. Maybe some months down the line this will be good. Maybe it won't. Time will tell.

_childDocuments_.review: Top Down Shooter Fans Looking For Simplicity  This is a weird one, and if there was a thumb to the middle, I definitely would be giving the game that. Lone Ruin is one of those games that is solid in its implementation: has layers of depth in the simple gameplay and does good in giving a good first impression. There's some elements of replayability when it comes to weapons and accessories, and each weapon does feel relatively balanced with small differences in play style to emphasize the game's basic movement and enemy aggression systems. It's nice to look at on the surface, and it's a game that I can't really focus on any one thing and say there's anything bad about it.But in the same breathe, it also doesn't stand out compared to others that have interesting gimmicks or a bit more in the replayability department. The presentation has nice elements, but the level design doesn't mix up enough over the gameplay to really make it look different in any sort of way, so it starts to wear on you. The enemy variety starts alright, but the big problem is that many of the strategies to deal with these enemies in combination with the weapons doesn't exactly change up in a lot of ways. It's great at the basics, but it also doesn't really stand out in any sort of way. Lone Ruin is a game that's fun to play, it's solidly design, but it also feels like it doesn't take any sort of risks. It's hard to recommend OVER other games that have some unique feature to really stand out, but I can't say it's a bad game. It's fine. It's just that, realize you're getting a game that's keeping things simple, and that's fine. It's just not a game that you will rememeber in a few years.

_childDocuments_.review: LONE RUIN is a short and stylish spell-casting rogue-lite that’s light on story and heavy on action. You’ll play as a no-name, no-words blue-haired elf chick who took a wrong turn at the rave and wound up in a descending neon temple of doom that’s undoubtedly seen better days. But this lone ruin is anything but lonely, as on each floor you’ll encounter a slew of increasingly angry enemies, ranging from bats to bugs to big ol’ bosses. Let's take a closer look! The core gameplay loop in LONE RUIN is fast and fun if a little too familiar. To start each run you’ll simply spawn and select a single spell from a set list and then gain more of them—as well as upgrades and perks—at the end of each level. There’s a nice variety of attacks and utility spells in LONE RUIN, and they range from the slower, long-range Rail, Fireball, and Boomerang, to more versatile mid-rangers like Barrage, and Chain Lightning, all the way down to the up close and personal Scythe, Flame Breath, and Nova. (And no, that’s not all of them.)  Upgrading these skills is immensely satisfying—I started each run wishing I had just picked whatever spell I had last time, but after buffing the new spell's range, rate of fire, damage, et cetera, it invariably became my new favorite.  Finally, the dozens of perks or “blessings” you accrue in LONE RUIN can dramatically transform your approach to encounters. Gain a floating shield of ice orbitals, double your damage giveth and taken, gain the ability to cheat death, you name it. While you can only fit four spells on the rearrangeable skill bar, you can sell any of them (or any blessing) at any time. But! You can only hold a set amount of gold, meaning timing your trips to the shop is key. The end result is just a super smooth and highly-playable rogue-lite that sports snappy load times, a sleek UI, and solid combat.   Now, if only there was more of it! Despite featuring twenty-one semi-randomly assorted levels, LONE RUIN feels a bit indistinguishable. Each room is small, straight-forward, and drenched in varying shades of purple, blue, and pink. There aren’t any secrets to discover or environmental hazards to avoid (unless you count gravity) and the enemies remain largely identical throughout. So, consider me disappointed as far as LONE RUIN’s world is concerned. At the end of each seven-level stage, you’ll face a boss. They appear in the same order, and—while they’re mechanically diverse—there are only three of them, meaning they get pretty old pretty fast. It’s also super easy to cheese the first boss if you start with Boomerang, so consider me underwhelmed by the game's bosses. As for value, LONE RUIN launches at $15 for PC and Switch and should net players five or so hours of playtime. Without a narrative hook a la Hades, however, this game doesn’t present much reason to keep grinding out dubs, though there is a leaderboard and a wave-based Survival mode for when you feel like mixing things up.  Finally, a few words on style. LONE RUIN is an attractive mashup of 2D pixel art and 3D objects coated in a cool blend of colors not often seen in this genre (or games, generally). While it’s a little hard to distinguish between enemy and environment at times, I still consider LONE RUIN's memorable visual aesthetic a strength. Ditto that for the dark and booming electronic soundtrack, which synergizes wonderfully with LONE RUIN’s cyberpunky color palette and makes me realize that elf chick didn’t take a wrong at the rave... she's been here all along! In the end, LONE RUIN is fast, fun, familiar, and probably worth it if you’re jonesin’ for a rogue-lite fix. I’m giving it an aggregate MEGA score of 3.3/5 (full scoring breakdown available in video format) and hope everyone has an awesome week. Peace!

_childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews Video Review: LONE RUIN is yet another case of new action rogue like titles that the industry has been offering us in recent times. Set on a group of magical ruins with a color palette that mixes between shades of pink, purple and blue, the main premise of this title is to find an ancient power, while you go exploring arenas full of enemies.In fact, the narrative is practically non-existent. It’s offered to the player small excerpts from cut scenes, where he is tasked with venturing into the mythical ruins to find the magic power found in the last level. It just sets the tone for the entire vibrant yet repetitive pixel art environment. The colors used are comfortable and don’t tire the eyes too much, however, sometimes it’s somewhat complicated to decode where the enemy attacks are, or even the enemies themselves since it’s quite likely to end up with the screen full.Unlike the narrative, the gameplay is quite complete and the main focus of the developers. The attention to replayability inherent to new runs and magical powers that the character can enjoy is undoubtedly where all the fun of this title is found. Powers like fireballs, curtains of ice spikes, among others, are part of an interesting range of different combinations that leave open a whole strategy that can be outlined between runs, by choosing different powerups.As in titles like Hades, it is impossible not to make this reference, as soon as you finish an arena it is possible to choose one of two doors, each one referring to an upgrade of a magic skill, the possibility of acquiring a new magic skill, money, and/or passive skills that helps the player in their demand. As in all Roguelikes, death equals starting a new run and losing all previously captured power-ups. Each run is a different adventure, where small adjustments to the approach to enemies make all the difference and make the learning curve more interesting.There are two game modes, the mode that follows a storyline, although almost non-existent as mentioned above, and where it is also possible to have encounters against Bosses. And the survival mode where the premise will be to defeat waves of enemies that get stronger as time goes by until the clock hits 0 minutes. Both modes have online leaderboards and it’s always possible to compare scores with friends which turns things a little bit more competitiveHere perhaps lies the Achilles tendon of LONE RUIN, its durability. Although it features the survival mode, the story mode ends quite abruptly with only 3 different bosses and a somewhat scarce variety of enemies. In about 30 minutes I was able to reach the credits on medium difficulty. By far I consider myself a skilled player, even though roguelikes are in a very warm corner of my heart. So a so-called “average” player won’t have any problems doing such a feat either. Something that is really possible to improve with some updates, who knows in the future, and that will make this an even more varied and fun title.LONE RUIN is fun for short game sessions as it’s short even for his sake and mixed with the lack of content it makes for a combination that leaves a little to be desired. The experience is somehow saved by the fun loop, accompanied by a soundtrack marked by beats that stick in the head.

For example, the spell blackhole does not stun enemies when grabbing them although you'd expect it to have a soft stun in the first or second frame to prevent enemies of escaping it. Stairs in the game feel a bit weird, making you slide to the side once you step on them and provide an almost unfair advantage to either player or enemies if they have the high ground. The game also lacks a compendium to show you all the spells, relics, enemies and enviroments you have already seen. Furthermore, some basic spells feel weird to use because of the speed at which they are casted.

_childDocuments_.review: Lone Ruin is a twin-stick shooter with some light roguelike elements. The main distinguishing factor is the use of a spell system. Rather than having a single primary weapon, the protagonist can collect up to four spells - a standard evasive move, one guaranteed offensive spell, and two other offensive or support spells - all of which are on cooldown timers. Spells can be upgraded but not dropped, so understanding what works for your particular play style is important.By twin-stick standards, Lone Ruin is pretty easy. It's probably best suited for people who are new to the subgenre, as there is a lot of room to forgive mistakes. More experienced players will need to turn the difficulty setting up if they want a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: Instant buy. The game runs like a dream and is visually stunning. The snappy controls combined with the art and music make this a deeply immersive experience. I'm a huge roguelike noob and tend to die frequently when I play this type of game. That's why I appreciate the three difficulty modes (easy, medium, hard) which all have their own leaderboard where you can compare your score against friends (if you have them) and other players globally. It didn't take long to clear all levels in the game. However, I feel like your first complete run is when the game really starts. You've learned attack patterns, how the spells and blessings work, and how to wring out every last bit of utility from the mechanics. The bosses are cool, but the last boss took it to the next level.

A few skills (spells) and passive items (blessings) to mix and match with combos and upgrades to each. The spells in the game feel really good and suit different play styles (though i have not tried them all) and give a satisfying hit when they land.Overall I believe it is worth the price, but the game is short and the replayability really comes in through the survival mode, not the standard mode. Seeing your scores and where you stand with others is a neat thing to add to the game as well and was fun to compete.

_childDocuments_.review: this game looks great, but the weapons are all terrible and are actively not fun to use (they all have some annoyance like ♥♥♥♥ range or ♥♥♥♥ cooldowns that ruin them), the enemies can shoot at higher and lower terrain but you can't (which is not fun or fair design), and hitboxes feel wonky. oh yeah, and salt in the wound: the music is bland. what a bummer.edit to add: the first boss is also shockingly badly designed. the scythe weapon and any others which are effectively melee due to their pitiful range are completely useless against the first boss, whose bullet patterns make it incredibly difficult to damage without immediately eating damage to the face yourself. it's like if the Bone Hydra never stopped thrashing its head around, if that makes sense. completely renders melee builds dead on arrival and feels like a middle finger for trying to use one.this has to be the single biggest step down I have witnessed firsthand in a developer's ludography. _childDocuments_.review: Fool's Errand UpdateDecided to give the game another shot after this most recent update.I like that some more rouge-lite features have been added.  The extra health from the first cloak makes the game survivable now.  Some weapons are still too crap to be useful; mainly the melee ones because almost every enemy is a ranged enemy.This game plays horribly on controller.  When I switched to KB/M, I found it a much better exp.The tower enemies need to be nerfed.  If you have a melee weapon, you just die to these full stop.  I had to get the Rail gun and some upgrades to it before the towers ceased being so much of a problem.Still think you should ditch the heart health meter and just stick to a gauge with numbers or rationalize what a heart is actually representing.  I get you are going for a certain aesthetic, however; hiding an actual stat number behind something abstract like an image just makes it harder to know how much damage you are taking.If hearts were set up so that one hit was half a heart of damage, that would be fine.  Instead its an arbitrary amount of the heart.  If hearts ate 20 HP chunks of the gauge, how can I visualize the damage I am taking?  1 HP of damage is 20th of a heart, but how can I measure that difference on the heart.This is why image based gauge UIs aren't a good idea unless the gameplay mechanic behind them is well thought out.  This one isn't.  A game like Zelda's is.  If a heart might be like 60 health, the minimum damage you can take in some Zelda games would then be 15 and that equals 1/4th a heart.  That is easy to understand.More updates like this, you are on the right track.Overall:On Controller: 5/10On KB/M: 6.5/10____________________Cannot recommend this game as it is at the moment.  It has a severe lack of content, there is no rouge-like progression system as apparent yet; this is something that should be showcased from the first death.There are some UI problems; the health element should not be icon based in a rouge-like, it should be a valued meter.Enemies do too much damage, even in normal, so when you get to the mid-way point you just die unless you have specific abilities learned.I like that the skills can be upgraded a number of times and given new quirks.  I also like that an array of skills are presented when you start a run.There is little to no story as of yet to explain how you came to be in the ruin and what you are seeking.Combat feels a bit strange; targeting and movement are not smooth and have a stiffness I cannot explain.  It is very hard to aim accurately without the aiming marker swiveling around more than expected.There is some promise for this game's future, but the devs have a lot of work to do.  The game does nothing to hook you into it, at all.  It just throws you into the dungeon and tells you to move forward.I lost interest within the first 30 minutes and I love almost every rouge-like/lite I have played.Wait for the devs to finish the game or get it on a steep discount.  5/10

name: The Good Life
detailed_description: Journalist Naomi Hayward is drowning in debt and is at the end of her rope. Having accepted a request from The Morning Bell newspaper to “uncover the mystery of a small English town”, Naomi finds herself far from her home in New York, in Rainy Woods. Upon beginning her investigation, Naomi – camera in hand – soon discovers an inexplicable phenomenon in which the townspeople transform into cats and dogs as night falls... Then, as just she’s looking into that particular mystery, a murder occurs... Join her as she attempts to reveal the truth about Rainy Woods. As a journalist, Naomi is able to earn money by taking photos of Rainy Woods at the request of The Morning Bell and the town’s residents. Also, if she can manage to snap photos of whatever happens to be trending on social media site “Flamingo” and increase her number of followers, she just might be able to earn enough money to make life in this small town that much easier. Naomi herself eventually becomes able to transform into a cat or dog. Turn into a cat, and gain the ability to jump and climb all over town to explore; or transform into a dog, and use your acute sense of smell to track the town’s residents. Use your respective abilities as a human, cat, and dog wisely to more easily solve the various mysteries and incidents you’ll face. In Rainy Woods, as long as you’ve got the money, a free and easy life is yours to be enjoyed. Growing vegetables in your garden, brushing up on your culinary skills, exploring the plains, sharing a drink with your fellow townspeople at the local pub... Stay fed, get lots of sleep, keep yourself looking nice and clean, and enjoy daily life in Rainy Woods. Rainy Woods is full of various spots, as well as an array of events just waiting to happen. Explore the areas around the town to unlock shrines and camping grounds, expand your field of mobility, and enjoy the comfortably open world. Hopping onto a sheep and riding around the hills is just so much fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Comfy photography game. Pretty fetch-quest heavy, but if you're looking for something unchallenging to wind down with, this is a safe bet. The characters are all pretty unique and stylised and there are enough dangling carrots to motivate the grind (camera upgrades, new clothing, a ton of recipes to learn).Still pretty early, so don't know if typical Swery weirdness will unfold, but so far it's ticking the boxes I wanted (i.e. NPCs having little clockwork routines & the studio's take on this quaint English village setting). My only criticism is I wish the fields were different hues - would make long-views a bit more appealing. Also I kicked a hedgehog to death. :U

_childDocuments_.review: I recognise the reviews mentioning the lack of more translation options, so I'll preface by saying I was not a backer and I'm giving White Owls the benefit of the doubt on that decision, as every element of the game indicates that it's a labour of love and I'm sure they'd have wanted better language support more than anyone.Where this game succeeds fantastically is the richness of the setting. It asks you to roll out of bed or work through the night at myriad repetitive tasks, such as rummaging through bins or brushing sheep, and so far I've been more than happy to do so each time because it's a joy to roam in. I don't play many open world games but it reminds me strongly of Yakuza Zero, where there's endless stuff to do in a fairly condensed space and the impetus to play is in being the best inhabitant of society you can be. So far, The Good Life does a better job at interweaving its mechanics and drip-feeding new reasons to engage with its many systems, subtly upping the challenge along the way by giving you more abstract goals without way-markers, requiring some puzzle solving or viewing the world holistically. Every moment I've been able to set out from my nicely tucked-away-but-not-too-remote home with a specific goal in mind, checking off busywork as I go, and I've a good idea of what possibilities will open up for me in future. The way that quests are typically ignored unless they're active is frustrating at times, but overall it gives you a ongoing sense of purpose, unlike other games in the genre where side-objectives can often be completed accidentally while doing something else.The tone walks that same line as Deadly Premonition where crazy things are introduced with enough context that everything feels very intentional, so it can get silly at times without being frivolous, or far-fetched yet internally grounded. The right choice of music and camera angle elevates otherwise ridiculous scenes to something meaningful or comedic, not to mention the preposterously capitalist character of the protagonist Naomi absolutely selling every situation. The acknowledgments of its own genre land as poorly as they always do, but the astute British humour, chariacatures and societal observations are surprisingly touching whether you're submerged in main storyline or side quests. And almost everyone of the townsfolk has their character's fleshed out in a satisfying way, with oodles of contextual dialogue, so it feels incredibly alive among the endless fields and dry-stone walls.There are a few moments where the game spills into timewasting. I'm slightly in awe of games with the audacity to ask you to commit to spending minutes walking at a snails pace, or after doing something 30 times to then do it 40 more. After spending in-game weeks looking for a deck chair somewhere nearby I finally found one by accident, and realised it would take 10 minutes just to walk it back home. In the dead of night with rain lashing down I staggered down the country lanes ekeing out my stamina, and as dawn broke I chucked it into a corner of my garden and went straight to bed - if nothing else it was an emotional moment!I've had a few interesting bugs both helped and hindered by the save system - the game saves during main quests but otherwise you must visit a bed, which I'd recommend doing often even if you're aiming to be sleep deprived. I lost progress when I managed to sprint to a wall-climb spot with a person in my way, doomed to rub my face into their knees for all eternity. On another occasion I fell through the floor while shearing a sheep - the game let me warp home, but due to the distance I'd fallen I gained 15,000 hours worth of exhaustion and became irreperably smelly. Luckily it hadn't saved so that could be reverted, but it's clearly quite limiting without any back-ups. Warping home is a great way to get a headache though, in case you need one~The rest of the experience has been splendid. I've often visited the Lake District and I can't recall another game attempting the aesthetic, let alone hitting it so well. The hills on the horizon are just the right amount of roundedness. I had pangs of nostalgia when I veered into a tea-room on a whim. The low-poly style is very well chosen, and everything here feels lovingly hand-placed. I can't imagine the effort needed to make a functioning open world where things are constantly shifting around, and as a small studio they went overtime with the models and textures - there's so much wonderful detail just in some of the optional interiors you can purchase. The camera mechanics work tremendously when there's so many small touches and cumberland sausages to see.The nature of kickstarter is that many of those who would purchase The Good Life did so before it was made, but I was dismayed to see such a unique and wholesome experience missing the Steam front-page and getting swiftly buried after all this effort, hence this is my first review. I hope this is enough for any who stumble over here to give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: The Good Life is an adventure game with life sim quests and survival elements.Take the role of Naomi Hayward, a no-nonsense journalist from The Big Apple, who is sent on an assignment to uncover the secrets of “The Happiest Town in the World”.It soon becomes apparent that the town harbors some deep secrets, one being that the inhabitants turn into cats and dogs on every full moon. Naomi inherits this ability to aid her in the numerous quests provided by the inhabitants, all rewarded with some much-needed cash to pay off her humongous debt.The Good Life is eccentrically quirky and rough around the edges. The townsfolk have bags of personality and are delightfully over the top. At first it caught me off guard and I was wondering what on Earth was going on. There are some really bizarre happenings but you must embrace it and French kiss it to fully enjoy this game. The dialogues between characters are the strangest thing to behold. Sometimes voiced but mostly partially voiced, I had the impression that some of the characters had Tourette syndrome. During conversations they would just shout out random words like “Seriously!?”The characters are interesting to know at first but they soon run out of things to say and resort to sending you on numerous quests, which range from fetching items and bringing them back, to difficult puzzle solutions like finding items and places from cryptic clues. The main quests were imaginative and interesting to complete. The map is HUGE but you are unable to mark waypoints, and sometimes it is difficult to find your current quest. During the game you will be doing a lot of travelling. I found this very frustrating at first. The dog runs faster but is not a good jumper and your path is full of blockades that only the cat can scale. Transforming between cat and dog could have been made easier, as you have to go back to human form each time before you transform. It soon becomes tedious.A lot of the quests will aid you in the game, and make travelling easier to swallow; unlocking campsites gives you the ability to cook outdoors and save your game, instead of travelling all the way home; activating transport shrines enables you to fast track anywhere where there is an active shrine; and catching and training a sheep gives you a very speedy ride. All of a sudden, those grindy, annoying quests, with slow endless travel, suddenly become more enjoyable and this is when I started enjoying the game a lot more. As the game unlocked, I found myself not wanting to put it down.Every element of the game has been watered down from its basic farming, to its primitive survival aspects. Nothing is detailed and nothing is particularly challenging. Looking after your vital statistics is just a matter of eating six jacket potatoes for breakfast and the occasional salad when needed. This routine completely circumvented any need to brew stamina or health potions; The farming is so easy; it is just a case of planting a seed and picking up the bounty the next day. I didn’t find the need to buy much food, as potatoes were incredibly easy to grow and simple to cook; The photography is an interesting idea but ultimately becomes obsolete because you don’t make much money out of it; and money becomes a deciding factor when buying clothes or adorning your house and garden, because it just costs too much, unless you want to grind for cash. There are also some pointless elements you need to do every day like take a shower and put your make up on.The game is quite lengthy. The main quests alone will take you twenty-five to thirty hours and if you enjoy the side quests then that will push it up to fifty hours. The achievements are very grindy and I wouldn’t be surprised to see you play over one hundred hours to complete all of those. For the amount of content, the price seems quite reasonable.As a journalist you are expected to take photos and report back to your newspaper with any interesting finds. Photos can be uploaded onto the Flamingo platform; a social media site which allows you to gain likes for your photos which in turn makes cash. There are certain buzzwords, for example, #fluffycat, which influence the popularity of your photo and could send it viral. Earn enough followers to be able to upload more photos.Your publisher will send you regular emails asking you to perform certain tasks like taking photos of inhabitants or questioning them for information. Completing tasks earns you cash which is knocked off your debt of £30000 which you owe your employer.You must manage various elements to survive like your hunger, sleep, stress, and appearance.You need to eat regularly by frequenting cafes or pubs. Once you have eaten an item in a shop you are able to learn that recipe and cook it at home, if you have the necessary ingredients. Meat can be harvested by killing prey, or buying it in the butchers, and vegetables can be grown in your garden. If your stomach is empty, your vitality depletes which could land you with an expensive hospital bill.Naomi must sleep regularly or she will collapse. You can travel home to your bed or unlock a campsite and sleep in a tent. The game saves when you sleep.Stress occurs when you travel home without using a shrine or when something horrible happens. Stress can be relieved by drinking tea or taking pills.Shower in the morning and put your make up on every day or else villagers will start to resent “your stank” and put shop prices up.Not looking after yourself can cause various ailments like headaches and toothaches. You can brew or manufacture potions and pills for this, or see the doctor.Naomi can transform into a cat or a dog.Cats can jump higher and scale walls with their super vision. They can also catch prey.Dogs can run faster, and dig up useful items. They also have the power to smell the scent of characters by sniffing a personal item of theirs. Getting around the map can be time consuming to begin with. Shrines offer fast tracking between each other and campsites offer sleeping and cooking facilities. The dog can catch and tame sheep which can be ridden at high speed.You have generous storage at your home for inventory items, which can also be accessed at campsites, and your bag can hold lots of items which stack up. Inventory is sorted out into categories for quick access but dropping items on the fly is not allowed and can cause problems when your bag is full.Money can be earned in numerous ways through your photography, quests, and selling items that you have collected or mined. Having enough money is a problem if you want to fulfill everything that The Good Life has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: You ever play a game where you understand and agree with a lot of the negative criticisms, but it's just so up your alley that you love the game anyways? That's this game.The Good Life feels like a janky relic of the early PS2 era, and I mean that in the most affectionate way possible. There is a lot to be desired in terms of missing modern QOL stuff (seriously, Swery, I can't buy or sell more than one thing at a time?!) but there's something oddly calming in just taking your time to explore the map, slowly go through a story that definitely goes places and just, well, live the good life in game.Is the game mostly fetch quests dressed up with the usual Swery oddball charm? Yes, but that oddball charm still entertained me immensely and the gameplay loop of planning out your day to find the needed materials gets strangely relaxing, almost Harvest Moon-esque.Honestly, the best advice I can give is if you're even remotely interested, just download and try the demo. It's pretty lengthy especially when you try to do most of the doable side quests; and while it barely scratches the surface of how weird it can get mechanically and with the story, I think whether it gels with you or you dislike it, you'll know pretty quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, an incredibly sloppy game that's bloated with tedious life sim mechanics.Here are two examples that I think encompasses the overall problem:1: You will be tasked with a side quest to find an item for somebody. You aren't told this item is rare. You will check the zone that you are directed to, to find the item. The source of the item will run out, and respawns later. Check again and again until the item drops. 2: You can learn how to cook specific food items later, you can do this for fun, or to pick powerful perks that the food gives. To learn food, you have to eat the specific dish several times from the restaurant. Can you purchase food in bulk to eat all at once? No. Some of these recipes require menuing and eating repetitively for 10+ times.There are over 80 recipes in the game to learn through this tedious ritual.The game's art? Fantastic.The game's music? Perfect, and perfectly cheesy for the feelgood story.The story though, is paced poorly, almost entirely due to the gameplay-tedium standing in its way of being told.

_childDocuments_.review: My boy Swery65 coming back again with yet another game that makes me get into that brain of his. The creator of Deadly Premonition gives us a more relaxed game this time, kinda comparable to DP and Animal Crossing? Not a perfect game for sure but an unique one, which is what I follow Swery-San for.So it's kinda hard to explain what this game is exactly. You move to the "happiest town in the world", get to know the people, have to solve a mystery, the usual, but added you have extra weird stuff which knowing the developer I'm sure you expect.You are also a journalist/photographer, so you get to earn money by taking pictures of whatever you find, among other ways too. Now for the bad stuff: the world fills quite empty outside the town, and the scenery often feels repetitive, which probably doesn't help with the feeling of emptiness. I also found it quite tricky to find some materials and other specific items for certain quests, so that made my quest list get really big in no time. That could be my fault though.Still I definitelly recommend The Good Life. Probably since I'm a city folk I don't get used to life outside the concrete jungle :PI give The Good Life 3 out of 5 beers.
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: Kickstarter backer here, so my review shows as a CD Key review, and will not count towards the overall review score.That out of the way...recommending with some serious caveats.It's a SWERY game, but not a 'typical" SWERY game. Weird, messy, a bit sloppy, a more Eastern POV and stereotype of life in the UK and the West.Kb/m controls are quite clunky. Controller is better, if the game and Steam recognize your controller (PS4/PS5 recommended- the game seems to reuse towork properly with my XBox One controller).Still some bugs, one hotfix out so far,hopefully a future patch ot 2 will fix up some of the more commonly reported bugs. If you have a console, the game might play better than it does on the PC port.But still... it's fun to take photos of everything and try to make the HUGE amount of money you owe.The quests are somewhat long and grindy, side quests are a bit vague on what you have to do, lots of fetch quests.Hunger and stress to deal with as far as needs meters go.It isn't like any other SWERY game I can think of- the weirdness is there, the strangeness is there, but the usual gory horror is not so much. I am enjoying it, though some of the quests can be a bit frustrating. (Intentionally catch a cold so the local doc can heal you- if you already have a cold before going for healing, it doesn't count.)A very 80s-90s feel to many things, but mixed with some more modern stuff and some really antique stuff.It's a weird mix- very SWERY, lol.I'd wait a bit to see how patches go, tbh. It's a bit buggy right now (not sure if the console version has the same bugs or not).Lack of Accessibility options and features is also a think- like i said- kb/m controls are really clunky, and there are some flashing lights and light flares that could be really bad for people with neurological conditions that are reactive to light triggers. Even with a controller, it's hard on the hands and fingers for people with arthritis or RSIs. So it gets a "NO" for Accessibility.It's not for everyone.Still giving it a recommended review, because it is fun and cheeky, but playing w/o a controller may be more frustrating than it is worth for some people.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a hidden gem like Deadly Premonition 1, but it sure as hell isn't a travesty like Deadly Premonition 2.  The Good Life is poorly devised, poorly written, an underachiever, badly balanced, grindy for no reason, too short but also padded, emotionally blank and an overall disappointment.  But if you just play the main story and a couple of side quests, it's a pleasantly tepid experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good Life might not be the most fun I've had playing a game, but I think it's the happiest I've been playing a game. As intrepid, resourceful, and heavily-flawed photographer Naomi, you're tasked with uncovering the darkest secrets of a whimsical village, chock-full of the traditional SWERY characters. It's not as campy or quirky as, say, Deadly Premonition, but the intriguing storyline and charming village makes for a great experience.My sole criticisms of the game are the size of its world (it's huge, and if you want to fast travel you have to pay 10 quid per trip), and the potential need for some quality-of-life adjustments (an in-game compass would be lovely). I highly recommend it, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Its alright, mostly consisting of of fetch quests and its also one of those meter-level crafty games. As in you have to hunt/scavenge bits to make materials to craft the stuff you wanted in the first place while watching how tired/stinky/hungry you are. This along with taking photos from a regularly changing list of items seems to be the meat of the game but there's (fetch questy) missions to complete and some mysteries to solve.I'd say this is kind of a dull game but i just played 4.5 hours and want to go back so its doing something right with it, and i haven't got to the sheep riding part.Should point out the voice acting's great so far, the graphics serviceable but i think i prefered the papercraft style myself.The country side in the UK really does look like this (our grit bins are yellow though-not blue) and we don't eat endangered species...Hedgehogs and red squirrels are of the menu.
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: If The Good Life was to be described in one word, it would be 'inconsistent'. I do not know what could be the reason behind the controversial resulting experience but SWERY seems to have completely lost their direction with this title in more ways than one.1. Strong points are not used properly.The YouTube theme song (The Good Life) for the title is pure gold. It plays better than many late Oasis tunes and could become a central hit for any movie.Where was it used within the game? Right, in the last 25% of it for like 2-3 minutes at a completely irrelevant moment. The same goes for many other opportunities ranging from multiple undeveloped background stories to underused lycanthropy ideas.2. Time spent on unnecessary or mundane things.We all know that SWERY tends to pay attention to unnecessary game mechanics such as fishing in DP1 or skate-riding in DP2. Ok, it was cool back then and added some craziness to the overall experience. However, this started biting their back in DP2 when players received a horrible game engine occasionally crushing to unplayable 5 fps rates but saw dozens of cool skate moves. Balancing priorities, anyone? No, let us just waste your limited resources and lose a once-in-a-lifetime chance granted by Nintendo to create a better sequel to your controversially received original game and smash all your critics.3. Unnecessary cringiness.Extremely gory or disgusting scenes in multiple SWERY titles including The Missing and DP1 were fairly expected. But The Good Life really breaks the next wall of CRINGE. Yes, the dog piss mechanics. I am not sure whether it is progressing reactive hypoglycemia that affected D4 development but I do not know a single person willing to play a main character pissing corners for a blind veteran to follow, following piss smell trails in dark caverns or doing other equally disgusting things further along the plot. Overall, I got the game for around $8 on Steam and it was well worth the money spent. However, I have to assume that the problems with the game are probably not connected to some horrible pressure from Access Games, some publisher imposing unreasonable deadlines upon SWERY or some financial constraints. In my opinion, it is the traditional Bioware/Obsidian/Troika Games syndrome where a company has no creative direction and is simply adding more and more elements to the game with the intention to crunch at the end of the development cycle and somehow make it all work. It worked for KOTOR1, Deadly Premonition 1, D4, and several other titles. It did not work for Arcanum (a great game killed by bugs), VTMB, KOTOR2, Deadly Premonition 2, and The Good Life. If you are playing this kind of a gambling game as a developer, you have to accept the winning chances of 50/50. With all great things produced by this approach (I still treasure my 2-disc soundtrack for D4), The Good Life is simply a patchwork of excessive mechanics that do not really need to be there. I think that a better plot with a solid explanation of Elizabeth's death and a quality killer search storyline could be preferable to sheep-riding, mining, cooking or beauty care elements that do not actually contribute anything to the overall experience. The final product seems like a Frankenstein cadaver assembled from different bodies that do not form synergies supporting each other but rather cause a mess of postmodernist deconstruction similar to The Last Jedi where good things get destroyed but no good things are created as a result. However, this approach is true to the Twin Peaks experience craved by SWERY where random elements are thrown in a boiling pot and nothing edible comes out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Technically Its not a bad game, but I honestly cannot recommend it, especially coming with good expectations after playing Deadly Premonition (and that one is a broken and buggy game that constantly crashes on PC, yet its somehow way more charming and fun than this game)This game lives and dies by the meta commentary that life sims are grindy, and will run this joke to the ground until the game ends, much to the detriment of it.All the optional grinding, as far as I know, is really pointless and barely affects your character. All the stats boosts you get from clothes might aswell do nothing at all, and you will be spending a LONG time running around grabing materials, oh and by the way, one of the most basic materials needed for alot of items in the game for some reason is a random loot with  a quite rare chance of appearing.The game's story is a murder mystery where you meet various colorful characters, however this cast of characters are unique only in appearance and lacking charming personalities. Also the game doesnt find a way introduce them to the player (unlike deadly premonition which has a scene where you get to meet everyone), so you might be several hours into the game and still miss a bunch of characters.The game is easiliy divided into main story quests and sidequests, yet there barely any difference. Some main quest are so bland they feel like sidequests, and the sidequests dont really offer good rewards and feel more like time wasters, you might aswell just do the main quest and you still wouldnt miss much.The main character is also very miuch like the rest of the cast: visually interesting but the rest of its personality can be summed up with "I hate this town" and, "yeah baby".In the end this game didnt even mett the measured expectations I had for it. The gameplay is bland, the grinding is long and unrewarding, the characters are bland, the story is cringy and the only charm I find are the visuals.Dont get the game if you expect something like deadly premonition.
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: I spent roughly a 1/3rd of this game with my eyes closed.If you decide to play this game, you will have to do the same.It's difficult to describe what kind of game this is. The closest to a primary game mechanic is the photography, which has you take pictures and upload them to the game's fictional internet, which nets you money based on the subject and if it ties to the game's randomized 'hotwords.' However, there's little to no challenge or creative problem solving when it comes to making use of those 'hotwords' as the vast majority of objects and characters they want you to take pictures of have only one example in one of the game's few interior environments. It's ultimately pointless, as you get far more money from selling the random junk you find exploring the game's English Countryside.Speaking of exploration, this is where the game grinds to a halt. The game quickly gives you the ability to transform into a cat or dog. The cat can jump over obstacles and climb some surfaces, the dog can run faster and for longer and can dig out buried items. However, you can't transform from one animal directly to the other, you have to transform back into human form first. So, you're running as the dog across the English Countryside, you encounter a wall too tall for the dog to jump over. You have to STOP, change into human, change into cat, jump over the wall as the cat, transform back into human, and then FINALLY back into dog. Each transformation takes a few seconds. And to top it off, each transformation makes the screen go ENTIRELY white to hide the model swap. My eyes literally started hurting from this. Thus, I instinctively started closing my eyes during each transformation.And that awful exploration is padded out with the awful grind. Many of the recipes and items you can craft requires resources that take an unreasonable amount of time. Like animal furs, which drop roughly 1 in 8 animals you kill, where just one is difficult to find, or aluminum cans, which you can sometimes find in the town's 12-ish trashcans, despite needing 50 for any one recipe that requires aluminum. (And there's a LOT of recipes that need aluminum).The story could have been the saving grace of this game, but it is not. I finished the main quest, and many of the side quests, and NONE of the game's big mysteries have a satisfying answer. Almost every major plot development ended with me yelling "WTF?" The characters are bland and uninteresting, the writing is passable at best, and the humor is little more than crude.Swery did not playtest his own game. Even the most amateur game developer would have observed the horrible slow down and eye-soar of the transformation. Only the most masochistic would consider the grind reasonable.Rainy Woods really is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hellhole.

_childDocuments_.review: deadly premonition but badhuge letdown, i'm trying to bring myself into finishing this mess of a game but it just feels like swery is trying to replicate his own charm, but failing at itsome of the worst game design i've ever seen, wish swery could do shorter games like The Missing or truly get enough funding to make an open world gamebut honestly, even if this game had a better budget, it would still have issues, because the main gameplay loop is the biggest issueif you want to play a swery game, just play deadly premonition, the missing or even D4's first episode instead, this is just eh

_childDocuments_.review: Worth playing despite it's flaws. Basically a chill life sim. Just do main story and some side quest content to enjoy the dialogues and certain rewards, do not play if you must complete everything.The game needs re-balancing regarding rng and crafting. Even if you go around collecting things a lot during the story, do side quests, etc... by the time you finish the game you still will probably only be able to craft 1 or 2 equipment items out of like 50. There are a bunch of potions you would never craft because it wastes your materials, so an entire shop is basically useless... It almost feels like the devs haven't tested non main story content, or they dislike/want to punish completionists or people who enjoy doing more than the base story, because the achievements and rng for materials are worse than most mmorpgs... Basically you need a full grind routine, which wouldnt be so bad if the rng wasn't so terrible, but as it stands the rng makes the grind painful. if you want to get anywhere regarding achievements and clothing, you're going to have to commit to the game like an mmorpg, hours and hours doing the same tasks over and over.I hope the devs would reconsider and change the grinding, the game is great otherwise, but the extreme grind doesn't make any sense.

_childDocuments_.review: After three tedious hours I ran into a game breaking bug on a main quest. The game also thinks it's clever and 'meta', but the writing it just feels childish. _childDocuments_.review: The core of the game is fun. I love running around the huge map, especially as a dog/cat, and managing Naomi's stats. In that sense, it's an engaging life sim, and I didn't have any issues keeping up with taking care of her health, hunger, etc.However, the minigames are just painfully bad. The controls are universally bad, no matter what, and the game expects an absurd amount of perfection for how bad they are. The drinking minigame? Forget it. Wasted probably about an hour on it before I gave up. The sheep trials? Absolute pain. And you have quests to complete these minigames that take up limited quest slots (shrine quests). Chunks of abilities are also locked behind plot progression, which isn't obvious at first glance. Definitely consult a beginner's tips thread or guide to figure out what order to do the routes in.The item economy is also absolute insanity. Aluminum cans are a special sort of hell. Just look up the item shop glitch and get yourself a set of aluminum chunks instead of trying to farm them the way the game intended. Farming is also somewhat annoying - you have to select a plot (which has a very small trigger radius), then hit "plant something", then scroll around in your inventory that does not sort seeds together and does not save sorting between planting, then select a seed, then endure a huge flash of white light, and then bam seed planted. Like, really? There couldn't have been a little animation there instead? Or it couldn't have been made simpler?Also, making me click for every individual item I want to store in my storage or remove from it is just cruel and mean. Sitting there and tapping a button 30 times to store 30 sage is not fun. It's tedium that should be removed with a simple "How many do you want to store?" button. Seriously. I digress. The game is fine - fun, even, at its core, with fun characters and silly ideas. It just sucks when you're cruising along and hit a minigame pothole that can disrupt the entire game for the duration it forces you to tolerate it. It just sucks! If you can't code a proper good minigame, just make them easy!
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I love Swery's previous games, this is just painful to play in basically every way.The controls are terrible. Trying to attack in Dog form will make you chomp empty air to the side 90% of the time, letting badgers get free hits on you. Naomi's idea of jumping is to skip a little. If you try to carry anything bigger than a flowerpot, as you're forced to do fairly often, you have almost no control over which way Naomi moves at all.Forced mini-game segments are a sin of game design. There are a TON of these, and not only do they lock you out of progressing through the game, but they also lock you out of going back home to save the game, so if you ragequit, as these mini-games seem designed to make you do, you lose hours of progress.The writing feels like having my gums scraped. I have a pretty low tolerance for "self-aware" "humor" in video games at the best of times, and oftentimes it feels like "hahaha the game knows it's a game" was the only joke anyone could think of. I backed this travesty on Kickstarter, and I have to live with that every day, but if you're reading this, you still have a choice. Do yourself a favor—buy literally ANY OTHER SWERY GAME instead. All the others have charm and heart behind their jank, but The Good Life is just plain bad.
_childDocuments_.name: The Good Life

_childDocuments_.review: Adorable, Charming, and FRUSTRATING. A great concept, somewhat marred by content.If you like open-world life sims that kill a lot of time without much effort or thought, or if you are a quaintified Anglophile, or if you just love cats and dogs, you might like this game.I plan to keep playing it, I really want to love it, but I must say my first impressions leave me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoyed.I like the world that runs on a schedule, I like running around as an animal, and I like the American Protagonist being stuck in a very twee English setting, and it's relatively easy to make money through photography, but there are issues that make the game extremely tedious:1. Combat is a joke.- There is no real timing or positioning that can save you. An enemy runs at you, you hit Attack, it is basically RNG who gets the hit. Every moment is wildly inconsistent, when you think you have a reliable pattern of fighting, it stops working.- Almost half the time I attack, my character spins around 30-100 degrees for no apparent reason.- Almost exactly half the time I land a hit, it does not deal damage.- When I do deal damage, it is very little. Pray you do not get the Attack Damage Debuff...- When fighting an enemy who dashes through you, prepare for CTS.- Combat takes a lot of energy. I started today's outing with plenty of energy, but passed out halfway through my 3rd fight, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ was the medical bill expensive. One death in and I do not see how I can recover the balance of my wallet.2. Inventory stocking is hellish.- Want to buy some healing items? Better spend 30 minutes or more scavenging in random bushes and hoping beyond hope that RNG gives you the right materials.- Need a specific cure for your debuff? Same as above but with rarer materials, some of which I have yet to encounter at all.- Collect EVERYTHING you come across, because you will need to eat A LOT, and eating the same thing over and over (even though it's the only readily available product based on materials you can consistently collect) will earn you a debuff - even after only 3 meals (in my case).3. Grinding a field full of corn with two beach pebbles.- As stated previously, much of the scavenging is RNG, so when someone wants you to fetch for a quest, it could take 5 minutes, or 40.- Carrying any kind of large item slows you down to all hell, and sprinting in this situation does not seem to speed up your movement in any immediately observable measure. Set aside plenty of playtime for travelling, even over a short distance. Also you will earn a nice fat debuff for your troubles.- The only fast travel is to your home. God I wish you could FT to Shrines. Maybe I'm spoiled by other games, maybe this game is too brutal.3 hours in and I have 4 debuffs, almost no money, and an inventory full of immediately useless tat (which will likely be useful later, but right now it's hard to imagine reaching later without suffering more setbacks). It's not even a case of 'restart now that you know what you're doing' - that would just resign me to another 2 hours of random item collecting. I may even end those 2 hours worse off than I am now.Oh, and when I died from exhaustion in the middle of a fight during a 5 minuute fight against a low-level enemy, losing all of my money to the vet, I was awarded MORE illnesses, not cured of the ones I died with. Illnsult to injury. The sad part is, I wouldn't of died if I had paid more attention to my stats, but it was so gruelling to spin my camera around constantly while fighting the fox I couldn't focus on anything else besides keeping it on my screen.I long for the day when I can update my review to a Recommendation, because I kind of love this game... For now though, I will be playing it in small chunks, and trying really hard not to be too frustrated.
