_childDocuments_.review: I love Swery games and love this game...when it works. The gameplay is a reminiscent of Deadly Premonition, Shenmue, Majora's Mask, Harvest Moon, Professor Layton and Animal Crossing, all mashed up together. NPCs have lives and schedules, plenty of quests, cool costumes to unlock, recipes to learn, a gorgeous soundtrack and plenty of soul.Sadly its crashes are frequent. It's awful. Optimization is super bad for a game that looks like a comfy PS2/PS3 game.Can't finish Route B since it won't stop crashing and asking for Unity libraries. Also had problems in Route A and the solution was skip some cutscenes. Also played the Nintendo Switch version and these problems were even worse there.Hopefully they'll fix this game one day. For now I can't recommend.And yet I want to keep playing it so bad. It's a better game than Deadly Premonition 2, but at least I could finish the PC port of that game without major problems, crashes or glitches. :(

_childDocuments_.review: So i first found this game because i had played SWERY"s other games. I was very confused as to why the creator of the weird near insane games that are Deadly premonition 1/2 and D4 would make what at first glance looked like...a rip off of stardew valley.Figured i would give it a try just to see what its about. And yeah. at the start, it plays just like a cute wholesome kid friendly life sim. Albeit with a bit of odd humor here and there.But well..lets just say that after a bit into the main story, there is an event that makes it not very wholesome. And everything just snowballs after that in the story. Each chapter growing more and more...well the best way to describe it is "SWERY".It even has the all the hallmarks and tropes of SWERY games, (mainly deadly premonition).-A mystery that grows ever more bizarre as you look into it-A open world small town to explore-Main gameplay consisting of what is essentially sidequests masquerading as gameplay, with random combat that barely works (cough Deadly premonition cough)-a...unique..form of transportation (Akin to DP2 but..englandier)-Detective (but not really) detective style theme, where most of the characters in the are are named and have personalities and routines (sort of like DP1)-and of course unique funky characters with lots of quirks that may or may not play into the storyonce you start looking into it, it has a lot of similar usage of themes and mechanics as DP2, at least vaguely.All in all..Its a shame this game has seemingly gone under the radar for..everyone i guess (except those who supported it in development) so, If you are a fan of SWERYs other work and want more...well this is  just that, but in a cute more (mostly) wholesome english themed package.

_childDocuments_.review: To succinctly sum up The Good Life is that it’s really half-baked but still charming despite its flaws and as a Kickstarter backer I’m happy that I did back it. The Good Life feels like what SWERY originally wanted for Deadly Premonition, a game with barely any combat where you’re just going around town interacting with the townsfolk and their daily schedules, doing random stuff around town, and solving a mystery. The Good Life doesn’t have the strength of Deadly Premonition’s writing though; said murder mystery pretty much goes nowhere as the story mainly focuses on the protagonist, American journalist Naomi Hayward, investigating other unrelated mysteries in the sleepy English hamlet of Rainy Woods. Naomi pales in comparison to the charm and likability of York; she’s rather caustic and whiny to an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ degree, though she does get better as the game goes on. The Rainy Woods villagers too also lack the depth that the folk of Greenvale had, but they’re still amusing enough. The game does have some eye-rolling meta humor though in the vein of "HEY, ITS REALLY ANNOYING WHEN  GAMES MAKE YOU DO FETCH QUESTS, HUH?"  and then they make you do a fetch quest.The main plot misadventures Naomi gets into are entertaining enough though even if they aren’t as gripping as past SWERY games such as Deadly Premonition and The Missing were.The Deadly Premonitions have become infamous for being buggy, but I actually ran into almost no technical problems with The Good Life. There are some physics jank when it comes to mechanics like the sheep charge and carrying heavy items around and I did get softlocked once by an instance of the game freaking out when I was carrying around a heavy item but for the vast majority of my playthrough I didn’t run into real bugs and the framerate was pretty smooth. I’d suggest playing on controller though, seems like it was designed for that more. Though as a warning there is a finicky thing where you need make a quest active in order to craft an item needed for said mission for it to actually count as well to talk to the person that will the advance the mission. That's rather unfortunately jank, but its something that can be feasibly fixed.The main gameplay loop seems fun initially; I enjoyed exploring the map, farming, taking pictures, and doing some sidequests. The two animal forms you can transform into aren’t super deep but they spiced things up some. Though eventually it started to sink in that a lot of the non-main story gameplay isn’t really worth engaging with. This is mainly because how grindy the crafting system to make new items is as well how much the sidequests are essentially busy work, which wouldn’t necessarily be bad, but the rewards are an absolutely laughable pittance, one of the worst I’ve ever seen in a game.  I spent hours scouring the, in retrospect way too large and empty, open world to activate fast travel shrines and camps and my overall reward of spending over 500 British pounds was around like 150 for both missions combined. No item rewards, just pocket change. It’s quite disappointing though I think it could something that can be patched, just increase the quest reward values and cut down on the crafting requirements and then it would be more fun engaging with the systems. Right now it’s only really worth accruing enough money by selling stuff likes dug up fossils and mined diamonds to get enough cash to progress through the story. (Which is like around 1000 pounds) Also some of the mini-games really suck, like the drinking mini-game that is mandatory to progress, that definitely needs some work too.It’s still telling that I kept coming back to the game until I beat it. As I said it does have its real charms despite the problems and the ending is goofy fun that makes it all worth it. It’s like a 6/10 game that can easily be elevated to a solid 7 if they addressed the quest reward and crafting problems like I said. If you’re a fan of SWERY’s oeuvre or just quirky games in general and have some tolerance for gameplay jank, Good Life is worth experiencing.*Edit* First update just dropped and its addressed my issues with rewards and the story mission drinking game, so that's nice.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Unique game that can get a bit silly at times. British people. There is a lot to do, and a lot of places to explore.Cons: The crafting system is VERY grindy with very low drop rates for rarer items, and it doesn't track how you get materials. Some items are hard to figure out how to get altogether. You can't cook or craft from your storage, even in your own home. While there is a fast travel system, the lack of being able to warp from your house adds a bit of lag time.Verdict: A fun game to play, but don't try to 100% it unless you are a masochist. Heck, don't try to do more than the main story unless you have a lot of time to kill. Maybe also wait for a sale before getting this one.

_childDocuments_.review: As always - wish there was a middling option.Is it fun? Yes.Is it repetitive, weirdly slow dialogues, and sometimes damn right weird, also Yes.It's not a great game, but it's a fun game. It just needs some more time in the oven.The one issue I do have is it feels everything was optimised for Switch. So expect the scenery to feel poor at times, and expect the FMVs to be potato quality. This can also be seen in the poor keyboard mapping.The map doesn't render properly and gives grey squares, most mechanics are explained poorly. There are quite a few bugs. _childDocuments_.review: I backed this mostly because I was a big fan of Deadly Premonition, and another SWERY65 game set in a countryside was something I wanted to see.It's certainly odd, and has plenty of flaws: I ran into a hard lock (since patched) and a soft lock. The UI is clunky, the writing all over the place, and the character's voice queues are grating and overused.But all that said there's something here, enough to compel me to finish it and keep on playing. It's comfy -- if you're a connoisseur of rain in video games, it rains a lot in Rainy Woods.Technically speaking, this is probably the most stable of Swery's games -- which may be damning with faint praise, but probably worth mentioning, especially if you, like me, struggled through the instability of DP's PC port, or DP2's Switch performance. If you're a fan of slow paced games, or a fan of Swery's previous work, it's definitely worth checking out The Good Life -- just be aware of what you're getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: A delightfully bizarre relaxation game made up of equal parts comedy and surrealism.The writing is an odd blend of Japanese westaboo (an Asian person who follows American media religiously), trying to write English humour but using Conker's bad fur day as a reference for what English humour is. It's weird but so odd I can't help but find it mesmerising. The setting's adorable "quiet little village" vibes are relaxing, and the frequent dark/crass humour is enough spice to prevent it from ever getting to dull.This is very much "Fetch-quests: THE GAME", but in a good way. You literally just want any excuse to run around the quaint paper mache country side, and say hello to the bizarre locals. This is helped by there being multiple forms of traversal making the jaunt feel a bit different each time weather you're riding a rocket lamb, transforming into a dog and marking trees along the way for bonus points, or just jogging and occasionally stopping to mercilessly boot every adorable critter you see for crafting materials.In short it's a cosy game with a very unique humour and bizarre atmosphere that only White Owls could possibly provide.Play time will very depending on your fetch quest optimisation, (you feel like a speed runner after doing enough laps around this country side), and your desire for completionism. The game has an "ending" but there isn't much compelling you to hit a finish line, just play the game any time you need to chill. There is a DLC out that will give the game more of a storybook ending but I haven't gotten around to it yet.

_childDocuments_.review: After you get past the rather slow start, like all massive world RPG's you eventually get into the swing of things. You know how to deal with food, sleep, and sickness. You have a pretty good idea where the characters are and you are freely going out and exploring. This is when the Good Life really picks up.Unfortunately as can be seen by many game reviews, I imagine most game reviewers (and many players) do not get to this point.  I don't blame them.That first little bit where you move at a snail's pace, then you get sick and move even slower, you have no cat/dog abilities, and Naomi (and many other characters) are just flat out annoying.... It's not great.Then once you get over that hump and really immersed in The Good Life Universe. It's so much fun! The world is massive with lots of NPCs. The character stories are detailed and interesting. Naomi starts evolving as a character. There really is an endless amount of things to do. There are mysteries everywhere! The ending is a really dramatic and emotional experience.It is a really great game. I just imagine a lot of people will miss it. For those that don't this will become a cult classic.Full Detailed Review -

_childDocuments_.review: I love this interactive, open-world mystery. It's full of colorful characters, rich storylines, a saucy script, and fun challenges. You can be a cat and dog and human again in seconds. Each form has its advantages and disadvantages. The NPCs have food and drink recipes you can learn to boost attributes, crafting recipes, tools to progress quests. You need to keep an eye on hunger (and hygiene!) Make sure you're on the desired quest when talking to the NPC, the dialogue changes. It's worth unlocking all the shrines for teleports. I really just love exploring, seeing what I can scout as a cat, dig up as a dog, and discover with opposable thumbs.

_childDocuments_.review: I backed on KS back in 2018 and I've been excited about the game the whole time, it looked great.Unfortunately despite taking more than 2 years to complete outside of the estimated delivery time, the game has lots of frustrating bugs, dodgy graphics, bizarre dialogue and unnecessarily awkward tasks.There are LOT OF GOOD BITS! The landscape is beautiful, its a real shame that the characters and dogs/cats didn't get the same artistic style and graphic design.Pros -- Beautiful and huge landscape.- Lots to explore, collect, craft and do.Cons -- Difficult to navigate the large map without changing characters or spending hard earned money.- As a native Brit I find the dialogue incredibly cringe-worthy.- Very buggy, making it frustrating to complete key missions, combined with...- ... Difficult save process. It would be better to be able to save when you need to.- The awkward references to drugs and alcohol.- Very many of the quests are exercises in frustration as opposed to puzzle solving.Overall, without major improvements, I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who values their patience. However, if you do buy it, you will enjoy it. It is fun. But don't buy if you are looking for the finished product, this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved SWERY65's Deadly Premonition, and actually quite enjoyed its sequel, so I was excited to play The Good Life after a heard he also developed it. I picked up both the base game and the DLC in a bundle when both went on sale. While The Good Life has a lot of that SWERY charm in its characters, setting, and story, there are too many frustrating design choices that keep me from recommending this game. I wish Steam had a "neutral" option because that is probably what I would choose for my review. While I did enjoy parts of this game, I felt the great moments got lost under a pile of bad and annoying designs.The TL;DR review is: if you like SWERY, you will likely find the narrative/character aspects enjoyable, and will probably enjoy the game if you just focus on the critical path and avoid any of the side content. If you aren't a fan of SWERY or don't know who he is, you probably won't enjoy this game because the core game and mechanics aren't really that engaging. If you are still on the fence about trying this game or not, I will go over what to expect with this game, as well as my major criticisms. *The "most playable* and least broken of the SWERY games I've played.*The game is marketed as a "Debt Repayment RPG," but this isn't the case. Unlike a game like Reccetear where you earn money through gameplay in order to pay off your debt as a part of the story, there is nothing like that. You have a large debt, but it gets paid off by just following the main story quest; there is no way to use your own money you earn through gameplay in order to affect this amount. It might as well not even exist.*The game is a blend of photography mechanics (taking and uploading pictures for money and to complete quests), and cozy life simulator (e.g. there is a day/night cycle where shops open/close and NPCS have a weekly routine/schedule).*You can upload photos of interesting or trending things in order to earn passive money over time.*You can earn money from farming, mining, and other resource gathering. *You have a garden you can plant and grow ingredients.*You can craft clothing to wear with different stats.*You can cook different foods with different buffs & can craft/buy concoctions with different buffs.*You can transform into a cat and a dog - each with different abilities that can be used to interact with the world in a different way.*Get to know the charming characters of the game through completing their side quests. *The map is too large for how little game there is. Most of the map is open, empty, and pointless. There are large areas of the map that you are never guide to or required to go to through the course of the game and might as well not even be in the game. There is a whole second town, but it has nothing of importance there besides nameless NPCs and a shop that sells some cooking ingredients. Most of the map I found myself visiting once just to see what was there, and never going back because there was nothing there.*The game is insanely grindy. It can take tons of materials to craft some simple things which are sometimes required for quest completion.*Most quests (especially side quests) are fetch quests that are repetitive and time consuming.*Many of the quests chains for NPCs are just doing the same thing multiple times. For example, one NPC wants you to "mark" (e.g. pee on something as a dog) 10 times. Then his next quest is to do it 20 times, then 30 times, then the final quest in the chains is... to do it 40 times - for a total of 100 times over multiple quests. This is simply not fun to do.*Side-quests feel mostly pointless because the reward for them is typically just a little bit of money (usually between $50-$100 per quest). You don't get unique rewards such as items, new features, or some other "advancement" or buff for your character. And sometimes to complete a quest you may have to spend money buying an item/material to complete it, so the reward you get is sometimes less than what you spend to complete the quest.*The economy is all over the place in this game. Camera upgrades can be around $700 up to $3000 each. That means it could take 7-14+ quests to complete - which would take hours - just to get the cheapest camera upgrade. Meanwhile, I could turn into a dog and dig a hole in town and get an item that I can vendor for over $100 in about a minute. I could also fast travel to a mine and spend about 5 minutes hitting up all the nodes there and get diamonds - which can sell for around $100-$180 each (with a chance of getting multiples). So if you want money efficiently you will be doing boring grinding.*But one of the most annoying aspects in this game is with the world and the transformation mechanics. Part-way through the story you unlock the ability to ride sheep as a way to travel the map faster. This is great, except that the map is divided all over by low walls that block your sheep's movement. The only way around is to dismount, turn into a cat, jump over the wall, turn back into a human, call your sheep again, then mount it and carry on. The problem with this is that the animation to transform into/out of an animal and to call the sheep takes about 3 seconds each time. So in that above example, it takes about 9-10 seconds of doing this series of actions just to get on the other side of a wall. And with how often you will run into this situation, you may be doing this every 10-30 seconds. This could have all been mitigated by simply giving the sheep the ability to jump these low walls, or at least making the transformation instant. While I generally enjoy the the characters and found the story intriguing (at least at first), I am frankly disappointed with the story on how it ended. From the game's trailer, it talks about uncovering the mystery of this town having its townsfolk turn into cats & dogs at night, as well as trying to solve a mysterious murder of one of its beloved members. The game introduces other big elements of mystery and intrigue, making the player wonder how they all tie together and are linked to the murder and shapechanging townspeople. However, NONE of these mysteries ever gets solved, and all the other aspects of intrigue are just non-sequitur one-offs that do not relate to the plot or mystery at all. If you are a SWERY fan and decide to heed my advice and just focus on the main story to maximize the enjoyment while minimizing the annoyance, and are wondering if you should pickup the DLC - DON'T! The DLC adds 12 new quests in the post game that are supposed to "uncover the mystery of Rainy Woods." It doesn't. It doesn't add any new NPCs, mechanics, or assets. The quests are all the standard fetch quests like the base game. The quests do not answer or solve the mystery of the murder or the shapechanging. It simply does the copout thing and says . I think the game wanted this to be an interesting twist, but it honestly comes off as making you feel that nothing really matters.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried (to keep) liking this game, but it just got worse the more I played it. Both the gameplay and the jokes and jargon get old pretty fast, and it's almost embarrassing how they're not even trying to hide how fetch-questy and bloated it is. Just like with certain massive movie studios making meta jokes through their super heroes about how corrupt the studio is - self awareness does nothing if the subject or reason for those jokes doesn't improve. It doesn't make the problem, that people clearly hate, suddenly okay and forgivable because you joke about how hate-inducing it is.  I honestly think the above would however be bearable if the gameplay itself were fun and/or smooth. But in addition, that is also extremely janky, everything from the shape shifting taking minimum 2 steps (each with a delay due to non skipable animation), slow basic movement, constantly empty stamina meter so running is barely an option, quests not tracking properly unless they're active (so it is way too finicky doing time/opportunity sensitive quests), and terrible mount steering. Last, the modern classic of treating the audience like idi*ts. By going with such a sloppy story and unlikely events, consequences, reactions and behavior, not thinking anyone will notice or care. Someone is killed, and both the village and your character just carry on like nothing, after half a day of initial shock and reactions. The village and eventually you having supernatural powers, waved off. You and several NPCs treating each other like trash with relentless insults, that's just something funny with no consequences next time you meet. I personally also get hung up on random animal species being unrealistically aggressive, like badgers or all wild birds attacking humans even if they spot them from afar. Also feels like the creators either think its audience has lived under a rock still believing those "all badgers will attack you at all times and bite you until they hear a bone cracking" children stories, or just lived in a city all their life and never saw a live animal and think all are ferocious carnivores.It's almost a shame the environments, some story elements, the animals and a few other elements is actually cozy and fun, because looking back at the game it makes you feel like it was fun at times,. Which it is, but not enough to be worth spending more than 10 minutes at a time in, before you realise you've wasted that time at a game not worth finishing.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as Swery fever dreams go, The Good Life is one of his weaker ones. Rainy Woods and its characters are a quirky, quaint vibe but the story is, I guess you'd say predictably wacky. You know what you're in for when it comes to a Swery project, but this one feels very much 'out there' merely for the sake of it. It's Werewolves, but it's also Vampires, except it's Aliens too. Does any of it connect or make sense? Not really, but as your protagonist will say, "Eh! Who cares! C'est la vie!" Sure, it may be self aware in it's goofiness, but it's never felt like Swery has used that as an excuse to be lazy before. This is the first time it kind of does seem that way.The same attitude also applies to the overall gameplay. It's a supremely tedious, fetch quest abundant, generic RPG but that's okay because the cast will break the fourth wall with "This is just like a boring video game!" jokes at regular intervals to excuse this apathy to its design. Again, I know you don't play Swery games for their mechanical prowess, but DP, DP2, D4 and Missing were at least ambitious in their approach in many ways in spite of their subpar execution. The Good Life takes many things already established from these titles but fails to add anything itself.So if i'm ripping into it so much, why is this positive? Well, I have a soft spot for Swery, and it's not like I regretted the purchase or anything; it just wasn't excellent. It was still good for extracting a chuckle and a smile every now and then. So if like me you like quirky japanese guys and their stories, you might get a kick outta this.He should put the bottle down and try harder next time though.If you want help reducing the tedious grind,

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played for 5 hours but happy to give this a thumbs up.As someone who loved Deadly Premonition for its understated and unadvertised merit of being a simulation of a small town, I was really disappointed with Deadly Premonition 2. I was really hopeful that The Good Life would deliver - and it kinda sorta does.Some things to point out (good and bad):* I've not encountered the technical issues in the negative reviews, but I've only played for 5 hours.* for a SWERY game, this is quite polished. The overall performance is good and the game has UI aesthetics that feel like a JRPG like the Tales games. Sometimes it still looks janky (low frame rate, music suddenly stopping and starting). * the jankiest aspect of the game is that while your quest log fills up with a lot of quests, only the currently active quest can be progressed. NPCs that you can turn in a side-quest with will completely ignore you unless you make that side-quest active. Conversely, a shopkeeper involved in your current quest might refuse to trade with you, but making another quest active will suddenly make their shop services available again. * there's not much combat and I hope it doesn't become frequent because attacking is crude and it seems like there is very little feedback that your health is being battered. * it needs to be said that a strength and simultaneously a weakness of this game is that it has no core gameplay. There's open world exploration; there's photography; there's fetch quests; there's crafting; there's an economy; there's combat. All of these are side activities. The game can feel empty, it can feel pointless; but at the same time there's a feeling of value that your choices are your own, and the apparent feeling that there's not much to do and the game is slow is part of the relaxed English setting.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying it so far. I'll write up a proper review once i'm done. So a provisional recommendation for now. It's definitely not awful, at least.:EDIT:Having finished the game, here is my review: SWERY, you are a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ schizophreniac. I love you....Ok but seriously, here is my real review.Basically, the most important thing to realise is that this isn't for everyone, and that's ok. I think it's probably a matter of perspective what you get out of things like this. Me, i'm a guy who can enjoy most things. I can watch those animated movies they churn out of the factory, and some of my favourite games are half-forgotten 7/10 games from 10 years ago. I don't need something to be AAA. And that's what you're getting with The Good Life. It's a perfect example of a good bad game. It's janky and unpolished, it has a bunch of bugs, the graphics look like they are from the Wii, and the mechanical depth is at the same tier.But if you can chillax past that, it has charm. Charm enough to be worth it. Sometimes, especially at the start, it really did feel magical.If you go into this critical, keeping an eye out for 'bad" stuff, I guarantee you'll hate it. For example, there is exactly one voice line for when Naomi uses boost while riding a sheep, and it replays every time you use the ability. It's really dumb. I could see that as terrible, as something that breaks immersion. But I, personally, didn't care. I just shrugged, because I know i'm playing a janky ass 7/10 game no one will ever hear about.So, for me personally, I enjoyed it. But it will drive other people absolutely insane. It's not really something you can give a blanket "yes, play it" or "don't play it" recommendation to. So, i'm giving it a Recommendation here and just hoping that people read reviews and realise it's an acquired taste, instead of just looking at the review % and clicking buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently unplayable if you're not running Windows 10.This would normally not be such a big deal, considering the minimum requirements on Steam list Windows 10, but I backed this on Kickstarter many years ago, and there was never any mention of it being needed when the game eventually came out. So now you've got a not insignificant percentage of people who made the creation of this game possible in the first place... being unable to play what they paid for. And the sole reason for this is because somehow the baffling decision was made that videos needed to be encoded with a codec that can only be installed on Windows 10, instead of one of the many equally viable ones that aren't exclusive to a single OS.Oh yeah, and then there's the whole thing about promised subtitles for other languages than English and Japanese that were ditched, and backers weren't told until the day before release. Classy.Will update this review if (and I fear that's a big if) the game gets updated so those unable to install a completely unnecessarily restrictive codec can also play what they've already paid for. I've been looking forward to this game ever since I backed it years ago, and am incredibly disappointed and frustrated at the sheer lack of thought and care towards those of us who funded it in the first place; it feels like a gigantic, 'well, we got your money, so we'll just do what we want now'.If I remember correctly, this is only the second game I've ever backed, precisely because there are so many cautionary tales out there.Add it to the pile, I suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: I Kickstarted this game all the way back in 2018, when I was still using Windows 7, and after people constantly told me about how great this Swery guy's video games are. I also was told that they were as well optimized as cars that run after they've been sitting at the bottom of a lake for five years or so.So after taking The Swery Challenge in 2018 and getting my key around October 2021, I was all set to play The Good Life, a debt-management RPG sim. Or I was, but I can't, because now I use the Linux operating system, and I get the black screen bug that occurs whenever the game loads a cutscene. This is because the game requires the VP9 codec to decode the videos. But! There's a workaround that's in the Windows App Store! (EDIT 10/19/2021: It's not the codec itself, it turns out. The devs goofed up on the way they implemented the 'mfplat' function, which is used in conjunction with a local webserver to play the cutscene files. For some reason. I have no idea why this was implemented this way, but there's finally a workaround for Proton. Every other operating system, unfortunately, will have to wait for a patch to play the game.)  Which I can't access because I'm playing this game via SteamPlay on Linux.So I will say that the game has a very nice menu. But after three years of waiting (or forgetting about this game and then realizing it was out because I got an email about it), I am immensely disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Backed the Kickstarter but didn't play it until the last month when i got my Steam Deck, plays perfectly in it by the way, i think all i needed to do was adjust the resolution after executing it for the first time and that was it. Very recommended, including the DLC which adds some extra quests and answers some questions adding more of them.  recommended, but with a catch: Some of the quests and achievements are locked behind grinding  to casual players, needing incredible amounts of grinding , as save for those you can do the vast majority of the game's quests, including many optional ones, without doing any serious grinding. The problematic ones either need materials that are locked behind time-limited randomness, and many that are drops from animals which are themselves rare, or simply need a time and effort investment that is beyond any reasonableness.So, either forget to 100% this game and enjoy all the utterly enjoyable parts of the game and the DLC ignoring the ones that are downright unreasonable, or prepare to spend possibly hundreds of hours of grinding for the achievements, which would rob it from all the enjoyment. _childDocuments_.review: I want to give this game a positive review, but I found it to be more grindy than fun.Pros:- Surreal story elements with a main story to follow- Fun characters to meet and help out- Able to run around and do your own thing without needing to follow the main story thread- Uploading photos for likes- I was often left with a "wait, did that just happen" moment while talking to people or exploring the game, which for me, is great. Lots of games are the same these days and I appreciate when a game takes risks on weird stuff.Would be pros if they weren't annoying:- Character customization: I've been wearing the same queen dress for the entire game only because collecting materials for the outfits can be difficult- Large world to explore: The map is fairly large, but unfortunately it's covered in walls which your mount cannot jump over. So you need to go through the tedious process of dismounting, changing to cat form, jumping, jumping again because you didn't make it the first time, changing back to human form, and recalling your mount now for this side of the wall.- Fast travel: I rarely use the fast travel system because the price is ridiculous. Once unlocked, fast travel should be free. It would make a lot of the more annoying elements of this game (walls, side quests, material collection) doable.- Camera: Early on the player is introduced cameras and lenses. I'm 20 hours in and have only seen one better camera and one telescope lens. So there are 2 items you can upgrade to, which isn't a whole lot of depth for a feature that's been built out. Side note: I'm 20 hours in and have only unlocked the telescope lens.- Animal swap: being able to quickly swap back and forth between forms would make the mechanics more worthwhile to useCons:- Inventory management: there are a lot of items in the game to collect and unfortunately you need to prioritize which items you want to hold on to when you hit your inventory cap. This makes the customization and cooking mechanics of the game not fun.- Double cost: purchasing items from stores have 2 costs, one is the price and the other is the materials you need to collect. I've given up on any sort of customization because of how hard to collect and expensive everything is.- Walls: as previously mentioned, needing a specific form to jump over them can be annoying. But additionally, all the walls look the same, which can be confusing when you are unable to jump over one. Suggestion: low green hedges for dog / cat jumpable walls, gray stone walls for cat-only jumpable walls, and red brick walls for absolutely no passing over this wall.- Overwhelming quests: I generally like side quests in games, however, the amount, frequency, and requirements for these side quests was more of a burden than they were rewarding. Often a side quest will have me running from one side of the map to the other, taking a day+ to complete, only to be rewarded with, another side quest.- Status: There are far too many mechanics for me to manage that prevent me from actually playing the game. Health, tiredness, beauty, stress, hunger, well-being, getting sick, cat/dog team, food boosts, time of day, and moon cycle. If the game was more focused on combat, health and food boosts would work and make sense. But it seems like the games focus is the main story and these mechanics are just tacked on.My recommendations: do away with the bloat. You don't need all these ancillary systems that are barely used and are more annoying than fun. Return to the focus of your game: Story, photo capture, cat / dog forms. That's it. Center the systems around these 3 elements and you will have created a more cohesive and enjoyable experience. Overall, I really enjoyed what you were trying to do. Thank you.Edit:Forgot to mention the "Yeah baby!" Say it once, then never have her say it again. Delete it from the code.

_childDocuments_.review: "A Very Swery Game"REVIEW UPDATE:The later part of the game gets pretty grindy and lacks some of the more poignant elements of Deadly Premonition. It's still very much a Swery game, but unless you really enjoy the kind of special jank he makes this one might not be for you. In my first few hours of game play I did little more than faff about and kick a sheep to death while yelling at it to get its attention and I loved it.Then I found out that sheep are also my vehicles and I felt a bit bad about my prior actions.And we're not even getting to the really weird bits.This is a SWERY game for people who like SWERY games.  Not what is traditionally considered a good game.  A SWERY game.  Lots of jank, the graphics aren't anything special, the animations are basic.  Sound is fine.  Then you kick a sheep (to see if you can) and fight music starts to play and now you're running for your life because the sheep is beating the tar out of you.  Then you figure out how to fight.  Then you're robbing people's gardens, stacking things on tables while people are using them, peeing on everything and shoving your animal bum into the face of the vicar just because you can.  In the meantime the game is occasionally stacking you sheep just because it can.

_childDocuments_.review:
Play as Naomi, a journalist from New York who moves to a backwoods British town called Rainy Woods in order to pay off her massive debt.

The only way for her to escape from debt hell is to take pictures of happenings in the town and report on them. Of course, 'the happiest town in the world' is not your average town... 

The inhabitants of the happiest town in the world are some of the most bizarre people you'll ever come across. You'll live alongside them as you solve mysteries and experience a hearty helping of craziness. We're sure that you'll eventually come to love all the mystery, horror, and good old charm that this town has to offer.

name: The Serpent Rogue
detailed_description: The Serpent Rogue is a botanical action-adventure game built around exploring a medieval fantasy world, mastering the art of alchemy, and taming wild creatures. Playing as a mysterious alchemist known only as The Warden, you will craft, brew, boil & concoct potions all in your stead to protect the realm from the dreadful Serpent Rogue! The ominous Serpent Rogue has laid down roots on Mount Morbus. Its evil is spreading quickly, and it threatens to overwhelm the realm. It is your task as the Warden to confront the Serpent Rogue and bring peace and tranquillity to the land. Explore every inch of the map, unearth secret passages, and expand your knowledge to stand against the incoming disaster. Using your alchemy skills, craft and experiment with different ingredients to create extraordinary potions each with its own unique effects. Take on quests from the inhabitants of the cursed land and earn resources to further your exploits. Each action you take will create interesting sequences of cause and effect. Keep too many creatures in one place and this will attract blood-thirsty reapers. Forget to bury the perished ones and you’ll start to attract corpse-eating ghouls. Hoard too many items in one location and attract plague-spreading vermin. Shapeshift into different creatures, brew potions that will alter your body, give you unique abilities and create the perfect balance between human and creature.

_childDocuments_.review: Save your money and play the demo. The demo contains half (not even joking) of the explore-able maps. There are a few smaller maps that contain bosses or stores, but where you will spend most of your time is in the the two large ones collecting resources between storms. The game loop consists of collecting resources from the explore-able maps crafting potions to sell for gold to hire NPC's and buy cleansing vats/potions (you can't craft yourself...) to complete the quests to advance the story. It starts out pretty fun, but very quickly goes downhill.It first starts to become annoying with the storms, they constantly charge up and then reset the two explore-able areas also rearranging the layout of the map. If this only happened every now and again it wouldn't be so bad, but its very frequent which forces you to rush to do whatever you are there for. To make things worse they have these gems that you need to find three of to open a chest (and a gate in the first area). They appear randomly on either mobs, chests, or destructible items somewhere on the map. So you have to rush to find all three randomly around the map, get to the chest or the gate before the storm. If you don't when you leave with any of them they vanish forcing you to start all over again when you come back. To add to the waiting around for stuff you also have to wait for the Boat to arrive to hire NPC's, the music to fill the woods to hire monsters, corpses to disappear on their own until you can unlock the undertaker, a few resources that only spawn outside of the explore-able maps one of which I only had respawn twice in my nearly ten hours of play so far. So get ready to sit around and do nothing while waiting for percentage bars to fill up and hope you don't miss the window because they only give you about two minutes before they reset and start all over with or without you.While you are waiting around you can do fun things like practice holding/releasing the sprint button. You will be doing it a lot since you have nearly no stamina and its maximum depletes to regenerate your health until you eat food again. So the less max stamina you have the more often you'll have to hold-release-hold to run around. This can be solved by eating food... if you can find food to eat! Lets take a diversion to crafting, you can find metal, wood, cloth, plus some other items to craft things like Swords, axes, torches, and accessories. You can even 'upgrade' them too! You'll be doing all of this very often if you can keep up your materials. Why? Well, because they all break extremely fast. Especially those nifty accessories that increase your damage, max hp, and protection from status ailments they'll fall apart halfway through one map run. Upgrading them consists of finding one of the million spectral fuel pieces laying all around the ruins north of the first map and whatever modifier you want to change that you'd use for potions. So you want to upgrade damage you need to find a Claw to up your damage from 10 to 20. At this point it doesn't matter what weapon you want to use since you can make any one of them have 20 damage! Wohoo variation!Lets talk about something neat - Transformation! You can totally change your character from a scary looking Plague Doctor to something like a Chicken, a dog, or even a rat! What? You want something vicious? Well, you can change into some of the monsters too... well until you need to eat food, or use any consumable since someone didn't think to allow your Consume key to be something different from your Revert Form key, but no big deal right! Those extremely rare materials needed to make those potions are a breeze to get right! :D I just hope you don't mind only laying two eggs per Chicken transform potion to cook you some food - that would be just sad. :(There are some other more minor things I could complain about, but I feel you already understand where this is going if you've managed to read this far. This might be acceptable for an Early Access game or a cheaper game. This however is neither, if you are interested seriously try the demo then go find a Lets Play on YouTube to see the other half of the game. For the $17.99/19.99 price tag you'll probably get about 12 hours of play if you're thorough and probably 7/8 if you just rush through it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's something like a cross between a crafting game and an adventure game, requiring you to explore and understand the world. It encourages you to try and break its system or find interesting solutions to problems. I was hooked for the first 5 hours.Unfortunately, so many mechanics go unused, or are largely not available until near the end of the game. For example: Want to tame a creature, which the game explains to you at the start as being a basic mechanic? It will need to be hungry first. Most useful animals aren't (such as the chicken). But the hunger potion is gated behind collecting ingredients from an infrequent drop on a semi-rare monster in the last main area. You could also tame creatures through another mechanic, but that doesn't open up until much later. One area I couldn't find until I'd actually beaten the game, because I don't think it unlocks until you die once.A lot of the game leaves you wishing there were more to it. Maybe that was the plan initially. It's ambitious, it does things other games have never done, and doesn't hold your hand. The right kind of person, who enjoys figuring things out for themselves, will enjoy this one. (For me, that's one of the main draws of gaming, being forced into a situation where I don't understand how to succeed, and then figuring it out.) Many others will not, or will be left feeling confused or underwhelmed by the end game. Still others will find the combat clunky or old-fashioned. It's still an absolutely unique game and worth a look.Also, most beautiful clouds of any game, ever, as far as I can tell. And isn't that what  matters?

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting ideas, tedious execution.I like the idea of exploring areas, collecting and researching flora and fauna and using that research to craft potions to help you in combat, however actually doing this is overly complicated and grindy. The melee combat system is clunky and overly punishing. Between the quickly draining stamina and the short time limit between corruption storms (where the world randomizes and damages you unless you leave the area) fights can quickly lead to a death spiral where you will die over and over before being able to recover your tools and food items.I want to like this game, but it's been too frustrating to get anything worthwhile accomplished.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, OK I'm in a very weird position here in that a lot of the reason I'm not going to recommend this game is due to flaws that I personally have a very high tolerance for, but I still recognize they are pretty big flaws.The fact is... This game is a chore to play, with it feeling like they tacked a bunch of features together to make a game as a proof of concept rather than an actual finished product. It feels very much like an early access game. There's plenty of features implemented, but absolutely none of them are polished. Well, maybe the actual potion crafting feels pretty well implemented, but you can't make a game around only that.OK, so let's start with the first really big problem. The entire beginning portion of the game. You are kind of given very little guidance. The game does point you towards beating a big bird thing in the wasteland, but by the time you discover it, you either have no weapons or you have an axe (which sucks), and if you fight it, you'll likely die. Instead what the game wants you to do is scour the wasteland for materials so you can slowly work your way towards beating it. Essentially you need a sword, which you either luck out by finding, or you have to luck out by finding it's crafting recipe. Because you are going to find out very quickly that the sword is the only thing that does a noticeable amount of damage per hit. The axe does exactly 1 point more damage than your unarmed strike. But now we've got a few more problems. They added roguelike mechanics which aren't very well explained. Basically every once in a while a storm wipes out everything in the wasteland, including you, and then replaces everything with random stuff. So you are supposed to go out, gather stuff, return, and repeat over and over again on the same map, doing the same stuff, fighting the same enemies, until you figure out how to beat the bird thing. This somehow manages to be tedious without actually taking that long. I think the average player will get sick of the wasteland after returning to it about 4-5 times, and you'll have probably done almost everything you can do there in about a half hour. Once you beat the bird thing the game opens up a bit, but it doesn't actually add that much either. You've already got a feel for what the entire game is.The game's combat is lousy, unresponsive, and boring. Enemies lack variety and have absurdly simple AI. The gathering gets stale quick. You can get AI helpers, but they have absolutely abysmal AI and you can't order them to do anything other than wait, follow, and head back to camp. The game just isn't designed that you really need them for much or that they can really help much. Honestly every individual feature and mechanic just isn't all that much fun to play around with, and it feels like everything needed at least one more pass through to polish everything up. Even the crafting isn't that much fun to mess around with, with the slight exception of potion making, which can only keep your interest for so long.One example of how the game's lack of polish kind of messes with players is actually in that bird thing I mentioned earlier. The game hints that you can purify it instead of killing it. Except if you try to do it, it doesn't work... Except you actually CAN purify it, but the game missed a chance to give the player some type of hint that it is indeed working. You can get purification potions, and you get 5 at a time. But even if you toss all 5 at the bird thing, nothing at all happens. What you actually have to do, is toss several more on top of that and it will suddenly work when you've tossed enough. Then if you want to tame it, you need to feed it a bunch of raw fish. How do you get raw fish? Not by fishing, oddly enough. If you fish you get some weird type of skeleton fish. Instead you need to turn into a rat (yes really), and get raw fish from upturned boats.  Nothing in the game even hints at any of this. You'd have to have tossed more than 5 purification potions at an enemy that shows no indication of being purified, then figured out how to get fish by turning into a rat and checking boats all on your own... Oh, and if you killed it. It's the only enemy that doesn't respawn. That isn't told to the player either. None of this is. Even how to get purification potions isn't really told to the player. Whatever. I'm getting the vibe that I'm already near the end of the game so I'll power through and if the game gets better, I'll update this. But man this game feels like it's not really giving a good effort/satisfaction ratio here. Most fun I think most players will get from the game is crafting potions and tossing them at their followers to change their species and gender for the lulz.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: Always happy to see a game with a focus on crafting/gathering instead of just having it tacked on as an extra feature. I love that kind of game but I know it's not for everyone.This game is all about exploration, experimentation, and discovery. Seriously, the tutorial tells you what button lets you sprint, what button lets you punch, and barely introduces the crafting system before leaving you to figure out literally everything else on your own. As someone that is absolutely sick of being babied by tutorials, I LOVED this. I spent the early game poking at every mechanic I could find just to see what it did and learned a lot in a way that was so much more satisfying than the game just telling me how to play. That sense of learning and discovery continues even after you've mastered the simple-yet-deep potion crafting system as you find new ingredients and learn what they do and how you can use them.If I had to complain about something, maybe that some of the ingredients take too much research before you can use them. I beat the game with a quarter of them undiscovered. I tried continuing to research the ingredients afterward just to complete my journal, but it ended up being too much of a grind. If garlic does what I'm guessing it does, it probably wouldn't be that useful anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: The artistic style coupled with an adventure/creature collector game really had me excited for this title. Sadly a lack of instruction on mechanics coupled with the starting play loop make this a no for me.You can piece things together getting to the first zone where you encounter a timer ticking up to 100%. If you're still in the zone at 100% and not near an exit you're more than likely going to die, because the stamina system for sprinting isn't all that great. Zone maps don't exist either, so you're stuck trying to balance exploring for items you need to make progress while avoiding imminent death. Moving between maps seemed to always result in coming back to the timer around 45-50% so I couldn't accomplish much because it increases pretty quickly. It makes exploring feel frantic and not relaxing.Within the first hour I also encountered a bug when discovering a creature that made it so none of my button inputs worked forcing me to Alt F4 out. The lack of save function made it so all the progress I made to that point was reset to when I first entered the zone. Frustrating to say the least. The creature AI leaves something to be desired as my first creature either did nothing or spammed attacks endlessly while just getting hit over and over. There's also friendly fire on your potions which led to a pretty fast death for my creature when paired with its AI.There seem to be a good number of ideas in this game that could have made it a nice little gem, especially with the overall aesthetic, but it becomes tedious trying to piece everything together.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the early confusion, The Serpent Rogue is a great pick for fans of craft-intensive games like Valheim. The focus on exploration will appeal to open-world RPG gamers, as well as those who like strong stories with dark or spooky themes. The game's crafting system is well-balanced, and the ability to learn about crafting ingredients adds an extra level of immersion that benefits the main character's role as an alchemist. While The Serpent Rogue may not be great as an entry-level crafting game, it is a fantastic and beautifully crafted fantasy adventure that is enjoyable and challenging from the second players embark on their journey.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: The Serpent Rogue is.. curious. Not strictly bad, but perhaps not complete enough to actually warrant playing - which is not altogether unusual for Team17 publishings. Evokes feelings of FATE and hints of some of the freedoms of Fable.Some the core ideas, the actual use of ingredients and potions rather than them feeling like an over complication or something to be ignored, work fairly well, but there isn't actually enough game to then put those ideas into practice. There are effectively only -two- gameplay areas  They're not that big or varied, and you have to leave fairly often and return to either get more ingredients to appear or because the rogue-lite element of the area refreshing is occurring.You can have an array of followers, change them, yourself, or your enemies with potions - but again there isn't enough of a game to warrant doing so. Most of what you will fight or encounter just feel like low level monsters. Rats, chickens, skeletons. Technically only one large enemy blocks your way to the end game and is introduced at the start - and once you deal with it it is no longer a problem.Serpent Rogue needs a lot more development. As another mentions: it is a very solid proof of concept or extended demo.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: Starts fun, cute graphical style, teases you with what the crafting systems will be like. But then you unlock a few zones, and realize that the entire game world is on the map you see at the start. And most of the "content" will be you farming the same few zones, over and over again.You can't adjust the camera, combat is terribly clunky, you spend ages farming in a few renewable areas in order to open chests to get rarer items in order to be strong enough to beat boring checkpoint bosses, the stamina bar is small, you have to hold shift to run, if you have any stamina because the food needed to replenish your stamina is mostly absent... And from reading other reviews these problems do not improve at any point. If anything your reward for playing further seems to be unlocking more unpolished, unplayable game.If you're thinking of playing this I would think again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: Got the game as a birthday gift after eyeing it pre-release for a few months.6.5 hour later i beat the main part of the game, BUT i feel like i've only experienced like 25-33% of it.Is it worth the price without sales? I'll let you decide, depending on what you like.The main loop of the game made me feel like i was playing Animal Crossing for the first time again - Going out, collecting loot with some distractions in the middle, getting back, crafting with what i got, waiting for more materials.The collection, recipe and crafting system is simple and fun, you actually feel like you're learning things as you go.The combat system --works--. It's not perfect, definitely rough to get into for the first time but the game manages to make it work. A simple hit and run strategy mixed with throwing damage potions at scarier things is what you will spend most of your encounters on. There's no dodge mechanic yet, but it would be a really nice addon, The stamina bar drains fast, but once you start cooking foods 1-2 hours in, it stops being a problem and survival becomes easier.If you want a chill and therapeutic experience of foraging with a great artstyle and beauriful soundtrack I'd definitely recomend experiencing the game. There's a lot of ways you could approach the gameplay, but don't expect an in-depth system that takes hours to master, it's a 600mb game.I hope the game will expand over time, new areas, mechanics, materials etc, because it is a bit small and empty even with the amount of materials and recipes in itI will definitely try to 100% the achievements at some point because it sounds like a really fun challenge

_childDocuments_.review: So, I know I haven't 100% the game and I know I probably won't. Therefore take my review with more than a few grains of salt. I personally did not like this game that much, that being said, I don't think others won't or shouldn't enjoy this game. It has it's aesthetics, everything looks unique and there are many things that are enjoyable, from the recipe hunting, to gathering and researching potion ingredients, or even taming and playing around with all the different critters, big or small. I personally think it did well on the crafting systems, weight balancing, journal and map refreshing. The crafting systems were unique in a way that if you had a general idea on how to puzzle solve, then potions were very easy to craft. Cooking was similar as it had stages to the recipes, but you would gain multiple tier 3 food items for each craft, making the resource loss manageable and it easier to tame bigger critters. Forging was less amazing since unless you ground out a ton of logs constantly, you weren't gonna forge a ton, especially if you just farmed moonstone chests like me. Enhancing was interesting though, albeit very small scale as a feature. It was basically plug and play with any highlighted modifier and you could change a ton about specialty tools.I'm going to combine the map factors and weight system here. My belief is that they did a very good job balancing weight in the game. Weight in The Serpent Rogue, was simply balanced. In more detail, the tools are balanced based off their amount of general use, whereas the smaller the tool is, the lighter it also is. Potions, food items and ingredients are weighted well too, meaning that you can carry a ton of a basic ingredients, but a rarer ingredient takes up more space so you have to debate what to keep and what to chuck, potions being all the same weight also helped. The map elements on the other hand seem to just be modular pieces, each piece moving, or even being exchanged for a different module. You could get a nest hill or a thorny hill then the next storm cycle, you have a moonstone chest. There's also a bonus where (as far as I know) every time you relog, the areas with no storms also refresh their contents, to some extent.Now for what I don't particularly like about this game that makes me dislike it as much as I do. I'll make this brief so it doesn't seem like I'm trying to drain every second out of your day. A major issue I felt, the game seems long, but it's just grindy, with not a super large amount of content at least not enough for $20 in my opinion. The kiosk is dumb cause every potion can be sold for 1-3 gold if it's sold too much, even highly priced ones (I know supply and demand stuff but from 40 to 1???). There are some trees with high roots that look like you could walk under, but you can't, meaning traversing is awkward. Researching is tedious and doesn't often make sense since resources are pretty scarce. Lower tier resources are incredibly hard to find sometimes, I took 2 hours for eggshells and 7 for seeds, meaning you need a ton of luck. Lock picks will break almost 100% of the time which means looting chests is pretty inefficient if you don't have good luck with scrap metal or the locks. Some key abilities of animals aren't explained on how they are used, or at least I never saw something about it, so you have to trial and error how to sneak as a rat or lay an egg as a chicken. Sometimes the moonstone chest doesn't spawn but it still allows you to gather all the stones, or sometimes 1 stone is just gone and you are stuck with 2 out of 3. I prepared some broken tier gear (20 dmg sword, 20 dmg claw necklace, 20 hp bottle, +food and pots) and the final boss fight just makes all my preparation useless. I have a ton of other nitpicks and complaints but they aren't as large in my opinion.Edit: I found out after a bit more play that the special chest or 1 of them can be locked behind a gate that happens to also require the moonstones so it's honestly not the best design. There also a bunch of other bits and bobs that I found out with a little bit more time investment, most negative sadly. All in all, definitely not worth the cost, and honestly, I wish I had realized sooner to refund it. I know it's rude but it's not the best for it's price. (Edit was made with a different frame of mind and mood)TL;DR Its a pretty game, interesting ideas and mechanics, but I have a ton of nitpicks and problems with some design choices which adds up to my negative view of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be fooled by the high praise in the trailers. I got this basically free from Humble Choice and still feel like I was ripped off. It's got a great aesthetic, but that's really the only thing going for it. Accomplishing anything takes far longer than it should, especially in the early game. Took a little more than 2 hours before I found the random bottle that allowed me to craft a  basic tool, an axe. The battle mechanics are extremely clunky and force you to rely either on throwables that you can't craft for too long or tools that break in less time than it takes to craft them. If the dev team hadn't completely abandoned this game, it might have a chance to at least be mediocre, instead it's left to rot with half-baked ideas and unfinished or entirely broken mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential to it. The crafting system is fun,and the aesthetics and graphic design is lovely, However, the game is essentially just about crafting. Which I would theoretically be happy with, BUT... there is a central, rogue-like element in that the places you go to collect crafting materials are on a timer. Once the timer is up, the landscape and what is available changes. So you're going back to the same area and having to re-explore it every time. This wouldn't be so bad if you dying didn't leave all your things where you died. You die a lot in the beginning of this game. And THAT wouldn't be so bad if your stuff wasn't wiped away with the next timer ending. And THAAAAT wouldn't be so bad if you didn't unpredictably lose your essential helpers in a variety of extremely annoying ways. With very limited carrying capacity, you need helpers running along with you to help you carry things. Until somewhat later in the game, they are so useless in a fight, it's best to avoid confrontations. But they are very stupid, so may throw themselves into a fight to the death behind you, while you are gathering something else. Thus you have to carry their burden, or dump it, so you can escape.What kept happening is I would slowly collect enough items to craft the things I needed. I would finally have got a halfway decent tamed animal, since they are the only helpers worth having.  And I would be JUST about to head out, when an enemy popped out and engaged all my very stupid animals. Which kept us long enough to be caught in the storm. Which wiped us all out. So I lost EVERYTHING. Every animal and every heavy crafting item I needed them to carry. And I would be left to collect everything all over again.It's tedious AF. It feels like grinding all the time. I was even legitimately upset at one point because of how much I lost in one, stupid, fell swoop. And! It's buggy as hell. I NEVER got to ride the Valravn, even though I had one and ran into several. The ride function just never, ever appeared. I never found enough sap to make hunger potions, and I never found enough Valravns to uncover their preferred food. Even though I looked it up on the internet, whether through bugs or bad luck, I was unable to do one of the majorly interesting to me things the game trailer promised. By the time this beast appeared in the game, I had become so fed up with grinding, I just didn't have the patience to spend another couple of hours slowly wandering and hoping they had spawned this time around and then looking at them, and then trying to find sap, and then crafting potions, and then doing it all over again because of the inevitable loss of everything in spite of all my planning, blahblahblah.All in all, this was a very frustrating game. I wanted to like it. But mostly I was just playing it from a stubborn refusal to be beat. I put 40 hours into it and I'm not sure I even had fun. As the final, most frustrating cherry on top, the apparent moral of the game is that having any personal identity will lead you to destroying the world to keep that identity. And only when you give up your identity and your life to save the world will you finally be "good".Oh and there's a literal soul slave ship that sails into port and you just purchase souls to serve you and be forced to follow you into the deadly wasteland where they would inevitably die in the first fight they encountered. You must have slave souls. The game requires it. So that's fun too.Ugh. I just wanted to ride big beasts and make potions. :( Not buy slaves and starve animals to make them my pets to feed into an endless grind of death and destruction. Gross.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to lie, this game feels more like a proof of concept with a really long demo rather than a 'full game'. There's enough here to justify the price, buuuut it is still a bit short (easily about 1/6th of my own playtime. I'm just really really slow at stuff).However, I do like the direction the devs are actually going with the game in general. There's a relatively easy to understand and solid Alchemy/forging system here (the game just doesn't really teach it well), allowing you to not just make potions or enhance stuff to items. But to actually change the properties of those items too! If you find a ring that protects you against "Souless", you can Change it to protect you against Burning or Poison instead. Feeling like that Silver Cross artifact is a little lackluster due to its 5% chance to avoid damage? You can jack that up to 20% instead!I love this, honestly, and want to see this in more games. It compliments the urge to go out and explore, collect things and 'research' them so you can discover what they do. How you can change items that you have and make new ones. The feeling you get when you come up with an idea is wonderful: "Hmm, this feather matches the same name as that griffon thing from the beginning of the game. Can I... Change myself into one of those!? Can I turn a chicken into one!?" It is beyond cool and absolutely love it. Speaking of changing forms, your main antagonist in the game is 'The Corruption', no surprise there. But what is interesting is that you can purge it- including the 'bosses' that you come up against. Giving you a unique option to getting around them- without even actually having to fight them. Instead, you can Tame them if you have the correct access to their preferred foods. The strongest monster in the game; the second to last boss, you can cure and tame. Having that option legit means the world to me as a non-human enthusiast.But sadly, The Serpent Rogue isn't all positives. The combat isn't... Great, but I've seen a lot worse. Your defensive option is basically blocking or moving out of the way (no actual Evade, just simple movement/sprinting. Abuse the fact that there's no body-blocking), however blocking not only tanks your stamina, but your weapon's durability too. Making it feel rather unreliable. There are no ranged options other than potions and throwing your weapon- which does sound silly, but it is surprisingly effective. It feels like the game wants you to utilize the Transforming aspect of the alchemy system but there's a very large Glaring issue with it...Weight.You have a weight stat for carrying capacity. Which kinda makes sense, don't get me wrong. You can't carry everything on you at all times and that's okay. However, it REALLY gets in the way when you want to transform. Found a little hole you can crawl into as a rat? Cool beans! Make a rat potion, use it- Oh no! Rats can only carry 10lbs of weight vs your normal 40lbs! So now you move like a turtle on morphine.Logically, this makes sense, don't get me wrong. But it is one of those Realisms that doesn't add to the game, and just breaks the flow of it. You have to abandon most of your gear ahead of time and plan around this one mechanic and it just doesn't feel fun. It makes the puzzles (OPTIONAL Puzzles, mind you, for like bonus items and loot) a chore, especially when you have to run back all the time or have an ally hold your stuff. At least those are options, sure, but the simple solution would be just have your main person somehow hold 40lbs at all times.There's more to the negatives than that, I feel like the corruption timer is a bit too short when it comes to 'resetting' the explorable areas. I always feel like I'm rushing, leaving good materials behind because I just don't have the time to collect them all. But at least there is an abundance, and I honestly like the concept: the storm coming through and absolutely decimating everything in its path before reforging the land anew. My hoarder brain just doesn't want to leave anything behind, especially when it could be useful.Anyway, I would recommend giving the game a try if it looks interesting to you. Even if its to experience the alchemy system in general, the idea of transforming things around you, or if you just want to tame an army of chickens and relive the Zelda reference from the other POV (not to that level of numbers, but its a fun idea honestly). TSR has a lot of unique ideas, and I honestly wish to see a sequel of sorts where it can flourish~That, and there are just not enough games where you actually get to play as a Griffon-thing. So, 7.8/10 Stars

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the style and gameplay of this game, but there is one large issue that will prevent me from playing more:Weight management leads you to depositing items into a storage chestGoing to the Forge, on the other side of the base, finding that you don't have items, and having to go back to the storage chest and pull specific items is far too time consuming.If weight management + item crafting is a core part of gameplay, crafting from storage needs to be the default while in a 'safe zone'.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, it's a broken game. Developers released it and abandoned it after just 1 week. I encountered more than a couple bugs and game also crashed. Some polishing is missing. _childDocuments_.review: Hello friends,Today i will review the game THE SERPENT ROGUE. This is a rogue game, as the title of the game says. It is a dark rogue about death, light, and darkness. The story is basic and not much to it, but the game is fun as a rogue game. Although technically, i liked RAD better as a rouge game. Anyways, here are the pro and cons list for this game:PROS:- Supports controllers. I used a logitech G310.- Ability to craft different potions to heal, to transform, to damage enemies, and to add to hunger.- Crafting ability to make weapons and enchant them.- Sometimes opening new areas require dying...- You can tame monsters to fight with you if you can find out what they like.- Works on windows 11 OS.CONS:- Semi buggy. Sometimes when i loaded a game after i quit it, it loads me in a frozen state on the map i loaded from. This can be remedied by force closing the game and reloading it. This ssemed to fix it.- Sometimes i feel thu the map doing things like brewing potions at the brewing station.- The length of the game is not long, and even people on the forum complained about adding a dlc to the game to make it longer.A buggy yet fun rogue game. I recommend only buying it on sale when it is as the game is not a long game, but can be fun if you like rogue games. I took my time and only had 22 hours total on game and did alot of the side quests and took my time.

Throw potions wasn't explained so i die several time trying to fight the first boss meleeing them with potions. Spent an hour trying to figure out how to get to the pier. Had the correct idea to use the torch but needed to light the torches on the wall not just walk down the path. Got ambushed in dungeon and my entire party died because I couldn't see the thorns growing arounds us because i switched to my sword instead of the torch. _childDocuments_.review: Firstly this is not a bad game, at it's price I wouldn't recommend purchasing it.  The game itself can be fun it is also a figure it out for yourself type of game which there is nothing wrong with.  Why did I give it a thumbs down?  I did so because this game seems very grindy for resources which seem to be limited many times when you are about to complete gathering the number you need of any particular item aside from the basic ones like Tea Leaves and Aloe plants.  To further complicate that there are random bugs that will cause your control to sometimes not work in the game if you use a windows controller.  Also followers can be fickle and commands like getting them to engage the machine sometimes just don't work.  If that happens you need to reboot the game, same with the controller issue.  Also there seems to be no way to mitigated damage from the cursed embers if you try to collect them for the undertakers area quest, or just to experiment with for making potions.  The game is also not that big in area as some have already commented.  The Art and the ambience in this game are very well done, it just feels like a 10 dollar game not worth 20 bucks in my opinion  I did get it on sale for 15, but it really doesn't feel worth that there just isn't enough content and I didn't even get an acheivment for beating the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed on this one.  The concept is really cool, it just needs a bit more depth and more play areas.  The struggle with recommending this one is that there's only two major play areas, so if you go hard on farming resources, you don't really have a lot to use all your resources on, except for some of the tougher monsters.  There are a few collectibles and side quests and tiny side areas to explore here and there but it was disappointing that the core gameplay loop, the "meat" of the game, only has two play zones.  I can't overstate that.I will say though, transforming an army of followers into a flock of chickens, then buffing them with artifacts is immensely funny to have them stomp the tougher monsters that the game has to offer.  It's kinda like having your own flock of overpowered birds akin to legend of zelda which was really funny--you guys get a point for that one, that was great!The exploration part of the crafting system was neat but it felt extremely limited, I would have liked some more variety in mixing species with other attributes.The combat is clunky at times (especially for followers), but it's barely passable.  I only ever experienced one major glitch that froze me in place while in combat with one of the bosses, very very odd, and I wasn't able to reproduce it.I don't know about the price point for the game, I'll say that despite how short it felt, I did really enjoy it (I played through it twice explicitly to mess with materials from the strongest monsters).  If there was a DLC or sequel that gave a bunch of new play areas to farm and gather resources in, I'd be all over it in a heartbeat.
_childDocuments_.name: The Serpent Rogue

_childDocuments_.review: Charming indie title that's fairly innovative as far as its alchemy mechanics go. Setting and characters are also great, plague doctors and all.However, it is too short. Although there's a lot of alchemy recipes, effects and strategies you can employ, there's not enough content where you can try them out on. As if that wasn't disappointing enough, the ending is disappointing and final boss strips you of all the gear you brought for the fight.I still think it is interesting enough to try out if you can get it on a massive sale (eg. $3-5),  but do keep in mind how short it is. It could be even shorter for you because I went out of my way to farm materials to try out alchemy recipes.
