_childDocuments_.review: I detest quick-time event “games,” and this game DOES deserve all of the hate which it gets, but I also give New Tales a positive review for the few weirdos who are really into the Borderlands series like myself so much that they are willing to endure this, because NT is fully reliant upon that madness to succeed.Critique will follow, but tl;dr: The story was good enough with some good laughs, the music is superb like it was in BL3, the art direction is consistent (good), and the experience itself delves more into the slice of everyday cyberpunk which BL3 gave us during Promethea. A 2 / 10 game for people not obsessed with BL especially including BL3, or a 6.5 / 10 for people like me.The reality to why it is “mostly negative” on Steam: The Netflix writer effect.“Millennial speak” (which is now Gen Z speak) written by out-of-touch people in their 40s, very “how do you do fellow kids” as it always is, for 2020s mostly American topics in this world of the 2800s including student debt, capitalism bad, non-binary gender, OnlyFans, and stale memes following an actual trigger warning at the start of the game. Mental health awareness but not actually, just multiple times noting mental health as generally important in the most useless superficial way without any respect for those who struggle with it. Haha repressed memories, right?? Also bullies are like so bad, am I right???Two “namaste lol” jokes, eight “literally” overuses, and one of the main characters is the sassy brown guy stereotype like Rick from Dino Crisis while being modelled after Barack Obama's face with young people comb-over dreadlocks, who in his very first introduction criticises the calzone maker’s “problematic accent” because man making Italian accent is bad, while later an even-worse execution of a woman doing a French accent for an extended period of time is completely ignored because woman doing it is good. The “man bad but woman ok” undermining of equality by a writing team who really wants to be known for their affectations of diversity comes up several times wherein a man doing or saying the thing would most definitely be criticised but we are supposed to find it funny when a woman does it, most notably with the male intern being repeatedly sexually harassed by his female boss in what is very uncomfortable for viewers without the “but it is ok because woman” effect which the writers assumed that we would all feel.There is also a rule at the BL studio that there must be at least two one-gender romances or expressions of romantic interest for every two-gender one, for the third game in a row (BL3, Tina’s, NT) because mandatory inclusion, yet in such a paradigm virtually everyone speaks only American because the writers have never actually met anyone not from USA, which is why all of the supposed shared experiences memeified in their recent games do not translate at all to non-Americans despite the very conspicuous effort to make sure that you are aware of their deliberate inclusion efforts and contemporary topicality. “Conspicuous inclusion” has to be on the writers’ inspiration board due to how frequently that the focus is made upon the concept.To summarise, the writers who made BL3 not ideal made NT not ideal in the exact same way, and that is why everyone hates this "game." Watch it on YouTube instead of supporting the design and writing financially, as it is not deserved. I paid $3 USD during a Steam sale for NT, which I think is fair enough. The default $40 asking price is not worth it under any circumstances.Also the robot with the psycho mask in the marketing and banner? It never comes up, it is just some unrelated concept or promotional art with a character in the story who never has any interaction with psychos or masks. A lie, really.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hard to review positively. And I really want to, because it had some decent moments. But I can't.I like the design Gearbox took with what is obviously an inspiration from Telltale's design style. It's a lot better to be able to free walk and actually turn the camera as you do so in order to see your surroundings. Gearbox's version also certainly stays true to the roots of Borderlands by allowing you to loot boxes for money which allows you to customize the appearance of your characters, and there's also collectibles to hunt for, which I personally love collectibles. That is, when you do actually get to walk around. I believe that this, compared to Telltale's version, has less opportunity for that player controlled movement but there's still plenty of dialogue choices and hard decisions to make. It's almost more of an interactive movie in that case. That being said, it creates a bad first impression by being full of cringy, cliched gen Z and younger millennial dialogue with a lot of overused tropes. And that's saying a lot, given it's a Borderlands title. It becomes slightly better after the first episode, truly, where a lot of those issues sort of disappear, but first impressions are important. I gave it the benefit of the doubt and the respect of the development team by at least playing it (extra time spent on this game after this review is for getting the rest of the achievements) but It's full of crybaby gen Z and younger millennial language and references throughout the entire game, such as when Octavio is accused of "victim blaming" all because you select a dialogue choice of neutrality. Game studios need to stop hiring writers who write this bologna thinking that it's funny or acceptable or enlightening to certain sociological issues. It's a video game. Stop. Preaching. Especially in a Borderlands video game of all franchises. Normal people just want to play a video game rather than being preached to because of their normalcy somehow being offensive to other groups of people. And only these people struggle to fathom how a video game like this can possibly be so negatively received, so they call you "racist" or "transphobic" because their warped worldview is challenged.You just expect more from Gearbox, where the Borderlands looter shooter version is usually great. What you have here was a unique style of gameplay that has its potential squandered to instead try and proselytize you with wokeness. Lots of cliches and tropes: -We're introduced to a lady who is obviously a diversity hire for Atlas and a Mary Sue, and Gearbox doesn't even hide it. Anu, the lady scientist with a phD in something -- it was never explained where her doctorate is from or what she studied, begins rather clueless and forgetful. The average IQ of a doctorate is around 125, which is still higher than 95% of the population. I don't even have a doctorate myself and my IQ is 150. She can't remember a 4-digit passcode to her office safe (which is, no surprise, "1234) and couldn't recall where she placed an important artifact that is integral to her scientific research, and yet, the complex mathematical equations on the whiteboard are supposed to be her workings. Which you learn were also incorrect. When it comes to this artifact, she proves her being a Mary Sue by being able to effortlessly harness its energy through a device she creates. When Handsome Jack, canonically, would spend billions of dollars on researching how to manipulate that energy that she is easily able to do. Your very first quest with Anu is to roam around her office trying to locate it for a prototype that she is working on because "guns = bad" and she wants to end all violence. She also goes on a rant later about "capitalism = bad" as well. She's a character with so many cliches stuffed inside of her that there's more dialogue choices than can be counted where you can literally choose for her to have a mental breakdown. -Octavio is introduced as this passionate, determined "future mogul" but his very first cutscene literally has him telling a guy to stop doing a fake Italian accent. Hypocritically, in his next scene, he literally does a lame, fake Irish accent to a dead Irish guy. So the POC is allowed to do bad imitations of foreign accents? He also makes a note about how "nine-year-old girls are the future" when a robot says that he sounded like a young girl after being frightened. Technically, all children are the future and there's no need to empower the girls specifically. Boys need recognition as well.-So then we see Fran. A heavyset (obese) lady in a wheelchair to put the final touch of sprinkles on the representation checklist that comes in her big bowls of froyo. Her friendly talking pocketwatch robot tells her to "calm down, woman" and she nearly throws it at the wall (or does, depending on your choice) while saying "do not tell me to calm down." This is such a pointless line of dialogue. People don't talk like that unless they're intentionally trying to push this narrative of misogyny to exaggerate its existence, thereby creating it where it doesn't otherwise exist, and that's clearly the point here because a woman being told to "calm down" happens twice. Once to Fran and once to Anu, by Octavio, and Anu has a similar reaction to simple advice when she was being erratic. Sexism literally does not exist in the Borderlands universe and nobody could possibly prove an example where it does. If anything, the women are sexist here.And when it comes to Fran, a lot of her dialogue choice seems to revolve around promoting body positivity. It's clearly forced and just odd and more virtue signaling to go with the rest of the video game. Her whole character is blatantly designed for the sole purpose of being "fat, sassy, loud" and that should honestly be insulting to actual overweight gamers or just people in general. And when you get to scan her as Anu, she's of course, a "flirty pansexual." I guess she couldn't be unique enough as she already was.When it comes to Rhys, Gearbox completely rewrote him into a person far different than how he evolves in Tales from the Borderlands. Gearbox literally retcons the entire character and has no idea what to really do with him, which is a shame because he was one of the heroes of the first game. This is all within just the first episode of the game, so within the first hour or two. The biggest trope afterward? Anu & Fran are clearly educated, smart women while Octavio is the idiotic, comedic relief to serve their intelligence. They decided Fran has a Master's degree instead of just being a simple froyo shop owner. Fran even makes it a point to mention how she enjoys emasculating Octavio. And in episode 3, she corrects him three times while he "misgenders" the two female protagonists who obviously identify as women. "Do you guys realize..." > "Just say women." > "Do you women realize..." > "Just say ya'll." . . .This is a character who supports women so why exactly does he deserve to be a punching bag for them? _childDocuments_.review: My review after playing it for almost 12 hours straight so I'm finally over with it❤ Audience ❤☑ Beginner☑ Casual Gamer☑ Normal Gamer☐ ExpertNew Tales from the Borderlands (NTFTB) is a game full of mentions and references of all previous games, so it's recommended to play them, the Delux version provides you with a copy of the first game Tales from the Borderlands (TFTB).☼ Graphics ☼☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☑ Beautiful☐ FantasticIt's the typical Borderlands cell shading, tho if you compare games it's closer to the Borderlands 3 style than the original TFTB looks, but nothing too off. The scenes and locations look really good, which is sad cause that's the best feature in ♬ Music ♬☐ Bad☑ Alright☑ Good☐ Beautiful☐ FantasticThe music in this one is okay, it's not my kind of music but taste in music is subjective so... The songs were okay and they kind of fit in; but I preferred the soundtrack from TFTB, it slapped more, and just felt better☠ Difficulty ☠☐ Easy☑ Average☐ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Hard☐ UnfairYou can't choose the difficulty in the game, but it's okay. It's not too bad, it has some frustrating moments but I'm going to talk about it in the Gameplay section⚔ Gameplay ⚔☑ Frustrating☐ Sleepy☐ Boring☑ Fun☐ ChallengingThe gameplay is your usual TellTale gameplay, you have dialog options and your regular QuickTime events. The only complaint I have is that you have three player characters and more often than not you can't tell which character the dialog option is for. You have a tiny icon in the middle of your options, that should indicate which action is for which character, but it is so tiny. By the time it takes you to tell what character you're choosing for, you barely have enough time left to read all the dialog options and then choose what you are going to say. In TFTB they had a better solution, for Rhys and Fiona you had different designs for the dialog options which made it pretty clear which character you're playing, but this time all you have is a tiny colored dot.§ Bugs §☐ Bugs destroy the game☐ Lots of bugs☐ Few Bugs☐ You can use them for speedrun☑ Nothing encountered☯ Story ☯☐ There is none☑ Bad (if you loved TFTB)☑ Alright☐ Good☐ FantasticOh man, here we go. First I have to say the quality of these episodes varies a lot. Like it had an okay start with Ep 1, got better in Ep 2, Ep 3 and 4 were still okay, not good but okay, and then totally lost me in Ep 5.In spoilerfree details: I know the beginning of a game is important to introduce the characters and the surrounding, but it's also important to capture the player's attention and interest to keep playing and bonding with the characters. In this case, it took a bit too long and kept dragging on and on, could have been a bit quicker and shorter. For example showing us characters and the relationship we have with them, only for these characters to maybe reaper once after Ep 1 and then never again (like what happened to them? are they still alive? did they spontaneously disintegrate?) It gets better in Ep 2 (which for me is the best out of all five) story kicks off and you get pulled in.Ep 3 kinda feels like a filler episode, but still okay.Ep 4 pulls you back in and at the end of it I had to finish the game cause I thought "finally now it's getting really good and interesting, the grade finally)Then Ep 5 the (not so) grand conclusion. It started well, the story got emotional and I thought this could actually end well, but jokes on me for believing that. It felt weird and kinda unsatisfying.Like TFTB did some Badass moves with destroying the Helios and after the fight with the Vaultmonster finally entered it and leave us in suspense about what is going to happen. Tales did a lot of bold moves and had good pacing. While in this game it felt off, they tried to be different then TFTB but in all the wrong ways. Even after that, it felt like a weird cheap rip-off from TFTB matched together with BL3. I never anticipated for it to be able to compete with TFTB but it feels like they didn't even try.It has its moment but when 75% of the game is either meh or just annoying that 25% just can't save it. My highlight of this game was the last episode's conclusion with Markus and the reveal of who he was talking to.۞ Game time / Length ۞☐ Really short (0 - 3 hours)☐ Short (4 - 8 hours)☑ Few hours (10 - 15 hours) [if you focus on the main story]☑ Some time (15 - 20 hours) [if you want all achievements]☐ Long (40-60 hours) ☐ Very Long (61-100 hours)☐ Extremely Long (101+ hours)$ Price / Quality $☐ Full price☑ Wait for Sale☐ Don't buy☐ Refund it if you can

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed this game. Its peak comedy, loveable characters and entertaining storyline really hooked me, while playing through it the first time. Just about every choice you make is more like a "choose the joke you want to hear", while all of the options are great. But, that's where the problem lies with this game. The choices you make don't really matter at first, and just have effects on your relationship-stats, which every once in a while could either get someone killed or save them. As with the ending, I think that it also depends on those stats, but I'm not sure. Without spoilering anything, at the end of the game I've lost characters without much explanation as to how I could have saved them. And reading up on guides and discussions, it seems that they really could have been saved. Just... how? As a game where some of the choices only take effect later on, I think it's very important to have something to tell you what does what. Like, for example, a New Game + where it tells you the changes. Or like Telltale's second season of Batman, let it have a page on the decisions-overview where it says how the characters felt upon certain actions. Because trying to figure it out yourself is like trying to find a needle in a 1000m²-field, while being blindfolded. You may come upon the solution, but really just by blind luck. And all that wouldn't be so bad, if the achievements didn't want you to see all endings. I don't think you can skip through any scenes, and if you don't know what-does-what, you'd have to see the whole game like a thousand times or more, until you may figure it out. So, if you really want all the achievements, have fun doing that. If you want to platinum a story-based game that doesn't just have unmissable ones that you get by completing chapters, play Detroit.Other than that, I'd also like to mention that the second chapter felt really short, especially in comparison to the first one. Overall, I would've liked the whole game to be longer. Although that could've been a problem when trying to see every possible ending. Maybe have some chapters completely different, depending on previous choices, so you'd see completely new things on a re-run and still be engaged. But, this may be asking a bit too much.TL;DR: Great fun playing through it the first time, although a real pain in the ass if you want to get all achievements, because you don't know how the decisions you've made affect the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Spoiler Free:If you like the world and story of the Borderlands play this game, if you don't then it's fine to pass it up. This is not a good "Tales" game, the minigames are repetitive, the quick time events feel almost pointless, and your choices don't really matter all that much. HOWEVER, its a pretty good story, that does what I wanted it to do, expand the Borderlands Universe, which it did as well as show another corporation in action. Spoilers: TLDR Episode three is the low point Episode One: honestly really solid episode, great humor, good job of establishing post invasion Promethea. It was really interesting to see how people viewed Handsome Jack, with Reba dismissing Fran when she explained why she went with a Tediore product instead of a Hyperion oneEpisode Two:  Another really solid episode, sneaking into the vault and an interesting vault monster fight though it lasted a bit too long in my opinion.Episode Three: Jumped the shark, literally. The empisode took a sudden turn with characters just shooting eachother for fun, which was funny at first but the bit lasted too long. Then going on sink or swim and starting a business just felt out of nowhere and was only really explained in the final episode. Also there was this whole bit about getting a corpse but it was never explained why they wanted a corpse just so that a character could die and then they'd be able to show the power of shard TBH they could have just done that by reviving pierre, but whatever. Episode Four: All in all pretty great episode arguably one of the best in this game. It was cool to see how the companies interact with one another with Torgue, Atlas, Jakobs, and Maliwan all present for Susan's Teed Talk. My only question why the hell was Athena there? Literally 0 explanation for that. Is she the new owner of Hyperion? I dunno, but other than that it was cool to see Katagawa Sr. Episode Five: Another solid episode with really interesting effects on the future of the series with the introduction of the Anahatium shards (Green & Red Eridium) and the being that is reunited in this game that has now assumedly possessed Timm-e. A big complaint that I do have is that for literally zero reason Stapleface dies in this game even though Anu runs up and touches her and we've established that the shard can bring people back from the dead and it doesn't care if they're murderers because well Anu is a murderer it makes zero sense why Anu wasn't able to heal Stapleface. Also when/why did fran die at the end of the game. That I don't really understand either. End Credits: FIonas back, has been in contact with Marcus AND alludes to her trying to find Sasha. Also in one of the episodes they throw out the line of there being six galaxies, which I don't remember being established previously followed by in the end credits Marcus pointing out that the shards trail leads to the Gladius Nebula so perhaps that is where future borderlands games will take us.

_childDocuments_.review: After Wonderlands, I went into this game with very low expectations. At best, I figured it would be fine. As one of the series' pickiest fans? I'm so, so glad I was wrong.I want to be up front: Gearbox still sucks at character writing. Dialogue exchanges often feel unreal - there are things characters say to each other that nobody would actually say. It's weird, disjointed, and sloppy, and it's not funny to write like that. The writers should have more confidence in their actual jokes than having to write a game where every character is an ADHD-suffering TikTok personality. But the characters themselves are great. They mesh well with the existing Borderlands universe and mesh well with each other - there's a constant push and pull of their personalities that shows that they were written with chemistry in mind, rather than as standalone pieces that just kind of exist in the same space (see: every other Borderlands game, including the OG Tales).The story itself is a little shaky. They planted a loooooot of red herrings at the start that kind of fizzle out into disappointment rather than a successful narrative misdirection. However, it's made pretty clear what the game is actually about: The relationships. It's using the grand scale of the Borderlands universe and all the cogs already present in the machine to make a game that's about relationships, communication, and empathy. Which is a weird thing to say about a Borderlands game - especially because it really, really delivers on those.And what makes it better is the performances. The cast for this game nailed it every step of the way. I think the weakest links were Diamond, Radon, and Stapleface. But only Stapleface has a lasting role of those three. The actors involved with this game really worked their ♥♥♥♥ out. Early in the game there are two comedy relief soldiers that trade compliments and even say they love each other. The amount of warmth in their expressed love was so genuine I felt giddy. The anxiety and anger and joy and stupidity of these characters shines through the motion capture and voice work to a degree I truly haven't seen in a "comedy" game like this. It's some truly next-level ♥♥♥♥.The faces creep me the ♥♥♥♥ out, though. They're almost photo realistic but you can see the series' iconic lineart creep up on while they emote. I think having some static lineart or just stylizing the faces more would have gone a long, long way. But the animations? Stunning.It really is difficult to talk about how special the narrative of this game is without just telling the twists and turns. It works - just not in a way that meaningfully pushes Borderlands' narrative forward and only in the individual perspectives of its main 3 cast. I think in some ways, I enjoyed this game more than Telltale's Tales from the Borderlands. And I don't feel the reviews for this game are necessarily the fairest. I think most people leaving negative reviews are upset that this isn't Telltale. But why would you want something Telltale from a studio that isn't Telltale? That's on you, not Gearbox Quebec. But people initially disliked Telltale's take on Borderlands, too. So we'll see.

Mindless violence and shooting and blowing stuff up'' when this is not what this is or ever claimed to be, this game along with the first one is a story driven, choices matter adventure just like all the Telltale games that they released in their time. There's not a lot of exploring the world, but as someone who otherwise enjoys story-driven based games, this one was nice to experience. The rest of the humour isn't half bad, with several references to pop culture that are, shall we say (mostly for the sake of my own ego), classic. The character development is pretty good, not too forced for something that can literally be played through in a single session, and there's growth there. The game includes a trigger warning for some themes and inclusive language which tends to peeve a certain demographic, which made that little fact an extra selling point for me. It's nice. You just have to be in the right headspace for it and approach it more like a movie, one that you actually have to pay attention to... put down your phone... or you'll miss the quick time events... which is inconvenient.. when you have as much ADHD as I do. I missed some things... ... dunno if I'll go back for them, maybe in a few months, when I've forgotten enough of the movie to warrant a re-watch.

_childDocuments_.review: For someone like me who's been invested in the Borderlands franchise from the start, this game has been satisfying in a few ways. The comedy shines at many moments and has the expected absurdities. I enjoyed the character development and their relationships and motivations. I thought each character experienced meaningful growth along the way, especially but not exclusively Anu.I found the group cohesion scoring (the  system) to be overly opaque: I couldn't really understand why the group was only rated around 67% by the end of the game. I find most of these systems in games of this genre to be a bit frustrating and inconsequential, and probably wouldn't choose to play many more of them if it weren't for the fact that this is a type of Borderlands game. I think this is more a consequence of me not being motivated by these systems as opposed to them being designed or implemented poorly.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I finished the game in a single sitting, and I still stand by my initial review.  This is a fun little game that let me play around in the Borderlands universe.Genuinely, I cannot figure out what all the bad reviews on here are about (I mean, I genuinely suspect it is just people being overly critical of games where the main character isn't a white dude).  I've played episode 1, and there were enough endearing and engaging moments to connect me to the characters and to feel like I am playing in the Borderlands universe that I love.I've played the original Tales from the Borderlands, and this feels pretty similar to me in tone and execution.  The pacing is a little slow at times, but Tales games aren't supposed to be action packed.  It lacks the full emotional impact of the Walking Dead Tales series, but I'm not sure I want to be making heart wrenching decisions every few moments in Borderlands.If you like the Borderlands as a story-telling playground and you like narrative games, then I'm sure you will find something to like here.  I have been waiting for the introduction of Tediore, and one episode in, I am excited with how they did it and how it looks to be going.

_childDocuments_.review: New Tales from the Borderlands builds upon the legacy of its predecessor, offering a fresh yet familiar narrative experience within the chaotic and irreverent world of Pandora. Developed by Gearbox Software and released in 2022, this sequel introduces a new cast of characters while maintaining the series' trademark humor and choice-driven storytelling.Set against the backdrop of a post-apocalyptic Pandora in the wake of the events from the original series, the game shifts focus to a new trio: Anu, a brilliant yet socially awkward scientist; Octavio, her ambitious and somewhat unscrupulous brother; and Fran, a tough-as-nails businesswoman with a troubled past. Their story revolves around a high-stakes quest involving a mysterious alien artifact, a lost city, and a series of increasingly ridiculous mishaps.The game's strength lies in its engaging narrative and character development. The writing remains sharp and humorous, capturing the essence of the Borderlands universe while introducing new comedic elements and emotional beats. Each of the new protagonists is distinct and well-developed, with their own personal stakes and quirks that add depth to the story. The voice acting is top-notch, bringing these characters to life with charisma and nuance.New Tales from the Borderlands retains the episodic format, which allows for a rich, serialized storytelling experience. The player’s choices influence the direction of the narrative, although, like its predecessor, the overall plot remains largely linear. The decision-making moments are compelling, offering a range of outcomes that can significantly alter character dynamics and storylines.Graphically, the game continues with the cel-shaded art style that fans of the series will recognize and appreciate. The visuals are vibrant and comic-like, perfectly matching the tone of the narrative. The animation and visual effects are polished, though not groundbreaking, effectively conveying the game's humorous and high-energy atmosphere.One area where New Tales from the Borderlands occasionally falters is in its pacing. Some episodes may feel slower compared to others, with certain sequences dragging a bit longer than necessary. Additionally, while the core gameplay remains focused on dialogue and choices, it sometimes lacks the urgency and variety that might have enhanced the experience.Overall, New Tales from the Borderlands is a worthy successor to the original, offering a blend of humor, heart, and chaotic adventure. It’s a must-play for fans of the Borderlands series and those who enjoy narrative-driven games. While it might not reinvent the wheel, it successfully captures the spirit of its predecessor and delivers a compelling and entertaining journey through the wilds of Pandora.

_childDocuments_.review: I mean the game on its own is not that bad, it's just that Tales from the Borderlands, Borderlands 1 and Borderlands 2 with all the DLCs set the standard too high...At first, I must say that the graphics are just awesome, the game looks really nice. It's really irritating to have to hold a mouse button and move it over an icon to loot a box or interact with a thing, but that's just a little nuance. This game is full of jokes and funny moments... maybe too full, it surely feels like the writers had no idea about the story and just thought it would be all saved by jokes - sometimes too forced in or just too dumb, it's not the usual Borderlands funny-dumb, it's more like a 40 to 50-year-old trying to stay relevant.The personal growth of the characters is none, Fran stays exactly the same as at the beginning, Octavio too, only Anu tries to grow in her shard-dream fantasy but once she is out, it's still the same.The choices you make make no real difference, even though you pick a response you feel like the response from the opposite character is still the same no matter what you choose.It just feels like Gearbox let the good writers go and brought in some really mediocre (I am sorry to say this). It is the same problem that occurred to me with Borderlands 3.. the main story was just meh... (I mean I loved the DLCs, not gonna lie) I am not even mentioning the fact, that this game just feels like a movie (not an interactive one, but you change little to nothing) more than a game. In the end, I would not recommend this game to someone who did not like Borderlands 3... there is some reference to the stories or characters that we like from the previous games, but this game is more suitable for someone completely new to the lore who has never played another Borderlands game and has no expectations (Even though this game is connected to the events of the game...). This game is like the bad bite of bread, you should take to get to the best part (everything else on the bread... but you can always just cut away the crumb...)

_childDocuments_.review: I initially gave this game a negative rating after an hour of gameplay, but recently returned to clean up the achievements. Turns out, putting this game down after just an hour was a mistake; there's actually a lot to enjoy here. Enough for me to unquestionably switch my review to a positive one. Long story short:The Good:The graphics in this title are amazing. Admittedly, it's easy to achieve when the entire game is essentially a cutscene. Nevertheless, seeing the Borderlands universe in this level of fidelity is truly remarkable. It's by far the best-looking Borderlands game and even tale-esque game to date.The writing is spectacular. From the absolutely hilarious Vault Landers guy to the random NPCs, it's all extremely well-written and quite the treat. The humor in this game is, again, the best the franchise has ever seen.The Bad:The first couple of hours of the game are quite boring and have a sprinkling of the "woke" agenda. For instance, scanning a particular character will reveal her sexuality as pansexual, yet nobody of any other sexuality has their dating preferences mentioned. Additionally, the two able-bodied main characters aren't Caucasian, and the one who is Caucasian is bound to a wheelchair, while her customers are mostly trans/non-conforming. One character feels the need to address herself as "her" but gets upset when a young male character says "Hey guys! ...and girl!" and suggests saying "ya'll" instead, as it's inclusive for those who don't identify as he/she. As usual, white men (and women!) play the story's villains, and the characters/world in general feel like a caricature of what boomers think teenagers are (fr fr, yaaas slay queeen, no cap). I'm not saying any of these things are particularly bad, or even trying to make this review political, but this modern trend of turning minorities into "everybodies," with the world's current "majority" being purposely hidden, has an extremely forced feel that a lot of people absolutely detest. However, it does get better as the story progresses. The tone set early becomes less important, and the great story of the characters and their adventures becomes brilliant (and focused on them, rather than irrelevant woke nonsense). The wheelchair-bound woman has severe anger issues, and depending on the choices you make in-game, this can become something truly hysterical.And finally, the game only supports a 16:9 resolution, leaving out those who use taller 16:10 displays or ultrawide monitors.If you're willing to push through the mediocre start, a quick woke pummeling, and a forced 16:9 resolution, there's an amazing tale here, and it's well worth a play, especially at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Prefacing by saying this isn't as good as the original. With that said this one isn't as bad as some of the other reviewers make it out to be. This game is 100% narrative decision and quick time event driven. If you hate cut scenes and quick time events, this isn't the game for you. This game narrative is mostly character driven, so if you don't like extremely expressive characters and lots of dialogue this isn't the game for you. I can't really express that enough. If you hated Borderlands 3 and think Borderlands 2 was the peak of the series you will not enjoy this game. This game is 6-8 hours long maybe, perhaps offers some replayability for different endings, but thats about it. You need the correct expectation going into this to get anything out of it.That said, the over arching narrative isn't amazing. Its hard to even call it good, maybe just ok, but certainly not terrible. As someone who wasn't fond of the BL3 story in general but enjoyed the game play, I can still appreciate what is on offer here. The voice acting was top notch. The motion capture was top notch. The animation is great. The music, eh Borderlands has had better, but its hardly a fault at all. Its hard to tell which dialogue options will be impactful later on. There are moments when the game tells you about the results of some interactions in the top corner in a Telltale style, but its hard to determine where that impact actually pays off later down the road. The minigame is fun and silly, but a bit basic and lacking any challenge. I did still make me chuckle about how silly it was every time I played it, and the NPC who plays with you is great every time you meet him. On that note, the Tediore soldiers in general tend to steal the show from the main characters. Their brand of comedy just works. The main characters on the other hand, its going to be hit or miss depending on your comedic tastes. I found myself more partial and laughing at Anu's type of neurotic personality, less so for Fran's bruser/crude and Octavio's wanna be hustler tropes. The assassin bot is probably the best character in the game, and there are some new characters introduced with rather small parts, but it makes me wonder if we might see them again in another game. The story however is filled with absurd reactions from most characters in every situation. I'm not sure if this was intended or an overlooked result of attempting to force comedy into every situation. Characters just do things that don't make sense. But if you are playing Borderlands and expecting everything to make sense, you aren't doing it right. Overall the game is sorta fun, short, but decent. My recommendation then is that, sure, its worth a purchase and play, but maybe not at $40 for most people. For complete fans of the franchise sure. I'll throw my support behind Borderlands simply because I want it to continue. The series is definitely suffering from a writing issue. That is no secret, but every game whether it is a mainline or spin off, has still given us characters to love and an evolving world/galaxy to have stories set in. I'm not a fan of Gearbox, but I'm hoping eventually they can figure out a writing team that works and this franchise can shine. People bombed on the first Borderlands Tales game as well. It almost didn't get finished, but now it has a cult following and is generally looked fondly upon. In time this may be the case here too once the initial wave of over expectation dies down. Don't doom them just yet.

name: The Game of Life 2
detailed_description: Prepare to live a thousand lives in The Game of Life 2! It’s the award-winning official sequel to the classic board game played by millions around the world. Gather your friends and family and dive into a bright, fun 3D world, bursting with adventure! A new Peg has entered the board! Choose from the Pink, Blue or the NEW Purple Peg. Select an Outfit and make your Peg your own. Browse a selection of cars, bikes and scooters and find a ride to suit your style. Will you wear your business suit on a bicycle? Or roll up to College in a Sports Car? It’s up to you! It’s time to fly the nest! Spin the iconic Spinner and set off on your life journey. Will you go to College immediately, or drive straight into a career? Whatever direction you take, the spinner will decide where you land along the way. You’ll be presented with decisions at every twist and turn, but crossroad moments will affect your life path. Will you get married or stay single? Have kids or adopt a pet? Buy a house? Make a career change? It’s up to you! And in this sequel there’s an added crossroad, so you can choose to make those important choices earlier or later in life. In the original The Game of Life game the wealthiest Peg won. In The Game of Life 2 decisions have been updated to fit with modern times, so you’ll also earn points for choices that bring you Knowledge and Happiness. Now it’s not only possible to win rich, but you can maximise your Knowledge or Happiness, or go for a healthy mix of all three, and come out on top! Life goes on! When you reach the end of the game you can choose to rest in a luxury retirement home, or ride off into the sunset and fulfil your bucket list! It’s up to you! Unlock new Outfits and Vehicles by playing the game and earning rewards! Collect 60 Happiness points, travel 100 spaces, collect 5000k; each accomplishment unlocks a puzzle piece. When you collect 6 puzzle pieces you unlock a bonus item, and there are eight to unlock in each world! Live life in enchanted worlds, make friends with dinosaurs in the Age of Giants and launch into the futuristic Lunar Age! Every new world features new Outfits, Vehicles, Jobs, Properties and more! Buy worlds separately in-game, or buy the Ultimate Life Collection to unlock them all! Join your friends and family, whether they’re on PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox, PC (Steam), Nintendo Switch, iOS or Android. Play together seamlessly on multiple consoles and platforms.

_childDocuments_.review: It's essentially a shorter, dumbed-down version of LIFE. Sure, it has "minigames" and crowns, but the novelty quickly wears off. Here's the real kicker, though--the online multiplayer is padded with bots, probably to make the game seem more active than it actually is. I've had multiplayer games with three bots. What is the point at that rate? And this isn't even mentioning the cash-grabbing DLC.If, for some reason, you hate yourself enough to want to play LIFE on a regular basis, buy Tabletop Simulator. You'll get a better LIFE game and maybe even some good board games if you're feeling spicy.

_childDocuments_.review: I know the game was first released on mobile with a certain format that fits that platform, although I got to say I was kind of hoping that a game would last at least a little bit longer than about 20 minutes on PC. Felt very rushed when me and my partner played it.I love the Game of Life in other formats and was really looking forward to this one too. It was fun, but it was too short. When you are able to get a 10 roll and almost skip entire sections it doesn't really feel like your choices of where to go matter that much. Like there's barely enough time to RNG your way into having a family or house for instance.Also it would be a nice edition to be able to rename local players.The game has potential, but I think it needs some game balancing in length to be more enjoyable and fit into the PC game style. So this review is mixed, but sadly have to give it a downvote for now due to these impressions.

_childDocuments_.review: First, I love the set up and the take off the classic. The variety of worlds and their unique activities. However, no matter how well developed and how graphically pleasing that's NOT what makes me love this game. I have two children and they play this game with me. The conversational opprotunity that comes with playing this game is what makes me proud of my decision to purchase this game.  First example: There's always a "winner" in the game and it always makes their little hearts sad if they don't see "winner" above their name. How did I turn that around? I asked them if they were happy with their decisions, if they had fun, if they would play again, and so on before I got to make final point: Stop comparing what you've accomplished to others to determine your own happiness.  There are a lot of unhappy people out in the world because they're always playing "Keeping up with the Jones" when what the Jones have might not even be what you actually want. Second example: Marriage equality has been a huge debate in our world. This game gave me the perfect opprotunity to show my children what it's all about. The first round we played my daughter said she had to marry a boy because girls cannot marry girls. "That's what my friend at school said!" So I said, "Is that so." and moved on with the game. Then it became my turn to either "stay single" or "get married". Going against my original plan I went "get married". I asked my daughter "I'm a girl... so I shouldn't be able to marry a girl?" She nods her little head and I said, "Well, I'm going to anyways" and I clicked the pink character as she gasped and the wedding bells chimed. It was so scandalous for her. Then, I explained to her that 1. we think for ourselves. we can listen to what other people say and we can acknowledge how they feel on a topic, but it's up to us to use our own critical thinking, moral compass, and empathy for others to create an ethical code unique to us. 2. If you want to marry in a traditional fashion, girl to boy, then that's okay... however, it's unethical to determine the course of action someone else takes for their own lives and happiness. Their life is theirs alone and maybe you don't agree with a girl marrying a girl, or a boy with a boy, it's just not YOUR thing... but you should support them because it's THEIR life and happiness and has zero effect on the quality of your life and happiness. This just a couple of conversations inspired by this game and I look forward to to having many more.

_childDocuments_.review: I come from a family of hard-core board game players, the kind that by the time I was around in the 90's the inside lid for our 1960's copy of Life was scored ink-black, full of the names and wealth of winners games past. We even played Ancestor rules (sometimes we'd play a game christmas or new years eve for example, and the next day play again but with all your stuff from last game as the grandchildren)The Game of Life 2 is very cute, but the base gameboard is just too small, I think maybe a third the size of the physical board game at best. The only real agency you have when playing is deciding which fork in the road to go down, but almost every split reconnects so quickly you can breeze past them in one or two turns without anything meaningful happening. Even the system for choosing which stat option to increase (Love, Knowledge, or Wealth) doesn't give you any agency because they all are worth the same score at the end and there is no disincentive to just pick the card which gives you the most stats for the least cost aside from bonus points if you have the most in a stat.Maybe the DLC boards are longer and have more player agency, but if that is the case it's actually worse because then it shines a spotlight on how the base board was probably designed badly on purpose to get people to buy DLC.The best ways to fix this in my opinion are to double or so the size of the game board, add options that can negatively impact the whole board or other players, bring back mini-games which were apparently in the last game but not this one, and introduce stat requirements and excluders for a lot of the stuff you can buy or upgrade. Don't got a lot in the love stat? Doesn't look like marriage is on the cards for you yet, but oh boy do you have enough knowledge for that Robotics pay raise.This reminds me a bit of 'The Game of Life: Twists and Turns' as well, so maybe they can find some inspiration there if they haven't already. I can also see this game being a lot more fun with a looping style split-path gameboard like 'Twists and Turns' and a predetermined round limit or win condition to see who can get the most out of their LIFE.Good luck Devs, I returned my copy but I'll be keeping an eye on development.

_childDocuments_.review: Was actually looking forward to chilling on this game. Aesthetically it looks great but that't about it for me.1 - The board is tiny, you can skip most sections with a 7 plus spin on the wheel.2 - Marrying, kids or pets does nothing in terms of your final reward so its pointless doing any of that3 - They've added a new fate square, land on it and the only thing your gonna end up doing is paying taxes seeing as taxes take up most of the wheel (which is ridiculous). So don't bother taking the risky route, all you're gonna end up doing is wasting the little amount of money you have collected on the board.4 - I think there's about 4 jobs to choose from in total to choose from.5 - It is impossible to earn money, somehow the NPC's can generate some extreme amounts of money but you'll be very lucky to reach even 700k tbh...6 - There's no mini games, in actual fact theres no fun in this game whatsoever, the only thing i noticed was that the game is actually ridiculously irritating - don't expect to win because you won't (the NPC's will)7 - On the last and final occasion i thought i'd give this a chance i managed to get to the end with 1 crown (pointless new feature) and around 800k which was great, but when it started counting the money at the end the game froze and i had to CTRL/ALT/DEL to close it down so actually if you manage to win at some point you won't get to bask in your glory, you'll have to close the game down and lose everything anyway.I hope to sh*t they update this game, until then it will be staying in my library in the (f**k that) folder.It really was a pleasure watching everyone else excel in the game of life whilst i'm sat in my front room contemplating sticking pins in my eyes (thumbs up!)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great if you are looking for a very, very, VERY simplified version of The Game of Life.  However, if you are like me and want a more authentic experience of The Game of Life, the first game by this company is much better.To start off, there is no insurance in this game.  Which helps to highlight the lack of danger throughout the board.  There is only one outright bad/dangerous tile type to land on, which is taxes.  There are Fate tiles that make you spin the wheel too and those have a chance to make you pay taxes as well, but other than that, there are no dangers across the entire board leading to a very boring experience overall.  The jobs are also very repetitive.  There are only a few different jobs that you will encounter so no career really feels all that special because most of the players will probably share a job.  Logistically speaking, the "scoring" system that determines the winner of the game is completely different from the original.  It feels like a completely different game at this point.  Children have no effect on the score.  The score is based on the players money and these "characteristics" which are wealth, intelligence, and love.  To be honest, it doesn't really matter how much money you have by the end of the game.  The winner is pretty much exclusively decided by who has the most of those characteristics.  Those are the ONLY two things that have any effect on the score.Overall, I found this game to be quite boring and repetitive.  If you are looking for a very simple board game to play with a couple of friends this will work for you, but if you want something that would take even an ounce of thought/strategy to play, this is not the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: The short of it: It's way too short, and way too repetitive.- You can easily spin eight 10's and be done with the game.- The game banks off of playing many rounds, because you unlock items for playing the game *many* (10-20) times.- There are probably like 5 jobs. Everyone that goes to college ends up with the same highest-paying job. There's no chance about it.- It's super easy to go into debt in the beginning, multiple times over. You start off with $200k, college is $100k. Land on an action/life tile and want to get life points? Also $100k. You now have $0.- If a player gets high rolls they can get married in 2 turns. Other players are required to give you a wedding payment. No money left after college? You're in debt, congrats.- After you get a job you're given the "lucky number" on the wheel, players that land on your lucky number have to pay you $50k. One player rolled two 10's and is halfway through the board, while you've rolled two 1's and are still in college? You're in debt, congrats.- Going into debt gives you loans tokens in increments of $50k. Repaying loans is only an option on *some* (randomly) of the action tiles. Don't land on those tiles? Your $50k loans are now $100k to pay off at the end of the game. You lost, congrats.If you want to play this game, at least get it on sale. I got it from a bundle.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game of Life 2 is a fun game when played with friends. The multiplayer experience adds a lot of unpredictability, making each round feel fresh. However, playing solo can get dull rather quickly, as most of the game’s features are already explored after just one round. On the plus side, in solo mode, you can speed up the wheel spins and other animations by up to five times, which helps the game progress much faster.The DLCs, while adding interesting new themes and options, feel a bit overpriced. It’s also a downside that all friends need to own the same DLCs to enjoy them together. Unfortunately, in online mode, you can’t fast-forward the AI turns, which can become a bit tedious over time.Despite these drawbacks, the game (of Life 2) offers an enjoyable experience, especially for groups of friends looking for a casual, easy-to-pick-up game. Overall, I’d rate it a solid 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: The Game of Life 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game that could be fantastic, but it's held back by lack of basic quality of life features and some minor coding choices that I'd have to pass up as a lack of ability/funding otherwise they'd just be strange. Example, I just came out of an online game where everyone had to quit because I player up and left AFK for whatever reason and never came back. We were waiting for what could have been easily 30 minutes. I'm not sure why this wasn't thought of during the design phrase of this game, but there NEEDS to be a way to deal with player inactivity. I'll make a post in the discussions area regarding ideas I have as well.Every stage uses the same board, and some even reuse the same jobs. The game needs more variety and I don't see why this is a hard thing. You've already got the assets and code for all of these at the ready, all it takes is some planning and slight changes to the code. Every stage should have its own unique board layout, and unique jobs. I don't think that's asking a lot. Minor things like these only serve to improve your game greatly. I have some other ideas as well but like I said I'll hash it out in the discussions area later. All in all it's a great game with great ideas but it's brought together in a very...what feels like halfhearted manner. I recommend it but only on a steep sale in its current state. Due to the issues I mentioned, all the dlc are just basic reskins. There's no reason to buy them. I own all, but it was during a major sale where I got it for next to nothing tbh.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game if you like The Game Of Life. I have only played it locally ("pass the mouse" style) with family. It would be nice to have a different course for each "world" instead of a reskin. Why, in the Age of Giants world, am I getting a LIFE tile for a flat screen TV?- Apparently, despite having the exact same map, online multiplayer requires each person to purchase the "world" before any player can use it (as opposed to it being "hosted"). Thus, if you want to use a particular "world" with your friend, you both have to buy it. Bottom line: Buy the base game and expansions, but not at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game of Life 2 is a board game, where you have to start your life, collect money and achieve your dreams in order to beat other players.The game looks good, it really does seem like a tabletop game and I do like about it. The basic gameplay is fun in my opinion, you need to money and other attributes, which gives you points in the end. You can get these by taking different routes and make your decision between family, career and wealth. The round of the game is not longer than 20 minutes, so you can play it basically any time. The controls of the game is pretty easy, you only need to use the mouse. The sound is all right, but in long term, it can be boring to listen to...and this is the biggest flaw with this game, it's boring after a few games. You can try to mix it up, by taking different routes and gameplay, but you will basically do the same thing on the same map over and over again. What about the world DLCs? Those are just reskins of the default map plus adding piece skins, but nothing more. What about the online multiplayer? I tried to find someone to play, and I got 1 person so far in an hour of searching... and that person also left the game mid game. You can play the game on one computer, which is pretty good, but sadly the game don't have Play Together, which is   unfortunate. There are freezes and bugs here or there, some of them even game breaking, but I only found 1 in my one and half hour of gameplay.This game seems and feels fun, but it lacks any long lasting gameplay. You can have fun for an hour of two, but you probably won't touch this game, except if you play with friends. I recommend you in general, but get it only, if you can get others to play with you, otherwise just skip this game. If you still interested in the game, I suggest you to get it for around 3-4 €, it doesn't worth 10 in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Today when I walked into my economics class I saw something I dread every time I close my eyes. Someone had brought their new gaming laptop to class. The Forklift he used to bring it was still running idle at the back. I started sweating as I sat down and gazed over at the 700lb beast that was his laptop. He had already reinforced his desk with steel support beams and was in the process of finding an outlet for a power cable thicker than Amy Schumer's thigh. I start shaking. I keep telling myself I'm going to be alright and that there's nothing to worry about. He somehow finds a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ outlet. Tears are running down my cheeks as I send my last texts to my family saying I love them. The teacher starts the lecture, and the student turns his laptop on. The colored lights on his RGB Backlit keyboard flare to life like a nuclear flash, and a deep humming fills my ears and shakes my very soul. The entire city power grid goes dark. The classroom begins to shake as the massive fans begin to spin. In mere seconds my world has gone from vibrant life, to a dark, earth shattering void where my body is getting torn apart by the 150mph gale force winds and the 500 decibel groan of the cooling fans. As my body finally surrenders, I weep, as my school and my city go under. I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate gaming laptops.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game of Life 2 is a fun game in a way that I can best describe as a nostalgic, "stuck with your family on a holiday," board game night, sort of way. In other words, some good nature competitiveness that won't send you crying to your room over a loss, and at the same time it's not exactly anything that will send you running around town bragging about your "BIG WIN" over the weekend. The graphics and game-play remind me of something that would have been played on the Nintendo Wii. It is priced right, family friendly, good for all ages, works as it should, and has enough modes to keep you entertained for at least your money's worth of time. I personally picked it up because I used to play a version of this game on computer around 2005-6ish. What I found addicting as getting some relatively easy steam achievements. ;-)-In order to save yourself some embarrassment:(Hint: It can be hard to spin to move dial using the mouse, therefore I found it much better to hit the space bar. You don't want to be like myself and attempt spinning the wheel for at least 3 minutes, which took everyone else a few seconds to spin, in an increasingly panicked moment of embarrassment. _childDocuments_.review: i appreciate that there is a third color option for pegs other than blue and pink, and that it is wearing a veil and a tux when you get married. there are limited options for outfits and cars unless you get the season pass, which lets you use any of the world-specific outfits or cars with any of the worlds. there seems to be no difference between the squares on the board or action cards between worlds, though the jobs and houses have changed to match the theme. you get to choose whether to have a baby or adopt pets on the baby square, but you don't get a choice of peg color or animal breed. after playing several games it looks like you always get a blue peg child or a cat first. there also aren't many opportunities to buy a house; more than once, neither i nor any of the ai opponents had the option to buy a house for the duration of the game. the inclusion of happiness/knowledge/wealth points makes the game more strategic than "just earn the most money," as well as the different retirement options. i own every version of life from the original 70s game to the "adventures" card game and while "quarter life crisis" is still my favorite, this comes in a very close second.  on a technical note, i would like the option to turn off automatic camera scrolling as it makes me dizzy. a suggestion for future expansions would be to tailor the action cards to the theme of the board and change the routes around a bit. possibly an option where you don't have any money to start with (like quarter life crisis) and have to take out loans to go to college.

_childDocuments_.review: Rock Candy recipeGather the ingredients.Wet each wooden skewer with water and roll it in granulated sugar. This base layer gives the sugar crystals something to grab when they start forming. Set these aside to dry while you prepare the sugar syrup.Place the 2 cups of water in a medium-sized pan and bring it to a boil. Begin adding the sugar, 1 cup at a time, stirring after each addition. You will notice that it takes longer for the sugar to dissolve after each cup you add. Continue to stir and boil the syrup until all of the sugar has been added, and it is completely dissolved. Remove the pan from the heat.If you are using colors or flavorings, add 2 to 3 drops of food coloring and stir it in to ensure an even, smooth color. When using an extract, add 1 teaspoon of the extract; for flavoring oils, only add 1/2 teaspoon. Make sure you don’t stand right in front of the pan because the scent can be very strong as it rises in the steam.Allow the sugar syrup to cool for 20 to 30 minutes.Quick rinse the prepped jars with hot water, then pour the syrup into them.Lower one sugared skewer or string into each jar until it hangs about 1 inch from the bottom.Carefully place your jar in a cool place, away from harsh lights, where it can sit undisturbed. Cover the top loosely with plastic wrap or a paper towel.You should start to see sugar crystals forming within 2 to 4 hours. If you see no change after 24 hours, try boiling the sugar syrup again and dissolve another cup of sugar into it. Then pour it back into the jar and insert the skewer or string again.Allow the rock candy to grow until it is the size you want. Don’t let it grow too large; otherwise, it might start growing onto the sides of your jar. Note that a top layer of crystal will form. This is OK. Once the candy has reached the desired size, break that top layer of crystal up with a fork before removing the candy.Transfer the rock candy to an empty jar or glass (keep the clothespins to balance it) and allow it to dry for 1 to 2 hours. Serve and enjoy, or wrap in plastic wrap to save for later.

_childDocuments_.review: Having grown up with the classic board game version of The Game of Life, diving into The Game of Life 2 was a delightful journey down memory lane with a contemporary twist. As someone who hadn't experienced the original digital version, I found this sequel to be a refreshing take on the beloved classic.One of the standout features for me was the inclusivity offered by the game, allowing players to choose non-binary characters. It's a small yet significant addition and I hope more games implement this features. The single-player mode's 5x speed option during other players' turns was a game-changer, significantly reducing downtime and keeping the momentum going. In just over an hour, I completed two games, which felt faster than expected. This feature not only enhances the overall pacing but also makes the game more enjoyable for solo players like myself.While there's a concern about potential repetitiveness after only a few games, the inclusion of different worlds and unlockables offers hope for continued engagement. Exploring these additional elements may add depth and variety to the gameplay, mitigating any feelings of monotony over time.Despite its reliance on luck, which is inherent in the original game, The Game of Life 2 introduces a stronger sense of choice, allowing players to feel more agency in their decisions. This balance between luck and choice adds an interesting layer of strategy and keeps the gameplay engaging. I purchased the game on sale (I think it was $3) so that is also a bonus.In conclusion, The Game of Life 2 successfully captures the essence of the classic board game while infusing it with modern features and elements of inclusivity. Although there may be concerns about potential repetitiveness, the game's additional content and strategic elements offer promise for continued enjoyment. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game as it's fun and relaxing, and there are some achievements to unlock.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to give this a thumbs up or down, because it really depends on what expectations you have going in. It's a very shallow play experience with only slightly more strategy than Snakes and Ladders but nowhere near as complex as Checkers.Recommended if you just want a simple low-stress party game to pass time with friends or kids. A colorful alternative if you're looking for a casual game but something like Mario Party is too complex. There are no timing challenges, and you're only ever asked to pick between two options. Even the worst options still being beneficial, and a lot of times the winner is determined more or less by random chance. Makes a good couch game to de-stress, especially if only one person is controlling it and making selections by others' request.Not Recommended if you are looking for any kind of depth of gameplay. You're allowed to make some decisions, but what you get is random chance, so you're not always able to achieve the strategy you want. Spinning the wheel with the mouse is incredibly difficult, but if you spin with the spacebar in an online multiplayer game the spin and result don't show. Even with paying for all the DLC there's still a lot of locked customization options which requires a lot of tedious grinding to access. You get a brief window at the start of the round to see everyone's location and status, but otherwise have to wait until it's your turn to pull that information up, when it would be much less cumbersome to be able to look around while other people are taking their turns. Your public username seems to be stuck to your Steam name, and if you select local multiplayer you similarly can't rename them away from Player 2, Player 3, etc. There's no way to communicate in-game at all, not even a small set of phrases (like "good job", "lucky!" or "oh no") or emojis.Unless you have a specific situation, or don't have high expectations, give this one a pass.

A suppose it's "inclusive" since for marriage you can choose blue, pink, or purple.It is a neat idea to not only make money the winning factor with the other items not being as high as money but still weighed in (I made sure to play some full rounds before getting an opinion on changing the games win state). BUT put the idea that life isn't just money in at the same time it could have bee fun. But as it stands it is a parody of real life at best, worse, it's almost mocking.

_childDocuments_.review: Adolf Hitler (20 April 1889 – 30 April 1945) was an Austrian-born German politician who was the dictator of Germany from 1933 until his death in 1945. He rose to power as the leader of the Nazi Party, becoming the chancellor in 1933 and then assuming the title of Führer und Reichskanzler in 1934. During his dictatorship, he initiated World War II in Europe by invading Poland on 1 September 1939. He was closely involved in military operations throughout the war and was central to the perpetration of the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims.Hitler was born in Austria, then part of Austria-Hungary, and was raised near Linz. He moved to Germany in 1913, and was decorated during his service in the German Army in World War I. In 1919, he joined the German Workers' Party (DAP), the precursor of the Nazi Party, and was appointed leader of the Nazi Party in 1921. In 1923, he attempted to seize governmental power in a failed coup in Munich and was imprisoned with a sentence of five years. In jail, he dictated the first volume of his autobiography and political manifesto Mein Kampf ("My Struggle"). After his early release in 1924, Hitler gained popular support by attacking the Treaty of Versailles and promoting pan-Germanism, anti-Semitism and anti-communism with charismatic oratory and Nazi propaganda. He frequently denounced international capitalism and communism as part of a Jewish conspiracy.By November 1932, the Nazi Party held the most seats in the German Reichstag, but did not have a majority. As a result, no party was able to form a majority parliamentary coalition in support of a candidate for chancellor. Former chancellor Franz von Papen and other conservative leaders persuaded President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as chancellor on 30 January 1933. Shortly after, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act of 1933 which began the process of transforming the Weimar Republic into Nazi Germany, a one-party dictatorship based on the totalitarian and autocratic ideology of Nazism. Hitler aimed to eliminate Jews from Germany and establish a New Order to counter what he saw as the injustice of the post-World War I international order dominated by Britain and France. His first six years in power resulted in rapid economic recovery from the Great Depression, the abrogation of restrictions imposed on Germany after World War I, and the annexation of territories inhabited by millions of ethnic Germans, which gave him significant popular support

_childDocuments_.review: "The Game of Life 2" is a digital-only sequel to the eponymous famous board game. The original board game was (and perhaps still is) extremely popular, but was never actually a "good" game - its core rules were designed in 1960, at a time when board game design was still in its infancy. This sequel tries to address and modernize some of the mechanics, but does not go far enough to turn it into an actually engaging experience.As usual, you compete against up to 3 other players in an attempt to have the "best" life. You progress on a track that starts at early adulthood and ends in retirement. To progress along the track, you spin a wheel that will point to a number between 1 and 10. At six spaces the track splits, and you can choose between two different lifestyles, such as "have a career and get a better job" vs "have a family" (yes, the game treats these as mutually exclusive at least for a while, and forgoing career opportunities is the only way to make sure you'll get married). To win the game, you need to accumulate more money than the other players (because the game thinks that life with $800k is much better than life with $400k ...), though you can also accumulate points for "happiness", "education", or "wealth", and get bonus points if you're the player with the highest score in any given category.The game design has a whole lot of problems. For one, its outlook on life is extremely simplistic and competition-oriented. You're only "good" if you make more money than others, and other potential goals like "happiness" or "education" only really count if you have _more_ of them than other people. While I understand that family board games can't be too complex and need to simplify real-life concepts so that players of all age groups can play them and have fun, I'd still say that this is a terrible conceptualization of the quality of one's life.Nevertheless, I wouldn't hold this against the game if it had fun and engaging mechanics. Unfortunately this is where the game really falls flat. Its main problem is that it is extremely based on luck. The main factor for success is still money, and money gets earned, lost, and redistributed based on the random results of the wheel. While you have more opportunities to make decisions than in the original game (which is a good thing), anything beyond the most rudimentary strategies (like "focus on collecting education points") is impossible to plan. Even those simple strategies can easily fail if you just don't draw the cards you're aiming for while another player gets them.For a family game, this dependency on luck can be beneficial, as it allows even young kids to legitimately win. But for a game that's offered on a platform that doesn't even allow access for anyone below the age of 13, game design that potentially lets you end up with 0 points for your attributes even if you focused your entire gameplay on raising one, just because someone else drew the cards that you needed, is just weak.Nevertheless, a luck-based game with a naive and simplistic outlook on life could still be recommended to players with young kids, if at least the production values and user experience were good. Well, welcome to the _worst_ parts of "The Game of Life 2".Graphics are without exception crude, cheap, and featureless. Player characters do not even have faces - while I understand an art direction that tried to stay close to the pegs of the original game, there would have been much better options. In theory there are ways to seamlessly move the camera across the colorful board and zoom in and out, but you can only do this when it's your turn, and when I tried it, the camera was placed below the board with no way of changing its altitude, I could not see anything. (It did work correctly when I tried it right now, though.) A few crude animations exist, which is a nice touch, but they cannot be skipped, which you really want to if you've seen them dozens of times. The background music consists of an obtrusively repetitive attempt at upbeat music that is fun for 30 seconds and then incessantly grinds at your nerves. Voice acting exists only in the form of occasional squeaky exclamations like "Yay!" or "Woohoo!".Sliders for volume control do not exist, you can only turn the music or effects on or off. Graphics settings do not exist apart from "Fullscreen", "Vsync", and a resolution selector that only caters to a 16:9 aspect ratio. Colorblind filters or other accessibility options do not exist. Keyboard controls _do_ exist, which is good, but cannot be rebound (which I wouldn't consider a huge problem for a game like this, but it would certainly help players with disabilities). Spinning the wheel requires some awkward circular mouse movement while holding the left button pressed (if your wrists are vulnerable to any sort of strain pain, this game will bring it out) until you desperately mash your keyboard and find out that you can also use the space key, which the game never tells you. On the positive side, you can save the game at any time.Judging from the crude graphics and missing usability features, this feels like a cheap mobile port that was thrown together without much care. Perhaps the simplistic gameplay might appeal to some players - there's nothing fundamentally wrong with playing games that don't require your brain to be switched on -, but I wouldn't consider it worth the 10€ asking price. What's worse - in a pretty shameless money grab, the game offers alternative "worlds" in a season pass for 25€. These packs contain just a few skins for clothing and cars, plus alternate graphics for the game board. They don't even adapt the gameplay to the theme of the DLC, meaning you can play on a fairytale kingdom world, but you'll still do actions like install solar panels or repair a computer. And if you host a game for your friends who don't own these DLCs, they won't even see the new graphics. The developers have really gone out of their way to deliver a substandard experience at above-average prices.I'm obviously not the target audience for this game, but I believe that this is true for the vast majority of Steam users. Nevertheless, I would recommend checking other reviews as well, as I am really struggling to find anything to praise. The thing that I liked the most is probably the inclusiveness - when you marry, you can choose between three spouses of different genders. I really appreciate the sentiment, but it doesn't save an otherwise pretty bad game.

_childDocuments_.review: Direct improvement over the first game; they've added multiple maps and vehicles, character customisation, and way more possible choices.Each time you land on a panel you'll usually get 2 choices, making it more skill oriented than the first. You focus on getting different bonuses that will help propel you past your friends, and you can keep playing past reaching the end, allowing you to catch up on the panels you would have missed by going fast, and win outside of just having a good paying job. While the first game had random events and mini-games, 'The Game of Life 2' gives you more choice and balances out luck. It's by far not even close to being heavily skill-based, but if you enjoy a chill board game with friends, it's pretty fun.The biggest downside is the other maps being DLC. This game doesn't scream triple-A, and I think the price is fair, which begs the question why the DLCs are a rip off. They're not THAT expensive per-say, but it's not something I would ever want to pay for, especially because you need both you and your friends to buy them. The game doesn't seem to have much upkeep or updates, so I personally don't understand. Not that it's much of a worry, as the base game is good enough imo.Overall, a definitive version of 'The Game of Life'; worth a buy.

Also, the default game only seems to have 2 or 3 minigames. The original had at least 4 to 6 minigames. Thus the original game had more variety in between turns. _childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this, it brings back a lot of good memories from when I was a kid and played the original board game version with my sister back in the 80s/90s. I see a lot of people complaining that each world doesn't change the options for actions or anything, but to me that isn't a big deal. It's basically a collecting aspect after the base, and makes perfect sense if you think about it. If each world changed and had a different board/actions and options, you wouldn't be able to play with your friends who DIDN'T own them. However, the Jobs DO change, and are tailored for the world that you choose. (cause lets face it, who would pick being a surgeon over a dragon tamer??) All I'm saying is if you're wanting to have a good time with friends and family, this is a good way to do it. :)
