_childDocuments_.review: The Game of Life is a classic board game that has been brought to life in a digital format, and it doesn't disappoint. With its colorful and engaging animations, the game provides players with a fun and immersive experience that's sure to keep them entertained for hours.If you enjoy games like Monopoly, then you'll feel right at home with The Game of Life. It features a similar gameplay style, where players make decisions that affect their future and compete to accumulate the most wealth and success. The game's mechanics are easy to understand, making it accessible to players of all ages and skill levels.One of the most enjoyable aspects of The Game of Life is how it lets you customize your character and path in life. You can choose your career, spouse, and even have children as you progress through the game. These decisions affect your future and create a unique gaming experience every time you play.The Game of Life is also an excellent time killer. The game's rounds are relatively short, so you can easily pick it up and play for a few minutes or settle in for a more extended gaming session. With its addictive gameplay and engaging animations, it's easy to lose track of time while playing.In conclusion, if you're looking for a great board game to play on your pc, phone or tablet, then The Game of Life is an excellent choice. Its engaging gameplay, customizable options, and immersive animations make it an enjoyable and entertaining experience for players of all ages.

_childDocuments_.review: I am having loads of fun with this game so far, but I have some small complaints. It's mostly in regards to the lack of STOP places in the game where they should be. For example, on the Classic board, you at one point have to choose between Family and Investment (basically Happiness and Wealth for the in-game stats). The problem is, there's no guarantee if you select that path that you'll get what you wanted. I can't tell you how many times I've bypassed the Family or House tiles because of poor spins. There ought to be STOP tiles at points along those routes to allow you to actually grow your family or buy a house. That's how things were in the original board game, and it doesn't make sense that this feature was removed.Aside from that, this is a fun adaptation of a classic game, and I do recommend people give it a try if they liked the original Game of Life.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely an upgrade from the original "Game of Life" digital version.There is a lot more content that lends itself to replayability of this game. It is much less stagnant then the first one. Still a very large number of online players so you don't have to play just against AI which works great for SOLO players.You can get Steam and In-Game achievements so there is always a reason to continue to play the game. Even when you buy the "Season Pass" you are only buying 50% of the games extra items. The SP also unlocks the ability to gain more items without further purchase you just have to continue to play toward the in game achievements to unlock the Outfits, Vehicles, and Avatars. In-Game Achievements - This is all done through the extra boards you unlock. Each board has 2 Vehicles, 3 Outfits, and 3 Avatars. These are separate and different from the 2 Vehicles, 3 Outfits, and 3 Avatars you get per board from buying the SP.I really like this idea since usually when you get a season pass there is no real reason or need to play the extra content more than a few times unless you really really like it. The extra items add to the games/players continued interaction thus leading to a larger continued (online)community involvement for the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I would only recommend this game for kids.It's still a fun and cute game, but if you are an adult it will get boring fast.This game puts a twist on a classic! Playing this version of the life board game made me realize how non-PC the original was. For example, you can choose to get married or to stay single! I feel like that is a bit more up-to-date than the original and not so brain washy! ^_^It's definitely a modern take! I was so happy that they gave the player a choice.They even change the objective to being the happiest instead of the riches; which in my opinion is a little bit based on how wealthy you are, but not as focused! I feel like this version is a better role model for kids instead of the old one.Why get married when you don't want to?#AcePower#GarlicBreadWith that out of the way, let me tell you why it's best if an adult doesn't play.Yeah, yeah, yeah. Play the game to spend time with your kids, but at the end of the day, you won't really want to play this for long. It's cute at first, but there isn't much content that would make the parent themselves (or any other adult) say, "Wow! This game is so fun that I would play this by myself without trying to use the whole 'Well, you know it's for the kids' excuse." The game isn't Shoots n' Ladders bad, or Candy Land bad, but you won't get much gameplay out of it. It's extremely short with virtually no content. There aren't that many career choices, and the how "Gasp! You have to pay taxes!" feature isn't that really much of a challenge. It's a true child's game in which the developers tried to take into consideration the motor skills, mental capacity, and the attention span of children. You will notice (eventually if not right away) how low the difficulty level is.I never played with any DLCs, so I can't say for sure if the DLCs add more value or not.But to end on a good note, let me just say again that I LOVE how they modernized it!I know it's just a game, but the classic Game of Life board implies that all there is to life is just earning money and then dying. But this more modern version shows that you don't have to have earn the most money in order to "win." That there is more than one routeAnd that was a pleasant change!

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but I can understand why it isn't for some people.   Put simply this game is a trimmed down version of Life where an average game is around 20 minutes give or take a little depending on rolls.   Gameplay is centered around spinning a wheel to move spaces and acquiring money and three attributes (learning, wealth, and happiness).   Most of the strategy comes from making decisions on which of these attributes to target while making all the cash you can.    Certain parts of the board also briefly branch and tend to have benefits that will cater to certain playstyles. Let's be clear here, it is a lightweight game.   It's very simple and casual.   You can absolutely bring some thinking to this game as far as when to try to hoard cash or when to spend on attributes.   But it's not a deep experience.  It's also over very quickly, if you roll a lot of 9s and 10s you'll skip entire sections of the board.   For me I'm ok with all that.   There is just something comforting about the adorable artstyle and music, and just feel of this game that just won me over in a big way.   And yeah i bought the season pass and I have no regrets.  Just know what you're getting into.   If you're looking for a true successor of the "The Game of Life" with longer gametime and decent level of complexity, this is not it.   This is Game of Life's adorable nephew who has infectious enthusiasm that makes you smile and but isn't old enough to have any interesting conversations.   It's just good clean, relaxing fun.   And I love it for that.

But it doesn't even change the Event cards to be appropriate to the setting. So you still get things like Buy a New Computer in the Age of Giants, which is based on the Stone Age. _childDocuments_.review: 1. The cut-scenes get annoying after a few rounds.  You get to speed up your opponent's, but don't get to skip/speed up yours.2. It's very difficult to spin the wheel.  The control is clunky and you have to jerk your mouse really hard to make the spin work.  A push button to spin will work much better than this current control.3. The RNG factor at its finest.  Upon reaching retirement first and spinning to get more points (50% getting points and 50% nothing), I got 7 out of 8 nothing.  I had to watch my opponent surpassing me bit by bit and eventually lost the game by a small margin.  Also, my opponent never paid for tax during the course of the game, whereas I have paid for tax 4-5 times.4. Some other reviews already mentioned this.  The first campaign map has like 30 minutes play (against one opponent, if you choose to play against 3 opponents, it'll be probably ~1 hour long due to the cut-scenes). _childDocuments_.review: Quite good and fun. Though there are some unbalanced game mechanics/features that could be fixed:1. Too much of a difference in terms of salary between the college path and the career path. Even though the college jobs pay more taxes, they are not effective as a balance because you only sometimes land on taxes. Therefore nobody can really win the game by choosing the career path.2. Fate wheel should give more benefits. Right now it's high-risk low-reward instead of high-risk high-reward.3. The house space is too OP (compared to the job space or family space). Because you get 2 wealth points plus the house will always net you profits at the end. There should be at least a 50% chance where you can lose profits when selling the house at the end.4. Could add some more job options, as there are only a handful of jobs to choose from right now.5. Overall speaking, too dependent on luck, very little on strategy (which could be good or bad depending on the player type).

_childDocuments_.review: There truly needs to be a middling option about these games. There are parts of The Game of Life: 2 that are absolutely horrible that will bother your game play so much that you may be turned off from buying it and it might alienate casual gamers and long time lovers of this game. On the other hand, it's a pretty good update.Emphasis on pretty good.If you remember being able to play mini games where you could sue the other player, play puzzles, find hidden objects, and other games to determine extra perks that could change the game for you... I don't believe that's ever returning to an edition of Life ever. I recall playing this version after theatre rehearsal while running lines and suing the pants off my AI opponent. This version is not it and it doesn't bring back that element either. I am pretty sure some of you are looking for the reviews for that so I'm gonna tell you that now. Nope, not here. Not even the weird "Red Light, Green Light" game from that one mobile edition, either.The forever-missing Life tiles are back, but they've been reinvented in the form of gaining points in Wealth, Love, and Knowledge. Confused? It's not too tricky. You land on a space or the new Wheel of Fate (spin when you land on these for a chance at something) and you may be given some points. These function essentially like Life tiles once did, assigning you points to help you at the end of the game so it's not all just money anymore. This is a welcome sight. Much like those tiles, each of the cards are fairly entertaining when you pick up the points. Learn how to make sushi from a master class. Volunteer with a charity. These are just the ones the peg people are achieving right this second in the game. There's plenty, but boy did I miss these. It gives anyone's life a little flavor. Now these colorful pieces of plastic really do represent people and I don't feel like I'm just mindlessly clicking... Which I actually am. Now I just have something warm and fuzzy to read. It's good, trust me.Some new things are dogs and cats included with children. Want to be a crazy cat lady? You can. Want to adopt children while z-snapping and declaring you need "no man"? You're allowed to pursue a route for this. The problem is, all of these routes are so painfully short that you never get to experience that new and shiny Wheel of Fate or enough family tiles to help you. You end up relying on some spinner manipulation if you actually want to experience what the game has to offer, which is a shame because they've gone through the work to give us some houses to watch our little peg hop around in front of and be a happy home owner of... and buy multiple houses.That's right, Life is letting us play the real estate market, baby!Unfortunately with all of these lovely additions (we get non binary pegs and non binary spouses!) it seems like choices were also ripped away from us. No matter how many rounds I play with the college route, I'm always stuck with cooking or robotics as the best choices. Not going to college gives me pop star, athlete, and some social media based items... What happened to teacher? We're still becoming teachers today. Brain surgeon? Really? Why not taking a step back and thinking about the classic board game for a moment. I still have my beautiful relic from the 90s and the jobs there are just as relevant then as they are now. I love the addition of social media jobs, but did we seriously sacrifice things as basic as retail jobs and teaching? Really? That's what most of us boring average joes are doing right now.It's also dawning on me that Hasbro has the license for Monopoly and Life. Yet Monopoly taxes you closer to real life than Life ever has. This is the only board game, this particular version, where you can be taxed before you ever get any sort of paycheck... That's a little screwy. Life as always needed to reevaluate their idea of taxes but it's glaringly obvious in this game.I grudgingly recommend the game. I do like it. Most of the improvements that were made are things many fans wanted for a long time. Being forced to do things in a game called Life felt a little awkward. However losing a little bit of choice that made the game fun in the career section seems counterproductive.It's honestly too short to enjoy what great changes were made. Price is pretty great for the base game, but you're just gonna play it over and over again hoping you can fill your car with as many cats as possible and you'll be shocked if you get even one.

name: Dorfromantik
detailed_description: Wishlist our new game Roadmap About the Game Dorfromantik is a relaxing building strategy and puzzle game in which you place tiles to create ever-growing, idyllic village landscapes. With Dorfromantik, you can immerse yourself in a quiet, peaceful world at any time and take a break from everyday life. At the same time, Dorfromantik offers a challenge for those who are looking for one: To beat the highscore, you need to carefully plan and strategically place your tiles. In Dorfromantik you start with a stack of procedurally generated tiles. One after the other, you draw the top tile of the stack, place it on one available slot and rotate for the best fit. Thereby groups and combinations of landscapes are formed, such as forests, villages or water bodies, and you are rewarded with points depending on how well the tile fits. On some tiles you will also encounter special objects that give you a quest: For example, the windmill wants to border 6 grain fields, the locomotive wants to be connected to 10 tracks or the deer wants to inhabit a forest with at least 50 trees. Fulfill these quests to get more tiles to continue the expansion of your landscape. The game ends when the tile stack is used up. As you expand the landscape, you can advance into new, colorful biomes and discover pre-placed game objects that give you long-term tasks. Through these tasks you can unlock new tiles, new biomes and new quests. What Dorfromantik offers Building endless and beautiful landscapes Unique mix of strategy and puzzle mechanics Relaxing and calming gameplay Idyllic village scenery Strategic placement to beat the highscore High replay value - every session is different Many unlockable tiles and biomes Original Artstyle with handpainted boardgame feel What Dorfromantik does not offer 4X Strategy Trading Resource Management Combat & Violence Multiplayer Dorfromantik offers options for any style of play! Take a short break from life in quick mode or try to master the game in hard mode. The Custom Mode allows you to create your own rulesets and share them with others, while monthly mode awaits you with a new challenge every month. If you just want to relax and build your own landscape with no limits, try the creative mode! Dorfromantik was developed by four game design students from Berlin. Together we have founded Toukana Interactive and want to develop many more small, original and high-quality indie games in the future. We are happy about constructive feedback of all kinds, so feel free to contact us! We will do our best to respond to messages quickly and fix any problems that may arise. :)

Thereby groups and combinations of landscapes are formed, such as forests, villages or water bodies, and you are rewarded with points depending on how well the tile fits. On some tiles you will also encounter special objects that give you a quest: For example, the windmill wants to border 6 grain fields, the locomotive wants to be connected to 10 tracks or the deer wants to inhabit a forest with at least 50 trees. Fulfill these quests to get more tiles to continue the expansion of your landscape. The game ends when the tile stack is used up. As you expand the landscape, you can advance into new, colorful biomes and discover pre-placed game objects that give you long-term tasks. Through these tasks you can unlock new tiles, new biomes and new quests. What Dorfromantik offers Building endless and beautiful landscapes Unique mix of strategy and puzzle mechanics Relaxing and calming gameplay Idyllic village scenery Strategic placement to beat the highscore High replay value - every session is different Many unlockable tiles and biomes Original Artstyle with handpainted boardgame feel What Dorfromantik does not offer 4X Strategy Trading Resource Management Combat & Violence Multiplayer Dorfromantik offers options for any style of play! Take a short break from life in quick mode or try to master the game in hard mode. The Custom Mode allows you to create your own rulesets and share them with others, while monthly mode awaits you with a new challenge every month. If you just want to relax and build your own landscape with no limits, try the creative mode! Dorfromantik was developed by four game design students from Berlin. Together we have founded Toukana Interactive and want to develop many more small, original and high-quality indie games in the future. We are happy about constructive feedback of all kinds, so feel free to contact us! We will do our best to respond to messages quickly and fix any problems that may arise. :)
short_description: Dorfromantik is a peaceful building strategy and puzzle game where you create a beautiful and ever-growing village landscape by placing tiles. Explore a variety of colorful biomes, discover and unlock new tiles and complete quests to fill your world with life!

_childDocuments_.review: The typical 'run out of cards and start again' mechanic.  And of course it's not a 'select a card yourself' mechanic but just the normal 'do the next card'.  Far to many of these things releasing and expecting people to just play random draws over and over.  Cards can also use more of a merge mechanic similar to the water based cards to look nice and the towns should grow and merge tiles.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This game was given to me as a gift and I absolutely love it. It's simple, repetitive, and rewarding. The creative mode is super fun when you just want to build massive maps and the piece diversity is nice. The music is super calming and relaxing, so whenever I'm feeling stressed I know I can boot up this game and just have fun expanding the map. There are quests and different goals to complete as well that offer new pieces for you to use, so its rewarding in that regard. I can easily see myself putting another 70 hours into this game as it is now. The different biomes and how they connect can make some really beautiful game maps. Would definitely recommend if you're looking for a relaxing and casual puzzle-like game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Misleading Tags. This is not a turnbased strategy game but a puzzle game. No resource management or tech tree, just random map parts which have to be arranged in certain patterns. I admit that watching a video makes that clear pretty quickly, nevertheless the tags are just wrong. This has little to nothing to do with strategy or building cities.Also: entirely not my type of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This game just feels right. I don't know how else to sum up how I feel about this game! I love puzzle games but only if they are FUN to play! So many games pull off the puzzle bit but feel more like a chore than something you want to continue playing. Among all of the many games I have, this is the one that seems to make time melt away inside the little ever expanding map. This game made me late for errands but I still didn't mind.The music is relaxing and you can definitely zone out plunking down little tiles. It can also be intense - carefully planning each move to maximize space. The plunking sound is just right and the mechanic of placement is satisfying. When you get in the zone and you're nailing the short term goals one after the other, this game becomes truly enjoyable. It took me around 10 hours to fully grasp more efficient placement and how to do things like, for example, start a new run of rivers one tile from the other run so if a short term goals pops up with a specific number goal you can use the separated run until that number is accomplished then a number+ goal comes up next to be connected on that single open tile onto the original run. (Those are a lot of words to explain a relatively simple concept.)Now, the only input I have for adjustment are the goals that are on the outlier of your starting points. If you can't tell what they are until you get that close to them, they should either change to the format that you have extended all the way to them (forest, towns, railroads, fields, or water) or they should be visible as soon as the round starts. It's a bit frustrating to make your way all the way to one of those goals only to realize it's the format on the opposite side of your map that will connect!Anyway, I HIGHLY recommend this game. I am a bit concerned I won't tire of this game and it will continue to disappear some of my waking hours. In the meantime, I will enjoy plunking my little world together!
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I was told that if I like one specific boardgame, I would very likely like this game too. They were right and once I start playing this game, it's hard to stop.The fact that I can play this on my own and choose between different modes from classic point collecting puzzle solution focusing mode to creative mode just to build something aesthetically pleasant is everything I wished from this game.The graphics are very lovely and the music very sweetly goes along with the game and it's quick to start and learn but also challenging if you really wanna go all in and try to get only perfect tile matches while in the mercy of rng waiting just that right piece to come up and score more points and get extra tiles to continue game just when you were about to get game over.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Reminded me at first of Islanders, but soon I realized how much more I like this game then Islanders. It's beautiful, relaxing, and interesting. Seems very approachable , and one you can go back to when you want  this kind of game.  Has that Euro game feel. The art and music is terrific. My wife bought this game after watching me play it, (and she is the one that told me about it). A household hit! Great for everyone!  Great job.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Very addictive, in a good way. High replay value, no two games are alike. Graphics are enjoyable, the animation adds to rather than distracts. The mystery tiles showing up as you expand are fun too. The goals very greatly from game to game so you are always coming up with new strategies. Well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Mostly succeeds at being the light fun game it wants to be, but is stymied by the baffling exclusion of an Undo function.  I'm mystified how this wasn't an important feature from the outset, and now they can't seem to add it without more work than they want to do.  So the result is a relaxing laid-back game that also intolerant of accidents or brainfarts.  Dumb.  That said, is it worth $5 to screw around with and then forget about?  Maybe.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and serene tile based city builder. Float in a purple liminal space and slowly create and ever expanding world while trying for perfect borders. Completing small challenges (ie have a city of at least 15 tiles) grants additional tiles, and certain achievements unlock new tiles. Slow, calming dopamine.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Really relaxing and enjoyable.  I hope the tile system gets advanced to the point where it feels like you are building a whole world space (mountains, hills, etc).  My only complaint is it feels like it is designed to end your game sometimes.  Maybe that's better stated as there's no way to earn more tiles, or the system forces you to make decisions that long term cause your game to end (cashing in on the flags to fend off the end by closing off sectors, then getting a tile that requires 100+ of what you just closed off).  I think if the number of active missions you have increases slightly as you place more tiles that would help.  I have only played 3 full games, but two of the three ended when I went on a 15+ tile run where I don't think there was any combination of ways that I could have used the tiles to stop the game from ending.  Having said that I understand the games aren't supposed to go forever (maybe an endless mode could be nice at some point?).
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: A relaxing and visually stunning tile-placement game where you create picturesque landscapes. It's easy to learn, with strategic depth, calming music, and beautiful visuals. Perfect for puzzle lovers and those seeking a stress-free, creative experience. Highly recommended for casual and meditative gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This is a super relaxing game. I highly recommend it.I love both the regular game mode and creative mode so much! I even signed up for the public beta to get the experimental stuff to try out. The devs are very active in their Discord community and also very responsive to both bug fixes and general questions.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderfully relaxing game. The game play is simple yet challenging. When I first saw the game it sort of reminded me a bit of Sim City - that build up your city kind of game play is what I anticipated. The game is like that in a way, but you build your landscape by using the tiles as they are "dealt" to you. So... it's kind of a cross between Sim City and Solitaire. As I said before... the game play is simple yet challenging... a bit of "relaxed strategy". The music that plays in the background is very pleasant as well... I look forward, with excitement, to the further development of this game. I highly recommend getting it!
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Ill be completely honest. When I first started this game, it was after an impulse purchase of no real reason, and I was thinking of refunding it. The game was good, but didn't really hold my interest. Had a 1 hour session and got bored and closed it. However, something drew me back. I wasn't sure what it was, but I felt this strange desire to keep going. Unlocking more and more tiles, building massive cities, all to the tune of relaxing music just hit an itch I didn't know I had. I easily blasted through another 2 and half hours straight without a single regret. I enjoyed my time building a massive moving world.Another thing that kind of goes unnoticed is the degree of freedom you have over how you move the camera. A very subtle thing to add, but I can tell that it definitely makes a difference. You can drag the screen around. You can move the camera regularly with WASD. You can hold SHIFT to move it faster like you're sprinting, and even rotate the screen around. Little things like that make the game feel just that much more fluid to play and make it very enjoyable.TL;DR If you're looking for a relaxing and enjoyable puzzle game to pass some spare time, this is definitely the game for you. I definitely enjoyed it. Even losing by running out of tiles felt strangely enjoyable, a charm not shared by many other puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Sit back and relax people say... Well sure, but it requires a lot of focus and thinking as the game moves on, which makes it hard and not that relaxing.Overall It's a nice game. Unfortunately the content is very limited and gets repetitive and boring, so try to get it on a discount. I got bored after ~30 hours of game play, though i still recommend it but only on a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Adorable (and challenging) little game that you can lose hours of your life to. It's the perfect blend of chill vibes and genuine puzzling that I found supremely enjoyable. Recent updates to the game have also correct the tiny issues, like not being able to undo an accidental tile placement, all in all 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Don't believe the lies this is the most stressful game. There's an inevitable end that is constantly teasing you with an ever-changing tile count, and each tile asks you to scour you map to discover the most optimal place which takes and increasing amount of time due to the nature of your growing landscape. Each new objective is another extra responsibility required to keep playing and adds to your decision time. This exploration into twisted cosmic horror gave me an existential crisis. And if you don't have OCD it's probably a great game. 86/100
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik is the definition of what a best friend would be if they were a video game.You can just relax with them and you can also find joy in doing something engaging and challenging together. They're always there for you and the more you know them the more you like themThere is a certain magic in this game that pulls you into a wholesome and peaceful space. The visuals and the audio is just perfectly simple and simply perfect.I can play this game with my kids and get absolutely excited with them to see new biomes and vehicles for the first time. I can play this game at night to wind down and relax. And I can also play this game for a few minutes between work sessions and try to beat my own records. Whatever the setting, Dorfromantik is my most beloved game at the moment and it will always have a special place in my heart.Dear Luca, Sandro, Timo & Zwi and all the other people who contributed to Dorfromantik!Thank you for pouring your heart and soul into this work of art and bringing more magic to our world. I wish you the best and will be looking out for the future projects of Toukana Interactive!Sincerely, Bernát from Hungary
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: The aim of this game is placing hexagonal tiles next to each other, in such a way that they make a beautiful landscape. The landscape created will include forests, villages, fields, rivers, railways... Occasionally, you'll be given a quest to place a certain number of structures adjacent to each other for a score bonus. There are also quests that track your score over several games and unlock new types of tile. As of the time of this review, the sandbox mode has not been implemented yet, so the number of tiles you can place is finite.This is one of those games where I wish Steam had a star scoring system. This way, I could have given Dorfromantik 4 stars. Because while it's relaxing, satisfying, easy to learn, pretty and reasonably priced, I feel that the quests are often grindier than they need to be, especially the ones which unlock new tile types.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Got this originally as part of the Bundle for Racial Justice and Equality on itch and really enjoyed the game. When it was announced to be coming on Steam, I wishlisted it and purchased soon after release. It's a great game to sit down for a few minutes or an hour and just place some tiles trying to meet quests. Would recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most refreshing zen AND strategy/puzzle games I have ever had the pleasure to play. The aesthetic is amazing and beautiful. I love the art style of this game and it's very thoughtful how it blends from season to season on the same board. If you are looking for just a feel-good zen gaming session, this is it! Alternately, if you are looking for a challenging puzzle/strategy gaming session, this is also it! You can approach the game differently depending on what mood you are in and what you are looking for. Not very many games can pull that off successfully - this one does impressively.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I am so happy to have found this game. _childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Without a doubt one of the most fun, challenging and relaxing games i have played the last few years. I like that every game is different and there is no clear road to getting the highest score. The more time you spend placing each tile, the better your score will be. Not for people looking for a fast pace game or with a low attention span. The achievement system is what keeps you going and going. Not paying attention for one second and accidentally misplacing one tile can ruin your whole game. I love it, hope they never add an 'undo last tile' button or something. _childDocuments_.review: This game is very relaxing and satisfying, highly recommended if you're looking for a game to play during a 10 minute break or when there's time to kill. Straightforward and simple goals but mastering the game takes more strategy than placing tiles that look pretty next to each other. The full release improved on lots of minor issues as well. A must have for the casual gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik is a pleasant and relaxing game with clean and clear presentation. It reminiscent of Civilization and jigsaw puzzles having a baby. The games I have played (which are 3 playthroughs on twitch) lasted anywhere from 1.5 hours to 4 hours. It's fun and easy to learn and the very few complaints I have may just be related to the way I play, but I also wish they were explained a little more thoroughly in some capacity through the game. One is that at some points when connecting pieces, you can sometimes run into a problem where connecting the common pieces will block you off from getting the achievement, but it never explains why or when this is going to happen, and with what pieces because they are so varied and only certain tiles have this feature. So, sometimes you have to start a new section even though you have the opening to put the tile down, it will cancel your achievement out. Now, I haven't found any explanation as to why this happens or what the reason behind this is. The other issue I have is the last game I played had Flags you have to block off, and I believe my game glitched to where I could not close off those tiles, because I surrounded the tiles with my last few of the game, and where you are supposed to block off these tiles is usually lit up. Well, there was no light indicating where to block these two flags off, and I lost because you gain tiles by gaining these achievements. Other than these two issues, this game is a solid, fun, casual, strategy game, again with very clean, clear, simple presentation. This is a very access-able game for any isometric/strategy and/or puzzle fan.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game because I was looking for something relaxing and casual, but that did posed some kind of challenge. I found this game to be extremely addictive, it is very pleasing when you're able to properly connect tiles. What really makes the game imo is having some challenges or sort of quests, and I really hope they will add much more of those since without them I think most people will eventually feel it's lacking purpose and will lose interest. Also the game is pleasing to the eye, though it drives me nuts that the farms look like stone (I was positive it's like a stone mine/deposit or something). Give it a try if you're into puzzles and OCD-like tile matching.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a real gem. Don't let the "early access" thing scare you - it is already a fun, stable, interesting masterpiece. The design is top-notch: both simple yet atmospheric artstyle and music pair real nice with simple yet challenging gameplay.The only "problem" about this game is unclearness of scoring. For example: a reward says to "place tiles without connecting incompatible edges", but I have no idea what that means. I can make a couple guesses, but I'd rather get a clear explanation. But it doesn't really mess the game itself, as it's fun enough to try and beat own score, or just place tiles to create something neat.Would I recommend this game to my friends? _childDocuments_.review: Be careful. This game is deceptively addictive! "Oh, I'll just play for another few minutes" turns into hours!  The game mode is only "relaxing" if you're not a perfectionist. Thankfully, there is a creative mode where you can just build whatever you want, too. Even in game mode, you can always just leave the game and pick up where you left off later. There are no timers and no pressure - except for finding perfect tile fits which can be maddening, but when you find a perfect tile to fill a hole, it's so freaking satisfying. I often turn the soundtracks to games off, but this one is so relaxing and peaceful that I keep it on. It's a perfect complement to the game. Contemplative and calming. I can't wait to see what the developer adds! Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little puzzle game with a simple UI.  Scoring is not clear at first, but becomes understandable after your first few rounds.  Experience will help you as some bonus pieces are impossible unless you have planned ahead.  The randomness of the pieces can sometimes cause frustration when trying to manage separate biomes (rail and river on the same piece).

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks relaxing. It sounds relaxing. But it actually isn't.The game only counts as relaxing, if you don't play for score or achievements, but just for the visuals, and don't care about how far you come. I imagine that the creative mode will actually be quite relaxing - but not really a game, since there's nothing to gain or to lose.Because if you play for score and achievements, you will inevitably become frustrated. No matter how well you plan your moves, 90% the time it is impossible to reach the achievement goals. It doesn't matter if you see to it that you fulfill every quest to get more tiles, while also having an eye on the achievements, which, once completed, also give you tiles.Of quests, there are those types: 1. Group tiles of a certain type together, which is parted in:1a. AT LEAST that many tiles or1b. EXACTLY that many tiles. 2. Close off a group. Those groups get marked by a flag. The flags are usually earned through 1b. quests.3. Find hidden tiles on the map and fulfill their quest.Achievements come in different versions. Some are global, meaning you can finish them over several games and some have to be completed in one run.1. Group at least that many tiles together (e.g. form a forest that consists of at least 800 trees) Usually one run.2. Score perfect placement (means that all edges have to be aligned with an edge of the same likelihood) Come in both versions.3. Close off tile-groups. (e.g. form at least 50 closed-off field groups having at least 10 tiles) Usually global.Example: I just finished a run (which prompted me to write this review) in which I planned everything perfectly. In the 30 mins I played, I managed to complete every quest, while still lining up achievement requirements. I connected every train and water tile I could connect (as I had achievements going that prompted me to form a train track of 50 tiles and a body of water with 60 tiles) and in the end, the run ended, with me falling short of 3 train tiles and 4 water tiles. Tiles I could have added to the train track, while adding them to the water body, would not have made any difference (there are tiles that can be used for both).There was NOTHING I could have done better. Yet, the RNG did not even PROVIDE me with the tiles needed. It was simply impossible to get the achievements!I see two major problems here:1. The (badly designed) RNG has complete power over the game.2. More complicated quests to complete don't gain you higher rewards.ad 1.) If the RNG decides to only give you tiles you can't use and no achievement tiles, then that's that. If the RNG decides you not even get enough tiles to finish your achievement, then that's that too. Also, the tiles you get get worse the longer you play, making them unusable at a certain point. This isn't fun.I would suggest adding a mechanic like in "Islanders", in which you get to choose which type of tiles you get next when you reach certain score points. To explain for "Dorfromantik": Let's say you have 3 quests for a forest open, and you hit 2000 points, you should be able to choose to get a certain amount / more forest tiles for the next 20 tiles. This way, you could influence the game a bit, without killing its gameplay.ad 2.) The longer the game runs, the higher the requirement for the quests are. E.g. in the beginning, you need to connect 20 houses to finish a quest and get more tiles, later you need 200. Problem is, you only get 5 tiles as a reward, and it does not matter how many you needed to complete the quest. Which means, ultimaltey, that it is impossible to keep going. I get that this game is not meant to go on indefinitely (in classic mode), but it is frustrating to not get higher rewards for harder quests. That is one of the basic principles of quests, which should be adhered to. Otherwise, why even bother with the harder quests? Oh right: because you don't get easier ones later on.TL;DR: The RNG, on whose mercy you have to cast yourself, and not getting higher rewards for more complicated quests and achievements kills the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing casual early-access game. Having a great time and the challenge level is very reasonable. I have two suggestions, both of which I have seen in the past, but was hoping to emphasize.1. I think there should be a limited-use "undo" feature, maybe you made a mistake or you didn't realize all the aspects of a given tile and you would like to rethink its placement. Maybe you earn 1 undo every 50 tiles or something2. I think there should be a "skip" feature similar to the suggested undo feature. Very limited use, but sometimes maybe you're low on tiles and really trying to complete a trial, and you get a tile that will be monumentally unhelpful; it would be nice to have an occasional skip without consequence.Thanks for this great game, and I hope to see it continue to develop going forward
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for those who just want to relax and not use the keyboard for once (unless you use the keyboard which is optional). I got this thinking I would examine every hexagon for the perfect match, but what I ended up doing is slapping fun villages and forests together, creating the world's most twisty rivers, and watching trains run along the tracks I set out. Exactly what I needed without even knowing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This has been my go-to game to relax and concentrate. Reminds me of Carcassonne but far more relaxing.The gist of the game is basically place tiles adjacent to eachother to complete tilesets, get your points rinse repeat, all the while creating a lovely landscape in the process. Unlock special tiles as you continue to play and drop those beauties down as you go. Keep an eye out for white highlighted tiles for extra goodness.Def recommend this gem if you enjoy relaxation and concentration whilst relaxing.Exceptional for those suffering from Anxiety + Depression or other mental illness. Super relaxing.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I felt that the games are very long, very addictive, and very frustrating. If you want to perform well, the game will take more than an hour; however, the tiles are random. That means the perfect tile you are waiting for won't come, and suddenly it's "GG", "Try again". And you do, thinking that this time it will be different, but after some hours of effort it's "GG" again. After 3 hours, you played only two games that ends like nothing happened in here. And if you close your eyes, you can see the game trees and houses, which means it is seriously very addictive.But now I see the game becoming better, step by step, with updates.I have some suggestions to it: add different architecture (Romans, Aztecs, Middle Ages, Japaneses), add different themes (Halloween, Christmas, Middle Earth), add different game modes (build a labyrinth), maybe open the game for mods in the steam community tab.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game to play a couple rounds of whenever you're feeling down or bored, no rushing involved. The music and the relaxed atmosphere both help improve your experience, too. Some of the achievements are slightly bonkers and not exactly easy to get, but it's not like they change much about the game anyway. A solid 10/10 from me!
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, very chill and soothing. That being said it might be a little too chill. I could see myself sinking 5 hours into this game seeing how far I could get and trying to get achievements. When I thought about it I decided that I could spend my time in a better way. This is a cool and fun game, but I feel like the rewards and replayability are lacking.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: It is simultaneously relaxing and challenging. I play it almost everyday after work. Like others, I'm interested to see what the devs might add in terms of tool tips/better tutorial. I read an article that gave tips and my scores significantly improved. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because I wanted to be able to play a chill game either to relax or to play it along with a stream/movie/yt video on my other monitor. (This works perfectly btw)Little did I know that I would descend into madness. PART 1: Ignorance is BlissI didn't know how the point system works so I just kept building cute little maps and I was pretty proud of myself for increasing my points after every run. I was happy as long as the world made me want to quit real life and instead get on the cute little train on tracks that looked like a 5-year-old designed it. But I wanted to get even more points and so instead of going for aesthetics I was paying more attention to maximise points. PART 2: Perfect Tiles = DopamineOne thing led to another and I ended up watching a 40 minute YouTube video talking about the point system, some general tips and the overall thought process when putting tiles together. Basically, you have to try and match each side of the hexagon tile with an adjacent tile, for example house borders house. If you are able to match all sides perfectly you add more tiles (and points) to your stack. The 'goal' is to not run out of hexagons. Another way to accomplish that is to fulfil quests that will pop up randomly. Tasks involve connecting one type of tile (e.g. tree, field, house..) to reach either a specific number or plus. This awakened something in me that has been absent for most of my life; ambition. I started to get the hang of it and my maps were getting bigger and I finally reached over 10k points. I considered that an achievement; my friend called it an addiction. Apples and Oranges. Every time I completed a matching set of tiles and the "perfect" animation popped up with the cute sound feedback, I got a small dopamine dosis that kept me going. Coffee? No. Chocolate? No. Perfect tiles? Oh yeah, that's the ♥♥♥♥!Conclusion:What started off as a game to past some time quickly turned into a personal challenge. Don't get me wrong though, I can still relax while also trying to be more efficient about it. Sometimes I do get a little grumpy when there is a tile that ♥♥♥♥♥ you over and doesn't fit ANYWHERE :) But, on the other hand, you feel the opposite when you finally see a tile you were waiting for the past hour. There is also a creative mode for all the people who don't want to deal with points and quests and prefer to build aesthetically pleasing maps. 10/10  I dream about putting tiles together. No, I don't need help.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't want to buy another game in EA, but this one is so polished already, I couldn't resist. There are regular updates and the devs listen to the community. If there wasn't a roadmap ahead, one could think this game is already finished. I didn't run into any bugs, it even works perfectly fine on Linux with Proton. I can only see this game getting even better with each update. This game is very pretty, the music is very chill and it's just an enjoyable experience. Also slightly addicting, the "try again" button is right there once you finish a round.There are some things I'd mention, but they are already on the roadmap; controller support, undo button, being able to save a map and start a second one. I also can't wait for creative mode, as my maps never get as pretty when trying for points, especially sprawling train tracks can become a bit annoying. I'll probably uninstall until a few of those features are in, if only to stop myself from "just starting another quick game because I have 5 minutes" and to save myself the headache of insta-regret after placing down a tile. But before I do that, I'll just do one more quick game.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, it is a four-dollar game, which is pretty good for a ten-dollar game in the first days of Early Access. It would also be nice to be able to turn off some of the unlocked biomes---one of them is pretty ugly, to my eye, all grey and red and yellow. It's also fairly empty, still. _childDocuments_.review: This is NOT a city builder/sim/resource management game.  It IS a STRATEGY game.For those of you who have played Carcassonne, it is very similar but it is play alone and, from what I have read, they do not plan to make it multiplayer.  Which is fine by me; it doesn't need to be.  Caveat here that it would be a good game for two or more people to sit down together to plan a strategy.For those of you who have not played Carcassonne, it is a tile game with different landscape elements:  Forests, villages (houses), grasslands, rock fields, railroad lines and water/river/oceans.  (More biomes are promised.)  The basic premise is laying down the tiles in such a way as to build on those areas.  But that's not all . . . each play through (session) has different "quests" and/or rewards so you are doing something different and changing your strategy each time you play.  Example of a quest may be that you must match tiles with a certain number of houses exactly, or sometimes at least that number and sometimes you must close off an area of houses so the area cannot be made bigger.Very addictive game.  Devs are hands on and listening to the players.   I've played for 10 hours at this writing and I'm not bored yet.Highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Lordy this game is adorable!I am a fan of Cataan, but this game is much better. The similarities really end with the hexagons. The birds and the music and the little boats and trains are just so soothing to watch. All in all there isn’t much animated, but that helps you focus on the puzzle.  The devs say it doesn’t include strategy, trading, resource management, combat or multiplayer. They basically removed everything I hated about city builders! I mean, I don’t mind the last two but you get what you get. I cannot WAIT for creative mode to come out! There is still competition cause I really do need to learn to catch my four friends who got this and now take great pleasure in their higher scores. I enjoy puzzles, but I’m not very good at them. This was super fun without scoring high. Every time I play I will learn more, and do better. Every so often you get really intent on the puzzle, but then the birds chirp and you zoom out and look at the little town and just… all your tension goes away. Hope you try it!

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: A relaxing, beautiful, and surprisingly challenging puzzle game about building a countryside.  A great game if you love those kind of build-as-long-as-you-can games.  Even for Early Access, the game is fully playable, merely lacking extras.Dorfromantik is NOT about romancing Tim Conway's famous character Dorf.  Sorry.The game's core loop is simple.1) you have a pile of procedural tiles with grassland, train tracks, rivers, forests, houses, etc.2) Line them up to match as many sides as possible to get points.3) Some tiles provide quests to connect as many lands types, perhaps with limits or to be "closed" off.4) These quests provide points and more tiles.5) You may find quests you can connect to to trigger them.6) Quests grant more points and tiles.7) You unlock various tiles and achievements.That's it.  But the game is deceptively simple when it's often complex - more than it may seem, and for some more than may seem relaxing.As you  play, you start discovering a variety of possible strategies and complex situations.  Do you take a quick win on a quest to create a space you can't fill later?  Do you line up as many ideal connections to gain a few points or complete quests?  Will that river tile interfere where your railroad tile may go?  If you obsess over the game, you can obsess a lot.The game is also well-presented.  Lovely graphics, relaxing music, easy controls, a pleasant attitude.It's easy to compare this game to Islanders - another lovely puzzle game - but it has a different feel.  This is more puzzle-like alignment than zoning.  But if Islanders scratched an itch, you should buy this.So who's it for?* If you like alignment-puzzle games and path-building you'll almost certainly like it.* Did you like games of build-your-own lands?  This might be for you - it's that in puzzle form!* If you like puzzle games in general, it may be for you, though the random nature might frustrate you.Overall a great game and it's hard to believe it's Early Access.  Mostly what it's missing is some extra features, but the core game is solid.

_childDocuments_.review: A very chill solo infinite Carcassone-like game with great music and pretty aesthetic. It can get a little glitchy at times, like undo's breaking locking me out until I restart. But it retains the game state pretty consistently, so I've not had too much trouble.Updated (~133 hours):I haven't had any further lockouts for quite some time now, the game has been completely stable. The game's longevity is found in its Award system which keeps me from purely seeking higher score games, I hope to perfect this game this year. Truly up there for me in on my list of chill side games that keep challenging me at every level, much like Into the Breach, Inscryption, They Are Billions (only "chill" cause you can pause it,) and Roguebook.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game! I found myself playing for hours, staying up way too late just having to finish one more layout, trying to best my previous scores, find new tile pieces, unlock new biomes, etc... Each play through is different. You learn as you go along, setting yourself up for a better chance of prolonged success each time. It's so relaxing and also surprisingly challenging if you are looking to make the most of each play through. I love watching the trains, boats, and wildlife, and seeing new biomes unveil themselves, or communities grow. It's rewarding to build giant forest areas or fill in all of the sections of a water path. And then we have the art style, gorgeous, simple, quiet, yet striking. I love it! I highly recommend this game to anyone looking to enjoy a calm, relaxing game night.

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing, atmospheric, beautiful. This game is perfect, if you are looking for something very, very, very specific.If you are looking for a game that is "fun" I don't think that this would fit the description for many people. It is a puzzle game that isn't really all that much of a puzzle. You have fields, farms, forests, and village tiles that will only give you points if you connect them to tiles the same type. Then you have rails and rivers, that can only be attached (at certain angles) to tiles of the same type.That is it really. Connect them perfectly on all six sides and you will get extra bonus points and more tiles to keep building with. Honestly, combined with the in-game music, or your own soothing tunes, this can be a really calming experience.I would recommend it, but again, only to a certain type of person who is looking for a very specific gaming, almost meditative, experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Sure the game is pretty relaxing and zen-like played casually, however if you're trying to beat your high score and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pieces just wont fit the way you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ need them to because you've gotten like a billion of those useless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ train track junctions and the trees on all sides tile that would let you complete 3 quests at once seems to have gone to the other dimension and hang out with the line piece from tetris it can be a little frustrating as well.For anyone wondering Dorfromantik is a weirdly named building / strategy game where you draw a tile from a pool and have to place and rotate it so it ideally matches on all 6 sides - trees to trees, houses to houses, water to water etc etc. Matching on one side only is 10 points, getting a perfect fit is 60 plus an added card to the pool so you can keep building bigger and bigger. This game is the definition of easy to learn, difficult to master. Mixing up this formula are quests, either to build certain types of land bigger, or to close off segments that are already large. Completing a quest awards 5 cards so they're essential to progress, however quest requirements scale with what you've built already so it becomes a pretty interesting and in-depth balancing act between building well enough to score high points but keeping segments of your build contained and separated so the quest requirements don't blow out of proportion. It's an unusual and interesting deep layer mechanic that pairs beautifully to what goes on at the surface, making this game deceptively complicated. Cracking past 15k or so on the scoreboard requires big brain times.

_childDocuments_.review: I like Dorfromantik for the most part. It's really meditative when you get in the flow, and the music is calming.For some reason I thought there would be levels, but it's just one main level where you try to beat your high score (plus a creative mode, too, which is nice).There will be quests and requirements that get you thinking about tile placement and how to achieve better scores. You'll get better as you practice.In the menu you will also see challenges you can work towards as you play the game. You can get new tiles/skins by completing them. They are linked in with the Steam achievements. There are base challenges such as "place 250 tiles in total" and "gain a highscore of 10,000". But the other challenges you need to unlock.This is where I feel a bit iffy. To unlock a new challenge, a pre-placed tile will appear on the board, slightly further out. You then have to build up to that point to "uncover" that tile. It will have its own quest which you must fulfil to add the challenge to your menu.These extra challenges will be things like "score two perfect placements at once" or "build a forest with at least 250 trees". In my opinion, these should already be unlocked from the get-go. It feels weird to have to obtain the challenge card first - especially if you've already done some of these requirements! I don't know, I just like getting achievements without stipulations...That aside, it's a good puzzle game. It's pretty to look at and my favourite part is the different biome tiles which give you different colours across the board.I'll keep playing for sure. I recommend this game on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Easy to learn, a lifetime to master is a saying that applies to this Carcassonne-like puzzle game.A number of the reviews focus on the aesthetics, and though it is an element, it's not the core of this game. You can build a board to be beautiful if you want, but it has little to do with the scoring system.The mechanical core of this game lies in the infinite complexity that comes with the fact that if you want to play to score big, every single tile is a source for hefty deliberation and the potential joy or alternatively dismay, when you find that it does or doesn't fit the board you're making. And not only do you want it to fit on all the sides you connect, but you also want future tiles to fit on ALL sides without really knowing exactly what tiles will come. Jeez! On top of that you also have to consider all your quests, which ones you want to pursue and how, and which ones to ditch and how. The result of these considerations determine how many tiles you get to play with and how much you'll score with each tile. Once you get into this (perfect placement) you're going to get hooked, IF you have the patience for this kind of thing. These are not all the elements in the game, but it's the essential ones.I recommend you start by reading an external explanation of the scoring system and some general strategy. It's not complicated, you'll learn these mechanics and guidelines in 5-10 minutes. Once that's done you're ready to make your choices (which IS complicated) and puzzle your creation, potentially until you die of old age because the replayability is through the roof here.Needless to say, it's a thing of beauty for patient people who enjoy deliberation. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Grudging thumbs up - more 50:50.Game's relaxing, if you liked Islanders, it's more of a similar thing.The music's great, exactly what you'd expect, and the mini animations for the boats + trains chugging along their own little paths is p cute. There's obviously been a great deal of care put into the game.But I have a bone to pick:The randomness of the pieces you receive coupled with the restrictions on the "quests" you fulfill to gain more parts leaves far too much to rng. Some of the quests are of the "n+" type and others are "n" - that is, exactly n things must be linked to that piece or the quest fails. There's a certain level of strategy around planning your resources, but ultimately this splits your resource pool into groupings of "many" and "a few" without any concrete indication of what you'll actually need. If you split resources too thinly, you won't be able to complete the "n+" types, which increase requirement as the game progresses, but you'll also run out of parts if you forego the "only n" types since quest completion is what generates new batches of tiles. Now cascade this over multiple types of tiles and you've soon a messy clusterfsck which becomes less of a relaxing hamlet building experience and more of an exercise in frustration and sameness as you try to minmax placement to ensure you actually complete the quests.Removing the "only n" types would solve this frustration but I guess the devs intended it as another layer of depth or something idk. It's just not very fun. Particularly since you have no control over what parts are generated and often you'll end games with 5-6 active quests and just no tiles that can be used to complete them.

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik is a delightful gem of a game that has truly captured my heart. If you're seeking a relaxing and visually stunning experience, look no further because this game is an absolute masterpiece.First and foremost, the artwork and design in Dorfromantik are simply breathtaking. The hand-drawn landscapes are so charming and picturesque that you'll often find yourself just gazing at the scenery. The attention to detail and the vibrant, calming colors create a tranquil atmosphere that's perfect for unwinding.The gameplay is easy to grasp, yet it offers a surprising depth of strategy. The concept of placing hexagonal tiles to build a pastoral landscape is both intuitive and creative. You'll quickly find yourself engrossed in the challenge of creating the most beautiful and harmonious world possible. The game strikes a perfect balance between being relaxing and engaging, making it suitable for both casual players and those who enjoy more in-depth, thought-provoking experiences.The relaxing soundtrack complements the gameplay beautifully. It enhances the tranquil ambiance and is just a joy to listen to while you immerse yourself in the world of Dorfromantik. It's a game that encourages you to slow down, take your time, and appreciate the simple pleasures of life.One of the most appealing aspects of Dorfromantik is its endless mode. There's no rush or time pressure, and you can play at your own pace, creating your dream landscape without limitations. This design choice allows for a highly personalized and meditative experience, making it the perfect game to unwind with after a long day.Dorfromantik's replayability is impressive as well. Each new game offers a fresh opportunity to experiment with different tile placements, develop new strategies, and improve your high score. It's a game that you can return to time and time again without it ever feeling repetitive.In a world filled with fast-paced, high-stress games, Dorfromantik is a breath of fresh air. It's a peaceful, engaging, and visually stunning experience that will soothe your soul and provide hours of enjoyment. If you're looking for a game that helps you relax and appreciate the simple beauty of creating your own idyllic world, Dorfromantik is a must-play. It's a true work of art in the gaming world, and I can't recommend it enough!

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't review Early Access games, but this has been such a gem that I want to help spread the word on it. You know when people ask those questions like "What's your downtime/chillaxing game?" This is another one to add to your list.Dorfromantik is a puzzle game in the guise of a citybuilder. You start with 40 tiles and have to strategically place them on the board to get the highest score you can. You get points by connecting things together like buildings, trees, and rivers. But 40 tiles can go by pretty quickly. Luckily you can earn more tiles to make your world and score bigger. One of the easiest ways to do this is to complete quests. Some of your tiles will have a number hovering above it. These are quests you can complete and they start off simple like "connect 5 houses together" and upon completing them, you get more tiles. As your world grows, so do the quests so you'll have to develop your own strategy to maximize your points and size.While there is a global leaderboard for competitive players, I personally just enjoy the calming nature of the game. The music is beautiful to listen to, the tiles and pieces look great as you build, and the overall feel of the game is perfect for when you need some downtime. You earn new tiles as you play, so there's always something to look forward to as you get better and better at the game.I think my only gripe I have with the game so far and many other players is the lack of an "undo" button. As you world gets bigger and bigger, it gets a lil harder to move around the screen and sometimes you accidentally place a tile down that you didn't mean to and now your whole run can be ruined (this has happened to me a couple of times). An undo button would be a nice addition for when this happens. Being that it is Early Access, this can be added later and I hope the devs consider it.Final Verdict? If you are looking for a nice, relaxing, and charming puzzle game, then you need this in your library. I look forward to getting better and better at the game and making more bigger and better worlds as I play. This game is a gem and definitely deserves to be your next downtime game. Thanks for reading!

But quality of life (like an undo button or a mulligan) would be nice benefits. So, SHOULD YOU BUY Dorf Romantik right now, in this state?Maybe.I love these kind of games, I can just sit back, throw on a video and let my mind wander aimlessly as I put down little tiles and clap my hands, but other people may get annoyed with the RNG and other factors that are difficult to predict which makes the game somewhat "unfair" as you just get shafted by not having the right tiles, or just odd where you're building these long strands of railway or rivers going nowhere because you keep drawing them.So, it's your call, do you want a game to vibe to, something reminiscent of Grizzly's Islanders or do you want a "fair and balanced" game where you can get the highest score possible without praying to RNGesus? If you want the first, go for it, it'll only get better, if you want the latter, than wait on it until they add MORE stuff to the mix.
