_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, this game (to me, at least) seemed pretty similar to Islanders, when it really isn't. Islanders is a relaxed city-builder, while this game is much more akin to an endless mode to a puzzle game. That being said, it's still relaxing to play, and I'd highly recommend it if you enjoy puzzle games or want a game to chill with when you're low-energy.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Quite addicting puzzle game. In theory, you can always just play a few turns and return to your run later. But the "just one more turn" addiction strikes hard.A nice quality of life improvement would be to offer slightly more convenient first turns. In 90% of the games, you are forced to play a bad turn within the first few cards (i.e. unfitting borders or a flood of water and rail tiles), which makes it mandatory to restart the run if you are aiming for a high score. That's obviously not a big deal because restarting the game costs like 5 seconds. But a more polished game would come up with a smarter solution here. Maybe having a multicolored starting tile (e.g. a random distribution of 3x meadows, 1x corn, 1x village, 1x forest) and suspending water+rail tiles for the first 3 turns would already be sufficient.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik is chill and cozy with just the right amount of dopamine hits per minute. It's the definition of easy to pick up and hard to master.The tile artwork is gorgeous and they slot together pleasingly. Movement and rotations are crisp and responsive.I appreciate that there are lots of little unlockable goodies like little carrots on the end of a string. It has the same kind of time compression Civilization does, where you start playing when the sun's out and you snap back to reality 12 hours later in the pitch darkness.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: So much fun, I suck at this for now but I'll definitely get better. It's really interesting and there are endless ways to set up your township and turn it into a sprawling landscape. I can't wait for more content to be added but I would like to suggest a possible feature to the devs for the future. There are often times I make the mistake of placing a tile, I'm not sure if I just over looked it or not but is it possible to have a undo option for maybe between 3 or 5 tiles? Or some kind of reward where you can unlock the undo option by hitting a particular mile stone and you get to accumulate a number of undo. Perhaps if you undo a tile it subtracts points or resets milestones. I'm not sure if that make sense. Either way this game is quite alluring and I'm enjoying myself a lot.  Give it a try if you enjoy puzzle games, building and chill environments.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love Dorfromantik!  It's so simple to play, I can just sit and chill to play when I need to relax, yet it doesn't feel repetitive or boring.   I love strategy games and especially love when I can find the kind I can play without straining my brain when I'm just needing something to do to destress when I'm feeling tired.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik is one of those rare gems of a game that seems to do everything right: Offer an extremely simple basic game idea that allows for gradually intensifying difficulty, give it an easily understandable visual style and gameplay mechanic, add challenges that make sense and seem to grow naturally with your ability, and add flavor by playing with the style, look and feel of the game.This is one of the best games on Steam, period.

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely little game that is almost worth playing in its current state.Dorfromantik calls itself "relaxing" and "meditative" but is so restrictive in its puzzle elements that all your games will be cut painfully short unless you stress over every single tile placement from the start. The only two ways to receive additional tiles are to get "perfect placements" where all 6 of a tile's sides are compatible with their respective adjacent tiles and to complete quests, which require varying amounts of a specific kind of tile or object (like houses) to be connected, and both are structured to not encourage but  careful play just to sustain your tile income and stay in the game.Presenting a challenge like this is fine, but requiring the player to to weigh the potential location of every tile on  spot on the board at  available angle of rotation against 1) their surroundings 2) your next few tiles 3) the many, many little permutations of each individual possible future tile and 4) water and rail tiles which place hard restrictions from the start is not relaxing. It's exhausting, and not in a good way.To the devs: in my opinion, relaxing quest requirements substantially for the first 10-15k points would be a good starting point to allow for much longer sessions without stressing over much before the 380+ forest and 17+ rails quests show up while still not allowing infinite games. Either that or a separate mode (NOT creative) with relaxed quest requirements and increased tile rewards to smooth out the challenge over a much longer session.Rivers and rails suck. I don't know what to do to make them better. They're restrictive and end up creating horrible nonsensical patchwork terrain that's anything but pleasant to look at. I am NEVER happy to see a river or rail.Also, that "game over" sound is anything but relaxing and calm.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This game offers strategy, without constraints: No time limits, no resource acquisition, no PVP, no PVE, no pay-2-pay. When you buy this game, you receive a complete product. The main strategy is this: Laying tiles the best way possible that allows your tile-stack to grow. Overall, I give this game somewhere between B and A-.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big city builder fan but, despite countless tries, I just don't think Dorfromantik is a good one. It gets very dull and boring, rinse and repeat mechanics with no upgrades, and the most exciting thing imo is being able to change the colour of the trees. It feels more like a puzzle game than a city builder, and the hype around it confuses me. Much better products out there than this one
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and relaxing game, it somehow feels very satisfying to create giant forests in the middle of the map. It's only a little frustrating when you get rail pieces or river pieces and can't connect them anywhere - but well, that's how the gameplay works. But that doesn't make it any less good. Recommended to anyone who wants an easy to learn / hard to master (which is not required to have fun) relaxing game.

_childDocuments_.review: There has been a renaissance of city builders recently. I suppose in this case it’s more of a “world builder,” but the result is similar. Of course, this is just as much a mild puzzle/strategy game as well. While the premise, design, music, and overall goal is to mellow out and enjoy the ride, there’s still an underlying level of challenge to keep you coming back for more even when it’s 4:00 AM. That’s what makes this early access title worth checking out even before the full launch.Abbreviated Review: Dorfromantik is a simple game at its surface. All you really do is place hexagonal tiles beside one another and collect points. However, there’s a bit more going on underneath the hood. The tiles you place are limited and if you run out, it’s game over. You can get more with special pieces that prompt you to connect them to tiles of the same type. Each tile can represent several different types of environments at the same time, so one side of the hex may be a river, another a forest, a third and fourth side covered by houses, and so on. Piecing these together cohesively takes just enough planning and strategy to keep your brain active while you drift into the experience.As the world you’re building comes together, it’s easy to stop and admire the beauty of the gently muted colors of crop fields, quaint villages, and expansive green forests. Considering my haphazard placement, it’s impressive how cohesive it ends up looking and feeling. When you combine this with the soft ambient sounds and placid soundtrack, the whole experience is perfect for getting lost in a trance for hours and losing track of everything. If the auditory experience wasn’t so pleasant, I’d say it was a great game for listening to other music or podcasts as well, but so far I just want to stick with what I’m hearing.While the core loop of aligning your hexes to gain more tiles and slowly raise your high score is enjoyable, there are also quests that make the game a little more dynamic. You only get three at most per session, so if you complete one or all of them, that’s all you’ll see until you run out of tiles. It seems the game is geared toward limited sessions, so I’ve never even finished all three available quests on one map. They include basic things like building a certain number of forest tiles or more complex tasks like placing several “perfect connections.” Most of these continue between sessions, so it’s not often required to complete them in a single world.Finishing these quests will unlock new types of tiles and skins for previously unlocked tiles. New tiles may function almost identically to others, like a clock tower that is essentially just a standard house tile, but they each seem to have some unique aspect that makes them useful. For instance, clock towers usually give you a chance to get more tiles when properly connected. Some new tiles, however, have more unique functionality like connecting dissimilar pieces. One is a “Water Train Station” that can bridge the gap between streams and train tracks – which can be invaluable when things get a little messy toward the end of the game.There is also a progression aspect in the map itself. As you build into the void, ghostly hexes may appear that you can build your way to and unlock. Once you get to them, they’ll show the new unique tile and display a requirement (much like other tile-gaining hexes) to connect them to a certain number of a specific type of tile. When you complete that little mini-quest, you’ll unlock the new piece and have it added to your randomly assorted stack of future tiles.It seems like Dorfromantik has a great start in early access. I’m not entirely sure what future content is being developed outside of the “creative mode” listed in the “new game” menu. However, even as it sits, it’s worth the price. The replayability is outstanding and it’s hard to put down even when you do hit the game over screen. Yet, there are a few quirks worth noting.The first and most prevalent one is the difficulty to discern what is on each side of a tile. Sometimes it looks like a side is, for instance, a forest, but the forest doesn’t quite extend to that side. If you’re careful, this isn’t much of an issue, but it can easily be a problem if you’re hasty in placement. Even more so down the line when you’re trying to put pieces near already placed tiles.I also have a more personal issue in that I sometimes feel like I’m playing the game wrong. I’m not sure how to explain that, but it seems like I always get to a point and lose right before I can unlock new tiles. The game is session-oriented and not meant for gigantic maps. The scroll speed becomes painfully slow when you start to get there. Yet, I can’t help but feel like I’m missing something when it comes to keeping enough tiles toward the end of the game.The future is bright for Dorfromantik though. I plan to keep returning to the experience as more is added and hopefully unlock some cool hexagons to build my fantasy world. Maybe it’s just my environment talking, but I hope they add some rolling hills to the game. Then I can start singing Country Roads…

_childDocuments_.review: Its a cute wee game, with a simple unlock/progress checks. Scratches an itch. The artwork is cute, the music is relaxing but limited. Its essentially 6 way chess where you can work towards a simple goal - like create a forest for the deers. I've played 15 times now and rarely get over 15000 points. I think the more you unlock the easier it becomes with certain randomised pieces. I try to fail on purpose and it just keeps going on tediously with minimum satisfaction. Its okay game, solid 7/10. _childDocuments_.review: I'm really glad I gave Dorfromantik a try. As someone with pretty high-functioning ADHD, it's always been hard for me to "shut off" my brain - not to stop thinking, but to focus on the here and now (sort of like mindfulness) - but with this game, I find I'm able to without any trouble. Dorfromantik has just enough challenge that I don't zone out, but I focus on it and stop thinking about anything else, and it's really relaxing. Not only is it a ton of fun (as well as fulfilling, knocking out task after task) but it's a great way for me to wind down in the evenings before I go to bed. The art is charming, as is the music, and I would definitely recommend it to anybody who wants a nice puzzle game to help them relax.

_childDocuments_.review: This review comes in three parts:If you're in the same position I was a few weeks ago, you've just clicked on the page for this game you've never heard of because you thought the game looked pretty. I cannot overstate the importance of the beautiful design in this game, though I suspect is speaks for itself. Every little world you build will be absolutely adorable, to the point where you'll want to spend a few minutes looking at it from every angle when you lose before you move onto the next game. I have friends who were content to just sit in my room and watch me play even before they learned the rules. Even if you don't want to go all in on trying to get the highest score possible, you can always treat Dorfromantik like a mobile game you just play brainlessly while you listen to music or a podcast or something (not to discount the beautiful soundtrack!). Quite delightfully, the game incentivizes you to do things that look nice anyway, so playing to make a nice looking village doesn't ultimately feel that far removed from playing optimally anyway!But what if you really do want to aim for the highest score? Admittedly, I'm not the most skilled village builder (my current high score is around ~20k), but I do feel like I'm getting a hang of the strategies. I won't try to explain my approach to the game here because I'm sure other people have already posted much better ideas, but I will say that the process of trial and error to improve my score really has felt rewarding. I've intentionally avoided reading strategy guides/watching other people play the game, because I've really enjoyed figuring everything out for myself. The game only takes a few minutes to learn, but thirty hours later, I'm still finding ways to raise my score, bit by bit. I've yet to play more than two or three rounds in a row without breaking my high score, so I never really feel like I'm getting stuck.While this game definitely challenges you, part of it's draw is that it can be so mindless. If you're putting 100% of your brain power into getting a high score and optimizing your play, you're going to be less than 100% satisfied, because that's not the point. You can focus in really hard and spend minutes on every tile if you want to, but if you do that, you'll probably end up getting a high score in the hundreds of thousands without ever appreciating the beautiful world you've made. Of course it's a little ironic for me to get on my high horse and talk about how the game isn't the most strategically interesting it could be while I'm stuck around #15,000 on the leaderboard, but my point isn't necessarily that the game is easy, more that I find that the game is significantly less fun if you're really trying to play optimally. Obviously your mileage might vary, but I'm a person who usually likes to optimize every game and play perfectly in any way I can, but I feel like I just don't have as much fun in this game when my only focus is winning. I can spend five minutes on each tile and I play a lot better than I normally do, but I get so bored.That said, if you're not playing optimally but you still want to get a high score, the randomness can occasionally feel a little frustrating. Every round that I get down towards the bottom of my stack, but I also have a lot of quests I'm close to finishing. All I need is for that last tile to have some trees, a house, even just an empty side so I can place it next to this other tile to get a perfect placement and... it's a railroad. Of course I understand that it's my own fault, it's not like I played perfectly, or even like I got particularly unlucky, but it's just a fact of how the game is set up that once you get a hang of the rules, nearly every game ends not because you made a bad decision on your last move, but because you drew a bad tile on your last turn. The devs have already said they plan to add some of these, and I am not a game designer by any means, but I still feel like there's some small changes that could improve the game a lot for me. I should take a moment to say that while I do think there are some features that are glaringly missing, this game feels surprisingly polished for a game in early access. I've found no glitches, and there's already a lot in the game to make every round feel different. That said, there's more I would like to see:-Undo button! In my opinion, this is an absolute must for the game. It feels like every other round that I mess up my village because I've accidentally placed a tile in an awkward spot. Every way I've thought to implement the undo button does feel clunky to me, but that's why I don't make video games. I'll take the undo button no matter how weirdly it needs to be implemented—it's just too painful to feel like I've screwed myself every time my finger slips.-Some indicator of perfect placement. If you're unaware, surrounding a tile on all sides by matching tiles awards a new tile in your stack, and these "perfect" tiles are really helpful (if not absolutely necessary) for improving your high score. The problem is, it's not always obvious when you're about to score a perfect placement. There are some completely unintuitive mechanics that I've still yet to figure out (I think lakes next to empty edges count as perfect, but only if the tile with the empty edge has no water on it, but water train stations absolutely need to be connected to rivers/railroads to count as perfect? Correct me if I'm wrong—I genuinely can't tell). It would be nice to have some explanation of these rules somewhere, but it would be even more helpful to just have some simple visual indicator like a little glow around a tile if you're about to perfectly surround it.-More "classic" (i.e. not creative mode, but I'm also excited for that) game modes. I would really like to see some twists on the game, even if they're really simple. Something like a mode where there are only rivers and railroads, or a mode where you can't gain new tiles but you try to get the highest score possible with what you have. I'm not sure exactly what I want (my ideas are probably terrible, but I feel like there must be some small edits that could add a new challenge), but it just feels like there must be lots of subtle variations on the main game mode that could add a lot of new life to the game. I don't expect this any time soon, but I think it would be really great to have a few small spinoff modes.Don't let my long, rambling negative sections alarm you: this game is amazing, and it already feels like a finished product even though there's so much more to come. I feel challenged by the mechanics, but also mesmerized by the beautiful design—I can zone in and feel like I'm playing a regular puzzle/strategy game, but I can also zone out and spend hours just ignoring my quests and just trying to create a cute little world. There's certainly more I hope to see from this game, but the only reason my hopes are so high for the future of this game is that it feels so great already. Even for all my frustrations about how I feel like I can't enjoy this game quite as much when I really try for the highest score, I've still found my own very satisfying middle ground between completely ignoring my score and agonizing over every move, and I'm sure you could too.Ultimately, this game is just too adorable to not love. I've gotten lost in it countless times, only to look up from my computer a couple hours and a thousand tiles later to realize I have to sprint off to a meeting. The developers have done a fantastic job creating the relaxing atmosphere they set out to create. Dorfromantik is a game I really feel motivated to play more of and get better at, yet I never feel too bummed when I lose; I just take a few screenshots of my world, and move on to build a new one.

It's only as complicated as you want to play, super calm and peaceful experience, great art style and chill music. 9.5/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually don't care how it's categorised, It very neatly balances between the puzzle genre trappings of games like Triple Town with the delightful trimmings of a city-builder. No matter how you like to think about its categorisation, it is a . It balances so neatly between playing for the beauty of the landscape you create and playing for the objectives of getting to play more. it's very rare to come across a game that balances those things so neatly but Dorfromantik does so, all the while singing relaxing tunes to create such a zen experience.It builds on the storied legacy of Carcassonne to show another dynamic to tile laying games but it also scratches that itch from other puzzle/city-builders like Islanders. I can't help but heartily recommend the game to those who love a good puzzle challenge. But also to those who just want to relax alongside the beautiful visuals that you create. For everyone in between, Dorfromantik balances on that precipice between aesthetics and strategy expertly!

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik has been on my mind since it launched in Early Access, and let me tell you, it’s hands down my favourite time-killer in my massive library of games.It’s super easy to jump into, doesn’t bombard you with a million things to do, relaxed to the max – but here’s the kicker: It’s surprisingly deep. I mean, it depends on what you’re expecting, but bear with me.Dorfromantik doesn’t have fancy gimmicks or make use of confusing elements. Nope, it keeps it simple and sweet, hooking you with gameplay that’s consistently enjoyable. Just place your tiles on the board and try to score as many points as you can – and here’s the deep part, I suppose: Points vary based on placement, like, what you placed it next to, how many of the same tiles are connected, how many of the tiles next to this one has matching corners. And on top of that, you got little mini-quests that need fulfilling in order to bring in more tiles for you to place, and more tiles = higher score. As a bonus, you unlock new types of tiles by finishing achievements.But even with all that, it’s the kind of game that lets you genuinely relax – from the relaxed gameplay loop, to the pretty visuals, and the soothing musical score. Honestly. While the game can be considerably more involved if you want to chase score, at no point does it force you to do this. It even helps you along with where to place tiles.  Oh, yeah, the friggin’ music! Let me tell you, it’s like the musical equivalent of, well, whatever truly satisfying thing you prefer. For me, a hot cup of instant coffee with a splash of milk and an episode of The Wire. What? I’m a simple man.In the world of casual games, Dorfromantik is the one that shines the brightest. It’s got an undeniable charm. It’s a bit like Civilization, not in terms of gameplay, mind you, but in that ‘just one more turn’ kind of way. You’ll find yourself stuck in it for way longer than you intended. If you’re in the mood for a casual/puzzle game that’s the absolute chilliest something can be, do yourself a favour and dive into Dorfromantik.Trust me, you won’t regret it.Read this review and many more @

_childDocuments_.review: Played it for a couple of hours, but it very quickly became monotonous and boring.Since you have limited tiles you need to complete missions by matching up certain types of tiles to get new ones, and eventually I just sat rotating every tile to see how I could maximize my chances of completing missions and score, at which point it just felt like a chore. Or I sat waiting for some rare railroad or river tile to stop my map looking like a snaking mess.Personally it felt like placing dominoes ad infinitum, but if you enjoy the mindless repetition and looking at, potentially, pretty landscapes it might be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy this game. The variety of puzzle possibilities ist fun, the design is very cute and the overall look relaxes me greatly.As others have pointed out, the fact that the amount of tiles is limited and the need to gain more tiles by completing quests can be stressful, but I personally don't mind the challenge of it. And challenging it is! I'm still missing 9 Achievments and haven't reached highscores above 25k, but I can see my own learning curve which I love.For those looking for something more low stakes I'd suggest to wait until the full version drops with an open game option. Generally worth the few bucks, without a doubt!

_childDocuments_.review: It's like if Carcassonne was single-player.  It's super chill and relaxing to play.You get a stack of tiles.  You get points for connecting the objects on the tiles.  Sometimes the tiles will have an objective like "connect X houses" or "connect exactly Y water tiles".  Completing the objectives adds more tiles to your stack.  Repeat!  It's one of those games where it's very easy to lose track of time.  Civ has "one more turn", Dorfromantik has "one more tile".As far as Early Access is concerned, the game is pretty much done but they've been pushing bug fixes and quality of life updates.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like puzzle games or want to challenge yourself. This is your puzzle game. It's relaxing and charming. _childDocuments_.review: Games is a good time killer. My criticism would be there's very little progression. What I mean is I am continuing to unlock goals/rewards simply by achieving the same 15-20k score - and this sort of seems by design. The unlocks don't allow you to greatly improve on your score which I think is a fairly missed opportunity. I expected, with the goals/rewards, to earn tiles that would actually have significant impact towards progression. Reality is I'm just playing the game over again never getting past my average score.Or I'm just useless and hit my peak with this game, lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute and utterly relaxing (until the tiles start running low!!) strategy/puzzle game. The goal of the game is to build as extensively as possible through strategic tile placement before running out of tiles. You score points placing tiles down - the more edges your adjacent tiles share, the better. As your village grows, you can complete small quests to unlock more tiles. Every round is unique and challenging, while the atmosphere brings maximum chill. Players can enjoy sitting down for an extended session, or to play on the side.Totally worth the $10. Good luck creating your magnificent village! 👍🏻
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This is a relaxing builder/puzzle game. It's good to zone out and just match your tiles and watch a beautiful landscape grow. I like that you earn more tiles by completing the challenges and that the game does have an end when you run out of tiles. The creative mode is super nice to have if you really like the landscape you've built and want to continue adding to it or complete it when you run out of tiles.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Do you enjoy Carcassonne, but think the most fun part of the game is when it's your turn? Did you enjoy Mini Metro? Are you fond of an occasional, low-stakes game of Mahjong? Are you looking for something fun and casual, while still wanting some light strategy? This game is ridiculously enjoyable, super chill, and has some great Civ and Rise of Industry vibes while absolutely being the right wavelength to play on a long Sunday afternoon parked on the couch with a beer. I bought this thinking "yeah, could be fun" and here I am, five hours later, furiously researching how to get Steam to work on my TV because I NEED to be on my couch right now playing this on my big TV with a beer.

_childDocuments_.review: For years now I have stoutly resisted the siren call of the Eurogame, standing aloof and immune to its perfumed blandishments and honeyed solicitations -- and now it appears that I've fallen victim to some sort of Trojan horse of a Carcassonne-like solitaire that could very well rudely disrupt my sleeping pattern and cripple my seating posture. And I'm perfectly okay with that.

_childDocuments_.review: Dorfromantik stands out with its undeniable charm, offering a particularly sympatic gaming experience. The clever management of tiles to create picturesque landscapes is simply incredible. This game manages to capture a relaxing atmosphere, inviting players to get lost in the construction of bucolic villages.The magic of Dorfromantik lies in its balance between simplicity and depth. The addictive gameplay mechanics encourage extending sessions, as each placed tile contributes to the artistic expansion of your virtual world. This strategic management quickly becomes a genuine ludic pleasure.In summary, Dorfromantik distinguishes itself with its harmonious combination of factors, creating a gaming experience that surpasses expectations. It is a title that captivates with its simplicity while offering a deeply rewarding and engaging experience for fans of relaxing games.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the chill minimalist buildery of games like Islanders and Mini Metro, this might be a good game for you. You can totally play this like that and gradually get better as you go while chillaxing.If you like strategy games where every placement matters and opens or closes possibilities, this might also be a good game for you.This is kinda like Loop Hero in the sense there's actually more depth to the strategy than there first appears to be - not quite to Loop Hero's level, granted, since that game has a ton of interwoven systems - and that you can either play it as a way to keep your hands busy and turn your mind off, or take your time and try to be as strategic as possible.Anyway, yeah, it's pretty great. _childDocuments_.review: LOVING this game sooooo much right now. Perfect game to relax and chill with. The world building with puzzle aspect is shockingly engaging. I find myself getting so excited when the little challenges are completed. And the music! Oh just love the relaxing music. This game scratches a bunch of happy itches and is quite the mood booster.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the most relaxing and rewarding games I've played. Even if you run out of pieces and have to start a new set, you don't feel frustrated, but happy to make a new one. It's simple, your progress is saved between sessions and there are plenty of achievements. Good for a lazy day where you don't feel like murdering anyone but still want some neurons to be active.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly calming and enjoyable game.There isn't much to it and that's the joy of it, whilst I will say it was confusing at first to understand the 'mission' aspect of the game, once you do you'll be creating satisfying worlds in no time.There is just enough progression to keep you attached throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really fun and calming, the only goal is to complete simple objectives to get more tiles to place down, otherwise you can just keep building a little world.I can't wait until they release the sandbox mode so I can build with unlimited pieces.Edit: It has been a while already since they released the sandbox mode, but it is very fun, I love making spiraling patterns with river/lake pieces. _childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: All the reviews that say this game is charming and calming are 100% correct, and that's how I experienced this game for a good 5 hours. And then I started trying to play well...If you want it to be, this game is low key one of the highest cognitive load games I've ever played, and it's immensely satisfying. If you love board games and sometimes just wish you could play an amazing board game by yourself, this is it full stop. Play to relax, or play to challenge yourself, or anything in between. Absolutely worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes I get overwhelmed by my game library, I want to play everything and all at once! A lot of games - I cannot just launch and play for 15-30 minutes as they require more concentration and time investment, and thus comes anxiety. But, not with Dorfromantic, I absolutely adore this game, it has no pressure, it has no limits, it doesn`t ask for any long-term "relationship", it is just there. So I launch it, I play it, I unwind, and I close it as an accomplished man.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be challenging to beat your previous high score or unlock the next tile types, yet it is also so incredibly relaxing.  It reminds me of taking all your Carcassonne tiles and trying to make an imaginary land.  The music is soothing and when you make a beautiful world, there is a feeling of accomplishment.  I thoroughly enjoy this game and recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's the perfect level of chill and engaging. It's simple to grasp, but also has the ability to be complex. You can kind of choose what experience you want to have: do you want to just place tiles and make it pretty and aesthetically pleasing and not have to focus on much? Do you want to really focus on knocking out the quests and objectives to get the highest score and expand as much as possible?I also love that I can walk away to attend to real life or just quit at any time and come right back to it. 10/10 would absolutely recommend you get this if you enjoy cozy games.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: Dorf Romantik gets a tepid thumbs-up from someone who's played quite a bit of the game; not because the game is bad, but because the developers refuse to implement simple optional controls and visuals for the visually and physically impaired. There are simple quality of life options users asked for back when the game released that still haven't been implemented to this day. Other visual cues the devs finally did add - such as tile-edge match highlighting - are very difficult to see.Overall, the game is fun and relaxing, unless you need to strain your eyes and/or can't constantly hold down the left-shift key for hours on end.So thumbs-up for the great concept.Thumbs-down for not even trying to accommodate accessibility needs after nearly two years of being live.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an amazing stress-reliever. The concept for the puzzle is quite simple: place tiles down to create a landscape, yet it's also very rewarding to see as the game plays out. The tiles themselves are also very nice in appearance, the houses, trees, and fields give you the image of a peaceful little world that you're sculpting.I don't find myself coming back to this game often, to be honest, but it's relaxing to jump in every once in a while and throw on some music while playing it. I recommend it to people for whom fast-paced games are not always a great stress outlet for.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I enjoyed the ~30 hours I spent with this game although I also think I'm about done with it.  (That's not really a knock - I got my money's worth)  There's some strategic depth - my scores went up significantly over each of my 5 plays, so you can definitely "get better at it" but there's not a lot of gameplay variety - I could play again but I think it would be pretty much the same thing.(Caveat: I did not try creative mode - wasn't really interested - but that could certainly be a draw for people)The strategy is a decent mix of long-term planning (how will I lay things out so I can complete future quests to keep earning tiles) and short-term optimization (especially when you get down to your last few tiles).  And if you're building well you're probably also making something that looks fairly nice (mostly)It's also very "one more turn" when I should be turning it off and going to bed.Overall, I'm glad I bought it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful, relaxing, yet strangely addictive game! Don't worry about that "Early Access" tag - this game is polished and after 8 hours I'm only about 30% of the way through the content. I have encountered zero bugs and zero issues. Full Video Review: Things I Enjoyed:+BEAUTIFUL game. The tiles are gorgeous, the sound design is lovely, and you create beautiful maps as you play.+Simple, easy to learn mechanics (with a good tutorial to teach them) that lead to a surprising variety of gameplay.+Full of smaller and larger goals to keep you engaged.+It's a puzzle game that feels like a sandbox.+Just plain relaxing. After a stressful day, sitting and playing a few rounds of Dorfromantik is really calming. Even when you lose, it's not discouraging - it just makes you want to jump right into the next round with new ideas on how to do better.Issues:-Creative mode is still in development and not available yet.-A little too addictive. It's easy to lose a lot of hours to this game without meaning to.As you can see, overall this is a definite thumbs up from me. Well worth its price, and I can't wait to see what they add to it next.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: TWO PARTER:Really disagree with most of the reviews here. I found the game frustrating, stressful, and honestly completely not the relaxing experience I hoped it would be. Do you get gorgeous vistas and peaceful music? yeah! absolutely. But the stretch goals to unlock new content seem frustratingly just out of my reach. I spend so much time checking tile placement, splitting out rails from rivers to reduce placement, and trying to dial in all the quests but despite my best efforts and plenty of skin unlocks I can't complete a single major challenge!I'm going to keep attacking this game on the good faith assumption that I suck and don't have enough practice and that I got some bad luck thrown in the mix. I'll see if I can put another update in after a few more hours.ALRIGHT well I came around to liking this game. you have to un-learn some stressful and short-sighted strategies that other games praise. I prioritized building a puzzle that fits together best, and made every other concern secondary. It's going quite well so far! this game taught me to chill out   L:-D

_childDocuments_.review: I love the relaxing vibe of this game , and the ability to play at whatever strategy level you like. Want to try for perfect placement of tiles for high scores? You can! Want to just chill and build something beautiful? Also great! The only improvement I would make would be to expand the soundtrack with more music.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very cute and relaxing but with a lot of scope for challenge if you really want a high score.The rules are simple and accessible with train tracks and rivers providing the only barriers to tile placement, but optimal placement is important if you want to go far. It really rewards thinking ahead and taking your time and is balanced well so that a game can go for a very long time if you are playing well. It has a very addictive "just one more tile" kind of a feel.It's in early access, but it's already feeling quite polished. Though I imagine that in addition to the planned sandbox mode there are hopefully some QoL features coming. I'd love an undo button just because of the number of times I've left clicked and placed a tile when I meant to right click to rotate. It'd also be nice to be able to have multiple saves, or to be able to revisit old games.Actually, on that thought, this is a really minor point but it'd be cool to see a slight frame change. Instead of saying "game over" when you run out of pieces it would be cool if it said something like "map complete". Just to emphasise that relaxing, constructive sort of feeling the game fosters.
_childDocuments_.name: Dorfromantik

_childDocuments_.review: After discovering Islanders a couple of years ago and eventually getting all achievements done and having over 200 hours played in it, I had this hunger for something similar. A game that has pretty, but simple graphics (so that I can play it on my weaker device), but still makes you sink in for hours without realizing. Dorfromantik was the answer. I’ve been playing it before it went into full release and I can say that it has been brilliant since the start, constantly improving the experience of it’s players. It’s worth every penny, whether it’s on or not on sale. If you want to have huge fun and just chill while playing a really pretty game, it’s great for you. If you want some puzzle challenges, it’s still for you. Just go buy it, dammit!

name: ROBOBEAT
detailed_description: Join our Discord About the Game Beat. The. Bot. You're Ace - a famous bounty hunter after your latest target, the eccentric robot-showman Frazzer. To find your way through his twisted techno-playground, you’ll have to master the art of shooting, wall-running, sliding, and bunny hopping, all in sync with the beat! Get ready to dance till you're dead and then suit up for the remix in rogue-like rhythm shooter ROBOBEAT. Shoot to the Beat Shoot to your own beat with the custom music feature. Simply upload & trim your track or leave it as it is in our in-game editor to auto generate beats that suit your play style. Change custom songs effortlessly in-game anytime anywhere without interruption. The feature will support .wav, .mp3, and .ogg files. Maximise your damage and shorten your cooldown time by shooting in sync. Master the art of charged shots, damage multipliers, armour piercing rounds, and more! Move to the Music You’ll want some slick moves to go with those slick new weapons. Your enemies aren’t going to wait around for you to take a dance break, so you’ve got to keep moving if you want to survive. Wall run, slide, double jump, bunny hop, and grapple hook your way through technicolour levels to give your enemies the runaround. Keep it fluid, keep it funky, and keep it moving. Rewind, Remix, Replay ROBOBEAT is a rogue-like remix. Fast forward through procedurally generated levels, equip an arsenal of finely-tuned weapons, and accompany your arsenal with a symphony of modifications. Your playstyle is on continuous shuffle, so you never know what each new run is going to bring! Will you have what it takes to break the infinite loop and stop Frazzer in his tracks? Features Make your enemies face the music with an orchestra of guns and melee weapons; Choose from a diverse playlist to find a track that suits your playstyle; Unlock new songs, weapons, and utilities as you progress through the mansion and uncover its secrets; Shoot to your own beat with the custom music feature. Feel the beat with environments and visuals that adapt to the music; Mix it up with a range of modifications to give you an extra boost; Use your smooth moves to master platforming levels. ∞ Shoot - Remix - Repeat ∞

_childDocuments_.review: Robobeat is a very good action roguelike rhythm game that I'd personally recommend. It has quite a few issues, particularly with the roguelike elements, but the FPS gameplay is  well done and makes up for its faults. I 100% the game yesterday, and I thought I'd leave a review on what I like and what I don't like about the game.Those are my thoughts on the game. As an FPS, I think it's one of the best of the genre I've played. As a Roguelike, however, it leaves a lot to be desired. I'd probably give it a solid 7/10 overall. A lot of its problems could easily be solved by a few updates or a sequel and I'd love to see this game expanded on in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: it's funi like the game overallpositive:as someone who played BPM and has couple other rhythm games, I think the rhythmic elements were incorporated well, and the automatic beat placement thing for custom songs worked well enough most times. I adore the thing where you can change the song any time.somewhat negative:I have been having an overall good experience with the game, but design-wise practically every weapon doesn't reward parrying as much as the usual headshot revolver does. As someone who can parry consistently and hit headshots, I often don't see much reason to swap off such as weapon, as the others feel somewhat gimmicky (excluding the sword, it's fun to dodge around with that thing) .For context with the ability to parry, I P-ranked P-1 on Brutal in Ultrakill. (no dice on P-2 so far though lol)When you hit a parry and have the headshot revolver equipped, you can charge it twice and fire to deal a crap ton of damage to nearly every enemy in a considerable cone around your view. It's to the point that I was able to get by through just parrying barrels and the very easy eyeballs, then pressing three buttons to deal with more than half of the wave. Compared to that, every other weapon feels underwhelming; Oftentimes, I'll replace my revolver with something else, only to realize in the very next room that my parries had lost around 60% of their effectiveness. I understand that it is by nature a skill weapon, but why must every other weapon only have a single combo where parry is involved? Their parry combos often deal either middling damage in a larger group or large damage to 1-2 enemies; It feels weak. Maybe include more combos that involve charging before parrying??Random gripes and suggestions:The dash doesn't seem to recharge often enough to be used on every other beat.^ Tying into that, please make every cooldown based on beats instead of seconds.For the custom songs, please allow us to group cassettes into albums or something. The way it is, I've got Clustertruck music being mixed up with Crypt of the Necrodancer, which makes it annoying to find the song I'm looking for.^ Also, put a place where we can describe the BPM, so I don't have to include it in the song title.Something that rewards you universally for having a beat streak.More weapons that offer a greater reward for getting a kill with them.Make the ricochet gun deal comparable damage to the headshot revolver.More interesting shop (perhaps you could purchase minor-ish stat buffs or something???)Guarantee against getting duplicate quick cooldown starting weapons (Two headshot revolvers, for example)Early-game difficult challenge rooms, like the ones in BPM where you pull a lever to summon enemies in exchange for more rewards.More transparency about what it is you're unlocking.While the movement is fine as-is, there are some mechanics that I wish were there:Slide-jumping. (._. please)More transparency on the amount of air-jumps and wall-jumps you have remaining.Some form of B-hopping, like crouch-jumping.Swinging grapple hook instead of just pulling you to a point.Shooting the ground to achieve a higher jump.More apparent stamina bar or removal of the mechanic entirely.If crouch-jumping were to be added, it would be nice if doing it out of a slam gave you a lot of horizontal velocity.Also, I like all the little beat indicators you can pick from. I like the difficulty of using no beat indicator (The Professional) , but it was fun to play around with them.yes im neurodivergent lol how could you tell

_childDocuments_.review: Finally finished the game after being stuck on the horribly long final boss fight. (only 3.3% of ALL players have beaten the game on Steam)There are some things I really like about this title and its a great concept as a whole. but...Holy moley there are some insanely annoying bugs and really stupid mechanics/design choices that make me never wanna play again and really hesitantly recommend it.Positives: -movement feels pretty good, slam jumping, wall jumps and dashes all feel pretty solid. near ultrakill levels but not quite as complex and with lower speed-some weapons are designed fairly well and feel/sound great to shoot on beat-adding your own music is fun (when it works..ill get to that)-the first 3 bosses are awesome to fight-loads of secrets and unlocksthats about it..honestly, past that its really hard to give the game any more compliments. here is some bugs as well as design choices that really hinder the experience. I'll list bugs first:- (bug) adding your own music will have it automatically try to guess/fill in the beat spots. out of the 15 songs I added, about 11 of them had serious issues at several points in the song that needed fixing- (bug) the custom volume slider for songs freaks out constantly and will not save your choice, often resulting in tracks that are super loud or too quiet.- (bug) parrying any attack that is not the (!) homing track shots works about half the time.. seriously. parrying on beat is supposed to result in "increased range of the parry" but this also doesnt work for any non homing shot. often making you whiff and take a ton of damage- (bug) when changing keybinds for equipment, the HUD will show the incorrect prompt no matter what you do- (bug) jumping will make the beat indicator by the aiming reticle stagger which counts for a shot's beat causing ruined beat streaks and damage- (bug) especially in later levels, some enemies will get stuck on terrain/stop attacking. sometimes just until you turn a corner then they are already mid animation attacking youNegatives:-some weapons are downright useless. Now I get its a roguelike and not every random loot can be overpowered, but its so bad that genuinely wish some would never show up. (shield and kunai in particular)-damage is incredibly high, especially on further levels and if you have a gun augment that can make you take more? expect to get 2 shot by nearly everything. Unless you have the best of the best upgrade cards.-like the weapons, certain utility items and upgrade cards are also completely useless-no use for blips/unlock currency whatsoever after youve unlocked everything you can. Genuinely, why even have the doors show up then? why give the currency on boss kill? The ability to buy a heal instead, an upgrade, or ANYTHING would be better than this.-the last boss is an absolute slog, I'm talking a 5+-7+ minute fight unless you have the best dps possible at that point, with no option to heal beforehand. Seriously why does this guy have so much health? You better play near perfect and know every one of his attacks otherwise you're toast. Took me 7+ attempts and I never wanna do it again.----------------------------------------------I know this was a long review, and it honestly really sucks I'm this bent out of shape about it, because I think there's a great game in here, but these issues have gotta get fixed, and I'll change my opinion if they do. Otherwise, maybe consider staying away.

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like a game I'd come back to with some updates, but as it stands I'll probably be moving on for now.I think my biggest issue is with the custom music editor. It's the feature that drew me in initially, but it's a nightmare to use. The game does make an attempt at auto-mapping beats, but often places beats in between others or misses beats. If the bpm is off, or half/double what you think it should be, your only option is to manually set the bpm by clicking on where the first beat is on the waveform and typing in a number, there's no option to just double or halve the bpm. There's also no snapping for beats, so if you maybe want to add or remove a beat here and there to spice up difficulty, you're again stuck just clicking on the waveform. Additionally, if your song has some silence at the start or end and you want to cut that out, it's only possible for the song to loop from where you set the end point back to where you set the start point, which often means the beat will shift when looping and throw you off. No snapping for these start/end sliders either.For songs in general, they don't really mesh with gameplay outside of setting the overall pace, but there isn't any indication  as to how this pacing change will affect the difficulty. I've found that while faster songs mean faster enemies and more attacks, up to a certain point it's easier to keep on beat. It's really just preference, which I guess is great for some but didn't feel especially compelling to me. You just choose what song you listen to, and then it loops, forever, which means that runs feel very same-y unless you're changing the track a bunch, which halts the fast pacing the game has going. There is the mixtape feature, but it also feels lacking. There's no major indication of when a bpm shift is incoming, and when changing areas it loops back to the first track. There's no way to set things to change the song only when changing areas, or to assign certain songs to certain areas, etc. I think in a perfect world I would like a more tailored soundtrack, but as it stands I  don't hate the user-curated music idea and I really just want either more ways to automatically change a song, and/or a way to assign songs a difficulty or something like that.The game's visual style felt somewhat lacking, at least for me. Relatively muted environment color palette outside of highlighting colors, and fairly unchanging room layouts make, again, for very same-y feeling runs, even in just the first hour. Yet despite these bright highlights against muted greys and blacks, the palettes used for pickups all seem to lean pretty white and have a similar effect to the enemy spawns, meaning there would be times I'd just end up shooting at pickups for a few seconds before realizing what one was. I'm not sure if doors stay locked until you've collected all pickups, but there's absolutely been occasions where I've beat a room, blazed into another, and then stopped and went "wait did I miss a pickup?" The visuals are appealing to look at, but they don't make for a great experience, everything mixes well which makes stuff hard to pick out and identify. Some enemy attack suffer from this issue as well, like the grey shockwaves some enemies send out, or the melee attacks that don't have any kind of visual effect attached to them.Tutorials and tooltips are also pretty lacking. I have this issue with a lot of roguelikes, where there almost feels like an expectation that you know the basics of how run builds tend to go in various other games and as a result you can easily go "oh yeah, this is like this other roguelike, I know what I'm doing", without the game really explaining how mechanics combine. Take for example the fire data chip, which applies fire to all of your attacks. If you saw this card on its own, you'd have no idea what the point is in picking it up. Because I've played Roboquest and the game seems to use a similar weapon effect system, I knew to expect that some weapons would have effects that proc on burning enemies, burning kills, etc. That's really what I mean. If there was some kind of tooltip, say "Fire adds continuous damage, and some bonuses allow for additional damage or effects to apply to burning enemies when hit or killed", that would literally be enough. But it doesn't do this, and fire is just one of many potential mechanics you might end up basing a build around, meaning that you end up having to teach yourself a lot of what feels like things that should be explained.Next up, the parry system doesn't feel especially intuitive for me. Some attacks will arc up on one beat and swing back down on the next, while others just travel at consistent speeds, with the firing being on beat. It makes for an odd feeling rhythm, and if you want to get parries down consistently it feels like you just need to stand in place and let stuff come to you. There's no incentive to chase down and parry projectiles like in Ultrakill since if your positioning is off and you have to do it off beat the whole sequence might end up being pointless. It almost feels like the parry should have been an AoE pulse rather than a contact thing. I am willing to concede skill issue on this one though since I haven't played a ton, though maybe some practice room where you could spawn enemies could help mitigate this.Other reviews say you can beat the game in just 3-4 hours which, if true, means that me getting to the second boss means I've probably experienced about 40-45% of all the major story content. The replayabilty of roguelikes for me isn't inherently motivating, I do still desire story content. Especially with what I've described I wouldn't see myself coming back after beating the four major areas. Which is a shame, because there are tons of weapons and abilities, and they keep adding more, but without any new places to use them in or enemies to use them against, I just don't really see a point to going back for them. For me, that means the ~$15 price point I got it at didn't feel especially worth it.I guess that really sums up my critiques. It needs some tweaking in tutorials and UI/UX, and maybe some more diverse areas and enemies, but the fundamentals are there. Shooting on beat is always fun and mixing it with an Ultrakill-esque style/movement system with roguelike abilities based on these actions makes for a ton of neat interations and shifting playstyles.
_childDocuments_.name: ROBOBEAT

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels amazing to play, though I really hope development won't stop for a while.It's hard to describe how this game feels to play. The game has amazing juice, gives you slowmo when you pull off stylish moves, tons of visual effects to enhance how great everything feels. But somehow, despite all this, it does not lose on visual clarity, I've always felt like what went wrong was my fault. Pulling off some of the add-on combos feel extremely good, especially when you're rewarded with juicy slowmo, so much so that I really wish more weapons felt as good as the revolver does.The songs. Oh good gosh the songs. They're pretty much all killer, and feel amazing to play along with. Doing actions on beat is so so so satisfying, so much so that I often end up also dashing, jumping and slamming on the beat, despite it not being required at all.Movement felt a bit clunky at first, especially the wallrun, but once you give the game some time, your movement options just flow into one another. Really, really solid movement, which I'd argue is probably what's makes this game feel extremely good. It's what splits it apart from Bullets Per Minute, and it does an amazing job at it.The revolver, crossbow, cosmic, and bouncer feel really, really good to use. And so do the Hookshot, Nuke, and Finish utilities. Just, lots of opportunities to be stylish and they're fun to play with.At the moment, it feels like I'm playing a vertical slice of what the game could be. There needs to be more viable weapons (or please add more add-ons to the current weapons that feel as good as pulling off the revolver's Aimbot add-on). Either that, or add modifiers that will  make me consider whether or not I should grab a weapon I'm not comfortable with. Force me to go melee because the hammer spawned with some crazy modifier. The flare gun and the Electroshock only exist to be used along with the 2x damage on burning/zapped enemies. The Contact basically just allows you to hit two enemies at once. There's a couple of weapons that really feel unique and good to use, I just wish more of them felt that way.There aren't enough cards to pick from, and a lot of them feel like they don't affect the run much. Grabbing the "Shoot both guns at the same time" card is a no-brainer, and I wish there were more good cards so that we're forced to make actual choices. Some cards also need a bit more info. Having a card force you to alternate between your two guns for more damage is nice and all, but what kind of damage increase are we talking about? I've never really felt like that card did much, even when I picked it twice during a run.The currency used to unlock new items gave a way to heal yourself before bosses, but that's removed while playing a "real" run (the final "path" unlocked). The currency then becomes completely useless, but you're still being given the option to pick rooms that give it as a reward. I'm not asking to bring back the healing stations, but maybe bring in a shop that accepts said currency? Right now, this feels like a big oversightI also have some small nitpicks. The second boss feels exactly like the first boss, except it's got two additional attacks that are pretty trivial to dodge. Definitely would like a bit more variety there, but they both feel good to fight against using parries, so really, I'm not complaining too much. I love having to parry multiple times in a row, and wish the bosses would do some stuff similar to the final boss' second phase. Also, when you get unlucky during a run, you can still pretty reliably get through without ever getting good damage options. But that makes the third boss feel like a bullet sponge, and the final boss even more so. It did make for some fun battles of attrition though. I know I've mentioned a lot of things I wish were better, but these really come out of my love for the game. I feel like this game could shine ten times brighter, easily, like it's a few steps away from becoming a roguelike I'd sink hundreds of hours into. I'm still hella recommending it. If you liked BPM, play this. If you like fast-paced shooters, or you like rhythm games, play this. If you like both of these genres and loved BPM? Why isn't this game in your library already?

_childDocuments_.review: This is what you get when you cross BPM: Bullets Per Minute with the movement and style scoring system of Ultrakill. It works amazingly and feels really good to make combos in.If that wasn't good enough on its own, it also lets you import custom music and even has an in-game editor to fine-tune where the individual beats are placed throughout the song, letting you make practically any song work. I really appreciate the freedom provided through these tools. My only complaint here is that the game doesn't recognise FLAC files, which any music enthusiast is going to generally have instead of MP3sYou can switch tracks on the fly, the game doesn't force you to use any specific song, they're not tied to levels and you can even swap mid-level if you're in the mood for something different.A decent selection of weapons and secondary tools with roguelite progression to unlock them, random passive upgrades found in-run and an alright amount of level variation keep runs interesting.I don't have a strong opinion about the art style one way or another, it's got that same deep fried look BPM had whilst making enemy colours contrast massively, it helps keep you focused on the enemies but I've found I struggle to see things like pits in the floor from time to time.There's a very high skill ceiling with the style points system, learning new ways to clear rooms in as cool a manner as possible will keep you busy practising and trying new things for a long while.Overall just a lot of fun, if you like rhythm games, boomer shooters and Ultrakill-esque movement, this is the perfect combination of all of those things.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure the game is fun, I really like the concept, but I can't get the calibration right on my set-up to have the audio/visual timing to be precise. There's only a slider to adjust the timing +/-0.25sec. This isn't intuitive enough for someone to calibrate on their own. There needs to be a built in calibration tool for people to be able to dial in the calibration, something like Guitar Hero's calibration. A set timing offset also doesn't work when the BPM changes, it has to be a percentage, otherwise the offset might be too fast on one song and too slow on another.  I've requested a refund because without a precise timing calibration method, this game is unplayable as a rhythm game on my system. As a musician, it's particularly frustrating because I know how to count music and reel rhythm, I don't need timing indicators on screen, nor do I want to use them. If you're not a trained musician the timing mismatches might not bother you as much, but I play rhythm games because I want to feel the music, not try to time my clicks to an indicator.I will happily update my review if they implement a proper timing calibration system.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished it yet, but from what I've seen, it already gets an extremely positive review from me...ROBOBEAT is a rhythm shooter with a futuristic theme and RogueLike features, where you'll need to advance to uncover its story while enjoying the beats that come with the game (incredible in my opinion) or your own music thanks to its audio import function. Its gameplay takes a lot from other games like Ultrakill, Hellsinger, or Dusk, making it extremely frenetic yet very polished and fair; the more skill you have, the better your gameplay looks. Thanks to its different weapons and combinations, parry mechanic, and strictness with health, the skill gap is quite large, giving you many hours of fun mastering the mechanics (especially with high BPM songs).If you like futuristic settings, electronic music, Ultrakill, Quake, Dusk, or frenetic shooters in general, this game should definitely be in your Steam library. Now, changing the topic, let's talk about the few negative points (2) that I could mention about the title:BPM in custom songs: It's not something alarming since in most genres and mainstream songs, the BPM adjusts automatically to perfection. However, there are some tracks, especially glitchcore or hyperpop, where I had to find the BPM manually and then hit the exact part of the song where it should start. This is extremely tedious as the track editing system is quite poorly designed in my opinion. Additionally, when you move or change the beats of the song, the markers don't update, so you have to exit and re-enter the editor to hear them synchronized again.Movement: Coming from Ultrakill, where one of the most important mechanics is the ability to maintain momentum, I feel this game could benefit from a similar system or a way to move faster than the normal slide, which sometimes falls quite short.Even with these slight issues, this has become one of my favorite shooters by combining my two passions into something truly fun and clean. With nothing more to say, I'll keep shooting to the beat!

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine you are at a restaurant. You notice a juicy looking description of a dish in the menu. It's described so pretty, that you can almost feel the taste! You order this dish. But at the end, the most delicious and memorable part of this was a .That's how I feel about ROBOBEAT.I like . Art style is more consistent and appealing than in BPM. But at the same time, it feels so dim and uninspired. Most of the enemies have no distinctive features. Enemies are often just some coloured dolls.The enemy design (gameplay-wise) is good though.The ! And I like the variety of a music repertoire (especially different BPMs). Also there is manual import of tracks!I liked secrets and Easter eggs with references to other games.There is some story, but it's not so significant and notable. But it was fun exploring some backstory in the game.And that's all what I can say positive. The main parts of the game feel lackluster.OK, first of all, there is a controversial decision in the design. The player should start runs from the beginning  to complete the game. I don't like this concept at all. Look at DEADLINK. The game lets you to try to reach final boss from the first try. works . Often there are identical items at the start of the run (or in the two separate reward rooms). Or the random can decide to throw at you three consecutive parkour rooms.There is a  like in ULTRAKILL. Successful parry deflects projectiles in the direction where the player currently looks at. Or parry just negates melee damage from enemies.Also there is a . Every weapon has some number of combos. Reloads, shots and parries are all combo elements. There are many weapons in the pool though. But most of them are not as effective as a start revolver.See, the revolver has an ability similar to McRee from Overwatch. Essentially, this combo grants you multi-headshot (critical) to a limited amount of enemies in front of you. None of other weapons have same overbuff combo with that big damage.There are  that is a novelty in the genre. But it's very hard to have fun with them as they tend to be slower or less powerful than range weapons. Using melee places the player in a close proximity to enemies and limits player movements. And constant movement is essential for surviving. I can imagine boss battles with melee as a nightmare 💀The variety of arsenal should present an opportunity for multiple builds. But I believe there are only couple of good builds which is a sad. Also there are abilities. They are OK and gives you some utility.There is a system of upgrading character which allows the player to pick some buffs for the current run. For example, slow-mo after skating (yeah, main character is like on rollers) or giving you a boost to the damage at the price of increased recoil. Overall, idea is OK, but why the buffs are presented in the form of "tarot" cards? I don't know, it seems out of place.There are two unlockable rooms:  and . After successful completion of a room (hitting all target within a time limit in "challenge" and reaching a certain point in "parkour") the player can choose random generated reward (ability or weapon). Often, rewards are not worth the effort. But I see a potential, like in DEAD CELLS. The parkour segments could be challenging platforming areas with cool rewards.. They are OK.  However, all of them lack complexity. Bosses have a lot of HP and they spam same attack sequences. So the player just avoid attacks and keep shooting. Boss battles very quickly become mundane and boring encounters. It would be cool if some of them had different weakspots. Or several phases. There is definitely room for improvement.

It's like diving headfirst into a pulsating neon dreamscape where every move, every shot, is a perfectly choreographed dance to the beat. As Ace, the fearless bounty hunter, you're not just on a mission to capture Frazzer – you're on a quest to become the ultimate rhythm master!From the get-go, ROBOBEAT immerses you in its electrifying world, where the music isn't just background noise – it's your guiding force. With each beat, you'll find yourself effortlessly wall-running, sliding, and blasting your way through waves of robots, all while feeling like an unstoppable force of rhythmic destruction.ROBOBEAT is a feast for the eyes, with its vibrant colors and dynamic environments that seem to come alive with every beat. It's like stepping into a neon-lit dance floor where the party never stops.But what truly sets ROBOBEAT apart is its ingenious integration of rhythm and shooter mechanics. It's not just about shooting – it's about shooting to the beat, syncing your every action with the pulsating rhythm to unleash maximum carnage and style.Oh, and did I mention you can set up your own custom soundtracks? That's right – you can turn ROBOBEAT into your very own personal rhythm symphony, adding an extra layer of excitement and personalization to an already mind-blowing experience!In conclusion, ROBOBEAT is a must-play for anyone with a love for rhythm games, shooters, or just pure, unadulterated fun. It's a wild, exhilarating ride from start to finish, guaranteed to leave you breathless and begging for more. So, strap in, turn up the volume, and let the beat take control – you won't regret it!Consider checking my gameplay before making your purchase

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Good game but if you aren't a skilled at rhythm fps and likes to actually finish the game you will be a bit frustrated.The game is a roguelike but the only progression is:- Codex: Tells a bit more of the story.- Songs: The songs dictated how fast you can shoot but it doesn't mean that unlocked songs become faster and faster the farther you get, they are, in the most part, something tied to the story or themed after the level.- Weapons: As any roguelike you can't actually pick any weapon from the arsenal, they will appear at random, also the new weapons aren't straight up upgrades, some can deal more damage but they have some limitations on how to actually deal good amounts of damage with them.- Utilities: Same deal as weapons.So yeah, the most precious progression of the game is your own skill and knowledge of the enemies patterns.There is no "increase max health", "heal X amount of health at end of each room" or "unlock re-roll on shops", so yeah, pretty much the only thing that matters is you getting better, and it shows, only 3.3% of players beat the game as of writing.The good:- The songs are great;- There are some good concepts for combats such as parry and utilities that allow you to get a free parry;- It is really satisfying to clean a  room up when you are feeling the groove;- There are some good enemy variety;- Lots of secrets;The bad:- There are some enemies and bosses that require you to dodge or parry melee attacks, if you dodge you extend the battle, if you dodge you run the risk of missing the parry. The melee attacks should be tied to the beat, so, if you parry on beat you are good, but sometimes it seems the parry misses even though you feel like you are doing it on time;- The game is composed of 4 levels, each having a bunch of rooms and one boss, the game also has 4 difficulty options, the problem is, the difficulty option caps your max level progression, therefore you can only beat the game on the hardest difficulty, and to top it all off on the hardest difficulty you can't use currency to heal before boss fights, lower difficulties allow it, in other words, if you want to have a chance to learn the final boss patterns you better not take any damage on the last level.Suggestion for the developer:-Implement the same concept of "pay for a re-roll of options" from the cards into the weapons shop;-Make the "heal before boss" an optional feature, by default it is always on, if you choose to turn it off you will have some sort of bonus, maybe more currency or better odds of better items;-Create a "forge room", allowing you to pay for an upgrade of your weapon, maybe even re-roll the bonuses. I like weapon variety but there was some weapons that worked better with my play style and many times I enter a room "oh a gift room, maybe there is something good" and I see something I don't really care much about;-Create a "sandbox" mode, for training, by default you can enter and use any weapon you have unlocked on a dummy target.Also on the "sandbox" mode you can summon any common enemy you've defeated before for you to train against it.I say the "sandbox" is a good option because I got the throwing blade that "splits your shots" and I just couldn't figure out how to use it and I wasn't about to lose a run to try and figure it out.
