_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game.  The UI is clunky and the story is, uh, poorly-presented to say the least.  But the core game loop and soundtrack are *chef's kiss*.Essentially it's a very-lite roguelite where you're magically bound to a car in a zone full of anomalies from unobtanium nonsense science.  You take individual "runs" into this zone, going deeper as you progress.  There are no "enemies" or combat, as such, but there are still lots of dangers to deal with and learn about.  Exploration is key... don't just go to the map markers, look around.  Also, it's got a bunch of great little features, like "quirks" where the weird sciency radiation in the zone causes unrelated systems in your car to suddenly link in weird ways and you have to accurately diagnose the problem before you can fix it.If you're the kind of person who prepares meticulously, you might find this game very easy.  If you play by the seat of your pants, you might find it unfairly difficult.  It's one of those games.But seriously, you should buy this game just for the soundtrack alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: I like crafting games with survival goal and some neat extras like in this case, with a car and anomalies.What i don't like is when the Devs want you to play in a certain way without letting you know and a weak story.The biggest issue and strength are the anomalies, they are quirky and unpredictable but also tedious and appear many times exactly in your way or chasing you way too long.When you do story missions or exploration, the Devs expect you to do things in a certain way or order, that don't come clear straight away. For example the second story mission: you have to drive to a big thing in the middle of the map, no big problem except there is radiation around it and the mission demands, that you get closer to the big thing once you entered a certain area around it, hinting to drive higher. But in order to drive higher, you have to drive out and find a way up a mountain, which you could have done straight from the beginning on the map, having avoided the radiation and explosive dummies.Another example, the third story mission: You have to activate three towers, alpha beta and gamma. Again, appears to be no big deal except, if you do the order wrong and have alpha last, you have to drive through the map in order to enter the exit, all while a frickn storm closes in fast, making you barely survive it if you are lucky when it comes to the other anomalies.This is also not proberly explained, leaving an area via gateway. When you collected the charges needed to exit and activates the gateway, the storm is coming straight away in highspeed. So you have to be close to the gateway, but not too close otherwise it turns red and you can't activate it, and then floor it in order to keep the damage minimal.Also neat, when you collect charges, anomalies appear quickly around the anchor, which housed the charge.Also is the car way too easy to damage, ANYTHING can damage parts of your car, and even loose parts, just because you didn't had enough repair patty or no sealing kit to keep the wheels full of air, because you need to collect mats but also need space for tools. Which midly frustrates me as you can only stack 20 of one mat as it forces you to start a new stack.Way too many things are not great, some QoL changes could make it more bearable like toggle sprinting or picking up certain things with one press, not staying on the button to take something.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: A "survival" driver with a creative inventory system and a completely customize-able car. Despite only being able to save at your base and auto saving when you enter a zone, it doesn't feel bogged down or terribly annoying. The car quirks that start creeping in can be annoying at times, but always find a way make a tense situation comedic! With a minimal HUD in the field you'll rely on your car's dashboard to help you out on some long drives. All in all I keep finding myself coming back not long after I finish a session to see what else I can discover or loot!

_childDocuments_.review: Good all around game, inventory management could be a bit better and it could explain some things better but those are minor issues.I switched to controller half way through for a more laid back experience and apart from taking longer to move items in your inventory it works great with a controller and the car is nicer to drive.I noticed it has some good difficulty options if you want a more forgiving playthrough though I don't think it's to hard on default.You do benefit from pushing some way into the narrative before any major farming or exploration, speaking of narrative the story is pretty good and well told with some great voice acting.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: No game has ever got the feeling and spirit of owning a car you form a bond with quite so well, I've bonded with this wagon as if it was my own irl car. The maintenance is fun? It's quite fun to see a headlight clicker so  you have to either fix it, let it run out or replace it on the fly. Not to mention that the game itself is actually tense, but there are so many gameplay and accessibility options that you can tailor the game to be exactly what you want. Don't want storms? It's there, don't want to take damage or even die? Sure, won't get trophies but you can do that. Don't want your car to drain battery with the headlights on? That's possible too. I'm not very far into it so I can't say much for the story but it's truly something interesting so far. As for optimization the game is 17gb and even on my old 1080 I still have to turn the graphics down a bit but the game's style doesn't require your game  to now look all muddy, i have numerous things on medium and it's still just beautiful. Music in the game is incredible, sound is top notch. Just remember to Drive Like Hell.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: I should have hated everything about this game. Its everything I don't like. It's a Driving sim, it's a rogue like, it's got timed events, the story flaggs a little at the end, it's entirely repetitive. Yet I still love it. The characters, whilst suffering from the aforementioned dodgy plot progression, are really cute and loveable. The radio banter  from them as you drive around the (very lonely) zone is a very welcome addition, and the humour is spot on. I found myself laughing aloud on numerous occasions. The gameplay's repetitive nature somehow feeds into its addictive properties. The skill involved in methodically plotting a route, preparing items, avoiding obstacles and choosing (and reaching) your escape route are all such a powerful adrenaline rush. I couldn't put the controller down, honestly. It's so addictive I played the damn thing for 90hrs and collected every achievement and I still feel I want to keep going. I can't emphasise how often I just finish a games plot and dump it. Not this time. Even better, the rogue like settings are adjustable so you don't have to grind as much if you don't want to, or stress as much about background effects like radiation (although only at low levels, high levels will still hurt). This hugely improved my experience of the game, and I have to thank the Devs for (mostly) letting such options go unpenalised (choosing to never die for example, is an option, but warrants no achievements and is entirely pointless in my opinion- but most other adjustments can be done without achievement locking). This makes the game more accessible to a much larger audience, instead of just hardcore rogue like fans.I could go on and on all day and type a dissertation, but honestly, just play it for yourself. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

Getting back to the garage with your car held together by duct tape, spit, and luck is an awesome feeling. Working on your hunk of junk station wagon in the middle of the night with the banger OST radio playlist on in the background and rain pouring down outside... It's a feeling I didn't know I needed. _childDocuments_.review: Game sucks.  Nothing is really satisfying to do, for instance the scrapper tool you use to get your scrap parts deteriorates after a few cars and you have to make a new one.  Why not just make it permanent, then picking up each little piece that comes off is just annoying.  I tried to use a controller to give a more delicate turn and it is just atrocious, slow and sloppy takes way to much to get the wheel to turn and by the time it turns you're already over steered too much.  Then you get back to the auto shop and "repair" the car by making and throwing putty all over it. Its so dark in the world and they do not give a flash light or anything to use so you cant see.  The lady will tell you to get close to something so you drive up and you just get dragged and tossed around (Then you really can't see) and I'm like "Is this what you wanted? Am I doing it right?" then get sent back to auto shop so I'm thinking that's not what she wanted but how are you supposed to know.  Map in the game is way off, I'll be driving on the road and it shows me way off in the grass area somewhere. If you want to play a REAL survival car game then just get               My Summer Car, they even have you look at the ignition to start the car and look at the shifter to put it in gear like My Summer Car but in this game just feels forced and shallow.

There is a bit of a learning curve to all the nuances and it's easy to miss some of the options. It also takes a few hours to understand the gameflow. There's a lot to this game and I think it rewards players who explore. However I think the difficulty ramps up at a comfortable pace - especially since a lot of it depends on how you plan your routes and what activities you do on each level.Aside from that it's a great game - just prepare to search online for some answers to basic questions like "What does an Arc Doc do and how do I install it?"

_childDocuments_.review: After 15 hours exploring everything there was to learn from the demo, and now after 8 hours with the full game and just a handful of drives under my belt, I can offer a tentative... YES!Pacific Drive is absolutely fantastic. It can be relaxing, spooky, scary, and terrifying at different times. Heading out to a new junction shrouded in mist, plagued by anomalies that are yet undiscovered and others that you wish weren't there, with little more of an objective than to just explore the Zone, your car newly beefed up with off-road tires and improved storage, is a pure thrill. Pacific Drive is a game of exploration, discovery, purposeful crafting and loot collection. The Zone is a mystery wrapped in an enigma with a linear narrative but the freedom to move at your own pace.And after a successful drive to a new junction, which opened up the map some more and netted some valuable materials that will make survival incrementally easier the next time out is a completely satisfying experience. I suspect that once the mysteries are all solved, there will be ample room to replay, too, because no repeat trip to the same junction is exactly like the last.Pacific Drive is X-Files on steroids. It's a brilliantly designed and executed game, and a MUST play.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. I love driving around in my car, crafting, gathering parts, unraveling the mystery the story, and then when you get back to the garage you can upgrade that as well. There is also research so that you can get better car parts, better tires, better technology to survive. Once you begin upgrading your car, getting off-road tires and over all better equipment, beating the storm surrounding you and getting to the exits points is easier, so you just got to hang in there and continue playing to get better equipment. I have had some close calls and every time it’s an adrenaline rush. I see people complaining about this game being “too harsh” or “too difficult”, but the devs put settings in the game to customize your difficulty (if you are changing graphic settings how do you miss these settings). So if you wanted to make your game easier you can do that. After I get through my initial play through I am going to mess with the setting. I feel like I am surviving the paranormal in my sentient ghost car. Driving the car feels really good, and your car can develop quirks as well that you can diagnose and fix. My most recent run I had finally found some crystals for the turbo engine upgrade and my car decided to develop a quirk to throw the engine into reverse every time I turned the steering wheel. That took awhile to figure out and it turned into a close call with a storm closing in. I almost didn’t make it to the portal in time! This game also runs buttery smooth. I have a 4070Ti on a 2k display and I have everything cranked up to ultra with vsync turned on and I do not notice any hitching, stuttering, or frame drops. It's rare that games will run like this these days.This game is part supernatural mystery, part shipbraker, and part car mechanic sim. There is an exit save when you are in your garage, and you are able to save manually as well in there. This 6 hours of game time at the time of review is one sitting because the game loop is so addictiveThis is like the hardcore version of trucking simulator for breachers

_childDocuments_.review: Pacific Drive offers a unique blend of survival mechanics and driving simulation set in a mysterious, post-apocalyptic version of the Pacific Northwest. The game’s central feature is a station wagon that players maintain and upgrade while navigating through the treacherous Olympic Exclusion Zone. The car becomes a companion of sorts, its condition directly impacting the gameplay.The game’s atmosphere is one of its standout elements, with a setting that is both eerie and captivating. Players can expect a challenging experience that rewards ingenuity and perseverance. While Pacific Drive does not revolutionize the survival genre, it provides a solid and engaging experience with its combination of car maintenance and exploration.The narrative is intriguing, though the game can be punishing at times, with a learning curve and unforgiving dangers. However, those who enjoy a challenge and are fans of survival games will likely find Pacific Drive to be a rewarding journey worth taking.

_childDocuments_.review: As a game developer, I feel bad leaving a negative review on an indie title but I’m not enjoying the game too much. It’s scoped out of it’s mind I tell you. Everything feels cheap and student project-ish, characters are kind of lazy and played out. The premise is cool idkCouple things I wanted to mention too. For a game about driving there's not a lot of driving. Mostly running around and clicking on objects with half a dozen goofy gadgets you have to craft. You could argue that you can't make a game about just travel, but it could actually be nice and atmospheric I think, like a road trip. There's just not enough art to support that, so gameplay is padded out  with random on-foot chores. That's where my scope argument comes into play. _childDocuments_.review: Pacific Drive is often mistaken for a horror game, but it’s more accurately a survival experience with a tense, atmospheric setting. The primary challenge in this game comes not from supernatural entities, but from the harsh, unforgiving environment. While there are a few bothersome bots and environmental hazards, the real adversary is the world itself.At first, Pacific Drive offers a captivating experience with its unique mechanics and intriguing exploration. The thrill of discovering new areas and managing your vehicle creates an engaging sense of adventure. However, as the game progresses, the constant need for travel and the lack of fast travel options begin to wear thin. The “highways” provide a more direct route but only marginally reduce the extensive distances you need to cover. This relentless traversal through the same areas becomes monotonous and exhausting.The game's world, though visually striking in some parts, suffers from a lack of biom diversity. As you traverse the same environments repeatedly, the initial sense of wonder diminishes, and the game starts to feel repetitive. This repetitiveness is compounded by the game’s tendency to require you to backtrack and cover the same ground over and over again.The narrative has potential but is often overshadowed by constant dialogue and on-screen distractions, which detract from immersion. The game’s resource management and car upgrades offer some satisfaction, but the frustration of losing items upon death and having to retrace your steps diminishes the enjoyment. By the end of the game, the grind had become so wearisome that I opted to forgo further upgrades and venture out with a stripped-down vehicle—no doors, no panels—just to escape the tedious cycle.Despite initially enjoying the game, my enthusiasm waned over time. By the end, I was relieved to be finished rather than feeling a sense of accomplishment. The repetitive nature of the gameplay and the constant need to travel the same routes made the experience more of a chore than a pleasure.Pacific Drive is a niche game that will appeal to those with a strong appreciation for survival mechanics and exploration. However, the lack of biom variety, relentless travel, and repetitive gameplay can make it a challenging experience. For those who choose to play, adjusting settings to tailor the experience may help alleviate some frustrations. Overall, while the game has its unique aspects, the eventual grind and repetition overshadow the initial enjoyment, leaving players more relieved than satisfied upon completion.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm going to say no, I wouldn't recommend this, but what I really mean is "you should be warned first." Let me explain.This game is self-described as "a roguelike". So what is that? If you boil it down to the simplest possible essence, "a roguelike" basically means "a procedural death labyrinth". It's a game where you go on dungeon crawls into procedurally-generated dungeons to gather loot and resources you need in order to progress. You have specific goals to reach which require certain amounts of various things, but whether or not the treasure chest(s) you open contains those things and if so how much, is random, as are the specific hazards/monsters you have to face in order to reach them. And dying carries a stiff, persistent penalty - in the older Roguelikes that meant permadeath, as every game was Hardcore, no exceptions.In Pacific Drive, it means "lose the last four hours of your  progress and start all over again because the game is now unwinnable". If that sort of punishing difficulty is your jam, well, go right ahead. But be warned - you can do everything right, make zero mistakes, and still be brutally killed and lose all your progress. This happened to me multiple times in 55 hours of gameplay and this "punished when I haven't done anything wrong" theme is what put me off this game. I could cite multiple examples, but I'll try for a non-spoilery one.In order to successfully complete a run through one of this game's dungeons, you have to collect a certain liquid which is used to unseal the exit. This liquid is contained inside objects that are scattered randomly throughout the dungeon, and are never clustered together. How much liquid each object contains is random, as is how much of it you need. You might only have to open one, or you might need five. But 'winning' is contingent upon opening these objects and you can't get around that.Here's the thing, though.One, the objects poison you when you touch them, doing damage over time. Doing what you literally have to do hurts you.Two, whenever you open one, all hell breaks loose. Environmental hazards spawn, monsters come running like you rang a dinner bell, plus a timer starts counting down, and when it reaches zero, you die.And lose all your progress. Again.The final time I died, and what prompted me to stop playing was when I opened one of these things a hazard spawned directly underneath me which launched me up through the air and into a second hazard which launched me into a lethal trap.This could not be avoided in any way - it was impossible to dodge as it appeared literally beneath my feet, then I was juggled through the air until I died. After that initial launch, I never touched the ground again.I literally did what the game makes you do, and I was killed for it.Which cost me about three hours of careful progress because the game was now unwinnable and I had to start over. My vehicle was an utter wreck and I lacked the resources to repair it and continue.To be both fair and transparent the game does contain a mechanic that technically lets you continue from something like this, but your vehicle will lose all the improvements and upgrades you've put into it and basically starts over from scratch. Your base and character retain their upgrades, if any.So if the threat of losing hours of work to what comes down to a random roll of the dice sounds like fun to you, this game might be right up your alley. I hope you have a good time.Me, I'm uninstalling and never playing again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very atmospheric game, the kind where a good third of your enjoyment is in traversing the world while listening to the radio as you make pit stops to collect materials or fix up your car after surviving an acidic storm.If you are a player who is always on top of the situation and rarely gets caught off guard then you won't experience many of the tense situations you could get yourself into, like limping to the portal on two flats and two spares with half your doors gone with anomalies trying to end your run. Instead it'll be a pleasant cruise with a few frustrating moments. Your enjoyment will be however much pleasure you garner from the environment you're passing through as you make another run to get the resources you need to get that next upgrade.If you are a player who's terrible at driving games and/or frequently forgets to ensure their ride is in tip top shape then your experience will vary quite a bit more as your car will deteriorate faster, exposing you to hazards and additional frustrations that'll either bolster your enjoyment or make you quit because this is the fourth time you didn't fix your rear door and so your internal batteries leaked out along with your gas tank, leaving you stranded in the zone.In either case there isn't much else for players to sink their teeth into. The story is lack luster and it feels more like you're just listening in on radio chatter between survivors with no real plot carrots to keep you going. The only reason I wanted to go deeper into the zone was to gather new materials for better upgrades, not to further the plot. Eventually I had everything and I made a beeline for the ending missions just so I could finish the game, not because I was overly excited to find out how it ended.Simply put it is an open world driving simulator in the STALKER world, with touches of Subnautica vehicle building, but the story goes nowhere so you best just enjoy your drive as you strive to build the ultimate zone wagon.

_childDocuments_.review: This game checks a lot of boxes for me:  exploration, driving, survival-crafting, etc.  What makes this a special experience is the world building.  There is certainly source material to draw on the internet, e.g., the SCP database, but making it a cohesive narrative and interesting environment to discover is the real accomplishment.  The Frequency Files was my favorite in-game lore and I went out of my way to discover the recordings even when I was essentially done with the game.  I admit to being captivated with the setting being a Washington native.  The only glaring issue was the lack of texture for the rocks; the boulders were weirdly de-rezed compared to the rest of the scenery.

_childDocuments_.review: I were to put a genre on this it wouldn't be 'My Summer Car meets Roadside Picnic meets Pacific Northwest creepy pasta' or 'story-rich adventure survival with a sci-fi twist' or... No, I have a much more concise game tag: 'North American hipster indie'. You know, games like Firewatch, The Long Dark, Road 96 etc. Hey, there's nothing wrong with North American hipster indie! You should probably strive to play one in between each triple-A title. It's the healthy thing to do. They give you a brain break, have lots of charm and, besides, Pacific Drive is rather fun. _childDocuments_.review: This game, to me, gives the same feelings Subnautica did, possibly better than that game's sequel does. You are alone, with radio transmissions you can't speak back to, there are no other humans to run into on your drives, it's just you against an almost alien environment. Progression involves you learning about this environment, you getting better equipped to handle it, and you getting more skilled at dealing with it. You get comfortable in the shallower zones before you trek out to the deeper, more dangerous ones, as the dangers ramp steadily upwards, and the encroaching storms enforce a soft time limit on each of your stops along the way. It's not a tight time limit, but it is meant to keep you from bogging yourself down in visiting every little POI along the way. The gameplay loop can get a little repetitive, but also strangely addictive. I find myself being satisfied with one or two trips for a day only to come back the next day eager to run a couple more. Progress is both vague and yet very tangible: there's enough to unlock that you could dwell in the outer zone for dozens of hours, constantly unsure of when you feel ready to push further, but you can also very clearly see your car become increasingly developed and outfitted with the upgrades you achieve in a way that makes it feel considerably more personal. Which has a fun and very likely intentional implication when considering that your car is [REDACTED], but that's more just flavor than anything. I don't think the developers intend you to unlock EVERYTHING before you finish the game. There are too many unlocks for not nearly enough slots, and the energy (research currency) you get is too limited to make that a speedy process. But the option is certainly there, as no technology is forever gated behind your choices, and so you can choose to linger in the zone for however long you wish. Honestly, you could probably make it through the main storyline with just basic steel and a stockpile of fuel, repair putty, and a jumper or two if you wanted to. But the fact that the game makes you play through the drive along every junction towards the destination you're on, highways included, is a pretty clear tone indicator that the game wants you to enjoy the journey. The story itself, which I've largely left on the wayside for this review, is more for added flavor than a real narrative that you'll want to blitz to the end to see, but the VAs do a really good job that makes participating in it feel enjoyable.The game is no snoozefest driving simulator, but you don't have to constantly be on the edge of your seat either. As long as you aren't driving directly into every anomaly you see (or don't see, but that's, and I mean this both gently and self-referentially, a skill issue), it's not hard. There aren't very many games like this out there, and for all of them that give you a mobile base to work with, there's something particularly quaint about this one just being a plain old car. It helps that they came up with a pretty good selection to play on the radio, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I've got your attention, when I finish the game I will provide an update here at the top in place of this sentence if any of my opinions have changed. So a lot of the review as I’m typing this have like… an hour? Thats perfectly fine and every review is valid bla bla bla, but I do think having gotten to a point in the game where you can at least say you’ve well passed the point of the demo should be a prerequisite for  writing out a full on review lolI was one of the very lucky creators (streaming/Youtube video making) that got sent a copy of the game a day early so I was able to do a whole stream just exploring things before the game fully came out. I am one mission away from hitting the “mid” point in the story, having done a good bit of unnecessary exploration and resource gathering,  I’ve upgraded most of my car parts to the mid tier level, I’ve dripped the car out, and I’ve named the car BethanyCan I just put in an official request to have the community call the car Bethany? It just fits, thats all I’m sayingThis was, since the first trailer really, one of my most hyped games this year (the other being Balatro and thank god that game slapped so hard too).  That being said I was a little worried when there was a MASSIVE visual glitch in the demo that had a flickering invisible wall that was kinda artifacting in the garage, and when I booted up the full version the same thing happened. It sucks to get through at the start, but just trust me if this happens to you and suck it up and get past the first garage visit because beyond that, this game has been absolutely bug free. Like, seriously, not a single issue. Performance has been great on my middle end rig running max on all fronts, and I have yet to encounter a single bug, which is more impressive if you know me and my track record with games. If theres a problem yo I’ll find it, check out these game breaking bugs while the DJ revolves it, Ice Ice BabyBeyond technical polish and performance, the game is just fun as hell. I really appreciate the full send the dev team went for on recreating the feel of the PNW, which is rainy as hell and trees everywhere. Alan Wake 2 is the only game in recent memory to nail the feeling so well and Pacific Drive kills it in that regard. The graphical style is “simplistic” but its not really lacking, moreso they focused on making everything look good with a more restrained art direction than making everything hyper realistic which helps the overall mood of things as well as the performance, I’m sure. I was initially a bit skeptic about the whole mechanic part of the game, I don’t mean game mechanics, I mean literally being a mechanic in the game, but my worries were unfounded. Sometimes going through the PNW Stalker Zone (lol) your car will develop… problems. For example when I put the car in Park my passenger side front door would open, every time. You develop these quirks and get to do a little guessing game to figure out the exact causes of it, but the game doesn’t go HEY YOUR CAR IS ACTING FUNNY, it took me like 5 times of going “damn why is that door open again” for me to realize something funky was going on and that was a really cool bit of emergent gameplay. This whole game is teeming with stuff like that where the information is there but doesn’t bonk you over the head, it just gently nudges you to address it, or in the case of the anomalies, sometimes not so gently nudges you. The home base has this really great and tangible sense of progression to it, as you slowly invest in upgrades replacing the cardboard boxes and junk all over your garage with functional (and stylish) new facilities that slowly increase the capabilities you have as the player. Its really cool seeing the transformation from rinky dink little sh*thole to a one man pit crew. Pacific Drive is more or less everything I wanted it to be, which is a tall order. It has all of the right influences worn on its sleeve, its silly, its serious, its scary, its stylish, and its so very fun. Also, if you happen to stream/do content you can have your chat pretend to be backseat drivers with TTS as seen here, sh*ts fun as f*ck. If you are at all interested in more indie game reviews, follow my curator page. I do my best to review games when I’m 100% done with them, but I figure 7 hours is better than all the 1 hour reviews as far as first impressions go. I got this for free technically from the devs (ty again guys) but I would 100% have bought it myself if they hadn’t hooked me up and there would be zero purchase regret. This game slaps. Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: Good and unique game. For those that like survival/crafting, it's a nice twist on the genre.I was saddened when I wound up on a path that forced me to route to the endgame before I wanted to. I wanted to unlock everything first. But in the end, I finished the game with only mid-level gear. I think the game should be harder. It seems hard, but if you are a good boy-scout and come prepared, you can survive most anything the game throws at you. I wish the game gave more freedom in route choices, like even the ability to drive home if I wanted.I did encounter a No Signal bug once and had to reload. I'm not sure if that (or some enemy I missed accounted for a lot of lost resources I had just collected. But overall, the game is not buggy.. just that one is a bit game-breaking if you encounter it.On the whole, it's a good, enjoyable, even relaxing game punctuated with 'oh crap!' moments. The creativity and uniqueness is a big plus. I'm just sad I could not get more play out of it before being led to the end. Somehow, now that the story is over, I have no motivation to unlock the rest of the equipment...what is the point?It should not be so easy to survive the final zone with mid-level gear, imho. I'm surprised so few finish the game. They probably rage quit after having something stolen by a critter, or find it hard because they don't spend proper time preparing before a run. That last run for me was 7 locations in upper-mid level gear (all insulated or lead doors and panels, and I could have done another 3 or 4 with the repair equipment, gas and battery I had. Little hint - you can use your gas cans to siphon gas from the many abandoned vehicles, so essentially endless fuel if you are taking your time, especially in the early zones.The game has a very spooky feel and some threatening sounds... ignore the sounds..they don't hurt you (mostly).  Not equipped to deal with a certain obstacle? Just drive around it. It's not as hard as it seems if you are prepared and cautious. The core concept is essentially a press your luck mechanic. Just don't be too greedy.The whole game, I only died once, and that was my 2nd run when I was still learning the ropes. My regular load out (aside from doors and panels) 2 side turbines, 1 solar panel, 1 side battery, Jump jacks and expanded rear-seat fuel tank, Live generator, Lim shield, Roof storage rack. I'd carry at least 3 of each type of repair kit, 1.5 to 2 of each important tool, 2 spare all terrain tires in the top storage, and Loot and scoot to have resources for crafting if you need more than that.So, Very good game.. but I wished they did not make route planning so inflexible, and I wish the game was harder near the end. I found mid-game actually harder with the rarity of chemicals for putty, until I unlocked the blowtorch. Come prepared and pay attention to what you are doing and end-game is easy, even if they are forcing you to go where you don't want to go.

_childDocuments_.review: The beat up station wagon I've found somehow holds together through the freak electrical storms, bladed jelly things and an ornery floating steel mass which I've taken to calling a "crash bastard." I'm also faring better since I discovered this car. The coughing fits have eased and there's less blood than before. Maybe something I can exploit when I escape this place. I've settled into a routine of driving along shifting roads and scavenging from wrecks that I know will be swallowed up by the instability storm after I leave. The car, my one companion, is a jealous friend; The coughing fits resume if I stray too far from it. It's got good taste in music at least, which makes it a more tolerable friend than most. The car might be talking to me. It seems affectionate, but this sparks a new conundrum as I'm not entirely sure we're separate entities anymore. Can a finger feel affection towards its hand? For that matter, am I the hand or am I the finger? I need to get out of here. The car is definitely talking to me. It thanked me with a playful beep when I swapped out a ruined tire for a fresh one. Will it one day be grateful when I am replaced, ruined by the Zone and swapped out for a fresh driver? I'd like to think it would cry for me in some way. Maybe spray some wiper fluid in my honor. I've started waking up in the car. While this ought to concern me, I'm more concerned that I can't remember going to sleep. The last thing I recall is switching off the ignition. That and vivid nightmares of jagged metal beasts erupting from beneath me, slashing at my  . . . was it my feet I saw? Start. Drive. Scavenge. Drive. Refuel. Repair. Drive. Drive. Drive. Off.- Fans of atmospheric survival games.- Anyone who wants to play in a homebrew D&D game based on the film/book "Annihilation" - Anyone who names their car.- Anyone who played Subnautica and resisted the temptation to Wiki anything before completing 1 play through.- Saving during trips not yet available. Be prepared for long hauls.- Some performance chop in tunnels or during heavy weather effects on my well above specs PC.- UI takes some adjusting and game systems are not always transparent (and not in a "The fun is figuring it out!" way. More in a "I have no idea what scans are or how to use them, but I have 3 of them." way.) - Strong world building and some of the most captivating AI I've seen in these types of games. If you enjoy the classic base building trappings of the survival genre, this is closer to those roots than Pacific Drive. Also a more classic horror experience, which might be more up your alley if you prefer terror over dread.Are you a terror or dread player? I've got a test if you need it: If mentioning  forced you to pause and ponder the end state of the protagonist just now, you're a dread person. If you've never heard of the short story, give it a read or a play (there's a Steam version), and if you turn out to be a dread person, I'm sorry.Like this review? _childDocuments_.review: This is unironically one of my favorite games of the past several years. It's *not* a hardcore survivalcraft or a high-octane driving simulator, despite what some of the trailers might look like. Instead, it's a fairly chill meandering ride through a couple different biomes with occasional bouts of frantic scrambling to get somewhere fast. Between each run, there's a cathartic pause where you swap worn-out parts, upgrading your tools to be better, and just kinda chilling around.There's a story, it's told entirely by voices over the radio and is pretty boilerplate, but I enjoyed the voice acting and found the back-and-forth actually endearing, even if nothing felt particularly new. But speaking of radio, the soundtrack is *incredible* and might be the most thematically appropriate collections of songs I've ever heard in a game. I don't think I've felt compelled to buy a VG soundtrack since Bastion, but this one (and several albums and EPs from the artists featured) was an almost immediate buy as well.To be clear, I don't think this game is for everyone, and it's got plenty of rough edges (that I'm hoping to see cleaned up). But that's mostly like weird UI bugs and some unclear mechanics/limited tutorial. But when it's all running together and you're blasting the radio while you scramble at top speed through a dark forest, watching the HP of your last spare tire and praying it holds long enough to let you limp home with your loot, man, what a game.,
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: Guys, you simply cannot lose 2-3 hours of progress because you have to leave. Read the tutorial, it's made extremely clear that the game saves at every level transition. A level takes 15-25 minutes to complete, so that is the most you can *ever* lose if you have to instantly leave and must shut the game down. The highest possible estimate for how much time you would lose to an average interruption is something like 12 minutes, and if you're very unlucky and are at the very end of a level but HAVE to leave instantly you may lose 25 minutes in this worst-case scenario. That sucks, I get it. But it's not hours of progress. A momentary distraction comes near the end of a level? Just pause the game and finish the run when you get a second. This isn't actually an issue in my eyes especially compared to a lot of roguelikes (I simply can't play RoR2 for example because of its save system), I had to leave a lot while playing and never lost significant progress at any point.If you're reading negative reviews about how the game is unplayable for people with a job or children, ignore them completely. I don't have the ability to sit and play for long sessions and have interruptions all the time, yet the most progress I ever lost was when my power went out and sent me back by about 10 minutes. I don't know if people just don't know how to read or can't see the save icon or whatever, but you don't lose a *run* when you quit the game. The save system is a non-issue unless you genuinely can't play for more than a few minutes at a time, and the ability to instantly return to the shop with everything intact nullifies any problems entirely.Finally getting to the review, the game is very good. It's paced very well to keep feeding you new content and gameplay until about the 25 hour mark, and if you were to rush through the game you'd finish the story in 15ish hours. If you get a lot out of progression that's one of Pacific Drive's strongest points; upgrading your car feels fantastic and the progression tree will keep you occupied for as long as you want to keep playing. For me (not a completionist, but I am generally pretty thorough) my playthrough lasted around 31 hours; if I were more geared towards completion filling out the entire tech tree would take about 50 and I think the gameplay loop would run out of steam long before that point, so completionists beware.The game runs pretty well for how good it looks, but cranking shadows up (which is the most important setting for making the game look good) takes my performance down by half going from Medium to Ultra. On my 1070ti and Ryzen 5 2600x I averaged 65fps and basically never saw a dip below 55fps at all Ultra settings with Medium shadows, which dropped to 35 avg/30 min on Ultra shadows. I imagine an up to date PC could easily crank out 80+fps on maxed settings, but being able to stay over 60 with almost maximum settings on my ancient rig is pretty solid considering how good the game looks as a whole. It's not fantastically optimized, and an improvement to performance on high shadow settings would be welcome, but it's far from an unoptimized game as well.Visuals: 8/10Atmosphere: 10/10Performance: 6.5/10Stability: 9/10, I have never had a crash but some reviewers say they have issues with crashingSoundtrack: 10/10Story: 7/10, the story is above average and the voice acting is excellent which bumps it up a notchGameplay Loop: 8/10, it's serviceable and is carried by really satisfying progression and fun driving mechanics, but harvesting resources can get slow and repetitive at timesAccessibility: 9/10, the only game I've played with a more robust suite of accessibility settings for gameplay is Celeste with its assist mode, which is saying a lot.Overall: 8.4/10, This is one of the best games of the year so far in my opinion.

Definitely worth the money for the amount of gameplay. The saves aren't that big of a deal and does add that risk/reward thrill. I only died like twice through my play-through. I love the scaling of the upgrades and zone difficulty. Tbh the game is the hardest at the beginning-middle section of the game. My longest time in a zone was like an hour and a half (looting every POI on the map). One thing I would change would be a better Pneumatic locker system to where you can sort alphabetically or by type of item as it was a bit annoying trying to find the dumpster pearls I would throw in there by accident lol. I think the quirk system is really neat and some I left on my vehicle because I liked them such as when I put the car in park the passenger side front door would open making it easy to grab an anchor quick and save a button press. Overall I really enjoyed the game and think the Devs did a great job with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Outstandingly well designed game. Massive recommendation from me.The overall game is just dang good. The gameplay loop is really enjoyable, though I accidentally turned it into a chore a few times by ultimately just not playing intelligently. The base away from base (car = mobile base, garage = home base) is such a delightful move. The quirk system! Ohhhhh the quirk system. Hilarious to experience, sometimes frustrating on the surface, but an absolutely boss little mechanic of troubleshooting turned into a minigame. Progression feels good once you understand the elements. The story, flavor text/lore, world, and characters/writing are great.I only encountered one event that would cause a crash, and a scant few bugs that weren't significant. One downside I found throughout the game was the endgame resources, which are incredibly hard to find, and the craftables you make with them, which are better than everything else but also entirely unnecessary. That feels like it either needs a rebalance or it's in the game currently in preparation for future content that'll be tougher. Or, I guess, the third option is that it's just something for folks to do if they really can't get enough of the game and just want to keep playing. I suppose another, which is commonly complained about, is the 'wearing out' of items. I don't mind the mechanic, but I definitely struggle to appreciate the unpredictability. What I'd love to see is some kind of stat that shows the likelihood of 'wearing out' given the amount of damage its taken (or whatever metric the game uses to determine this) when I scan the vehicle/item. Ex., if the item has taken X lifetime damage, it displays "40% chance of 'worn out' (or whatever) status," then after the next run the item has taken Y lifetime damage and displays "67% chance of 'worn out' (or whatever) status." This way, I can take a backup of the item in the car if I want to sacrifice some storage space for security.TIPS (no spoilers per se, but includes some vague notes on progression and gameplay loop). 1) It's a better idea to progress the initial story/missions rather than overstaying in the starter zone. 2) Scan EVERYTHING. Not only is there good lore and flavor, but scanning is also literally necessary for research progression as well as being notified of the upcoming threats on your next planned trip. Ex., you have to scan X to research A; you'll have ??? on your maps for your planned trip, which is a threat you haven't scanned, so you don't know what exactly to expect until you get there even if you've experienced it before but didn't scan it.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw this game, all I could think of was the car segment from Half Life 2: Episode 2. I thought of how instantly attached I got to that rust bucket, and how cool it felt driving it around in a mad dash with hybrid sort of on-foot/on-wheels gameplay.Whether or not this was inspired at all by that, it really fits the bill. The entirety of this game is spent scavenging for materials as you traverse a dilapidated, overgrown, and extremely hazardous rural PNW-inspired environment, a so-called exclusion zone. You're semi-tethered to your multi-purpose shelter/storage container/transportation as you roam about. Your mission is largely focused on scavenging, upgrading, and delving deeper into the more dangerous parts of the zone. There's an overarching plot told by way of radio conversations, it's well acted & delivered and at times quite engaging but ultimately a bit limited by how disjointed it can feel from the gameplay. Many a time one of the characters would be pouring their heart out about their life's work, meanwhile I'm being harassed by a hovering alien tow truck dragging me off a cliff and into a pile of exploding mannequins. It's there, it's worth following along with, but it never really shakes the feeling of being a bit... draped over the core gameplay.Speaking of, the core gameplay loop is perfect if you like that sort of The Long Dark style scavenging where the environment is actively hostile. The zone is full of all sorts of things you need to keep an eye out for, and if you die you might lose most of your stuff. You mostly bounce around landmarks carefully looking for things to take back to the garage to upgrade your car. Available upgrades span a wide array of utility options to the point where you ultimately will wind up with a car that's all your own and more reminiscent of KITT or the Batmobile than a normal car, replete with active and passive countermeasures for all sorts of challenges.Customization actually tries to play a big role in the game  (because they really want you to get attached to this car). You're encouraged to decorate it with paints, decal kits, stickers, accessories, etc. that you find in your travels. My main problem is that what my car looked like had more to do with the function (i.e. what kind of armor or tools were on it) than with what I wanted aesthetically. Some of the panel types don't accept paint or decals very well and I wish I could be way more specific with the paint than only being able to pick the main color for the entire panel. I don't expect every game to be Armored Core but... it's hard not to compare. I was ultimately pretty happy with how my car looked but it felt very much like I filled in a paint-by-numbers and less like I created anything my own. Even something as simple as being able to select secondary colors on panels would go a long way.Speaking of customization though, the level control the player has in this game over the experience is unprecedented and extremely cool. You can adjust just about anything you want as far as difficulty goes. Don't like having to repair after each run? You can turn on an option that full heals you when you complete a run. Want to reduce the material grind? Lower the amount required for crafting with a simple slider. You can change the consequences for failed runs, change the consumption rate of gas, anything really. This game is as casual or hardcore as you want it to be.Also I have to mention: the custom radio update was brilliant and I had a ton of fun with it. I did just so happen to have an old mp3 player full of 15+ year old music laying around so it kind of just worked out perfectly. Highly recommend trying it out.I'm all over the place and this is getting a bit long but I think I more than got my money's worth out of this game, and it's an experience all its own that I won't soon forget. If you're in the mood for a bit of a self-guided, (at times) pensive experience, give this one a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: The game hooked me for about 3 hours, it was a ton of fun and the idea was great, the anomalies were interesting and capturing.Unfortunately after 3 hours I saw that it was mainly the repetitive task of gathering scrap which was uninteresting especially after doing it 100's of times. Another problem was not being able to save during a mission, it meant that I'd have to do the same mission that could take hours over again if I had to leave IRL. The UI is very intimidating when starting the game, and I feel like I still miss a lot of the important information when taking a quick glance at it.I'd hate to criticize without recommending changes to make it better, so the below tips would help a lot:1. Create a checkpoint system that doesn't make you abandon your trip! This would add a lot of value to the game and fix a lot of heartache.2. Add more loot to containers or more containers. The scrapping grind is ridiculously long and repetitive. 3. Reduce the amount of time it takes to scrap things, this would further reduce the amount of scrapping which is annoying.Overall, its a great start and has potential to be a fun game to come back to.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: This is not what I expected this game to be. The graphics are terrible and the lighting is about the worst I have ever experienced in a game. In the day time when you enter a building it is pitch black inside. You need to be using road flares to see anything, even after boosting the brightness in the game settings. There is no flashlight. At night, everything is pitch black, so you need to be making road flares all the time just so you can see 5 feet in front of you. There is no way to fast forward the night either, which seemed to last for about 2 hours or game play.Since it is a driving game I started using my controller, but it is seriously bugged out. When you are in any of the options screens, the controller skips windows and options. For example, scrolling down the controls list in the option settings, it skips every second option or so, making it impossible to change any type of settings with the controller. Even in the car, the controller causes you to miss half of the options by skipping over them. You push once and it skips the next one and highlights the third instead.The car is such a piece of garbage that I just stopped caring about it after a few hours of game play. Driving it about 2 miles or so deteriorates every part of the car including all body panels (even if you don't hit a single thing with the car). So, you need to be repairing it all the time which is tedious and annoying. Also, it drives like a WW1 tank.The game is very linear, there is no replayability to it. You drive down these single roads that are point to point and every 50 meters there is a something blocking the road. Pointless road blocks like a barrel with blockades around it or a huge pile of rocks that looks like it just dropped from the sky. There are also these flying robots everywhere that stick suction cups to the car and then it drags the car into the roadblocks or just smashes you into trees.In the beginning I was spending all my time trashing old abandoned cars (which all look exactly the same) to get materials, which in fact, I found out I didn't really need. There is no save function, unless you are back at the garage, so when I left the game after 1.5 hours to go get something to eat, I ended up losing all my progress and it started me back at the beginning of the game.The buildings in the game are all just copy and pasted from about 5 different models or so. The world is empty of any life, other than yourself. The entire experience just felt bland, pointless and frustrating. Since I cannot get a refund, being past the 2 hour mark, I will just be uninstalling and hiding the game, as I won't be touching this dissapointment again.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: The game's fun if you're part of a certain archetype of game enjoyers, one that I happen to be a proud member of.So! It's a fun game, especially for the first bit of every area where you're just exploring and looting. It's generally paced well, though having to go through every previous junction to get to areas 2 and 3 is really annoying in terms of gameplay. If you're one of those people who has the virtue of patience and has decided they want a mind-control station wagon as their best friend, this is for you!Verdict: Good if you're patient enough to actually enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: It has a certain vibe going, especially with the ability to add your own music. (but not streams as far as I know)I will give it that. There aren't a whole lot of games that will cater to this.You won't hear much of it though, because contrary to the trailers, I find myself spending more time outside of the car than in. That said it has an unforgivable sin to me. You cannot save mid mission/map!It will reset you and put you back at the start. These missions are long, so if you die, or simply want to stop. You loose everything. And if you didn't save on a multi map tour?..oof. There go potentially several hours down the drain.It also tries to inconvenience you at every stop.Half my inventory is assorted tools that I need for exploring. Flashlights, crowbars, disassembly tool, radar(ish), hammer, and more....And if they break along the way? you have to track back to your car because you cannot craft even the smallest thing yourself. And some stuff you cannot craft mid mission at all.This isn't an open world either, you go from map to map.There is also an odd mix of high rez and low-rez to even ...no-rez stuff. where it will be purely vertex colours.It's atmospheric, but not particularly pretty up close.I dunno, I'm not gonna say it's a bad game, but it can be exhausting. You're not missing anything by not playing it either.The deathknell to me was finally getting stuck on a tree with no way out except for loosing all my progression for that map. And I did not have it in me to continue after that.

_childDocuments_.review: The first half is really rather enjoyable. The core gameplay loop of entering areas and exploring is really well done. The variety of random factors really makes it feel like you're doing something new and interesting. Nice soundtrack. Neat details about the car, like manually controlling the hand break and lights, as well as the little quirks like wipers turning on when you slam the door. There's a satisfying feeling of getting things done and improving your car and base. The story was also compelling, up until the whatever that ending was. There's enough fun in the first half of the game to recommend checking it out.Now, there's still issues though. Chief among them is hard crashing the entire PC once every five hours of gameplay for me.  No improvement with the recent big patch. The performance is also rather poor. I had to crank everything to Medium on a top end machine to get stable 60fps. And this game really benefits from all the higher end environmental effects and details. The gameplay gets kinda repetitive in the second half. Exploring is fun, but maintaining the car can get really rather dull. A lot of the upgrades fell like they're mostly similar, a lot more expensive, and you know they won't last very long anyway. It's generally rather hard to grind some of the high end materials too. Finishing the game is a lot easier than getting through the tech tree. I think I would enjoy the upgrade path a lot more if it was more permanent and linear, rather than having to choose between having radiation shielding or corrosion resistance.There's also no way to save while the run is in progress. The game kinda saves when you enter a new area, but it does't make it obvious and it doesn't feel reliable. I only know because of the crashes.
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, if for no other reason that it's innovative, maybe even unique, in that I haven't seen anything else like it, but then I'm not a big time gamer.  The idea driving this game is just short of genius.  You're a person in some kind of post apocalyptic era with only a car to help you survive.   There are some glaring bummers with this thing.  For one thing, the collection of resources is mind numbing.  It feels very much like work and not play.  It would be fine if the caches of items got bigger or more plentiful as the game wore on, or if there were large caches (besides the trucks that are too uncommon) once in a while.  Or if there were some device by which to harvest these resources without the same, soul destroying process of breaking into a place, opening crates and lockers and whatever and collecting TINY amounts of stuff at a time.  Also, there are a few resources that are more necessary than others and they are too scarce.  Way too scarce.  The other MAJOR problem here is that to advance to the new places you have to DRIVE THROUGH THE SAME TERRITORIES OVER AND OVER AGAIN.  This one is very nearly a fatal flaw from which you're tempted to just walk away from this slog. But the game is just good enough to keep you going.  If there is a way to teleport, I haven't seen it or discovered it yet, after many many dozens of hours of play.  A few of the anomalies are too hard to find also.  IF the dev team could fix this stuff, this would be a true work of art.

I haven't modified any myself but it was good to see.  More points to the devs for allowing players to customize their experience the way they want. _childDocuments_.review: This is a perfect example of a game that makes me wish steam had a deeper review system at times.I somehow have 40 hours in this game, it in no way felt that long but it also doesnt feel like it was really worth it. Theres points in the game especially early on where it clicks right and feels great, at other times this game feels like an utter slog. There's what I will call 3 sections to this game, Looting, Exploration and Car.Looting is the really basic, you either loot a container, possibly locked behind an item requirement or you harvest a thing with the needed item, not really much to complain about hereExploration is discovering and learning the lay of each map section- this is done via a map, I personally really dislike this as it prevents you from continuing down a line you know exists (because its pointing towards an already discovered map section) or sometimes the random event happening there marks the point as a dead end preventing you from going there or you'll fail your run outright (unless you change the difficulty to prevent loss of items)Last section is Car: Car is driving, car is maintenance, car is inventory management. You can craft new parts for the car some with special abilities, some with extra storage. The issue is a lot of these are frankly pointless, the game is a massive grind for resources to build anything or get enough core energy of the right kind to research and then build everything and I found it so pitifully easy most of the time that the "difficulty" amounts to just annoying you by needing to fix everything again or damaging parts of the car, early on I could spend ages looting every map meticulously and id come back to the garage with zero issues, late game Id get back to the garage spending the same amount of time going 4 maps deep and the car would just naturally be so damaged from everything they throw at you that apart from a few times nothing was in dire situations but you'd end up spending like 10-20 minutes sorting and replacing everything. Then they introduce Quirks, sometimes boones, usually annoyances ranging from unnoticeable like your fuel gauge not displaying right to your doors flying open or falling off when you turn your wipers on.The driving feels pretty good but the game clearly feels like its meant to be like Chernobylite but lacks the actual development and variety that has to keep it going. Now one thing I will commend this on wholeheartedly is that its nice to see more engaging action focused games that don't centre violence and has a nice bit of queer rep in it, but this leads onto the story. I think the story is very hit and miss, it has you do active things to progress the story but you are also a completely passive entity in the story. You are not important or a main character, the car is and the 3(-4) characters on the radio you hear are the main characters. You as The Driver are exactly that, you just drive to the points you do and never directly interact with the characters, and as a silent protagonist that clearly arrived in this area for SOME reason we never find out why they ended up here or why they just end up just staying here. Im usually alright with silent protags but usually theres more evident reasons why these happen and from a meta standpoint when youre asked to keep going after the story ends you have to ask, why.Theres only to my knowledge one single required car part to finish the story and you will likely need to grind to get it, the game also never prevents you from accessing the map that forces you to use it so you can end up softlocking yourself (This was my single "death" where I had to abandon the run, as no exit was provided on the side of the map I could access) it just leads me to ask whats the point of 90% of the upgrades. Yes armoured panels and doors are useful, offroad tires are useful and some of the tools are useful but again most of the tools dont get you much more than what you need to get about.I cant say I didnt enjoy this game at times but it feels so disjointed at times between the pointless progression, the repetitive maps that take too long to get through, the scarce loot especially on the high end. If you are wanting a good driving game with roguelite elements and dont mind being bottle necked by the story pulling you about and like a good grind this will be great for you. I do genuinely hope either updates or DLC down the line can rectify this but I personally dont see myself returning to this anytime soon

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, unique in many ways, and I really like how quirky it is. The menus and the amount of information on screen can be overwhelming though, but there is a certain aesthetic the game maintains with the cluttered menus. I really like the scifi themes explored here (so far at least), it seems to share a lot from the Strugatsky Brothers' "Roadside Picnic," but is more accessible than the film adaptation "Stalker" (Tarkovsky, 1979).
_childDocuments_.name: Pacific Drive

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a very surprising experience for me, and let me tell you it's a positive one. A game about driving around in car isn't something that I would normally be interested in because it sounds simply dull and pointless. That was however not the case here. Primarily it was two things that kept me engaged:. There's only a few characters and you don't get to actively interact with them - but it's clear that the makers of the game wanted to make flawed but loveable characters who you actually care about. The characters was one of two big highlights for me. The second one was :Driving the car slowly at night, full rain hitting the roof of the car that almost becomes deafening. The wipers are on, there's some lightning strikes in the far off. You see creepy statues staring at you that almost seems as if they are becoming more and more... Sometimes I was actively spooked and completely hooked (no jumpscares, just creepy). Sometimes I was just driving and listening to the rain, and completely lost in the world as "The driver". Characters and atmosphere, it's a full journey. Much else is good too. The gameplay is surprisingly complex without going over the top. The story is intriguing, but not the best. The save system works fine for me, but I can understand certain frustrations with it. The cosmetics and building of the car, upgrading, is fun. All in all, other then a couple of bugs here and there, I have nothing to complain about. The game is worth it's price and more.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played a game quite like Pacfic Drive. It borrows from so many genres, yet the end result is quite the original experience.At its core, the gameplay loop is looter-extractor a la Escape from Tarkov. It has atmospheric elements and an exclusion zone setting straight out of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games. It has survival mechanics and a crafting system similar to games such as The Forest, The Long Dark, Raft, etc.More driving simulator than walking simulator, the car is the real star of the show. It's pretty much your custom mobile base. Much like Subnautica series, you'll be exploring instances of the zone (called junctions) via your car, driving from POI to POI, getting out only when necessary to loot and occasionally scan new anomalies (which unlocks new research). Wash, rinse, repeat then return to your real home base (a garage) so you can unload everything only to plan your next trip out in the zone. If, like me, you're a sucker for looting and hoarding, you'll love this kind of game loop.But that's maybe where the game's limitations start to show. Because that's what you'll be doing 90% of the time. This is a single player game and there is indeed a progression albeit paper-thin narrative. The game does not force you to progress the story, so you are free to visit or revist locations at-will.The character voice acting is excellent and there is a little bit of lore building via audio logs. At times the main story can not progress until your tech research has advanced sufficiently. This is done on purpose as to give first-time players some time to catch up on the game's reasonably deep tech tree (that loot is there for a reason). I really appreciated being able to play the game at my own pace. If you only care about plowing through the main story, you could easily beat this game in less than 10 hours. I spread things out and spent 80 hours on my first playthrough.Oh, and the music is excellent.One detail I would like to point out is that this game allows you customize many of its "quality of life" features. Basically, it lets you turn off the hand-holding (i.e. highlighting items you can interact with). A polarizing topic these days for sure. The point here is that we are allowed to tailor the "quality of life" aspects of the game beyond the defaults. This is something rarely found in a game today. Gaming studios take a real good look at what these devs are doing here, because you should be doing it too. I can't tell you how agonizing it is to watch some hype gameplay of some upcoming title only to witness the same "quality of life" feature that I utterly loathe due to its immersion ruining. If instead you present options to tailor these features in your game, then not only will I be more inclined to purchase your game, but the only thing left to debate is what the default should be. It's win for everyone.I think the developers are on to something here. The game itself is a great concept and there's certainly ideas yet to be explored (something a bigger budget could make happen). I'm already looking forward to a Pacific Drive 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, this is an *incredible* game with loads of promise. I feel bad saying "don't buy."However;The game disrespects your time and isn't balanced at all towards you ever failing. It has numerous ways to screw yourself over. It's quite buggy in dangerous places like mission checkpoints. It has a clumsy upgrade pathway that means if you ever want anything nice you have to forgo future progression. Explanations are minimal and scattered in the lore, which stinks when you get "fragile" and your car is destroyed in moments because you didn't know that fragile was a nightmare, not a mild downside. The most essential pathway upgrades are locked behind obscene resource costs, and worst of all: the hardest mission is the midpoint, which has a number of unintended consequences:If you fail it; you're exceedingly likely to screw yourself over twice if you can make it back. The resources necessary to try again are then all locked in that final location, and therefore can't help you. The precautions you take from that point on are basically pointless because the difficulty nosedives again.... and this difficulty spike is the very first time they give you the "drive quickly through checkpoints" test with barely any explanation.The game is tuned to hook you. It's tuned for nothing else. They're *almost* generous with the difficulty settings, but there's no way to get a helping hand on the materials grind... and no hints that the entire back half of the tech tree is basically pointless and you can easily complete the game with crude parts and a functional **mission critical bumper.**I hope they'll eventually iron out the kinks. I also hope to come back to this game and this review and swap them to a "worth the cost" once they release some DLC that gives you something to do once you've completed the decent story.. and maybe gives you a better ending. Right now, the game is just too rough after the intro gameplay loop falls off to justify this price point. One day it might be, the engine of this rust bucket is a diamond. (ironic as I never even got **near** the final engine upgrade).Final afterthought: in other roguelikes you bypass the boring looting you do in the early game, or speed it up. That never happens here. You only ever gain in efficiency of usage, so your handful of bulbs go slightly further. You'll have a zillion scrap, and still be opening the same chemical lockers right before you complete the story that you were opening in the start. It's cool that the car is never all that good. It's lousy that your experience is never all that much better. Sap condensers feel like the devs going "oh no that's not fun", but there's 3 other resource trees that also need that refinement pass, or a slider to turn in difficulty settings.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a middle option on steam, not just yes to buy or no, do not buy. This game is addicting and fun when it works. So thumbs up for that. However, there are still a lot of bugs. You can go into game play options and set them how you want, which is always a cool feature, but for me at least, those options do not stay that way. They reset themselves back to normal settings constantly and I have to keep going back into the settings and change them to what I want again and again. I have turned off the  car quarks many many times cause I think their super annoying and the system to figuring them out is also annoying. But, even with that feature turned off, my car still has like 5 quarks.... yes, I said FIVE! Remember, I turned quarks OFF in the settings... so I should have zero quarks... but I have 5 of them. So the option to turn off quarks does not work at all. it's pointless to even try. Five quarks is a lot of issues to deal with at one time. I have solved and fixed 2 of them already, so why do I still have FIVE? One of them is a  game breaking quark for me {if it's even a quark at all and not just a bug}. I have had to restart my game many times cause my car will only drive left... not straight, and not to the right.... only left... no matter what I try to do... most people know 3 lefts just makes a circle. DUH. lol. Which equals to "game over for you" cause you cannot drive at all. Can we please not make a quark that is a game breaking thing? When I get back to the garage after being killed by driving in endless circles, I cannot leave the garage because, again, circles... not straight, no right turns. I can't go anywhere.  I have to restart my game...which fixes the issue, but I lose hours of precious gaming time...but then I can drive like a normal person again for a while, until it happens again... which can take a while, but is always during the worst times. _childDocuments_.review: I really love this game, so this may seem a little lengthy...In it's current state, there are a lot of unfortunate bugs I ran into that honestly brought the game down a bit for me. There are also some issues with the way the UI works and the way certain game mechanics work that could be improved with some tweaking or just an explanation...literally any kind of explanation. Yeah, there is a *lot* that the game doesn't tell you, for better or worse, depending on how you look at it. I am a fan of discovering things for myself but some of this stuff is confusing. The biggest issue for me, by far, was the route planner map. At 60+ hours, I just finished the game and I could never understand how I am supposed to properly use it. I understand the basics but also had to go out of my way and do some Google searching to figure out other things. But even THEN, there are still multiple questions I have that remain unclear: What do certain symbols mean, what is the point of scanning areas, why can I only scan *some* areas, why does it not let me go in a southwards-direction, why can I only initially pick an area that has an exit *yet* I can still end up traveling to a dead-end anyways, etc. The whole things needs a complete re-work in my opinion. I only had 1 hard crash but I did run into several game-progressing blockers that forced me to "end" runs prematurely. (thankfully, you can quit without penalty to loosing your items!)However, the good stuff here that really had me hooked is the presentation of it all. The aesthetic, the spooky atmosphere, the colors and tones, the 90's vibe and style, the writing, the music, and that car! It all works really well together and it's right up my alley. The gameplay loop is great and I was always excited to test out new upgrades on my next runs. While the story is fairly basic, the voice-acting is what really helps to sell it. Really solid performances from everyone. My only gripe is sometimes it can be impossible to pay attention to the more important story bits happening because I would be busy trying to make it through a harrowing area and wasn't paying attention to what was being said.Pacific Drive is very much a game about getting in and out of the car hundreds of times, looting and crafting, having to repair hundreds of components, and spending a lot of time at the garage in-between runs. You will be pulling on the hand brake, turning the ignition, and getting annoyed at anomalys for dozens of hours. This is not going to be a game for everyone, for a lot of completely understandable reasons. But I loved it.To give it a number score, I'd have to give it a 7/10, and that's a HIGH 7 btw, but I'd bump it up to an 8 if they patch it up. I really hope this studio gets to make a sequel. There is so much room for improvement, and I really do mean that in the best way.Pacific Drive 2 could be a perfect game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a loot goblin who drives, why wouldn't l like this game.To expand on this a little more, this is effectively an extraction looter (as mentioned by another review). The main pull for me is the exploration aspects of constantly discovering new places and anomalies, the world building, as well as the surprisingly good writing and voice acting by the characters over the radio.Some low-level anomalies can appear to repeat, but you come to find not all anomalies are actually detrimental. You can learn to use many anomalies you come across to your advantage (either by design of the initial enemy, or by creative uses).I found the log entries you come across and can read/listen to were actually compelling, as there is a pretty fascinating story being told both within and outside of what is being directly fed to you in the main story missions. I'm only in the middle section of the game at this point as I've taken my time in the beginning to really stock up on loot, but the world hasn't lost its grip on my interest yet.As a final note: The dialogue and voice acting from the three main characters you're introduced to (Tobias, Francis, and Oppy) is surprisingly compelling. I don't know why I didn't expect it from this game, but it caught me by pleasant surprise regardless.If this game intrigues you, please pick it up. This is one of my favorite single player games to release in recent memory and it can only get better with additional content that will hopefully come in the future.Now open that gateway and drive, Breacher.
