_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review after I've 100%'d the game.In short, it's quite good. As other reviewers are keen to point out, the visuals and general aesthetic are incredible. The gameplay feels vaguely Bioshock-esque; use elemental abilities (and occasionally a bow and arrow) to defeat the endless onslaught of demons from taking over Shibuya. These abilities can be upgraded over time, as you save more souls and collect the power from the supernatural folklore creatures roaming about Japan. There are an insane amount of collectibles and side missions and interesting little tidbits to find out and about on the city streets.However, it is quite repetitive. There's a lot of the same kinds of missions, and encounters with any of the folklore creatures are almost always just copy -> pasted, albeit in a different, still pretty location. You gradually encounter more and different enemies to fight, but there isn't enough variety to keep the encounters constantly engaging and it can just boil down to "click on the bad guys". However, I did encounter a lot of enemies, given that I put the time in to save all the souls and collect all the collectibles, so if you're not looking to be a completionist then perhaps it'll end up alright for you. It was an enjoyable bout of fetch-questing, even if my brain was off for a lot of it.If you decide to buy the game, I would rush for the Summon Tengu ability as soon as you possibly can - it makes the platforming a lot less frustrating by being able to summon and then grapple onto something atop buildings. And you spend a LOT of time on buildings. I wish that the progression system was longer, since I found myself having reached max level with almost a third of the souls left to collect.There are 6 chapters in total, but the last two are very short. The bulk of the game will likely be played within the 4th chapter, as that's when you gain access to the entirety of the city. Completing it in its entirety took 35 hrs for me - I imagine a regular playthrough w/o collecting everything likely hovers around 15 - 20 hrs. I got this game as a birthday present, but if I was going to buy it myself, I would say what most others are - wait for a sale. I had quite a bit of fun playing it, but I know that I almost certainly won't play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire Tokyo is a slick action game with detail levels that require attention at all times lest you miss a tiny environmental story. The world is full of these. A person's last moments captured through a dog or cats thought. Or clothes laid out in an everyday task with a note nearby. It all has an eerie feel and, if you're like me and enjoy Japanese culture, you'll soak it all in. I've always wanted to visit Japan and this has stoked that fire with a stunningly accurate (from what I know) downsized version of Tokyo. It looks marvelous. The gameplay isn't incredibly deep but it did keep me going till the end. Most of the game is open world till the last two chapters and it let's you know well in advance that you can't go back. I could go on about this game but take out of this review that it's a lovingly crafted, ghostly, ethereal jaunt through Tokyo with a ghostly sidekick imbuing superpowers into you. I loved all the Japanese ghost story lore side quests and missions and the main story itself is worth seeing through to it's emotional conclusion. A solid 8.5/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves a really strong 7.5/10. I would recommend this game, but only buy it on sale. I played this game for (according to Steam) 34.8 hours and have 100% of the achievements completed. This is including the half hour that I've probably taken a break from the game, and the other half hour trying to look up a game guide for the food in this game as it is a part of one of the achievements for 100%.This game is fantastic in all sorts of ways, in terms of visual styles, gameplay, lore and general feeling I enjoyed it for the most part.I played with a PS5 controller and the haptic feedback on, and I can tell you that there is pretty much no other way that you should be playing the game. (So much so to the point that I probably wouldn't recommend the game without this feature otherwise.) It's a big feature that had me tied to the game, and I think that it gave me a greater feeling of immersion that you absolutely cannot get with a keyboard.I think one of the big drawbacks for me was the fact that this game seemingly was terribly optimized/ or just didn't run very well on my system. I bought a 3080 12gb to enjoy a lot of the games that have been coming out recently, but this game just absolutely kills my system and itself while playing. I had to play with RTX off to be able to get anywhere in the game, and whenever a cutscene would come on it would skip and stutter while the audio would keep playing which absolutely killed all feeling while playing through the game. (I looked up guides and was told to switch off of my native 1440p to 1080p just to make sure that my cutscenes wouldn't completely die while playing. Which... :/ )Aside from the obvious technical issues that I faced, the story was short and simple, but very well too short. The story took up probably 10 of the 34 hours that I spent on this game, which is a bummer because I really enjoyed the story beats and the characters that they introduced. They're not necessarily colorful by design, but the personalities were enjoyable.The side missions are an 11/10, and I really wish there were more. A lot of them included traditional folktales with a spin for inclusion into the games lore, and it works amazingly. The side missions are also where the most jumpscares are included and made it terribly fun for me because I love horror.The gameplay loop is kind of stale. You go from clearing an area of enemies to clear an area of fog, you explore the area where you can collect any one of the 7 collectible item types, you upgrade your magical attacks and then you do the whole thing over again. While I was able to do this within 34 hours, the 24 hours/ day's worth of time that I took to collect all of these collectibles was a grueling task that I wouldn't recommend to most people.I honestly think that you can complete the game without the loop getting too stale, but only if you don't go out of your way to 100% the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Weirdly unadventurous for an adventure game.Everything else aside, that’s my biggest gripe. Clearly Bethesda has an appetite for ‘safe’ at the moment, because they’re publishing stuff that doesn’t really innovate. Ghostwire is exactly the kind of environmental explore-fight-collect RPG they love, molded in the image of games like Prey, Deathloop and the hallowed Dishonored. Unlike these predecessors, Ghostwire feels very paint-by-numbers. It is obviously mimicking, and in doing so loses a unique identity of its own. Evil Japanese spirits meets pixelated elemental abilities should be a stand-out gimmick, but Ghostwire manages to make it bland.The story is really shaky, and from the very beginning things are grim, with a hackneyed ‘save  your sister’ motivation. The story beats are labored and the scripting minimal, the plot veering between laughably vague and deeply insipid - but the glaring issue, narratively speaking, is the protagonist. Akira is so , and KK so pointlessly vague and smug. The whole plot rests on them, as the repetitive nature of the side-quests and the empty nature of the world do little to immerse you in the story. But they’re both utterly wooden and uninteresting, so the end result is you left wandering around on the sidewalk with two unpleasant dudes.For those who don’t care for narrative, the visuals are probably the main draw, and they’re a matter of taste. Some will find the detailed facsimile of Tokyo endlessly appealing, and others will be underwhelmed at what feels like any other digital cityscape. Ultimately, I didn’t find that the looks alone could sustain my interest.The final nail in Ghostwire’s coffin was combat. There’s a lack of variation, both in enemies and in approaches you can take. All encounters boil down to ‘stealth, or ping away at range while juggling ammo’ and it gets old fast. There’s no interesting combo system, and no real depth or payoff to the skill tree. Those awesome looking spirits all have very limited combat behaviour, and I found myself avoiding encounters only a few hours in. With this, the anemic Redfall, and the excruciatingly bad reception Starfield received, it’s starting to feel like Bethesda has dropped the ball in a major way. One can only hope that they wake up a bit and return to innovation over these sorts of cynical repetitions. In the meantime, I’m going to start looking at their products with a lot more cynicism, and I recommend you do the same. You can start by not buying this one.

The side quests, the collectibles, and even loads of notes dotted around the map all contribute to the worldbuilding of this fictionalized Shibuya and it's absolutely fantastic. Expect a ridiculous amount of detail as well as the entire thing being just a gigantic wad of fanservice for Japanese folklore and culture. Whoever invented that Daikyo omikuji achievement though? There's a special place in hell just for you.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Visually pretty and somewhat fresh, but suffers from a somewhat repetitive gameplay, uninvolving story and tiny niggling issues.Ghostwire: Tokyo is a  horror-themed first person parkour action in a sandbox urban environment with both ancient, modern, and sci-fi-ish influences on its aesthetics, set in Tokyo.Gameplay-wise it's  like your typical Ubisoft sandbox formula, except that instead of "exploring" from this game's Ubi-tower analog, you cleanse a deadly mystical mist, thus allowing you to access the areas that you previously were not able to. Otherwise it's not that much different: there are side missions, main missions, lots of enemies all over that you can fight, sneak past, or parkour away from, and, of course, lots of collectibles.Combat is definitely somewhat unexpected: first, it's very much action-heavy, with blocking, parrying, and dodging (all in first person), but also your offense is actually shooting elemental magic from your hands, so it's definitely not a survival horror or anything like that. While it  works fine, I personally have two main gripes with the game's combat: first, out of the three "weapons" you have, only one (Wind) has both a decent projectile speed AND range, and even then it's not even close to being a hitscan weapon. Combine this fact that a lot of enemies in this game can be pretty fast and move in somewhat unpredictable ways, and some can fly, it's  easy to waste your very limited "ammunition" for anything other than the Wind (which also has the lowest damage, but the highest possible ammo cap by far), and not so easy to regain it mid-combat. Second, some enemy types are truly obnoxious: invisible ones that teleport when you hit them, underground/water ones that can stay there pretty much indefinitely (a few times they literally  while there), and pretty much all the flying ones bar the basic tiny ghosts are huge pains.Visually, the game has a lot of cool tricks, and, especially with RTX on, it looks pretty damn good. I'm not sure I understand  design decisions in this regard, like, there's a lot of almost Matrix-ish floating symbols, the glowing lines on the protagonist's hands have this circuitboard aesthetic, and the villains are all dressed in this very modern urbanwear with glowy lines on it, but they were still interesting.Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the story. It's a sandbox, so it already is at a disadvantage there, but I was just not really sold on it at all. There's a disaster which already claimed hundreds of thousands of lives and is about to result in a total apocalypse, but it's somehow all supposed to be a personal story about taking responsibility, communicating your feelings, and not running away, and it just doesn't work. You barely interact with the villain, of which only one is actually , and your sister, who is supposed to be the main emotional anchor for the protagonist, disappears from the game in the first chapter and is not even seen conscious until the very last one.On the other hand, every shopkeeper in the game is a floating two-tailed chubby cat wearing a tiny cat-sized kimono and singing in teeny adorable meows, so it's the best game ever.

I'm a big fan of the Japanese culture, going out of my way to learn various things about the country and its folklore so the setting is a big plus for me. The main gameplay loop of combat is a bit repetitive but not terrible (though I wish I could figure out the timing for the perfect blocking better, I've done it now two times in frantic moments) and the exploration gameplay is fun if you are a fan of collect-a-thon games like I am. I'm still only on chapter 2 as of this review so I can't say with full certainly if the story will be good the whole time but I am enjoying what I've gotten so far and if that opinion changes I will probably edit in more thoughts.I remember when this game was announced years ago that it looked really spooky and scary! The final product isn't that, though I believe there is one jump scare near the latter half of the game in a side quest going off some discussion I've seen. For the most part the game isn't scary, at most you'll see a few ominous visuals and a feeling of dread as you walk around the streets so if you are worried the game won't give you a moment's peace from horror, worry not.

_childDocuments_.review: Great visuals and huge emphasis on Japanese mythology. The amount of detail just scattered throughout the world make it feel more real and engaging.The gameplay is pretty snappy, albeit the character is quite slow-moving. Breaking open possessed demon-like enemies is satisfying, each time you manage to do it.There are three basic elemental spells you can use + a bow (mostly for long-range take-downs), some traps and moves that can help you disable enemies pretty quickly, given you're in the right circumstance.Lots of things to pick up, look for and go through if you're aiming for a longer play.The story itself seems to be alright, generally speaking, nothing spectacular though.The main problem players might be facing is the general repetitiveness. Even though you have a range of tools to defeat the enemies, at the same time you can take all of them down by just basically wailing on them, so the combat challenges are more up for the player to create, rather than the game presenting them to you.For me personally it was more interesting progressing and opening up map areas just so I can find more extras, than progressing through the story. However, that also got a bit stale and now I'm more bent on just finishing the game and crossing it off of my list.Generally a good experience, nothing too intricate or memorable, but a decent play-through.7-/10

_childDocuments_.review: To start off - most of you will be looking at this game, expecting fast-paced combat, tense horror and varied content. While the latter is true to an extent, the first two are just not present in the game and I honestly believe it is only worth half of the price it had on release. If you are fine with just "ok" combat, atmospheric but not really scary horror scenes and a good 40+ hours of content (which can get repetitive though) and see this game on a 50+% sale, do take it under consideration. ;-)Ghostwire: Tokyo is an FPM (First-Person Magic) horror game, which takes inspiration from Japanese folklore and is set in more-or-less contemporary Shibuya (a popular commercial ward in Tokyo). You play as Akito, a Japanese student (University, I think, but am not certain) who nearly dies in a traffic accident and is saved by KK, a spirit detective pursuing a mystical person in a Hannya mask who tries to bring about the end of the world and abducts Akitos sister Mari towards this goal. To achieve this he summons a mist, which turns all the humans into spirits and lets in legions of "Visitors" (Japanese negative spirits. I guess you could call them "demons", but the Japanese "Yōkai" is not the same as our perception of this concept, so lets leave it at "negative spirit"). KK lets Akito perform "Ethereal Weaving" (cast spells), which is done from the first person perspective. However here is the games first shortcoming - there are only three elements with two modes of use - quick and charged. The former is quick, but a tad weaker, the latter creates a more powerful effect (wind charges up to four projectiles with a single piece of ammo, water creates a broad "scythe" which strikes multiple opponents and can break visitor umbrellas, which are acting as shields against wind, and fire creates a ye-good-olde-fireball). You either strike at an enemy until they dissipate, or until their core becomes visible and you can tear it out (which is, to be fair, VERY satisfying). Lastly there is the earth shield, which either reduces incoming damage, or (provided you manage a "Perfect Block", which is blocking exactly when the enemy attack would have landed) negates damage altogether and damages the attacker a little bit. However there is no dodge system, no way to improve the shield to absorb more damage and Akito moves fairly slowly (which makes him more grounded in the "contemporary" setting, I guess). This means, that you will not move around much and just spam attacks, block and spam some more attacks, maybe try to avoid attacks via running. There is also a stealth mechanic, which is the classic "crouch to move silently". In case you get tired of magic, you can use the very powerful bow (there are enemies which are highly resistant to most elements and are easiest to kill with a bow) or even more powerful talismans, which can distract Visitors, paralyse them, expose their core (or cause a lot more damage than normal attacks) or create a bush to hide in. How you utilise these skills is entirely up to you, but mostly you will just use magic over and over and over again...When not fighting Yōkai, you can run and parkour through Shibuya, which, I am happy to say, is rather faithfully recreated. Naturally it is not 1:1 photo-realistic (several landmarks, such as the Hachiko statue on Shibuya crossing) are replaced with something more generic, as many of these things have trademarks associated with them. But generally - when I approached the Shibuya Crossing station and went to the spot "where Hachiko is", I recognised MUCH of the surroundings, which is one of the reasons why I even bought this game. :-) (seriously - do you know how much it would cost to run through empty Shibuya streets? :-P) As I have mentioned - Yōkai is not the same as "demon" and on your parkour adventures you will meet many spirits, which are technically Yōkai, but are actually benevolent (or at least neutral), such as the Nekomata. These are "cats which lived a full life" and thus ascended as spirits, which made them grow a second tail and now spend their time .... peddling wares to spirit detectives. :-D The game explains this as "... they want to make some Meika (spirit money) to buy Nether Catnip in the spirit world." Be that as it may - you meet these merchants either running convenience stores, or peddling special wares from stalls. Always check with them if you choose to play this game, as food and drink restore Akitos health. On that topic - health restoration is quick and substantial, further removing from the sence of danger ("just pop a rice ball!" should become a catchphrase in this game, as food restores up to like 80% HP, making it pretty hard for enemies to kill you, despite how squishy the protagonist is).The exploration is very fluid and pretty pleasant. Akito clings to ledges VERY well and is the first protagonist I have played who knows how to lift their arms above their head, as you do not have to hit the ledge on face-level, it can be a bit above you. I think this very cool, as the whole "you can only interact with a ledge if it is on-screen or in head-level" to be kinda dumb. Your spirit powers allow you to also glide through the air for a few seconds, which means you can glide from rooftop to rooftop. Lastly you have a skill which scans the surrounding area, revealing points of interest, and you can equip beads which will alert you there are certain items nearby. Most combat is not mandatory either, so if you just want to explore, you totally can.The story is ..... well its "fine". I found the end to be a pretty touching story about coming to terms with personal loss and grief, so if stories like this are your jam - this game has you covered. I am not able to confirm, whether the game has multiple endings, but the narrative is VERY linear so I do not believe you can affect the ending in more than one way (which doesn't actually change anything either, it just give one of the characters closure). Also (and this was probably the biggest selling point for me) you find a lot of lore on Japanese culture, history and mysticism, which is pretty abundant and "fed" to you in fairly small chunks.The atmosphere is pretty much spot-on and while it is not scary (you having a means to defend yourself pretty much takes the edge off the horror elements), it still does the supernatural aspect VERY well, with "glitches" happening around the Yōkai (the weaker Visitors just cause shutters and bin covers to open and close frantically, but the stronger ones can openly distort space, cause the visual to change color and so on). The side-quests are particular about this, as mostly what you encounter in the streets are the "weaker" variants. The side-quests are varied and can either be just calming benevolent spirits, or full-on exorcisms of malevolent wraiths, which will try to distort space in order to scare you off. All-in-all the game is not bad, unless you are expecting something fast-paced. I came into this from playing Cyberpunk 2077 and the combat experiences between those two games cannot even be compared. Why I am satisfied with this game, despite not being able to recommend it to everyone is, that I wanted a game which will let me parkour through Tokyo, read up on lots of cool lore and meet lots of cute critters (such as the Nekomata, or stray cats and dogs), all supported by a fairly satisfying combat system, but wasn't necessarily looking for fast-paced combat, an involved levelling system and a branching questline which asks very deep and interesting questions (the final three I find is what plenty of gamers have come to expect from franchises). If you see yourself in that first part and are willing to look past the more tedious aspects, this game may still offer you a good 40+ hours of pretty solid entertainment.P.S. the core game and story is about 10-20 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes I wish I could give a 'meh' review without a thumb up or down, usually I give a game the benefit of the doubt and will give a game a thumb up even if I don't like a game but something has stuck with me or the game clearly had love and passion poured into it. This is a funny example in which the game is interesting and different enough to your typical games (especially fps games), is based on Japanese Yoki which I'm interested in and was clearly developed with love and care by Tango Gameworks (who out of the 3 games they've made I've only enjoyed evil within 2). But despite all this I struggle to recommend this game unless you're really interested in the subject matter or really need something forgettable to cleanse your palette with because for me this game is so forgettable and bland that ultimately if I had to choose between a thumb up and down I'd have to say thumb down. The combat at first seems like it'll be a fun spin on the heretic/hexan combat system, you utilise magic based on japanese tradition which is quite refreshing and the first ability hits enemies in a satisfying way, you then pull out their cores which is also fun at first. The issue is however is that besides what I just mentioned that's all the combat is and with so few weapons to use it really doesn't feel fun and quickly turns into a slog. Sure you can quick switch weapons like it's doom but really I found there utility in comabt to be underwhelming and it got boring fast.The open world isn't very fun to travel, it looks good and the neon painted city scape is nice at first but when you travel around the map completing the most basic open world fluff quests it gets repetitive.The story is so forgettable that I forgot what happens.In truth I think giving this game a negative score might be harsh and I don't want to push people away but for me I had some hype going into this and was ultimately left disappointed and don't think I'll ever replay this game again.

_childDocuments_.review: It is fun enough. Just be warned that there is no NG+. Certain cosmetic items do appear to be global save based, so after a certain point, cosmetics are unlocked automatically, but only cosmetics.The items for beating the game 100% are great, but are kind of pointless at that point.Gameplay is reasonably fun for the most part, although trying to complete the game can be a pain.Controls are usually fine, but just be warned that if you are on the controller, it is hit or miss whether or not the hand signs will work. Fortunately, you can automate these.Sight duration is very short, so expect to need to refresh the sight surprisingly often.The end portion of the game is extremely slow and forcibly drawn out, but it may still be faster to finish the game once to obtain the end game reward if you are going for 100% collection.The hyakki yokai event should be farmed as soon as you are strong enough to do so. This event can respawn about once every 30 minutes and you need to eventually beat it 8 times for 100% completion. If you wait to farm them, you might end up at a point where you are just waiting for the respawns with nothing else to do.Arrows are great for many things. Just be warned that you do have a limited number of arrows. With the headshot and beads 3 bonus for bow, you can one shot most non-boss enemies. Combine this with certain other beads, such as the stealth beads, and you can play extremely safely with a ranged stealth build. Otherwise, you can combine this with beads to maximize your ability to kill enemies. This means that both stealth builds and frontal battle builds are viable for non-bosses. For bosses, you are best off with a build designed for combat.There are certain parts of the game where it makes more sense to just run instead of fighting, but you can fight if you desire. There are certain parts of the game that suddenly force you into combat rather unexpectedly. Save reasonably often.You can switch equipment in most battles, so if one weapon isn't working well, you can switch your equipment, although this isn't "realistic".There aren't many jump scares, but be warned that there are what many might consider spooky points in the game and enemies can spawn behind you, so you might check an item and find that you have an ambush waiting for you when you turn around.Be warned that there are certain points where you might want to make a manual save because the section after can be annoying.Also be warned that farming can be rather tedious here.

_childDocuments_.review: Run there, float here, collect that, do this, upgrade that. Yadda, yadda, yadda. Repetitive, right? Yes, but name a single open-world game that isn't. Can't knock it for the genre pitfall. They all tend to follow the same formula, however, I feel what sets Ghostwire apart from the run-of-the-mill open-world game is the sheer amount of detail to Japanese lore, culture, and the urban landscapes. It simply nails the atmosphere of Tokyo, while providing an immersive and detailed story most players will be invested in seeing through to the end. Add in the paranormal/spiritual urban legends and you have what makes this game, its story, and it's setting one the best in recent years. As for the combat, it is very similar to Control or Infamous (if you played either of those). I enjoyed the unique take on the elemental powers without the bullet hell landscape of Destiny, CoD, or Far Cry. I don't have the beefiest machine and I didn't experience any FPS drops running on an ultrawide monitor and 2080 RTX. All settings were on Ultra with RTX enabled. Some people have mentioned memory leaks, but I didn't experience any (nor a single crash) while doing long play sessions. As for time to beat, thankfully, it isn't drawn out and really allows the player to play at their pace. The main story took me about 25 hrs to complete with approx. 33% of the spirits found. Yes, it could be completed faster, but why rush a game if you commit to spending the dollars on it. Will I go back and collect the other 67% of the spirits, including all side quests and additional content? I plan on it, which says a lot, but my backlog may get the best of me. In either case, it's remaining installed with the intent and hope of revisiting this beautiful, spirit-filled world in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This is just me but this game got me hooked about everything. It gave me the same feeling as playing Arkham City in terms of atmosphere and exploration. It's been a while since I felt like I don't want to sleep and rest just so I could play this game more. The main story is short but I had so much fun exploring the whole city so here's what I think of the game:PROS:- The overall feel of the game is fluid. The combat, the movement, the camera, they all feel smooth. - Since this is a first-person game, I commend the team for making the hand motions and gestures realistic- The enemy designs are great! They're not scary but they're creepy in a good way.- Graphics is good and it feels like you're really in Shibuya- Combat is not that hard and not that easy either. The enemies are easy when they're alone but it can be quite challenging when they attack in groups- If you're a fan of exploration and looting games, this game gives you just that- There are many secrets and collectibles in the game but there are abundant features that make it easy to find them- The game has yokais in it. This may be the closest you'll experience being an exorcist lolCONS:- The main story is short. Heck, it feels like they put more side quests in it. You'll spend most of your time exploring and looking for secrets.- Majority of my hours in this game was spent looking for spirit collectibles and that's quite tedious for many players- While the combat is fluid, it's quite straightforward. I feel like the game is more of just shoot whatever comes at you.- They enemy designs are good but they don't differ that much in terms of how to kill them. Just keep your distance and shoot- There are weapons/tools that you won't be needing at all. One good example is the decoy talisman. I didn't find a scenario where it would be practical- Side quests are more of running errands literally. Just run into that area and find something or beat the enemy- The skill tree is lacking. I hate upgrades that focus on fire rate with minimal differencesBottomline, this game is a good experience for everyone. But buy it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire is on those games that flew under the radar. I've had my eye on it for a while, waiting for the juicy discount to hit 50% or more off, that day came and now that i've played and beaten the game, i can understand the lack of interest. Ghostwire is fantastic in nearly every department, except the one that arguably matters the most, the gameplay. Things start off great all around. Visually the game is stunning with incredible detail and particle effects, I don't recommend raytracing often... Actually never have i recommended that gimmick feature, but given this game's environment and tone, its actually almost worth the massive hit to FPS.Tokyo has never looked better, and i've played alot of games centered around Shabuya. The detail is incredible, the streets lined with cars and neon lights, the sounds of shops nearby that have appropriate music playing, although the inhabitants are gone, the city is still alive like nothing happened.Now onto the biggest con, the gameplay. Ghostwire went with an open world setting, allowing you to explore and find one of the several different collectathon items. At first its a fine experience. Glide around rooftops getting souls, find a shrine or two, look for some treasures, do a side quest, its all good enough fun. But after 3 hours of gliding around, finding shrines and souls, looking for treasure, you realize something. None of it does anything for you of any real value. Money is used to buy food, but food is plentiful and the best healing is from food you find floating around. Souls= massive XP, but the upgrades are mediocre across the board, and the only good weapon is the wind attack. Treasure gives different rewards, but most of it are cosmetics or emotes in a SINGLE PLAYER FPS. Even as a completionist, i found the whole thing tedious with little change in the formula as you progress.Ghostwire is a damn good game if you do some side stuff then rush to the finish. The story is decent enough, and the characters are ok, but nothing that incredible. I would love to see a sequel, taking everything here but amping it up. Make the movement more enjoyable, make the combat more interesting, make the upgrades more impactful, maybe even some co-op to spice it up. The foundation is set, the world is built, the characters are introduced, all Tango needs to do is build upon what they have. Mark my words, if they announce Ghostwire 2, it will be a fantastic game worth the wait.

_childDocuments_.review: Agreeing with most of the other reviews here. Had quite a lot of fun. Probably not for everyone, but it's a beautiful game with a beautiful story. The notes and information gathered throughout the game, had me researching and reading up on a few things I didn't know about as well, which was pretty awesome. The food just made me hungry... Also, because I was achievement hunting and going for all the spirits, I managed to skill out to max, so, wasn't much effort in killing them at that point.  I guess majority of the time I was just walking around looking at everything. For those wishing to get all the achievements, I felt this needs to be mentioned before you attempt them:1. Get the summon Tengu skill as soon as you can, it helps a lot to get to those spirits on higher locations. 2. Collect all the spirits before Chapter 4. You can't collect them after.3. Don't avoid the Hyakki Yako/ Demon Parade. They might be difficult at first, but once completed, they drop spirits that you will need. I saw someone else mention this in the reviews as well. I had to run around endlessly at the end, praying for them to show up at specific locations... So, yes. 4. Check the phone booths/ pay phones when you're dropping off those spirits, they usually have voice logs in them. 5. There's an audio log in Chapter 5. Do not miss it. You can't go back for it. _childDocuments_.review: Hello friends! Welcome to my review of the game GHOSTWIRE TOKOYO. This is a open world game with many quests and side quests. It features lore from japan including yokai and ghosts familiar with that region. The game also features buildings from Tokoyo such as the 409 building, the tokoyo tower, and many other real life buildings set in the city of tokoyo japan. The game is split into different chapters which most consist of a open world area where you can take your time to do quests. There are also many side quests that can be done by the player to enhance their game. There are also collectibles and hidden things to find around the world. Despite being open world, this game tends to be more horror in essence compared to other open world games. There are even jump scares on some of the quests and side quests. Anyways, here are my pro and con list:PROS:- Open world game with horror elements.- Many japanese lure about yokai and ghosts.- Collectibles.- Controller support. I used F310 logitech.- Beautiful music.- Very good graphics.- The game seems to still being developed and given additional free things and new patches.CONS:- Sadly, this game suffered from the ubisoft same open world format, thus degrating the game using the same formula which can make the game seem boring to some people.- Repetition of doing some things in game can cause bordom. As with all games, if you get bored, change to another game and come back to play it later.- Very little stuttering, but otherwise worked fine.- The game does not take long to beat. It only took me 36 hours casually to beat the game. Hardcore games might even finish the game sooner than that.I do recommend the game because i love exploring mythology and lure of other cultures, as in this game, it is japanese lure about fantasy creatures and different ghosts.NOTE: If you get the game, do not play the prelude chapter until after you beat this game. The storyline in the prelude ruins many aspects of the main game and is not very good in my personal opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Tldr: Ghostwire Tokyo is a First Person "Shooter" RPG hybrid where you survive a hostile takeover of a portion of Tokyo thanks to the soul of someone who possessed you, "KK". You and KK go through a now haunted and empty (of people, things to do, and charm) Tokyo as you try to break the curse that a group of people have laid upon Tokyo and rescue your sister who is a key part of their plans. I did not enjoy this game much at all after the first 3 hours or so. It becomes quickly repetitive, the combat was fairly bland IMHO and I ended up stopping about halfway through the main storyline.Gameplay loop - You are given places to go to and find things or purify shrines. That's pretty much all there is to it. On the way you fight battles with a growing cast of ghoulish enemies with three main elemental attacks, and a sweet bow. As you play you gain experience from fighting, completing quests/side quests and saving spirits (a collection game). At each level you get more health and can upgrade your abilities. You can play this as a stealth game for certain parts or go in all "guns" blazing. After the first 3-5 hours, I found it to be repetitive and after a few more hours exploring you realize this version of Tokyo is absolutely empty and devoid of anything interesting to find. The map at certain points has a hard time of telling you where to go (when something is located up or down) and searching for incredibly small items to pick up to advance the quest or find small side quest relics is more of a pain than anything else. I give this a 2/5.Story: The story, at least to the part I got to was pretty bare bones. You lucked out in how you were able to "survive" the rapture of Tokyo and luckily got a "partner" who bestows you with spirit fighting abilities, your sister who was hospitalized happens to be key to the nefarious group whose objectives remain unknown and you're now the only chance for saving everyone. There's a few small side characters that pop up from time to time via logs, recordings and ghostly interactions but it was pretty minimalistic from an engagement and character development point (at least as far as I got). I had no real interest or vested motive to see the story any further. 2/5 for me.Music: Suitably ominous and minimal for this kind of game. Some jump scares got me but nothing memorable here. 3/5.Graphics/design: Some decent graphics but the setting could have been way better than what it presented here. Tokyo is an incredible city to explore in real life, but the lack of inhabitants and anything worthwhile to find really dampened exploring this Tokyo's bland buildings and streets. 3/5.Fun factor: For me the fun wore out quickly. I had started trying to clear the map of all side quests and collectibles and quickly realized how much of a drag it was. Doing the same fights over and over again with the gameplay loop just wasn't fun. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire Tokyo surprised me a lot. It is a solid first-person action adventure game set in a stunning recreation of a Tokyo where its inhabitants have been spirited away and replaced with modern reinterpretations of yokai.The two aspects I would highlight from it are the combat and, particularly, the overworld and its exploration.While I would not use "first-person shooter" as the genre to primarily describe the game as a whole, the combat certainly could be summed up as such. That being said, its entire design is tightly put together so that the act of engaging enemies can be picked up by anyone, while also allowing for a slightly higher degree of strategizing and satisfaction as you upgrade your character. The tools and upgrades that the game puts at your disposal beyond your basic "ammo" does push you to use and favor certain tactics, which does not leave a lot of room for super in depth tactical gameplay, but it will keep you entertained for, at least, the duration of the main story. Another thing to consider is that it really isn't a hard game. Some bosses took some retries, but as long as you have a good grasp on the mechanics and the controls, it good portion of the game becomes fairly trivial. The challenge does decrease as you gather more power ups and upgrades, but the enemies don't scale up with you.In this game, exploration is deeply connected to character progression. It is a key element to the game as the overworld becomes another important character you interact with. That being said it is a bit of a mixed bag:On the one hand, Tango has made an impressive effort to create a stunning and beautiful recreation of Tokyo. Whereas other games make timid use of ray tracing, Ghostwire goes all out on it and the presentation is significantly improved with this on.A big effort is made to immerse the player in this world as much as possible, not only through the world itself, but in the ways you can interact with it and what you can discover. The game offers enough context for you to understand it through the "glossary" where message logs, information about collectibles, enemy origins, etc. is provided.You are invited to not view the map as simply another gameplay element, but one that should take the time to appreciate. I did, and it's one of the things I enjoyed the most out of this gameOn the other hand, though, the value that the elements I've just described creates is diminished by the side activities design that mar many modern open world games. No matter that the incentive (acquiring context for the world, exploring the world itself) that the game gives you to engage with the additional activities, it innevitably becomes tiring. Side quests do not go beyond the "go to location - fight enemies - retrieve item/help spirit pass to the afterlife" (though some do provide interesting stories and locations), and there's sizeable amount of collectibles you can find to finish up the "checklist design" that defines most of the side content. I do enjoy this sort of thing with measure but, as player progress and exploration is so tightly connected, I had to take long breaks from the game to finish it playing it this way.While I feel these two elements are what defines the game as a whole the most, I also want to briefly mention some of the other things that make up the experience:Ghostwire: Tokyo is one of the more interesting AAA games to come out in recent years. It mixes tight gameplay design paired with a fantastic game world that should be explored with both calm and measure to fully enjoy it. A game very much worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommending this based on the "main quest," which is very good. It's a 10 hour or so FPS (yes it's an FPS even if the bullets come from your hand) with great level design, enemy encounters and story. If you can play it as that, and ignore most side content, then you should have a great time and enjoy a uniquely Japanese take on the genre.If you insist on playing it like the Far Cry game it occasionally tries to be however, be prepared for a boring slog through repetitive city environments and holding right-mouse on endless numbers of things. Stay far away from that, and enjoy what the game does well. Do some side stuff here and there on your way through the main campaign and you should have no trouble, as the upgrades are mostly unneeded anyway.Graphics are extremely good and ray tracing actually isn't a gimmick and adds a lot. The extreme realism isn't really my thing, but the main quests change this up with lots of fantasy content. Performance is great once you put texture streaming on "auto." Pretty much every issue I had and have seen on the forums was fixed by that. Mouse and keyboard controls are just fine, and in fact it's a pretty fast-paced shooter so it feels right at home here. Make sure to turn off acceleration and auto-aim.Ghostwire Tokyo is a 9 out of 10 linear FPS in a 5 out of 10 open world shell. Go in knowing that and you can have a lot of fun with it.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game that has some problems. - it gets pretty repetitive, finding all the spirits and other collectables is a grind- there are some very annoying enemies which are either bullet sponges or can be one-shot, which makes them feel more like a chore, especially since just fleeing from some of them takes more time than fighting them- in general fighting isn't the most fun- the person who created the Daikyo Omikuji achievement should have Daikyo applied to them in real life. an achievement that's basically a RNG with 1% chance and a 10s animation plus the need to reload the save on fail. Designed only to waste the player's time- the school dlc is not fun, especially the part where you need to walk around blindly, with the camera fixes on one point, in a library with the tables and bookstands.- starting the spider threads mode with level 0 character is a bad experience, being used to everything maxed out and then thrown into fight with the base version of all abilities just takes the fun away until levelled up. A much better choice would be something NG+-like, with everything you've earned in base game unlocked, but with new special abilities added on top, instead of the lazy choice of copying the same skill tree and zeroing it.+ the setting is perfect if you like Japan+ a lot of folklore included, plus the dialogs are in Japanese+ visuals - it's beautiful+ the various "other dimension"-like parts are fun, it's a shame they appear only in a few places+ exploring is fun, especially after unlocking the longest gliding and summoning Tengu+ the spider threads mode is surprisingly fun after some skills are unlocked, I was very sceptical about it but it's better than I thought+ denuvo was removed

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire: Tokyo has been a highly anticipated game for me ever since it was first shown at E3 2019 because the TangoGameworks studio headed by Shinji Mikami, who is the father of the original Resident Evil games and my favorite developer, makes his games at the highest level and tries his best in every title to get the most out of it, I honestly wasn't sure how a horror movie with elements like Evil Within would work and also how they want to bring some elements into this title, however they succeeded but it's not as perfect as I expected. Ghostwire: Tokyo, as the title says, draws you into Tokyo, which is currently facing an invasion from another world, you are Akito, who has been "possessed" by a spirit named KK, who gives you supernatural abilities and how to defeat the so-called Visionors, who are drowning all of Tokyo in fog, everyone people mysteriously disappeared and you're the only one who can do something about it but it's worth it KK thought you were dead which is also half true when he got inside you practically caught your second breath and KK kept you alive but here the priorities are a little different, Akito is trying to find his Sister Mari and KK is trying to defeat Hannya, who is behind this invasion, on your way you will get better abilities and you will also meet other enemies, since the people have disappeared, they are now surrounding Tokyo Visitors who live here as ordinary "people" will also find gentlemen with umbrellas, headless schoolgirls, old ladies, flying monsters and big ladies with scissors who will try to separate your head from your body. Your power comes from Etherium which gives you KK it's kind of like elemental abilities it gives you Air which when charged makes a few swirls in a row then Water which is melee and does area damage when charged it makes a huge swirl in a slice , which looks like a water blade. And lastly there is Fire, which works like Arrows, which have huge damage and can shoot through several Visitors at once when charged. But you will not only have these "weapons" you will also find various scrolls that will give you abilities such as slowing down time in a certain area, or "Wire In" which acts as a Rage mod that allows you to use your abilities to the fullest extent, but this the ability has its own cooldown, which is not short, so think about when you use it. When you wander around desolate Tokyo, you will find various bags or even shops where you can buy some food, drink, etc... Food and drink will regenerate your health and add a small bonus to your maximum HP. In addition to fulfilling your "Main Story Line" here, you also have side quests that will give you pretty good bonuses. But you can't save Tokyo just like that, along the way you will also see the souls of people who stayed in Tokyo, if you capture them in the Emblem you got you can then transfer these souls to another world where they will turn them into people again, but God knows how they will end up where. Since it's a game from the creators of Evil Within, a Skill tree must not be missing here. I have to say that here is something that probably slowed down the creators a bit, because the abilities you get are useful, but some of them you almost don't use during combat or exploration. Do you have Attack Speed ​​bonuses, Charge Speed ​​bonuses, different combos or attack speed, and I have to say that yes, some skills can help you fight Visitors, but it won't be so necessary, since the combat system will fall into your hands after a few hours of playing so perfectly that you will no longer perceive any abilities, but you will simply do combos and exchange abilities like on a treadmill. The scenery of Tokyo itself is really nice and I have to say that just enjoying the view and the graphics never stops entertaining me in any game, but what is a bit "Anchor" about this game is the Optimization, most of the game I had 45FPS which on my monitor looked like 25 I'm not saying that I didn't enjoy the game, but I had to reduce the quality a lot and take a big chunk from the Visuals of the game itself, although the game is more stable now, I had to use AMD FSR 1.0 and throw it on Balanced, otherwise the game would give me a lot take. Although my setup is successful with this game at least on Medium details, even Low Details it looks like my PC can barely run this game. Not to mention the choice of Cinematics, where you can choose Quality mod or Performance mod, where Quality mod plays Cinematics for you in 4K and Performance plays it for you in Full HD, and even though I put Performance on, I still see some drops, although I'm quite sad about it this is really a big anchor of the game, although it is not alone. After playing for a while you will feel like you are doing the same thing over and over again, which is true, the side quests get repetitive after a while, and the only thing that will drive you forward is the Main Line, which gives you other things, but if I take it around and around you practically do the same things all over, except for the parts where you have the Boss.Ghostwire: Tokyo met my expectations about 75% honestly the game I waited 3 years for I could have waited 2 more years for the game to be in a better condition than it is now I'm not saying it's bad I'm just saying some things could be changed or even modified, with the exception of Optimization, which could be improved. However, even if I squint, this game is really fun and can hold you for a long time, Shinji Mikami has done his job really well and brought us a really good game with a touching script, fun fights and Easter Eggs on the Anime... But if you were thinking about this piece, so if you don't mind a little labile optimization and repetitive tasks, Rating: 8/10Played on:AMD Ryzen 5 2600 (6-Core)GeForce GTX 1660 Super (GDDR6 | 6GB VRAM)Corsair Kit 2x8GB 2666MHzWindows 10+ Beautiful visuals+ Soundtrack+ Duel system+ Story- Weaker Optimization- Repetitiveness of tasks

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire: Tokyo....this game is not a horror game, nor is it a survival game.Ghostwire: Tokyo is closest to a collect-a-thon. a slow, meditative, artistic, atmospheric collect-a-thon. and yet it is the perfect embodiment of a phrase ive come to call "blissful isolation." there is so much to this game, in an opposing direction of anything i could have expected, and i love it. Ghostwire: Tokyo is a beautiful tour of modern japan folklore, set in an exceptionally rendered and realized version of Tokyo, told through the lens of AAA open world game design. Marketing butchered the handling of this game, but that does not take away from just how fleshed out and beautiful this game is, while maintaining an atmosphere of isolation and mystery, while rooting itself in the vast world of japanese folklore. Ghostwire: Tokyo is not a game for everyone, but it the perfect game for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game, but I think it would've done better as an atmospheric horror game as opposed to an action game. Generally I like action games, but the combat in this is a little underwhelming for me. It isn't particularly fun and the enemies aren't particularly interesting either (aside from maybe their appearances which are kinda freaky) and you'll be engaging in a lot of combat as you progress through the game. There's a lot of variety in attacks you can do, but I haven't found much reason to experiment since very few enemies take more than a couple of hits from basic attacks to vanquish. It doesn’t feel like any of the enemies really challenge you in interesting ways which can’t be overcome with just more of the basic attacks.The environments look amazing and is a feast for the eyes, but I think it actually loses it's luster a bit when in motion. I haven't really had a moment to just stand and stare as I’m constantly going from one place to the next, but whenever I take a screenshot and get a chance to look at it later I'm blown away by just how good everything looks. They definitely nailed the atmosphere, and I think that is one of the main draws to the game for me.As with many open world games it can start feel like a never ending to-do list after a while. Go here, fight some enemies, do the torii gate, get to the next area, suck in some souls, help some spirit to get their peace, deposit the souls in the telephone and then on to the next marker where you’ll do the same. Thankfully, to counter this, there are moments in the story, and sometimes in the side missions, that really do pull you in. Suddenly the game throws a curve that isn’t just the same routine. Maybe you need to find a thing, or avoid a spirit or solve a puzzle. It's a real shame that these seem so rare… On a 50% to 75% discount it makes sense, but certainly not at full price…

To be honest, I really enjoyed my first "full" playthrough of Ghostwire: Tokyo. Being someone that normally doesn't finish games, this was a pleasant surprise for me. I have always really enjoyed horror, and while this game isn't inherently scary, it provides a great atmosphere of feeling alone to some degree, all with that voice of reason (KK) in the back of your head to keep you sane. That being said, I personally really enjoyed the story, while falling flat in some areas, I think it wrapped up the game nicely towards the end. The side quests in my opinion are really what makes the game shine (Collecting TP for a ghost stuck in the bathroom as one example lol). My main gripe that I have with the game are the Tengu. THEY.NEVER.SHUT.UP. Hopefully this will be fixed in a later patch with a mute or volume down option. While the move-set for attacks were also a little repetitive, this didn't make me like the game any less, other than it taking a rather long time to collect all the spirits, I was definitely satisfied after finishing. _childDocuments_.review: I would rate Ghostwire Tokyo a "maybe" on the recommendation scale, leaning trowards a no. I enjoyed my time with it, and found it worthwhile to purchase and play for about ten dollars alongside some other games in a recent bundle. There's a lot to appreciate here: Tokyo itself is fun to explore, the art and sound design are excellent, and there's some real highlight missions I had a great time playing, like the new school one that came with the free Spider's Thread DLC. All that said, Ghostwire fails to wrap this all into a package that I can recommend to everyone. Rather than an engaging, super-powered first-person action-horror, this game winds up being a weirdly packaged collectathon that still has some value, but falls flat due to those former intentions. The story and characters are uninteresting, there's no atmosphere of tension (even with harder enemies), and the combat/traversal abilities you can obtain lack the depth to drive this experience home without a strong narrative to support it. I ended up putting a good amount of time in, mostly doing extraneous content and exploring the city and what this game had to offer, but I'm not compelled to finish this game's story content, and I don't see that changing with so many stronger contenders in the open world genre. If you want to run around a well designed Tokyo and collect things, shooting spooky monsters as you go, this game's probably worth some of your time. If you're looking for more depth in a super-powered survival-horror than that, I'd suggest Prey (2018) instead, even if the set and theme are completely different.

It also helps that the main protag and his little hitchhiker are different enough in personality that their dialogue doesn't get too stale. The map design is pretty alright, although the fog can be quite annoying as the resident "Don't go here yet" mechanic of the game. All in all, not worth $60. _childDocuments_.review: Got this gifted by a friend. Really enjoyed the story, scenery, mechanics and character development. I did all the side quests, but not all the collectibles, and thoroughly enjoyed exploring and listening to the stories of various ghosts. I will say that the difficulty level isn't very high, as I played on hardest and pretty much first timed each boss encounter - however playing on the highest will inhibit your ability to gain XP completely. All in all, fantastic game and really fun interactions with various characters, and it's even more enjoyable if you are interested in Japan as I am.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very good! Though i have only 30 hours played and almost a 100% completion, I cannot recommend a 100% completion. The spirit parades known as "Hyakki Yako" spawns in far to little for a late game completion attempt. The game also doesnt incentivize another play through even on harder difficulties. save yourself some pain and play through on the easiest setting and visit the shibuya crossing scramble in game for the "Hyakki Yako" they will probably be the hardest things to get done if you leave it for the end. Good luck to you on the parade hunts!

_childDocuments_.review: I will update this review once I have made it further in the game.  I am purposely avoiding spoilers! ^_^After 5+ hours played, I am can say with certainty that I am absolutely loving the gameplay and atmosphere in GhostWire: Tokyo.  I typically play open world games slowly because I like to take in the sights, sounds, and atmosphere on offer.  I find myself in awe of the game world that is available to explore.  Everything is highly detailed and beautifully rendered.  In this respect, Ghostwire completely delivers!I am playing on Normal difficulty and it has just the right amount of challenge.  I find it interesting that there aren't as many in-game enemies as I would have expected given the events of the game.  I assume this is a game design choice because if the environment was overloaded with enemies it wouldn't be as easy to enjoy the atmosphere. The story so far is engaging and intriguing.  It is pushing me to move forward and make progress while at the same time isn't instilling a sense of urgency that would preclude me from continuing to explore.  I absolutely want to understand why the events are occurring and that pushes me forward.  My primary criticism so far is with the mouse and keyboard controls.  Mouse inputs are slow and laggy when your mouse DPI is set to a high level.  The on-screen action lags behind, like there is some kind of mouse smoothing implemented.  I am playing with a Razer Basilisk and I have to set the DPI no higher than 800DPI for a smooth experience.  About twenty minutes in, I decided to switch over to using an Xbox controller and it plays much better.  It seems this game was intended to be played on consoles based on this observation. Overall - at this juncture I absolutely recommend this game!  I will update my review as I make it further along.  ** A note regarding system requirements and in-game performance:  If you are looking for an ultra smooth gameplay experience, get ready to tweak the settings until you find your own performance sweet spot.  I have historically upgraded my PC components whenever I can't get games to run really smooth but the cost of components nowadays prevents that mentality - so be prepared to adjust the settings.The intro cut-scene appears to be in-game rendered so I used that to fine tune things.  Here is my core hardware setup (Stock voltages and clocks - no overclocking involved in my rig):Motherboard - Gigabyte Z390 AORUS ELITE-CFCPU - i7-8700kRAM - 32GB - Corsair DDR4-3600 (8GB  x 4)GPU - Nvidia RTX 2080 Founders EditionMonitor - AW2721D connected via DisplayPort 1.4 / GSYNC EnabledMonitor Resolution - 2560x1440HDR - DisabledI started out with the following settings:•  Native screen resolution (2560x1440)•  Framerate unlocked•  Ray tracing enabled  The intro ran choppy so I turned off Ray Tracing and lowered my resolution to 1080P (1920x1080) and the intro ran smoothly.  After playing for an hour I increased the in-game resolution to 2560x1440 and I haven't noticed any differences in performance except for certain scenes where there is a lot of environmental detail.  It is totally playable, I am just very picky :)I bet an Nvidia 3080 would resolve the Ray Tracing and other performance issues I have experienced since my 2080 is more than three years old now but I can't justify paying what they cost nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and unique game! The animations, graphical fidelity and accuracy of Tokyo plus the designs of yokai and visitors are very interesting grasps at folklore. My only gripe is how repetitive the combat and collection aspects are, this game really needed some extra combat animations and more variety of things to do.Edit: I'll never forgive Microsoft for taking the axe to Tango Gameworks. _childDocuments_.name: Ghostwire: Tokyo

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great open-world game with some small gripes. The open world is massive, the enemies are varied and original, there is lots to do and some of the effects used are straight up the best ive seen in a long time. Seriously some of these effects that give you creepy/ghost vibes are just perfect. Like upfalling rain when a certain enemy is nearby, zebra crossings and street markings flowing, shadowfigures on walls. The world looks and feels awesome. My main gripes with the game are that one, the combat does get a little bit stale towards the end, especially if you do lots of the optional stuff and two that some of the optional stuff gets repetitive fast too, like waiting behind a rock before you can approach a kappa. The story stayed somewhat in the background for me mainly because i spent so much time doing optional stuff that it didnt feel like the story mattered as much. The ending was great though. So even if you dont like doing lots of busy work, I would recommend this game just for jumping into and experiencing the world and enemies. If you do like lots of busy work then you have even more of a reason to try it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostwire: Tokyo

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very interesting experience, but it doesn't feel like there's much of a game. The environment itself is absolutely impressive (albeit held back by the heavy Post-FX) and all the missions have very interesting stories to tell, but nothing about the overall experience is really *fun* to play. I think if there was a stronger soundtrack presence to fill the mood of the world, and the combat were completely revamped to feel more powerful & less reliant on pinpoint aiming, I would have enjoyed the experience more.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl,Dr: Great fun game that seems like a trip through an abandoned TokyoPro:+Great soundtrack+Fun combat+Good story+Interesting side quests+Beautiful visualsCon:-Some of the open world soul hunting can be a bit repetitive, though that is only a minor annoyance for completionists like me- a few of the Yokai events are reused, the fact that this is one of the few downsides is incredibleProbably the most fun open world game I have played in years, the somewhat slow pace may not be everyone's cup of tea, but for me it was damn near perfect. And despite me claiming that some of the spirit gathering was a bit annoying to fully complete it, the game gives you options of making it easier and with less than forty hours to 100% this game, so it is nowhere as bad as some other games do it.I truly hope that they will make a second part in a different culture and city, as the setting really lends itself to it.

_childDocuments_.review: It might not be the best game I ever played but it is very good. It looks great (I think it runs pretty well too), plays great - combat is actually fun and controls are responsive, the environment works really well with the traversal mechanics. No part of the game is bad (probably the worst part were these chase/defend/sneak yokai "quests" to get an upgrade material and late-game gate cleansing) so its just a question of how much you like the varingly good parts. Whats really great is the overall mood/feel and side content. While often times you just find an object or fight a larger-than-usual enemy there is usually a nice little backstory for why you are doing what you are doing. I should say that the main story didnt necessarily make sense all the time but at least it felt like something new. Which is true for combat too - kinda like an fps but loads of special moves and abilities that change it up.tl;dr every aspect is at least good (the overall mystical feel is especially great), really interesting and fun to playhappy to see a game that tries to do something new and actually fun

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Nice world design. Despite the mediocre graphics, it's an immersive representation of Tokyo with genuine Japanese vibes. The setup of a city empty of people, but with lights, open shops and scattered clothes everywhere creates a weird, eerie atmosphere full of mystery.- Addictive, fun gameplay with responsive controls and some interesting mechanics. Parkour movements, jumping, gliding, grabbing are so fluid. Battles are great, aiming is precise and kills very rewarding. Stealth mechanics are decent too. Overall, there are a lot of abilities and upgrades to match your preferred playstyle.- Some of the best animations out there. The movements of Akito's hands are amazingly smooth and detailed. Movements of enemies, their attacks, their reactions when receiving blows, all those floating particles and effects during battles, everything is top notch.- This multilevel city along with the fluid parkour mechanics is perfect for exploration. Jumping from rooftop to rooftop in top speed makes you feel free.- Although the main story is shallow, its lore is great and pretty deep. They have perfectly combined traditional myths, spiritual creatures and religious artifacts with technological objects and modern world (e.g. katashiro - phone booths) creating a unique result. - There are some fantastic cinematic sequences with great rhythm and surreal elements. They're short trips that you are thrown between real and spiritual world through illusions, distorted geometries and every kind of trippy, crazy things.- Cool main characters with interesting personalities. Akito and KK are like mainstream super heroes, but more earthy and sentimental. You'll like them both.- Awesome enemies' design. Their lack of facial characteristics make them even more dark and creepy. Bosses are uniquely designed too, while battles against them have some interesting gameplay elements.- Nice, convincing voice acting performances, although sometimes they're a little bit over the top. Japanese vocals enhance even more the atmosphere.- Good sound design. It's so cool and weird that you can hear city's sounds or music from shops and cafes like everything is in tact except there are no people at all. Sounds of spells, kills, blows during battles are highly addictive.- You can learn many things about Japanese art, culture and tradition via all these objects that you collect.The bad- Well worn structure. Like most open world games, you have to follow missions' dots on the map from the beginning till the end without exactly knowing why. No creativity at all. Even worse, KK keeps constantly telling you what to do next, where to go, whether you have to turn left or right at the next corner.- It's full of low quality content in order to make it lengthier. Some side missions have fun, but they're mostly silly mini games or repetitive battles. Storywise, it makes no sense to selflessly run errands for all these people. Also, there are tons of collectables and cosmetics scattered inside the world that have no function and offer absolutely nothing to the lore. They developers should have focused more on the main story plus three or four deeper side missions instead of spending time on adding all this garbage. - Mediocre, cliché main story. You try to save your sister and the whole world from the villain that wants to destroy everything and likes to talk a lot about his big plan. Also, towards the end it gets extravagant with a classical blockbuster battle finale.- Graphics could be better. You'll find many blurry textures and bulky models. I'm not fun of the overall aesthetics either. Too much contrast and glossiness. No, ray tracing is no excuse for neon lights and pools of water everywhere.- Wider enemies' variation would be nice. They're awesome but you face the same guys from the start till the end. They never evolve or get tougher. At later stages they're just more.- Mediocre writing. Most dialogues are too simplistic, almost childish. Akito and KK keep repeating the same phrases after each of your actions. It gets annoying after a while.- Bad PC optimization. A lot of frame drops and some minor glitches here and there.

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool visuals and story held back by a lacklustre combat system. By 1 hour in, you have already unlocked all your major abilities. All bar one skill are simply stat increase: "Charge 10% quicker", "regain 5 more health" etc. The only interesting perk is being able to grapple anywhere, which is the most expensive skill in the game.This game truly shines in the side-quests, which frightened and amazed me multiple times. There's your "normal follow person then fight enemies" or simply just "kill x amount of enemies" quests. However, some of these quests will take you to really interesting areas. While the main story does have some of these moments, I found that most of these came from the side-quests.While I have been critical about the game, I don't dislike it. The flair of the game can make you forget the monotony of combat, and gliding around the map is pretty fun. I would recommend buying on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR I enjoyed playing this and would recommend that you do it as well.I got this from Humble Choice, which is good because I was getting to the point of wanting to buy it anyway, and I very much enjoyed the gameplay. I waited a bit before doing the side quests, which was a mistake because some of them are actually really good, I expected generic fetch quests and was surprised with new set pieces and short stories. They nailed the empty city feeling with abandoned clothes and stuff everywhere, and the atmosphere, there are just so many tiny details like rattling trash cans or hands reaching out at the end of alleys that genuinely caught me off guard. I went in expecting a horror jump scare game, but it felt more like Dying Light in a way. There is a lot of interesting case files and stuff to read about mythology, so if you are into that I would recommend it.The next two paragraphs are just tips and about saving time 100%ing the game, so there is probably very light spoilers about game stuffOnce you get to like chapter two and game opens up more, first go to the map legend and uncheck "show completed" at the bottom so you can avoid confusion about what there is still to do. Pretty much everything can be found without a guide, one thing I didn't notice until near the end is that when talking to the nekomata, you can select each of the items they request, and it will show on your map the rough area of where the object is, which I wish I had known earlier. For the Jizo statues and tanuki, at the shrine offering boxes, if you donate 500, there should be an option for  "I wish to find more Jizo Statues" or tanuki and yokai, which will mark the nearest one on your map. Stealth attacks are very powerful, sometimes you can just dash around the side of an enemy before they notice you and backstab them. For the missions where they are attacking boxes, you can backstab them while they are focused on the boxes. I would advise against Tatari difficulty, as it removes xp from the game, so you can barely get any skills, which is where a lot of enjoyment came from I think. Buy the DJ Multiverse songs from the collector nekomatas, I was vibing to them while running around killing ghosts.Took me about 68 hours to 100% including the spiders thread mode, which I did after everything else (that took 29 hours, but a decent chunk of that was just running through levels looking for the stupid cats). If you enjoy 100%ing games, bear in mind there are two particularly bad achievements here, them being "Don't worry about it," where you need to rng pull a specific blessing from the shrine stick things (took me two hours of save-scumming, someone on a forum said it took him 18), and then 100%ing the spiders thread mode, which I finished in like 18-19 hours, then spent like another 10 running through levels to find all 20 stray cats (equip fleet foot and max upgraded spirit vision beads, and listen for a meow when the level loads in.)

_childDocuments_.review: The main story feels unnecessary and went nowhere, the protagonist does nothing wrong. He was just in the wrong place at the wrong time. I still don't get on why the antagonist is so hellbent on the plan  Fortunately, The presentation of Tokyo in this game is very on point. The nighttime atmosphere is very eerie, the city is very lonely and even scary at some point. The combat is alright, not perfect but also not too bad. If you having fun with Assassin's Creed RPG styles gameplay you'll enjoy what this game has to offer. (ex. using stealth kill, finding how to reach high ground, range combat using arrow and elemental attack, melee combat using block and guard, etc.)The side-quests seem more interesting/engaging than the main story, it also nets you a very nice reward to use in the main quest and make life easier so no complaints here. Oh and you can pet the dogs in this game.Still recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the story line is great and the graphics are , if you're looking to get 100% achievements on this game, have fun, I noticed one of the achievements requires you to finish the story line AFTER you transfer 100% of the souls in the game. Which sounds easy enough, but even with maxed out spectral vision, it will take you  to find each and every soul in just a single area. Especially if there is just a single soul left in a massive area like the Onten Shrine. After about 10 hours of play time, I started focusing on getting every single document, message, statue, soul, etc. After another 18 hours I am now stuck with my Onten Shrine at 99.35% souls transferred, and a couple other shrines in the same way. Even when walking around the streets spamming spectral vision I just can't find the last souls. I won't stop trying tho.Although I find the souls to be a massive pain, I still completely recommend Ghostwire: Tokyo, because not only is the story line great and immersive, but the graphics are top tier, and the combat is easy to get the hang of.
