_childDocuments_.review: i was completely wrong about this gamethought it just beeing a generic openworld-grinderboy was i mistakenfirst off: yeah, it's kinda like a checkbox game, but very light on the checkboxes and it's realy designed around em. not like Ubisoft games where the world is just populated for the sake of it. it's less, but deliberatly placed.just as an example: a core aspect is "collecting" souls, to deliver at phonebooths, which nets you a whole lotta exp and money. these souls are placed all around the city; but often enough at places where you have to use your mechanics, almost like playing a light-jump run. you glide, grapple and jump from roof to roof, building to building to collect all of em. it's actualy quite fun and rewarding.which comes down to how "thight" the gameplay feels. no matter if it's traversal or combat: it's great.you unlock jumping, gliding, grappling (a tiny spiderman influence here), etc. but the thing that makes it work is the world-design. it's not a randomly generated openworld, not even a live-like design like Cyberpunk, it's more "blocky"; which is actualy hard to desicbe. but the world is design around your abilities, which makes it feel gamey, but very fun. same goes for the combat. at first it looks like a bad ego-shooter. but the more you get used to it and unlock new abilites, or levelup to improve existing abilities the better it gets. even in chapter 2 combat already offers so many possibilities. there's a perfect block, almost like a Fromsoft parry, but with a much more mainstream approach; the parry-wondow is pretty user-friendly and with upgrades each parry nets you ammo for your shots; same goes for your melee punch, then you unlock specific ammo-types (like an aoe fire attack, or a shotgun like water attack) which you can interweave; ad to that a very strong bow and talismans (aoe-stun, etc.) and combat is much more than just an ego-shooter. it's like a little dance and everything from stealthing around to 1-hit-kill most normal enemies to taking on some large crowd feels very entertaining. you can run around and just shoot things, but you can also use all the available skills and make combat a dance. technicaly the game run almost perfect on my end (i9, 3070/3080, 64, Game HDD, Win10 SSD). everything maxed out, full RTX 1080p+ and constant 60fps (v-sync) without any frame-drops. the games looks technicyl not as impressive as a Cyberpunk...tbh. they are worlds apart. but Ghostwire has a great art-direction and a almost Metal Gear like, clean aesthetic. the comparsion to Metal Gear also applies to how the story is represented. larger cutscenes mixed with small ingame cutscenes, which often gave me the old-school MG feel (pre 3). both maincharacters also often comment on what's happening or have inner dialogues, which was also very entertaining.both the voice over and the writing are great. doesn't feel forced woke, neither does it feel edgy for the sake of it. especialy the relationship between the old KK and the very young protagonist was almost endearing in places. great characters, especialy later on when more human characters appear.none of the small little sidetasks is something to write home about. you collect cash from destroyables to buy some rare upgrades or cosmetic, you collect rare items for demons, or hunt rare demons, etc. . it works because it fits in the world. and gain: it's not an Ubisoft game. at no point is more map filled with little symbols to give you anexiety. i realy do love this game and i'm kinda bummed i skipped it on release; but it was kinda hard to measure what it actualy is. i can fully recommend Ghostwire even to people who got enough of open-world-collect-em-all-ego-shooters ala Ubisoft and co. it's great and i do hope a sequel is already in the making.

_childDocuments_.review: As many others have said, this was not what I expected it to be at all. I think most of us went in looking for some kind of horror / mystery experience, but what we got was a weird mix of Japanese folklore, generic fps combat, and what feels like 3 Assassin's Creed games worth of collectibles. That aside, there is fun to be had here, and nearly anyone that plays this can agree that this is an absolutely gorgeous vision of Tokyo. The city really is the best part and the level of detail is astonishing; it really feels you are running through an abandoned version of Tokyo. It is almost worth recommending just for this, but the bland combat, nearly non-existent story, and overall lack of enemy variety really leave you wanting. In its favor, while all the other characters and villain were not memorable, I did enjoy the interactions between Akito and KK (the main character and his spirit/ghost partner).Despite its many flaws, I had fun with this game and I would still recommend a buy when it is on sale. You will get a solid 40+ hours out of it if you are going for 100%. I know we will probably never see it, but I would really like to see a sequel where the game and world they are trying to build can be more fully realized. Achievement rating: Very simple with no missable achievements taking an average player 35-45 hours depending on how fast you are. Be prepared for tons and tons of collectibles (some are related to side missions which are actually enjoyable and do a better job building the world than the actual main store at least).Update DLC: The rather substantial free DLC update to the game (Spider Thread) adds on a good 20-25 hours of content if you go for full completion. The additions to the main game itself are short but very welcome and the alternative mode is a nice change of pace although it was not nearly as satisfying as the new side missions and content for the main story. I imagine this was all added for the recent Xbox release, but it is still refreshing in this day and age to see such a large update for free. They even added Steam badges.

_childDocuments_.review: The good: great setting, interesting combat mechanics, some great music tracks, effective rtx effects without heavy performance impact. You can pet the dogs  the cats.The bad: it's a  ubisoft game with multiple collectible categories, and hundreds of items in some of them, (one category is required for good ending). It's dark af, and your flashlight is useless 99% of the time. Not a great variety of enemies, the game falls back on "higher tier" pallet swaps quite fast. Vertical traversal is a chore, even when you unlock the free anchor points it's still quite limited on where you can use it. I had a progress-breaking issues a number of times where interactive triggers didn't do anything and I was stuck with the only option to reload from the latest save. Sometimes performance just vanishes (I usually get 80-120 fps, but sometimes it just drops to 30-ish for no reason, and what's weird, it goes worse if you look at the sky). Mouse sensitivity is way too high for me, but there's only one slider for both mouse and controller.The weird: you increase max health by eating food, but you can't eat food if your health is full. So you either do self-harm by going into fog, or let the food go to waste as enemies do almost no damage generally (most encounters end before they even register you as an enemy unless you explicitly taunt them). You get lots of clothing items and costume sets, but the game likes to force specific outfits after story cutscenes for no reason, which is annoying. Some missions have  invisible walls in the most obvious paths to railroad you into intended direction, which is a huge level design letdown considering that most of the time it's very good.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really wanted to like this game. I enjoyed both of the Evil Within games, and was looking forward to this game.  I started out not really liking the game because of the limited combat, but I was engaged with the story and interested to see where it would go. This game is not scary, like the previous titles from the devs Tango Gameworks, but the game looks just as fantastic as them. Its rendition of Tokyo might be worth the asking price just for the virtual tourism.  The game is also very Japanese and I mean that in a historical sense, not a weeb one.  You’ll be learning a lot about Tokyo, yoki, shintoism and some other Japanese traditions.  The game's love of Tokyo and Japanese culture is the high point.  After about 6 hours with the game I was starting to enjoy it.  It's the typical open world game with way too many map markers.  The side quests for the most part seem to have a decent amount of work put into them with most of them having unique areas to explore.  However what you are doing in these areas are largely the same.  You either be killing waves of enemies, catching a yoki, or running around the area cleansing it. This is where the simple combat really drags down the entire experience.  The game is an FPS with only 3 weapons.  Yes there are others, like the bow and the talismans, but they are not bound to the scroll wheel and are not picked up during combat like ammo for your "finger guns". Your finger guns all have 2 different attacks based on if the attack is charged or not.  The other piece of combat is pulling out ghost cores.  If you do enough damage, the ghost core will be exposed and you can pull it out.  A ghost can be killed without doing this, and you can pull multiple cores at once.  It takes a couple of seconds to do this, so positioning is important for this move.  And that is all there is to combat, 3 weapons with 2 shots each and you can pull cores for 15 hours. It gets old fast especially because enemy variety is only okay.  Character design is another thing worth mentioning.  From the look of the fodder enemies all the way to the main big bad, all of the enemies have a strong visual style.  The bosses you’ll fight as a part of the main story are another highlight, not necessarily mechanically, but visually. The last thing I’ll touch on is the story again.  After the interesting start, it ends up being a fairly generic story that you have seen before in countless other forms of media.  The thick veil of Japanese culture kinda makes it somewhat interesting, but overall I was largely disappointed.TLDR; Good rendition of Tokyo and Japanese culture, repetitive combat, generic story but great visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire Tokyo is a game that captivates players with its truly unique graphics and atmospheric design. The graphics reminds me a lot of chilla's art games, Yakuza and even Yume nikki.Graphics and Atmosphere:One of the standout aspects of Ghostwire Tokyo is its graphics and atmosphere. The visuals are stunning, blending realistic elements with a touch of the supernatural.It leans more towards the artstyle than being very photorealistic. Which is a plus in my opinion.Story and Combat:While the graphics and atmosphere shine, the story and combat can sometimes fall short. The narrative, though intriguing, may feel a bit stale at certain points. The pacing could have been improved to maintain a consistent level of engagement. However, it's important to note that these shortcomings do not detract significantly from the overall experience.Positive Aspects:Despite its flaws, Ghostwire Tokyo manages to overcome them and deliver a very positive gaming experience. The game's setting and unique feel make it a standout title among its peers. The exploration aspect is particularly enjoyable, as players are encouraged to uncover the mysteries lurking within the hauntingly beautiful Tokyo. The attention to detail in the game world, coupled with the underlying themes of loss and mourning, adds depth and emotional resonance to the overall experience.Criticism of the Gaming Industry:In recent years, the AAA gaming industry has made its fair share of mistakes, and Ghostwire Tokyo is not exempt from some of these issues. For instance, the installation of anti-piracy software that causes frame drops can be frustrating for players. Additionally, the inclusion of repetitive missions or elements can dampen the excitement and hinder the overall experience.Conclusion:In conclusion, Ghostwire Tokyo is a game that stands out for its unique graphics, atmospheric design, and exploration opportunities. While the story and combat may have their shortcomings, they don't overshadow the overall positive experience the game offers. Despite the issues faced by the gaming industry, Ghostwire Tokyo manages to shine through with its attention to detail . If you're seeking a game that takes you on a nostalgic journey and provides a unique atmosphere, Ghostwire Tokyo is worth exploring.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to start off by saying I'm a tad biased when it comes to this game. I absolutely LOVE Japan and have been desperate to go back since my first trip to Tokyo, so a game that is set in Tokyo where I can recognise streets that I have been down, it absolutely up my alley. Especially since this game allows you to talk to stray cats and dogs, and rewards you for doing so with in game currency or helpful tips. Hits the nostalgia bone hard as when we visited Tokyo we made a point of trying to spot and get a photo of every cat we could find (big animal lover).With this bias in mind; I felt that the game was hands down gorgeous, It captured perfectly the wonder of visiting Tokyo, how the city makes the most of every space available, how dazzling neon lit areas look and how simple and beautiful the little parks and spots of nature can look in contrast to the city.  Finding different Yokai and shape-shifted Tanuki was really fun and I really enjoyed that all of the spirits, other-worldly creatures and enemies seemed to hold true to their inspiring myths and legends in Japan and had a simple breakdown of their mythos. While I feel that if you just follow the main story line it could be a really short game, and can understand people finding the side tasks repetitive, I personally really enjoyed the aspect of helping people pass on after death and found quite a few of the mini story-lines very touching or humorous. I'm not particularly good at games so while I did die on numerous occasions I found that the normal setting was rather forgiving on someone not used to playing on PC and who admittedly flinches away from things running towards them in first person. The controls seemed fairly streamlined to me and i didn't have any major issues out side of my own panic when surprised. Personally, I would definitely recommend this game, especially if you enjoy the aspect of getting to thoroughly explore a map (which I do) and will be giving it another play through after a short break to see if I can find more hidden goodies.The only possible gripe I could have with the game is additional things I would have liked to see at the ending: (spoilers)I would have really enjoyed seeing the main character Atiko potentially meeting the other half of the team that you only hear over the phone Ed, but I also can't imagine how that would play out so I understand not including it. Or getting a glimpse of the world returning to normal, do people realise something happened? how is it reported on the news if they do? but similarly I understand leaving it out.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this a thumbs sideways, but since I can't I'm leaning towards down.  The good things I liked about this:  the graphics are great, I love the aesthetics, the setting is neat, and the dynamic between Akito and KK was fun.  For an open world game, it also does not overstay its welcome.  I did a ton of side stuff and nearly maxed out the skill trees in 20 hours.Now the bad...I felt the open world was pretty boring and had little incentive to explore.  The main collectible in the game is lost spirits, of which there are hundreds to pick up.  Each one requires an animation (sometimes extras for "afflicted" souls!), along with you having a max you are allowed to collect before you have to drop them off.  And the only thing this grants you is money (which I found worthless in this game) and xp (which you will cap out on long before you collect everything).  It really dragged the game down for me and the entire mechanic feels designed to waste your time.  They must have even realized this, as there's a branch of the skill tree that only exists to speed up those animations.  Getting around is also somewhat slow until you unlock a certain upgrade about midway through the game.  Combat is fairly dull.  The story felt completely forgettable to me.  There are a couple cool set pieces in the main story missions but it left me wanting more as they are few and far between.All said I would like to see what a Ghostwire 2 would look like, but I doubt we will see one.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the general vibes of this game: it's a horror first-person "shooter" (not guns, but with supernatural powers) in which you fight Japanese horror tropes (e.g. different types of spirits), and the glossary function was nice for learning about the cultural aspects of each of them. The graphics of the world (e.g. the water reflections, the textures, etc. ) were also great!I think there were three main negative aspects of the game in my mind. First, the pacing was way too slow: the cutscenes and so many of the tasks felt way too drawn out. Second, the gameplay got  repetitive pretty quickly into the game: go to the next gate, cleanse it, go to some places for the plot quests, fight spirits/bosses, etc. Third, I ran into some performance issues that I didn't expect: I tweaked the graphical settings to get a consistent 60 FPS, but after 20-30 minutes of gameplay, the FPS would drop significantly (e.g. 20-30 FPS), but if I just saved and loaded the game, the exact same area would be at a solid 60 FPS again. Not the end of the world, but it seems like something that could be patched up by the developers.Overall, I definitely recommend trying this one out, but I would wait until it's pretty deeply on sale. It's interesting and pretty entertaining, but it gets a bit too repetitive after a while

_childDocuments_.review: As ever Steam's insistence on a simple thumbs up or down is frustrating because I think it really depends on how tired you are of the same forumla.Do you like modern open world RPGs?  If yes, then you'll enjoy this game.  It's well made, good pacing, I have encountered no noteworthy bugs and it's graphically pleasing.  The story missions are fairly interesting, the plot isn't anything groundbreaking but it's solid and will keep you engaged.  The biggest plus is the enemy aesthetic design, very creepy and to my novice eye a fascinating look at some Japanese monsters from folk lore that we don't often see in a major release to a western audience.However, there's nothing new or different here, if you've played anything in the open world genre in the last 10 years you have played this game.  Go to a place, kill the enemies and do the input that unlocks the next map area, collect the collectables in that map area, do one or two of the same half dozen side quests, repeat.  It's not that this is particularly bad and says more about the industry than this game but it does mean it grows a little stale after a few hours, and I fine myself rushing through the repetitive side content so that I can focus on the story.I picked it up for £25 ish on sale in store, to me that's good value.  Full retail... wait until the next sale.6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Purchased the game one year ago because I thought the concept was interesting but also one of the deciding factor was that, unlike a lot of recent games, it didn't include Denuvo and I wanted to support AA/AAA devs not using it.But now,after more that a year I just discover that they added Denuvo I cannot say how disappointed and angry I am.I mean I can understand that devs uses Denuvo for the initial release windows and if they remove it after some months / a year, I don't mind purchasing their games once it's gone. (for example like recently in RE Village)But here they are adding Denuvo on an already released game, one year after release, and worse once people are outside the refund windows so they are stuck with a Denuvo game whenever they like it or not. I find that to be incredibly scummy and dishonest from the devs, if you want to use Denuvo at least have the basic decency of do it from the start, mention it on the game page, and let peoples decide if they care or not, don't force it on peoples afterward once you get peoples money.If the devs had a minimum of honesty they should at least offer unconditional refunds for peoples who purchased the original Denuvo-less version.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE AS OF APRIL 2023: WARNING! DEVS HAVE ADDED DENUVO, AN ANTI-CONSUMER DRM MALWARE TO THE GAME. Why are they adding it now after all this time? Who knows! Even scummier because it isn't listed on the product page. AVOID!I write this after just having 100%'d the game. I wanted to give it a positive review, I really did.Issue one: Frame drops. After a certain period of time, the game will suddenly start chugging and you'll have to save/load to restore your FPS. Not sure if there's an optimization problem or a memory leak, but it's incredibly annoying. Often, you'll get a fatal error message and the game will crash entirely. In one case, I had to force shutdown my computer because it just crashed everything.Issue two: Soul collecting. Granted, this will only matter if you're an achievement hunter or a completionist, but there is an objective to save every soul in the area. All 240,000 of them. Now, when you find souls, you'll always get around 100-700 at once, but that's still a LOT of hunting to do even with the items that allow you to track them. Not to mention, for at least 15,000 of those souls, you need to pray to RNG to find a demon parade that randomly appears in the streets so you can run into it and do a battle to retrieve some of the souls. I spent a good few hours before the point of no return just running around the streets trying to get it to spawn.Issue three: Limited combat abilities. You have wind (fast but weak, single target), water (short range but wide for close combat) and fire (everything must die now). You'll quickly learn that you'll want to charge every single shot, as charged shots are both more effective and make the most out of your limited ammo supply. You also get a bow early on that feels woefully underutilized - the only upgrades for it increase your quiver size and let you draw the bow faster (yeah, you'll want to charge that too). Combat ends up with you running away and spamming charged wind shots in 90% of cases, because while you do have a melee attack, it is weak and you should never, ever use it.Issue four: The story. I played the prequel visual novel and it did a better job fleshing out the characters there in 30 minutes than this game did with its cast over the entire course of the game. The final boss was pretty underwhelming too, and things just kind of...come to an end pretty quickly.On the plus side, I enjoy Japanese occultism, and it was fun seeing a number of legends brought to life or have cameos, however shallow they were. You can also pet dogs and cats and feed the dogs, who reward you with a little more cash than you spent on the dog food, but come on. You should feed them anyway, even if there was no reward.Also, in terms of glitches, I experienced none in my playthrough. No falling through floors, no enemies getting stuck in unreachable areas, etc. The game, while the main content is fairly minimal, is still pretty well put together.

_childDocuments_.review: .: Story :.Not wanting to spoil much of the story with this review, but the story was good. You have your typical protagonist and antagonist. What captivated me more was the character dynamics between the main characters. Listening to them talk, and how they bond the more you play the game shows that there was a lot of love put into this project. Side characters with their corresponding side quests are a great way to introduce them to the player. Side quests aren’t a drag like other games, where they were made into fetch quests and so on. The more side quests you complete, the more of the world, as well as upgrades will be presented to you..: Sound :.The soundtrack is amazing, each song has its place within the cutscene. And the fact that you can unlock them throughout the game and listen to your favourite track as much as you like is a great feature. If you aren’t craving the looping of the game's soundtrack, you can count on the ambient sounds of the game. Expecting noises in an otherwise well known busy city, and suddenly hearing nothing makes you feel like you are truly alone with all the spirits and Yokai… and dogs… and cats… and Tanuki..: Graphics :.For me the graphics were great, some of the cutscenes were blurry for me. But other than that, the game gives you the option to enable motion blur and what not. A cute feature they added was the camera function, so you can have a new wallpaper background as you pose your way throughout all of Tokyo.. : Controls :.Simple enough to learn and master, once you get the hang of it, it makes you feel like a ninja sometimes, if you go for a more stealthy approach. The game supports those that want to go all in and loud, and those who are more of the sneaky, assassin types. .: Content :.The game has enough to keep you busy, it has achievements that you can unlock by actually caring for the game and putting time into it rather than rushing through the story. The side quests are amazing, and packed with lore of japanese history, myths and legends. Looking for everything in the game will intrigue both Japanese culture and the game's story..: Replay :.Sure? If you want to challenge yourself with the Tatari difficulty.This mode will require you to make split-second decisions and take advantage of all of the supernatural tools at your disposal. All XP rewards in this mode are set to zero, and you are unable to change the difficulty after starting the game - (credits Like I said, if you enjoy a challenge, then there is definitely replay capabilities here. Or if you are the kind of person that likes bomb rushing through the main story, then you can always replay the game to do a 100% run. Collecting everything, while reading about the lore once you collect said items..: Fun :.I had a lot of fun with this game, I would definitely recommend it to others that enjoy a single player game like this. It's time consuming, you don't have to think much. For those that are interested in Japan and its mythology, you’d find yourself at home here. I didn’t find myself getting bored at all while playing this game, and was eager to get all the achievements for it, and I encourage those that have this game to do the same. Although I am a bit agitated at the hardcopy price, I would say that the price matches the game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun enough for what it is - an open world action adventure and collectathon. The world of downtown Tokyo and the enemy and combat effects are all visually appealing.What holds the game back is that it executes on this formula about as well as games were 10 years ago. It's pretty rough around the edges. Let me get into more detail:The story is okay. It keeps things moving fluidly from section to section and the cutscenes don't drag on for very long, at least - but the main characters are typical moral paragons and the only interesting conflict between them gets resolved almost immediately, leaving the rest to be saccharine and formulaic.There are many different small things to collect and do around the city. If you've played games like this before, you know the drill - there are little hidden items, larger non-hidden items, special enemies and side quests to clear out, and the obligatory "towers" that reveal more of the map. For the first few hours this is a nice excuse to roam around the city, but the repetition starts to stack up fast, the more you collect. There's not a ton of variety, especially in spirits, the main item you are most incentivized to collect.This is where the game really does not shine, and the main reason I don't recommend it. The combat is somehow both boring and frustrating. One out of your three main attacks (water) is quite useless, and the more powerful one (fire) has so little ammo you'll run out in half of one fight. This leaves you with spamming the most basic one (wind), which is a mindless mash-fest taking down one enemy at a time with what feels like a BB-gun.There is a finishing move you can perform, but other enemies can interrupt you in the middle of it and they always travel in groups. There's a stealth mechanic, but it's poorly tuned and enemies usually aren't thoughtfully arranged to make it work well. This means most fights in the game will end up being normal combat, strafing side to side while you pick off enemies one by one. Little challenge, no special moves, no strategy.As for the enemies, though there is some visual variation and their visual design is one of the more appealing parts of the game, many of them fall into one of just a few categories with very similar movesets. The more challenging ones end up having a shield or some long-range projectiles - things you still defeat just by continuing to strafe around and spam wind.Finally, the ammo - you have limited ammo and the way you replenish is by punching random objects scattered around the world. There's no other incentive to do so, you will have to do it after almost every fight, and it gets old very quickly.After 10 hours of play I found myself avoiding combat in the open world because it was just getting tedious. It's more fun just to run from destination to destination and pick up spirits since they give you experience as well, but it's still mind-numbing in its own way.I have to note this too because it affected my experience a fair bit. There is no field-of-view (FOV) slider, and the game has it set way too tight, with no third-person view. If you're susceptible to motion sickness from games, you will almost certainly get it from this game, especially if you're playing on a larger TV.If you really like the visuals of this game from watching its trailers, like me, you will probably enjoy the game as much as you would any other collectathon. It keeps you immersed and moving and enjoying the world that it's built, for a few hours at a time.But if you are expecting to be blown away with super rewarding and well-tailored gameplay -- perhaps you want to wait for a generous sale to play this one.

_childDocuments_.review: So this review is going to be a bit of a mixed bag. First and foremost: TL;DR I think this game is about a 6.5 or 7/10 for me and you should only pick this game up on sale. For reference sake as of writing the review I have 100% completion. Now to the nitty gritty details. One of the first things I dealt with is an issue many players have complained about: cut scenes. I don't exactly know what the issue was but I believe it has something to do with playing the cut scene in 4k even when the settings are turned to non cinematic 4k and 1080p. Due to that issue the first two cut scenes that begin the entire narrative of the game were abysmally  desynced and the framerate was equally poor. I immediately began tweaking the settings and ultimately what worked for me was setting the game to run in windowed mode with the non cinematic 4k setting off. Restarting the cut scene it played perfectly and I actually understood what I was seeing and hearing. Barring this initial setback, I never had an issue with the cut scenes again in my entire play through. Ghostwire: Tokyo plays really well. The combat is intuitive and the creative Visitors and Yokai you encounter make it the world feel like there are genuine threats and mysteries to deal with. However, no matter what anyone says I cannot emphasize enough that this is essentially a Bethesda skin to a Ubisoft open world title. Instead of Towers and Bases and clear out and expand the map, this game uses Torii Gates and monsters. It is uncanny how easily I was able to slip into the game play loop because I have played many Assassin's Creed and Far Cry games. If you are not looking for that type of content I highly suggest skipping this game. With that major criticism out of the way, I did have a blast running through the world. As you run and explore your main objective other than completing the main quests is to collect spirits left within the world. They are littered everywhere and I mean everywhere. The game does offer you equipment that allows finding them easier and leveling up feels good as your mobility and combat skills upgrade and you can actually feel the difference when you are able to one shot basic enemies with a bow or nuke a group of foes with a well timed Fire Charge attack. One of the most useful abilities allows you to summon a Tengu (which are scattered all over the map) at will to traverse vertical areas. Completing this game felt natural due to Spectral Vision, aka Eagle Eye, which highlights objects you can interact with. There are a lot of collectibles to find and only one kind of collectible is not needed for 100% completion, so completionists beware. One small criticism I have personally is that the main story is rather short. If you ignore all side content you are missing out on about 70% of the stories and experience of the game. With a world so tightly packed with goodies to find it is one of the main appeals for this game. I like the story and feel like I did get my moneys worth (which I bought this game during the Summer Sale) but that doesn't mean it wasn't obvious how short the main campaign is. I had more fun running around dealing with yokais and spirits trapped due to X or Y reason than about the threat and villain of the game. So, I have already mentioned above that one of the main objectives is collecting spirits. There is something I feel I should mention about my time, which seems to be shared across the community. There are various ways you can obtain spirits: finding them in the world, completing side quests, finding Containment Cube events and finding Hyakki Yako (Demon Parades) in the world. Both Containment Cube and Hyakki Yako are random events that can found while exploring past Chapter 2. The initial time you encounter a Hyakki Yako in Shibuya Square, your ally K.K. mentions to avoid it as it will suck you in to the underworld. So, naturally I avoided them until I fell into on accident. It creates an arena and you fight and are rewarded with some spirits. Not terrible on paper, however the Hyakki Yako are on some form of timers. You need 15k spirits from these events in order to complete the game and the last 10 hours of my time were spent running around the world hoping they would spawn. It is easily the worst part about completing the game 100%. Some players reported finding them roughly every 20-25 minutes at major street intersections and that if you just wait they will return, but I found no actual method that worked. I had looked up countless guides and forum posts compiling where the event spawns. I cannot stress this enough: if you see one at any point in the game, as long as you are confident in your fighting capabilities you should absolutely do them, as many of us waste hours desperately trying to find them with absolutely nothing else to do but wait or wander aimlessly. Another minor gripe I have is that there are cosmetic unlocks and even some full outfits to wear, but the game is a first person game. So you only ever see the outfit choices in some cut scenes because others force the character model to be in the default outfit. So ultimately, why even have cosmetics? Even more, most of the cosmetics are just boring. There are 3 different glasses, 2 sunglasses, 4 different kinds of generic looking pants and that goes for the majority of them. It's so odd that the options aren't even really fun or wacky minus masks and a few hats. Everything else is just a different set of normal looking clothes it wildly not fun to dress your character minus the full outfits which there are only four of them. Alright, still with me? So I know it somewhat looks like I just spent this entire review bashing the game but honestly it's only a few issues except the technical issues of cut scenes, that bar this game from being really worth the price tag. I truly enjoyed my time and loved reading and listening to all the lore and fighting these creative fights but at the end of the day this game is just alright. It's solid but other than this being a Tokyo Skin to a Ubisoft-esq game, finishing this game made me realize that I've played a dozen other games just like this and the wheel isn't advanced any one way. Some may say that it is worse because of the faults, but I think it's just as good as the competition. If Far Cry 6 and Assassins Creed Origins launched at retail $60 I don't think it's odd that this game did too, but a majority of my time was spent collecting things and not exactly doing anything of real value. Also, some of the achievements basically require you to save/load until you achieve the result you want which is boring. Bethesda please stick to RPG it clearly is your strong suit.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, so much so it's one of the few games to 100%, however I do have some criticisms despite this.First of, a special mention to the accessibility of the game when it comes to difficulty. It doesn't lock anything away whilst allowing you to not only play on the easiest setting, but also has a separate toggle to switch off timers on timed events. I know this won't be for everyone, but for someone like me that prefers a stress free game and is just along for the ride it really is a great feature. Although, it does have moments where music is playing, tensions are high and without the urgency of the timer it can fall flat. Still appreciated.The story I actually enjoyed, as well as the side missions that are more unique that just starting to collection side quests. That said, it is also where my main critic is. I want more. The main story, while good, seems short. The set pieces and engaging portions are few and far between, and seem like the time is inflated by the open world and the collection mini games. The same for the side quests, it's one of the few games where I enjoyed seeking them out as a few of them were truly unique, and sometimes uncovered more lore into not just the game but Japanese culture. I need more of this.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire Tokyo was one of the games that I've wanted to play on release and when I finally got a PC capable of handling it, I dove head first. It's a great game for people who want to explore Japan's horror stories without ever leaving their room. Monster from mythos along with cute tanuki and every one in a while a helpful spirit makes the place feel alive despite the lack of people. It really also helps that city is to scale to real life. I cannot go to Japan to visit on my own but it did scratch that itch of visiting it. You can feel the care they took in making it as accurate as possible. The ending is great and it had a twist I wasn't expecting(more like expecting to happen but didn't, nonetheless a twist that didn't happen is still a twist to me). The texts on unlocked phones, backstories of other characters, the random piles of clothes of people who got raptured made it feel eerie and a blimp in time. It was truely a fun game even if the gameplay loop was repetitive. The repetitive nature was almost meditating in a weird way and going rooftop to rooftop collecting souls made me feel like Spiderman. The connection between the 2 main characters developing was fun to watch and reminded me of the connection between Yugi and Yami in Yugi-Oh. Now a gripe: I have a completionist attitude and I desperately wanted to save all the souls in Shibuya. I had finished the base game without the dlc but before the final cutscene. Shibya should have been 100%. It wasn't and there was one section where it was 98%, yet after checking it repeatedly with the highest tier soul seach bracelet, I couldn't find it anywhere. Only after googling on reddit that it said that was supposed to happen and it will update to 100% after the cutscene. I wish I didn't waste at least 2 hours before searching but you live and you learn I suppose. Bigger gripe: It is truely a shame that Microsoft closed down the Tango Gameworks studio. I would have loved to see more from them. My love for this game made me want to play Hi-Fi Rush, another title of Tango. I would have never played it if it wasn't for the love I have for this game. I hope that corporations look at the love for making games and not only focus on the profits that can be gained from it. This game is a labor of love and I hope the industry reverts back to passion projects where they get popular due to the effort put behind them rather than yet another remake of the same game with minimal updates (looking at you COD, NBA, FIFA etc).

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I liked this game a lot. It is absolutely *gorgeous*-- just walking around Shibuya and taking in the sights and sounds is wonderful. Enemy variety is somewhat lacking at least for the length of this game.However, I have two BIG caveats I'd like to mention:1) This is NOT A GOOD CHOICE FOR STEAM DECK. _childDocuments_.review: ahhh, this was a fun one. Ghostwire: Tokyo is a soap opera constructed out of repurposed Japanese folklore that uses a dense environment and an array of creepy enemies to bind it all together. i played the game in Japanese language with English subtitles and found the acting to be very well done and the story itself to be entertaining. Akito, the lead, is a bit bland on his own but the devs decided to add in a sassy mentor figure of K.K. to serve as foil and the end result carried me as the player through forty plus hours of enjoyable gaming.a caveat: there's A LOT of stuff to collect which is right up my alley because i find that kind of mechanic soothing, but if you're irritated by finding X amount of weird out-of-the-way stuff then this probably isn't the game for you. also of note, i found the game to be very well optimized on my 2019 Acer Nitro 5 laptop with 8GB of RAM, but i also turned all the settings down and the resolution was at the second to lowest setting. had no crashes to speak of, and it only lagged badly at one point which i fixed by restarting the laptop.in conclusion, this game is now one of my favorites and i fully intend to replay it every year or so in the future. i hope it does well enough in sales that Tango Gameworks can continue to make games with this sort of aesthetic and tone.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't do reviews. But this was an absolutely fantastic game! As someone who loves Japanese culture and folklore, this game was a real treat for me to experience. _childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire: Tokyo is an open world Action-RPG with Horror Elements. It has what you can expect from an open-world RPG, collectables, side quests, upgrades and so on and so forth.The game, which might be obvious, is set in Tokyo, specifically in Shibuya; which is, as far as I know, one of the main districts of Tokyo. I recently read that the area you play in the game is faithfully recreated for the most part to look like how Shibuya looks in real life, however I've never been so I'll just have to take their word for it.Regardless, the map itself is very well crafted, it genuinely feels like it is (or was) a lived in City. It's very dense just like how you would imagine, big tall buildings, flashing neon lights and even the more suburban areas are taken care of so well. The map is a genuine joy to be in and for me it didn't get boring once. I loved exploring all that Shibuya had to offer, it's probably the closest you can get to wandering around Shibuya-Tokyo without actually going there in person.One of the best parts about Ghostwire: Tokyo is how the lights change depending on your detection level. The game is -not- a stealth game but it does have stealth elements. If you're wandering around and nothing is going on, everything looks normal. If you're being detected, the lights start to go yellow-orange, when you've been detected and combat begins, the lights go red. I don't know what it was about this but it just made everything feel like the environment was reacting with me, giving the game a more horror-like feel.The game borrows almost all its horror aspects from Japanese Shinto Mythology, but the most interesting part is seeing how they correspond in a real modern life setting. We're used to seeing Oni's and Kappa's in games like Sekiro and Nioh, but to see them in the 21st century? I thought it was pretty cool.As far as I'm aware, the game originally started its life cycle as The Evil Within 3 and things got too off-track so they made a new IP instead. However if you've played The Evil Within 1 & 2 you will 100% see its influence bleed through, namely environment shifts and how certain enemies look.You have three "Main" weapons in your arsenal, each corresponding with an element, Wind, Fire and Water. To put it plainly, Wind/Gust is your semi-automatic rifle/pistol, Water is your shotgun and Fire is your Grenade-Launcher/RPG. You have other weapons at your disposal such as talismans and a bow but I rarely ever used them.The combat is... I wouldn't say it's boring but it is repetitive, since you have a limited arsenal at your disposal, you'll find yourself using what you have, which isn't a whole lot. I found that in the beginning all I was upgrading was my Gust attacks, and near the end of the game I discovered that upgrading the water abilities turned out to be very strong and satisfying. So please experiment and use everything at your disposal, which as I said isn't a lot. However what I will say is, there's one thing about the combat that -never- gets boring. And it's core removal. Whether you've got one or whether you've got five exposed cores and you start extracting them at distance, the sound effects, the animation of the yellow wires as Akito pulls on them. It's divine and ever so satisfying.The main story is a alright, effectively similar to Shadow of War in the sense that you've got some bloke inside you telling you what to do and your goals eventually align, each with their own respective motives for doing so. It is the Side Quests that really show off the world the developers have built. Some of the side quests in this game are some of the best content I've ever played in terms of self contained storylines and the environments in which it puts you in. Genuinely some of the best side questing experiences I've ever had.I see some people complaining about enemy variety but I thought there was enough for the game, considering the length of it. Albeit some of the enemies are just different coloured variants of the first one you encounter, but they at least have some extra little niche to them. If you're like me as well, and enjoy collectables, and enjoy games like Assassin's Creed and what not where you just go around picking things up, this game has this in abundance. Souls, Nekomata Items, Yokai, then you'll have a great time. It's a good game for completionists.The only sort of bug I ever encountered was that sometimes when you try to charge an attack, it doesn't charge and makes you expend a shot before charging the second, this can be a little problematic when you're using water and fire abilities, considering you get significantly less ammo for them that you do Gust.Overall, the game's a good new IP and definitely worth a shot, pick it up on sale if you don't fancy the full price tag. It's worth the full price if you're going to collect everything in it. Pick it up on sale if you're just going for a one and done playthrough. It's an enjoyable game and the horror elements, although you'll never be scared, are executed well. 7/10, I hope they make a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a big fan of Japanese mythology, and are craving a Ubisoft-esque free roam title, then this is the game for you. Otherwise, it's most likely not worth the price. The two prime examples of this being the fact that there's only four weapons,   and that almost all of the side-quests follow a very similar premise with the same spirit npcs handing them out. Despite some of the shortcomings, I found the combat / collectathon game-play loop very satisfying and addicting. I also loved pretty much everything about the setting, enemies, and bosses. (yokai included). I would love to see a sequel or dlc in the future that fully expands upon all of this game's mechanics, and gives the people like myself, who thoroughly enjoyed this game's world something more. _childDocuments_.review: I rarely have a love/hate relationship with a game, mainly because games I rate poorly REALLY have little to no redeeming qualities, while those I praise I enjoyed wholeheartedly. Yet Ghostwire: Tokyo - a game I was beyond hyped when the first trailer was announced, and later when game's launch drew near was stoked to play it - is a game of conflicting visions. Like Yin and Yang, it offers plenty of good (the story, characters, lore, worldbuilding, visuals) and plenty of bad (f&#%ing collectibles galore (Ubishaft-style), stale combat after your 100 enemy encounter, no respect for player's time with quests like Spirit Photographer, where you cannot carry all photos but must return after 3/4 have been purged). I still cannot wrap my head around the developer's idea as to include the utterly terrible open-world elements like collectibles (relics/spirits/clothes/graffiti/music tracks/tanuki/jizo statues/yokai i.e. magatama/food & drink/landmarks/voice logs/KK notes/figurines) into a game that has some 10 hours of story-related content that is actually good. Would've been way smarter to have strong narrative focus through-and-through, without artificial playtime extenders (or, if there was a need for collectibles, stay around the sweet spot of 50 total, not over 600 (!) with the Spider Thread Update (STU)).But then there is combat, which visually looks amazing... the first couple of hours, at least. Then you begin routinely taking the enemies out, more in quick purge style due to bullet sponginess (I was playing on hard, mind you) than duking it out, or avoiding the combat altogether! This is a problem for a game that hooked me on hand sign, Shinto Onmyōji shtick, and more so when I was (in late game) only using two modes of attack - one resembling submachine gun fire, the other literally flamethrower...And don't even think about playing Spider's Thread - a roguelite mode that is unlocked early on (past Chapter 2) in the story - IF you are a completionist. It is one of the grindiest experiences I ever encountered, and feels like it was just tacked on and sloppily made (wonder if Bethesda, encouraged by terrific PREY's Mooncrash roguelite DLC, urged Tango Gameworks to add something similar to Ghostwire: Tokyo). It also doesn't respect your time with how little content there actually is, urging you to get better at the game, slowly climbing those permanent buffs/skills with each attempted run, only to give you f#&@ing beads at level 50 which which you can ONE SHOT ANYTHING (yes, even the 'bosses', which are basically recycled bosses from the base game)! Of course, you can also be one shot, but since the enemies have A.I. that is dumb as rocks (plus the majority of enemies won't even attempt to fling projectiles at you unless they can reach you in melee) it becomes trifling to deal with them as you breeze through all 30 levels that took you thrice as much to complete without them, Overall, with the caveat that you get this game dirt cheap ($10 or less), you throw your compeltionist ambitions out of the window at the beginning (or suffer like myself - masochist that I am, apparently), are into Japanese folklore observed through eyes of a modern man, and give one or two spins to the roguelite mode (just to confirm what I wrote here for yourself) - I'd say it is worth it. In any other circumstances - stay away, not worth your time at all (unless you are REALLY into collecting stuff and are tedium-proof).

_childDocuments_.review: What makes a good open-world game? As far as I am concerned, two things: an effective base-routine and an abundance of micro-plots. Anyone can see what I mean by effective routine: whatever the action the game is based on (assassinate dude in Assassin's Creed, shoot the bandit in RDR, etc.) As far as this gameplay loop is concerned, Ghostwire does quite well; the action is fluid, and while rather simple and repetitive, it remains mostly fun. Now what do I mean by abundance micro-plots? I mean the presence of elements that engage the player and contribute to immersion: elements that both make the open-world 'alive' and that make the player 'invested' in that universe. That can take many forms, from memorable characters or location, to engaging side-quests, world-altering player choices, or simple quirky details. What's important with those 'micro-plots' is that they should not be mandatory (so that the player feels they result of their choices) and that they should be unique (as soon as they are repeated, they stop to make the world 'alive' and enter the realm of the gameplay loop).Well as far as 'micro-plots' are concerned, Ghostwire: Tokyo is a train-wreck. Let us speak first of the macro-plot, the major story itself. It's not good. We've certainly seen worse, but we've also definitely seen a lot better. The characters are all mediocre (one-dimensional and effusive), the dialogues are flat (and the English translation is both poor and inaccurate, and the story is barely coherent. That's a shame because the premise (kinda Ghostbuster meets Shrine-maiden) appealed to me: but we end up with a very generic 90s anime story.Now for the all-important mini-plots--those little optional bits that made games like Red Dead Redemption or The Witcher 3 such compelling experiences, quite aside from their main story-line--well there is not many to speak of. Very few things in this game you will need to do only once. Most villains, most quests, most challenges and even most loot you will encounter three or four times. That cute Ghibli-style Yokai you saved from hungry ghosts? You'll have to save the same one at least four times. That mission where you have to follow the foot steps of a girl throughout the city? You'll have to do that five or six other times. That mini-boss that freeze the ground under your feet? She'll become a run-of-the-mill monster half-way through. To conclude: there's potential in this game, because the gameplay and the graphics are quite good. The design is not all it could have been, but the idea of using Japanese folklore in a modern setting is a good one. The city itself is made well enough, although assets, buildings and even whole blocks are re-used ad nauseam, and most areas look entirely the same. There is potential, but there is not enough work put in. I don't know if it was rushed or if the developers were just lazy, but it feels like they did not have the resources to make a good open-world, but still refused to make a linear adventure game, and therefore had to copy-paste much of it. I paid about 20€ for the game, and I feel I might have overpaid a little. At any rate it is not worth the 50€ price tag usually asked for i.

_childDocuments_.review: 1. Beautifully realized game world that showcases Tokyo, and Shibuya in particular, in gorgeous detail.2. Very unique enemy design.3. Awesome music.4. Occasionally interesting side content.1. Incredibly boring gameplay loop. Hundreds of pointless collectibles and the same mission structure over and over again lead to an ultimately mindless experience.2. Bland story that fails to do anything meaningful with its otherwise intriguing premise.3. Combat has some interesting animations but there's very little strategy or challenge even on higher difficulties.4. The open world takes all the negative aspects of "Ubisoft" style games with none of what makes them (sometimes accidentally) fun. Clear tower (torii gates in the case of Ghostwire: Tokyo), kill enemies, find collectibles, move to next area, rinse and repeat. It's so incredibly lifeless and boring.5. Why is Akito sooo daaamn slooow??? The guy looks fit enough yet sprints like somebody on life support.DON'T WASTE YOUR TIME WITH THIS GAME!!! Sure it's pretty, sure Tokyo looks amazing, sure the combat might seem fun and the enemies weird & disturbing but they're all superficial elements. Replace them with anything else and you'll see Ghostwire: Tokyo for what it really is: just a pointless time sink. It's so unfortunate that such a beautifully designed world houses such an empty shell of a game. Respect your time, watch a playthrough on YouTube at most and move on.

_childDocuments_.review: Had a pretty fun time with this game. The story gets a little lost in the sauce with all the other collectibles, side missions, and yokai you can hunt down. The combat is fairly simple with an upgrade system that makes you close to a god once you get everything settled; you'll end up plowing through mobs with no issue and the final boss won't stand much chance either. The majority of collectibles are fun to collect, from hunting down tanukis or finding different yokai that all are hidden or require a chase; everything except the Kappa (I f**king loathe doing anything related to the Kappa).Didn't have much issue with crashing. The game performed well on higher settings and the art of combat and the background of Tokyo really add beauty to the game. The new DLC was free and nice, adding a haunted school side mission to the game, which provided a different feeling, along the lines of abject horror set in a Japanese cult horror film. The spider thread DLC was mediocre imo. The levels became repetitive and trying to complete the catalog is purely based on random encounters so you could be screwed going 60+ levels and never finding a cat (you'll get it).All in all, I had fun and got my money's worth out of it. I received this product as a gift and it was a pleasant one to get.

_childDocuments_.review: The main story is undeniably its weakest link! Very rushed and and lacking depth. But despite these shortcomings, the weird blend of cyberpunk+supernatural theme surprisingly worked. Exploring Tokyo, especially at night, is where the game truly shines! The world is undeniably beautiful, teeming with secrets to uncover and mysteries to solve. From hidden alleyways to towering skyscrapers, there's no shortage of places to discover. BUT! the absence of human life in this game creates a sense of emptiness. While the spirits and demons may populate the streets, the lack of human presence makes the world feel very lifeless.The mechanics and combat is very underwhelming! It could have benefited from a third-person option imo. Not a bad game, but not that good either. .

_childDocuments_.review: Tango Gameworks deserves massive applause for achieving the impossible and hitting the sweet spot in Ghostwire: Tokyo's open world design.  There's enough to do, the world is immersive but not over-large, rewards and feedback are satisfying, fast travel is accessible, the story is cohesive, and traversal is ideal.I am tempted to 100% this game, not for the sake of completionism, but because I am genuinely interested in seeing the outcomes of everything the player is asked to do.Admittedly, I'm sure I was particularly drawn in because I am a folklore buff -- if the theme and content doesn't interest you for its own sake, you might get bored, but I have to say that I'm not /sure/ you will.  The game has the same repetitive activities that all open world games have, but in Ghostwire they each felt unique /enough/ to me that I never felt like I was grinding through the game.I made an unusual choice at the beginning and decided to play on Easy.  I am glad I did, because the net result was that I found the combat visceral without being too challenging.  That being said, the game gives you a whole arsenal of non-standard weapons and tools that on higher difficulties I'm sure are required to be successful, not to mention satisfying to anyone looking for a more tactical experience.Wholeheartedly recommended.  I hope to see more from Tango, in this universe or otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Please play this game, but don't bother platinuming it. The game is a brilliant experience and the achievement hunt is bogged down with 500+ collectibles, not including spirits, that turn the platinum experience into an incredibly tedious and frustrating experience.You know, I think that there's a lot about this game that feels kind of mediocre or overdone. A lot of the open world design feels like it's taking cues from games that we collectively ran out of patience for a few years ago, the combat is middling to okay. But I think this is a whole that's way way greater than the sum of its parts. The music is stunning, the story is totally fine but elevates to great because of a phenomenal set of performances from the entire cast (in Japanese, anyway, I didn't play the dubbed version). I cried three or four times during the last two chapters, which isn't hard to make me do but certainly means I was halfway invested here and there.I have about 20 hours, with a bit of cleanup to do in postgame still to go, but I also spent a fair bit of time before beating this game doing the collectathon stuff, so I think the average player probably gets 10-15 hours out in a playthrough with relatively minimal ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around.Worth 60 bucks? Probably, just to support Mikami and Co. There's a postgame there for you to clean up achievements, so you'll get more than just the first playthrough out of it if you so desire. In general, I think that this kind of game is cool, and while I think that a fair bit of it feels a bit uninspired, the things that *do* feel inspired make this game a really memorable experience.EDIT: Coming back to this after wrapping up the platinum after another... seven or so hours. I think this game is worth playing for sure but the platinum is just. not worth the hassle. There's at least two if not three achievements that are very RNG-centric and the achievement to collect all spirits is not only incredibly tedious but, if you haven't been doing them at intervals throughout the game so far, locked behind random event spawning that, for the life of me, I cannot figure out the pattern for. The collectathon that this game turns into for the platinum honestly really takes away from the otherwise really cool and really fun experience that this game had been up to then. I absolutely still recommend this game but with the stipulation that you should probably simply play it for what it is and not plan to platinum it. Was not an enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire: Tokyo is an amazing experience, even if the game itself is a fairly standard open-world action affair. It's pretty repetitive in terms of what you can actually do, but the gameplay isn't really the main selling point. All that said, the action is pretty solid, it looks and sounds great, and the world itself is the most vibrant representation of Japan I've ever seen. The story isn't going to set the world on fire, but it's still well told and has some interesting characters. The two main protagonists don't have the most compelling screen presence in the story, but they share a ton of banter as they go around the world that goes a long way toward establishing their relationship and also providing a window through which to see how they view modern Japan and its culture. It's the perfect palate cleanser to something like Elden Ring, which asks you to keep track of everything on your own and doesn't offer much in the way of guidance, but Ghostwire: Tokyo is still a smart game that constantly engages, especially if you play on harder difficulty levels and especially if you love exploration. An absolute must-play for virtual tourists, a solid choice for anyone looking for a good popcorn action movie type shooter, and a pleasing playground for those who love to just jump all over a big open-world sandbox to find collectibles and mark off side quests. Come for the stellar visuals, stay for the ridiculously stunning, detailed representation of Tokyo and fun facts about Japanese history, culture, and food.

_childDocuments_.review: From the icy realms of HowlStrom, where magic and lore intertwine, I ventured into the hauntingly beautiful world of "Ghostwire: Tokyo". As an Ice Wolf with over 36 years of gaming wisdom, I've traversed many digital landscapes, but this game... this game is a masterpiece that resonates deeply with my soul.The narrative is captivating. Tokyo, a city I've dreamt of visiting, stands desolate, its populace vanished, leaving behind an eerie silence, broken only by the whispers of vengeful Yokai. The premise is intriguing: a city once bustling with life, now overrun by supernatural forces, and a dangerous occultist pulling the strings from the shadows. As I delved deeper, the story unraveled layers of emotion, mystery, and suspense, reminiscent of the ancient tales told in HowlStrom.Visually, "Ghostwire: Tokyo" is a feast for the eyes. The juxtaposition of Tokyo's modern skyscrapers with its traditional temples and alleyways creates a mesmerizing tableau. The attention to detail is impeccable, from the shimmering reflections in puddles to the ethereal glow of spirits. Iconic landmarks like Shibuya Crossing and Tokyo Tower are rendered with such precision that I could almost feel the chill of the HowlStrom winds against the neon-lit streets of Tokyo.The combat system, while seemingly straightforward, offers a depth that requires strategy and finesse. The elemental abilities, reminiscent of my own ice magic, added a layer of complexity to the battles. Ascending Tokyo's skyline, soaring over its streets, and ambushing enemies from above felt exhilarating. The recent "Spider's Thread" update further enriched the gameplay, introducing new areas, extended cutscenes, and a roguelite game mode that kept me on my paws.However, it's not just the combat that shines. The exploration aspect is equally enthralling. The city, though haunted, beckons with secrets waiting to be uncovered. Every corner, every alley holds a story, a piece of the puzzle. And the Yokai? They're not just foes; they're a bridge to Japan's rich folklore, adding depth to the narrative.Now, no game is without its flaws. Some tasks felt repetitive, and the combat, at times, lacked the challenge a seasoned gamer like me craves. But these are mere nitpicks in an otherwise stellar game. The developers have poured their heart and soul into crafting this gem, and it shows.In conclusion, "Ghostwire: Tokyo" is more than just a game; it's an experience. It's a journey through a city where the boundaries between the natural and supernatural blur, where every moment is a dance between light and shadow. From the frozen heart of HowlStrom, I, Kiba Snowpaw, wholeheartedly recommend this game to all who seek adventure, mystery, and a touch of magic. May your journey in Tokyo be as enchanting as mine.

_childDocuments_.review: I am still playing through this game, and only in chapter 2. Will update my when I beat it as well. That said, exploring Tokyo is a real treat. I have never seen a more detailed Tokyo in any game ever, the neon signs, the verticality, the random stores and other locales you can enter, the residences its all very authentic to when I visited! Additionally, this PC port seems to run really well for me with DLSS and raytracing turned on for me at 1440p. Worth calling out since this isn't always the case.I really take my time with games, and I noticed that the game really does its best to make you want to explore. I see many people complaining that collecting spirits is repetitive and I do agree, but they do a really good job of guiding you around the map. Sometimes you stumble upon fun little landmarks that really have no bearing on anything other than like 'oh I found this place'. There will usually be a spirit or something ambush you but really if you are an urban explorer or are curious of Tokyo, this is a really fun time.Learning about the japanese food and culture is also kinda neat, though can get wordy over time. You also collect relics that cut pretty deep culturally, I feel like I'm learning all kinds of new stuff by reading through item descriptions and even just random messages left around the map.Combat is fine, it feels a bit secondary but things open up the more you play. There is an exhilaration in deciding the vanquish foes or keep firing at them since there is a risk reward tug of war. I am playing on hard mode and I have died going in guns blazing a couple times, so it is not completely mindless. If you want to cheese the game, you can, but if you want to challenge yourself and switch ammo type and look cool - well you can do that too. I still think the real draw is the environment here, that said it still impresses me as I continue to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Tango Gamework's rendition of Tokyo is stunning to behold. The atmosphere of the game is excellent and immersive. However, the game falls short in all other fronts. Combat gets stale very quickly and the story, while not horrible, isn't really something to write home about. Main story missions can be repetitive, but side missions are usually pretty interesting and provide insight into Japanese mythology. Now, on to the completionist review. The spirit collection is horrendous and the other map completion stuff is very repetitive. It's a mindless slog with no variation between areas. Unless you're a virtual tourist looking to sightsee, I unfortunately cannot recommend this game. It is either mediocre or bad in all aspects aside from the visuals. It might be worth it if you manage to grab it on a very steep discount, but at full price there are much better games you can buy.Positives: Visuals, Japanese mythology which is mainly explored in side missionsNegatives: Boring combat, stale story, repetitive main story missions, horrible collectibles and map completionFinal score: 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire: Tokyo : By Triple F "Ghostwire: Tokyo", developed by Tango Gameworks and published by Bethesda Softworks, is a mesmerizing and enigmatic journey that seamlessly blends elements of Japanese folklore, urban exploration, and supernatural mystery into an unforgettable gaming experience. From its captivating narrative to its meticulously crafted world and unique game-play mechanics, "Ghostwire: Tokyo" is a testament to the potential of video games as an art form.The game opens with a mysterious event known as "The Vanishing" in which the entire population of Tokyo disappears, leaving the city eerily empty. You step into the shoes of Akito, a gifted medium who possesses supernatural abilities that allow you to see and interact with spirits. Tasked with uncovering the truth behind the Vanishing and the sinister spirits responsible, you embark on a haunting journey through the streets of Tokyo.The storytelling in "Ghostwire: Tokyo" is both compelling and emotionally resonant. The narrative is richly layered, drawing from Japanese mythology and folklore to create a world that feels simultaneously familiar and otherworldly. The characters you encounter, from the enigmatic spirit guide to the tormented spirits, are well-developed and contribute to the game's eerie atmosphere. The central mystery is expertly paced, keeping you engaged and eager to uncover the truth."Ghostwire: Tokyo's" gameplay is a delightful mix of action, exploration, and supernatural abilities. As Akito, you navigate the beautifully recreated streets of Tokyo, which are dripping with atmospheric detail. The city feels alive, even in its emptiness, thanks to the meticulous attention to detail in environmental design. The eerie silence punctuated by occasional ghostly apparitions creates a tense and immersive atmosphere.The core gameplay revolves around using your supernatural abilities to combat malevolent spirits. Akito can harness a wide array of powers, such as elemental attacks and telekinesis, to fend off spectral threats. Combat is fast-paced and intuitive, offering a satisfying blend of magic and martial arts. The variety of abilities at your disposal encourages experimentation and creativity in dispatching foes.Exploration is a key element of the game, and Tokyo's open-world design rewards thorough investigation. Side quests, hidden collectibles, and hauntingly beautiful vistas await those who dare to explore every nook and cranny. The incorporation of traditional Japanese elements, like shrines and torii gates, adds depth and cultural authenticity to the experience.The game is quite the visual marvel. The attention to detail in recreating Tokyo's urban landscape is astounding, and the game's use of lighting and particle effects creates a hauntingly beautiful aesthetic. The contrast between the mundane and supernatural elements of the city is striking, making the game's atmosphere truly immersive.The audio design deserves special praise. The haunting melodies of traditional Japanese instruments mixed with eerie ambient sounds amplify the game's sense of unease. The voice acting is top-notch, with the cast delivering emotionally charged performances that draw you deeper into the narrative.To sum up, "Ghostwire: Tokyo" is a masterclass in storytelling and world-building, offering a captivating narrative set in a meticulously crafted urban playground. Its unique blend of Japanese folklore, supernatural abilities, and atmospheric exploration results in a gaming experience that is both haunting and beautiful. Tango Gameworks has created a game that pushes the boundaries of what can be achieved in interactive storytelling. "Ghostwire: Tokyo" is not just any ordinary game; it's a hauntingly immersive journey through the supernatural heart of Tokyo that will leave a lasting impression on players long after the credits roll.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostwire: Tokyo is a game that is both frustratingly mediocre and deserving of a sequel. Had it's potential been reached, it could have been game of the year, and if a sequel ever allows the IP to reach the heights in view throughout every idea, it could be a masterpiece. The presentation is great. It ran well, looked good, and sounded good too. Pulling cores and firing off attacks feels fantastic. I wish I had more to say about it. It's simply good. The gameplay on the other hand is shockingly worse than bad; it's boring. You just shoot enemies and occasionally strafe. New abilities are consistently introduced but they always achieve the same thing, and with the same mechanical input from the player. Movement feels subpar, but at least the shooting looks good. The open world bored me, which is a surprise given that I normally love a Ubisoft-esque open world game. The story was fine. Individual moments were hit or miss, but at least the finale was very well done, nearly justifying the 8 hours of tedium to get there. Overall I hate that I have to either "recommend" or "not recommend" a game because Ghostwire: Tokyo lands so harshly between the two. I'd say I would recommend it because it is an exceptionally unique concept, but only if it is on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a breath of fresh air in a sea of never-ending open worlds and online features. Tango Gameworks really nailed it with this action-adventure packed with scares, and the best part? You can finish it in less than 20 hours.So picture this: You're in Tokyo, a metropolis where everyone has vanished, leaving behind yokai, folklore creatures, and vengeful spirits. You play as Akito, a survivor who merged with a spirit named KK, granting you some badass supernatural powers. And guess what? You've got a to-do list: collect spirits, find your sister, dispel evil fog, and stop an evil mastermind. Easy peasy, right?The combat is a mix of action and first-person shooter vibes. Forget guns; you've got magic. Wind, fire, water – you name it, you use it. It's like Doom but with spells and heart-ripping. Yes, you heard that right. Rip out hearts for magical bonuses. It's weirdly satisfying.Now there some missions where you have to rely on yourself without your magical powers, relying on stealth. Bows and silent take downs do take the forefront and it's a nice change of pace that adds some variation to the game. It forces you to think methodically.Now, navigating Tokyo means taking down hordes of enemies, cleansing shrines, and saving lost souls. Think of it as an experience system. The more souls you rescue, the more upgrades you get. Simple, right? Plus, it's got that indie exploration game touch, with heartwarming sidequests and a love letter to the city itself.Speaking of the city, Tokyo is astonishingly detailed, with familiar places and hidden gems. Cats run the convenience stores, by the way. Ghosts, creepy monsters, and atmospheric details – this game has it all.Ghostwire: Tokyo is a unique gem that respects your time. It masterfully blends action with exploration, and the stories you'll uncover are fascinating, sad, and sometimes hilarious. If you're tired of endless, time-consuming games, give Ghostwire a shot. Trust me, it's a hauntingly good time.

That said, the game is bloated with side content (following the steps of every open world game nowadays), but thankfully grinding is not necessary to progress. The combat is relatively simple but satisfying. I would compare it with a good FPS where different weapons work better for different situations. Overall, I would definitely recommend the game, especially if bought on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to recommend this game but I can't.   The story, skills and city are really fun.   The thing that kills this game for me is the amount of bugs, crashes, and corrupting game files that shows the lack of QT that went into this game.   The first major cut scene is a KNOW issue that de-syncs the video and audio.   The graphics that chug and stutter even at low settings.  More de-syncing cut scenes. 1 auto-save slot that when, not if, the game corrupts can cause you to loose hours of playtime.  Manual saving even corrupts from time to time so it's smart to make the same 2-3 times on different files.It's utterly stupid.   I want to love this game so much but it's so damn buggy that I can't.
