_childDocuments_.review: There were a few tricky platforming parts, enough that I considered stopping as early as the level with the lady bugs.  Had to resort to flipping my controller upside-down in order to make it through the last level, but that just came down to how my brain works. Generally relaxing though with beautiful visuals and a nice orchestral soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful platformer with a wonderful story, fun and intuitive gameplay, stunning visuals, and beautifully moving music. Takes just a couple of hours to complete but I'm really looking forward to playing it again. Nice balance between being spoonfed instructions and figuring things out for yourself, not too challenging but super rewarding. Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Cute, quirky, with a Ghibli-esque feel to it.  If you want something to kill a bit of time and not stress about it, this is it.  If you're into Ghibli movies and the like, this will probably connect with you.  On par with the game Journey (spiritual, little dialogue, short gameplay in a 2D platformer style)PROS:  relaxing, artistic, easy to pick up, music was nice, no major frustrating mechanics, quaint storytelling, achievements were not a struggle, ability to pick any level on the main menu if you want to repeat it, no micro-transactions, the user interface was easy to use.CONS: pretty short (less than 3 hours to complete).  An expansion or sequel would be nice.  Described as a puzzle-platformer but most of the puzzles were very straightforward.  If you want difficulty in puzzle-solving this isn't it (not necessarily a bad thing, I enjoyed the ease of the game)9/10 would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful and lightly challenging game. Its feels nicely paced, the controls feel fluid, and the music is atmospheric, the sound effects fitting. overall the story with game are good, I would recommend this game to the casual platform player due to the fact it slow pace and there's no real danger in going slow or you never get so set back you have a hard restart.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: The artwork  is so pretty, the characters are so cute. The storyline is full of hope and you work hard to guide the main character on his adventure to keep that for the other characters in the game. I was excited about it from the moment I saw the trailer and it truly lived up to that excitement. I recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a strange experience and I feel like the developer really didn't know what kind of game they wanted and how to tell the story. The storytelling is very weak and limited, with random cinematics. I would recommended this game if you're looking for a simple, linear, and basic platforming game that gives somewhat of a Studio Ghibli feeling. However, I would say this just passes as a recommendation, and the visuals and music alone are really driving that recommendation. If I could give this a numbered rating it would be a 5.5/10. Total time to complete was 2.3 hoursThe only issue I had playing was while using my xbox 360 I was forced to use the D-pad. Anytime I used the thumbstick my character would autorun about 60% of the time making platforming navigation difficult and unpredictable. There are no customization of key binding in the menu and while using the D-pad autorun never engaged.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Hoa is a short and mostly art-focused platformer. It's simple and very easy, it won't give you any deep gameplay or puzzles. It works, it feels good enough, and it does its job. That's about it.Then we get to everything else; the art, the set pieces, the atmosphere, the music, the overall audiovisual presentation in general. It's a true delight to play and look at. Cute and charming as all hell. I know many people already described it as such, but it does kind of feel like playing a game made by Studio Ghibli. Albeit with a small indie budget.It's absolutely recommended for the experience alone. It's about two and a half hours long and if you feel that the price is too steep for the value - wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely recommend this game if you love whimsy, beautiful artwork, and storyline. I cried like a baby at the closing scene because you get to learn the actual reason you're playing the game. It's a phenomenal, phenomenal piece that's very relaxed and wholesome. No 'death' or 'time count', so if you're looking for a game with ZERO respawn, this is the one. (Just be prepared to have to redo some platforms if your aim is wrong.)
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Short, but sweet.Hoa is a game deserving of the title "Underrated Masterpiece".Graphics: Stunning. Straight out of a Studio Ghibli film. Every point of the game pops, and it's as though you're inside of a fairytale.My personal favourite part was the factory which seems to take inspiration from Howl's Moving Castle.Music: Fantastic. Instantly immerses you in each scene. The music doesn't just play in the background, it'll make you stop and listen to it.The inspiration from Ghibli is prominent here - with one song blatantly incorporating the leitmotif from Spirited Away's "Name of Life".Gameplay: Simple, yet creative and effective.One part of the game - which I shall not spoil - is particularly mind-bending and innovative. It's worth experiencing.Story: Nothing life-changing, but particularly beautiful and tragic.Like I mentioned, it's fairly short, but it's an experience. I highly recommend this charming little game.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Hoa is a very peaceful and serene game with absolutely stunning visuals and wonderful music. Several times I caught myself thinking of the energy of Studio Ghibli or even games like GRIS, especially because of how beautiful it is. I found the last level very difficult, because of my garbage perception, and I definitely didn't keep turning my laptop on its side to make sense of the controls in that level. Beyond that it's not a particularly difficult game, unless like me you struggle with platformers. I found it challenging in some places but not impossible, as you can see from my play time. Overall it's a beautiful, incredibly cozy little game, with a gorgeous soundtrack and backgrounds, and a touching story that had me tearing up a little. It's going to sit with me for a little bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Ghibli, playing this game recalls me of many scenes of their movies that I've watched. From the music to the assets used in the game, they are so nostalgic. I almost cried after finishing the game :<<. Of course, the game play is not so "game" but personally I think it's like a book that we go for after many hard-working hours. =((( Shout out to the viet team for having created a wonderful work like this <3
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: It's gorgeous, obviously. But the controls were clearly intended for a gamepad, making keyboard play somewhat clunky and unintuitive. I also thought it was strange that all of the important parts of the story, including the backstory, were saved for the ending cutscene. It already feels plausible that the story was tacked on to give that veneer of narrative cohesion to the different play areas, but in this case its also actually tacked onto the back.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved the first 4 stages of this calming/cute little platform game where you bounce off bugs, fly, swim and jump on leaves etc. It's really sweet. The last level is all backwards controls which I don't really enjoy. However I completed the game and would regardless of that level recommend the game. Plays on steamdeck perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: It really is a great game, artwork, music, cozy feeling. But what I dislike is that it crashed a couple of times, especially when you're midway through with that level and then you have to start from the very beginning which made me lose interest in continuing it.Would I still recommend this game? Of course I would.
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Hoa starts off as an easy, slow, breathtaking, and blissful play by just watching its background and hearing its great calming piano back-sound...seriously this is the first game that made me took a lot of screenshots whenever the screen slide...but idk whether I'm bad at playing game with a lot of jumping/double-jump, body-swing, flying and slide control, it started to get me frustrated from the rock map and the top hit was on the forest of Ladybug and now I'm stuck underwater...like bruuh why I got a light headache after playing it.so, nope...this isn't for me but in case I miss playing it, then I'll just replay the first 2 mapsNevertheless I still recommend this game for those who are fine with much jumping/double-jump, body-swing, flying and slide control
_childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful studio ghibli-esc art with the perfect music to accompany your adventure. A simple puzzle game that is perfect to make you sleepy and relaxed when you can't sleep at 3 am. It does not have a particularly outstanding story but it definitely makes up in terms of visuals and the general vibe of the game. (minor spoiler) The only "challenging" part would be the final part where the controls are reversed and the screen gradually rotating which did give me a slight headache but otherwise, a fairly easy game :D buy on sale to make it a more worthwhile play

_childDocuments_.review: Very chill platformer. Can be boring at times with no enemies and mostly just collecting butterflies its pretty linear and platforming is just ok. _childDocuments_.review: I don't even know where to start with how astounding this game is!! I will say it's very similar to 'GRIS', but Studio Ghibli-style. Yes it's a short game, perhaps 3-4 hours of gameplay if you keep at it, but it's absolutely worth it for the gorgeous graphics, beautiful music, and emotional story-telling! I really love how each scene has been laid/drawn out, and all of the characters in it are so adorable (you will see)! You play as this cute creature named 'Hoa', and navigate through various levels trying to get 5 butterflies each time in order to 'awaken' or activate the current character you need to talk to. The different levels can be a bit challenging, but prepare for a mind-boggle on one of the last levels, which is why it reminded me a bit of 'GRIS'. You will push, jump, double-jump, fly, bounce, and more! Overall, I recommend this game 100%, It's a mix of Ponyo, Arriety, Howl's Moving Castle, and all that beautiful floral scenery similar to Kiki's Delivery Service'. I'm so glad I came across it, and I hope there'll perhaps be another in the future some time!

_childDocuments_.review: Hoa is a simple, short little platformer. You play a little fairy guy who traverses the levels collecting butterflies and activating sigils to wake up the guardian of each level, who teaches you a new move that allows you to advance to the next area, and more of the story is revealed as you go. There's nothing really tricky or groundbreaking in the gameplay; the real star here is the art direction and music. There's a fanciful, almost Ghibli-esque look to the characters and environments, with a calm, piano-led score playing throughout.The game will only take you a few hours to knock out, so I'd get it on sale for the most bang for your buck, but if you're a fan of atmospheric, low-stress games this is a good one to check out.

_childDocuments_.review: It was extremely cute. The music, the art, and the story came together to feel like you're playing a story straight out of a Ghibli movie. It's a relaxing and immersive experience, but it is not going to give you the elating feeling of solving a really difficult puzzle or overcoming an impossible platforming challenge. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I'd recommend it while it's on a sale, mostly on the strength of its presentation.First off, the game looks beautiful; It really nails a 'playing a Ghibli movie' feel. Despite the story being pretty light, it's not hard to get wrapped up in the world of the game thanks to the visuals as well as the great soundtrack. The whole thing as a package creates a world that's easy to get lost in for a couple of hours (well, mostly... see below)The game doesn't set out to be challenging, which is totally fine, but there were one or two little things that I encountered which felt unintentionally challenging during my playthrough.Early on there is a section where you need to swing and jump between flowers to progress. I found myself always falling short of grabbing the next one (and in some cases just moving straight up when I tried to jump to the next flower). So I thought 'oh, I must need to unlock double jump first' and decided to come back... only to find out I needed the collectibles past this point to unlock double jump. I ended up watching a YouTube guide to make sure I wasn't doing anything stupid, but I was doing what they were doing. Eventually I got it, but I felt more like it was luck than skill. These same flowers also need to be grabbed from a fairly precise location - if you hit the side, it just shoves the whole thing out of the way and you fall. Later on, there were also a couple of gaps to jump through that were so narrow that I hit off the top and didn't get through. None of these are a huge deal themselves, but each feels like it requires a needlessly precise action from a game that seems mostly about just kicking back and enjoying the world.Aside from the above, the gameplay is pretty relaxed. It doesn't ask anything too taxing of the player, and also doesn't do anything that hasn't been seen before in a game like this (think Limbo, Inside, etc). That's fine though, I think the visuals are really the main draw here and the standard but pretty solid gameplay is a bonus.I played it on Steam Deck, which for the most part ran perfectly. One issue I encountered though was that, after sleeping and waking the console, cutscenes were choppy - they'd play for about half a second, freeze the display for a second, then skip ahead and play another half second etc. Maybe a reboot would have helped, but it did take the reward out of the ending a little.

_childDocuments_.review: Hoa is a beautiful puzzle-platformer game that features hand-painted art and an orchestral score that makes it feel like it’s a playable Studio Ghibli movie. Although simple and basic, Hoa stands out for its non-violent and entirely puzzle-driven gameplay. At the very beginning, the player will have access to basic controls like moving and jumping but as the story progresses different abilities will become available, like flying or double jumping. The maps are very small and linear with very clear and easy to find objectives.  The puzzles are also easy making this game accessible for children and adults who just want a sit-back-and-relax gaming session. Story-wise, the plot is a bit rushed and unfinished. As you progress through the game, there’s really not much information about who you are and what happened to you. However, one single cutscene at the end of the game will try to clarify things. Overall, even though the narrative falls a bit short, Hoa's stunning visuals, soundtrack and atmosphere were enough for me to enjoy this from the very beginning to the very end. On a side note, the game is short lasting around 3.5 hours and all of its achievements are unlockable in one gameplay; very satisfying for completionists.

_childDocuments_.review: - Gameplay: A decent puzzle-platformer. The game knows what it wants to be: a beautiful experience where the player can enjoy its Ghibli-esque art direction, story, and music. The game does throw some curve balls at your by the end. It's not frustrating, just significantly more challenging. If you have played Ori or other metroidvanias with some tricky platforming/puzzle sections, Hoa would be a cakewalk most of the time.- Story and animation: The story tugs your heartstrings a bit but it's not an Ori-level tear-jerker. The animation looks nice but still lacks some nuances here and there that would have made it excellent. For an indie team, they did quite a remarkable job.- Soundtrack: Eargasm. Highly recommended.- Replayability: You get the chapter select menu after beating the game and that's it. But this is the case for most story-focused/walking sim games anyway.All in all, a good 2-hour journey.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful puzzle-platformer that offers a fun but fleeting adventure. Top-quality art and music reminiscent of Studio Ghibli, though it doesn't offer the most robust platforming challenge. A pleasant experience with less than a 2-hour runtime, but those that prioritize gameplay might want to wait for a sale before grabbing it.  is a puzzle-platforming game about a little fairy named Hoa, who travels across a land full of friendly creatures in search of a lost friend. The main goal of this game's design is to be relaxing and easy to pick up, and it succeeds at this across the board. If you have any sort of background with platforming games, . Sticking to the theme, gameplay lacks any significant "failure states" aside from the risk of falling off your platform onto the ground below. This means no bottomless pits, no health bars, and no combat; and while the game does include enemies of a sort, their only real threat is that they can kick you around a little and maybe knock you off a ledge. Whether you consider this simplicity a good thing or a bad thing is a matter of opinion; I personally didn't mind the relaxed pace of the game all that much, and I feel that it serves as a good introduction to players that aren't very familiar with the platforming genre. That said, if you're looking for a platformer that'll offer a substantial challenge, you're better off looking elsewhere.While the gameplay is fine overall, where  really shines is in its artistic elements. , with every environment and creature in it full of subtle detail; and many scenes feel like they belong on the wall as a work of art just as much as they belong in this game. The art isn't the only stand-out element, however, as  that gives every level an almost dreamlike quality to it. . Though the team at Skrollcat Studio may have taken inspiration from Ghibli works, upon further research I discovered that its design is actually more based on Vietnamese religion and folklore, such as the belief in a spiritual essence that gives significance to every little thing around them. These themes manage to make their way into the story and overall design of the game, and it's interesting to see a brief glimpse into a culture that I admittedly know nothing about.My only major concern with the game is that , with maybe a few minutes extra to go back and complete the optional achievements. Combined with the overall simplicity of its gameplay, it's admittedly a bit of a tough sell at its full $15 price. The Soundtrack Edition sweetens the deal, offering its amazing 17-track album for just another $4; but if that doesn't justify paying full price to you, you're better off picking it up when it goes on sale.  Despite wishing that the experience lasted longer, it did manage to keep me in high spirits the whole way through, so I do think that it accomplished its intended goal. Skrollcat Studio have certainly raised the bar for the level of artistic quality that a small development team can achieve, and I do hope we get to see more works of art from them in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Love that a small indie team made a game this artistic. The environment art really can't be praised enough. The music is good (but cuts out very abruptly in certain map regions and it gets really annoying) and the overarching story is okay but the actual dialogue writing isn't very good (I suspect this is just a localization issue).Unfortunately, that's pretty much all I can praise. The mechanics are super basic. Jump, double jump, push, walk, glide and smash (ground pound). You can also access the map, but only about half the times you press the button since most dynamic platforms count as the player being airborne and lock off map access. Most mechanics are introduced and then never really get used again. The push in particular is just bizarre in this regard. The smash actively stops behaving correctly in a later level. Camera work and general programming polish is not really acceptable for a fully released title in my opinion.The end of the game rewards you with a video, but it feels like the video would have been better at the intro since it explains what happened before the game started.A few segments involve mechanics that aren't introduced until after they've been found and overcome. A lot of mechanics just involve waiting for things, which gets frustrating.Lastly, the biggest issue I have that made me leave a negative review is the final chapter (gameplay spoilers ahead). The final mission requires you to replay a large portion of the game again, but with reversed controls and no environment artwork. This is...not fun. It isn't hard either, it just isn't fun and I'm here for the visuals that are no longer present.In summary: I appreciate what they went for here, but the mechanics, level design and general progrmaming quality just drag down the music and visuals.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played a lot of platformers in the past, Hoa is def. one of the more simpler ones. There are a handful of gameplay mechanics you'll learn on your way and which will help you to get around. But it's not like you would find yourself having a hard time because of a jump you have to study gameplay for. Getting closer to the end though there is a slight change in gameplay that is more challenging. Especially people that struggle with reversed controls and/or screen behaviour might want someone as backup to help them go through.Comparing this to other game of the same genre I'd give it a 7/10. There were minor problems in the animated cutscenes that made the cutscene go back and forth. Also, the story is not as deep as I wished it to be, it's rather lovely and flat. _childDocuments_.review: Washed ashore in mysterious circumstances, you play as the titular character, Hoa, on a quest of self-discovery. What we have here is a puzzle platformer about returning home and exploring the past	And it’s a really relaxing experience.  The game is broken up into a series of levels, all of which follow a similar gameplay loop. You have two main objectives, to light up symbols or hieroglyphics scattered around the area, and to collect butterflies. The latter provide new powers necessary to progress.  Hoa is not a challenging game. There are puzzles, but not the sort you’ll have to rack your brain to solve. Platforming is simple too. There’s no falling to your death here – in fact you can’t die. The deliberately straightforward gameplay allows all focus to be placed on the Studio Ghibli-esque graphics and the superb orchestral score.  With that said, it’ll probably come as no surprise that Hoa is a short experience. I completed it one sitting, in just over two hours. As long as you go in with that in mind, there’ll be no disappointments here.  For fans of puzzle platformers like Gris, Limbo and the recent Out of Line, Hoa is a must play. It tells an intriguing story of industry corrupting nature, and you’ll learn by the end how you came to be on the leaf you floated to the shore on at the start of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one where I wish Steam had a 'neutral' rating, but since one isn't available I've gone for a tentative thumbs up (with the caveat that I'm not sure I got £11-worth of enjoyment out of this, so maybe buy it on sale if you're unsure).Let's start with the positives - the music is absolutely gorgeous, and the artwork/scenery is beautiful. Each separate 'kingdom' feels visually unique from the last, and I enjoyed meeting each different chief. All this combines to create a really calming experience within a world that feels vibrant and richly-detailed.Where the game really fell down for me is the story - which is to say, there isn't really one. You wash up on an island where all the creatures seem to know you, and as you work your way through the levels it becomes obvious they all had a hand in helping you escape something. Which is fine, but there's no evidence in the surroundings that anything bad has happened. I don't know if I missed a cut-scene, or something else obvious, but this seems a bit of an odd loop (i.e. we were rescued and set adrift on a leaf-boat, and yet that leaf-boat has now washed back up on the same island but everything seems fine, and now we go back meeting everyone who saved us).This leads in to my other main issue, which is that there's no real threat in the game. Yes, there is the occasional robot that can kick you, but it doesn't send you that far, and there's no depleting health etc. so the worse that will happen is that you fall off a ledge. This no-danger atmosphere might have worked if the levels were engaging enough to hold the player's attention, but although there are some minor gameplay changes between them, the format is generally the same (light up runes to wake the chief, bring the chief five butterflies, gain a new skill and move on to the next level). I think an element of threat, or even a sense that we were changing the world (e.g. there were burned or damaged areas that we brought to life) would have really helped the pacing/gameplay depth, because as it stands the game is very quick.All that being said, if you're just looking for a chill platforming game, with some beautiful music and lush scenery, then this will definitely scratch that itch. I came away from it with a feeling of hope and cheerfulness, which was nice, but it wasn't really what I was expecting in terms of gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello everyone.This is an overall great game, really relaxing, especially the music. I never in my gaming career caring so much about a game background music, for me it is just a little touch, but not very important, sometimes I even mute the music so I can concentrate to the game sound. But this game the music is so great, I can even continue to play if the music stop, and it stops for some reason at random moment while I play. I don't know if that is my problem with my setup or it is a minor bug that is gonna be fix in near future (ASAP I hope). And for any confuses, this kind of music is really similar to what I used to listen to, like in the 2000s, where my childhood is.I played like ~1h and I got 9/18 achievement, I don't know if those represent the length of the game, but I do read somewhere on the Internet that this game is kinda short. But it's okay, I think there are still rooms for more development, more levels, secrets, achievement, etc.The design is pretty, it kinda reminds me about the whole races thing, elves, dwarves, orcs, etc., you know, like in D&D or some movies. I think it's clever to turn them into some natural creatures like that.The gameplay is really simple, but I feel like it is a little... tedious. Sometimes you have to run all the way back to where you already explored to get the stars or pass a level, and the freaking lilies ropes (or some kind of flower idk) is really drive me crazy, you have to swing like a lot to get to the safe place.In conclusion, the game is good and simple, really love the music. Worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Hoa has beautifully designed hand-painted artwork and an outstanding original soundtrack that makes it feel like you're in a Studio Ghibli movie. _childDocuments_.name: Hoa

_childDocuments_.review: Both the music and the art are like something straight out of a Miyazaki film. Absolutely beautiful. It's worth playing just to submerge yourself in the outstanding aesthetic.It's very easy to recommend, but you should know that this is first and foremost a PEACEFUL and RELAXING game. In genre terms, it is very much a platformer, but there is no death and the platforming is mostly pretty light and easy. It's more of a peaceful activity than a serious challenge. In that way, it is more comparable to games like Marvin's Mittens or Here Comes Niko. It's not intended to get your adrenaline pumping. It's intended just to make you smile and feel good, and it succeeds if you're asking me.It is a little bit repetitive, progressing in terms of "areas" or "zones". Each of these areas has some kind of an elder creature that you must awaken by collecting 5 butterflies in the nearby area. Once you find all five, you show them to the elder, who gives you a new platforming skill, which allows you to move on to the next area. Rinse and repeat.Did I mention that it feels like Miyazaki? It really just has a great personality.

_childDocuments_.review: Hoa is a beautiful adventure with relaxing music and no frustrating gameplay elements. You just jump, jun and fly through forests, lakes and factories, awaken old creatures and collect butterflies with which you can extend your skills. It is based on a Vietnamese fable of a fairy who awakens the nature around her. It reminds me a lot on Ori, but without the frustrating parts. name: Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga
detailed_description: At the turn of the millennium, the world of Tahnra is headed for a reckoning. The long and bloody conflict of Veridian Succession left the Empire of Veridia scarred, its people subject to brutal hardships. Under the reign of Empress Florina, the vicious cycle seemed to be broken, until a rogue General abducted her from the capital, mustering his own armies and raising the flag of rebellion. You, a young academy graduate, will command an expedition against these forces… a conflict that will set off a chain of events and shake the very foundations of the world. 2D Turn-based Strategy RPG Squad-based player army Story-rich 30-40 hour Campaign with huge replay value 50+ Character classes for your troops Massive depth of tactics you will learn through natural play Limitless possibilities for how to build your characters and squads The gameplay focuses on grand-scale operations, outwitting and out-planning the opponent, while individual battles are carried out automatically and are thrilling to watch unfold. Maneuver squads of up to 9 soldiers across battlefields and seize the advantage by grabbing high ground, holding chokepoints, ambushing from the woods, and more P ay attention to the weather, or fall prey to a sudden blizzard or heat wave Liberate towns and capture resources to bolster your reputation and sustain your armies Break the enemy's morale, while maintaining your own Eliminate enemy squad leaders to shatter their chain of command Tactics win engagements. Logistics win wars. Once the dust settles, it's time to collect the wounded, rally the troops, and prepare for another battle in the long march to peace on Tahnra. Assemble squads from more than 50 unit classes, including heavy infantry, archers, shock cavalry, medics, arquebusiers, dragons, battle mages, and more Outfit squads with equipment and artifacts obtained through looting and victory Nurture your conscripts into elite warriors, or hire mercenaries to instantly boost your army's fighting prowess Research upgrades through your faction’s tech tree across a multitude of classes to specialize or generalize your troops for the job The graduates of the Imperial War Academy were sent to quickly contain a rebellion, but became embroiled in a vicious plot far beyond what they could imagine. Meet friends, heroes, allies, and rivals from the many different factions across the world Manage a dynamic relationship system, unlocking iconic conversations, unbreakable bonds, and powerful bonuses between your characters Experience an epic tale brimming with malice, treachery, and ambitions, as the fragile peace of Tahnra unravels

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for April 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 7th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A Song of Fire Emblem and … just fire Fire Emblem.Symphony of War starts with the main character and a friend going off to fight in a war to get a kidnapped Empress back.  During that battle, they met up with people they knew when they were cadets. This is all done in the background of a large Strategy RPG where players will move their characters tactically around a map and take out units. It’s a lot like Fire Emblem, and that’s a good thing because the battle system here is solid but adds a few new tricks. You can fill out your squad as you want, change your character’s classes to try out new things and build a larger army than the Fire Emblem games.  At the same time, this is more of a pure strategy RPG with the focus more on roleplaying and tactically maneuvering troops rather than just overpowering the enemy.  The maps feel overwhelming when you first reach them but then almost feel too small once you finish them.  Also, people have pointed out this has a lot of RPG Maker assets, but if that is what enables a team to make a thirty-hour or more game with a small team, the more power to them.  This is a twenty-dollar title after all, not a big sixty-dollar one. Pick this up if you like the Strategy RPG genre, this is more Fire Emblem than anything, but there’s a little bit of a feel of Advance Wars, or Wargroove as well and so far it is delivering on all cylinders.  There’s an obvious turn coming but it would be worth playing more to see the story. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've taken a while to think of how to write this review. I knew, from the beginning, that I'd be giving it a thumbs up, but there is one thing that just needs to be talked about. While the game has an interesting take on new game plus, and I enjoy the gameplay, squad building, and 90% of the story...I genuinely think it flounders the ending, primarily. Again, I do heavily suggest it to anyone that looks at it and goes 'thats my type of game' but the actual ending of the story(the last 3 missions) was so rushed and threw so much stuff at the player that, while there was resolution, it was unsatisfying and almost felt like sequel bait.But yeah, still recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Had a blast playing it.And by playing I mean min maxing the ♥♥♥♥ out of it.Loved the systems and how they interacted.Especially the Leadership system, that made it so some Units could grow to be as relevant gameplay-wise as main characters.I spent a ton of time on the Squad Management, great balance on the micromanagement.I played on hard mode with permadeath and found it too easy on the last third of the game.It's quite difficult early on, but as with other permadeath designed games, your run can be snowballed or ruined.I also abused the Force Surrender mechanic and maxed out the Tech Tree too early, so it was pretty much my fault.The story is okay, although somewhat cliched,It had some nice characters and pretty decent writing.Bonds were shallow but I liked how they affected the epilogue.As for the graphics, there are 4 distinct styles...Cutscenes: RPG Maker art, honestly not bad, especially considering it's not shown that much;Overworld: Simple but distinct enough, well done;Potraits: Honestly disliked it, took me quite a while to get used to it, feels cheap;Battle: Absolutely loved it, and it's the main reason I gave the game a chance.This might be my favorite SRPG.Loved the unit progression and customization.All in all, I quite enjoyed the game.Some minor feedbacks:Names could have a wider pool, but at least I got to make a Squad out of Magdalens;Raskuja overworld art is too gray-ish, I always forgot he hadn't acted yet;Achievement for level 12 is almost impossible on hard mode, so I had to restart on easy mode to get it, and that was boring.AHThe key under ESC speeds up the game by a ton!I only discovered that near the end of the game, don't make the same mistake.

_childDocuments_.review: This has everything I love from games like Fire Emblem and Ogrebattle. If that stirs something in you, you found your game. It's got a decent story and great replay value with the army variety, difficulty options (including permadeath) and romance options that you have. Players on discord are already sharing "no kill" challenges where they only win through surrenders. For how much this game costs it has a fantastic amount of content.I am extremely excited that this game exists, mainly because it means if it does well we may get something grander in scope from Dancing Dragon Games in the future. There is so much already here, and so much that can be built on. I try not to get hyped about things anymore but it's hard not to feel a little giddy about what comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great little game. The story is serviceable, and someone involved in the art seems to have a lonely teenage boy's fondness for anatomically improbable women, but the core game itself is brilliant fun. The army management is a particular highlight, and the battles are detailed and engrossing but never outstay their welcome. I've happily spent a lot of time noodling around in squad organisation screens, and (unusually for me) I think I'm going to make it all the way to the end of the story.I've been playing on the default difficulty settings and there isn't much challenge, but it's a lot of fun finding new ways to obliterate squads of enemies. I've not tried the permadeath or other harder settings, which I'd hope would require more thought and careful planning; the default difficulty is very forgiving. Would love to see this series continue, ideally with fewer gravity-defying chests and more classes, skills, and stories.

_childDocuments_.review: The game holds up to other top tier old-school grid-based tactic games such as Fire Emblem and Shining Force.Story is great from start to finish. Combat is smooth and plays just as you would imagine from other similar games. I love that they have a speed-up button that you typically see in emulators to let you quickly zoom through the enemy turns. I look forward to coming back to playing again in future versions when they add new modes. Absolutely worth the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. It hits the nostalgic vibes of the older tactics style games and certainly reminded me of the things I loved about Ogre battle back in the day. But it does this in a clean modern style. A nice enjoyable experience from start to finish from a team that's clearly intent on supporting it post launch.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Symphony of War is a mechanically a modern Tactics Ogre, and story-wise and attempt at Fire Emblem: Genealogy of the Holy War. I think it starts really solid but after the halfway point it gets a little too simple (tactically and lorewise).  6/10It worked really well for a while but after some time I felt it repetitive and too loud, even when I lowered the settings. 8/10It looks really solid throughout most of the game. The character models, the effects, etc. I am giving it a lower value however because pretty much all the girls have busts bigger than their heads and because some of your units look strange.  7.5/10If you enjoy Fire Emblem, if you’ve played Tactics Ogre, you will find pretty much the same gameplay. They added some new features like technology upgrades and they are really interesting but the numbers can be meaningless sometimes, and combat is really fast. My biggest gripe with the gameplay is that upgrading your troops require them to meet a specific number in some characteristics, which upgrade randomly through the game (unless you use an item), that means that, you can stay with lower tier units for way too long. 7.5/10I enjoyed the first part a lot and while the dialogue isn’t as good as I would like and some interactions are strange, it does shine. The second part, I think it lacked some characterization that could have been explored further via support conversations. I think that most of the characters are one-dimensional and they fulfill their role, which I understand is also something similar with the FE games it was inspired on. But overall, enjoyable, nice world-building and leaves room for more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game worth your time, with some annoying issuesI'll focus on the negatives here, but do keep in mind that I give the game a solid thumbs uppart 1, combatIt plays like a mix between Ogre Battle and Fire Emblem, as one would probably expect just from looking at the screenshots. I completed 25 of the 30 missions on the standard difficulty, plus all the side missions which all drop at the same time, rather late in the game, for I don't know what reason. The combat is fun and fastpaced, unless there are 20,000 active enemy units on the screen, in which case you can watch them shuffle around after every turn. And speaking of 20,000 enemies, in the later missions you will notice that the enemy units usually like to wait around in clusters that won't activate unless you move into attack range, which to be fair, is pretty much what Fire Emblem is STILL doing as well. - Sidenote, they did include a button to view the active range of all enemy units, but they forgot to make it a toggle, which means you can't issue unit orders while . I suspect it's either a engine limitation (RPG Maker), or design oversight. And, spoilers, there's more of that in the gameback to the enemy unit clusters - so, in most missions, the enemy wants you to come to them, and if you move into their attack range, you will likely get alpha-striked by a whole bunch of units, and that could overwhelm even some of your tankiest units. However, somewhere around the halfway point of the game, you unlock special rechargable abilities like teleporting, a damage spell and so on. Of particular note is an ability that ups a unit's defense and gives them a taunt that makes every enemy in range attack them. So, what you can do is to send one of your stronger units into an enemy cluster, use the ability of them, and watch them wipe out 12 enemy units in a row while barely taking any damage. And you may do it again one the next turn or the turn after. And all your other units get ignored and can kill with impunity. Yes, that trivializes the game. But it's rather on the easy side on normal difficulty, anywaypart 2, menus and army managment the game has a pretty good unit variety. A somewhat odd design problem is that you unlock most of the available unit classes relatively early on, so that kind of removes the excitement of getting new toys in the later stages of the game. There is a fair bit of possible mirco-managing of every single of your units, like changing units stats and giving them traits, but you have hundreds of them, you can recruit new ones all the time. I didn't personally bother with it at all. I barely even equipped items and traits on my squad leaders, mostly just to increase their army capyou will spend a lot of time in the squad menus, switching around units/items and so. The single most glaring issue of the game is that the menu system is frankly quite bad (understatement). To change anything at all, you need to click through at least 2 or 3 submenus every single time for every single squad. Add/Remove units, move units positions change order of squads, give items, give traits/stat boosts, everything is it's own submenu, you constantly have to switch between multiple submenus for every single little change, you can't even see which character has what item or trait equiped unless you directly click on them, inside at least two layers of menus. It's baffeling. This is either again a symptom of the aformentioned engine limitations, or the designers had some serious tunnel vision. I did however read that the menus are the top of their to-fix list, so maybe they can do something about itpart 3, story"Mom, I want a generic Fire Emblem/JRPG story!""We have a generic Fire Emblem/JRPG story at home"The generic Fire Emblem/JRPG story at home:it's pretty much what you'd expect from small indie games emulating all their favorite Japanese RPGs. All the typical tropes are present. It's the usual stuff, but hey, that may be just your thingthey copied the support conversations from Fire Emblem, but I started fast-skipping most of them pretty early. It doesn't look like there is a real support system in the game, I believe the conversations become available automatically after each mission---right, that's about it. The game does plenty of good things that I'm just not going to mention at all, it seems like. It's fun to play, it likely worth your time, it isn't anywhere near perfect, that's about all you really need to know

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of things to like about this game.  The gameplay, the mechanics, are all fun and even fantastic! I enjoyed building squads and experimenting with artifacts; I thought there was a great variety of units and unit types that allow for a great experience with lots of customization.The rest of the game was.... not great.  Putting aside the RPG maker story segments, which were visually mediocre or offputting, the story dropped the ball on what would otherwise be a solid game.  The plot is strange and almost nonsensical; events happen and more or less follow from one another but... there's not really any consistency beyond that?  The game waffles on taking any kind of moral stance.  Eugenics, breeding programs, extra judicially executing surrendered POWs, total war in the actual definition... these are all things uncritically accepted by the "good guys," yet killing enemy conscripts on the battlefield is a sign that the MC has lost her mind and gone too far.  And of course, the villains are ontologically evil because they kidnap children, brainwash children, indoctrinate children, use children as hostages....  together with how often the bad guys target children and how often breeding, offspring, and having kids comes up on the MC's side, it really does feel like the whole game has some kind of hang up about having children.  It was... pretty uncomfortable.I would be remiss not to mention the support conversations and dialogue in general which is.... incredibly bad.  Like, one romance occurs because the "dashing rogue" character kept hitting on a girl despite her rebuffing him 2-3 times before.  She just says "oh you outlasted me, congrats on getting a date."  There's incel-y conversations, a "nobody liked me when I was a nice guy" rant... god, I honestly can't describe it all and would recommend just skipping all the dialogue you can if you decide to go for the gameplay.  Just.  Wow.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Game of Thrones if all the budget went into the action scenes, resulting in the writing and presentation suffering over time. Or to put it another way, it's like Game of Thrones.Rated from someone who has never Fired an Emblem or Battled an Ogre (at least not Tactically).- Forming battle units is an engrossing puzzle thanks to formations, class interactions, capacity and more.- Good mix of classes with specialized roles, which enhance the battle unit puzzle and tactical space.- Encounters are quick and occasionally have a shake-up to keep you engaged.- Lovely pixel art and animations in combat.- Obscure mechanics. Traits and tactical interactions are all buried in guides that are difficult to navigate.- Default difficulty is pretty easy (so far)- Permadeath option more tedious than challenging.- Character writing inconsistent to the point where it gets distracting.- Multiple contrasting art styles also distracting. - Fans of "dudes on a map" board games.- Fans of tactical games who skip cut scenes on first playthroughs.- Pixel art fans with selective memory.- Aspiring cosmetic artists - I haven't yet found the tutorial outlining the beauty routine these war torn veterans must practice, but it's gotta be a doozy. - More a Heros of Might & Magic kinda game, but it provides a lot of tactical depth while addressing many of the issues I have with Symphony. Better teaching tools integreted within its campaigns, sharper dialogue and a steady difficulty curve (mostly). It gets bonus points too for doing more with the music motif in the title via its bard songs.I'm still enjoying my time with Symphony of War. While the elements surrounding the gameplay need help, the gameplay is substantive enough to keep me coming back. If you're a 'games are to be played, not read/watched' type who can spice up your own experience with self imposed challenges, I think you'll get a lot out of this title, but if you need some presentation to get your feet marching, consider my alternative first.Did my review help or amuse you? _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Decent combat system bogged down by a painful UI and anemic story and characters.The Good:-Tactical combat is good, with nice differentiation between unit types and uses. Particularly in the early missions it can feel very rewarding to put the right units in the right places and feel like you're coming out on top.-Fairly simple to pick up and play, particularly if you're a fan of the genre. Fans of series like Fire Emblem will feel very much at home.-Lots of customization for individual uni`ild a lot of nuanced units for specific purposes or functions. Want to build heavy infantry backed by healers? Cavalry units to run down archers? Gunpowder units that can absolutely shred heavy infantry? All options here.The Bad-Later missions ramp up difficulty in the wrong ways. Instead of presenting more complex challenges they tend to either throw masses of units at you or position glass cannon units in such a way that they're impossible to get past without letting them get a hit in that will devastate whatever unit it hits.-The Menus could use some work. Lots of nest menus and repeated clicking can make squad management a real chore.The UglyThere are some deeply, DEEPLY problematic tropes at play in the character interactions. Aspects of female possession, gamegate/incel mentality and the like abound with most female characters playing out like someone's fetish wish fulfillment. You're better off skipping the dialogue entirely if you're going to play the game.Overall while the game was fun to begin with, I steadily soured on it over my time with it, with the writing being a real nail in the coffin. I'd be curious to see it with a dedicated writer or something similar, but absent that I don't be giving any more $ to this particular dev.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this make me wish for a "maybe recommend" option.  This is the kind of game you will play once or twice and never remember again.  It is by no means a bad game, but it's also not an amazing one either.  Graphics: 6/10 I played with the art upgrade, and I think the character designs fit their respective areas.  Every sprite had a level of detail put into it.  That said, many of the unit sprites (including other story characters) look exactly the same as your generic army units.  It becomes more noticeable in later levels when you field a large amount of units. The nice character portraits clash with the RPGmaker sprites that make up most story events.Story 4/10: A young recruit in his kingdom's army is tasked with dealing with a former hero turned rebel.  What he learns on the way will soon involve him and his friends in the fate of the entire world.  Does it sound like many other stories out there?  It's because the plot is incredibly weak and serves to get the players from map to map.  The game does add it's own glossary for the lore, but the plot does little to make you interested in it.   Even the few twists in the story come across as unexciting.Characters: 3/10: to put it bluntly, the characters are very flat and very forgettable.  Most have little (if any) dialogue during the main story.  While the game tries to add side events during the chapters, the characters remain bland and two dimensional.   You see little development of them aside from a few love (bond) scenes and events where people become friends.  Some major characters have less dialogue than this paragraph.Music: 6/10: There is nothing to write home about.  The music fits for the environment, and the game does have multiple tracks for different levels and battles.  While none of the music is bad, most of it is not memorable either.Gameplay: 8/10: The thing that makes this game worth playing is the gameplay.  The player controls customizable squads made up of a leader character and whatever other units you choose.  Each squad has a high level of customization from the units in it, the skills you can assign to them, and where you position them on the battle grid.  Unit types also matter along with their placement.  You can protect your fragile spell casters by putting heavy infantry in the front lines.  Certain classes (rogues) can counter this by attacking the back lines, and ranged classes also have this benefit.  Your leader starts with limits to how many people can join their squad, but this number increases as they win battles and take locations.  You can also upgrade classes into more powerful versions as you progress.  While promotional classes have stat requirements, there are items that let you boost and change your character.  You can also equip skills and artifacts that allow you to further tweak your characters and their squads.Challenge: 6/10: The game does some things well, and other things poorly.  The game does very well with terrain.  Elevated  positions allow your ranged characters to shoot farther,   Forests can allow certain classes to ambush.  There are buildings on the map that have different effects (such as a temple allowing you to revive fallen units).  You can also make broken squads surrender for extra exp and end of battle funds.  The  army eventually gets access to powers that can also help (such as teleporting units or giving a character a second turn).  Maps also had a level of variety with things such as choke points and variations to map design.That said, the game is very hit or miss with difficulty.  It's very easy for a few of the main characters to become extremely powerful without any exploits.  It is feasible to use the armor blessing on a squad, send it into a group of 8 enemies, and watch you squad wipe the floor with everyone when they attack on the enemy phase.  Aside from the last chapter and a few legends chapters, most of the games missions are incredibly easy to S rank.  The game does have things like increased difficulty settings and permadeath for non heroes, but the game is still easy to manage if you properly build your squads and utilize basic tactics.Overall, I would say this is an enjoyable game for people looking for a tactical RPG with some good customization options.  The gameplay is one of the few things that makes this game worth finishing.  People looking for engaging story and characters are sure to be disappointed.   Final Score 5.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War is one of those games that makes so much sense once you begin playing it. So much so in fact that it almost makes you wonder how it took so long to get here.I suppose the best way really to describe this game is to call it the natural evolution of the "Fire Emblem" style of strategy, at least in the terms of game play. It's similar I suppose to tactics ogre in the sense that instead of individual units you are controlling squads. Each individual unit has an evolutionary path, and there's a good amount of variety overall. Also you don't have limited use weapons, too. There's some secrets to be found in the game, but not a lot of side missions.  I would say the balance of the game is quite good, regardless your play style. There's a few challenging parts but once you're knowledgeable of how every unit works the game does end up getting pretty easy. Especially if you do any grinding. The story is alright, it's a unique take on the whole good vs evil, heaven vs hell deal, but nothing too extreme. Diablo shares the same theme in that the "Nephilim" are the catalyst for what drives the story. Overall it was a fun game, a good experience, and if you like Fire Emblem or Tactics Ogre, this is right up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems heavily inspired by Fire Emblem, and oh what a cracker it is!  This game is absolutely superb; clean, crisp, colourful pixel art, beautiful, fitting music and meaningful and satisfyingly strategic combat system that really rewards experimentation.  I've spent hours tinkering my army to the last detail and it's so satisfying watching my carefully configured units dominate the battlefield by fulfilling their roles exactly as I intended.  The controls are very well designed as well, making it a breeze to play on a controller, keyboard or even just the mouse alone, which is how I've been playing it.The story is okay... don't expect a masterpiece of story writing here, but it's interesting and enjoyable enough that I actually want to read the dialogue and it provides plenty of context for the each battle.  There's a nice variety of different battles which makes each one memorable in some small way, which is really nice.As for downsides... honestly, there's nothing really major to say, other just the usual nitpicks and issues that are in pretty much every single SRPG: the AI is pretty bad and the menu systems could be a little bit more streamlined.  The 2D artwork for the characters seems thematically different from the rest of the in-game art, which is also a bit odd.  These little issues are not stopping me having fun with this game at all.If you like 2D SRPGs like Fire Emblem, Ogre Battle, Shining Force 1 or 2, Advanced Wars or Battle For Wesnoth, you should definitely give this one a go.  It's thoroughly enjoyable and I would love to see what the devs at Dancing Dragon Games could come up with if they had some serious budget.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I have no major complaints about SoW’s performance. The game crashed once, but I did not otherwise encounter any game-breaking bugs. That said, the U.I. can be a bit finicky, and very late into the game, I encountered microstutters when initiating combat.The overall quality of the writing is far and beyond the worst part of SoW. The best way that I can come up with is that it reads juvenile, and I am not describing it like this to be mean, but rather that this is the genuine impression I’ve had. This comes partially from the presentation, featuring Fire Emblem-esque map-crawls between chapters, but also from the caviats of the worldbuilding, such as featuring support conversations between playable characters.The basic idea, however, is that you are playing Lindly, canonically the female avatar and name, though both can be changed upon starting the game, and the name whenever you’re in the menu between missions. She is being enveloped in what seems to be a political conflict that, however, soon expands into the usual high fantasy, prophetic war.The basic story isn’t bad in itself, but suffers a lot from being overly wordy, throwing tons of regions, names, and nobles at you right from the start that make it incredibly obnoxious trying to keep a firm grip on the overarching story, but more so the intense tonal whiplash that some scenes evoke. It tries to be incredibly gritty with genuinely not terrible twists, but then tosses cartoonishly evil ‘villains’ like the Black Knight at you, committing war crimes while brandishing their evil, glowing sword "Balmung hungers..". It’s atrocious, and where it's not, it’s boring.Supports are barely worth mentioning as each character has merely a handful of scenes, all of which suffer from the same issues as the above but with the added weight of pacing. Characters that barely know each other will start romances; hell, characters for whom it makes no sense at all even within their own dialogue will do it, and it feels like it’s all just there to be formulaic.Beyond this, I’ve spotted numerous other quirks with the dialogue, like grammar errors, inconsistent capitalization, and naturally, the cardinal sin of obnoxiously spelling rhoticity like Rrrrrrrraskuja.Graphically, SoW is okay. The sprites and combat animations are fantastic, and so are the once-atrocious-looking portraits after the recent graphical update. That said, the maps and in-game cutscenes still have a distinct RPGMaker vibe to them that is just a bit too low-quality to not stand out in comparison. There is also no option to tweak the graphics or the resolution, for that matter.Sound mixing is a bigger issue; while the music and general sound are perfectly fine, certain elements are off, such as the voices of specific characters being vastly quieter than the others and two late-game units having no voice acting at all.The main gameplay is split into two major parts: unit management and playing the actual maps. For the former, unit management happens in between chapters wherein your army is split into squads of 3x3 units; those same units are tiered and upgrade through reaching experience in their current class while secondarily leveling up like in any RPG and gaining stats according to their nature and archetype. The upgrade tree is expansive and, at first glance, the game's strongest point, although the game can be obtuse about what the point of all the different classes is. Instead, unit descriptions are buried within a submenu, while during upgrading you merely get a throwaway sentence of the broad idea of what the class is supposed to excel at. Furthermore, during my Captain playthrough, some classes severely underperformed in comparison to others, such as the entirety of the Archer archetype; the overall difficulty seems to be designed with Warlord and Permadeath in mind, although the latter comes with its own issues. The answer for most any map was to just vomit more units into any of my squads and merely play around the movement type.Now, having put around seven hours into Warlord, it is a more engaging experience, but I can foresee the same issues arising there as well, namely, that stat bonuses from items are simply too explosive, to the point that any game would have trouble providing a consistent experience throughout different difficulty modes. Permadeath provides some much-needed pressure, but that pressure ends up being more obnoxious than a real influence on player strategy as you can’t control your squad's attacks and defense past their baseline formation, making character death largely a part of natural RNG.It's too many turning gears that all end up shallow. Too many unit types that aren't balanced and different enough to feel worthwhile; too many traits that feel ultimately superficial. A nature/element system that's just a headache to fiddle with. I'm sure this sort of management is the reason why a lot of people enjoyed the game, but I don't feel it has enough depth to warrant engaging with it.Symphony of War isn’t terrible. Despite all my criticisms, it does its best to emulate and build upon a genre that the developer is very clearly passionate about. Even now, I’m still tempted to go back to my Warlord save and just give it one more map to experiment just a little more, but at the end of the day, I just don’t think that this charm and passion are enough to recommend the game on. Ultimately, for me, the game suffers a death from a thousand paper cuts, starting with inconsistent writing, even if it might have some genuinely interesting ideas here and there, a difficulty curve that is utterly incomprehensible due to a myriad of design decisions, and just not being a very tactical experience. But by Donar, do I want Diana to pick me up by my legs and tear me in half like she’d a sheaf of papers.

_childDocuments_.review: Made from scratch and heavily modified in RPG maker, Symphony of War manages to take Fire Emblem and twist it into its own thing. Out of every Fire Emblem fan game/spiritual successor/copycat/whatever you want to call them, this game has been my favorite so far. Dark Deity, Vestaria Saga (Keep crying Kaga fanboys), etc have been defeated by Symphony of War. Let's talk about how and why.This game has Fire Emblem mechanics like different classes, grid based and similar battles. Similar to the battalion system in Three Houses, you form squads which take battalions to another level. Instead of just being a stat boost, you form linked squads that act together. It's insanely satisfying to just look at your huge, badass squad, and even cooler to see them destroy an enemy squad. This is the best part of the game, even if it has some problems. Menus are a little cumbersome and unit capacities are inconsistent. I look away for one second and a leader has 65+ capacity, and then I grind another unit and that leader has only 40-45 capacity. I know it's rng but it feels weird and favoritism based from the devs.There are tons of different classes and for the most part all of them feel different. And unlike most Fire Emblem games, you can reclass and even declass. My favorite class by far are DRAGONS. Yes, there are playable dragon units. Not manaketes. Not Corrin. Actual dragons. There are other weird classes like units with muskets and cannons. They pierce armor quite well but can't attack as much as other units. In terms of tactics, the game eventually gives you more types of battle initiation. You can make enemies "surrender", which gives you bonus gold at the end of chapters, execute aggressive/defensive orders, or target the unit leader to break morale. Oh yeah, morale. A neat little system that determines how effective a unit will be in the moment, and makes surrenders easier the lower a unit's morale is. Visually the game is mostly good. There is some slowdown/stutter with unit animations at certain points even though someone who plays the game a lot said they patched that out. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Otherwise, the art style, sprites, and animations all look fantastic. They didn't need to make all the units look sick, but they did and I appreciate that.The story is alright but there were some twists/events I didn't see coming. Overall it's your basic FE story.If you're a Fire Emblem fan I can't help but recommend this game. It's quite well made and for the price tag, well worth every dollar. The learning curve isn't even that high, which surprised me. The game teaches you enough in quick bursts, instead of long and slow tutorials in most games.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Hybrid game that reminds of a mix of Ogre Battle and Fire Emblem. Has some downsides but for fans of the genre it is a steal at its $20 price. As others have mentioned the game play is a bastard sibling of Ogre Battle 64 and Fire Emblem, with squads comprised of your classic fair of tactics style classes but remaining turn/grid based like Fire Emblem. There's a lot to customize with this system and adds it own flair with its leadership system. Leadership is its own stat that allows for more units to be added to a squad as the game goes on up to a max of 9 (some large units take up 2 squares though) and impacts which and how many artifacts can be assigned. Artifacts are a nice mix of providing squad customization without going in the absurd level that Ogre Battle 64 did where every unit in each squad had assignable equipment. Overall game play has enough similar mechanics to feel familiar but enough new features to encourage experimentation. I would not call the story amazing as it goes down the cliche path often but there is also nothing wrong with it. Just do not expect it to top some of the JRPG classics.Balance still feels a bit off and on the standard difficulty it was quite easy to out pace the difficulty curve of the game and become pretty much unstoppable by the mid-game. The game offers optional challenges in most missions that help give some variety to how you play a given map. There is a hard mode but the prospect of playing this type of game with perma death seems like a massive jump in difficulty and would more encourage a deathball style of play that I would not be as interested in. Game is still being patched so this may be fixed in the future. (Update perma death has been split off on its own, separate from difficulty selection so maybe no longer a problem)Ultimately the most important thing is that the game is fun and if you're a fan of tactics style games the game play alone is worth the pickup and at a $20 price point the game is basically a steal. Would highly recommend and only writing this review to help boost the games visibility to hopefully help others see this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the games this draws inspiration from (especially Ogre Battle March of the Black Queen) then you'll probably be happy to see this entry in the subgenre. + Easy to learn, hard to master+ Fair class selection with some additional unique characters+ Advanced play will find you using a lot of the small mechanics that exist within the game in an interestingly wide array of applications without it feeling like it's shoehorned in + Offers Permadeath mode and non-Permadeath mode to suit your preference+ Most of the things you do feel rewarding + Being able to combine an increasing number of unique leaders into very powerful individual units as the game progresses is a cool option to steadily unlock (Stefan + Raskuja and Narima makes for an insanely strong offensive ambush unit, for example) + Decent item variety and great item relevance + Some story points hit with emotional depth a la Tactics Ogre + Well thought out map design on most maps- Some story beads seem genuinely stupid, cliche, or both simultaneously- Characterization is generally cliche in my opinion (but it's not all bad) - Only playable large classes/characters are Dragon(rider)s, playable monster diversity is sorely needed- Some specific things that happen in the game and grant the player more combat options should probably happen earlier- Getting every tech by the end of a playthrough ultimately homogenizes your tech choices  Rating: 8/10. Really like the game. After first playthrough I started skipping all cutscenes. Gameplay is great. If you've been looking for anything even remotely like this, you will probably be as happy as I was while playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War is an amazing game that is well worth your time. It has an blend of Ogrebattle 64 and  Fire Emblem that you don't see very often. The combat is as easy or as complex as you want to make it and there is no shortage of interesting campaign missions to play through. It's items and artifact system allow you to customize your armies to fit your play style, and again it can be as deep or shallow as you want it to be. The main story of the game is really well written for the first 80% of the game, but as with a lot of games they struggle to really stick the ending. By the end of the game it felt like they were rushing to a conclusion and not really giving any of the events time to breath, but this is only a minor detractor as the story still landed pretty well for me. The writing also came up short when it came to relationships with your party. In a few cases I saw multiple conversations that had progression from one conversation to the next, but most cases the conversations felt disjointed and in some cases had absolutely zero build up. In the romantic relationship I sought for my character I had no idea if the option for a romantic relationship would even pop. When it did it seemed to be irrelevant to the main story. There was also a huge gap in missions between private conversations actually happening. This could have been alleviated by having a few conversations after each deployment, and this would have allowed the relationships between the characters to feel more natural. I would have also liked to have seen more from the surrender system, like a system that allows you to try and capture leaders and then interrogate them, this would have given them a great way to sprinkle in another something that is another complaint of mine. Not enough side missions and they aren't spread out enough. But again these really are all minor gripes that I hope are addressed to some extent in a sequel. It really can't be overstated how good this game is. And maybe that is because to some extent I had very low expectations, but this game really knocked it out of the park. I would gladly pay $70 for another game in the series. It doesn't even need to follow this story it could be a whole new story in a whole new land. Either way they have earned my attention and I look forward to playing more from them.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a great game that's worth a purchase.The game is a great return to the fire emblem / advance wars strategy genre.  Completed a game a little longer (37 hours) than others because I liked the grind in the Arena and the menus (more on that later0.  The story line is pretty basic but keeps the player engaged.  The game play is pretty solid with combat and units feeling like they have impact.  There is a need to use the players units well as the player is frequently outnumbered.  The use of terrain also gives some great advantages (though it's not readily apparent unless one delves into the help / tutorial files).  On the captain difficulty the AI seems to make some pretty novice mistakes such as having melee squads shoot with their one ranged unit.  AI composed squads also need some work with even the late game squads seemingly a hodgepodge of units.  Furthermore there are squads in missions that do not move or do not move when every other squad moves making it easier to isolate and destroy in piecemeal.  The soundtrack is alright though could use some additional options.  The voice acting is pretty good for a small studio as well.     The menus are an absolute mess.  The amount of clicks to get through setting up squads and assigning items is just ridiculous.  There are huge lists of items with no filters / no way to sort.  There is no way to re-arrange squads so a player can keep their favorite squads up top so one does not have to scroll needlessly in the deploy screen.  When placing artifacts the player is given the name of the squad leader but there is such a short list of names that there are frequent duplicates making it hard to quickly assign artifacts.  The game would really benefit from a re-work of the menu and item system.  The Tech system is a bit opaque with no entry on the tutorial on how tech advances (it's through faction ranking up).  Some more tool tips around battle and benefits of certain abilities would be helpful too.  A player cannot at a glance see what's going to happen during battle.  Damage ranges / percentages for surrender would be a great help.  Lastly, the market seems a bit anemic / the resource drops.  It should always be an option to get resources for gold.  I captured every mine / stable in the game and still ran short gems, horses, and iron until very late game.  I had plenty of gold but nothing to spend it on because I didn't need recruits and the items in the store were not useful.  The last store seems to be a better system where it's an infinite store.All the negativity aside, this is a great game.  It's worth the price and will be a fun romp.

_childDocuments_.review: I have incredibly fond memories of playing Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones and Final Fantasy Tactics Advance when I was younger. I've played a handful of grid based TBS games since then but for one reason or another none of them lived up to the experience of those classics. Until I tried this game. The combat is extremely polished and exciting. You really get the sense that you're commanding an army. I opted to play on normal difficulty with perma-death on. I think it adds a huge amount of investment in the characters and combat. It is incredibly satisfying to crush a larger force with superior tactics and not lose a single unit. I only have a couple of personal gripes. The time spent managing your army between combats can really drag on in the later game when you've got 15-20 groups to manage. It kind of kills the pacing, although obviously not enough to keep me coming back for more. I had some other issues with the interface but large strides were made in that area midway through my play-through and it's much more fluid now. If you enjoy turn based strategy I highly recommend this game.
