_childDocuments_.review: Summary:This is a fun game that pulls very heavily from the Fire Emblem series and other Tactics Strategy games in terms of both storytelling and gameplay. It doesn’t seem tired, however, because it does the tried and true things quite well, and includes a couple significant innovations which freshen things up.Note to developers:It’s unlikely that anyone who worked on the game will read this, but it’s possible, especially since it’s an indie developer. If they do, I just want them to know that I enjoyed the game and appreciated their effort. Great job!Story-VibeThe story of the game was not as bad as I expected, considering that some of the reviews mention that it’s not strong. However, it was also the least interesting part of the game for me. I would say that the story is “Good enough.”The setting might as well have been pulled straight from Fire Emblem. There are nations which fight and politic, there’s magic and dragons, and divine powers which compete. The characters vary wildly in terms of both how interesting to me they were and how much story content belonged to them. Relationships are actually a mechanic in the battles, although a very minor one, and you can see what relationships characters have to each other on a certain screen. At the end of the game, most characters seemed to only have one or two relationships. The main character is the least interesting character in the story, which kinda dragged down the stakes for me. This is probably because they’re an audience insert, whose name and gender you choose. A lot of places which focus on the side characters' relationship to the main character fell flat for me. The main is part of a kinda generic Anti-hero/Hero/True Villain triangle, and all of these characters lacked spark IMO.On the strong side, the deuteragonist of the game is a character named Diana. In terms of the story, she actually could have been the protagonist. I ended up caring about her relationship and ark more than the real protagonist. There’s also a secondary Anti-hero who I found much more interesting than the main anti-hero as well.I can’t say, however, that the story never caught me by surprise. Most of it runs exactly by the book, but there was one particular twist that caught me a bit off-guard. I’ll save you the spoiler. Gameplay:The gameplay is a LOT like other tactical strategy games. There’s different classes of units that you level up and they fight on a grid. The outcome of the battles is determined by a set of stats that you’ve probably seen before. Some types of units have advantages over others at the cost of being weak against yet other unit types.That being said, they applied these elements well. One thing I appreciated about the game was that everything was explained quite clearly in the instructions. The right things seemed complex and simple. For example there didn’t seem to be a bunch of insignificant elements to track, which can happen in strategy games. Everything seemed both relevant and clear to gameplay. There were a couple small exceptions to that- I didn’t really figure out how “Ambush” worked until late in the game. The main innovation of the game was that each square on the board is filled not by a single unit- like in fire emblem, but a squad of units, which you can customize and adjust. This is a good concept and the core of what makes the strategy of this game tick. It also makes the scale of the game feel a bit better- rather than having an army of 14 people, you can field an army of 140 people, without it seeming unmanageable. For me fiddling with the squads was one of my favorite parts of the game. It adds freshness because the Rock-Paper-Scizzors element of unit combat is basically connected to how you build the squads, not some arbitrary thing like Fire-Emblems sword-lance-ax thing. That you can make the squads in many ways means that this is a complex and engaging question.In theory you can use any unit as a squad leader, and could make massive changes to the makeup of your army for every single battle. In practice I used the named characters that I was given as squad leaders 90% of the time, and mostly kept similarly composed squads. Part of this was that there’s limited variety in terms of what the different missions require from you, so I didn’t feel much need to make drastic changes, just marginal improvements. Actually, I think that this is where the game had missed potential - if the game had fully pushed me to change and rethink the makeup of my army more often I think it would have gone from being good to great.One complaint is that you have some limitations in terms of what units you can access. The game includes both gun units- think muskets and cannons, as well as dragon units. Until the last 5th of the game you basically either get to have one or the other. I was a bit disappointed when I finally unlocked the dragon units full capacity only to find that there wasn’t really any situation where I might use them, but was delighted when I earlier pulled together a unit of mounted gunmen that could wipe out practically any enemy squad.I started the game on warlord difficulty, and did not find it hard. If you’ve played tactics ogre, fire emblem, advance wars, or even XCOM I’d recommend that you do the same. This game is relatively easier than those games. The game has 30 main chapters, and 6(?) side chapters. That was about the right amount.I started the game with PermaDeath enabled, and played through chapter 19 with it on. This made it more challenging, but I did eventually turn it off. At some point the game seemed to punish the player for choosing permadeath. For about the last third of the campaign the enemy starts fielding a lot of glass-cannon squads which are practically guaranteed to kill your units if they hit them, and fields them in numbers which are more than the number of squads you have. Additionally, up until then there’s a building you can revive lost units in- this is taken away around the same time. Rather than seeming like a natural increase of challenge, it kinda felt like the developer was intentionally trying to make permadeath more difficult. The drawback to switching permadeath off was that it really simplified the strategy. By that point in the game you’ll have a couple squads which are really powerful, and they carry the bulk of the battle without you having to think about the strategy too carefully.A bigger brained person than me might be able to play the game at that point in terms of profit and loss- judging how many units it was OK to lose in the battle, but since you’re cultivating each unit of the squad over time, I didn’t really want to play it that way. I think the game actually subtly discourages that type of play by having tiered class advancement- The number of battles a unit has to survive in order to advance to a higher tier is too many to have a lot of your units dying each scenario, and by the end of the game literally all of your opponent’s units are in the highest tier. Conclusion/ReplayI enjoyed this game, but I don’t think I’ll replay it. I think that the 40ish hours that I’ve spent on this basically let me have the whole experience, and that there’s not much left to enjoy. Still, it was a good time, and if this is the genre of game that you’re into, then I totally recommend that you give it a spin.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the Ogre Battle 64 sequel I have wanted for over 20 years. There are some mechanical differences, but the key elements are all there. Don't be put off by the RPGMaker graphics, simple tilesets, or predictable story. The gameplay is what matters, and they've nailed it. There is a surprising amount of class depth and map depth. Each mission is a unique puzzle board to figure out. I would advise playing on the maximum difficulty + permadeath OFF. This keeps the game strategic and interesting, without ever becoming tedious. You don't want to play on standard difficulty and end up in a situation where one squad (Diana) just crushes everything thrown at her. That's not strategic, nor is it fun, and you're a nerd playing tactical RPGs, so start off on "Ludicrous" and enjoy the challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: In Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga, you play as the Blue hair protagonist in Tarhnra, a land ravaged by the war of Veridian Succession that only brought Chaos and instability for all parties involved. In one last attempt at rebellion, General Antares, once the war hero, kidnapped the Empress, and you must go and save her for the Empire.The Story happens in Tahnra, a land ravaged by the war of Veridian Succession that only brought Chaos and instability for all parties involved. In one last attempt at rebellion, General Antares, once the hero of the war, kidnapped the Empress, and it is our goal to go and save her on behalf of the Empire. A scenario filled with intrigue, cliché and some Game of Thronesque moments will meet you in every corner until the end of the adventure. Without revolutionising the concept, the scenario held on its own and kept me engaged for 30 hours. Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga (referred to as SOW past this point) surprised me by the depth of its content and the overall quality; it is an excellent game that hits all the right notes.Indeed, the Lore is well-built, makes sense and is quite in-depth; you will find details about the history of the characters, places, famous locations and general history that you will be able to read about or discover the more you progress. The worldbuilding exercise was on-point, but sadly, the character development was not equally distributed amongst the cast. Some have a personality, some are extremely boring, some are charming, and others are completely cliché.Mechanically speaking, the game is not reinventing the wheel, but you are at the command of your army; you will build it up from scratch and design it around the idea you will make of it and along your very strategy going into the battlefields. With a 25+ hour runtime over 30 missions, the world of SOW will keep you busy and for a good reason.There are so many options for your army; you will decide their class and their items (artefacts), and you can honestly try so many variations that it is extremely overwhelming at first. The skill trees and talents you will unlock will also help you refine your strategy, and these elements were extremely well designed and implemented in-game. The game will favour trial and error and experimentation.The game plays out on a grid, with each army taking a turn to manoeuvre and play; your job as the commander will be to defend your base, attack the enemy base and seize the objectives. All at the same time.I regret not trying to mix up my strategy and strongly encourage you to try to diversify your armies. While playing in normal difficulty, I didn’t experience tremendous challenges, and if you are familiar with tactical RPG, you should consider starting the game on the hardest difficulty. There is also a permadeath mode that will add a substantial amount of complex situations for you.Graphically speaking, the game is extremely pretty, the maps are well done, and the characters are well designed and inspired by various other similar titles, which only contributes to some nostalgia factor. The design meshes well with the environment, and the animations of battles are extremely fluid and of high quality.The Music was also quite reminiscent of the 90s JRPG games and meshes well with the rest of the game.Finally, SOW is an amazing tactical RPG with surprisingly rich lore, fun mechanics and a great duration; while being inspired by big titles of the same genre, SOW mixes it all up and makes up something that stands out at a reasonable price.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Fire Emblem, Final Fantasy Tactics, Langrisser, and overall Tactical and Strategy RPG enjoyer, I can confidently say that Symphony of War is a fantastic product overall, especially given the price, and all of the problems the game has currently are actively being ironed out and worked on by the developers. _childDocuments_.review: The closest to a true Ogre Battle spiritual successor in decades... if not the only one that has ever existed. Has elements of Fire Emblem and the Langrisser series.Improvements I would like to see:1. More complexity in the AI battles and/or more interesting units. Having only one type of healer/support is boring especially.2. Mounted units are just copycats of ground units. This is extremely boring. This is one element where I wish they'd taken more inspiration from Ogre Battle rather than Fire Emblem. Game really does not need mounted units, just units that can make squads go fast. 3. There should be more fantasy units and less horsey stuff. This is a fantasy game with dragons and beastmen, not a pre-1800s-themed strategy game (i.e. Dragoon).4. Some units like Ranger and its predecessors (Skirmishers) I could not tell at all what the point of them was. If it's not a tank, healer, archer, mage, or dragon, it is very unclear what the real benefit is if anything. Assassins seem like they might be useful but I honestly cannot tell if they're really that impactful or not.5. Leadership & capacity mechanic is interesting but it's frustrating starting a new party with only 3 units. Parties should be 4 minimum.6. In the manage army screens, the UI takes up the whole screen which is fine except when you hover over a menu item such as Change Job, that hover menu covers up the units in your reserve completely. Looking at Ogre Battle, a game with tons of units, I think the original did it better as the scaling of the windows was much smaller which made micromanaging less painful.7. I wish there was an option to turn on a sound effect for dialogue. The actors don't speak so having some kind of typing / writing / or a "beep-boop" sound fx would be nice.8. I like the idea of the tech tree but the benefits seem mostly invisible. A big part of the problem is how the tech tree is laid out. Might be better if the tree verticals were divided by specific roles (I think 5 or 6?) plus a general catch-all one. Another problem is very early on you get a whopping 8 tech points which allows you to fill almost all of rank one techs, but later missions you hardly get any. It would be better if they were spaced out more.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been enjoying the hell out of this game so far and the storys been good with some plotwists. Now, there is some issues I have with this game.1. Due to the limitation of arena tokens, grinding can be difficult to do early game.2. The difficult spikes are a bit random if you choose the second option as your difficult. There's been times I go 'wtf' when a unit  with 30% - 50% less threat level suddenly destroys my units even though previous chapters they were fairly tanky, ESPECIALLY near the end of the game where black mages and champions are thrown at you as they tear through your units like butter, even if you overleveled.3. The 'bonus challenges' are unnecessary. Oh sure, it'll get ya lotsa money and such, but.. .Your main character unit, Diana, and Abagayle? They are your powerhouses for most of the game.  MC due to Spoilers: Once he/she returns from the dead and is promoted, Attacking first they get to cast a AoE lightning spell, destroying most of the units if you've got two or three mages or dragons to attack with him/her. Abagayle as her passive helps overlevel dragons, and Diana, who BECOMES A ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ BEAST. She's tank, has high crit rate, and destroys most units in the front. Add two/three healers and two paladins and she'll destroy most things that isn't an assassin that destroys healers. Due to those three, I've often found myself not bothering to buy new units.Suggestions to improve this game1. Quality of life improve inspired by Fire Emblem games such as showing an 'arrow' path whenever you order a unit to move. 2. add an option so that after you finished ordering all your units, the game will automatically end turn and not have you to select it every time.3. After enemy units move, make their sprite greye out so I know which one has moved or not.4. Adjust the Blackmarket, or at the very least make the shop change every time I train in the arena rather than I need to complete a chapter to see new goodies.5. remove the tokens and instead make it so that you pay in gold coins similar to Fire Emblem's Arena. If you lose in the arena, you don't have all that exps vanish as if I loaded a previous save, instead let my units keep it. Failing to beat the chapter will mean I lost gold. But of course, you could replace the arena with the option to revisit previously beaten maps to find random units who have taken over it.6. the AI is so far, its.. kind of 65% intelligent but often times they would rather attack a unit with high threat level than to go for low weak threat levels. Sometimes  they'll outright ignore taking over your base in favor of attacking others. I believe the AI should be tweaked to go for threat levels lower than theirs and if their HP gets low, make them flee to a Fort or Church to get healed up per turn.7. dragons need a buff, they're suppose like a more tankier mage, but for them to fall SO quickly to physical attacks? Considering how they take extra slots, it makes them useless at front row.8. While buying units is good, I believe you should have a new spell where you can capture units much like Fire Emblem Fates, but of course you may keep that idea for a future game instead programming it here.Now, considering this game was made with rpg maker, the suggestions I made may or may not be possible to do, and I understand if you can't do them, or if you disagree with my suggestions. _childDocuments_.review: Nice SRPG that where maps play relatively quickly. I haven't felt the need to turtle like I normally would in other SRPGs, since the squad composition and healer mechanics allow you to take some punishment without seriously handicapping yourselves for the rest of the map. The ability to reset turns and quickload, while it can be exploited, also allows you to just be more free with your tactics rather than trying to plan out every little tiny detail before turn 1. I really enjoy the progression between maps, using resources you've captured to level your soldiers and tweaking squad compositions. You also have an option to do a little grinding (limited by somewhat uncommon items) in case you feel you're falling behind/ want to give that last little boost to a squad before a tough battle.If you like SRPGs, this one does enough well that it is 100% worth taking a look at. I'm very excited for the potential sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War allows for more customization than any other tactical RPG I've ever seen. The class structure for each unit is robust and intuitive. Additionally, they can be put together in all manner of combinations to form squads of various roles (punching bag, finisher, healer, etc.). And in turn, the combination of squads helps to form the overall army and corresponding strategies. The game gives you complete and total freedom by fully refunding of all resources and maintaining all class XP as you experiment with builds. It's hard not to like a game that lets you play how you want to play.SoW's other great appeal is the nuanced storyline. When you've played enough of these games, it's rare to see anything unique in the plot. Although the story is largely linear, there are plenty of twists, and a few options that players can choose between, which will lead to slightly different endings, ala Chrono Trigger.If these two traits appeal to you as a gamer, you'd be hard pressed to find a more enjoyable game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! If you're a fan of older Fire Emblem games like I am and Three houses felt like a huge letdown for you the same way it did for me (waifu wars school simulator edition just isn't my thing, no judgement if it is yours), this is a great alternative. I especially like the way the game lets you customize whole squads so you feel like you're actually commanding a small army rather than a ragtag handful of soldiers.The only major complaint I have is with the game having a few stats that it doesn't explicitly tell you what they do or what's contributing to it. I keep running into instances where a unit has a certain capacity number and the squad leader has enough capacity left, but it won't let you add the unit to the squad. Some kind of tooltip with stat breakdowns would be a really nice quality of life improvement, but it doesn't ruin the experience for me. _childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game. It takes a bit to take off and the story is more or less predictable (at least up to the chapter I'm on).Where it shines, though, is in the tactical options and gameplay. The setup of your armies and squads is very customizable to your preferences and play style and it really impacts each fight. You feel you have options, even though you'll always have a lingering feeling that your army could be more optimized. Most chapters after the initial part of the game play out as multi-front battles, forcing you to split your forces and this creates tension and ramps up the difficulty a bit. It generally feels very good, as you'll be rewarded for sound tactical decisions and punished for rash and impulsive ones.Overall, I recommend this game to any turn-based strategy fans, particularly those fond of Advance Wars, Fire Emblem and other similar games.

_childDocuments_.review: To start with the cons, this game's story and some of its minor mechanics fall apart under their own scope especially at the end.The story starts off alright and gets pretty strong in the middle, but definitely is a lot weaker in the end when a lot of themes and subplots they've been building to either don't resolve or end up not making any sense. Some of the support dialogue can be weird, like characters falling in love despite never interacting before. As for mechanics, unless I messed something up they introduced "side-missions" you could do before continuing the story, but there were only like 5 and they all started at the same chapter meaning I did them all at once and they never showed up again. It could've been expanded a bit.But, I still recommend this game because gameplay and mechanics-wise it's one of the most fun turn-based strategy games I've ever played, if a touch on the easy side (I played on Warlord Difficulty and Permadeath and didn't find myself struggling once).The squad-building and recruiting mechanic is incredibly well thought-out and makes permadeath mode very fun to play, since now you can  weigh the pros and cons of sacrificing units. It also made the battles feel very large in scope without making them feel slow since you could fill your deployment slots with squads led by other generic units.Every soldier class in the game felt unique with their own niche that made them worth using, and the equipment system gave that extra bit of customisation so that even similar units would operate differently.I think the hardest difficulty could've been made to be a bit more difficult. The quicksave ability is fine because it helps you not reset constantly, but I think that the enemy quality could've been a bit higher. When some characters can wipe entire enemy squads in one round of combat, it becomes a bit easy. Especially after you unlock some extra powers which let already powerful units basically solo entire maps. (Edit, the roadmap looks to include a harder difficulty, which I hope solves the problem. It mentions locking in harder settings/ironman mode which I'm not as big of a fan of, but I'm looking forward to tougher enemies)Still, a very good game and well worth the price if you're a fan of Turn-based strategy RPG's like Fire Emblem, Langrisser or the FF Tactics games. Even less RPG-focused fans of games like Advanced Wars or War Groove would get a lot of fun out of this.

Only 2 "real endings" I believe.I would give this an 8.5 out of 10. Get it, you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid turn-based tactical RPG.The good:- Each unit is really a "squad" of units, and building them up, and watching them grow through the game is fun as you'd come to expect from the genre.- The amount of micromanaging you can do is fairly deep if you want to get into it. Maximizing the stats on a squad but staying under their capacity makes for fun management.- Music is solid.- The game-play itself is fun, giving you options between what kind of attacks you want to do. There's "more offensive" or "more defensive", normal and "target leader attacks". The morale system makes for a fun "bonus" if you want to take the risk of making enemy squads surrender.The bad:- The UI is not good. For a game with this many abilities and small attributes that are important on characters, you would expect tool tips on hovering. Instead you need to click a separate button to show what they do and wait for it to scroll, or go to the tutorials page to find it out. Not a deal breaker, but definitely something that can be improved, and to the devs credit I think they are addressing it.- The story devolves into tropes. It almost feels as though it was just going through the motions in the end. It starts off decent, builds some intrigue, but then for me it started going downhill. There were some nice twists here and there, but overall I'd say it didn't hit that spot where I was super invested to find out what was going on.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! A mix of all the old school favorites (Ogre Battle, Fire Emblem, little bit of Final Fantasy Tactics).Writing is a bit wonky, but I can get past that. You'll have a great time training and creating your different squads, looking for the right combination of troops.Overall good game play and what you want out of a game like this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm keeping this review positive despite having no plans to finish the game. As many have said, the idea behind this game's combat mechanics is awesome and I really want to see more from this developer. The game is also only 20$ and even with the problems I'll list you'll still get your money's worth from the game's charming features.What's crazy is that my list of CONS is much larger then PROS and I'd still give the game a 7.5/10 for the price tage because the PROS are just that good.PROS- Fighting in this game is awesome, I really loved the variety of units and possibilities that could occur.- Conquest of objectives makes you really feel like an army winning a war and it's very satisfying.- The main character is likable, if not a bit generic.- A basic romance system exists, which is nice but held back by the game engine.CONS- Linear: This may be a personal bias, but the story and everything that happens is set in stone. A game with such great war mechanics and ideas would be fantastic as an open world game.- The Story Is Meh: I paid close attention to what was going on for about 8 chapters but after that it really started to get bogged down. This is a huge part because this game is made using RPG maker which is extremely outdated at this point.- Character relationships are extremely boring: Again, heavily influenced by the game engine, I just could not care less about the dialogue that you can have between each of the companions.- Scripted Battle Losses: This is a huge pet peeve of mine, and while YES you can technically win the battle if you knew everything before hand and built an exact army to counter your enemy, that's not how I enjoy playing games. All the more reasons the game would be even better if it wasn't linear, that way any loss you suffer will still feel like I had a choice.- Shifting Scope: Another personal preference perhaps, but for me the game is at its peak when you're on a large world map conquering towns and forts, but at certain times you'll have to play a whole chapter when you're breaking someone out of prison or into a sewer. And it uses the same mechanics as the world map wars so it really feels....small. Insignificant. And it breaks the feel of the rest of the game.All and all, I got a bit frustrated after the forced battle loss that happens in the story, but pressed on just to find the story really gets slow afterwards so I've stopped playing completely and I don't see myself coming back. However, due to the nice price tag I'd still say I got my money's worth. A sequel/spin off for this game has HUGE potential based on what they did right for this game. I really look forward to see future developments from this company.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone that grew up with the Nobunaga's Ambition / Gemfire / RotTK Nintendo era and moved through FF Tactics, Fire Emblem, Ogre Battle and the like... _childDocuments_.review: I was involved in the beta for Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga (from here on SoW) so that's how I've got 30 hrs of gameplay before purchase.The game: SoW is a srpg where instead of moving a single person around you control a unit of soldiers on a 3x3 grid.  Think Fire Emblem meets Ogre Battle.  A few characters (such as the MC which you can choose between a male or female avatar) have set classes that change with the story, but for the rest of your army there's a branching class tree that ranges from your basic guy-with-sword up to dragon rider or cannon.  As you progress you upgrade your army through a branching skill tree that improve your army, artifacts to improve your units, and items for your individual soldiers within the units that give you a lot of opportunity to customize.The Good: SoW gets the joy of building an army and unleashing them on your unsuspecting enemies soooooooo right.  When you find that one unit/skill/item that feels unstoppable it gives me that pure OB64 (which is my favorite time) good feelings.  If a game gives me that "one more turn" feeling I have to recommend it flat out - and SoW gave me that one more turn feeling night after night.The battle sprites are gorgeous.  Battles themselves are joy to watch.I generally don't listen to a game's music while playing (unless it's rimworld), opting for my own playlist.  Add SoW to the list of games that I'll play with the speakers on because the music, even the menu music that I've got playing in the background right now, is fantastic.Also, Devs are extremely responsive and have been patching at a furious pace over beta.  The meh: Graphics outside of combat are meh.UI is clunky sometimes but as said above, the Devs have been patching so there's a good chance this won't even be an issue in a month.The Bad: As I've said, what makes me giddy is building my own unstoppable monster units.  Well, sometimes the game will take away those units for chapters at a time to only focus on story characters/units who I hadn't been focusing on.  A few chapters eskew the unit as a whole as well, focusing on only a single character.The Ugly: The story can be at best called "over ambitious" and if I wasn't a member of the discord I'd think the writing was a poor foreign localization.  A thing taken from FE games is a between mission conversation system, which gives you a tiny bonus to getting up the skill tree and can cause story characters to gain bonuses fighting against each other, which is a lovely little mechanic I'm loath to use.  Best part of the cutscenes is that you can skip through them, although if you do you won't know why you suddenly have lost a portion of your fighting force sometimes.Summation:  SoW gets the gameplay right and to me that's what matters.  Some nits I have are big, but they didn't stop me from throwing my money down the moment the game launched.

_childDocuments_.review: Without being dramatic, this is possibly the best RPG Maker game I've ever played. The influences here are clear, invarious greats of the Tactical RPG lineage like Ogre Battle, Fire Emblem, and the Shining series. Impressively for a game developed independently, this game is not just a lighter rehash of those ideas, but rather a modernized retro that can genuinely stand alongside it's inspirations.  Many of the core ideas are familiar: like all the above mentioned games, this mixes a grid-based tactical map with jumps to side-view autobattle screens when units attack. Basic units follow branching upgrade paths into more elite types and form a rock-paper-scissors style counter meta against each other. Units are arranged on a 9x9 grid, using row and column based attacks and blocking priorities. But the details are where the game shines: it's more than an X beats Y beats Z beats X, but rather offense/armor/magic/ranged, cavalry/anti cavalry, ambush, skirmish, glass actual-canon gunpowder units, healing, and more, all additionally dependent on unit grid position. Adding unique unit skills, squad leader skills, and squad items, your options, if not limitless are certainly vast.  The end result of this a  great deal of creative expression and exploration (my personal eureka moment was when  I realized I could mix rogues with light cavalry), and the ability to create some extremely powerful units that feel great when they tear into the enemy.  The game's AI does struggle to keep up with this through most of the game if you try too hard, with only a battles that can test your ability a bit more - but the devs have been working steadily on improved AI and higher difficulty modes.While the unit/army design is the biggest standout, the game also boasts some truly great art, with both the in-battle sprites and the visual-novel like story section character art both being lovely to look out. While the game's story is fairly generic and full of JRPG tropes (evil empires and chosen heroes and the petty political struggle eventually culminating in fighting gods), it still serves as sufficient to provide context to the various battle maps. There's a light character link system as well, as in many of the inspirations, where you can pursue romance or friendship among the various hero characters in your army. While this is all definitely a side-offering to the combat, it's still pretty satisfying, and a few of the characters really stand out for memorable designs, personalities, and backstories, with some world-building elements I wish we got more than just a quick taste of. If I have one negative to ascribe to the game it's that their unit customization system is so advanced, so detailed, so complex and offers so many options, that you can easily find yourself burning away more time in the army configuration screens than in battle by a pretty significant margin. This is a draw at first, but can eventually feel somewhat tedious especially with the size of the armies that the later parts of the game support (and sometimes expect) you to field. There's also elements of min-maxing that feel awkward or grind-y (like having to hire and fire units to find the best base stats, element combinations, etc), but ultimately these are things you don't need to obsess with if you don't want to.What else can I say? If you like this genre, play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a grand slam or a masterpiece but it's okay. I'm sorry to say it did not meet the hype of all of the other reviews and ratings. I'd give it a solid C+ grade, passing. I'd recommend it, with some notes. 1: Gameplay is pretty easy, but I can see potential for a death spiral in some extreme cases.1a: Building and outfitting your forces is fun! I enjoyed the twist on the old "fire emblem" formula.1b: Enemy unit surrender and morale was cool, but it was not clear how it affected ally units. 1c: Enemies are all the same unit types, player has significant advantage most of the time. This made for boring and repetitive combat. Enemies didn't have items or special tactics. 1d: No way to inspect or adjust squads in the field. 2: Perma-death doesn't apply to main characters. I dislike this. No Iron-man mode a minus (though with iron man, the aforementioned death spiral becomes a strong possibility). 3: Scenarios were bland and side objectives ridiculously easy to meet on the standard difficulty. I will not be replaying on higher difficulty. I was never in ANY danger of running out of time, ever. 4: Writing was middle of the road, some good, some not. No sense of meaningful choice, things just "happened". Low replayability.5: Some of the art needs sharpening, most character art fell flat for me.5a: Unit art was good, with classic Game Boy Advance Feel.5b: The character art clashed with the unit art pretty hard. 5c: UI was clunky, but usable.6. music was okay, appropriate to genre of game. No bangers though. (frankly, I think that music is one of the hardest things to nail.)I got my money's worth, 33 hours for ~15-20 bucks. I would probably buy something from Dancing Dragon again. I wish them luck with their next project. Making games is hard, just getting a finished product to market is a herculean effort. I can appreciate all the work that went in to this even though I am lukewarm on the finished product.

_childDocuments_.review: Really excellent game, and brings a lot of new stuff to the table. Hoping this isn't the last we see of this style of game from this developer.The customization allowed by the squad system is fantastic, and the way you set your army up will seriously influence how you approach each map. I started with mostly heavy infantry with healers, an archer squad or two, and one heavy cavalry squad - these served me well enough, but as I progressed I learned the value of having a few light squads for increased mobility in rough terrain and the ability to *ambush*. When a light unit starts its turn on rough terrain (woods, hills, etc) and attacks from light terrain, it gets to ambush for a massive advantage in the fight. Normally combat has turns like: attacker->defender->attacker->defender, but in an ambush the defender just straight up doesn't get to take their first turn, allowing you to blitz them down. Makes up for the reduced defensive capacity of light units, since they'll end up taking less in retaliation. Just one of a bunch of excellent tactical mechanics in the game that were entirely new to me.Regarding difficulty: I played on the hardest difficulty with permadeath off, and found it to be a nice, consistent challenge (although the last few chapters were a bit too easy). Permadeath would have made the early stages of the game *substantially* more demanding and difficult, but the game gives you "arena tokens" with which you can grind resources/XP. Few and far between early but you'll be swimming in them later (and thus swimming in available funds, if willing to grind them out). With the appropriate tech researched, you'll be able to refill and replace depleted armies without issue as long as you aren't losing lots of units every chapter. You can also make use of quicksave/load in combats if you mess up. While the game supports the permadeath mechanic in this way, and it certainly changes the way you approach the game, I think I would have found it a bit more tedious, spending extra hours over the course of the game refilling my army to replace losses. It is *hard* not to lose units against certain enemy types - musketeers are just devastating, for instance. The game gives you tools (special classes, artifacts) to specialize defense against them, but in the absence of such a squad setup you can expect to lose some or all of your frontline if you ever let a firearm squad get the jump on you.Also - weird design choice on the arena tokens. You can trade up/down for tokens that give you harder fights and more rewards, but the more expensive tokens don't give enough of an increased reward to make them worth using over the cheap ones. Much more efficient to trade down, but that kind of sucks because it takes longer to grind out. Wish the higher level tokens had higher droprates for rare artifacts/traits, at least. The most expensive token does give you a class capstone item (not a huge effect, but nice simple stat boosts to a veteran unit) which is otherwise hard to come by, at least.Anyway, that's just one minor gripe about an otherwise great game. Worth mentioning as well that I was expecting some garbage story based on the other reviews for this game, but I found it to be totally fine. On par with (and very similar structure) to most FE titles. I'm aware those aren't necessarily known for their stories either, but it's perfectly serviceable and I had reason to follow along. Outside of a couple exceptions I found the character writing to be solid as well.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, my main motivation for trying the game was the similarities of the battle system with one of my all time favorite game series Ogre Battle and other games like Fire Emblem, Soul Nomad, and Advanced War.  I would recommend trying the game if you are a fan of the aforementioned games, especially if you are starved for anything similar to Ogre Battle.  Although, this game doesn't have as much depth compared to Ogre Battle when it comes to the units and fights themselves.Total gameplay will run you about 15-20 hours depending on how quickly you go about things and if you run some of the optional arenas for money/items.StoryThe story was better than I would have expected.  While odd at times the story telling was decently written and coherent. They use the tried and true story formulas used so often in games like Fire Emblem so you will be in familiar waters if you have that background.  You start off as a no name soldier at the beginning of a rebellion and end up as a leader of an army. You are then caught up in political intrigue backed by sinister forces and end up becoming one of the chosen ones.  Fire Emblem type of ending is a plus, although some unique characters were missing.MechanicsThe meat of the game is through the battle system which takes a lot inspiration from games like Ogre Battle and Soul Nomad.  To more younger people you could view it as a sort of simple autobattler like TFT without the traits. You place units on a 3x3 grid and when fights happen through the Fire Emblem / Advanced War battlefield movement the unit involved in the fight do their actions automatically until both sides have exhausted all actions.Morale for each unit lets some individual units take extra turns and affects how easy it is to make enemy units surrender. Artifacts lets you further customize your units at the cost of possible unit space. There are battlefield powers unlocked halfway through the game that provide some global presence during chapters. Tech tree is a cool idea to improving/customizing your army, although you just end up getting everything in the end. There are some terrain effects. Unlimited quick saves and even redoing turns means there isn't too much difficulty during a chapter.Some other relevant mechanics include support conversations between missions, although these are seemingly gained automatically after certain chapters rather than as a rapport sort of thing one would expect from games like Fire Emblem.It gives some background and interrelationship context between people but definitely less than I would have liked as most of the conversations are between the main characters.  Some conversations will affect minor details in the ending.CharactersThe characters are alright.  They are not very complicated and there is only a bit of character development as the game goes on.  There is very little going on between most of the cast excluding a handful of the main ones.  This would normally be where support conversations fill in the gap, but again those conversations are specifically for the main characters.SoundThe sound bites for unique characters are adequate.  The music is somewhat generic but serviceable.  The sound effects are appropriate with nothing really being too out of place.GraphicsTypical Fire Emblem-esque sprite work for most of the in battle sprites. The effects and animations all look quite good. The sprites used in cutscenes look a little too chibi-like than I would have expected, but they are serviceable. Unique sprites for the main characters are appreciated, though some people lacking unique sprites seems a little odd.  IssuesThere are definitely some issues that detract from the experience a bit.  Some of these are balancing issues, but others are more with the game itself.  The UI leaves much to be desired.  Here are some of the UI issues I had.  Having to go through multiple menus just to realize you need to check something before making a decision making you have to go backwards to another set of menus is more than a little annoying.  Not being able to see the threat rating of units on the battlefield without entering a menu.  Not being able to see what a unit does in a fight without consulting an article in the tutorial section.  There aren't even tutorial articles for unique units.  I had no idea one of them had a ranged attack until I accidentally triggered one.Not knowing if a units attacks/spells scale off of different stats.Not knowing the growth rates of the different classes despite most other stats being shown.Not being able to see at a glance what terrain does without having to check tutorial articles between missions.I never bothered with looking at traits as it was such a bother to even see them and most of them weren't even important enough to consider.Some unique units have silly affinities which do nothing or harm their class.Difficulty on the default "Captain" difficulty is on the lower side for the most part.  There is a drastic drop in difficulty at chapter 20 which I assume is for leveling purposes.There is a drastic jump in difficulty at chapter 25, although still on the easier side of things if you are at all familiar with these type of games.I felt that money was a bit lacking in the early-mid parts of the game (although I did have a few arena coins I could have used) when there are tons of high value things you wish to buy.Later in the game you are so inundated with money, but you don't really have anything to spend it on.  Having the shop refresh itself like how it does in the last chapter could have been nice.I am unsure on the number of legendary/unique units there are to be bought (I found 3).  I was hoping to find more during the latter chapters, but never saw any.Why can't you sell consumable items?There are only 5 "Gaiden" or extra chapters.  These were interesting and fleshed out some characters, but they all occur during chapter 20 which is very odd.Most chapters while usually on interesting tile sets are pretty generic in their objectives.  There were only a few chapters with interesting gimmicks.Below are things that I found lacking or appreciating when looking for a game like Ogre BattleLack of depth when it comes to the units and classes.  Very small pool of classes, many starting classes are just branches that lead up to certain tier 2/3 units which means there are very few "prestige" classes.Complete lack of non-human classes aside from dragons.  There were very few unique enemy-only classes too (2 to be exact, although one was a boss).Positioning has limited impact.Lack of rapport related things like combination magic casting.  This was one of the coolest things about squads in Ogre Battle so it is a little odd not to see something like it in this game.Lack of agency during a fight, although they moved those options as a prefight choice with pro/cons.Lack of secrets.  The game is incredibly linear like most Fire Emblem games.Direction not being a factor during fights.  I almost feel like units should have a speed stat affecting order during a fight instead of one squad then the other doing their actions.  This made attacking the far superior option.I did appreciate the Fire Emblem battlefield movement although you do lose the time of day aspect that Ogre Battle had.Morale was an interesting mechanic and I think it fits the army theme.Artifacts are an interesting take on equipment, though it cuts down on individual customization.  Traits and affinities are nice in the other direction improving individual customization.Overall, I still think this is a game you should definitely give a try if you are looking for anything even remotely similar to Ogre Battle.  This game is probably the closest modern equivalent I can think of that captures much of the same essence as Ogre Battle while being its own representation of what the developers wanted in their game. I really can't thank them enough for creating this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This one was a surprise, flew under my radar from the getgo. Im glad it was brought to my attention. The game manages to throw me back to my kid days, eventhough i never played Ogre Tactics / Fire Emblem games until recently, it felt like i was back there.  The Story is surprisingly engaging, and the variation in tactics and options is great.  If i'd wish for one thing, then it would be that there is some spreadsheet mode to see the warriors in your army so its easier to pick the best. That can be at times a bit of a hastle.  Another positive note towards the difficulty, the game has 3 settings (easy, normal, hard) and the option to switch on/off Permadeath for your dudes. This way everybody can play the game the way they like it (it is NOT A COMPETITION you "hard mode is the only way" sayers).  I think if you get to understand the game, towards the end Normal "can" get a bit easy if you really theorycraft every squad from the start and exactly know what you plan to do with them.  But also on Easy, mistakes got punished until 3/4 trough, hard. I really enjoyed my 40-50ish h with the game, was just about the right lengh. If you like turnbased strategy, and a game that respects your time (it has very minimal grinding) - go for it. The Dev's deserve their success!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty flawed game on an amazing concept. As a big fan of Shining Force, Ogre Battle and other ancient tactical RPG:s this did scratch an itch. Only the completionist in me made me finish the game though as squad progression was pretty meaningless and arcane after about half the game.The good - Fun strategy RPG with great art, competent music and fun early progression. Well worth it's price if you're into these kind of games. It also runs solid 60 fps on a potato.Some rambling feedback:The tooltips needs to be made much much clearer. Overall the UX work is far below what's acceptable in this state and it's highly unclear what various things do. The items were mostly left unused in my inventory as it was bloaty and too much of a hassle to drop items on every single soldier in every single unit. Stats and levels were pretty much totally unnecesary as I never looked at them or gave them much thought after a certain point in the game. The idea that you need certain stats to promote to a certain class is a good one but you should make it clear what the soldier needs to do to build these stats beyond unga bunga and items. A Karma-system like ogre battle is pretty cool where you get worse karma if you kill weaker units. It's a great way to ensure you don't just build 2-3 juggernaut units because you literally wont be able to promote to some of the higher tier classes if you have 0 karma. Class mastery is also a cool idea and right now it's just a tier xp meter to be filled. It could add passive bonuses to the soldier so that if you max out archer for instance you get a permanent +5 to SKL so that maybe you need to master both Archer and the light infantry soldier to make ranger.To make the end of the game better I would have preferred fewer units so that each chosen soldier becomes more important. The Rock paper scissor-esque vibe where certain units are stronger against other unit types is also pretty redundant or at least very unclear. I played the game on captain so maybe it is better matched at warlord but I had my strongest units and they were strongest against everything, and could one-turn any enemy and also counter terminate enemy units whereas other units couldn't do either even when they were evenly matched on class tier and levels. I would reduce the total amount of units, or more clearly specify what they are strong against. I would remove unit traits or reduce the total amount of soldiers because it becomes too much to manage for my taste. Same with affinity., It's a half baked idea that doesn't really add any significant value to your soldier, it just confuses the player.. So tip to dev to make the game even better - Reduce total army size, reduce the systems around each soldier (XP, CP, Stats, Affinity, Items, Traits could be automated like 'defense focus' 'ranged focus' 'magic focus' and the unit becomes more adept that way when leveling up.) More endgame challenges would be cool too, and more soldier tiers, or make the last tier further away as I had most of my army maxed out about midway through the game.Now when it comes to the story it was alright. The cutscenes could do some work, and should have been presented in a much less opressive way. They should have been integrated into the combat like they were in one of the missions for instance where some characters are talking to eachother whilst the fight is going on through shoutouts. I always hated when the 'conversations' tab lit up and I had to go esc out of a conversation I didn't really care about to get some rank points. Rank points, on that matter, also become redundant as you can literally unlock every perk. Overall good value purchase that I enjoyed a lot and will continue to come back to as the devs keep updating and fixing.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth buying if for nothing else because the tactical meat of the game is frankly one of the best in the genre - I spent hours playing around with creating different squad compositions (like many players) and the battles, though quite lengthy, are sheer fun to play out. In fact, in terms of the actual gameplay and tactical layers, this beats out most AAA titles and literally every other indie SRPG I've played and I've played a *lot* of games in this genre (it's my own personal favorite).I'd describe this game as a fusion of Ogre Battle, Langrisser, Fire Emblem, and Vandal Hearts. There's influences I can see from each of those series at play here. Worth noting: all of those are excellent SRPGs (Vandal Hearts being the underrated one far too many people are not familiar with).The story: Some people love it, some people hate it. Keep in mind either way - this is only the first episode of a franchise series, so this is just setting the stage for a longer tale. Personally, I liked the story and while it has some technical flaws (the characters are somewhat tropes, and I found myself skimming the dialogue in cut scenes because it had a been there/done that feel), the overall narrative kept my interest and it does some interesting things with a predictable plot formula (which I won't get into because spoilers).But like I said, even if you hate the story, the actual tactical gameplay and creating and readjusting your squads as characters increase their Leadership Points (the currency that determines how large your squads can get) and you add new characters either via story, the mercenary shop, and/or generic recruitment... that is so spectacularly done, you could gloss the story and still feel as though you got your money's worth - if not an outright bargain.

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War is hands-down one of the best tile turn based strategy war games on Steam, and possibly one of the best indie ones ever. It hits a lot of the notes I was looking for in terms of a "Fire Emblem but on PC." The biggest point of enjoyment is within the core gameplay: squad-based units with each soldier being customizable is great.- No single units, each 'unit' is a Squad that you can endlessly customize between different soldiers, classes, traits, stats, and group artifacts. This allows for creating different groups with different roles on the battlefield, or whatever you want! (You can have a 9 unit archery-only squad to deal insane range DPS, for example, or just a squad with a little bit of everything. Only just run a single unit by them selves!)- The world and lore is actually interesting. I find myself not impatiently clicking through dialogues boxes and do check in on the lore dump documents sometimes just to get more immersed. - The missions are balanced pretty well and there are a lot of interesting scenarios in the mix that break away from typical play.- There is a break point in the middle of the story that was super interesting to me, and I really enjoyed those chapters.- There are some great tunes here, especially in Sayunaa.- The story is fine. It's good. It lands around the 'typical fantasy-war rpg' territory. What with Gods, ancestors, evil politicians, so on. Save for the few chapters in the middle of the rising climax I mentioned in  the story is just fine.- While the pixel art design overall is just wonderful, the character and UI art sometimes feels a little...out of place. It begins to grow on you at first, but something about the characters seeming under-detailed but also realistic put in the foreground of a GBA-styled pixel RPG feels mismatched. It's still good, but it feels like there were two departments for world/in-game art and character/UI art and they didn't mix together quite well.- There are side quests, which show up later in the game, and they're nice to have! The game doesn't give you too many chances in the first half to farm and grow your strength, so these showing up were nice. But their existence is the only good part.Now, don't get me wrong. This game is a wonderful piece of work and loads of fun! Anything here in The Bad is mostly just gripes and nothing that prevents you from enjoying what the developers made here.- Relationships: The game has a unit relationship function which is something I personally loved in older FE games. However, it is executed sort of poorly here. You do not have to do anything to unlock a relationship conversation from appearing. They will appear after a chapter every time. You can chose to ignore it if you want but you still don't have to work for it. Some relationships will grant a bonus involving the units, but some do nothing. The romances are nice to see and I do have my own ships, but they're nothing to write home about. Overall, it feels like this feature was meant to be baked into the game more than it ended up being, which was sad to see.- Side quest STORIES: there aren't many side quests, and when there are, they don't have any fun little story to go along with it. Sure, you get a small blerp about what led you to the battle you're about to fight, but that's it. No intermission conversations, cutscenes, or anything. A real missed opportunity for extended character development.Symphony of War: Nephilim Saga is an awesome indie game that gives you that Fire Emblem need, whilst doing its own thing. I've played Dark Deity and War Groove, and neither of them have satisfied me in the way this title has done. And to be quite honest, I will always prefer the Squad-based structure of the single unit structure of FE going forward.If you like War games, Fire Emblem, both, or just good turn-based RPGs, play this game! It's worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War is a love letter to classics like Final Fantasy Tactics, Advanced Wars and Fire Emblem, and (more importantly) it plays better than most. It has an interesting story and setting (strongly inspired by Ivalice and the FF Tactics deeply political story arc) which is enough to give a sense of meaning to the game. But SoW truly shines in the strategic department: it's a fun pick and play game but with a surprisingly deep system that will keep you doing numbers in your head on how to best approach every scenario. If you are remotely interested in the genre, go ahead and get this!The interface is a bit clunky (again modeled after PS1 classics, but 25 years have passed since them!) and the 2D characters are somewhat stereotyped and bland (what's with the ENORMOUS err chest properties of all the women characters?) but once you get past those flaws they don't detract from the fantastic strategic experience.Congrats to the dev team and looking forward to seeing the updates that they can bring to SoW! A better interface, more balanced difficulty and even more units would be great!

_childDocuments_.review: A good tactical rpg where the devs take a lot of fun things from various other titles and stuck it in. It even has a good story, though not particularly exceptional, is well written and has enough charm, interesting moments, and fun bits of lore to keep me interested the whole way through. Though the game isn't perfect, the ui is a bit poor, not in its layout but you will have to click too many buttons to get where you need to go and due to the units being squads, each with their own small things that can can be managed, it can get to be a bit of a pain later on when you have 15 squads with at least 6 units in each. This would be greatly improved with better mouse controls as in the current state you have to click buttons to interact with different buttons that are already visible on the ui.There also isn't a whole lot of interesting builds which you can do with units which would be the main upside of the the customization. The only one i could make was a low cap squad build with a mage unit that hits the whole map.I would also suggest any veterans of the genre play at the hardest difficulty, the game is fairly easy on the captain difficulty only having a handful of squad deaths throughout the entire campaign. The game gives plenty of opportunities to level and upgrade your characters so you can always make your squads stronger if you need to.The game is great fun and if you are looking for a game to scratch that FE itch I would definitely try it out.RIP Zorro

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR- Amazing Ost- Sick spritework- Satisfying to min/max or structure your army- An absolute joy to play if you like Tactical RPG'sWow, what a game, how do even I begin? I have played the game through twice now on Warlord (Highest difficulty) before the option to remove Permadeath, if I were to play again I would be too stubborn to turn it off due to having played with Permandeath twice already which was the default.For me, this game could have been easily priced at 29.99, so I opted to buy the extra DLCs to support the devs since it isn't.In an age where games are more about the presentational front and marketing power; Symphony of War easily stands as a testament to what small developers and a lot of love can accomplish if they lack that power. It still confounds and escapes my mind that Symphony of War was created within RPGMaker, and each time I start the game I am only ever reminded of this when a cutscene occurs whenever you get to see the iconic character(or chibi) sprites of RPGMaker fame.If the initial art style and screenshots of its highly stylish sprite work didn't captivate you at first, then this game is most likely not for you. This game is a love letter to the presentation, love, and work that went into the older games with its style; like Fire Emblem and Advance Wars, as the most glaring examples. There haven't been many faults within the art style that I've taken any deep notes on, the style is consistent and you'll notice a small difference and quality between certain units (Such as Sorceress and Paladin, and the animation differences between certain classes being much more visceral- Probably due to different artists interpretations). These details are however minimal on the whole, and the consistency throughout remains with its fantastic presentation.Gameplaywise it is an absolute joy for people of all different styles who love Tactical RPGs or would very much like to get into one. The game is backed up by a fantastic OST that gets you into the mood to watch your army fight; The only downside is that enemy-turn OST is the same throughout the game (Which isn't a bad thing, but it gets boring when it doesn't loop/change either!). The tutorial explains everything that you could need, so I am not going to go too deep into the gameplay in general. But if you are familiar with both Advance Wars and Fire Emblem, then the game will very much fall into place.It's satisfying to spend time thinking about the purpose of each group, what units they should have, what affinity is best suited for the role you want them to have, and then seeing it shine. There is nothing quite like watching your 6-7 Archer units rain down a hailstorm of arrows when fully upgraded with extra arrows or a shield-wall of Sentinels taking on 4+ groups of enemies as bait while healers are in the back-formation stitching them back up to full.The plot does what it's supposed to; it's to the point and it's sweet- though the pacing falls off slightly towards the end. If this is the buildup to a sequel or something much greater, I am more than ready to play it. I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and I wish to see more from the developer going forward. The game is so fantastically well structured and creating your own ultimate army is its own little game. I'd rate the game a 9/10, it's so satisfying to play, and the amount of work and love that went into it is abundantly clear. I still can't believe it's made in RPGMaker.______________________________________*old review back when I first got the game*What a stupidly amazing game, I'd make a larger review if I weren't playing the game right now and enjoying the toughest difficulty, even if I am losing and I have to reload I am not even mad.Things to note before full review:- What an amazing OST- The sprites are sick and consistently cool with the artstyle- I forget 99% of the time that it's an RPGmaker game, this is hands down the best RPGmaker game made yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. It will be familiar for fire emblem players but it's entirelly its own kind of beast. The squad-building is a very unique, very complex and very fun mechanic and the story and characters are quite enjoyable. Dialogues ranged from cringe inducing, to fun to actually well written character development and world building. The music is just decent, but the artwork is excellent. Get the DLC too, as it's very cheap and adds about a 30% extra content. It also includes some of my favourite units and develops some characters. Warcats and oracles are the real way to win wars in this world. PERSONAL HIGHLIGHTS (spoiler-free, of course):- I hate Chapter 27 with a passion. It's a very frustrating gimmick map that took some attempts to get right.- Absolutely loved the ending. it's grand, epic, heartfelt and quite uplifting. Can't wait for the sequel!- An absolutely random mercenary carried my entire playthrough. His name was Warlord Tatar, and, honestly no idea why, but this absolute beast of a man and his team dealt way more damage than the MC's squad and was able to withstand more punishment than the entire army combined. Absolute legend of a gigachad, Griffith would be proud.

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony bills itself as a tactics game, and harps on the importance of utilizing tactics in battle, but the mechanics don't lend themselves to that end. For example, cavalry are unimpeded by hills or terrain such as woods, meaning that they can simply charge through what should be movement impediments and attack your ambush troops with ease. That's inane - cavalry should be punished severely for fighting in unsuitable terrain. Heavy armor units should also be at a severe disadvantage when fighting in unsuitable terrain against light units. Also, if a unit is capable of performing ambush attacks, why can't it hide in the appropriate terrain? Why is the damn thing still visible? Some ambush.There is little to no information, save what is provided in text blocks during tutorials or the game's encyclopedia, about the properties of all terrain tiles. Even the entries there are woefully incomplete and inadequate. What constitutes 'rough terrain'? Anything but grasslands? Is a wheat field rough terrain? What are the properties of swamps? Do forests grant added protection against arrows (they should)? Do hills do something besides provide 1 more range unit to ranged attacks (they should, such as increased defense)? This means it's first and foremost an RPG - NOT a tactical game - where stats are more significant than any sort of tactical capability.Speaking of the woefully inadequate game encyclopedia, it is missing explanations for a slew of status effects or further information for properly triggering charge and ambush attacks - sometimes they work, sometimes they don't. There's no explanation as to why - according to the cavalry unit description if I move maximum range (or 6 tiles) before attacking an enemy I should get a charge attack. It also contains just blatantly incorrect information. For example, it states that siege cannon take up two tiles when they simply don't. Then there are the mission objectives and extra objectives. Mission objectives need to be met in order to finish a map. Some of them are simply stupid - for example, the swamp monastery map. The objective is to get your protagonist's unit to a particular tile to end the mission. However, I had completely destroyed all enemy units, including reinforcements. I still had to waste several turns moving the protagonist unit to the specific tile in order to end the mission. The extra objectives grant you extra faction experience if completed. They include things such as ensuring that allied units survive. However, the allied AI (and enemy AI, for that matter) are utterly brain-dead. For example, allied cavalry units consistently charged to their deaths against enemy units filled with pikemen and crossbowmen. One of the side objectives was to ensure no more than 2 of these cavalry units died. Of course I failed the objective due to their insanely suicidal and cavalier (heh) attitude toward life. Failing that objective was not on me - it was on the developers for coding cavalry units to blindly charge to their deaths against units specifically designed to destroy them. What sort of idiot commanders did the allies hire?There's nothing inherently wrong with any of this, and the game is fun to play in order to level up different troop types and see how they function. My issue is - don't claim that tactics are relevant when you don't even take basic terrain factors into consideration, the AI is brain-dead and suicidal, and you give the player super units who can unga-bunga their way through an enemy force by simply being present.Edit: 6/13/2022 (Note that today's patch may have addressed some of the issues above)Other problems include certain tactics not working correctly. Zone of Control has no effect, as enemy units can still move full speed past my units.Magic is apparently less effective when used 'consecutively', so I'm assuming that means if a healer uses a healing spell twice in a row it is less effective. Is that if used on a single unit, or just twice in general? Is that per caster, or for your army overall over the course of a turn?The morale system is silly. You can kill a squad's leader, utterly destroy the squad except for two archers or two casters (who will get wrecked without any covering units), and they still might have a low to nil chance of surrendering, regardless of the size or composition of the unit attempting the surrender. Two unarmored casters out in the open getting attacked by a full squad of heavily armored knights? Nope, no surrender, their morale is still 'fair'. C'mon, that's just stupid.Edit 2.0:Chapter 12 is stupidly long and boring, and consists of you watching an overwhelming amount of enemy units move around. I guess the benefit is you can try to take as many out as possible to farm XP for your units. Honestly, they should've ended the chapter so I didn't have to waste an hour of my life watching the enemy army shuffle about, waiting for them to kill me.Escort mission. This map is pure RNG - if you can luckily one shot whole squads as they ram themselves to death against you, great! Otherwise, quickload. No one likes escort missions, especially when the AI is brain-dead and is only set to run to an objective, not avoid enemy units. It's like babysitting a lemming and trying to ensure it doesn't run off a cliff every five seconds.  Enemy super units. You spend quite a few chapters avoiding, or running from, enemy super units that can one shot an entire squad. The devs fall back on this mechanic far too often. Boring and trite design.Valkyries. They're an utterly useless Tier 3, suffering from a massive identity crisis. They lack the healing power of a Tier 2 mounted healer (despite the game specifically saying they have the healing capability of a hospitaller, lol) and the attack power of a knight, making them pointless and a waste of a slot. You'll keep your mounted healers at Tier 2 if you want them to be effective. The class needs a mechanics re-work to be useful.Flying units can't fly over walls in certain maps that they can fly over in other maps (lol why? You're artificially limiting my "tactical" options). They also can't move or stop on certain tiles with no rhyme or reason - for example, where mountains meet plains. They also move more slowly than cavalry. What's the point then?Stun is useless when ambushing - it applies to the missed attack due to the ambush, not the attack the enemy actually gets to take. What is this game's obsession with water units? Water unit recruits, water units in my starting squads, water units in recruited squads... water, water, everywhere, and not a drop to drink.Terrible map design - move a turn, bait minimal enemy units with heavy to soak, punish with light / ambush troops, repeat ad nauseam. Some maps are designed with enemy light ambush / stealth attack units already situated in rough terrain. There is nothing you can do to avoid this - you have to bait and soak the damage with heavy units. These maps typically have Donari temples past the rough terrain with enemy ambush units, as if the devs knew they set up the map to screw you.If you don't recruit as many units as possible early on you'll get severely hosed later in the game. Late-game recruits, including uniques, have horrid stat spreads that don't match their level, regardless of affinity. You'll see level 40 units with 30s and 40s in their primary class stats, making them worthless.I can see now with getting deeper into the game the devs spent too much time trying to craft a narrative instead of focusing on game design. The narrative they did craft is rife with spelling errors, at that. What a disappointment - if I want a good story I'll read a book or join in on a TTRPG, not play a video game. I'm here for the tactical combat, not what your OC Donut Steel Amazonian mommy fetish paladin feels about Donar.I have no more room to express my dissatisfaction with this game. It's BAD.

_childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga is a love letter to old 2D tactics games from the glory days of 16- and 32-bit consoles. In particular, it's inspired by Ogre Battle (though I'm not familiar with that one). This is good and bad, as the game copied some of the bad parts of those old games as well, but it's mostly good! The developer also seems slightly incompetent, unable to fix certain bugs or implement certain requested features in a reasonable time frame. Nonetheless, what they've created is good.I'm too tired at the moment to go into all the details of how the game works, so I'll just add a few comments that relate to the most common complaints in the negative reviews.The UI is pretty darn bad. It's pretty much lifted straight out of an old SNES game, and not even one of the better SNES games. It works and it's understandable, but it's missing important quality-of-life features. It's clearly designed for a gamepad, not a keyboard and mouse. In fact, the keyboard and mouse support seems to be layered on top of the gamepad support, as if the keyboard and mouse are emulating a gamepad. Obvious PC features, like drag and drop, simply don't exist. I'd recommend not using the mouse at all in the menus, or hardly at all, and sticking to the keyboard, or (presumably) better yet plugging in an Xbox controller if you have one. The negative reviews have this right, but the game is still playable and enjoyable, especially if you can figure out which keyboard keys do what. (There is no key rebinding or key map. You just have to figure it out through trial and error.)The writing is not so bad. Many negative reviews complain about the writing. It's not amazing, but it's on par with those old games and there's a fair amount of intrigue and lore. The big picture of the story is actually really good. The details of individual lines and sentences could use a bit of work. Overall, I'm enjoying it. Some parts are silly, but it's par for the course I suppose. Some of the romance dialogue is awkward, though.The art is beautiful pixel art, although the battle backgrounds lack some variety. The sound effects are good, but the voice acting is bad, lacking in variety, and heard way too often with no way to reduce the frequency.The mechanics are good. There're a lot of details and ton of options for people who like to optimize and customize their characters and squads. I haven't seen another tactics game with the squad concept, and it's fun. The UI makes managing squads a chore, though.There's still no iron-man mode, even though it'd be almost trivially easy to implement one. There are some bugs, like some game options not really saving (or else getting reset somehow) and not really taking effect reliably. The important parts of the game, however, seem to work flawlessly.The game is good for 30-40 hours of play.In summary, if you at all liked those old tactics games, you should really give this one a try. It's a fun and worthy successor!
