_childDocuments_.review: This might be the only game in this genre that I hate and most disappointed. I completed the game with Ludicrous difficulty. I didn’t feel that AI is as smart as it claimed when selecting this difficulty, they just attack you when you are in range and don't place their position or select the target that is most effective.Here is the main reason I hate this game.The tactical game where you can’t calculate anything, you don’t even know what your damage or defense is. STR provides physical damage and physical resistance but how much? SKL provides crit rate, evade, hit rate but how much? When you use an item to gain an attribute to unit you never know how much it affects. Is 10 STR or 15% more damage better? You don’t know because you don’t know how much 1 STR turns to damage.Terrain effect, there is so much terrain and skill that relates to terrain like ignoring desert movement penalty. But fun fact is you don’t know the cost of the penalty from the first place so is that skill good? High morale may gain extra turn, low morale decreases attack power that’s all they told you so is it worth to maximum morale by sacrificing damage? In the game you win a battle and show as the winner but then your morale decreases even if not a single unit dies. With so many ambiguous details it results in a game play experience that you don’t know it’s a bug or somewhat untold mechanic.The UI is also the worst, never playing a game and feeling so annoyed when customized units like this. Can’t even rename the unit squad, when showing the equipped artifact it shows the name where I have 20 squad and only some of them can rename. When adding a new skill you must select skill then select slot then you can read what that skill effect. Another option is to select that skill and want the slow text to slide up line by line.There are so many more annoying things in this game so if you don’t like the ambiguous detail and horrible UI like it never gets tested I think you should avoid this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A cleverly disguised muscle-amazonian-woman fetish visual novel, with some copy-pasted FE gameplay between cutscenes.On a more serious note, this is a Fire Emblem clone, but you control squads instead of individual units. It does emulate the feeling of the games quite well, but it doesn't improve it in any meaningful way.The other aspect that can't adequately be summarized by "FE clone" is the plot. It is a fanfic. I'm not kidding, this has every trope in the book and a good chunk of obvious self-inserts and waifus. It's so cringy, nonsensical, and terrible I laughed a few times - which is a plus in my book; god knows the industry is riddled with mediocre, boring stories.The game may be a poor copycat, but it is competent enough to be enjoyable. It gets a pass from me, but don't buy with high expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: I got the game a week ago and blazed through it by sinking 35 hours in the past week. I've rarely done that with games, I'll be honest. Its hard doing that working full time jobs and having a social life lol. The game is great, for sure. But it's not without some glaring issues. WARNING - Spoilers ahead! - The whole appeal is the auto-battle with the customized squad you create and set up. Its incredibly fun. To see a squad you hand crafted win tough battles and survive till the end of the chapter, especially in the beginning 10 chapters or the game where it felt like there was so much you didn't know or understand of the game and what it had to offer. - I thoroughly enjoyed the campaign when it was outdoors, when you'd go from one fort to another fort and there'd be like 20 battalions of enemy troops coming at you and it felt like an all out war. The feeling of pitting your hand crafted customised army against the enemy's in such a large scale feeling battle was amazing. I did NOT like it when it was having those indoor battles. I didn't hate it. But it kind of took away from the fun side of this game. The feeling of war was lost in those chapters. - Talking about the story itself, its whatever. The characters are EH and its a very generic setting. Its not gonna win any awards for the story. But I guess it helps set up some plot points. It helped keep the chapters going which I didn't mind, I guess.- It was also weird seeing the weird titan form of one of the characters. It just looked so out of place with the rest of the character designs. Even some of the regular female character designs were kinda over the top. Like, the people who designed some of the women designs definitely did it with only one hand and then realised they can't use those designs and decided to draw tight clothes on them. For example - The character Diana. Her body shape is what you'd see in anime/manga like One Piece. That being said, I don't mind the muscular women tho. Warriors have muscles. It's not unrealistic or anything. - The dialogues were corny/cheesy/amateurish at best. But eh. Not really something that bothered me too much. Some of the dialogues could've been cut but there's a "Skip all" button, which is great for those who cannot deal with it.- I think the game is at its strength for the first 20-23 chapters. The last 7-10 chapters were its weakest. The first 10-12 chapters were its strongest I think. - And most importantly, the final 2-4 chapters were bland AF. I was hoping the game would've gone a whole DIFFERENT direction. I wanted the last few chapters and battles to be monumentally larger in scale compared to previous chapters. But instead, the second to last chapter was so weak because it was just you controlling 4 individual characters, not even 4 squads or armies. Just plain single characters. And despite that, I felt the whole final battle with the main boss in the following chapter to be even weaker. It felt like the game was leading up to bigger and bigger battles only for it deflate so hard at the end there. - I was HOPING there would be more classes and upgrades possible but I was kinda surprised at how limited that was. But seems like the game designed with that limit in mind. So, it works. But it kinda feels like there was potential for like at least the double the class types/upgrades. But like for a fantasy setting, they have dragons and that's it? When I first saw a dragon in the game, I was pumped because I thought I'll see more creatures. But no. That was it. Just dragons.ANYWAY...Why did I say I rarely play games for 35 hours in a single weak and then complain so much about this game? Because I still loved the experience for like 95% of my time with it. The last 3-4 chapters I played today were the weakest.I also think the devs have the ability to make a perfect game next time. They have all the ingredients they need. The foundation is incredibly solid. The ideas are on point. They just need to to understand what the strengths are of such a game and capitalise on it better by offering more customisation, characters, upgrades, larger scale battles (especially towards the end), a more unique story and better dialogues. Right now this game is a solid 7.5/10. Honestly, if it was 2 days ago, I would've rated it a 9/10 or higher. But the last 2-4 chapters brought it down for sure. I felt the game needed to end on a much grander scale of a note than how it ended. It felt very anticlimatic after all those battles. Just cannot shake the feeling that the ending was weak AF and that this could've gone a whole different ending direction. But if you enjoyed games with autobattles before, you might definitely enjoy this one. Support the devs. They have potential to make the next game, in this genre, ground breaking. I hope they learn from this and push it forward and expand massively in every possible.

I appreciate the efforts, and think if there will be more games in the same franchise that they will really be able to build off this strong foundation. Gameplay is strong, and has so many options to work with. Different styles of units make for a wild change in the entire squad and how well they function together with just a mere swap out of one or two characters. The gameplay difficulty scales up pretty perfectly. I dig it, hardcore!Ultimately, this game is a great time. If you like Fire Emblem, Langrisser, Shining Force... this is a must play in the same category and I would ultimately highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game shows that ingenuity goes a long way when designing a game. An rpgmaker game for $20 that surpasses the battle systems of full priced strategy games is worth picking up on that merit alone. While I have criticisms of this game, none of them are meant to take away from this accomplishment, but rather give feedback on how future releases might be smoothed out so that every element matches the quality of the battle system.The strength of this game is undoubtedly the ability to customize and tweak your squads as you see fit. There are endless examples, but for example you can put together a squad of exclusively archers, which are exclusively meant to pick off enemies from afar, or from atop walls. Or you could have a squad with archers in the back row with a front row of heavily armored soldiers/pikemen meaning you can strike from range, but aren't going to get wiped out if an enemy does reach you. You could even throw a healer into the mix to give the squad some sustain, or sandwich your archers between a front AND back row of armored units incase assassin type units who get to strike the back row of a squad attack you. I could keep adding "you could even's" to this until I am describing a completely different squad, but you get the idea.The customization goes even deeper, with you being able to equip artifacts and teach traits to units which will really make you think about how you are putting the squad together.This is without a doubt the secret sauce to the game, since you will get invested in not just your main story characters, but the units that make up the rest of your squad. You'll be excited as they level up and grow, and devastated when they die. That is, if you play with permadeath on which I strongly recommend, since it adds much needed weight to encounters that you would otherwise be able to barrel through with just a couple survivors- Main characters don't die even with permadeath so it strikes a happy balance between deaths hurting but not making you feel like you absolutely need to restart.On that note I will pivot onto my criticisms, the first of which is that even with permadeath I found the game a bit too easy. This is unfortunate since it felt almost properly tuned, except that my super leveled up Diana squad with Paladin's and healers were nearly unstoppable. She alone could hold a whole front of a war, particularly when you unlock certain powers later on. I'm unsure if the issue is with her in particular, or my tanky team composition with armor artifacts equipped meaning they never died and just snowballed, but either way that was my experience. Adjacent to the issue of difficulty is that not all missions are built the same, with some having quite a large map, lots of enemies, points of interest, and some challenge, whereas others are tiny with only a fraction of that, while still allowing the same number of squads deployed or close to it. This can lead to some of the missions feeling like filler and a waste of time, doubly so for the ones where you crawl through a short dungeon with enemy squads comprised of a single unit. These have no thought in terms of deployment or strategy during the missions and are absolutely the gameplay low point.The concept of controlling the battlefield is an interesting one, with you needing to seize certain locations to get resources- However this needed something more to flesh out the mechanic, since rather than being something to think about, the only downside to seizing them is that it might take your units a bit of time and cost you an S rank, though I can't think of a time it actually did that for me. I feel these needed to either be temporarily available at a bare minimum, or be able to be taken back by the enemies(though this would require more enemies being spawned in over time). Spawning enemies in as the chapter progresses, or something that applies pressure to the player would be ideal in general. Despite there being a whole mechanic where your base can be taken, and your ability to garrison it, including traits that have to do with that, I only ever garrisoned a base for two turns out of every turn I took in the game. Because the enemy doesn't push in on you, with the exception of one map I can think of, there is no need to play defense and you are just pushing forward. At least in my experience, even on the maps you were meant to just hold out, I still wiped all the enemies out as opposed to playing defense. Its a shame because in theory the framework for good defensive missions, or partially defensive missions is here and would add a lot to the gameplay loop. Additionally in general the game needed more unique missions, such as the mission where you have to protect certain fleeing NPC's. _childDocuments_.review: Deep customization and fulfilling tactical battles overshadow a lacking narrative.Symphony of War: the Nephilim Saga is a high fantasy turn-based tactical RPG in which the player controls an army of units as part of a military campaign. Each scenario in the campaign features different objectives for your squad to accomplish, which will require varied tactics and squad compositions, especially for players who are interested in completing optional challenges. In between scenarios, players can customize their squads by recruiting units, equipping them with artifacts, changing their classes, and investing in upgrades through a tech tree.The greatest strength of Symphony of War comes from how deep its customization is. Instead of controlling individual units on the battlefield, Symphony of War puts the player in charge of several squads which are each composed of individual units. Squads will have different strengths and weaknesses depending on the type of units they contain. For example, a squad could be composed entirely of mages in order to shred through highly-armored opposing squads, agile light infantry in order to ambush foes in rough terrain, or a balance of different unit types to allow a squad to be capable in all situations. With over 15 different unit classes and a variety of way to further customize squads through artifacts which improve stats and bestow special effects, there are tons of ways to build squads and customize one's army. The only limitations are one's creativity and tactical prowess.Overall, scenarios are not tactically difficult, but optional objectives and challenges allow players to customize the difficulty of their game. There's also extra settings that can adjust the difficulty of the game, such as permadeath for any of your units that should fall in battle. This makes Symphony of War a great game for both tactical veterans and casual players looking to try out the genre in a stress-free way. The enemy AI is very predictable, which is both a pro and a con; it allows the player to make better tactically-informed decisions by anticipating what opposing forces will do, but it also makes some scenarios stale, especially in the latter half of the game, where enemies play extremely defensively.Narrative is Symphony of War's weakest point. Characters are relatively shallow, as are their relationships. A shoehorned romance system and optional unit conversations add little depth to gameplay and even less to the characters themselves. The plot is generic JRPG-like fare in which a chosen group of heroes must defeat a powerful evil force, and while there are some mildly interesting twists along the way, the cutscenes are overall nuisances that feel like extended loading screens before the next scenario. The artwork, music, and sound design are serviceable, but nothing special.From a gameplay perspective, Symphony of War is a breakthrough in the fantasy turn-based tactical RPG genre and a must-play for any fans of similar games. Its customization options are unrivaled and I had so much fun spending hours in the army management menus customizing my perfect squads, and would highly recommend this to anyone who fantasizes about builds for characters in their RPGs or people who love watching their carefully-designed tactics execute on the battlefield.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic, 8/10 score. The main appeal of playing is to watch your army grow from a ragtag band of peasants to an unstoppable force. Not only your army is progressing, but the entire world is slowly shifting from late medieval weaponry to early firing lines, complete with cannons. There is something very special about blowing up an entire brigade of elite knights with a few cannons.  Another feature I love is the force surrender mechanic. You can demoralize the enemy by surrounding them and picking off their leader, then forcing them to surrender. Later you trade these prisoners for riches. This game has some fantastic highlights but also many aspects to improve. Luckily the good aspects easily outweigh the bad. Things that could be improved are: - Player convenience and quality of life. Force surrender takes too long with all the slow level up popups, menus are clunky, it is hard to get an overview of your army, controls feel weird and unpolished overall. - Class balance. I feel like some classes are massively more powerful than others. Valkyries for example can take damage (including magic damage), they are mobile, they hit like a truck and they can heal. Rangers on the other hand don't do much damage, die quick to any attack and can only fight in certain terrain. - Tactics. There are no tactics in this game, you just send your best squads into the enemy like a wrecking ball. You win or lose in the battle preparation and army organization phase, the actual battle is just a power trip (I don't mind this too much, army organization and power trips are great fun).The game takes inspiration from the Fire Emblem series, and compared to Fire Emblem this game is vastly superior. This is because Symphony of war takes out all the random diceroll nonsense and adds the squad system.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is good if you're into this type of strategy game. First and only play-through on warlord difficulty...that was an absolute struggle, but a good challenge. Wouldn't really recommend it for most players though. Warlord difficulty puts a very strong emphasis on developing elite squads capable of withstanding multiple attacks - the AI in this mode almost always will single out the unit with the lowest threat rating to swarm. Hence, there's a very steep learning curve to learning game mechanics and deciding how to organize/develop your army.Story is decent. Storytelling a less decent - there is a noticeable lack of meaningful dialogue between characters so you don't really connect with any of them. There is a bare bones amount of dialogue to force character development along. I suspect this has to do with the "choose your own adventure" aspect of the game. It seems that the story is more or less pre-determined by the questions asked at the start of the campaign - essentially just asks what type of main character are you (what do you value in a partner...how do you know you lived a good life...). Hence none of the story-lines are particularly meaningful or well-written.Overall...I'd give the game a 7/10.Note: many of my hours were AFK, so I'm unsure of my actual completion time. However, it was a very long campaign to beat on warlord difficulty first try.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing squad building fun with decent combat. 8/10, definitely recommend if you enjoy building your own army.Story exists and links the chapters together. The writing is questionable but somewhat works for the game. 5/10Combat is pretty well done. All of the maps have special objectives and soft turn limits for bonus rewards. Surrender mechanic and unit variety is quite good. Every unit has a place and purpose in the game. 8/10Squad building is excellent. The main draw of this game is how enjoyable it is to set up individual units into squads and manage them. I enjoyed being able to shuffle developed units out of your best squads to build up your other squads (Essentially removes a part of rpgs I dislike which is the power difference between your most used and least used squads: Most of my squads became useful very quickly in this game). The capacity mechanic also plays pretty well with this by encouraging turning highly experienced units into their own squad leaders. I have spent a good chunk of my playtime just messing around with making squads and shifting units around. 10/10 Permadeath (optional) is balanced pretty well and is made fun by the individual unit system. I am usually not a fan of permadeath in rpgs, but it works really well with the unit system here to create an actual feeling of attachment to my units and makes it feels like an army. It opens up goofy playstyles like conscript medic squads or suicidal conscripts to protect a single dps (beatrix + sin credo + vengeance). Donar temples (Revive stations) add an exhilirating feeling to maps as it gives an incentive to retreat your injured squad before it fully dies and can no longer be revived, while also being reminded to consider the turn limit. 9/10The difficulty is great. I have just finished one full playthrough (warlord permadeath), but there are many opportunities to grind in the form of arena tokens (side missions you can grind for money / xp / items). I finished the game with a significant amount of these tokens still remaining so I always had the option of grinding to improve my army if the game became too hard or I lost too many units. Enemy units were generally fairly challenging and fun to fight on this difficulty. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: A top-of-the-line tactical RPG with outstanding depth of customization, a diverse array of interesting classes, excellent sprite graphics, and really, really mediocre writing.Coming from a Fire Emblem background, the squad-based system of combat and all the tactical possibilities it brought to the table was incredible. Each unit on the map is like a mini-JRPG team that you can customize to suit your playstyle. If you prefer a balanced, safe approach you can field an army of typical tank/healer/damage dealer squads. If you're really feeling like a turtle, you can cut the damage dealers, and build an invincible front liner of shielded knights and healers, to draw aggro. Maybe you want to field a squad of all archers, to pick off enemies before they can reach your soft units, or maybe you just want to pretend you're a imperialist power and mow down melee fighters with a battalion of firearm troops. Your options are endless, and the balance of your army as a whole can shift greatly based on the individual squad decisions you make.The unit classes are widely varied, and each endgame class has a scenario where they feel powerful. Firearms units are monsters on offense, especially the cannons. There's nothing more satisfying than getting the drop on a group of soft enemies and blowing them away in one round. Light infantry can also shred tough squads with their ambush attacks, and the game provides enough rough terrain that their mobility feels relevant. Cavalry's excellent mobility and charge attacks make them incredibly useful throughout the game. Mercifully, though, heavy infantry and mages receive a huge power towards the end of their class lines, which means that cavs aren't the absolute most ubiquitous troop type like they often are in these sorts of games. Fliers are also complete monsters, but they require extensive investment and only pop up towards the late game, so you have to work for that power trip. Each class has an excellent set of sprites, and all the unique characters get their own as well. If only they had unique crit animations, I'd feel like I'm playing the old GBA Fire Emblem titles.The writing really let the excellent gameplay down. I can't say it's flat out terrible, but I think the script needed a second pass. There isn't a clear theme to the story. It sort of toys with destiny and fate but it just doesn't have much to say on the matter. Character writing is all over the place. Serious or stoic characters will use modern contractions or slang that hurt their credibility, and the tone of support conversations is sometimes difficult to read. I'm not sure if I'm supposed to read certain characters as flirty, creepy, or overtly hostile to their support partners, and that's a problem when shipping your units is a prominent feature. The story goes to fairly dark extremes, but I struggle to take it seriously when the characters make quips or use anachronistic phrases so often. I also guessed a few plot developments ahead of time, but personally I'd rather a story be predictable than attempt to subvert me every chance it gets. Also, I like the character portraits, but the stern and serious looks most characters have just don't lend themselves to humor or romance, which the game attempts frequently. Overall, this is a very strong game. The customization it allows you is incredible, and each of its unit types feels distinct and powerful. I just wish the writing was as good as the gameplay. If you like SRPGs, this is absolutely something you should pick up.

_childDocuments_.review: How can I explain this in a way that most will understand?This game is simply amazing, but I have to talk about something else to explain why it's amazing.Recently, I was having a conversation about how Gamefreak could've focused less on graphics and more on improving upon the gameplay experience of pokemon. With every generation, they sort of overhaul the engines by upgrading graphics in some way shape or form, which forces them to spend a lot of time rendering new stuff...which takes away time that could be used to simply build upon the game's core mechanics. I digress about this...but Fire Emblem has started down the very same road. Good graphics make for flashy trailers which lead to great sales...but that does little for the game mechanics and how memorable of a game they might make. In the same way that some of the best pokemon games i've played in recent years have NOT come from gamefreak, but from groups of pokemon fans who come together to make romhacks...this game...THIS GAME...is better than every recent Fire Emblem I have played. I love the comparison of pokemon and fire emblem because the core of the game is the same. Acquire new units or creatures to do battle with...strengthen them over time and have fun. But I've been waiting for both franchises to simply enhance that core... the core of battling. And not the small details of...oh we have new abilities and what not... but HOW we battle.The Squad mechanic of this game is absolutely genius. The least realistic thing about Fire emblem is the idea that the games center around war...when sometimes you're just a single unit riding into battle. Or a group of individuals against armies of people. It's ridiculous. THIS GAME though... A thing of beauty with the squads. It is my favorite aspect of this game and it is further enhanced by the leadership mechanic and the mentoring and the traits and the randomness of units you find.My small issues with the game come in the form of what I see as missed opportunities but it's all so refreshing that it's not a big deal. This being the first of its kind (if there are more, please tell me), it can always be built upon. And I do so hope this can be built upon.Also, my larger issues with the game have to do with the genre itself. This style of game tends to revolve around the medieval setting of kings and queens and war...and I think it's limited in ways that more fantastical franchises are not. Think final fantasy for example. One of their more celebrated tactical rpgs is the tactics series which features a slew of monsters that you can fight as well as add to your team in some cases. I think a loot system could expand the game. A game mode that doesn't center around the story is probably my most wanted thing in this genre...Other than that, it's super solid. While I feel inclined to keep referring to it as a fire emblem clone or something along those line...saying such a thing really doesn't do it justice. It really has earned the right to be called by its own name. Like a child of a famous person who worked hard enough to make a name for themselves. Symphony of War takes after Fire Emblem, but it has it's own identity! This game quickly skyrocketed up my favorites list. And I do mean of all time. Again, it could be improved upon in various ways, but it is solid. Has loads of potential.!!!

_childDocuments_.review: I appreciate how hard it is to be a one or two person team and put together a finished product that really reaches the potential you set out in hopes for.This game feels like a successful trial run for a very exciting new series. As it goes and picks up steam, I hope to see a lot of the stock RPG Maker tiles melt away into a fully realized and internally consistent style of its own.The gameplay is good. Backroom strategy games where the action mainly happens in the menu between fights are right up my alley.The music is forgettable, probably mostly royalty free stuff, but more critically, I found a lot of the core sfx unpleasant.The writing is where it really trips up, for my money. The little heart-to-hearts between missions lacked context and felt ham-fisted. The characters were mostly not interesting--effectively placeholders for fantasy tropes. The romance was a weirdly clunky thing tacked on, I'm guessing because people would ask for it if they didn't put something in.The world did not feel realized to me, either. The place to the north is cold and the place to the east is hot.The last thing I want to convey is that the politics were weird as hell. For at least 3/4 of the game, you are supposed to sympathize with the "good guys" (main char and co.), but I don't! They're all insane! They are all obsessed with protecting their culture and securing a future for their children. I don't know if this is a consequence of inexperienced writing or something much more sinister, but I am not squeamish about this stuff and it just kept slapping me in the face.Grievances aside, the gameplay is fun and carries the experience into a positive rating. Hope to see an even better second attempt.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute gem -- I knew I would love this game the moment I saw it, and once I started playing, I simply couldn't put it down.A few comments/suggestions:-- There really should be an 'auto deploy' option at the beginning of each level for those who want to use it instead of always having to manually click through each squad.-- A button to quickly locate the next available squad would be nice.-- Ultrawide support would always be welcome.-- Except for 2-3 achievements, the medium difficulty (Captain) is just too easy and I have never had any trouble with any level whatsoever.  Perhaps Warlord will be more of a challenge -- will find out I guess.-- Due to the incredible customizability of squad and units, the user interface can sometimes feel a bit clumsy to use and takes a while to get used to.  Personally I actually wouldn't mind sacrificing some of the customizability in exchange for a  simpler and cleaner interface.-- I would have preferred the unit progression trees to be narrower but deeper, and here is what I mean.  It is surprisingly easy bring a unit to tier 3, but after that there aren't lots of options.  Towards the later stage of the game the majority of my units (100+) have the 'gold arrow' while there are not nearly enough 'proof of merits' to make them gold.  So I would say either there should be more tiers for each unit type, or it should be harder (and more rewarding) to bring units to tier 3 -- and I wouldn't mind if this means having fewer options when it comes to converting unit types. Anyway, congrats to the dev for such an incredible game -- well done!

_childDocuments_.review: Rating - Harmonic Strategy Symphony (8.5/10)"Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga" weaves JRPG character customization, tactical grid-based strategy, and grand narrative into an engrossing orchestral performance.Gameplay - Complex Conductor (9/10): Symphony of War takes the baton and leads an impressive ensemble of unit customization and strategic command. It's as if Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics formed an army and marched onto a grander battlefield. The depth of squad and army management provides an entrancing core loop that keeps you itching for one more turn.Graphics - Pixel Art Performance (7.5/10): The game's visual offering is a cheerful pixel art canvas that breathes life into your battles and dialogues. Its charm and character might not be AAA spectacle, but it will strike a chord with retro-style enthusiasts.Sound - Melodious Battle Hymns (8/10): The soundtrack sets the tone for every maneuver and clash, enhancing the overall immersion. It might not have the most expansive playlist, but the tracks it does offer hit the right notes.Replayability - Endless Ensemble (9/10): With a wealth of squad composition possibilities, choices in battle, and an upcoming endless training mode, Symphony of War promises countless hours of strategic immersion. The replayability here is as vast as an open symphony hall.Accessibility - Learning the Score (7/10): The game's complexity is as layered as a symphonic masterpiece, but it offers a comprehensive in-game reference manual that serves as your personal conductor guiding you through the performance. It’s a challenge but far from an insurmountable one.Verdict - Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga is an artful blend of strategy JRPG and army management that delivers a refreshing take on the genre. Its depth of gameplay, charming pixel art style, and compelling soundtrack craft an engrossing strategy symphony. For those ready to take the conductor's baton and orchestrate their army in a grand performance of tactical mastery, this game is your stage.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine you are a soul reincarnated in a child with blue hair (yes, I swear). Later, you become a soldier in the service of the empire. Accompanied by your best friend, you embark on a military campaign to rescue the young empress captured by a group of brigands. Seeing that this campaign is bogged down in drinking and inaction, you take the initiative with a small group of soldiers to accelerate the rescue mission. Will you manage to free your empress? Only your bravery and tenacity will see you through this adventure, or maybe not. Will narrative twists save you from the worst possible dangers? Let’s pray for deus ex machina to save us!Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga promises a lot with its store, epic music, old-school JRPG-style pixel art graphics, and the promise of a customizable army that will accompany you throughout your adventure. Heroes, romances, and political intrigues. Unfortunately, this is not the case. You can sense the intent to do well, but perhaps the budget didn’t follow, because everything is subpar: a campaign with a clichéd story whose resolution is obvious from a mile away, poorly written and utterly absurd dialogues, linear and uninteresting romances, caricatured and boring characters. The environments are lifeless and repetitive, with nothing to explore or mysterious to discover. The gameplay is dull and repetitive, with no tactical challenge, and the missions are almost all the same. The only attraction of the game is the army you recruit, nurture, see evolve, and equip with various weapons and enchantments. It grows stronger as your adventure progresses. The game could have been wonderful but is just an empty promise.For those aiming to achieve 100% of the challenges, it seems impossible at first glance, but you realize that the difficulty level doesn’t matter. Just lower it, and it’s a breeze... No challenge or difficulty.Note to the developers: I saw that you are making a second opus. Despite my disappointment with the first, strangely, I believe you have the potential to create a masterpiece. First, recruit a good writer who can craft an original, interesting, and truly epic story. They will create characters with depth and soul, real romances with choices, disappointments, and consequences. You urgently need a skilled dialogue writer as well, because we can no longer stand these nonsensical and absurd dialogues. Please create a real map where we can truly explore with your army’s movements, towns to reach for recruitment, unique units in different regions, secrets to discover, creatures to capture and ride, technologies and items to acquire, heroes to meet. You need to go into detail, make the environment come alive with animations, such as inserting fleeing civilians. Have a system for prisoners who can be recruited or bodies that you keep fresh to resurrect, or, if too late, to zombify... There are plenty of little mechanics that can be implemented to make the game less monotonous. In any case, I am convinced that it is your desire to improve.

_childDocuments_.review: I understand that people are really crying out for an Ogre Battle style squad based tactics game. And yes - this game does scratch that itch in many ways. But I think overwhelmingly positive is really surprising when you consider the story of this game and also some of the annoying mechanics it introduces as the story comes to an end.I'm going to say here I'm not recommending it because I feel like there are too many caveats to that recommendation and I understand that the UI is being updated which reduces some of the annoyance the game has but honestly the story and character interactions need to be completely re-written before I'd recommend it.You're a general tasked with putting down a rebellion against the empire you live in. The slice of the game world you see consists of your empire, a desert east asian themed country to your south east and a tech themed country to your south. You're a new general and your buddy Zelos tells you how to control the game through the first three chapters. You also recruit a guy whose parents adopted him from the desert kingdom and a random lady who is with him. It tells you that you went to Officer school with this guy and yet you have a single dialogue with him in the entire game. This is how almost all the character interactions are. They work a bit like fire emblem where there's a screen you go into and you chat, then it upgrades your relation to them.However, there's basically "friend" or "romancing" and that's it. They're also all story locked, they just happen when you get to that point in the story. I feel like they exist entirely because Fire Emblem has them and for no other purpose and they're extremely arbitrary.They also read like a really old person wrote them, utterly packed with elipsis. Yes we need to...get to the western part of the continent and...defeat the enemies there I...do believe. It makes the dialogue FEEL really slow and it's jarring.The gameplay is very similar to Ogre Battle and classic Fire Emblem. You get hero units and you build a squad around them. There's 50 or so classes set around 8 weirdly gender specific paths as well as the Dragon path. The female healer/mage path, the female heavy fighter path, the male archery/crossbow path, the male heavy fighter path, the male light fighter path, the male spear user path and the male mage path. The named characters mostly do not participate in this and their classes only change with the story. Honestly I dunno why it's so gender specific but you're definitely not having any healers that are men apart from the story one and no archers that are women apart from the story one.It does give you a nice amount of customisation for your units and encourages you to experiment with what you have. Aside from the archers (who can fire a few spaces) I had pretty mixed units and I do like that it encourages this. You do pretty much HAVE to have healers in your teams though which narrows down the options a bit.Valkyrie healers seem to have been recently fixed and they were a standout interesting and fun idea for how I built my units, as well as the variety of different magic users (say a fire user is different to a lightning user) that alter how your units attack.Your unit has a leadership stat and every squad member has a "capacity" tagged to them that denotes how many units you  can fit in your squad. They also have 6 elemental affinities that affect their stats and abilities they come with to differentiate them. Honestly on Captain I didn't really need to pay attention to this side of it. And I'm glad - the UI is a struggle and all the time you're using your squad screen you're fighting with it. Why can't I fit this guy into my squad? Oh I'm below capacity. How much by? Just gotta check 3 menus to see that. I want to change my class so I click on it, but oh no I have to be in the screen for that particular squad to do it. So I back out of that menu, click the squad menu, click the squad, click change class, click the unit, click once to get into the list of new classes, click the class AND THEN click to confirm. Then as many steps out of it to return to where I was. Using items is basically the same too. I honestly have no idea why you can't do it from the first squad organisation screen. It's one of those games where you can easily see very simple changes that would make it work (I'm not saying they're easy to implement, just to see!) and it's frustrating how much messing around you have to do in order to make simple things work. I also found that by around chapter 18 of the 30 most of what I was doing was already set and I was tier 3 classed up with most of my units. I really like promotion stuff so it was a shame I fought so many battles without really having any promotion/etc to do.As the game goes on as well fights become "does the enemy have cannons/assassins and if it does can I attack them first". They're the only squads that are a true threat, suddenly killing a unit in one of your squads. Which is then quite annoying to resurrect. It's not really making the levels harder either, just...annoying.In one chapter a ton of cannons spawn at the base of the map and I had to wipe to them (they're REALLY powerful) then reload and leave a load of guys down there to deal with them which I think is kinda bad, I'm honestly not sure how you'd do that part of the chapter without savescumming.There's also artifacts. This is a colossal list of items that add buffs and boons to your troops. They come in four rarities as well as generic white ones. Again I mostly ignored them, there's some very powerful ones (take a second turn for example!) which I used but most are quite small buffs and I tended to try and use them to increase capacity. With 12 squads, 3 artifact slots each and about 80 artifacts its a bit much though.Again it's an idea I can SEE being good but at the moment it's so much struggle it becomes not worth it.The writing beyond what I mentioned above is strange. There's a lot of really creepy incel style stuff for one - a dialogue that specifically says a character is friendzoned, one where someone falls for another character because he's a "bad boy". The characters have very little agency and just fall in love immediately with whoever hits on them. .Then in the ending it pretty much tells you each character had loads of kids It felt very small c conservative, kinda an older american white guy's view of how a happy ending (or even a romance!) should work out.The world building is strange and kinda all over the place. It establishes the 3 nations and yours as the strongest but at the half way point suddenly the baddy has conquered the other two kingdoms with very little fanfare and it's all one big nation now. The southern one I can't even remember the name of because it just matters so little to the game. This conquest is directly contradicting the difficulty they had stamping out the early rebellion and other things that have happened in the story before. It doesn't quite feel RANDOM, but more like they introduce a thing, that thing is dealt with and has no reprocussions in the story whatsoever. One chapter your character is called an imperialist and goes mad at some regular people, attacking and killing them. It has no fallout, no return to it. It's just a thing that happens and they move on.The whole game's story is a little like that. "Oh I love you." "We'll be together forever" is super common as well. There is one "realistic" romance in the game, two characters that at least have a little bit with each other. All the rest are one and done. There's even a bit where your guy who is adopted turns out to be super important to the place he was adopted from. He's never been there! Although his sister (likewise adopted) has a Japanese accent for some reason.I understand what they're trying to do and I get it's their first game, but right now it definitely needs to be updated to be less weirdly old fashioned writing wise

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game immediately because I'm a fan of the Ogre Battle series. Haven't played much yet, but leaving my thoughts so far:Positives:The gameplay is good. _childDocuments_.review: Symphony of War leaves a very positive impression right off the bat - it's an obvious love letter to games like Fire Emblem and Ogre Battle. Combat plays out on a grid much like Fire Emblem or any other grid based SRPG. Units are comprised of several troops, much like Ogre Battle or Langrisser. Individual troops level up and gain access to promotions for more power. Leaders become capable of commanding more units or equipping more powerful artifacts. Creating strong units of different types and knowing when to leverage them is at the core of the strategy component.After beating the game, my thoughts are largely the same - it's an incredibly fun SRPG with awesome unit mechanics and lots of class diversity. Maps are varied and fun, and have lots of optional objectives to accomplish (some FAR more difficult than others). There is some respectable challenge in many of the later maps, especially on higher difficulties. You can steamroll many maps early on without a handle on the mechanics but later game requires understanding of positioning, terrain and how units interact against each other. While the game has a lot of polish in some areas, others need some work. The dev has stated they are working on a lot of this and given their previous output, the final result will be polished to a shine. All that said, if you have any love for the genre this is a must purchase. Easily one of the most fun SRPG experiences in a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr; Great SRPG. Certainly good enough to pick up the dlc for another play through at the next difficulty level. Thanks Humble Choice!Couple of gripes but the positives first. Took twice as long to finish the campaign as I probably should have because...+++ Really interesting and flexible squad system. If more than half the units in a squad are the same type, you'll get the benefits of using that type which opens up a ton of options. Most walking units can catch a ride with your cavalry, or a few heavy units can sneak around with a light squad and participate in ambushes. There are some exceptions, dragons can't ride allied horses for example.++ Interesting item system. Each is used by your entire squad which exponentially increases possibilities when tinkering with your army. Most seem useful but several have way too much downside or are so niche that when the time comes for them to be applicable you'll forget they exist. (-60 HPs to take 35% less damage from archers and firearms or -50 HPs for +16 magic for example. Maybe if we knew how the damage calculations worked? More on that later)Can spend a few minutes swapping around units and items, trying to squeeze every last bit of strength out of your squads, then look at the clock and realize it's been two hours (or more!).+ Resources are well balanced. You won't feel too stretched, but can't just buy everything. Maybe you have to decide between that unique artifact or high tier mercenary...+ Speaking of which, the unique mercenaries seem well designed. They get an extra skill and feel strong but not overpowered. You may find some that make great squad leaders, if you can afford them. Regular mercenaries can come with good skills and may occasionally be useful.+ Combat animations are quick and interesting enough, never felt a need to turn them off. Watching what's happening can help to devise new strategies and squad formations.+ A redo turn button is always available so you won't be punished for misclicks or major mistakes during battles.+ Comprehensive in game guide covers almost everything, only had to google a few times trying to figure out some nuances.+ I don't play games like this for the story, but it was compelling enough to feel invested in the characters with closure at the end.Some neutral things.Morale system can be a bit finicky. Winning combat means higher morale and more damage on subsequent fights, losing battles has the opposite effect. I set up a heavy spear squad with a few healers to counter enemy cavalry. When several appeared it was their time to shine! Sent them up front and they performed even better than expected. Not a single unit lost while killing several members of each enemy squad. But, their morale kept dropping with every attack. I guess it's the game's way of saying they're tired? After a few attacks they were doing almost no damage because of low morale. The in game guide says "Morale can be hurt via combat defeats" so I'm not really sure what happened. Not a huge deal, was able to mop up the remaining cavalry on my next turn with other units while my still fully alive and healed heavy spearmen were shattered (the lowest morale).Individual units are pretty good about targets in the enemy squad, but if you're not careful with formations and/or which enemy squads you attack, you can do a lot of overkill damage and leave several enemy units untouched. As an example, say you have an entire squad of assassins (probably never would) and the enemy has 3 units on their front line, 2 in the middle, and 1 in the back. Assassins always attack the rear most units on their first offensive turn, so all 9 could target the back line unit (depending on how the middle line is positioned), which would probably be killed by the first attack. The opposite could be true if you had units of the same type that only attacked the front line, and the enemy squad was in reverse. There is a turn order for attacks for each different type of unit so you'd almost have to be trying to create a scenario where you lost a significant amount of damage output, but it could happen. Each unit has an affinity tied to an element which affects their stats (earth gives extra HPs as an example). The system is fine and adds another strategic layer to customization but there are clearly some affinities that are better for certain unit types in most situations. The issue is, when picking up rank one conscripts (most of your army, the little guys who you build up), you can only see one of each type at a time and they each have their own affinity. After hiring one fighter, a new fighter pops up with a random affinity. If you're specifically looking for a fire fighter (not that kind, a fire affinity fighter silly), you may have to roll through several. The issue is, it's always better to save scum.  Don't get the affinity you're looking for? Just reload. Either that or potentially hire dozens of guys you won't use since you can't effectively take them in to the next combat and they'll be out leveled by the new conscripts after the next mission. An option to choose affinity when hiring conscripts (not the mercenaries) would resolve this issue and I don't see how that would be over tuned, since you'll probably be save scumming anyway.If you're in to muscle mommies, let's see... Thick thighs, check, dump truck, check, corset several sizes too small, double check. Interesting that the game can be played with one hand using only a mouse.Couple of gripes - Limited opportunities for combat and experience gains. There are only the main story missions, a few side missions, and arena battles which require tokens. Arena tokens are pretty rare and the result is if you change your mind about squad composition and want to train up some new units, the best way to go about it is trade all your tokens down to bronze (then probably get shot by archers over and over), not ideal. Since experience is almost completely hard capped when your squad is a few levels above the enemy, a "training ground" where you can't get loot, enemy levels are set to bronze arena level and can't surrender would be helpful. Then if you change your mind about some units and want to train others, there's an option. Running platinum arenas would feel much better, maybe even make the tokens untradeable. Would probably make permadeath mode easier but that doesn't seem to be the intended way to play, there's not even an achievement for it. Losing gold units would still be a hit there. (very minor spoiler) --- Every calculation is hidden. This is actually a pretty major issue for this type of game. It's impossible to have any confidence in decisions about skills and gear when you don't know the actual outcome of any of it. Do I go with the +15 skill item on my light ambush squad or is +7 strength better? No way to really have any idea which is ideal since we don't know any of the calculations behind the numbers. It seems the entire system is intentionally left abstract as part of the game design. This works fine on normal difficulty where you can keep it simple with heavy guys up front, a healer or two and a few damage dealers. Both items in the example would have some kind of benefit, it's just not possible to know how much. The damage calculations should be available for those who are interested in maximizing their squads or trying out the hardest difficulty.These weren't deal breakers on normal difficulty, we'll see how the next one up goes.  Maybe potentially bricking a save with an under tuned squad is intended design.  Just picked up the Legends dlc and looked through the new units.  Interesting stuff.  Should have dozens more hours played in the next week or so.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so let's get the obvious part out of the way- yes, this is pretty much "We Have Fire Emblem At Home", There are some differences, but it's obvious what this game's influences are, and that is definitely a strong one. There are additionally some aspects of the game that are simply byproduct of a limited budget and a small team, such as some aspects of VA and character art that are clearly done by well-meaning amateurs rather than experts in their craft. But that's a minor quibble, and honestly I stopped noticing it before long.That said, this game is legitimately one of the most in-depth, engaging, and enjoyable strategy games I've played in the last 10-15 years. The almost 24 hours I've played of this thing are within the last 2.5 days since I bought it. Everything works exceptionally well, and there are design decisions made in this game that improve on the typical point-based, squad-building, massive battle formula in ways I didn't even know I wanted until I had them.Possibly the single most significant one is that units in a squad remain the same points cost they were when they were inserted in the first place. Meaning, a unit that costs 10 points when placed in a squad will always cost 10 points in that squad until removed, even if it is promoted several times and its actual cost has gone up significantly. This not only rewards unit cohesion over many missions, but also serves as an interesting decision creator that forces you to have a clear plan for what you want a squad to evolve into.Oh, and play on the hardest setting. I don't typically like permadeath, but the concept works so well with the writing and mechanics of this game that I actively prefer it to not having it. Nothing about this difficulty setting is unfair or feels significantly unbalanced.Overall, I highly recommend it. I actively look forward to replaying it, and i haven't even finished it yet.

_childDocuments_.review: This game managed to scratch a very particular kind of itch that I didn't even know I had.Symphony of War is a turn-based tactical RPG that feels like a mishmash of elements from Fire Emblem and Ogre Battle. Your big army fights the enemy big army on a big battlefield, taking turns trying to murder each other while taking objectives and resources and what not. Each unit you control is actually a squad of soldiers that auto battles when attacking/defending against an enemy unit, and there are all sorts of different class combinations you can use to round out your squads. Each class has its own distinct advantages and disadvantages: Heavy Infantry are your front-line tanks that protect the rest of the squad but can't do much beyond attacking what's in front of them. Light Infantry deal lots of damage and can ambush enemies, denying them the chance to counter attack, but have low armor. Archers can attack at range, but are highly vulnerable to melee attacks. Cavalry can move -> attack -> move, but are weak to units with spears and polearms. Healers help keep the squad on their feet, but are easily defeated and have no offensive capability. Mages drop fireballs on your enemies, but their spells have a wind-up time and they are very squishy wizards. There are plenty more advanced units you can come by later by unlocking advanced classes like horsebows (archer/cavalry), paladins (heavy infantry/healers), and even dragons (idk, it breathes fire), to name a few. Story characters of course have unique classes that do their own thing as well.Game took me about 40 hours to complete, which honestly feels refreshing when you have a market full of open-world AAA titles that take over 100 hours to get through everything. Story isn't really much to write home about but it was interesting enough to keep me playing. Pretty standard "hey go kill this evil guy doing a rebellion" but the guy actually wasn't evil and it turns out this other evil guy wants to form an evil empire backed by a cult that worships some ancient evil and also the main character is like the reincarnation of Warlord Jesus I guess?TLDR; overall a very solid indie title, absolutely worth dropping 20 bucks on a game that'll keep you busy for a couple of weekends, especially if you like tactical RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Ogre Battle borrowed the best of Fire Emblem and ran with it in the world of Triangle Strategy. Between the satisfying & diverse battles, and the deep character customization, I had a great time. The story is serviceable, and with the hand-drawn portraits even the visuals are a net positive. Really, my only knock on the game is the absolutely insane menu designs, which make the significant amount of army tweaking way more time-consuming and painful than it needs to be.Protip to the developer: when your army can include up to 200 soldiers, every item/trait/artefact decision starts with the item in question, not with the soldier. The question is never "which of these 100 artefacts should I put on Bob?", it's "who should have this new sword I found?". That aside, it's a fantastic game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can really only recommend this game on the fact the gameplay is fairly good as are the visuals.  There are plenty of units and making your own little army is pretty enjoyable with gameplay that ultimately feels similar but different to fire emblem.I can't recommend this game for the story though.  It falls into the same trappings of the rather terrible way Fire Emblem has gone.  You are some magical chosen one and dying really doesn't stop you.  You are also the only person who can save the world and you also get magical powers no one else actually has.  Except this time you have a few other powered up friends and thats about it.  The characters are not great in total and the story loses it on your character for no reason by the end.So more spoilery based bellow about the story.The characters want to say your character is or is turning into a tyrant when you haven't said you want to rule and the main enemy is a cult that actually kidnaps kids and does ritual sacrifices.  And part of your team actually joins this group to fight you.  So ya apparently our character is the bad guy in this situation and evil?  The most evil thing our character does is fly off the handle wanting to kill people who cheered when they were shot dead the first time.  Which to me doesn't sound that unreasonable considering the situation and they were enemy soldiers who you had already killed hundreds if not thousands at that point even when trying to spare people.  The game almost pretends no other army was conscripted until that exact point in the story.The game wants to treat being hot headed as being a tyrant.  It just doesn't make a lot of sense.  I feel like whoever wrote it was trying to make some moral standing and preach to the player but forgot to make our character actually bad because its our character and they can't do that with us still sympathizing.  You could make that argument for Zelos considering all he did by the end but it honestly feels like the game focuses less on the fact he helped kidnap kids and murder untold amount of people for two years than it is about saying your character is a tyrant and bad for being vindictive and traumatized from being executed.Also the game wants to raise the moral question of is it right to force people away from the cult.  Yaknow the cult that is kidnapping kids, doing ritual sacrifices, and trying to return a dark god to the world?  You can't really make that argument with the player when we know what the cult is actually doing.  Sorry that I don't really feel bad for the random towns people who converted to the cultist religion who commits actual atrocities.If they wanted to tell a story where our character was questionably nearly as bad as the villain you have to try a lot harder and have our character do a lot more questionable things.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Ogre Battle then you'll probably like this.  Not nearly as complex, however, it does begin to scratch the itch a little.  The story isn't awesome, but it's not horrible either.  I really hope the developer decides to make another with similar structure.Some things that needs to be improved:- Game is really far too easy.  I played only on normal with permadeath, but even still I blew threw the game with really no problem at all.  I may try again on hard.- UI is pretty terrible.  I realize it was made with RPG maker.  I hope the next can have a more fluid UI.- Better balance between classes.  There are some characters that really don't seem useful.  This is similar to Ogre Battle, however, Ogre battle had just so darn many classes and usually the top tiers all had their purpose.- The game does feel kind of like an experiment.  Some parts of the game seem like they were added just to make use of some RPG Maker options/functions.  For example, the "Side Quest" portion only occurred once and there didn't seem to be any reason not to do them except as a time sink.  I think adding some branches/choices can make a game like this more re-playable and incur more investment from the player.- Better explained battle system.  It appears the battle system has quite a lot of randomness.  This might be ok, however, understanding the rules and choices where they exist vs what is random would be great to know.  I would especially recommend a more structured rules based system like ogre battle had if the standard difficulty were to be raised (which I really think it should be).  Normal mode really did feel way to easy even with permadeath. Some things that would be great for the next- Expanded class system with deeper tiers.  The distance between tier 1 and 2 is small, between 2 and 3 pretty large.  More tiers - Better rules based battle system.- Diverging story that could have a couple of endings, even if they are small adjustments.  I think you have a few things in there that affect ending, but I wouldn't say they are "alternate" endings.  Some things that are already great- I do like the mix of turn based movement with auto-battle. - The conversation/relationship portion was interesting.  I think it is a little too linear and predictable.  A couple more branches and possibilities would make this neat.  Also some potential battle mode options other than moral, perhaps a combo attach or something of that nature.I really hope the time investment vs payoff was worth it and you decide to make another in a series.  Hopefully this has provided enough funding to put some investment into some key areas that Ogre Battle fans really love and capture a niche player base that has gone unfulfilled for a while.  I think a few of the things I mentioned above are a push in that direction.

_childDocuments_.review: Great turn-based rpg. The affinity system is easy to learn but it takes time to get a good enough handle on it to make the strongest units possible. Balancing the resources needed to upgrade units means you need to make meaningful decisions on which of your units you invest in and by extension which heroes you invest in. The way you can mix different damage types and attack orders adds to the puzzle of figuring out how to make a squad that will have the right attack to get through certain enemies, all the while the enemy formations change so different combinations are better at different stages of the game. A deep and fun game that I highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really good. SRPG in the style of Fire Emblem, but one of the few that actually evolves the formula into something better.Disclaimer: I played this with a controller after that proved easier than mouse and keyboard.The squad system adds enormous customization and player choice to the core formula.In similar games you collect dozens of unique soldiers and choose ten or twenty to use and upgrade.  In this game you collect dozens of unique soldiers and combine all of them into ten or twenty units.Individual soldier customization is well done. Soldiers have individual stats that affect their class options.  There are several different class trees with many different end tier classes, and each end tier class offers something unique. There are also many individual traits with wide ranging and interesting effects. Story characters have unique classes and abilities, and the game gives you just enough of these to be interesting without pushing out the non story soldiers you have ranked up.Squad size is determined by the squad leader's leadership stat, which rises as they gain experience. This means instead of each squad being a static size, your starting squad leaders go from 3-4 soldiers to 8-9,  giving that sense of weak beginners developing into powerhouses.While not revolutionary on their own, the game combines various combat mechanics to make it more than just competing stat sticks. Cavalry gets a bonus for moving long distances before attacking. Units on walls get bonuses against attacking ground units. Surrounded units take more damage. Gunpowder units, unlocked later, ignore most armor. Light infantry can ambush enemies in rough terrain.Squad formation matters. Melee units hit the front line first, rogues and assassins can hit the back line, archers can hit everyone. Heavy infantry gives defense bonuses to soldiers behind them.  Mages are slow and only attack once per fight, but their attacks ignore all armor with high AOE.Squad composition also matters. A squad with mostly rogues and assassins will count as light infantry, a squad with mostly mounted knights counts as cavalry, and a squad with mostly dragon riders can fly. In this way you can still use more standard classes (such as a healer or tank) with specialists and not give up the specialist benefits.The devs provided many quality of life utilities. There is a button to vastly speed up the game that works at any time. There are features to let you redo a turn, or save scum, as much or as little as you want. There is a quick save feature that works like a single save state on an emulator. There are also options to quickly restart a mission or return to the preparation screen at any time, instead of making the player mess around with saving and loading different files.Updates continue coming out to improve the game in various ways, often addressing core issues. I was going to criticize this game for its hard mode having automatic permadeath. Since buying the game, new updates let you play any difficulty with or without permadeath. On the day I am writing this, devs released a new update with short and long term roadmap that sounds great and addresses my core criticisms.As a final note here, game length is very solid with a satisfactory number of unique story chapters plus some bonus missions and gladiator fights. Won't spoil the exact number but it holds up in comparison to old classics of the genre.The UI is not all bad, but sometimes it struggles. Specifically, the menus to customize an individual squad can be very clunky or inconvenient. This is a big problem when I spent a large portion of my time in this game customizing squads. If I could ask the devs for one more thing, it would be ways to sort the artifacts menu by squad capacity taken and equipped/unequipped.The game is also hit or miss on how well it conveys information. This occurs in several ways, but the two I will mention here are that it is unclear how most stats affect combat, and you can't determine the outcome of a close fight until it happens. In Fire Emblem there is RNG, but you can determine the exact hit chance, damage, and crit chance of each combatant just by comparing stats. In this sense you are gambling, but you know the exact odds. Not the case for this game at all, instead you just make your best estimate on which side is stronger. The devs seem to realize this, and they actually give each squad a single "threat" value based on its combined stats/abilities. This is better than nothing, but far from perfect.The difficulty. Like I mentioned above, they improved this enormously since I bought the game, with plans for a new super hard iron man mode. While this mostly solves the problem, it is still worth mentioning that the game is easy on normal mode. I steamrolled my first playthrough, smashing every secondary objective and doing it fast enough to earn an S rating on almost every mission except maybe one. There is always a turn recommendation you must meet for an S rating, and I usually came in with many turns to spare just by playing normally.There are some difficulty spikes throughout the campaign, and the overall challenge rose as the game went along. For me it was still too easy on a blind normal mode playthrough, and I would have gotten bored if the squad system and rpg elements hadn't captivated me. In defense of the developers, both the squad system and the recruitment system mean that two players might have armies with very different strength levels, making difficulty impossible to perfect.Since then I started a second playthrough on hard mode (without permadeath), and the game feels much better. I still have the very minor criticism that some of this difficulty comes from giving the player fewer resources to recruit soldiers, instead of just making the fights harder (which they also did).The writing. In some places it is quite solid, or at least smarter and more mature than you will find from others in the genre. In other parts it is clumsy or wooden. The story is not amazing, but it starts out solidly. Unfortunately it runs into pacing issues, and roughly halfway (again at the end) the story takes some wild swings that just don't have the impact they could have had.Related to the writing, the support system. This game heavily streamlines supports, in that they mostly just unlock automatically as the game progresses with no need for extra effort. I prefer this system to the old FE games, but it feels tacked on. There are fewer conversations than you would get for an FE game, and therefore less characterization, humor, romance, etc.  The writing is often very uneven here as well, with some conversations having interesting worldbuilding or tackling mature topics while others are nonsense, or possibly lost in translation.Related to the story, the first half of the game very often gives you story characters to use and upgrade, and then temporarily takes them away. This is not too extreme (arguably with one exception), but there is a relative lack of communication about it.  Once the player figures this out, they feel incentivized to level their generic characters and ignore the story ones. In one situation, I didn't use a story character and their level fell behind. Later they were involved in a sidequest that automatically leveled them up to a certain point, and I was glad I hadn't wasted experience on them previously.Relatively few reinforcements, trigger events, and huge changes halfway through each mission. There is still some of this, and personally I preferred this balance to other games that over rely on it.It's really good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really takes me back to my younger years for sure. I have read a lot of reviews for this game and they are all trying to compare it something. I have played just about every tRPG since Final Fantasy Tactics and Ogre Battle. This game is really more akin to Ogre Battle more than anything.
