_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic turn based strategy game! I Highly recommend this game  10/10 from meShort review:Are you looking for an addictive and creative strategy game??? This is a game for you. "SoW" sets itself apart from other Strategy games with an excellent squad creation tool that lets you form your army as you see fit. Want a cav army to charge enemy armies? Get a squad leader that can ride and form up around him. Lacking mages? turn your horseman into deadly fire, ice, dark and lighting mages to devastate the battlefield. Campaign is fun and puts you into plenty of different scenarios and map types while adding different mechanics to keep it varied and fresh. The game had me thinking through my moves on harder difficulties and I had no problems re tooling my army to face the challenges they encountered if I faced defeat and had to re play a board. I thought for sure I would get tired of it but scouting out the best recruits and molding your squads to be the best killing machines on the battlefield was a blast and I highly recommend it!Long winded review: You spend your times in 2 distinct sections of this game. Half the time and fun comes in building your squads. A 200 unit cap is placed on your army and at the start I thought their was no way you would need that many units. But as the game progresses having a variety of different units always made tuning your army to the next levels challenges much more enjoyable. Most units start out as a basic class and a default set of skills and attributes. As they fight they gain xp and level all par for the course. Now for the fun part when they are ready to get a promotion depending on their skill set they can be 1 or all of the classes granted you have the resources and skills on the soldier to pay for it. Going all the way up to tier 3 and some classes a tier 4. Now lets say you want to make your heavy swordsman into a cavalry unit. You can demote the unit for free!!!! and get back the iron you spend to make a heavy swordsman and then pay a horse resource to promote up to cav. don't like the cav, demote to get the horse back and re spend the iron. The system feels great and once you get a little ways into the campaign you will have enough resources to begin building the army you want! Units have a variety of stats that are tuned to their affinity in game(light or dark for example.) Which after learning the affinities you will get a quick summary of how that unit will level up and will shape up at the higher levels(Light for example will give a unit higher loyalty and leadership stats as they level making them better squad leaders.) As the game progresses new unit types are made available and shake up your compositions. Units can also be effected by weather, time of day and even terrain so take everything into account when choosing new recruits to get the most out of them. To get your army to fighting shape a squad leader needs to be selected(Generally a unit with good leadership skill.) Once your squad leaders start leveling up this skill you can assign more units to the squad up to a maximum of 9 units. These units slot into a 3x3 grid where unit position does matter. Units in the front row facing the enemy can tank for the units in the back, some units can hit the entire row or the column of this grid or other units have area cleave damage and spells focused on different areas. While units like rouges can get into the back lines and do crit attacks on your poor mages, healers and archers. Units can be individually killed off from your or enemy squads. take too many losses and your squads morale will plummet and their combat effectiveness will drop. Units with High morale will get free actions and higher crit chance. Lose a squad leader and the rest of the squad will mourn the loss. Getting them back to a friendly monastery will allow for a revive in mission at a cost of your gold reserve(Unless your playing on Ironman, good luck.) Sometimes the squad leader is best placed in the backline, other times he needs to be on the flanks. The grid allows for some really interesting unit setups. The system takes some getting used to but the end result is well worth the learning curve. I actually felt like I had an army of useful units. I compare this to 3 houses where the mercenaries felt like a clunky add on to single 1 man/woman army killing machines. With "SOW" the entire squad feels awesome to watch attack and achieve its purpose. (Not bashing FEH3 Houses have hundreds of hours and enjoyed that game for different reasons, but its the most popular game that is similar to this game to come out recently that iv'e played in my opinion)Of course the other half is the battlefield, the campaign does a good job of putting your army to the test. New units and mechanics are added every few levels. Weather and terrain is always a consideration and if you can get a good amount of bonus objectives your army will be trucking from the rewards in no time. As units fight near each other some key characters get relationship bonuses like in Fire Emblem units will speak after battle and become friends or more if they fight enough. Items will drop that allow you to fight outside the campaign in an arena to keep your bloodlust going. Earn enough money and you can buy items to equip your squads. Their is a shop that can be found on most levels to spend gold in mission or you can save it for back in the war room. Short on money you can command your troops to attack in different variations(Force surrender for example will have your troops taking prisoners for ransom if the enemy morale is low enough.) Say your troops are going up against a lot of archers you can command your tanky units to fight with caution and less damage will be received during the enemy faze. Later on more squad manipulations are added but I wont spoil what or how its done. You will have to play to find out!End rant.

name: We Are OFK
detailed_description: Pop. Love. Panic! Start a band in this dreamy, musical journey from indiepop cuties OFK . Cry, skate, date, and run for your life in 5 interactive music videos, across a heartfelt story of what you risk to chase your dreams. A Making-of-the-Band Series & Interactive EP Itsumi Saito just moved Downtown and broke up with her long-term girlfriend, leaning into her dream of making it in music. But juggling practice, friends, a brutal commute to the west side, and a full-time job... Itsu is struggling to establish herself in the cutthroat music scene of LA. When she talks her way into a shmoozy Hollywood party and makes friends with a rising music producer, she sees a chance to bring her dreams a little closer. We Are OFK is an interactive tv show of arguing over lyrics, sending sad texts, and playing Interactive Music Videos, including OFK’s debut single “Follow/Unfollow” and more! Features 5 Episodes of the interactive animated series 5 Interactive Music Videos: with debut tracks performed by OFK Fully-voiced interactive dialogue from a star-studded cast Emotional texting, thirst texting, meme texting, emoji spamming Original Los Angeles locations. You're gonna love the boba shop it's wild Full cast of We Are OFK: Ally Maki (Toy Story 4, Dear White People) Syhaya Aviel (Vinyl, The Circle) Fiona Rene (ABC’s Stumptown, I Know What You Did Last Summer) Teddy Dief (We Are OFK creative director) Deedee Magno Hall (Steven Universe) Greg Chun (Squid Game, Judgement series) Erika Ishii (Apex Legends, Deathloop) Yuri Lowenthal (Marvel’s Spider-Man, Bugsnax) Sara Amini (Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart, The Twilight Zone) Kimberly D Brooks (Psychonauts 2) Kaiji Tang (Yakuza: Like a Dragon) Miguel Caballero (Killer 7) Krizia Bajos (Far Cry 6, Gotham Knights)

_childDocuments_.review: I love story-based games, as long as they have an actual story. This game is based entirely on following the lives of the central characters, and they are just awful. They start off pretty privileged - living one of the most expensive cities in the world, employed in jobs relevant to their interests, multiple friends and seemingly no major obstacles in life - and things only get better for them from there. I'm not rooting for things to get better for them, because things are already good. All the 'drama' they actually go through are just minor setbacks that massively overreact to, like contrived misunderstandings or opportunities falling through. Characters' personalities rank from bland to downright unlikable. Drama comes from stakes and there simply are no stakes in this story. Also, most narrative-based video games usually make some marginal attempt to actually justify being told in an interactive medium. Here, the only interactivity is dialogue choices that have no effect on the story whatsoever. This story will play out the same no matter what choice you make. It is entirely arbitrary and just feels so phony.All due respect but when I found out this game was written and made by the voice of the one character who does all the singing, keeps worming his way into every scene even if it's not about him, and has a much flatter performance than the rest of the voice cast (a decent repertoire of television actors), it all started to make sense.

_childDocuments_.review: So, this was a surprise, but not an unwelcome one. I wishlisted the game the second i saw the trailer, so i was kinda aware of what i was getting into. But let me say this outright: This game is not for everyone. If you like gameplay with your game, this is  for you. Why am i still recommending this game? Let me explain...You switch between 3 characters: Itsumi, a young woman going through a tough breakup, Luca, a young man trying to balance his lovelife with his job, and Jey, an (older) woman trying to hide her sexuality from her parents, while simultaneously forming a relationship and perform at her job. Since all characters know each other their stories intertwine and play off each other, while still focus on their unique problems.The Story (or the premise of one that exists at the moment) is really captivating, well told, and well paced. The characters are loveable and their problems relatable, but its the artstyle and the music where the game really shines. The art is very minimalistic, but in a good way. Its hard to describe, but every detail that needs to be there is there, while everything else melds into the background. The music helps to bring the mood across, but in every chapter (so far) there is this one track, kinda like a music video, that totally steals the show.Also, this game is voice acted all the way through by professional voice actors. Even all the different answers you can choose during dialogue are voice acted, so probs for that.This game reminds me of the first season of Life is Strange, in a good way, a game totally focused on the story where gameplay takes a backseat. And I  Life is Strange. However.... Where LiS succeeded, and this game fails, is that LiS had actual gameplay. Here, there is only gameplay during the music videos, and it does  have any impact on the overall story. Same with the 'gameplay' during the rest of the game. You will be able to make decisions in texts or conversations, but they are the typical 'illusion of choice' decisions, that do not matter. I'm not sure why they are even implemented.So far, only the first 2 Episodes (of 5) are playable, so maybe the decisions you make will matter later, but for now they seem entirely pointless.Now, why am i still recommending this game when the only gameplay this game offers is meaningless? Because, when all is said and done, the only question that matters is this: Did I have a good time? And the answer is an easy: ♥♥♥♥ Yes!I love the characters, i love their story, and I totally want to see how it continues. The voice acting is superb, the music (while honestly not my cup of tea) is still good, and the story is well told and interesting. This could easily be a real animated series and i would watch every episode. Give it a chance if you have not already.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the intent behind the project, but man, the execution of this game was so poorly done you just recoil and cringe. As someone who doesn’t play a lot of VNs, this is a game that tries to do more with its story than its capable of in its current form.Unlike many talking simulators, your dialogue choices are of no difference to the story. All that changes is a few words and you’ll get a callback to them in the ensuing conversation a few minutes later, to convey the illusion that the game is dynamic. In reality, you are on a track for a fixed amount of time and no dialogue option makes any difference as to how those 40-60 minutes progress. The only truly “interactive” moments are the music videos where you can do things, but these are limited to the length of the music itself and seem to be there just for show.This project seems like that it was shopped to Netflix (to make something like Bandersnatch), and when it was turned down, it was flipped into a game. I don't see  they (theoretically) would have turned it down - the audio quality and delivery of the voice talent is not lost on me. Neither is the fact that the assets are fairly polished and artistically consistent. If you can forgive the moments that the models literally slide from place to place, it’s not at all hard on the eyes.The premise (being that you’re four people in SoCal trying to get together and make something for yourselves) is something noble, and elements of which I am incredibly familiar with myself. Specifically, getting the project done and distributing it, networking yourself as a creative, and dealing with interpersonal drama via DMs are all things incredibly online people like us can relate to.None of the characters are caricatures or walking stereotypes, which defied my expectations in a good way. However the fact that all the characters have it too good and there are no real issues like housing security or what they actually do for money marginalize the “life” part of “slice of life”. These characters have it easy - and seem out of touch to the Angeleno who might be working two or three jobs just to live in their home and pay the bills. Everyone appears to be solidly employed (even Luca, who ), or in the case of Jey, a creative with a very nice expensive house and home studio that is either being funded by her parents or some incredibly successful career we don't get to notice until now. It doesn't conform to the economic realities of most artists.Further, it drives me nuts that a lot of the story of We Are OFK was changed from the first time it was revealed. Back in 2020 at The Game Awards, viewers were treated to a virtual live performance by Luca and the rest of the band. You never get to perform as a band in We Are OFK, and I think the origin story is great and all - but where is that big performance you are building towards?The fact you can’t change anything about the road you go down is the biggest disappointment though. The game seems to have gotten all the attention it can organically obtain. As I said, it looks like a project that spent a lot of money and ultimately didn't recoup all of it. It could have done a handful of things differently to be more successful. Namely - it needed to be more relatable, needed more options for its characters, and needed to be more of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: The first two episodes of this are hard to watch.It's just hard to relate to or sympathize with a bunch of privileged LA queer artists. I know a lot of people who wish they were where these characters are at their worst moments.After the second episode the series really starts to shine. By the fifth episode they've managed to pull everything together in a mostly satisfying way that leaves you really wanting them to succeed.I feel like this game fell into the writing trap of making their characters unlikable so that they'd have room to grow into better people.This is REALLY annoying at the start. If you get through it, what you get on the other side is a beautiful queer game that's worth the time it takes to play through it. By the end I really wanted things to work out for them so please consider buying this game so that we can get a sequel.Despite the rough start I really hope we hear from Team OFK again soon.

_childDocuments_.review: This one has been on my radar since it was revealed at Summer Game Fest last year. It’s got a bright, poppy art style, some solid tunes, and targeted a niche that I’m generally a fan of. Now that all the episodes are out though, I’m left with just disappointment.We Are OFK is an episodic adventure game centered around a group of friends trying to make a living in Los Angeles as musicians (the absolute classic). Of course, that is not an easy path, so a lot of the story is the little drama that pops up along the way towards this goal - my main complaint there being that a lot of it is just so predictable and not really all that interesting.I will try to keep spoilers to a minimum. The producer character, for example, receives an offer from a big time musician to work full-time for him. Good pay, good benefits, but she will have to leave her friends behind and you bet the game makes the entire following arc about how “big music is soulless” and that it's the indies that truly shine. The bigshots are made out to be absolutely idiotic and even evil at times and the whole time I’m sitting there like - yeah, I could have written this in middle school, especially given how the characters fluctuate between acting that age and acting like adults.I guess that comes with entering adulthood, but it also doesn’t help that the characters here all share very similar personality types - the “let’s go out and get some boba” every day type. As someone that used to live in Los Angeles, it’s actually impressive how overly “quirky” they made the characters here and the dialogue writing often makes it hard to take anything that’s going on seriously despite serious topics being discussed.I started off relatively interested in the story after episode 1 and part of 2, but by the time 3 came around, it just wasn’t cutting it anymore and the following two episodes after that were just outright boring. I couldn’t escape this feeling that this game was made by an indie band that just wanted to get their music out and thought wrapping it up in an interactive movie would be a good approach.Don’t get me wrong, the music absolutely slaps - both the insert songs and the soundtrack - but the rest of the experience pales in comparison. You do get the occasional bit of gameplay, but it’s limited to selecting choices that don’t matter and only change a line of dialogue or two, music videos that are a bit more interactive, but have clunky controls and offer no real reason to even interact with them in the first place, and a story that lasts five hours but feels like very little actually happens during that time.This is the type of game that would have been better off as a 6 or 7/10 Netflix movie or series to digest and forget by next week, but instead it’s that in video game form and feels worse off as a result. I wanted to like this game, especially given the music, the visuals, the overall aesthetic, but it was honestly a struggle.So no, I cannot recommend We Are OFK. It does some things right with regards to its visuals and music, but the story is just not interesting as a video game and the lack of anything else really to elevate it leaves this as an experience best left forgotten.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: OK so first, a disclaimer. I think there are parts of We Are OFK that are a bit annoying. Those characters are very self-centered, and they have problems I could only dream of, and yes, that can be rather jarring - and even drag some people out of the experience altogehter.That being said, it is still a pretty cool experience! If you take it more like a TV show with characters that are more cliches than actual people you're supposed to relate to, that is. The music absolutely rocks, the interactive videos are fun, the voiceover talents make an awesome job breathing life into their digital alter egos, and the writing can be really neat at times (beware though, it's also full of references that non-US natives will have a lot of trouble catching).In the end, I recommend We are OFK, but be warned: if you're not into dreaming about being a LA hipster with no actual struggles in life apart for the drama they bring on themselves, it might not be your jam.

_childDocuments_.review: It plays more like a movie, I wish it was longer but the music slaps, visuals are incredible and all of the characters are just so much fun to watch / listen to chatter.Obvious pros for the incredible representation they have in OFK, as a half Asian, it hit a lot closer to home than I was expecting to with one of the characters ongoing family "drama" on the side. It's not blown out of proportions, but they hit that sweet spot of portraying that "toxic encouragement" (i guess lmao) that I've had to deal with my whole life.TL;DR this game rules and you should sit with some friends and watch it for a movie night.

_childDocuments_.review: Discaimer: I am a friend of the director, Teddy Dief, so while I'll do my best to remain objective, a lot of what makes this game special will rely on subjective appreciation because it is a closely-connected collection of what I feel are very personal tales.  And much like when I share my own, many people will be simply, unable to relate, while many will listen for hours wanting to understand me.This is a game that wants to be noticed and understood, but also asks for your patience as it makes you follow the characters meandering left and right until they find the right words or actions to state their point. I believe this is done intentionally to tell the player that it's ok for people to feel emotions that they can't articulate, because it's often the attempts to do so that's required to understand them fully.I recommend this game to mainly 2 groups of people:- anyone with any kind of creative goals, whether they're personal or professional.- anyone who is curious to take a peek into what life FEELS like for young, creative professionals trying to find happiness in the hip LA scene.  As someone who used to fit that demographic, I can attest to the accuracy of the physical atmosphere and the emotional tones the game conveys in various scenes in which the characters appear.( I have only played the first episode so I will write a full review after a full playthrough. This is also my first time writing a review and I'm learning that it's very hard )

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like We Are OFK. It has beautiful art, a star-studded, diverse cast, and an incredible musical score, yet the story of this visual novel (and it is a VN with minimal, arbitrary choices that have no real impact on the story other than on while voicemail you get at the end) itself is more or less non-existent. We follow a cast of characters who are more or less flat, uninteresting, and pretentious (all except for Debug the holographic cat that is); they're privileged, have little character growth or development, and the stakes and objectives for the characters aren't big enough to move the story along in an interesting way. I think the most interesting point in the narrative was the storyline involving Jey's character arc in chapter 3. Unfortunately, this does come across as more of a vanity project. The majority of the dialogue doesn't add anything of interest either. I appreciate the ambition of wanting to promote and transform an album of songs into a video game (especially considering OFK is virtual and comprised of members intimately involved within the video game space), but despite having so much going for it, the story (or lack thereof) just makes the whole game fall apart. 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: There's not a whole lot of *game* in here. Your interaction is mostly just getting minimal choices in instant messenger text that doesn't really seem to have a lot of impact on anything. It is almost frustrating how little the game needs you to be present for it. But that's the whole thing: It's a short animated film cut with music that every once in a while needs you to click a mouse.But the music is great and the design is wonderful and the hellish depiction of Life In LA for the Youngs is pretty much on-key.  It's seems all entirely too realistic, such that the bowlderized brand names like "Twibber" and "Cinamongram" are jarring.I liked it a lot, but I'd be hard-pressed to recommend it to most people. It's a 6-hour long slice-of-life story about a generation that isn't mine and has both the same problems I had, and also brand new ones.  It is kind of touching, but it asks a lot of down-time from you. I recommend you turn off the time limits on interactions so you can do other things while the show is playing without out.  It's not a bad way to get some laundry folded or something.

_childDocuments_.review: We Are OFK is a musical visual novel following queer millennial musicians just trying to get by. The art for this game is charming and had a vibrant but cozy feel to it. I enjoyed the characters, especially how imperfect and, in some cases, unlikable they were. This is a game about what it means to shoot for your dreams, and it shows the ugly sides of risk-taking and what horrible things people might do on such a journey. I'm not much of a music person, but the game's main focus is its music videos, and these were pretty cool. They sound fresh, and though the interactivity in these music videos is minimal, it was still fun exploring the experience of them. I had fun with this game, even if the achievements are a little frustrating for completionists, and I'd recommend it for those who want a more relaxed experience with a good story, well-rounded characters, and catchy music.

_childDocuments_.review: OFK is a chill, movie-like game. The characters are down to earth and relatable, you can easily empathize with every one of them. Great game to just wind down after a stressful day.
_childDocuments_.name: We Are OFK

_childDocuments_.review: We Are OFK is a interactive animated mini-series presented in a format somewhat akin to a linear visual novel, with choices primarily changing the course of short-term conversations and altering later dialogue by referencing earlier choices you made. Different people will have slightly different experiences as a result, as we gravitate to different options based on our personalities or curiosity. These options come up during both spoken conversation, by default with a 10(?) second timer that can be disabled if you prefer, and during text message sequences (which, as far as I can tell, don't run on a timer even when enabled). As each episode plays, your point of view will shift regularly between one of four characters. The story itself is about these four, notably queer characters- and I mean that with intense love, as a bisexual musician myself- trying to make ends meet and pursue their dreams. Some are looking for love, some fall in love, some have fallen out of love, some are still in love with someone else, some are trying to move on, some simply don't know how. It gets messy. That, on top of each character's personal background struggles, their jobs, the doors that open and close, all wrapped up in Los Angeles while trying to start a band with each other, priorities become difficult to navigate and organize, and people's feelings get hurt when they feel overlooked. It's all too familiar feeling, and the story itself plays all the right notes. None of these characters are perfect- but we absolutely relate to how they feel, and how they react to those feelings.I mean, unless you're a straight cisgender man. Shrug.  Guess I should just speak for myself.The only other interactive element in the game, besides the menus and playback controls, are the interactive music videos, and admittedly, they don't feel very good to "play" as mini-games. My biggest problem with them lies primarily in the controls, which are plenty simple and shouldn't stress even the newest gamer out, but the /feel/ of the controls, in the context of their mini-games, range from straightforward and pretty good (Episode 1) to uncomfortable and awkward (Episode 4). This is unfortunate, because some of We Are OFK's achievements are attached to completing certain tasks in the music videos, and the feel of the controls sometimes works against you. On top of that, those tasks don't really add anything of interest to the experience (sans Episode 5, but the criteria for its achievements appears to be, "happens at random"), but if you're achievement hunting, you are able to replay any of the music videos from the main menu once they've been seen for the first time.Despite my gripes about We Are OFK's music videos, the songs themselves are absolutely fantastic (though admittedly, my distaste in Episode 4's game-play partially transfers to Episode 4's song). Produced in part by one of my favorite music producers and engineers, each song is a variety of pop music, from more upbeat and bright tunes to darker, heavier ones. The soundscape is frankly unreal, and the production is top notch. Much of the score throughout the rest of the game is similarly good, though obviously geared towards complimenting the overall feeling of each scene. My biggest issue audio-wise is that sometimes, the voices are fairly quiet and difficult to hear over the music- a scene in Episode 1 comes to mind- but this issue doesn't get too in the way of the overall experience for me.(That said, I play this game with the music turned down slightly from the default settings. I would recommend it for now.)The only thing I want from We Are OFK, more than anything else, is frankly, more of it. A season two, following a timeskip, would be frankly spectacular. But critically, I actually feel like it needs more... in the actual game as it is right now. The five episode format is very convenient for the EP released alongside its final episode- one episode was released each week at launch- but the pacing, starting with the end of Episode 3, almost feels like there's too much that needs to happen to make it all fit together. There's a significant absence in Episode 4 that is predominantly felt throughout the episode, and we are given very little time to resolve that absence within Episode 5. If it were up to me, I'd try to fit one or two more episodes around Episode 4, and dilute parts of Episode 5 across them, so that things felt less rushed.Maybe a "Director's Cut" would fit the bill here. I dunno! I'm not the director.Anyway. Here's hoping for more We Are OFK sometime. For now, I'll just listen to the band as their new music comes out... whenever that will be. :)

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this experience quite a lot and I think that a lot of people would. The story mostly revolves around creativity and the struggles one finds when trying to express yourself. While I never had much of an issue with that, I was still very immersed into the characters' struggles. And, for some reason, this is the first time I thought about the whole concept of getting heavily into a story without being able to directly relate to it.With a game that's almost entirely focused on character interactions, dialogue can make or break your enjoyment of it - here, I definitely liked it (wouldn't finish a single chapter otherwise). There's instant chemistry between everyone that makes you feel welcome, exposition is smooth enough to make it seem natural and the occasional cringy line works in favor of the story.The music layer of this game is thankfully fantastic - given that the story revolves around forming a band, expectations were high and they were met. Background music perfectly accentuates the scenes it accompanies, the music experiences (?) at the end of each episode are well crafted. I don't think I got as much out of them as a native English speaker would, but I'm still satisfied.Visually, while the game looks simple, it's far from lazy - with minor exceptions, everything is expertly crafted and makes for good-to-gorgeous scenes.Overall, I'm really glad I played this game, bummer that it took me so long to get it.I do have a small addendum though - I don't think this game will hold a significant place in my memory for long, and that's because of the last episode, which fumbled the bag hard, especially compared to the one before (which was stellar!). It is the longest one, but it doesn't use that time wisely. There was no mystery as to where the story was going, so everything is in the execution - it ended up feeling stretched thin through all the little subplots that most characters received, with the finale defying expectations in a really unsatisfying way.Don't get me wrong, even after that last episode my impressions of the game are very positive and I wish that more people played this game - not only because they'd like it too, but I'd like to see another experience from the same studio. But that last episode, for me, turned this game from 'amazing' to 'great' - and there are a lot of 'great' games out there, yet so few 'amazing' ones.

_childDocuments_.review: Now that episode 5 is out, the game is complete. Having finished all 5 episodes, I now feel comfortable reviewing.First and foremost, "game" is a stretch. This is effectively a 5 episode series with some interactive music videos. The story plays out the same way regardless of what you do, most of the choices are nothing more than jokes hinting at the character's inner monologue and how it differs from what they are willing to say out loud. If that's okay with you, great! Just keep this in mind.I really enjoy the characters and the representation of LGBTQ+ diversity. Everyone feels real; they feel like people that had lives before the game began, and it feels like they will live on after its conclusion. I really felt connected to the main cast, even as they go through some bad spots. As for my mention of diversity, these people just exist in the world. They never go out of the way to shove someone's identity or sexuality down your throat, which is IMO, exactly how this should be done; it seeks to normalize rather than shine a spotlight. The music from the titular band OFK is primarily modern pop (what some would describe as bedroom pop), which isn't *everyone's* jam, but I enjoyed it. There's a little bit of deviation between each song, with "Infuriata" in particular standing out. (Although "Fool's Gold" was my favorite)If I had any criticisms to make, it felt like the pacing from episodes 3-5 was a loooot faster than episodes 1 and 2. Each episode focuses on one of the 4 main characters, with the last being a wrap-up that brings them all together. Perhaps another episode between 4-5 could have helped with my perceived pacing issues. Episode 4 features something of a deviation from the norm (characters travelling) which I believe is what adds to this feeling of rapid pacing.Altogether, I really enjoyed it. If you are someone that liked Life is Strange or any similar Western choice/visual novel game, you might like this as well. I hope to see more from OFK in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're thinking about checking out We Are OFK, it's important to understand what you're buying.You're not buying a game, you're buying a season of an online streaming show. This is obviously something new for a platform like Steam, but while I've never owned a Steam game like this before, I hope this is the last one, too. I come here for an interactive experience, and that isn't what We Are OFK provides.We Are OFK is about a group of offbeat friends exploring their musical dreams and forming a group to work on those together. The characters are memorable, and for the most part are pretty relatable. But the whole time you're "playing" you're really just watching an episode of a cartoon, and picking a different option on a different watch will hardly change anything.Was it a good show? Sure, it was a fun show to watch, and I said why. Still, after I finished, I uninstalled it and I plan to leave it that way.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface by saying I wanted so much to love this game - I mean, it literally has everything I love in a video game. It has queer characters, an interesting premise, and a cool stylized art style, although unfortunately it happened to fall flat in a couple different ways.Now, why would I say that AND still recommend it?I played OFK a couple months ago, and it took me until now to organize my thoughts on this. It's hard to say that whether or not I recommend OFK or not. On one hand, I did enjoy the time I DID put into the "game" (more on that later) and I enjoyed most of the characters, even if they all managed to get on my nerves at least once. There was an intriguing narrative that I believe started really strong, but somewhere in episode 3 or 4 is where it really began to fall short for me personally.After that point, character's started to fall flat, and it was becoming very obvious that my choices didn't have any meaning to the story, even though the game does a really good job in making you believe you do. In matter of fact, if OFK was just marketed as a linear story, I would've preferred that much more over the artificial choices we get in game. At the end, it felt really underwhelming as nothing I did thus far had any real impact on the characters or the events of the narrative, which is fine i guess if it works for the narrative but I don't believe it earned it. When the credits were rolling, I was wondering "is this it?" which is never a good sign.There were many things left unresolved for me, and an extra episode (even a short one) could've helped round things out a little more.Now, for the characters.I'm not gonna lie, the only character that I believe behaved realistically like an adult was Carter. I think they were one of the most compelling characters in the game, and their backstory was really interesting to learn about. Other than them, however, it really felt at times that these characters did not act like adults (for me, personally.)And now for the big gripe I had - this was barely a video game. If I had to categorize it, I'd most likely put it closer to a visual novel if anything. The main game loop of OFK is you watch dialogues play out with a couple choices sprinkled in, then near the end of the episode there's a music video that you play along with but that's really it. Think of it like an interactive TV show where it'll prompt you every once in awhile on what one extra line of dialogue you want to hear.That being said, here's what I DO like about the OFK:* queer friend group!!!* Songs were pretty good* Nice stylized graphics* great banter between characters* interesting character designs* each episode was neither too long or too short* each episode focused on a characterSo do I recommend OFK? The closest answer I can give is it depends. If you're looking for something more character driven and queer to settle in with for the weekend, then yeah. If you're looking for a more polished overall experience to sink your teeth into then most likely I wouldn't. But, if it's on sale and you want vibes and low energy outputs, then why not give it a try. Although I do have issues with the game, I did enjoy parts of it enough to still have reasons TO recommend it, which has to account for something.

_childDocuments_.review: We Are OFK is amazing experience of what feels more like being a fly on the wall of peoples lives than playing a visual novel. While I could say a lot about this game, I will choose to keep it brief and mostly spoiler free. Also, EP rating included at the end.I’ll start with a little bit of negative because the positive very much outweighs it. There is a little jank in the movements of the 3D models and some of the animation. Some of the controls in the music videos can also feel rough. Plus I had a few errors during the game where either a line of dialogue would be skipped and the only one the 4 choices were displayed as something like “PLAY SCENE 88, PLAY SCENE 7.9, PLAY SCENE 10, PLAY SCENE 55” while technical errors none of this took away from my enjoyment of the game.With that out of the way We Are OFK is a game about four (sorry Debug) friends that start a band and the events that they went through to the release of their EP. I think that the writing for these characters is fantastic, hooks does a great job at really hooking (no pun intended) the player into the lives of these characters and their stories. I also love that while each episode has one character it shines the spotlight on, the rest of the cast still isn’t forgotten about. By the end of loops, it was fully invested in what felt like four real people’s lives, I think having the option to influence the dialogue works well actually. I like how its less of making a major decision and more of what feels like influencing the tone or way a point is made. Some of my favorite options honestly were where you would pick a dialogue as an internal thought and not what the character says. While at first I thought the whole texting thing was going to be annoying or take away from the story it actually is really satisfying and I think adds a lot to the experience. I loved how sometimes you start texting after a conversation the player never saw and can scroll up to get snippets off, another very great way to make the characters feel real. I think that the casts faults and irrational choices really help to add to this as well, I found myself even more immersed watching them make poor decisions. The following that is blocked out is spoilers  Overall, I’d highly recommend We Are OFK, it is a very fun, relatable, and shockingly real story told in the medium of a visual novel. I can’t wait to see more from the OFK team, fantastic work and thank you for the memories as well as the six new songs for my playlist.Follow/Unfollow (7.3/10):Great opener, sets the vibe perfectly and lets you know what the general theme and journey of the EP is going to be. I really like the production and vocals on this track, making it a dance track with lyrics about being on the brink of happiness or sorrow is perfect. Fool’s Gold (8.8/10):My personal favorite, I love the pace change from the previous song. This also steps the band into showing how they can work with a much slower and sadder song and that they aren’t another indie pop or dance band. Yet again the theming and story telling in the lyrics is fantastic. I just really love how distant feeling that the song creates, honestly, I think it could have ended at the 3:00 mark but I don’t think the repeat of the chorus hurts it in the slightest.Infuriata (6.3/10):My least favorite sadly of the EP, I don’t’ think it’s the production but the vocal fry that bothers me with the track. It has the same effect of any Living Tomb Stone song where after the first 5-7 listens it starts to really grow on you and doesn’t throw you for a loop anymore. Outside of that, this song easily has my favorite theming of the entire EP, hearing “don’t get to say it’s up to me, then hold it all against me” is so powerful, yet again I adore the story in this song. I wouldn’t mind hearing more of these dirty more industrial sounding tracks with the soft vocals on them, it’s a very fun contrast it’s very well done.Footsteps (8.9/10):This rotates with Fool’s Gold as my favorite track on this EP, it’s just so comfy and the opposite vibe of Fool’s Gold IMO. Great story, production, vocals, and story, I’d say this is the best on the EP. Honestly it reminds me a lot of some of the classic 2012 fandom music in the best way possible. thanks, (8.4/10):A wonderful outro track for this EP, don’t think they could have done a better job capturing the feel of the entire EP. I love the message of its okay to not be okay, while some find it cliché, I think it is able to avoid this by adding and complete the arch of the story throughout the entire EP.We Are OFK (7.9/10):A fantastic debut EP that sets up the sound and vibe of the band perfectly. Plus, the range included in a short five tracks really expresses how much range these artists have in their music. Highly recommend even if you don’t play the game at least listening to the EP, if you are planning on playing the game avoid the EP at all costs, the songs hit ten times harder in context to the story. I love how much like the game it feels like it tells an entire story start to finish, makes it feel like skipping a track or listening to them out of order creates chaos. Even with that said all 5 tracks stand very well on their own as individuals.

_childDocuments_.review: It's more than a visual novel, but still not really a game per se. You can do the whole thing in about 5-6 hours. But it's really charming, unapologetically queer, and the characters feel pretty real. Definitely wanted to shake a few of them vigorously, but it makes them all the more real for all their flaws. The story feels rooted in the late 2010s in terms of technology and feel, and the storytelling itself mirrors the time period with a lot of texting as well as face-to-face.The "music videos" portions are okay as far as trying to mesh minigames with the music in an artistic fashion to continue telling the story in a sense, but in a lot of cases the controls were mushy or strange, never explained, and it's mostly just something to do while listening to the cool music? It's a neat experiment, but some chapters were more successful than others, and most of the time I'd say not super successful. But the music was great.Overall a cute, neat experience. Would recommend. A+ for authentically queer storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this on steam and have been "watching" it on my Mac.   Four episodes in it has been flawless technically. The art style is interesting and the music is good.  The characters are unique and different  but are so relentlessly "hip" that it makes me feel really old.  (I am really old) There are seemingly no plain folks in the world of OFK anymore.   Everyone is super fashion conscious, super gender fluid, super into their tech and their music.  As an old dude who grew up the east coast and have lived in multiple states in the east and southwest,  I've never met such a concentrated group of artistic, eccentric tech obsessed people in my life.  Makes it a little hard for me to connect with the characters, but maybe I'm just not the target demographic.   The plot moves a little slowly for me.  Some of the text message interludes seem to not add anything to the plot, but just burn time.    There is a whole lot of character introspection and more than a little negative energy portrayed.    Characters are referred to by multiple nicknames throughout the story, which was hella confusing for the first few episodes.I don't hate it, but I don't love it either.   I find it culturally broadening. Will be happy to watch the last episode.  I hope the story has a good ending.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for the release of this game ever since I first heard about it on Tumblr, and it was definitely worth it! I can tell so much love went into We Are OFK, and I'm constantly blown away by what I've seen from the first two chapters so far! The character designs are amazing! They're all so distinct from one another, but each are so wonderfully attractive in their own way. I'm so weak-kneed for Jey, and then the little "soft dom" comment in the text messages had me dead. ADFLAKSDJF Like, you can't just come for me like that! LMFAO! But I squealed in absolutely delight when I saw her and Itsu kissing in the sound booth, and I can only hope their relationship gets developed more. Beyond the character designs, I also love the environments and backgrounds. It just makes everything feel so alive, and when we get into the music video sequences, I can't help but be awed. And just the music in general?? Omg, it's so lit! So right up my alley in terms of what I like to listen to! I'm looking forward to the story development as we progress toward the remaining chapters. The subject matters we've seen so far deals with what I feel like almost every young adult goes through at some point. There's heartbreak, the uncertainty of change, and just the sense of being stuck in a rut without knowing how to get out of it. With Luca especially, I could empathize with his desire of wanting to create while simultaneously being stuck in an environment that severely limits his ability to do so. Then, there's also the subject of being afraid/not ready to try something new, especially when you don't know how things will turn out in the end. We can sometimes end up sabotaging ourselves by trying to hide it behind different things without facing the real root of the problem. Change, unexpected ones especially, can be scary. That he was able to admit to his faults, apologize to the ones he hurt in the process, and try to move forward gives me hope that I can face my own fears and shortcomings and move on as well. Really loving this game! Can't wait to see more!

_childDocuments_.review: For narrative choices and gameplay to be meaningful, they don't have to be grand story-altering decisions.  They can be moments that put you in a character's shoes, and let you explore how they think.  They can be moments that ask you to express yourself, and force you to put yourself out there creatively just a little.  "We Are OFK" is a game about these moments, about the joys and terror of creativity, but mostly about empathizing with multifaceted and flawed and charming people as they try to find a way past personal uncertainties and make something authentic.  It's a vacation to a Los Angeles where everything is the color of sunset and everyone works in the arts, with graphics and audio polished to a pop-perfect sheen.  You can play it with friends, or on substances, or alone wishing you had an overpriced boba to clutch as a talisman against your own crushing uncertainties.  All OFK asks is that you chill and enjoy the story for a few hours.  It wants to introduce you to some people who might seem intimidatingly cool at first, but I think you'll like them once you get to know them.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been very hyped for this game, and aside from the teaser trailer went in totally blind. This is a beautiful game, clearly lovingly crafted with some FIRE music and really deep characters. I love getting to learn about these characters, see how they deal with their screw ups and messy lives and am excited to see how their story continues. (edit: the final chapters are out and I LOVED IT this game is *chefs kiss*)I was a little disappointed that there is not much of "gameplay" so to speak, but i think that may be on me for going in to the game without understanding that its a visual novel with some interactive bits. As a whole it feels like your just experiencing a linear story and your choices don't really matter. The interactive bits are a way to keep you engaged in the story. This isnt a bad thing, just something to note. i'd definitely recommend this game. 10/10 great story, music, art, everything. <3
_childDocuments_.name: We Are OFK

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this ever since the Palm Tree Project days, and was stoked to get in there and play the game as soon as possible. I finished the first ep, "Hooks", and well, this is one of those rare games that made me laugh, cry and actually have me feel SOMETHING after so long. It wasn't a chore unlike most games I play these days (am a gamedev myself, and it becomes a chore as you play more and more stuff.) and man, I don't think I have the emotional energy to go on to the next one at 1 AM at the time of typing this review.OFK is amazing, absolutely brilliant, and the characters are so darn fleshed out. The experience is definitely a lot better if you've worked in the game industry, and GOSH do I relate with Luca and his whole thing with Leviathan games, and the Hyperlight Drifter reference jump-cut got a chuckle out of me, only to be followed with the whole party/networking creeps and likeI'm just,, a bundle of emotions right now, and this game hits home, especially hits home. This is also the first time I've bought a game on day one! :DLove y'allxoxo ~Ashe
_childDocuments_.name: We Are OFK

_childDocuments_.review:
Itsumi Saito just moved Downtown and broke up with her long-term girlfriend, leaning into her dream of making it in music. But juggling practice, friends, a brutal commute to the west side, and a full-time job... Itsu is struggling to establish herself in the cutthroat music scene of LA. When she talks her way into a shmoozy Hollywood party and makes friends with a rising music producer, she sees a chance to bring her dreams a little closer.

We Are OFK is an interactive narrative series of arguing over lyrics, sending sad texts, and playing Interactive Music Videos, including OFK's debut single "Follow/Unfollow" and more!

name: Venba
detailed_description: Venba is a narrative cooking game about family, love, and loss. Play as Venba, a South Indian immigrant mother connecting with her son through the language of food. It is a short and sweet cinematic experience that you can enjoy in a 1 to 2-hour sitting. Cook (and learn!) authentic dishes from regional South Indian cuisine Idlis, dosas, and biriyani! Whether you’re a new or regular enjoyer of South Indian cuisine, there’s something delectable to discover Venba's cooking puzzles. As you piece together a tattered recipe book, cook authentic dishes inspired by real-life cuisines. Once you've cooked them in-game, try cooking them in real life with the brand-new in-game Cookbook! Discover a heartfelt story of family, love, and loss As you restore lost recipes, discover the story of a family over the years as they grow and change through a journey of love and loss. Join a mother, father, and their son as they reckon with culture, self-discovery, and acceptance. Jam to catchy tunes inspired by Tamil music Move over lo-fi beats! Cook along to Venba's unique original soundtrack, inspired by Tamil music throughout the ages. And when you can't get enough, return to the newly-added in-game radio to listen to the OST on-demand! Feast your eyes on delicious visuals Venba's warm, stylized art brings the game's food and story to life! So good you can almost taste it.

short_description: Venba is a short narrative cooking game, where you play as an Indian mom who immigrates to Canada with her family in the 1980s. Cook various dishes and restore lost recipes, hold branching conversations, and explore South Indian food in this story about family, love, and loss.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, absolutely wonderful story! I enjoyed every minute of it! If I had just one small critique, it's that I wish there were more actual cooking parts to it - the story was more visual novel than cooking game (which could've also just been my misconception when getting into the game). But I absolutely enjoyed all of the little information bits incorporated with the cooking - learning about different cuisines and different cultures. I would definitely recommend this to all of my friends! ^-^
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't expecting feelings in my cooking game! Venba made me cry more than once, and while my own experience doesn't come close to that of an immigrant family, certain aspects definitely resonated with me. Absolutely beautiful writing, so much weight and thought condensed in an hour-long experience.Some of the recipes I will definitely try to make myself. 10/10 sound design, those sizzling spices and chilies made my mouth water! Maybe I won't make rice flour from scratch, but a few of them seemed very doable. Now, brb - going to the Tamil restaurant around the corner to sate a powerful dosa craving.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a lovely little game that delivers big on emotion and nostalgia in a very small package. This is definitely a good choice for a casual gamer who likes good storytelling but doesn't have a ton of time to invest. I really enjoyed the background of the characters, the soundtrack, and the story, and also the cooking minigames (for the most part). I will say that I was disappointed the dialogue choices don't seem to make any difference and some of the minigames aren't really games at all - just click what they tell you to click - but overall this was a heartwarming ~90 minute playthrough. I do think there's a minimal amount of replay value, but that did not take away from my enjoyment and I'll definitely be playing again at the very least to master all the recipes :)
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I have never cried my eyes out over a video game quite like this. As a Canadian child to a family with immigrants, nothing has ever so specifically targeted the my deep regret that I never had the chance to learn how to make traditional (in my case Filipino) dishes from my grandmother. Thank you to everyone at Visai Games for making this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game just expecting a fun challenge of figuring out the missing steps in the recipes, I got that along with many tears. The game play itself is very fun and I am inspired to try and make all of these recipes myself and to discover even more recipes to try, but honestly my favourite part of this game is the story telling. It is a beautiful story of a mother trying to keep her culture alive in a new country while her son is rejecting it, and ends with the son understanding why she wanted him to connect with their culture and starting to fully embrace what he was hiding from. This game will make you cry and it is worth every penny spent
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a really touching, yet bittersweet, story about the lives of foreigners living in canada and raising a son. It touches on a lot of raw emotions and really goes down to the feeling of losing a culture you had in favor of trying to fit in. At an hour and a half it can be beaten in an afternoon and that's honestly the best length for a game like this.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased Venba quite a while ago. I’ve also played it once but quit at the first cooking section, which was the very first section of the game, because I thought I had to memorize and work hard in order to progress into the story. For a story I don’t even know what it was going to be about. This notion was built due to the games I played at the time. They all had the nature of demanding your focus and hard work. They all had the tendency of failing you for good, once you mess up. I was set on refunding the game then but it had already been two weeks since purchase so I couldn’t, and I am GLAD I got to keep this game.  Venba is a story-driven game. If you mess up a dish, you simply start over right then and there automatically like nothing happened. So there’s no pressure. Just sit back, relax, and immerse yourself into the story. It is a beautiful story. 😄

_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a beautiful game with a beautiful story. Playing through each level and discovering the recipes is fun and heartwarming. As the child of immigrants myself, I related so much to the struggle of maintaining your culture while trying to conform to your environment. The story hits home in a lot of ways and I think players really feel the impact of it.Yes, the game is on the shorter side, but it makes every moment count. I loved this game and there were times I got a little teary playing. I had a lot of fun going through the dishes and really appreciated the care it must have taken to select each recipe. So much love is shown through food and this game demonstrates that perfectly.

_childDocuments_.review: i would say something like “i wish it were longer” but im gonna be real: i want more short games made by people who are paid more to work less and im not kidding!!!!!!!!!!!anyways, the actual reviewVenba is a gorgeous game. Narratively, visually, and aurally. The story will tug at your heart (especially hard if you’re an immigrant/child of immigrants), the art style and attention to detail is beautiful, the music is a fun blend of traditional and modern, as well as referencing iconic Tamil artists from each era the game spans (), and the sound design. Oh the sounds!!! The sizzles make my stomach growl. That’s another “downside” to this game: you WILL viciously crave Indian food at some point while playing. If only smell-o-vision worked with games…The gameplay is simple: click and drag with an occasional spin of the mouse. The recipes are vaguely given, and you’re left to experiment or use logic to fill in the blanks (literally). I found myself thinking about what would make sense if I was cooking the dish myself, (not that I have experience with Indian cooking… lol) and things are followed sensibly. If you do get stumped though, there’s a subtle and narrative-appropriate hint system you can employ.Some spoiler-y details I adore:1. 2. Overall, Venba is a beautiful, sweet, and heartstring-tugging game. I’ve been following development for a while, and I’m so excited to see more perspectives and narratives from South Asia. This game is deeply emotional, and I feel like no matter how professionally I write this review, my words will fall short of describing the love put into every aspect of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba beautifully illustrates the ideas of family, culture, identity, grief, and love. Each character has so much depth with their own quirks and the family dynamic brings so much life beyond merely "a short narrative cooking game." I would consider this game a life-changing, or at the very least, perspective-changing experience. While I personally cannot relate to the immigrant experience, it made me heavily evaluate my identity as a daughter and my potential future identity as a mother myself. This game has so much heart and soul and it was felt in every corner of the short time we spent together, down to the finest details of objects in the background or smudged dialogue boxes. I completed two full playthroughs in order to experience all of the dialogue options, then went back to a couple of chapters individually to get every achievement. This game deserves to be played at least twice all the way through because the dual perspectives of each dialogue option paints such a vivid picture of the characters and their lives. The art style is stunning, the food made my mouth water, and the soundtrack is incredible. Everything about this game is magical and I am so glad I experienced it. Highly, highly recommend to anyone interested; worth every second and every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game taps into something special. Family, culture, and food are the mainstays that guide you through the moving story. _childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This wonderful little game is dedicated to every immigrant or child of an immigrant who has had to grow up with the culture shock of moving across the world to have a better life in a first-world country.What I really appreciate about Venba is that they manage to nail the tension that always manages to form between immigrants and kids of immigrants without simply tilting in bias toward either of the parties, because, after all, that is how reality is, both sides are right and wrong in different aspects (I should know).The game is quite short, but it gets its story across quite well during the playtime. There's also some charming art, good recipes and nice music to boot.Definitely worth picking up if you are looking for something heartfelt and different.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a beautifully crafted story that will resonate with a lot of 1st, 2nd and even 3rd generation immigrants in a time where migration is so common and at times necessary. It tells a story of a Tamil couple that have migrated to Canada for a better standard of living with more job opportunities for themselves as well as a prospective future for their child. We encounter financial, social and familial struggle through these characters at varying degrees as the perspective slowly shifts from the 1st generation into the 2nd, but it is ultimately their culture that brings them together and allows them to move forward (This being shown in the form of the recipes that you cook). The gameplay itself is very straight-forward as the controls are simple, with a bit of intuition required as you have to decipher recipes that are half-there and half-not. The graphics are beautifully colourful with a cartoon touch, that feels very welcoming and comforting, whilst you have cultural music playing softly amidst the cooking. Reading some of the other reviews, the game apparently also exposes you to some very real recipes that you can re-create at home, which again adds that personal touch especially to those that are Tamil and playing this game. Overall, the story's length is about and hour and half, so this is a game that can easily be finished within one sitting and the achievements do encourage some replayability if that's something that you care about. It really is a touching story, that might even open up your own eyes if you are in the same shoes as the characters, as it touches on issues that hit quite close to home. Definitely recommend! :)
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: As a westerner with a huge appreciation for Indian culture, especially in South India, Venba was a wonderful game I am glad to have come by. I did not even know that a Indian-themed cooking game even existed. However, upon discovering this game I had to buy and play it to show my support since not many games focused on South Asian culture even exist.What makes this game particularly unique is not even that fact that it is focused on the culture, but that is specifically focused on it in a contemporary context and in the western world. Although Venba's story is fictional, I can say from my experience hearing sentiments from various individuals of the Desi commmunity that these are in fact real issues that many South Asians living in the west face. With that being said, the game does not shy away from depicting issues like internalized racism and discrimination, but it does it in a way that is genuine and relevant to the plot. It shows that these more politically/socially charged issues CAN be put in media in a way that actually adds to the narrative and is thought provoking. Overall, it is a well written story guaranteed to touch everyone, regardless of the community you come from.Although the game may be short for the price, it is definitely a situation of quality over quantity. Too many games are bloated with filler and/or just overstay their welcome. I can conclusively say, however, that all the content Venba has to offer feels put together with thought and care. That alone makes this game worth every penny.I want to see more games of this sort, showing off the rich culture that not just India, but all of South Asia has to offer. So if the game interests you in the slightest, I definitely urge you to just go ahead and purchase it; you definitely won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a great storydriven experience. It is important to note that this game is closer to an experience than a game. The gameplay barely exists. But this is not a bad thing as the game tells a great story. A story of cultural differences and what kind of an impact it can have on a family. The story had me interested from start to finish. When I started I imagined the game to be a sort of cooking mama but Indian style. Boy was I wrong. I got a sad, emotional story that I couldnt stop. I can only recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a such a love letter. It's not long; maybe 2 hours tops (if you take your time jamming out to the awesome music). Game play includes some dialogue choices, and an incredibly cute and easy-going cooking sessions. There's sometimes a bit of "logic-ing" out the recipes, but it's not difficult at all, and adds to the richness of this story. I highly recommend this to anyone that enjoys food, good music, and short tales with massive heart. And, I can't wait to make some of these recipes at home!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a beautiful game with a lovely story. I really related to it because my parents immigrated to North America and had me here. It definitely made me reflect on how I have treated my parents over the years up to now. It's such a wonderful touching story that really made me cry and want to build a better relationship with my parents because as we get older we will have less and less time to spend with them to learn about each other and learn about our cultural roots.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I was not prepared to tear up on New Year's Day after trying this! I lost my mom when I was young, and her love language was food (as is mine), so I knew I had to try this as soon as I heard about it. As the child of parents who immigrated to Canada as well, this was a poignant and touchingly relatable story to immerse myself in. I adored getting multiple perspectives in the same story. The music, art style and gameplay are all perfect for what this game wanted to accomplish. It is a game, but it's one you experience more than you play. I loved every minute of it and will be playing it again.Thanks to the Finest Indie Games Showcase 2023 for helping me discover this gem. I'm going to go make some food for my family now!

_childDocuments_.review: A short yet profoundly touching story that resonates deeply. No bugs or anything like that.Cons:- The game is a little short, maybe too short. _childDocuments_.review: Venba was a long-awaited game on my list, and I'm happy to say that it did not disappoint! The story, music, and food come together to create a wholesome experience that makes for a beautiful tribute to the Tamil, Indian, and South Asian culture that this game pays homage to. It was a refreshing breath of air to see the South Asian immigrant story—both its wonders, and struggles—be realistically and accurately told, with all of its nuance. As a South Asian myself, there were multiple parts of the game where I would stop and reflect on how relatable the situations were. I was even able to discuss some of these topics with my non-desi friend who watched me play. All-in-all a very beautiful game, and a very heartwarming experience! The game took me exactly 100 minutes to complete. Also, the Tamil bops here are 10/10, big kudos to Alpha Something.
