_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  is done and dusted. This is a short and fulfilling experience filled to the brim with feels and stacked with real life and tasty looking recipes that I intend to make as I acquire the necessary ingredients. I think the product description actually summarizes this game perfectly. I think where I want to start is with the story. You mostly play as Venba, the mom who the game is named after. You attempt to navigate living somewhere where you are viewed as an outsider by really focusing on family and raising your son. And to that end, you also focus on cooking the foods your own mother would make for you, and whose cookbook you are in possession of. The cookbook is old and beaten up, with text missing and such. So, as you dive into these recipes, you attempt to sort out what is missing in order to make these dishes you so loved when you were growing up. And in so doing, you hope this food will be something you, your husband, and your son can really identify with as something tangible that keeps you together as a family.Unfortunately, your son,  feels like an outsider in Canada when embracing his heritage and the family atmosphere you and your husband have built, and you watch as Kavin bit by bit pulls away from and ignores his heritage in order to be accepted by the mostly non-Indian people living in the area. Which leads to a growing disconnect between Kavin and his parents, something that the game does an amazing job of conveying in a way that really makes you, the player, share in Venba's sadness. Eventually, Kavin does realize the folly of trying to be somebody he is not, which leads to a heartwarming moment as well.Obviously, food is central to the theme of cultural identity and family in this game, and cooking these foods is presented in the form of cooking puzzles. Once you have finished a dish, it basically moves the story forward. And the recipes are all offered in a separate section of the menu, presented in great detail with the actual ingredients, amounts, the process of preparation, and the finished product. Very well written and easy to follow instructions really.The graphics are not the thing emphasized in this game, and they aren't going to wow you, but they are pretty and appropriate to the experience. And some of the finished recipes do look pretty mouthwatering. Additionally, while somewhat minimalistic, the artwork does do an exceptional job of conveying emotions. The audio features several cool songs which you can also revisit in the menu independent of playing the game, via an old school dial radio, which was cool.I think this is a fantastic game that hits you in the feels several times and really keeps you engaged throughout. And despite weighing in at under two hours, I think the experience plus the addition of all those wonderful real-life recipes makes this a game that definitely earns its $14.99 asking price. The messaging about being yourself regardless of peer pressure, of embracing family, and the simple act of making tasty food makes this a must play. This is a case of quality over quantity in my opinion. I highly recommend giving this game a look.

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is not a long game, nor is it really one you revisit, but it powerfully brings you through feelings and situations that some of us may not experience in a lifetime. The art style, music and foley work that were selected for the game truly help to create an immersive, authentic experience for the player. I gained a lot more than I paid for with this title. I've been excited for a full release since I played the demo, and this lives well up to (what I imagine) the developers wanted. _childDocuments_.review: The story is genuine, the art is pretty, the soundtrack is great.However, at a certain point, the cooking mechanics became purely following instructions to click on stuff, unlike the beginning of the game where you needed to solve some (very easy) puzzles to find the right order to do things. I know this game is not supposed to be a challenge or require a lot of input from the player, but compared to the puzzles at the start of the game which made you feel clever for figuring out how to cook a recipe as well as engaged for learning about the dish itself, the ones toward the end just felt like you are checking things off a list. It's very sad that this starts happening just as the plot reaches a nice resolution.Overall, it is still enjoyable as a piece of interactive fiction, but it definitely starts stronger than it finishes.

_childDocuments_.review: Veba deeply touched me. It's a narrative cooking game about an Indian immigrant mother in Canada, and the story's emotional impact goes beyond the kitchen. While I haven't experienced immigration myself, Veba's tale made me consider the struggles faced by immigrants, even within their families.The game beautifully portrays how Venba expresses her love through cooking. I loved the cooking aspect – the recipes offered a delightful puzzle-like challenge without being overly frustrating. The hint system was also a great touch, and I learned so much about different spices and recipes.My only wish is that the game were longer. I would have loved to delve deeper into Venba's story with her son and witness his journey of embracing his cultural heritage. Seeing the game from his perspective as a second-generation immigrant would have been fascinating.Overall, Veba is an enjoyable game, but due to its short playtime (around two hours), I recommend waiting for a sale before purchasing.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: The colours and art style jumped out to me immediately! I love the gritty texture the art style creates and how vibrant all the food looks! I loved seeing all the food drawn in this style. The soundtrack was just as bright and fun as the colours and worked perfectly within each setting. I found these elements a big factor in making Indian culture palatable to a wider audience.  The way they handled the struggles of immigration were very well-done and mature and unfortunately depict the life many immigrants start out with. This is especially relatable to many people in North America, especially older immigrants who were provided with less assistance during the 80s. The role of food throughout the game really highlighted the shared solace over something so simple. Here, food was a plot device that exposed not only culture, but the ups and down many immigrant parents and children face when it comes to what they eat. The story was amazing and encompasses the ability to be relatable to a wide breadth of people. Venba is a fun and beautiful game with many realistic life lessons. I truly enjoyed playing this game and learning a little bit more about Indian culture through food.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great short narrative game about immigration, South Indian culture, and the problems of moving to a new country. It's very heartfelt and very touching. _childDocuments_.review: Okay, so basically, yesterday I wanted to play a story based game. I wanted cute graphics, cozy gameplay and all that, but most importantly- I wanted an emotional story that felt real, something that seemed to have a lot of thought and lived experience behind it, and so I went searching for cozy story-based indie games on YouTube and thats how I found Venba. I started it today, finished it within an hour and a half. And I can tell you, it was exactly what I was looking for! The story felt soo real. It was so good, and really sad. Actually, even tho it was a sad story, it didnt feel sad while I was playing it, which I think comes from the genuine joy I felt cooking all these amazing authentic Indian dishes. Every sad moment had a certain food attached to it. I think it shows how food, and her culture helped the mother (Venba) to deal with all these various difficult (and usually sad) emotions. This game tells a story of the challenges faced by an immigrant Tamil family; a wife, a husband and their kid living in Canada as they try to live by in a country where they dont even speak the language fluently, and of course, of the ones that usually come up when talking about 1st gen immigrants and their children. It's really not that crazy of a story, its simple but it's really beautiful. I highly recommend it to anyone interested in the things I was when I went searching for this game. Just sit down, relax and enjoy an emotional, heart felt experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a story about the difficulties of leaving your country for another and seeing your children growing up in a very different way than you did.It's a cooking game, but at the same time, the food is only here to represent the duality of the characters life. Indian parents giving bith to a son in Canada, the son can adapt better than his parent and how the whole story goes back in circle.A very interesting albeit short game, I fondly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game has never made me feel so seen in my life. The "child of an immigrant" story is told pretty often though it feels like it may overlook some parts of the experience, This game somehow hits all the stops in the best (and worst) ways. Parts of the child's experience rang so true to my childhood, fighting with my identity as someone who wanted to be true to being an Indian-American but also didn't want to be... too Indian. It gave me so much more perspective on the parts of my life where I thought my parents were being difficult, but they were just.. doing what they knew. This was easily one of the most beautiful games I've ever seen. The recipes are flawless (honestly, try them! the steps are pretty much all correct) and so true to South Indian cooking - a part of Indian food that typically gets overlooked for it's more famous cousins.I started playing this at 1 AM and I wrapped up just around 2 AM. In that hour, I've cried upwards of 10 times and drafted close to 20 texts to my parents telling them how much I love them and how I'm so excited to keep learning from them. I didn't think I could respect them and really see them more, but this game probably single-handedly changed my relationship with them for the better.Thank you.. so much. Vanakkam. ❤️

_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: a short but incredibly sweet game about being an immigrant, tamil culture, alienation, and cooking. i truly cannot recommend it enough, it made me cry a LOT and i will be making my roommate play it some time soon. i myself am a second generation immigrant, but a polish one. this game still managed to hit really close to home for me in a lot of ways, and i've never been prouder to be a fluent speaker, reader, and writer of both my language and english
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: i have loved cooking games ever since i was little so when i saw and heard about this game, i was so excited and counted down the days for its release. i love the art style, the music, the story/message. It was fun to make food I've never made before and I like that for each recipe there is a trial and error aspect to it. why DONT i reccomend this game? For $15 and only 1 to 1.5 hours of gameplay... i dont think its worth. am i glad i tried it out? yeah. do i think people should spend $15 on it?... meh. if there were more recipes, more "levels" it would definitely be worth. also keep in mind that 60-70% of the game is the story itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: It's a short game, only taking 1 to 2 hours to beat it depending on your reading speed.This is 100% to its benefit in my opinion. The game tells its story, and that story is so genuine, so real, and so wonderful. It felt like someone who had actually grown up as an immigrant or an immigrant's child wrote this game.The soundtrack is wonderful.Absolutely astounding, please play this.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: It is a really wholesome game, focusing on mainly the story not the mechanics. The cooking mini games are fun and I think my biggest complaint is my biggest compliment also: that I couldn't get enough of it! It's a really short game but full of flavour. I'm really curious about the dishes shown, would have loved it if it had some recipes available from the menu, but I will look them up myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: The amount of warmth and heart and heartbreak in this game, left me in literal tears. A wonderful journey that hits really close to home, for me. Thank you to the team for sharing this beautiful slice of culture, of life, of hearts, of love, of loss. The graphics, the sound design, the story...everything coexisted together. Beautiful experience, thank you. ♥
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A short and sweet review for a short and sweet game.  Venba touches on the difficulties of immigrating and raising a child in a new country, while trying to keep your culture present in your life.  This short narrative is broken up into sections punctuated by Tamil recipes (and the sort of cooking minigames that go with them).  The art is beautiful, colorful and textured and so pleasing to look at.  The recipes are so fun to do (my only complaint about Venba is that I wish there were MORE recipes!), the story is compelling and touching, and the soundtrack is an absolute banger (seriously, I added it to my wishlist after playing, it's so good!).It is short - I beat it at an hour and a half, and spent another hour or so getting to 100% achievements.  At full price of 14.99 that might make some people pause, but I personally feel that the price tag on this one was worth the experience and I highly recommend this game at full price or a discount.I loved Venba, I think you will too - just prepare to be hungry after playing!If you liked my review and want to see more from me, check out my curator page at
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Very short game but with a very personal story.This is a touching story about a family of immigrants with all the hardships that comes with it,  A LOT OF THEM.There isn't anything supernatural or a villain for that matter, just a family trying to be accepted while trying to accept the new.Can't lie that the game is incredibly short, but the story is incredible and the gameplay conveys a lot of the problem of communication between generations and cultures.Wait for sale if anything but a good experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a brief gaming experience, wrapping up in less than 2 hours, but offers you a glimpse into a life of an immigrant family trying to settle into their new lives in Canada. Here's what stands out:- the visuals are breathtaking, entire art direction is mouthwatering. - the audio work is top-notch; the sounds of sizzling and clanking during cooking segments brought back memories of cooking with my mum when I was younger. - the dialogue flows naturally, though Venba's saint-like patience may strain credulity for some.However, the game falls short in exploring Venba's inner struggles, leaving events feeling somewhat disconnected from her emotional journey.It's a solid experience and I definitely get why it won Best Debut at both BAFTA Games Awards and at GDCA, but due to its brevity and lack of replay value, I'd suggest grabbing this on sale. Overall rating: 3.5/5.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, gives a good representation of what can happen when moving to another country with your family. I'd say just go into it knowing it's a shorter game. You're going through more of a personal story, a way to learn of what many people go through.I look forward to what they do next!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: perhaps my favorite of the Intimate Slice Of Life As Playable Vingettes games ive played...cooking is the bullseye golden idea for everything attempting to be accomplished, and if its the path of least resistance i cant resent a well chosen path. my favorite moments in other games of this type come from Repetition, when something is given ludic meaning and that meaning is then reiterated or subverted in another stanza, which i think is why i felt this so warmly, as its vignettes r almost entirely that. this type of tight focus, allowing for comfort and emotional expressionism, is the approach i think would take if i ever made one of these games. and besides all that, it is ofc deeply beautiful and humane and idealistic...no matter how difficult things are to navigate, its never too late to understand eachothers experiences and choices. the final conversation here feels like equal parts autobiography, aspiration, and healing
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a quick dive into what immigrant and first generation life can be like, and the conflicts within.  It's cute, very wholesome, and easy to play.  The sound design and music are both excellent - really like the little detail that you can hear Venba's bangles jingling when she moves.  And the story was really enjoyable.Couple notes - it's a very short game.  I finished the entire thing in a little more than an hour.  The cooking puzzles are fairly simplistic, but I think the trade off is you get to see some really excellent sound and visual design.  Definitely made me hungry!  Overall, it reads more animated story than game.  You get to make some dialogue choices, but I don't think they change the direction of the game at all.  There's not a lot of replayability value.However, I think the excellent visual, audio, and music design make up for the downsides.  There's clearly a lot of love that went into this game, and the story it tells is an important one to share.  If you're ok with paying a little extra to support a lovely game about a mom cooking for her family, then I think it's worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This was a charming and sweet story of a family, and I loved how they tied in the cooking as the game play as a way to connect back to 'home' restoring the recipes. The 3 main characters in the family are all written beautifully, it was such a wonderful, at times gut wrenching, story. I would recommend if you want a short and sweet game, that has a strong story element. I wish there was more cooking! It was a fun mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: call the 1800-sadcat hotline and hug your mother today.the story is short and it felt like there could have been more flavour texts that talks more about the different food items, especially in chapter 5. i wonder if it would've been more immersive with voice overs  instead of just the different coloured texts. and after playing it through twice, i still don't understand why sometimes kavin's text box has texture over like oil stains(?)

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting to play this game ever since I heard about it in early June. Personally, the price didn't matter because of how much this game interested me. _childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing game! Such a cute and very fitting artstyle, the recipes were on point and incredibly fun to discover and cook. The audio, the visuals, the story were all so carefully and wonderfully put together. It is a very very short game, which is not a bad thing, I just wish there was more because it was so fun! _childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a very  visually stunning game, it felt so immersive that it opened up a whole world to me and a culture ive never experienced from that perspective.   I was completely immersed in the story, and especially the family. I felt their struggles, aches, the love shared, and every bittersweet moment this game takes you through. The music was so fantastic, stunning work. The music was never overpowering it complimented everything so well and just adds another layer and way that the audience can dive into the culture with..   The pacing was wonderful and the real sound effects made it feel like I was really cooking, I could almost smell the food. created a realistic family that had many struggles but always kept on loving each other. I really enjoy that this was a sweet short game about family, culture, and the importance of  both in our own identities.  Kavin's mother reminded me of my own in the way she speaks even though my own family tells a different story, I felt empathy and could relate to many parts of the story in my own way.  I  was thrilled at how the game didn't tell you recipes directly it gave a fun challenge to it. It really helped you learn fully about this cuisine and how its made whether its smooth or by trial and error. I learned so much about the cuisine and tools used to make it!I suggest you buy this game for a relaxing experience into a world and culture either familiar or unfamiliar. With a beautiful immersive story that makes you want to dig deeper into the story even after it ends. Beautiful characters and the art style is breath-taking with a unique style. It was a wonderful insight into the culture and cuisine and the struggle many immigrant families face. the food and the music created a cozy atmosphere that anyone can enjoy.Love this game, played the demo and followed this game for long before its release from Tiktok and Wholesome Games. So happy it came out, fully enjoyed it. 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved Venba, although it's a little short for my taste. _childDocuments_.review: So, this isn't an awful game, and it absolutely has good themes/messages.The idea of making a cooking game based on faded/stained recipes is a good one, and moments of Venba are fun and enjoyable, as well as emotionally weighty.......so why am I not recommending it?Well, the graphics are a bit TOO stylized making it difficult to make out certain things (there are thankfully labels so you can tell that that stylized mound of yellow stuff is supposed to be shredded ginger {just an example by the way}) and it also sometimes takes away from the emotional heft of the story in the way that a more realistic graphic style wouldn't have.The gameplay of cooking is mostly fine (enjoyable even!) but the mouse and keyboard controls (well, almost entirely mouse) are SO awkward for a number of cooking steps to the extent that it detracts from the overall fun of the game.The plot and dialogue are fine (and the themes are absolutely good ones with a lot of relevance for a lot of people moving to a place with a different culture and values) but the transitions between "levels" (recipes) are too abrupt sometimes and not enough information is given about what events have transpired and how much time has in fact passed between chapters, resulting in a pretty big loss in emotional impact and even in emotional investment (hell's bells, it took me another chapter before dialogue between two characters even made me realize that in the previous chapter we were supposed to have figured out that ).  Additionally, some of the dialogue was a little trite and bordered on the ham-fisted side of things, which also hurts the impact of the themes.And as a final kibitz, the music isn't really enjoyable for me.  This is TOTALLY a highly subjective, YMMV sort of complaint (I love The Tragically Hip......but not everyone does and if a game had only Hip tunes for the background music it would kinda turn off those who aren't fans) but it did detract from my overall enjoyment.So, the graphics can be too stylized to really help the story and the gameplay, making the actual recipes can be kinda awkward and unfun with a mouse, the dialogue too often veers into the banal, and the storytelling takes a hit because of a lack of exposition in regards to events between the (sometimes vast) time jumps between chapters.It is absolutely NOT a bad game, but it isn't all that great either with too many nit-picks adding up to very mixed feelings about it.If you can get it on a deep sale you will probably find enough about it to enjoy it, but I can't exactly say I recommend it either.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game! It felt so warm and welcoming, I love the art style and the writing felt very heartfelt. I liked how when Kavin spoke in English his text sometimes became obscured the same way the recipe's from Venba's Amma were obscured. It drew a very sad parallel to how she felt she had lost or was losing both of them. Truly a beautiful game.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I so rarely write reviews but will for this one because it is so important to have representation in games. It was a lovely (albeit short!) game that did leave me feeling rather emotional. It was amazing to me to see Tamil script in the game and have so many foods I myself was familiar with + the soundtrack is great. I do wish the game was a little longer because I enjoyed it so much! _childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool little game! It tells an interesting story about family, identity, and culture from the perspective of immigrant parents and their first-generation son. The game is largely narration but the cooking sessions are fun, particularly when they're more puzzle-y. In addition, the cooking portions feel well-integrated with and complementary to the story, rather than just being tacked on for the sack of having "gameplay". The art's nice and colorful, the food looks delicious, and the sound design is solid. My only criticisms are that it's a little expensive for the playtime (about 1.5 hours) and that it needs an option to lock the cursor to the window. Overall, if you're looking for a cute little narrative cooking game, definitely recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Only thing missing from this game, is the full recipe book after completing the story.Learning Indian cuisine is one thing, but the insight you as a -in my case- Scandinavian, about the struggles of moving to a different county for a fresh start, the hardships of fitting in, and defining who you are as multi-cultured growing up, I was not prepared for. Fantastic game. 10/10.Have tissues within arms length. I needed them 3 times.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a touching narrative game that, despite its brief length of under two hours, masterfully explores the immigrant experience through the lens of food and family. The story resonates deeply with anyone who has felt the challenge of straddling two cultures - from navigating school as a child of immigrants to finding your place in society as an adult.What makes this game special is how it weaves traditional cooking into its storytelling, using family recipes as a bridge between cultures and generations. The cooking mechanics aren't just engaging gameplay elements; they're meaningful expressions of heritage and connection. The development team deserves high praise for crafting such an authentic and refreshing perspective in gaming.My only wish is that there were more cooking sequences, as recreating these cherished recipes was both entertaining and enlightening. When the game ended, I found myself hungry for more - both literally and figuratively. _childDocuments_.review: It was short but sweet. The visuals were well done, the food... I could ALMOST smell it thru the screen, and the story? Well I very much enjoyed it. _childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a short story game about a young couple trying to raise their son in Canada to give him a better chance at life. You get to cook dishes, go through the story line and sometimes get to pick the answers you want. While the game is hinting at a very important topic that still affects a lot of people today, I can't really recommend it at this price.I've played this game for 1.4 hours but paid the kind of price that nowadays lets you buy a decently good and long-lasting game on sale. I also hoped that this game would be more about cooking since the cooking part was the most advertised selling point during the Game Awards.I sadly can't recommend this game at this time and would highly suggest waiting on a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game is short, yes, but in that short amount of time the story told is impressive. It's hard for me to find the words to explain how this game impacted me. I had to sit for a while after I finished the game to take in and process the story. If you're balking at the price, then wait until it goes on sale, but I would still highly recommend that you experience what Venba has to offer. This story about family, food, culture, and growing up will sit with me for a long, long time and I'm so happy I gave it a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This is a story that is not told often enough in media in the USA. But in this game, the story of the experiences so many immigrants go through, at least, the beats many families perhaps experience, are told with love and care. You can complete the game in under a few hours, but it is well worth it for the cultural experience and information, and this tale of acceptance of self and culture. I waited for this game for a couple of years and while I wish it was longer, I was not at all disappointed! Thanks so much to the team who created this little masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game! I adored all the art and music, and making the food and reading the story was a lot of fun. The puzzles were fairly short and simple, and there are hints available if you need them. I recommend clicking on the speech icon just to read the descriptions of the food too, since there are sometimes fun little character moments there. I thought the story was well-written, and I cried while playing and had a lot of feelings, being a kid of an immigrant myself. I spent 1.5 hrs playing it. I had looked up how it long it was going into the game (consensus was 1-2 hrs) so that tracks. I think having that expectation helped, knowing that it was a short game. I think it's important to remember that good art costs money, and I think the game is worth the price. My only suggestion is to add a click-to-hold option (is that what it's called??) for accessibility. I played with my mouse and I don't personally enjoy clicking and holding the mouse button to drag things, which comes up a couple times in the puzzles.Overall, I thought it was a really great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a beautiful, soul-touching story about the struggles of identity, culture, a need to belong, and being torn between worlds. The art itself is amazing, and the gameplay mechanics with the cooking nicely scratch the puzzle-solving itch I always have for video games.The only gripe I have about this game is how short it is; my stats say 2.5 hours, but that's because I left my game running while I was doing chores. My actual game time was much closer to the other reviewers' 1.5 hours. There are only 7 chapters, and consequently only 7 dishes—which is a pity, considering that the game mechanics, art, music, and sound effects are so charming. I just don't know if it's worth the $12 I paid for it. It really was very, VERY short, and the puzzles weren't very difficult at all.7/10, wonderful experience, but points deducted for gameplay length.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: beautifully written; I love the story telling through food. Although I am not Indian or South Asian, I relate to many of the parts in the story/game. Food connects people in many ways. I found it interesting as a first generation, growing up in a predominantly white area that was relatable, especially in the BIPOC community.We share the ,now guilty, feeling of being embarrassed to bring or open up our foods to others who aren't like us at school. I remember making it a huge deal by begging my mother to pack me American sandwiches instead of our left-over Taiwanese dishes. I made it very clear that I did not want pork floss in my sandwiches. I regret it, and it probably didn't make a whole lot of sense to my mother. It probably did hurt to see me bringing home my untouched food. She would oftentimes worry if I ate anything for lunch.A lot of Asian cultures express love through food instead of words. It's important to us. Food is important to us. It's about family and love. The game made me cry multiple times. I recommend giving this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Man. Venba isn’t just a game about Indian family/food. It’s about so much more. It’s about the importance of culture and identity being preserved. It’s about leaving home and being othered. It’s about the fear of losing who you are when leaving who you were. This is one of the most beautiful & close to home games I have ever played. That scary feeling of unintentionally unlearning your mother tongue, not being able to eat or share the food that you grew up with cuz others think it’s weird/gross. Giving up home to fit in…This game is your mom staying up every night cooking all these dishes from your culture that will take hours to days to make but it’s how she shares her undying love for you.  It’s your mother struggling with life but still finding time to wash, steam and season your rice and marinate your favorite chicken or beef parts. It’s your mother making sure that you never have to order out or heat up anything canned even when she’s sick in bed…🥲Venba is your mother suddenly becoming an artist and cutting all the vegetables and fruits you dislike into the funniest and most beautiful shapes just so you get all the nutritions that you need. It’s just…so full of emotion. I miss my childhood.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game tugged at my heart strings. The game play is beautiful. I wish it was longer, and explored the nuances of the son's growth more. But the parts of the story that hits the tension between the characters were impeccable. The game comes across as a well-loved game, well-thought out, from the game play to the recipes to the story to the soundtrack. The attention to detail. Well done to the developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A visual delight! You can feel the warmth radiating from Venba's delicious dishes! The gameplay feels refreshing and rewarding and the soundtrack and sound design pair perfectly with the beautiful art style and the enticing recipes you learn to create! I loved watching the heartfelt story unfold and the short yet sweet pace and length of the game reminded me of the time it takes to cook a homemade meal! Sharing food with another is one of my favorite expressions of love and I feel inspired to try out a recipe myself and to treasure my own memories and time in my kitchen and hug my mom a little tighter!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: i'm a guy who's really interested in cooking games, and a dear friend pointed this game out to me when it first came out and bought it for me (thank you sarah!!!). i thought the game would mostly be about cooking so the story was entirely unexpected, but i still found it very enjoyable and heartwarming. i also really liked the gameplay, it's simple but it still felt engaging to me.it's a pretty short game and the price for it might turn people off because of that, but i do genuinely believe it's worth the price. there's an obvious amount of love and care put into it. i think my only wish is that the game had a sort of sandbox mode to just do puzzles once you complete all the chapters, but that's just my personal take, otherwise it's a very sweet game. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful journey to learn about Indian cuisine as well as learning to accept and love one's culture. As a Viet immigrant, I can easily empathize the story of how immigrant parents want a better life for their children but at the same time they are facing the risk of their children losing touch of their own root. I'm lucky and grateful to be born and grow up in Vietnam and I'm proud of my custom and cuisine regardless of the discrimination and judgement. I hope every immigrant kids will also learn to love and be proud of their culture as well since there's nothing wrong to be unique and be who they are :) <3
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Feels good to play such a heartwarming game after a long time . Venba's story discusses themes such as family and heritage and does so by using food as a means of communication . The gameplay's akin to that of visual novels , but it manages to keep it interesting with the cooking segment styled sequences which all play out like mini puzzles . The visual design and the food shown are a treat to look at , and the game comes with a cookbook and free ost's which is a novelty in steam . _childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with this game when I played a demo of it during one of Steam's many Next Fests.  The moment it was released I had purchased this game, and I have loved every moment of playing this game.The game highlights making traditional Indian foods while also going through each of the main character's milestones.  There are multiple chapters to play through, each of them with their own recipe (minus only one chapter) and each highlighting a core memory in their lives living in Canada.  The story itself is simple, but is very relatable with valid emotions about each and every topic.  There is no sugar coating anything, and the game keeps every moment of it real.  This is a struggle that many people do face, and I love that this game depicts that so well.  Despite having some of those heavier topics imbued in its story, there still is a fairly happy ending to it all, which I thought was healing for the characters.I do really enjoy the little food tips that each cooking session added in both because they give more depth to the characters and their opinions in addition to giving actual valid cooking advice.  They gave substitutions for a couple of the recipes too for healthier options, or how to make things a little differently.  It was a wonderful touch for the devs to add in the recipe book into the game too so people could make the recipes!  Many of the foods depicted looked absolutely delicious, so now we actually have recipes for what inspired the game we can try to make ourselves.  It's defintely something I plan on taking advantage of when I can!The soundtrack for the game was wonderful, with most of the music staying upbeat and inspirational though it did slow down and become more mellow or more upbeat depending on the event.  There was never a dull moment listening to the music, and it added to the comfort of cooking meals someone grew up making.  Listening to music you enjoy when you cook really makes the experience so much better and it really brought together the experience of learning these recipes and cooking them as the characters do.  Since every chapter had a new music track, it was super thoughtful for the devs to create a "radio" in the game for players to listen to all the music that was designed for the game.  I even say that they added in four songs to the radio that were not played in the game, which I find is super neat!The game itself is shorter and can be finished within a couple hours, though achievement hunting can add a couple more hours on.  I also think that the price point is a little steep for the amount of gameplay that was given, but I absolutely can understand this being from a smaller publisher and I can see all of the love that went into the additions and the game itself so I am happy to have paid that price.  This is such a wonderful game, and I am so glad that I had a chance to play it.  Hopefully the recipes that are added in taste just as good as they look in-game!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Heart-warming immigrant story about struggles surrounding cultural identity. Exceptionally multi-faceted and emotional for such a short game!Venba explores three main "characters": Kavin's parents, who want to raise a culturally Tamil kid; Kavin, who instead wants to assimilate into Canadian life; and that Canadian reception itself, which isn't quite accommodating of Tamil. All of these forces are treated with balance and nuance - Venba acknowledges the goodwill AND the flaws behind each perspective. Furthermore, they're depicted in both personal/familial and professional contexts. And there's also the theme of authenticity, and a nice catharsis at the end. Well-written!Nice cooking gameplay too. Recipes are partially obscured, which adds just the right amount of difficulty to keep things engaging without distracting from the narrative.(Although in particular, the dinner spread segment didn't have any of that difficulty, which made it boring for me. But I guess the absence of problem-solving made it go by quickly, which strengthened the build-up of excitement the scene was shooting for).Lovely visuals. Polished.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A really lovely little game with a story told through making food. Loved the point of view, loved the empathy for and humanity of the titular character. Very short, but honestly that's nice because I can recommend this to my friends who are parents. Cried a little bit after it was over because it tugged at exactly the right heartstrings for me. The gameplay is not incredibly complicated, but it's well made and satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet, Venba really was a roller coaster for me. Though I'm not from this exact diaspora, I could totally relate to a lot of the experiences being portrayed in the story (not wanting to eat lunch at school since others would make fun of my food, desperately trying to fit into Canadian culture while rejecting my own, struggling to speak my own mother tongue, etc.). It made me feel seen in a way that I don't think a game has managed to do in quite some time and it made me cry at points.Needless to say, I was starving and craving the food that was being made in the game after I finished it. I'm still thinking about getting some good biryani because that recipe was fun to work through. I loved the little tidbits about each of the dishes throughout. The soundtrack was unique and very fitting for the game. The mouse control for some of the activities felt a little "stuck," but I don't think it hindered my progress through the story. The art is beautiful and I just love how this game managed to tell such a compelling story without a whole lot of words. I implore others to give this a shot—if not for the story, at least stick around for the food.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly, highly recommend Venba. I spent about 3 hours playing through Venba, once for the story, and the second time jumping through the chapters to get 100% achievements. While the game itself is relatively short, the story itself is very moving and it punched me in the gut a few times. I was deeply invested in the cooking, life, and memories of Venba and her family. The game itself does a wonderful job of connecting the idea of family memory, and generational memory, to food and the game's recipe mechanics: We are put in a place of trying to remember our mother's cooking, or deciphering our mother's handwriting, in order to figure out the correct way to make each recipe. The game itself resonated a lot with me and made me think a lot about my own family while I played: my grandparents, my parents, and me, and the sacrifices that our families make for us, as children, to have a good life. The game itself definitely made me tear up a little at certain points, and made me want to call my mom. If you liked Venba, I highly recommend also checking out another cooking game that's about family and learning how to cook certain recipes to connect to our roots, tong jyun by npckc. The game is pay what you want on Itch.io and has really similar themes of translation, memory, connecting with your family when they're on another continent, and learning how to cook as a way of connecting with your family.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't hate this game but I do find it a bit lackluster. It felt like the game devs were trying to make a cozy cooking sim and a story about immigrant life at the same time but failed a bit at both. The recipes were okay and simplistic but there wasn't enough of them in my opinion, and I was a bit disappointed in one of the chapters (the one where Venba was making a feast for her son who was going to college) that the majority of the dishes were already half prepared for the player already. The cooking elements seemed half baked (not buggy or inaccurate just not enough of them to justify the game being a cooking game). The writing was okay. It felt a bit sporadic and vague at times and a bit cliche. I understand the immigrate woes as I myself am technically one but the plot elements involved seemed surface level and easily summarized by a typical immigrate couple has problems with integrating and faces issues like unemployment and a slightly strained relationship with their child who wishes to completely adapt and abandon his cultural roots. I wish there was a bit more robust writing involved. Like for example, Venba's relationship with her mother were more touched upon and while I understand Venba is the main character, it felt a bit unrealistic to not include anything about the father's family and his personal thoughts. (Also there was so many minor details that got sprinkled in the story that went nowhere. Key examples I can think of is Venba's mother's health, the bench incident, the relationship/opinions between Venba and her husband and that one dude in the first chapter [can't remember his name but I wish there was more in-depth details given on why the father character was so against working for him besides vague details], why the parents wanted to immigrate in the first place besides assumed money/opportunity issues back in India.) All these small things feel impersonal to Venba and the characters, like they can be used in any immigrate character story, nothing sticks out that could personally tie these elements to the characters, it's all just vague hand-waving bits of plot that feel like their existence is to showcase the difficulties of immigration (any immigrate character/family could work with this story, Venba and her family being the main characters are negligible.) Perhaps that's all the plot was meant to be, a story about immigration, integration, culture shock and a side of cooking with no other deeper story development involved. If so, ignore my gripes about the story I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: My parents came from nothing, and for people of their means back then in India, it meant moving from their forgotten villages to the nearest big city. They found each other in the early 80s and somehow made it work. Despite everything, despite all the odds, despite the distance between them, they made it work. Venba captures that experience so succinctly, it moved me to tears almost instantly. Kavin's internal conflict growing up is something I can relate to, and the fact that he cannot read the language of his parents, the language his father used to write in, hit me directly in the soul. I am 31 now, my family moved back to the city where my parents met. But that unique experience of displacement, and being connected to your homeland via food and the people around you are powerful motifs represent my own life via a medium that I love so much. Thank you, Visai Games. This is a very special game.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Venba is a very touching, honest and profound experience, and I was half-crying the entire two hours that it took me to finish the game. Venba is an interactive short story about a Tamil family that moved from India to Canada and focusses on various struggles the family deals with over a timespan of about 30 years and how they define and interact with their own cultural identity. The main lens through which we see the characters act is through their cooking, which is also the main game mechanic. From the first few moments of the game, I was instantly in love with it: the artstyle is absolutely gorgeous, the food in every scene looks incredibly good, playing the game feels very statisfying and the cooking parts have really well-polished animations. Additionally, I am usually not someone who deeply cares about game soundtracks, but the music in this game is straight-up SO good, that I would recommend the game alone on that basis. Gameplay-wise, Venba is just a LOT of fun and short enough that the idea doesn't become boring or repetitive and leaves you wanting 10 more hours of cooking Tamil dishes that you never heard of before. The cooking is framed like a riddle, in which you need to decipher an old cooking book, so it's not a "Cooking Mama" type game and more like playing a few very well-designed and visually appealing levels of a puzzle game. I don't want to spoil the story in any way, but the narrative feels really personal and honest and gets you thinking a lot, and is really good at immersing you into the situations and feeling tense and uneasy at the right moments. The only thing I would have wished for is for the game to be a tiny bit longer, because I was a bit sad to finish the story so soon after meeting the characters, and I had wished for one or two more interactions, to get to know them a bit better. Because while I liked that the story left a lot unsaid, there were a few things I would have liked to see a bit more of, especially since that would have also meant seeing (and cooking) more south asian dishes. I don't at all want to say that a game having a short playtime is a problem, but with this game in particular, I felt like the short playtime made it feel a bit less unique than it could have been. As someone who has read a lot of stories about immigrant parents and their children who grow up in a different culture than their parents did before, this game didn't say that much "new" stuff with it's story as it was, and felt to me more like a more surface-level summary than e.g. Crying In H-Mart by Michelle Zauner or The House on Mango Street by Sandra Cisneros - both of these stories also talk about most of what Venba talks about - food, cultural identity, language, growing up wholly different than your parents did, disconnect between immigrant parents and their more modern-oriented children, but these stories go a lot deeper with that and explore the main character's thoughts and relationships in more detail. And with a bit more playtime to get to know the family, the devs could have made the story even more "their own" thing in terms of that. That is to say, if this is a genre that you are very familiar with, the story may leave you wanting in a way or two, but that doesn't mean you won't enjoy the game anyways. And aside from that, if you like story-driven games, like cooking or just think the visuals look good, I would really recommend giving this game a try!

_childDocuments_.review: I had seen so many positive reviews of Venba, and I jumped at the chance to play it when I was able to get it on sale. I'll begin with my positive comments: This game has really interesting and beautiful art design and music. I think the sound design is also done well, specifically for the cooking scenes. There are also parts of the story that I found really endearing (Like the baby Idili!). My favorite part is that you can also have the recipes for the food you made in the game once you have finished the story. I do have a few critiques/what I was hoping to see in the game that I did not: There is honestly an overall lack of gameplay. This is more of a visual novel, but if a game is advertised as a cooking game, I expect a decent amount of cooking gameplay, which this game didn't really have. The narrative (That you have very little control over, it's mostly just reading) portion of the game is long and cooking game play segments are only once per chapter. At some point also it felt like the cooking game play got a lot easier, almost too easy. There wasn't as many elements to the recipes later in the game, and it felt a bit rushed, the puzzle element was practically gone. Also although the story was charming, it was somewhat predictable, and very short. There is so much opportunity for more game play and chapters in this game, but there is so much wasted time that we don't see between chapters (Chapters skip several years between). Overall, I liked this game, but I don't think I would replay it. I also expected more game play, and more cooking! I want a cooking game to feel like I'm doing a lot of cooking. At full price, $15 is a bit steep for the amount of time this game takes (It took me about an hour), especially considering most of it is reading dialogue and watching exposition (Which happens soooo slowly). I'm most excited to try the recipes I got from the game, but wish that I more fun actually playing it.

_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba offers a unique perspective of the first and second- generation immigrant experience in Canada, intricately weaving the narrative between touching cut scenes and mouth-watering cooking mini games. I'm legitimately excited to try some of these recipes myself. The art style is beautifully rendered, the characters feel real, and their struggles are relatable. Thanks so much to Visai Games for this gem. I'm excited for what's next!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Even from a different culture's perspective, this game feels personal in the themes it conveys throughout that are relatable to one if they are familiar with growing up somewhere ones family is not native to. What a splendid treat this little game was, and definitely worth the unique and short fun experience the developers put into it-
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A short sweet story puzzle game about a Tamil immigrant family in Canada. The music and recipes build the world nicely, the puzzles are straightforward but still have room for minor mistakes. I can see replaying it another time, to see if the different dialogue choices change much, but it's also a short game on purpose, and it does what it does in that time very well. It's nice having some games that don't demand weeks of play time but still have substance in what they do offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game for free, but I am going to be completely honest with this.==============================This game honestly made me really hungry, punched me in the face with all the feels, and is really well done. The art style and fluidity of the game was super cool. There wasn't any hiccups in the game play and super fun to build all the foods. It really hit kind close to home with the immigrant experience as a child growing up with immigrant parents who move to a new country for a better life. I also related to the generation who was born from the parents and had an internal battle between the two cultural backgrounds (the western identity to the X country identity) when most (not all) embrace it as they get older. The time progression was really cool and the pacing was great to move along the milestones and tragedies in Venba's  life with her family. Since this was a short game when I streamed it, I also did my own research on the recipes that were being cooked, which was so cool. Its quite different from the normalized view on Indian foods from the Butter Chicken, Tandori dishes, naans, and more. It's great to see it from a regional perspective to show the width breadth of any country cuisine.I feel it's work the amount they charged for the game, as this seems like a first big game for a small indie dev group.  The amound of work they put into this makes this short game worthwhile. Especially the sound experience with the cooking ASMR. The sounds were divine for a foodie like me who loves to cook. I would suggest to the devs (if you do read the reviews) is to maybe include some stuff for added content. One suggestions is maybe  a separate section for the recipes being used in the game, maybe even providing the full recipe of its ingredients and how its made. Also maybe an additional cooking section where we can cook other kinds of foods from the Tamil Nadu region. A little historical section talking about the region would be cool too!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game. It is definitely on the short side (1.5 hours without all achievements); I wish more gameplay had been included along with this amazing story. This is a common immigrant story within Canada - and it's told in such a beautiful way. It's very accessible - played on Steam deck perfectly fine, and all controls were straightforward, colours were artistic and not integral to gameplay, no bright lights, low movement for those with vertigo.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: It was a beautiful experience. I really loved this short game. The story, the drawing, the color, the cooking.I really liked the fact that this game tackle the problem of children of immigrants: keeping their parents culture or trying to fit the country's culture and feeling guilty.It was a beautiful story. If you liked emotional games such as What Remains of Edith Finch, Florence etc, play this game you wont regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: It's a visual novel with a moving story of an immigrant family that tries to find a balance between honoring their own culture while respecting the culture where they've arrived and raising a son in that dillemma.There are a few pointless text choosing options and a total of 6 puzzles where you have to add ingrediënts in the right order (but the biggest puzzle just gives you the ingrediënts one at a time, so that isn't really a puzzle)I was lucky to get it in a bubndle for cheap, and in that case if you're interested in the story it's owrth checking out, but 15 bucks for 1,5 hours of content (And I redid most off the puzzles for achievements) is ridiculous.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Some of these feelings explored in this game may have hit a bit too close to home for me, due to the demographic target.Phenomenal. Part of me wishes the experience (with the cooking mechanic) was longer, but the narrative probably wouldn't have the kind of impact it had if it were more drawn out. Simply phenomenal.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a neat experience. How the storytelling integrates with the gameplay integrates with the UI is really quite something. For example, there is a character speaking English, and when reading that from another character's perspective who is less fluent in English, the chat box has splotches that obscure some of the letters. Still totally readable, but you see how it is more of a challenge.Also the sound design is pretty great.Highly recommend, can be easily completed in one sitting.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Everything from the art, to the music, to the game play was a breath of fresh air for this game. However, probably the most impact part for me personally was the writing and story telling. It was beautiful and emotional, had me tearing up at different scenes. Kavin became my most favourite and least favourite character, but maybe that was cause I related with him so much. Abhi and the team killed it with this, and I would highly recommend it for anyone looking for a beautiful 90 min experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fun game however it was way too short for the price it didn't even take an hour and a half (with mistakes) to complete. The story was very touching however most of the recipes were just dragging things into a pot/pan and waiting. I'd be lying if I said I wasn't a little disappointed. The graphics and art were very good. If there were more recipes or the tasks were a higher difficulty I most likely would have recommended this game
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Sweet little gem! It's more like a story than an actual game, but it doesn't really matter as it is beautifully done. Heartwarming dialogs and, for some odd reason, the dishes looked very appealing to me, which made me quite hungry. A bit too short, to be honest; I would've liked to dig deeper into the story and to cook a few more recipes, but it was a nice experience nonetheless. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: As a second generation Indian immigrant (punjab), I can tell you that it was really hard to hold back the tears till the end. The story which many immigrants can relate to is told in such a beautiful way, that I didn't think was possible. Kavins inner conflicts growing up is really something that hit home.I also really loved and enjoyed the music and art. I could smell the food and home from the screen, it was such a nostalgic experience and I really wished that I could have played this game as a kid - I have never felt this seen before. Now I have to go out and hug my parents
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: The art and music is very nice.  I was under the impression this was more of a cooking game to introduce a cultures dishes to a new audience.  However there was very little game play, most of it was story.  The story felt a bit rushed and the cultural references were lost on me as I found it confusing being it wasnt my culture and I couldn't relate to it personally.  I would recommend this on a sale or lower price.  The game is also very short like an hour long if that.  So as much as I'd like to recommend this, for me personally I can not.Note: Yeah the story didnt appeal to me as I'm not an immigrant, but this was given to me by a friend of that ethnic group with immigrant parents,  who watched me play it, explained parts to me, and also did not feel it was worth the money.  They too agreed with my review, and I even showed them my review before I posted it.  So still for me, it isnt worth the price, and there is very little game play, and its more of a visual story book, which is fine, but was def gave off a different impression.  If this game was like 10 bucks, sure, I wouldnt review, I'd keep my opinion to myself, but for the price point, I cant justify it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: i'm ngl this game did make me cry a little. def a must play especially for children of immigrants :) a beautiful story depicting difficult subjects regarding immigration and the assimilation of culture and grow up a family in a foreign country. the game play was also super cute and i loved the recipe book included as well. loved it sm 10/10 <3
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This was one of those games i had been waiting for for soo long and I'm so glad that it has been released! The art style is very cute, the game play is very interesting and I adored the puzzles with the story adding so much to the overall game. I highly recommend this game to any one, as it is truly delightful learning how to cook each dish.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I loved it I think its really good, its a very nice story with some heartfelt messages- I liked the cooking aspect and it opened my eyes on many recipes and a different culture. The only thing I didn't like was that the game was very short and an hour of game-play isn't really worth it. It would've been nice to have more recipes to make, as well as decipher more of the recipes in the book. If you want a short cooking game thats also a visual novel I would recommend it but don't expect to be doing a lot. It's all up to you if you want to get the game but I really expected more out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: The narrative in the game was so well done, it really felt like you were in their shoes. The art as well and the small touches to the environment really make it hit home. There is definitely a lot more story to it, but the casual cooking is honestly really fun, and the fact that you can learn about the dish you're making is neat as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely heart wrenching and beautiful. A story of love, discrimination, assimilation, and finding oneself amidst it all. I grew up somewhere very culturally blended (in the sense that Chinese New Year, Ramadan etc. were celebrated on par with Christmas even down to arts and crafts in elementary) so I have always had a bit of a blind spot to what reality was within my country. It's gutting and I appreciate the way their story was told through such a universal medium (and fun little minigames that offered enough variety to avoid feeling like a chore).
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cute game. Ever since I saw the trailer on tiktok I planned on getting this. When I was a kid I really liked the toca cooking games so this reminded me of my childhood but with more depth and (tbh) nicer art. Its really worth playing for gameplay alone. The story touches you at the end (i was annoyed at the son ugh) but theres a lot of appeal to this game! Buy it!!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is a story about an Indian couple that immigrates to Canada and tries to make a life for themselves. I won't say anything else so as to not spoil the story, but it's sweet, heartbreaking, and shines light on the struggles of both the parents and children of immigrant families. I think Venba does an excellent job of doing everything it wanted to do- however, I will warn that you are paying $15 for an hour/hour and a half of game play, maybe a bit more if you try to unlock all the achievements. While this wasn't a problem for me, I understand that some people don't have the money to drop $15 on a game that's this short with no replay-ability. TL/DR: If you don't mind the price tag for an hour-ish long game, it's a very heartwarming story with cute art and fun cooking game play.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Game is quite short, but story-rich. Also I like the atmoshere. But If you're an immigrant and your parents are old, this game is the saddest game to play. Prepare yourself for it. Also I'd love to have an ability to see the flash when food should be flipped in real life too! it would be really helpfull.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I strongly endorse this game. Despite my limited knowledge of India or South Indian recipes and culture, this game resonated deeply with me. Being raised by my Thai mother and surrounded by her cooking, the mention of the food's aroma evokes vivid personal memories. Despite its brevity, this game is rich with meaningful experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Really beautiful game. I found it super relatable even though I am not Tamil, I'm the child of immigrants from a food and big family culture. Growing up isolated from your own roots in a foreign country, yet filled with memories of the delicious food your mother cooked that you took entirely for granted until you're old enough to realise... it is such a uniquely bittersweet experience and I'm so glad that this game exists. I'm actually working on my own game now with similar themes from my own culture, and I'm so glad I found this during the Steam cooking fest, and I feel a rejuvenated motivation to continue on my own story.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: What a gorgeously-illustrated video game that focuses on the Indian culture of foods, cooking, the Tamil language, loss, and growing up. I really enjoyed the whole cooking aspect of it and learning new recipes that shows off the Indian culture so proudly, and it's so clear that food is a love language for your loved ones (family, friends, partner, etc). The music is pretty nice to listen to as well, and I definitely loved the cookery noises, especially the sizzling sounds *chef's kiss*. I would say this game took me 2 and a bit hours to complete (especially if you're taking breaks in between because you need to go adult in real life). Overall, food brings memories, and your loved ones closer to each other. Whether you've moved out and live elsewhere that isn't with your own family or a loved one has passed away - your home culture foods will remind you where you came from, your roots, and who taught you how to make those recipes.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: this is a beautiful little game, more like a  very short novel with a little bit of guessing involved. I really enjoyed it. there isn't much in the way of a challenge but i enjoyed playing through and working out the recipes so much. I would really love to see more of this game. perhaps a sequel where you are kavin's son/daughter opening his/her own restaurant  and trying to decypher the tamil recipes in his/her grandmother's book? I'd love that the game was too short and i would like to play more like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: When I finished this game, I literally had snot dripping out of my nose like slug trails because I couldn't bear to leave before I was done to go blow my nose. I'm sure you can see from the trailer it's a beautiful game, and I'm happy to say the writing, story, and how they intersect with the actual cooking/puzzle elements of the game are just as beautiful. Have tissues near by, just in case.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Such a good game! It isn't long but I don't feel like my heart could have handled more of it. As a child of aging immigrant parents (though mine are Chinese and not Tamil), the relationship between the characters hit me so hard and I was crying by the end of it. But it was fun nonetheless and left me really wanting to cook *all* the food. I've even already looked up recipes and am pondering how to incorporate the things that were talked about in the game into those recipes!!This game is stunning both in terms of visuals and audio, the colours are so bright and the food both literally and figuratively looks and sounds amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing and beautiful little game. I loved watching the growth of this little family, learning a little about a different culture, and definitely cried quite a bit! The story beats hit in so many ways and is a very meaningful experience for anyone to have. I would love to see some more recipes if the game is ever expanded!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is an endearing and heartfelt visual-novel. It's not really a game and the food cooking, the only game part is too linear to slide the scale. It's definitely a visual novel. It's good for its length but it is very short.Cooking is kinda fun but pretty shallow overall, and well that's really the only interactive part of Venba apart from choosing some dialogue options. It's a tight story with some light themes. It's fun for the hour you'll play it and tugs at some emotions too, but overall it is far too brief.  Not enough can be said, not enough relationship to the characters can be built in an hour and well, the "game" leaves you wanting more. It feels like a demo.Overall it is enjoyable. Though it is a bit expensive for what you're getting. It should really be 5 dollars, but hey devs gotta eat. So thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: A game about food, family, culture, and being an immigrant. Some have called it short - I finished it in about an hour and a half to two hours - but the game is to me the right length to convey its story and atmosphere without being overlong, so I do not consider this is a negative.The story is poignant, sometimes funny, and always heartfelt, and the food looks delicious. This game managed to make me hungry *and* make me cry. That's a pretty good game in my books.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Short and bittersweet (and hunger-inducing!) Venba gives a very respectable nuance look at culture, people, food, the march of time, (food), and indian kitchen appliances. Wonderful menus. Wonderful scene setting. Hard-hitting truths...but if only there was a trashcan option when it got to the cilantro.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba is an incredibly touching game that packs a punch, even though it's pretty short. In the end, that is EXACTLY what makes it so good, any longer and it would have missed making its point entirely. It dives into themes like family, love, prejudice, sacrifices, and feelings of displacement. It keeps things simple and straightforward which makes it so charming. You'll be hooked in no time!And the cooking oh my god! Apart from it being a real love language between the characters it made me even more curious about Indian cuisine! I really want to try all the recipes presented in game and see what they actually taste like. Hope I won't fail much :)Two things that I love the most are:-the art style; both Indian culture and cuisine are very vibrant and the vivid art style translates this affinity towards colour, especially when it comes to how the food is represented-the sound Venba's bangles made every time, which I found very comforting; I don't know why this detail stuck with me but I absolutely love it!Thank you so much for giving us this little gem. I am really looking forward to playing more games by Visai Games and discovering more beautiful stories!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: As is probably obvious for my play time it can be a very short game so a heads up for that. It tells a pretty personal story which I certainly myself can feel for. The game itself is putting recipes together with context clues and a patchwork recipe book. I feel that it tells a good story but feel this is more of a interactive story rather than a game. I still recommend it as the food looks great and teaches a bit about the struggles of trying to start a new life. It certainly has sparked me wanting study some of the food I have seen.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Very short, but highly recommended.This is not so much a game as an experience. A look into the life of an immigrant family, the challenges they faced immigrating in the 90s, the challenges their children face growing up with another culture, the challenge to respect their heritage while also embracing their new home. The challenges for parents seeing their kids embrace their new home more than their heritage. Put yourself in someone elses shoes for a couple of hours, cook some biryani and dosas, and feel some big feelings
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This was a surprisingly small favorite of mine! The cooking was nice and I liked how it felt like a puzzle with the clues given. The story was honestly a gut punch to me in a good way, it felt very heartbreaking as someone who comes from immigrant parents as well. Makes me feel like I should call my own mom sometime.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I write this having just completed Venba in just under and hour and a half.  Make no mistake though, brevity is not to this narrative's detriment.  Much as one might call the shortest story ever written to be "For Sale: Baby shoes, never worn" Venba makes the most of the vignettes of the titular character's life that we get to see.  I could now talk about the puzzle elements to the Cooking Mama adjacent gameplay or the game's themes on food's ties to culture, history, and family or the narrative of living as a cultural outsider, or the things Venba never wanted to give up and sacrificed and the pain of seeing Kavin seem to not want that cultural heritage anyway, but many people have penned far better words on the subject than I could.  Words that convinced me of the importance of playing it.  Instead what I will say is this: Venba did a better job of making me feel tension and get invested in its characters, and delivered authentic emotional gutpunch better than any game has for me in quite a while.  There are games I've spent far more than ten-fold the time into that I've long since forgotten, yet I'm confident the almost 90 minutes I spent with Venba will stick with me for years.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the kind of story that hits so much harder if you are in Kavin's shoes. The dialogue from Kavin and his mom Venba hit's ridiculously close to home, and at times made me choke up because they reminded me of conversations I've had myself.The art style for the game is so unique and eye catching that you can't help but appreciate it, and how wonderful it makes the characters and the dishes look. If you are someone who can relate to this game, or even someone just interested Indian cuisine and how it relates to the people who cook it, I can't recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: before i say why it was a no for me-- this game's artstyle is beautiful, it looks really pretty and the cooking vfx/sfx are just wonderful. i really wanted to like this game but there was really nothing past 1 hour of actual playtime. the story is all right, but things moved too fast, and at some points there were little graphical glitches w sprites that just kinda took me out of watching the 'cutscenes'. cooking minigames were fun, but i wish there were more. ):
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: Venba - the main character of this game, is a woman from South India who came to Canada with her husband Pavaala in search for a better life, for freedom. What they found was a set of challenges, maybe too big to overcome... This game is just as colourful and warm as the preview images make it out to be. The art- and sounddesign are outstanding with great attention to detail. The main identifier for a game like Venba is this: Does it leave you wanting more? Yes, yes it does. As every independent game, there are some things to consider here. Yes, this game is not your 100 hour MMO. This is a heartfelt story that will leave you both hungry and thinking about cultures and the mixing of them and probably will leave you feeling a bit guilty about your own parents. It is games like Venba that need our support, they are the beginning of the future of a gaming industry that won't shy away from telling important stories, in a way that only games can. Highly recommend this game and now excuse me, I need to find the ingredients to make my own Biryani!Now nominated by me for "Soundtrack of the year" award!
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a short one but, in that hour or so I spent playing it I learned about Tamil cuisine and saw life through the eyes of immigrants. This game is beautifully powerful and it made me cry. I don't cry often. I would recommend this game to anyone and everyone and I will definitely be playing it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Venba

_childDocuments_.review: I went in just interested in learning about Indian culture and recipes (which I got).
