_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time with this one. It's really just a simple isometric puzzler with some portal gimmicks and a handful of moe characters, but it manages to stay interesting throughout. While some puzzles had me scratching my head as early as the first world, I was rarely frustrated, and when I was I'd say it was more the fault of the checkpoint system than the level design. Although I'll go into more detail about that later. While it is tagged as one, I'd argue QV isn't really a platformer. It does have common world themes, moving platforms, one type of enemy, and even collectibles, but traversal is moreso about using warps to teleport around the stage, and your wits to solve the puzzles in your way. Blocks and switches are the bread and butter of the gameplay, but Quby also brings some brush abilities to the table. She can draw her own portals on specific tablets, use inkwells to paint bridges over water, and use rain from water altars to extinguish a certain other altar. Not sure why that last one's a brush ability. At about the halfway point, the game introduces partners for Quby, and levels with a sort of tag team dynamic. Your first second, Varon, can't use any brush abilities, so he's basically just a remote control block that can push other blocks. But for the last couple of worlds your partner can use All of Quby's abilities. The game does a good job of gradually introducing these mechanics to to keep the simple block and switch puzzles fresh. Although my favorite is the flint golem. When Quby extinguishes a flame altar (via the aforementioned water altar) the corresponding flint golem will take whatever route is available to relight it, stepping on any switches that are in its way. Like most of QV's gimmicks, It's a relatively simple mechanic but it allows for more complex puzzles when mixed in with the others. In several levels you'll block or alter its path to flip different switches, or even trap it out right, and in one you'll race a golem through the stage completing simple puzzles before the golem flips the next switch and blocks  path. And also I like the the little jingle that plays when it wakes up. I had a lot of fun with the actual levels, although it was somewhat soured by some structural issues, on both a macro and micro scale.Starting with the macro, the level progression is completely linear. There are four difficulties, Easy, Normal, Hard, and QV (Very Hard), but Easy is locked until you try Normal or Hard on a level, and QV is locked for every level until you beat the game. I completed almost every stage on Hard first, with the exception of a couple levels in the last world. Frankly, a lot of the stages in the first world felt more like tutorials than actual puzzles on Normal, and I wanted a little more of a challenge. My problem is that if you get stuck on a puzzle, your only option is to lower the difficulty. The Easy mode acts as a concession, being a highly simplified version of the level with no collectibles. Personally, I think it would be better if there were some bonus levels on the side of the main campaign instead of so many different versions of the same levels with similar solutions. Although this is admittedly a nitpick. Ironically, the micro problem is a much bigger issue.My biggest problem with the game is the way checkpoints work. Instead of acting like a more traditional checkpoint, Memory Crystals are essentially quick save pickups. Whatever state the level was in before obtaining one will be the game state when respawning after a fall, a hit from an enemy, or a manually reloading. And when you pick up another it overwrites the last. Now this can work fine, but if you grab one say, before getting hit by an enemy, the enemy will be right next to you when you respawn. Your save is bricked. You'll have to reset the whole level. And there are a lot of different ways to lock yourself out of success. Even something as simple as missing a collectible can make a full reset tempting, as backtracking for it usually isn't an option. Pretty much from the fourth world onward I was constantly resetting levels, and while I wouldn't say this made the puzzles less fun, it did make the more elaborate ones exhausting.Overall, I'd say QV is a good game. It's certainly not perfect, aside from the issues above I also think the collectibles come off as an afterthought, but the core gameplay is fun and interesting. If you're looking for a platform puzzler it's an easy recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: QV is not a platformer in any sense of the word, contrary to the tags on Steam. Yes, there is a jump button, but it doesn't do anything. It's literally useless. And by "literally" I don't mean "figuratively", for a change. There is not a single instance of anything in the game that can be done by jumping while being impossible to do by simply walking. Jumping is only an animation. You can't jump on top of anything, you can't jump over a hole, you can't jump from one platform to another. If you can't walk/run from one field to another, you can't jump between them either. I advise to forget about the button altogether, otherwise you may try jumping over something in a time of weakness, and fall down.Now, what QV is, is a pure puzzle game which also requires a dose of agility. Some things work for a time, so you need to be fast. However, if you plan your moves and know what you're doing, you will almost never want for time. And even if you mess up, there are checkpoints you can activate.The game has quite a lot of content, including four difficulty modes (easy doesn't count towards completion, and it unlocks for each level when you enter it on normal or hard - supposedly it encourages players to at least try before lowering the difficulty), it looks and sounds nice, has a rather simple story and dialogues/cutscenes that can be somewhat funny.QV is usually pleasantly challenging and can even be hard on higher difficulty levels. The puzzles are diverse and well-thought.Some things that could be improved:- Checkpoints. Sometimes the first half of a level has 3-5 of them, while the latter part only has one, or none at all.- Finishing a level on hard doesn't clear the normal difficulty, which means you need to finish every level three times for 100% completion, including the hardest - QV - difficulty that unlocks for all levels after finishing the game once.- Jump button. Either remove it as to not confuse the player, or make it useful.- The timing while crossing from one moving platform to another is just strange.Overall, QV is a very fun game and its few flaws don't make it any less enjoyable.  8/10

_childDocuments_.review: QV is best described as a slice of life puzzle game with a hint of Portal.  Charming atmosphere, beautiful soundtrack and characters with cute banter for added spice.  It also has character customization so the player can change the look of Quby between levels which is overall just a nice bonus.First thing that needs to be said, a controller is required to play this game.  Keyboard controls feel clunky and can be an annoyance in some of the harder levels that require precise timing and speed.  With lack of keybind customization, the levels feel more tense than relaxing with keyboard.The challenge QV provides is pretty flexible, offering something for everyone.  Difficulty is reflected through easy, medium, hard and qv (basically challenging).  Each difficulty noticeably changes the level in some way, whether it be adding more doors to block your path, changing the layout of the level path or adding.  Levels requiring two characters to solve are some of my favorites and only wish there were more of them.  My only complaint is that easy and qv are locked at the start of the game. Unlocking easy requires the player to attempt the level (not even finish it) and qv is unlocked after completing the story.  Minor gripes aside, QV is definitely worth the investment.  It has enough replay value compelling enough to 100% the game.  I'd like to see more from this developer in the future.  Now time to add the glacier area's soundtrack to a playlist on repeat.

name: Loot River
detailed_description: Awake as a lone traveler in the mysterious, perilous world of Loot River. Befriend Iphis. Fight. Reach the Opulent Sanctum. Control the world beneath your feet. Cleanse the infinite universe plagued with the power of the relic. Be reborn upon your death. Grant the gift of eternal death to countless tortured souls or abandon your duty and attempt to escape the impenetrable keep. Master many formidable weapons. Learn the true power of magic. Disrupt enemy behavior. Combine armor, runes, headgear and powerful charms to deeply alter combat tactics and enhance fighting strategy. Slide floating ruins in a series of ancient puzzles. Venture through endless catacombs. Encounter beasts, lost travelers and demanding bosses. These cosmic grottos hold numerous new weapons and gear to discover. Unearth unholy knowledge for permanent upgrades. Game Features Challenging “Souls meets Tetris” gameplay in a lore rich world. Unleash your creativity with a level editor – design, share, and play unique levels crafted by you and the community! Defeat enemies your way - unlock abilities, items and weapons, each with unique animations, powers, and visual style. Discover 26 powerful weapons each with 4 elemental rune enhancements and 10 levels. Unlock over 40 charms, each alters and enhances your combat abilities. Unlock 9 game changing armor sets and 18 headgear options. Combine all charms, armor, headgear and runes to create a truly deep combat experience. Slide ruins of an old dungeon to defeat your foes and solve puzzles. Battle many horrifying beasts and bosses from alternate realities. Meet many characters, travelers, friends and foes who inhabit the strange world of Loot River. Immerse yourself in a beautiful, hand drawn, pixel art world with fluid animations, real time 3D shadows, and astonishing water simulation. The Relic grants its subjects eternal life, yet their frail bodies can still die. Knowledge is the one true constant. Discover the Loot River. Immortality is a bittersweet gift.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: The second patch to the game fixed basically all of my gameplay complaints, so now this is a full thumbs up from me, not to mention their swift response to the community giving feedback, absolutely impressed by the studio. Leaving the original text for posterity!------------------So my thumbs up does come with some caveats. I debated back and forth for a bit trying to decide because it definitely feels like it needs some patches that apply some TLC, but... overall it does still feel like a complete experience.It's gorgeous as you can see from the screenshots and videos, and the mechanics are fun to puzzle around with most of the time. The hub world feels nestled nicely, the balance of loot and exp to each level feels appropriate, and I felt like I was progressing during each level, getting better, getting loot, etc, I could see my stats taking effect and feel the damage or hp upgrades in real time.However, many have mentioned the combat feeling clunky, and I agree. Rather than i-frames, it feels like the dodge roll simply has you teleport a short distance, but if you don't time that just right, you get hit even though you're then behind enemies. Parrying is satisfying, with a nice little critical hit animation afterward, but the visual queues just aren't... popping enough. And the loot generation is... abhorent sometimes. I think on my third run, I went through the entire first city level, and only got charms, no weapons, none. I got multiples of most charms as I hadn't unlocked more, and yet I died in the second level... with the starting weapons... Progression OUT of levels is my main sticking point. Games like Hades or Dead Cells provide you the chance to spend your currency either in pieces, or keep it after your run. In this game... you have to have the entire purchase price of an unlock to buy it... and they're expensive. I didn't unlock anything for several runs, and that gets discouraging. I only managed to unlock the first couple upgrades after finding a rare sword way outside of my level to power through a couple levels and buy some spells, which then snowballed me into more. But it's not ideal.Hopefully these reviews are read, and we get a couple TLC updates and the game will really shine.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, but it just kinda... needs more work. I am fairly certain the devs just ran some 3D models through a 2D pixel filter, and it doesn't work very well. Animations and silhouettes are nearly unreadable most of the time and attacks are unclear, even with the outlines enabled in the options. On top of that, there doesn't seem to be any input queuing so inputs are often just ignored which is extremely frustrating. The player gets stuck on walls when walking next to them, which may be by design but it feels like a bug and it feels awful. The dash animation doesn't really have an animation, it's just a jarring teleport with no indication of a cooldown or anything. Again, it feels like a bug. Combat feels incomplete, using platforms in combat should feel satisfying but instead just feels cheesy. Your own attacks are animation locked and you can't parry or dodge out of them, this may be intentional, but it feels VERY clunky. Seems to be very few weapons/spells, shops only sell 1 thing at a time, etc.Overall, it feels like the game just needs some more polish before it is ready. Everything related to combat feels clunky and janky.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game wasn't worth it - if I'd realized that before the 2h mark, I would've refunded it.Pros:* Innovative platform mechanic gives you refreshing gameplay and creative combat opportunities* Entertaining base gameplay when it works.* Decent variety of equipment and builds, in theory.* Pleasant graphics and aesthetics.Cons:* Several opportunities for you to get stuck in a level with no way to return to where you came from (has happened a few times already), forcing you to forfeit a run and lose your progress and rewards* Buggy input processing (attacks don't register).* Buggy hit detection.* In practice you seldom get good synergies among the random weapon and equipment drops in a run.* Boss difficulty is all over the place - later bosses can be much easier than earlier ones.* Spells are underwhelming overall, meaning the absence of mana regen gives you little to no incentive to use them.* Short game.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, the game is very nice to look at (except the in-game font, which looks really out of place) and the world design is interesting, but unfortunately the actual gameplay doesn't do it any favors. Combat is rather dull and feels almost pointless - since you have limited healing resources and stages are chock-full of foes, it often seems like the best way to progress is to just skip as much as you can (which is actually shown in the trailer at :40). However, in doing this, you won't get any EXP to level up, so you're technically punished for doing this too. That said, even if you grind your way through the enemies, the fighting itself is very basic - most fights will devolve into either mashing the light attack to stunlock enemies, or abusing a platform to whittle away a tanky foe. There's a dodgeroll, which is obligatory for these Souls-inspired combat systems, but it never feels satisfying to use. It's not really a "roll", so much as a short-range teleport that I actually thought was an animation glitch at first. Shops only sell you one item at a time and you can't see the next items until you buy what they're selling, so if a shop is offering a pricey item you don't need or already have, tough luck.The first major boss I encountered  looked like an exciting fight, but it quickly wears off once I realized she only had like 3 attacks, and these attacks would just loop over and over if you were in "range" of a specific one (such as being far away = laser beam). When I climbed the platform she was on, she performed a hand-swipe attack to strike the entire platform (this attack can be dodge-rolled through) and when it didn't work... she just did it again and again and again. 7 times in a row, she just looped this attack until I eventually climbed off her platform. It just feels like a majority of the game is about manipulating the dumb enemy AI to cheese your way through things. Even in the Store description, there's a GIF of the player abusing a platform to get free hits on a bunch of enemies. Maybe some people might find this fun for awhile, but the game just wasn't a very rewarding experience to me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely gorgeous. I love the setting, I love the OST and I love the artstyle.The sliding puzzles are fun and a very unique part of gameplay that I've never really seen before.Unfortunately, I seriously cannot recommend this game. The combat is tragically dull, dodging is extremely unsatisfying and seems to actively punish you for rolling into attacks to maintain momentum, and as of the time of this review it boils down to cheesing enemies one by one through either stunlocking or exploiting the moving platforms. It seems like the game is being actively updated, however, and if these issues get addressed in the future, I will gladly buy the game again and most likely enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a rough launch but the developers made sure to address things real fast.  I think it's fair to say that where it's at right now, it's playable and enjoyable.  Note, there's still bugs lingering around, check the forums.  For the full price of $25, I feel it's expensive for what it is and the content it currently has.  It's got some replay value due to how the game's loop system is.  This is one of those games you can pick up and finish a run in about one hour average if you aren't rushing through it to speedrun.  If that's too long for you, the game has a feature where you can quit and resume at any point, which is great.Art direction-wise, it's a nice pixel look.  Not everyone will like this style but I definitely like it.  There's effort put into making the enemies and other details different such as the weapons, armors and spells.The combat and feel is of what's considered "souls-like" so it's not fast and snappy.  Most actions from your character are slow and so are the enemies' actions.  If you don't like this kind of combat, don't get this game.The "gimmick" of this game is the Tetris-platform movement.  You'll be moving throughout the levels by controlling the platforms.  It also ties into combat as you can strategically fight using the platforms i.e. hit and run to isolate or clear out groups of monsters.  I'm not aware of any other games that incorporate this into the game play but I enjoyed how this ties into the combat.As for things that could use improvement: the camera, more shop keeper choices, use of Knowledge after unlocking everything, and the RNG drop rate of equipment.  The camera design follows your character in a manner where it lags behind in a way.  This becomes problematic if you're moving from platform to platform fast as you won't be able to see what's on the next platform sometimes.  This can be fatal sometimes depending on what monsters are there.The shop keepers that take gold to sell you items only sell one item.  I wish there was more choices besides one item.  Maybe something like three?After you've used Knowledge to unlock everything in the game, there's nothing else to do with it at the moment.  I wish there was something to spend it on.Lastly, the RNG can make punish you and leave you with a weak weapon for a good portion of a run.  There's a shop keeper you encounter who will do a trade of sorts (won't spoil what exactly) in exchange for the possibility of a random weapon but there's no guarantee it's going to be useful.  I think maybe incorporating some kind of weapon upgrading feature to allow the player more control of what weapon they want to keep to deal with this RNG issue could work.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure if the price of the game is well deserved for the content in it but it definitely is not a bad game. I enjoyed every second i played. Anyway i have seen few people complaining about the difficulty, hard parries and dodge mechanic. First of all the parry, there is a visual indicator for parry but parrying just from this indicator is very hard as enemy attack animations are quite fast for most enemies. _childDocuments_.review: I really want to like Loot River. There's a core game here that has some interesting things going on, and I love both the Souls-like and Rogue-like/lite genres it draws its core gameplay from. The problem is, it just doesn't offer you a lot to love, and there are quite a few frustrating elements to it. There's minimal early-run variation (without dedicating a precious modifier slot to it), and the meta-progression feels underwhelming.This is a popular thing to complain about, I'm sure, but it's in the name: the loot in "Loot River" is less plentiful than you'd expect and worse, it's not exciting or engaging. With a name like "Loot River" I expected to have a Diablo or Borderlands-esque shower of loot to choose from, lots of interesting weapon and elemental modifiers, and to have the acquisition of that loot actually matter.The reality is that you unlock many weapons that feel pretty similar and you just generally lean into the movesets you like best or whatever goes with the stats you pick up along the way. Elemental attributes occasionally appear on weapons, but they don't matter as much as you'd expect. It's more important to stick to a good combination of damage and functional moveset.Unlocking weapons, hats, armor, and spells only gives them to you the first time and then they're added to the loot pool for RNG drops. You're also weirdly channeled into specific unlock paths with long dependent branches. At a minimum, I think it would help if the Spear was instead always something random from the pool of unlocked items rather than having to spend a modifier slot to get run variety.The loot experience just isn't very satisfying, but maybe the name is to blame more than anything for putting the focus where I don't think it really belongs. The platform moving is pretty neat. It gives you a movement layer to keep in mind any time you're engaging with the level, but most of the time in combat I just used it to slowly pull enemies out of a crowd by exploiting the simple pathfinding. Often I actually found the mild puzzle aspect more frustrating than enjoyable, but I think that's more due to personal taste in how a game should flow.The leveling feels strange. A little out of place, even. It's hard to bend the stat placement to align with the sparse RNG drops of weapons. Looking at another title that does this well, I would say Dead Cells gets away with it despite its single-run progression because it throws items at you constantly and only has three core stats. Here, we have many stats in Vitality, Strength, Dexterity, Endurance, and Intelligence.When it comes to Intelligence, I could never see a good reason to invest in it. Are spells worth spending precious knowledge to unlock? I don't know, there was no strong incentive to explore that path at face value, so I stuck with what worked: hitting things in the face hole as hard or fast as possible and throwing a few points into my health pool. Throwing points in Endurance didn't have an appreciable effect on parry timing, so I eventually stopped bothering. The stats seem awkward; a long-run RPG game mechanic placed in a permadeath rougelite that forces me to switch into a menu to arbitrarily assign them.Combat really doesn't read well. That's probably the biggest sin that Loot River commits, and I have no idea how the dev team could fix this very important problem without significant visual reworks. When engaging with multiple enemies, it becomes a mess of bodies. Legibility is completely lost and the best solutions is usually to madly dash through to try to get some breathing room. Getting mobbed with a supporter NPC that either makes platforms unmovable or everyone invincible is not a pleasant experience.However, even when you get down to one on one encounters, the graphics and associated animations don't convey enough information to inform what the enemies are doing. Ranged mobs are just miserable to deal with altogether. Enemies transition from an idle or walking state to combat with no real tells, you just have to keep an eye out for the red warning indicator and dodge or parry. Difficulty feels like it revolves around avoiding high-damage sucker punches rather than engaging with the flow of combat.Finally, some enemies just aren't worth engaging. There are times where you just run away because you know it's not worth the trouble of killing certain enemies, which can put you in a bad place for level and loot progression if you end up skipping sections due to unfavorable enemy generation.Parrying is  powerful when you get it right, but it doesn't read well. I eventually learned that I could pretty much just parry as soon as I saw the red warning icon and mash the attack button and that would always work, but that never really read properly in the combat animations that were shown on screen. Parrying is borderline required to succeed in Loot River, though, so you'd better keep an eye out for that red warning icon.Bosses felt awkward. They also often often boiled down to mobbing the player while evading the boss, and mobs of enemies are exactly where the combat feels worst. It seems like a strange choice for the game to take clear inspiration from the Souls-like genre but not to emulate that in the bosses. The AI is usually pretty simplistic, but it hits hard or underhandedly with long-range, teleporting, or homing attacks. There is no evident rhythm of combat in boss fights; instead you often engage in a mad dash to clear the lesser enemies out so you can then deal with the bosses directly.There are good things going on here, too. The graphical style is simplistic but visually pleasing, even it can be hard to read in combat. I liked the world-building and the hints at plot dropped as you progress along. The biomes offer more variety in experience than I expected even though the core level progression is the same. Despite the fact that many of them felt similar, there are a lot of weapons to unlock. Sometimes you can find combat flowing interestingly, and if the RNG blesses you, it's even possible to cobble together an interesting build from time to time.Even though there are some really cool things going on with Loot River and I really want the developer's vision to succeed, I think the game in its current state is too deeply flawed to recommend. Without a sizable rework of core mechanics, more opportunities for interesting build variety, and significant improvements to visual action legibility I can't endorse the game as an enjoyable or worthwhile experience.

_childDocuments_.review: i figured id write a genuinely helpful review given that most people are writing negative ones with less than an hour played...That being said if you're looking for a Roguelike that also has some Darksouls tones to it like parry into a visceral and generally challenging combat that it's helpful to know enemy move sets then this is for sure a game you'd loveAs far as Roguelike qualities this game has good progression with a town and NPC's and permanent upgrades as well as a variety of unlocks and areas to find and progress through with multiple paths overall it encompasses the genere pretty well while still maintaining the "sometimes minor other times major" impact of items again like in the Darksouls seriesThis game along with having familiar combat also has the ability to move any platform the player stands on allowing for unique positioning opportunities during combat and unique ways to approach fights this also gives the minor sense of puzzle solving between fights but id not buy it for it's puzzle feel if that's the kind of game you're searching for.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I've played plenty of roguelikes and metroidvanias, I was drawn to this game due to the innovative platform mechanic, however I was through disappointed for the following reason:-The combat is very slow and 1 dimensional-Very limited ammount of progression outside of different weapons that have abysmal drop rates to be stronger than what you currently have-The level design also got boring pretty fast since its very easy to get lost-Horrible button mappingIn the end the game just bored me after a couple of hours, I made it to the 3rd area? after the first boss fight, where there's an enemy with lighting aoe that completely melted me every time I fought one. The game could be better if:-They were more generous with weapons drops-Better magic that u get from start (I saw there was magic but I only ever saw the pushback spell, pretty boring)-Faster level ups or more impactful (only the hp level up feels actually impactful, the weapon scaling is pretty bad)Still think it wouldnt completely salvage it though, there's just a lack of depth to it

_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: This feels really rough.Combat feels sloppy, and having to move your pieces around instead of having a comprehensive dungeon quickly becomes annoying rather than interesting. Some boss battles make quite interesting use of the system, but for the most part it just slows the game down.Even if you're really into this type of game I'd wait for a deep sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: Give it a few runs & try to farm out Knowledge (kill all the enemies, open chests) to unlock some new weapons. Default starting gear isn't great, but things get really good once you expand the loot trees & find gear that clicks with your style. Don't forget to spend Knowledge between levels + you can pay partially, so if smth costs 50 but you only have 20, you can put down the 20 now & do the rest of it later.here's my current favorite approach for a high-mobility build, in case it helps anyone else (SPOILERS on unlockable gear):Bit of a squishy build but if you manage your dashing & spacing well, you can really shred through stuffnow, the actual review:I'm really enjoying this game! The process of learning the weapons, mobs, and levels has been really fun & challenging. Even after 15 hours & some pretty powerful builds, each attempt is engaging & I def haven't seen everything in the game yet.The movement & combat overall feels good. At first it felt a bit slow, but after more practice with platform movement + unlocking speed-oriented weapons & gear + being an unapologetic DEX user, I get the speed I need! On top of that, the devs have been continually updating the game to improve the overall feel & balance & it's definitely working.i have some minor nitpicks--sticky wall collision, enemy attack hitboxes "feel weird" every once in a while, other tiny, TINY things--but nothing devastating & definitely nothing that gets in the way of my fun or stops me from recommending the game.I look forward to further updates/patches & I really hope this game has a successful future
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I was on the fence about buying this but once I saw how responsive to feedback the devs are I decided to pull the trigger. This game is fantastic, if you're a fan of rogue-likes, it's definitely one to check out.  The sliding block mechanic is a welcomed change from the usual level design we're used to seeing. The combat is very responsive, I've read reviews that mention it's sluggish, but that's been fixed.  Parrying and dodging is very rewarding and killing have a chance to drop loot therefore it's not always best to run.  Reached the third floor and I'm giving it a Solid 9/10 so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the most unique roguelikes I've seen since One Step From Eden. I'm not sure why it got mixed reviews on launch, it wasn't THAT bad. But regardless, they have been progressively rolling out patches and listening to feedback, and for that alone, I can recommend it. Although I still haven't talked about the gameplay.If you like Souls games, you'll feel right at home. Stun-locking, attack animations that can't be cancelled, parrying and dodge rolling, only no stamina bar. Plus, if you can master the right stick well enough, you can learn how to flank, make dive attacks, and cut off enemies like a pro.The game has it's flaws though. Some notable sticking points are as follows.1) Dialogue boxes disappear. I'm not a fast reader and I would like to know the story before getting cut off.2) The first boss is unintuitive. I'm still not sure how I managed to beat it. The poison fog doesn't help that much. Especially when the bombers show up.3) Parrying still feels weird. Sometimes it doesn't connect at all and other times it I just take full damage despite timing it correctly. Although I think part of this also has to deal with positioning.4) I don't have epilepsy, but the Divider boss would probably give me seizures. Even with that aside, the flashing lights make it impossible to tell when an attack is about to be made, so maybe scale them back?5) Getting out in under 2 minutes is a good idea, but not everyone wants to be a speed runner and skip the whole level. Maybe add another challenge. Get through the first level with 90% enemies killed without using a potion?6) Lightening is far too inaccurate for what it's worth. At least let me cast it on the move so that I can spam it until it hits something.7) I'm very unsure how the bloodstained tool is supposed to work. I've tried and I see both no stealth or backstab mechanics when I use it.8) Shopkeepers don't offer enough. Would also be interesting to see them sell a healing potion as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: Game is poorly focused on Keybinding, hate to say it but it is.For example:Left Shift is for blocking, I want blocking to be on space instead though since I don't utilize that as much... HOWEVER; even if I wanted to swap the two, I can't. Want to know why? You can't set Left Shift as a keybind, nor any mouse buttons what so ever, not a single, damn, one. It's absolutely ridiculous, it baffles me in so many ways how and why this was released without these options. It's Mouse and Keyboard Keybinds for a reason, Mouse is literally *the* first keyword in the settings, you just can't set anything to your mouse or most keys though.My review is going to remain negative until they release a patch allowing us to set keybinds to Mouse and other keys.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: tldr; Game is very fun and addicting, most negative reviews are complaining about bugs that are being fixed or don't have enough playtime to have actually experienced the game so keep that in mind when reading them.Just got my first escape(which is the harder of the two endings for a run) and am absolutely loving this game, I'm not sure how much I will play the game after I fully unlock everything and have every trophy but so far It has definitely been worth the buy. My only issues with the game are some minor bugs as well as a few major ones, however, I am sure that these will be fixed very soon. If you are reading lots of negative reviews about the difficulty of parrying don't even bother continuing to read their review. You will get used to the parrying system within at most 30 minutes if you are actively trying to parry. Some other negative reviews may also say that their isn't enough "loot" for "loot river" keep in mind that these reviews tend to have under 2 hrs played and have not taken any time unlocking anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: This could have been good.This could have been better.But, the control scheme pretty much ruins what could have been a good time.Yes, you can configure your controls yourself, and that sincerely helps a lot.But it's weird and incomprehensible to say the least, that at no time during development did one of the devs go "huh, you know, it is really hard to control the character and combat with this control scheme".A "press and hold" button to move blocks would have been better than arrow keys.The game is basically designed to work with a gamepad. Mouse and keyboard does not exist - you can't do anything with the mouse to begin with. So, sit down, play the game once and then remap all your keys, because it is impossible to do well without putting in the effort of remapping your keys.Left hand WASD, also Q/E to attack, Shift, Ctrl, Space, and 1,2,3,4 - ALL on your left hand by default.Just arrows on your right hand.This does not work.You'd want to remap the arrows to JILM and attack to H/K I suspect.Or just use a controller,. face it, the devs aren't likely to improve the control scheme, or warn about having to use a controller.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I am leaving a positive review because I WANT to see this game succeed and don't want to hurt the games success by leaving a bad review.Pros:- The game looks amazing- Has very cool weapons and spells- Has a good variety of content (That I've seen so far)- Has one of the most interesting quirks I've seen from a rogue like in a long timeThe game is trying to be both Dark Souls and a Rogue Lite, it succeeds on being Dark Souls but fails on being a Rogue lite. Rogue Lite's are made to be exceedingly difficult while also being fair but the game feels incredibly unfair with wildly large enemy hitboxes, lightning fast attacks with almost no tell, bosses with undodgable attacks, enemies spamming explosive projectiles with far too large of an AoE that have too short of a timer etc.I've been playing Dark Souls and Rogue Like's/Lite's for as long as I can remember, I'm no slouch when it comes to these games but Loot River just doesn't give you that feeling of satisfaction since it feels like you either cheese the game or die to unfair enemy attacks/gameplay jank. Nuclear Throne is more fair than Loot River is at the moment.The game is trying far too hard to replicate dark souls that the combat ends up feeling clunky and incredibly janky; as if they sacrificed all their time to replicating dark souls to the T and nearly no time making it feel good.Dark Souls has methodical and reactive combat, you learn the enemies attacks and openings, Loot River has chaotic predictive combat where you need to know what the enemy does/is doing before it starts doing it to even have a chance of dodging.The combat is reminiscent of Dead Cells, the enemies will have a little quotation mark pop up to signify they are about to attack but without the polish dead cells has, it feels like dead cells with lag and heavier restrictions on healing. Cons:- Enemies waking up from a riposte after a successful parry to immediately attack, it would be as if an enemy in dark souls had no wake up animation and immediately started an attack after the player's parry animation finished.- Platform jank letting you unintentionally move between platforms, getting stuck on nothing and the enemy AI completely breaking due to changes in elevation/enemy position on the platform.- Enemy designs that stunlock you for 2+ seconds with no obvious tell- Bosses and Enemies with seemingly undodgeable attacks that come out lightning quick (The first boss has a giga laser that you cannot dodge and the laser moves faster than you do, so you just gotta eat the damage or pass a DPS check to kill them before they can use the laser)- Next to no actual loot in the riverI love what the game has shown so far but at the moment it isn't at the point where I can enjoy the game or recommend others to try the game either.If you want to pick up this game I recommend waiting a couple of months till the devs polish the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I felt this game had a lot of strong things going for it.  Sliding the platforms around was cool, especially when they have stairs that take you up and down to multiple level, and when things like fire spreads across platforms that are connected together physically.. The short breaks for the mental game of rearranging pieces to reach a special chest were hit or miss for me, but overall there were some great ideas here.Unfortunately, the combat and movement need a lot of improvement.  Getting stuck on a little piece of debris you can barely see, that blocks 180 degrees of your movement are a common occurrence.  It also seems inconsistent on how much a wall or pillar will actually hinder your ability to move between two platforms, again getting you stuck and prone to taking unfortunate hits when you were easily able to move through a similar-looking situation in the past.  Sometimes it's even possible to sort of glitch your way through a solid wall by moving the platforms in just the right way, at just the right time, and likewise get glitched out of place and stuck momentarily in the same fashion.The dodge is basically your character model appearing 2 feet in front of where it was, with no animation.   No stamina, so the dodge has an awkward cooldown instead unless you have certain equipment that lets you dodge twice in a row.  Countering after a parry is about the same, but followed by a slow and unsatisfying animation of... well it's kind of hard to tell because things are zoomed out and shown from a difficult angle. The spears suck, it's only worth using the swords.  Couldn't unlock anything else to try in my time playing because you can only spend 'Knowledge' that you safely make it back to the sanctuary with... never had enough on my first trip back there after level 1, and never lived long enough to see if I'd have enough on a second trip because the second level was REALLY big and complicated. This is unlike something like Rogue Legacy and many others, where you can spend your hard-earned meta-currency after death.. But the game never really warns you it works like this, even though you DO keep dungeon modifiers you find, even after death, without having to return to the woman that handles those first.The combat overall just feels kinda clumsy though.. the parry timing, for example, feels really early, and sometimes seems like it just doesn't work.  Often the parry animation would look like its completely over, but work anyway.. and if you try to parry the same kind of attack any later where the animation actually looks like it'd line up with the enemy attack, your character stands there and does nothing, tanking the hit.  There's some cool bits, like charging up the sword's heavy attack and zipping through a crowd of weak basic enemies, but that's about it.The first non-prologue boss or miniboss I found never attacked me, just kind of wandered around and attacked in the opposite direction of where I was standing almost every time.  The game put up a little barrier of flames to block me from leaving the area where I was supposed to fight this boss, but it would occasionally wander off, too far away for me to hit, for like 10-20 seconds at a time, making me wait for it to come back, only for it to start attacking in the wrong direction again, and standing there tanking my hits like a dope - easy kill, but only because the fight was broken.  Overall this game is pretty tough, but 50% of the time it's only tough because the combat feels clumsy, as I've mentioned before.Overall I think this game gets a 9/10 for ideas and a 3/10 for the feel of the controls, and the overall execution.  I'd say the price is way too high for how little fun it is to play it.  I wanted to like this for the concepts, but I have to give it a thumbs down.  Wait for 50-75% off.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this game feels terrible to play. The zoomed-out, overhead perspective isn't complemented with powerful mobility and wide, sweeping attacks. Your weapons have piddly range, awkward combo rhythms, and never—and I mean NEVER—deal hit-stun. I have no idea why so many Souls-inspired games fail to deliver on the most satisfying elements of Fromsoft weapon design.Also, parries and dodges don't interrupt the recovery of attacks. It is reliable to mash the parry button in front of enemies, but NOT to attack enemies continuously and parry on reaction. This is bizarre!While the piece-moving gimmick is fun, and there are combat applications, it's not as synergistic as you'd hope. It's like, any moment where enemies are packed densely enough that dancing on a piece would be beneficial, parts are clustered or locked or enemies are spread so evenly that the advantages of sliding around are dampened. The best use of piece manipulation is slowly kiting and isolating enemies, which feels cheap and bad.And that's the thing... The central conceit of this game sucks. Like, why do I want this piece-moving gimmick paired with punishing, high-commitment combat and randomly generated levels? Those elements don't have much synergy. I could see a dungeon crawler with this gimmick with  combat working... Or maybe pieces themselves are used to alter encounters and manipulate enemies beyond their ability to walk toward you... Maybe traveling far and slamming into another piece could stun enemies... There are 2 or 3 extra ideas missing to make it work that are entirely absent.Oh, and for a game with "loot" in the title, there's little to extract on each floor, and equipment often has trade-offs, which just sucks. I've loved games with trade-off loot as a core concept, like , but here it feels like a kick in the crotch on top of how little is available.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: This is a first impression review, but I had to write it down. I can't remember the last time I got pulled into a game this fast. It's a fantastic concept, the execution and controls are great, the art is beautiful. Moving the blocks around and fighting monsters just bloody works! It's not just this novel exploratory and combat tactical element, but also a great sensation of power when I'm able to manipulate so much of the world's mass. The beautifully rippling water and the sound effects add to that. I think you have to try for yourself to see. For me it's an instabuy.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: Visually a great game and some of the gameplay elements could really be exciting and fun to play. However, the combat feels incredibly unsatisfying and frustrating.Why would a game like this lock you in your attack animation for so long? This entirely kills any combat revolving around reactive dodging and parrying. When the best strat is to swing once, back up, swing once, rinse and repeat, then something is off. Especially if you incentivise fast clears in a game like this.The parrying feels very unreliable. Gating a potentially satisfying gameplay mechanic behind stacking endurance as a stat (as it increases your parry window) and therefore neglecting other stats feels more like a punishment than a reward. Especially since the parry windows for different enemies are not indicated by the enemies' attack indicator as it might seem. This on top of behind locked in attack animations quickly led me to abandon parrying entirely and investing in actual useful stats.Dodging feels bad for different reasons. Despite moving around on rectangular platforms, you get stuck on every possible object. Some attacks have a greater range than the distance your dodge covers like the purple explosives on stage one. Sure, it mitigates some of the damage, but still taking damage for "successfully" dodging feels again like a punishment. You swing at an enemy, see the explosive from a ranged enemy flying, spam your dodge while waiting for be finally released from your attack animation only to be still hit for some of the damage after dodging. Sure, depending on where in your attack animation you are, it can work out, but why not make it a little more lenient?I really hope they iterate on some of this stuff as the game certainly has potential. In its current state however, I just can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I guess I shouldn't be surprised that I'm seeing a bevvy of reviews for the game with mere hours played as it's only been out for two days.I'm going to do the exact same thing in argument with the negative reviews. I just wrapped up a two and a half hour play session and I was delighted with my time.I'll go down the list of complaints others have had and make my case for an alternative viewpoint:-"The game is clunky and flows poorly." Obviously personal preference will cause some variation, but I think that the game flows extraordinarily well. The loop for the game is a simple mix of kill enemies, shuffle platforms, and keep moving. The beauty of the slower animations in combat is that it times the process of killing all the enemies on a platform with the time it takes to multitask and move to the next section. There is a learning curve to the flow, but it is there and it is good.-"Parries are inconsistent and there are few clear tells." Downright not true through the entire duration of my playtime. Every enemy has clear telegraphs or very clearly has none at all, indicating that you can't parry them. Audio and visual cues are great and enemy AI is predictable enough that you can expect what they'll do once you have the moveset down.-"There's no incremental progression like in roguelikes." This has a variable degree of merit, depending on what you define as a roguelike. I personally consider games like Hades and Dead Cells roguelites rather than likes due to their incredibly important (and incremental) progression. If that's what you're looking for, you won't find it here. Think of Loot River's progression as a more punishing Enter The Gungeon, where unlocks are lateral playstyle openers, and you get meta-game currency (that you lose 50% of on death) from killing enemies. Progression is hard to get going unless you get a good run and can bank your meta-game currency, because you can only buy new items all at once. This can be changed and there's an argument that it ought be improved, but I personally don't mind it as it is now. The game expects you to get the fundamentals with the starting kit and then lets you expand laterally once you become more capable.I do have two concerns at this point:1) I worry about build variety. Stats like intelligence could be very relevant if the game has higher difficulties with more spells, but right now, I've seen exactly one spell and it has been completely independent of damage, making upgrading intelligence questionable at best.2) I worry about the length of a run. I'm either at the first boss, or both the first and the last. If it's the former, that has me very excited. If it's the latter, I might hold until a sale, because the base difficulty would require around half an hour to beat.If any of this sounds encouraging, I highly recommend watching some of the game to decide for yourself. I've personally had an amazing time and find the game incredibly rewarding and enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those "mixed opinion" games. I've found it fun enough to 100% it, so I guess I'd recommend it, but on a very deep sale only. It's got a lot of problems.For starters, the store page advertising it as a "narrative-rich roguelike" is absolutely lying. The "narrative" in Loot River is barebones at best, and both endings are extremely disappointing. There's not a whole lot of world building to make the setting unique or interesting. It's the Dark Soulsy "decaying kingdom stuck in a cycle" mumbo jumbo you've probably heard a thousand times. The game isn't always precise, and this can result in incredibly frustrating moments when you get hit (or die) because you magically missed an enemy or your attack simply doesn't start. It's a bit janky overall. The last negative I want to mention is the unlock system for weapons, armors, etc. It follows the Dead Cells system of "buying" items with a currency and unlocking them for future runs. I despise this system, and in this game it means that for your first runs you'll unlock basically jack, and you'll always have to deal with the default stuff, maybe a new weapon or two, tops. Unlocking items is tedious and slow, and the game isn't really difficult, so you'll probably finish the game before unlocking even a third of what's available. West of Dead and Curse of the Dead Gods had the same exact problem. The one way to avoid this is to know that there is a weapon that can completely nullify the grind by granting you a metric ton of that currency in a matter of minutes. This creates another problem: this way you'll unlock everything all at once basically, instantly diluting the whole item pool.But with all that out of the way... Loot River is fun in its gameplay loop. The moving platform "puzzle" element bring a new spin on the genre and it stays fun throughout the whole (brief) experience. When combat works, it's satisfying and feels rewarding. Bosses aren't anything mindblowing, but they're interesting enough. The game has a certain atmosphere that pulls you in. On top of that, it looks really good, and sounds nice.As part of a Humble Bundle I enjoyed Loot River, even if it took me less than seven hours to get the true ending and unlock every achievement. I wouldn't recommend it at its asking price, maybe not even at 50% off. But you could give it a try: two hours is plenty of time to figure out if you find it interesting or not.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: My concern before buying was that it would just be killing the same few enemy types over and over, with the same strategy; that the whole platform-sliding thing was just a gimmick. But the game is really well done and well thought out. There are all kinds of different enemies out there that require different strategies, and most encounters feel potentially dangerous. The game seems impossibly hard for the first several hours you play it, but then you start to figure things out, and it becomes a lot of fun. Some players will be bothered by things like the inability to cancel attacks, imbalanced spells (some are ridiculously strong, others just kind of lame), and the like, but the core game play is rock solid. While I haven't gotten the "true ending," the game does seem a tad short (but with some levels that are just gigantic). I'd like to see the option to play longer runs, and maybe with just a few more path choices. Lastly, you'll want a controller for this one. The block-sliding mechanic means 4 extra buttons to be allocated to movement.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: graphically very pleasing game however awkward controls and no real variety early on makes each run feel like your just rolling dice to get a lvl 3 weapon or higher which your comfortable using.Parry is very awkward and most trinket slot items are ever parry related or give +1 in a stat which does very little.Loss of your souls after dying makes it even harder to save and unlock new equiptment making it harder to increase what little variety you have.I hope with some future balancing maybe some problems with weapon spawns and such can be addressed however currently the main problems are in the lack of variety in the early Loot... which is a bit ironic given the name of the game

_childDocuments_.review: It's a neat concept, but unfortunately the only fun part of the game is its core gimmick: moving platforms. The combat feels and looks sluggish, and even with the most recent update letting you keep half of your Knowledge on death, the drop rate of Knowledge is too low and the cost of unlocks is too high for the progression to feel compelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of both the worldbuilding of this game, and the sliding-island mechanics. I can't really speak about whether the gameplay is objectively "good," since I'm pretty terrible at vidya games in general. What I CAN say for sure is that I find all the weapon animations satisfying and the combat usually feels enjoyably tense.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I "won" on my first run, proceeded to play another 4 hours getting my ass kicked every time while trying to unlock deeper secrets, of which it seems this game has many. Still finding new levels, items, modifiers etc, have a feeling the "true" ending will be much harder to obtain. Movement and combat takes some getting used to but is really satisfying once it clicks.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, and has an addicting loop. It also has a fair number of gameplay issues, however.Hitbox/Hit detection is spotty. This is mostly for NPCs. Attacks that missed will deal damage and attacks that hit wont.The navigation. The moving platforms as a way to navigate maps is a cool idea but entirely overdone. I think static maps with larger playable areas and moving platforming sections inbetween would have been more interesting. I've had more than one run end because there was no navigation solution and I didnt have the leap spell. The stats system is kind of pointless since I never found anything worth investing in besides health (which also heals you when you raise the stat). I would hold on to levelups to invest in endurance for a free heal.Easy Mode: This should just be called "playable mode" because being able to attack cancel is absolutely critical. This game has a ton of nearly unavoidable damage and everything is built around healing/health. The other stuff like lowering enemy damage (by about 30% Id guess) didnt matter nearly as much. This should be the standard for the game. It barely works without it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: level up u vig!---edit:As I said, vig is pretty much the only thing u need, since it also buffs heal accordingly, which means u can save more potions to be duped and heals a lot more! With 20 potions and a long HP bar any difficult levels in this game can be trivialized.Parry is already easy without leveling endurance, however it is harder to parry a vertical slash then a horizontal swipe. That's said, the stats balance for this game is probably non-exists, which actually can be a good thing for a single player gameIt turns out the as long as get enough coins you can purchase unlimited times from the same shop, and coins are kept to next round if reach the end of current run. So it is only usefully after you managed to play multiple rounds without death.I did't experience any obvious bugs during the gameplay, probably the enemy AI could be broken but that's actually making the game easier.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: My problem with this game is that, unlike most other roguey games I've played there is no resource which accrues between runs. There ARE upgrades to buy to improve yourself for future runs, unlock new weapons etc. BUT you have to buy them with a resource which dissolves if you die, a resource which I never seemed to have enough of to buy anything. Easy fix for this would be to allow you to BANK the resource at the sanctuary hub between levels. or just to make it persistent between runs. Without this, it felt very samey. It's possible I'm just terrible at the game. But for me, this meant that the game lacked the massive hook that other roguelikes/lites have.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: Still buggy after over a year, consistent softlocks either due to terrain or invisible walls that spawn due to mini bosses. The whole interesting mechanic of the game are the platforms and it seems there's no clever algorithm that prevents you getting platforms that can softlock you. So if you're unlucky, the random platform generation can block your progress completely.I don't agree with others about the combat, I actually think it's satisfying, even the controls are fine. The main issue is that enemies telegraphing and the timing for parries are inconsistent. You have to parry way before they start attacking to land a parry in most cases, which makes the visual cue feel pointless, the visual cue happens about a second too late. That would also be easy to fix...Game feels great overall and the art and ost is amazing but it baffles me that the tiniest issues that hurt the game so much and would be very easy to fix just aren't getting fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: Loot River is overall a unique experience with its sliding block mechanic, but the gimmick runs itself thin VERY fast and doesn't do much to progress or evolve itself. It tries to lean too much into being Dark Souls while also still trying to be a Roguelike.Pros:- Good aesthetic. Loot River has a very pretty art style that leans heavily into the "Soulslike" vibe of dread. - The sound design is fine and works for what the game is going for- The sliding block mechanic is something not seen in any other game priorCons: - Meta progression feels mostly non-existent. All upgrades feel superfluous and nothing is ever permanent besides the artifacts that only serve, thus far, to make annoyances less annoying. If I could freely choose hats, starting weapons, and garbs ON TOP OF more nuanced meta progression which currently doesn't exist, this would feel better.- Combat is incredibly 1-dimensional. You slap. You dodge/parry. You cast spells that don't really seem to do much of anything. That's really it. Any items you get add a smidge of flavor to the combat, but again seem more focused on the Dark Souls side of things with stat scaling and synergy. - Healing being tied to a merchant sucks. It just does. Investing is basically required to make sure you have ample potions later on, and this system only seeks to make taking damage INCREDIBLY frustrating and punishing. The whole point of something like Dark Souls is permanent progression through tough areas with occasional checkpoints. Loot River tries to be Dark Souls but without understanding what makes that game good. You don't keep any weapons. You don't upgrade any weapons. You don't keep any of the armor you unlock. It's Dark Souls but if every time you died you restarted back at the beginning of the game instead of a bonfire.

_childDocuments_.review: When I played on release, I had a list of issues with this game that really let it down overall and it felt like it would have benefited from an Early Access release instead. It was a huge shame after being keen to get my hands on it. However, in the short span of time since its launch, the dev team have acknowledged the state of the game, and already a fair few of the QoL issues have been tweaked/fixed to improve the overall game feel. To name a few of the improvements since launch:- Dash no longer a blink tp with no animation telegraph - now has trail and animation- First major boss encounter used to be too easy to safespot and cheese - now has added moveset variation and mechanics to make fight more interesting.- Parrying and overall combat tweaks / less instances of the moving platforms being buggy- Progression has been eased with half of your main unlock currency being halved instead of completely lost. (game felt a bit too punishing - even after getting quite far in a run there'd be nothing to show for it)I really appreciate the transparency from the team about this games short comings post release, and I believe this is a great foundation to work from. I can't wait for further updates and look forward to what the team will do. If you're on the fence I would say wait and see what more updates will bring, but I still think this game is worth checking out for its unique movement system, souls-like feel/atmosphere and visual style. The combat still could use some further tweaks to make things smoother, and more interesting loot pickup variations could be added for greater build variety, but from what I've seen in the 9 days it's been out - this will no doubt improve.

Getting frozen in place, enemies not being able to damage me, me knot being able to damage enemies just being a few I experienced from my last run.In addition to general bugs, the game suffers from pacing issues. The second level is way too long and repetitive. It makes future runs agonizingly boring to play. Also, it is not clear how to equip gear that you have purchased via the meta-run currency called knowledge. Im not sure that you can, which seems like an oversight.The lack of meaningful meta progression is a bummer, bc the gameplay is just not that fun without the ability to get stronger. The roll is bizarre, both mechanically and aesthetically. Seriously, what is wrong with it?All in all, it feels like a very early access title, not really a finished product. There is promise here, but feels like it needs serious work.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately commits the cardinal sin of game design and neglects to make the core moment-to-moment gameplay loop fun and satisfying.In terms of presentation, Loot River looks fantastic and sounds good. The souls-like inspired world and dialogue is well done. It has a lot of ideas I like, significant things like the moving platforms and smaller things like the ability to risk a lower potion count in the current zone for more in the next one.But the combat, which is what you'll be doing 90% of the time, just isn't fun. It's obviously attempting souls-like combat with heavy and deliberate movesets, parrys, and counters, but the view and the 3D-model-to-pixel-art aesthetic makes it very hard to see what's going on. In addition to the visual issues, there are plenty of control/timing issues holding it back. The enemy animations are so quick it's impossible to parry without spamming the parry button, but that feels cheap and isn't fun. Enemies will hit you when you think they shouldn't and vice versa. The player gets stuck on enemies/walls all the time, as if their hitbox was pineapple shaped.There a multitude of smaller issues that I could mention but I won't dwell on them. For example, I haven't seen any armour drops after the first run I did. You can buy an expensive weapon on one run (that's meant to persist), but you don't have the option to choose that weapon to start the next run with, you have to always start with the same two weapons and then wait for your unlocked ones to drop. Magic abilities are tied to weapons, so a weapon could drop that does more damage than your current one, but doesn't have any magic spells, so now you are forced to stop using magic.There is a _lot_ of potential in this game, and I really don't want the developer to be discouraged because it's obvious a lot of love and effort went into Loot River. However, it has been released much too early without proper playtesting and QA, which would have found these issues. It should have been released into early access and had time to gather feedback and mature into a great game, but as it's been released straight to 1.0, I have to be critical of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I like this game for what it is, but I would recommend it with the caveat that it's probably only for more hardcore roguelike fans.ProsCombat is simple but works well- dodge, parry, light attack, heavy attack, and various spells. Each weapon has unique traits and movesets. There's no stamina system but I think that keeps combat short and tense.The platform maneuvering system is unique and well implemented. It opens up some new opportunities and tactics you wouldn't normally see in a roguelike game. Occasionally it devolves into some light puzzle solving but it never really gets in the way of going through the game.Solid but short gameplay loop. A successful run only takes around 45 minutes or so, but there are multiple paths you can take so it hits the sweet spot of not taking too long, but not getting stale from repeating the same areas endlessly.Pixel art graphics are very well done.ConsReally only one thing I didn’t like about the game, but it is a big one compared to other popular games in the genre.The meta progression is bad. Unlocking new weapons, items, and spells just adds them to the pool of items you can find as drops or in chests. But there isn’t any way to influence what drops – you are at the mercy of the RNG. I get that roguelikes often don’t let you choose your ideal gear as an intentional part of the gameplay experience, but drops/chests are fairly rare in this game and once you have an expanded pool of items it really feels like a crapshoot. I’m fine with stats and weapons resetting upon death, but besides the modifiers there isn’t a lot of meta progression in your character. You never unlock new abilities that persist between runs. Not 100% necessary but for players looking for gradual changes as they complete more runs they won’t find it here.Gold is pretty much worthless. Vendors carry 1 random item and are rare. I’ve never really felt like it added anything to my runs.Suggestion to alleviate both of those- Add a merchant to the Sanctuary that sells a variety of items for gold, and allows spending gold to reroll the selection. This would give players more control over their equipment on any run while also giving gold a lot more value on individual runs.Offering a random selection of 3-4 sets of gear from your unlocked item pool at the start of a run would also be a nice way to reward players for investing in new gear.Knowledge shouldn’t disappear upon death. As the meta progression currency I should be allowed to bank it without investing it into unlocks ASAP. Not a huge issue, but was notable to me.Summary- if you don’t mind a more pure RNG based roguelike experience, I think the cool art style and unique gameplay mechanics make this worth checking out. It’s not overly difficult, though it is challenging most players should be able to beat it within a dozen attempts or so.That being said, I think that more casual players will enjoy a game like Dead Cells or Curse of the Dead Gods much more due to much stronger meta progression and control over your build/gear on each run. I think Loot River has a very solid foundation that it doesn’t capitalize on due to some interesting design choices that are to the detriment of the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: For a game called Loot River, it makes the cardinal sin of not having enough loot in the river.Most of the weapons, armor and spells you unlock as you progress will never be seen in-game, which is a baffling decision from the devs. The people who finished the game clock it at 10 hours… but, in my defense, I was playing with the High Stakes modifier which didn’t really give more loot but definitely buffed the enemies. I died often to hits that took half my health. Once I got rid of it, I beat it in one try.I think it’s a good game, bar one glaring shortcoming; the gameplay loop is boring. Now, you only notice this once you pass the 10 hours… so most people shouldn’t encounter it (stupid modifier).Now what I mean by boring gameplay loop is that the lack of loot makes every run feel the same, that you’re going through the motions, that you’ve seen all that there is to see AND STILL, the game withholds juicy, juicy loot from you. And that’s the whole point of dungeon crawlers… otherwise why in god’s name, would you face the dangers and darkness of the dungeon?The platform movement gimmick is awesome and many of the puzzles were satisfying to complete.Consider this a mixed review because although I enjoyed the first 10 hours, it became a bore thereafter.

_childDocuments_.review: Loot River is a crazy, hardcore, and fun, mashup between Dark Souls, Hades, and Tetris. Currently my only issue is that it can be a little too punishing at times with very little progress carrying over if you die before spending your resources. I am enjoying the challenge and difficulty regardless. I'll update the review as I progress through the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Loot River is an interesting game. I'd say that the Soulsborne aspect is mixed with some Metroidvania. The sliding platform aspect of the game creates a puzzle aspect as well and is a pretty unique way to approach movement through the labyrinths. If the sliding platform thing exists in another Soulsborne/Metroidvania game, I personally haven't played it. This creates a pretty cool approach to the genres.The combat itself can be pretty unforgiving and it's also kind of easy to get lost on the screen, but despite that and enemy groups tending to skip tactics in favor of swarming, some types of enemies do actually use minimal tactics to try to gain an advantage. Still, the overarching theme is to get as close to you as possible and then use whatever weapon they have available.Some enemies do however have ranged and magical attacks to spruce things up a bit, and there are some traps here and there.You have limited healing potions available, and your moveset includes two equipped weapons with their own light and strong attack plus special damage or effect AND a dash, plus defense which I haven't actually used lol.There are NPCs you will encounter, and when you die or finish a level, you are sent back to your Sanctuary, where various NPCs congregate much in the same way you'd expect in an actual Souls series game (most similar to Demon's Soul).The actual animations and general graphics look pretty cool and the audio is serviceable.I haven't decided if I actually enjoy this game, but it's definitely interesting and I don't feel like my initial time with the game was wasted. Especially since I got this game as part of a Humble bundle.It is perfectly suited to the Steam Deck and plays just fine on there.
_childDocuments_.name: Loot River

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, it's aesthetically and stylistically very appealing.Unfortunately, the basic movement and combats mechanics feel unpolished, and result in clunkiness, inconsistency and unpredictability that often lead to frustration rather than the punishing-but-fair challenge the developers are aiming for.A lot of minor issues contribute to this, such as:- Collision detection is awkward, your character easily gets stuck on corners, stairs, or small obstacles. Your character will get stuck walking alongside a straight wall if the control stick is angled even slightly into the wall. No attempt to slide along in the direction you meant.- Stairs work awkwardly in general. Sometimes you can walk onto them from odd directions and sometimes not. Sometimes enemies get stuck on them. Sometimes it's impossible to hit an enemy directly in front of you just because you're near the top of some stairs.- Usually you can dodge-roll through enemies to get behind them, sometimes you just get stuck on them and get hit.- Inputs sometimes seem to be ignored. Possibly an issue with lack of input queuing, or maybe cooldowns with no visual/audio cue? Not sure, but sometimes dodge or attack chain combo inputs just seem to unexpectedly not do anything.- Hitboxes feel inconsistent. Sometimes an enemy attack will miss even when your character is standing directly in front of the enemy and the swing clearly connected; sometimes an attack will hit even though you are standing behind the enemy and the attack was directed away from you.- Charged attacks sometimes seem to whiff when used across platforms that you just connected.Some of the boss encounters are not particularly intuitive and will likely kill an unprepared player who doesn't figure out the mechanics and intended strategy quickly. Experimenting with unfamiliar items can lead to a quick demise as well, like the charm which added bombs to my attack combos but it turns out the bombs deal massive self-damage, or the vision-impeding hat which, in a bossfight, zoomed in the camera and locked it on the boss, leaving important parts of the arena off-screen. Sudden deaths like this that don't feel entirely the player's fault would probably be less of a problem if not for the above basic mechanical issues, which make the prospect of getting sent back to the start to muddle through earlier sections all the more of a chore.Runs have high variance in difficulty depending on what loot you find, mainly weapons, but you don't have much control over this. A run where you find a level 5 weapon in the second area and can kill most enemies in one hit from then on is a bit of a cakewalk, but you can just as easily never see a weapon much better than your starting one and have no real chance at all.It's a shame because these are all minor issues on their own, but add up to make a game that otherwise could have been great just not that much fun to play.Would be happy to change this to a positive review if some of these issues got sorted out in future updates.

_childDocuments_.review: This game seemed to be off on rough start, but within two weeks of launch, the devs seem to have made some great changes and responded well to player feedback!First time I played this and I sunk over 2 and a half hours in, so it's definitely been fun. The game has enough content and randomization to make each run feels a little different and interesting, while remaining consistent: I don't feel like I got screwed over any particular run by RNG, but instead just by my poor decisions, haha. Modifiers do a good job of helping you out too after you get through the initial toughness. The ability to invest partial amounts of knowledge in items in-between runs is also very helpful.I enjoyed learning strategies on how to mix the platform-sliding mechanics with the combat. Lots of equipment slots, a stat-leveling system, responsive dash mechanics, and even a spell system all add to the combat and give you lots of reasonable options to work with, which I really appreciated. After a while you learn small additional techniques and what initially seemed tough to achieve becomes manageable, bit-by-bit. Overall, I think it's very well-paced for a roguelite.Occasionally the game gives you breaks from combat to solve sliding puzzles, which I think also helps pace the game out, especially if you're tensed up from combat, haha. Although sometimes these puzzles can require a good amount of back-tracking, so you have to work carefully to not set yourself up for failure.tl;dr well-paced but will get you thinking. If you like magic, melee combat, and puzzles, then this game is for you.
