_childDocuments_.review: was excited about this game as it seems like a good mix of some of the indie games i have played and really enjoyed. the moment side to side is really weird and tbh i feel it was lacking when it came to the characters movement when talking. i enjoyed the storyline but feel it was executed badly. there could have been so much more added to the storyline and gamep-lay in general but lacked.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: Each game from Annapurna Interactive is unique and full on charming narrative and heartwarming story. So buying Open Roads I expected a short but cozy and inspiring road-movie. Unfortunately the game dissapointed me hardly.I was aware of its strange visual style combining 3D environment with 2D characters but thought it is an artistic choice that would benefit the game. Instead I got a cut-costs decision with barely animated sprites that almost do nothing. The game has a lot of boring dialogues about noting like "Hey mom, here's an old hat, what do you think about it?" or "Hey mom, I found a picture of our old dog. But let's forget about it."The story pretends to be a mystery or a detective but reveals itself like a simple parent-child drama with no deep morale or philosophy. And it's not like a "good old simple story", it's . The final plot-twist from one side can be seen hours before ending, and from other it turns out to be unpredictable and stupid.The exploration itself is very simple and sometimes force you to walk around for minutes after you already found a solution. Aaaand btw there're no puzzles - just things like "walk around the house, say Hey mom, find the key, go back, open the door, then repeat to open the 2nd door". If you want a good exploration walking simulator game,  from the same publisher.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: The actors performances for the voice overs were top notch, and honestly that is what really made the game good.But I felt there was a bit missing as well.  The black screen instead of cut scenes was one that that caught me off guard, it gave it a slight unfinished feel.  The other area that made it feel unpolished, was the characters were not animated when speech was happening.  I did enjoy the artistic style, and the story.  For the cost it was about the right length, and I loved how well the professional actors made it come alive.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: Cute graphic styling but this game was literally 2.3 hours long, fairly boring, and not worth the money, even 30% off. $13.99 for 2 hours of gameplay is a ripoff, and I would have been even less satisfied had I paid the whole 20 bucks. When I read the credits it said that it was developed over years... for what? I don't see how this could have taken so much time and resources for what little was delivered. Buy it if you have money to waste and are easy to entertain, otherwise spend it elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't recommend it because for me the game mechanics just weren't my particular bag (bit more detail below). However! - I think another player might really love it. I will say that the voice acting by Kaitlyn and Keri is beautiful (as one would expect). There were some nicely scripted scenes and I think the writing was definitely heartwarming and the game pace was good if you're wanting something meditative :)However, it is very walking sim, which I didn't think would be quite so one-track. There are little to no puzzles and a strange lack of logic in which things can be picked up/opened and which can't. I don't imagine that everything you touch should yield something interesting (that would be worse), but to have 15 cleaning products in a room and you can pick up 4 or 5 of them for no reason but not the other 10 or 11? Maybe just make everything interactive or certain categories of things not (like cleaning products)? I think a good percentage of game play was just picking up and putting down random things. This I found a bit puzzling because when there was something to find it was always in an obvious place that required little to no discovery. There was some information to be observed on objects (rather than found inside them) which became relevant later in the game, but nothing the would really require you to be able to pick them up. Also, I figured out the story in about early Chapter 2 and then I'll admit I got somewhat impatient as it continued. But a charming game, I'm sure there are many who are just in the perfect mood for it!
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: The story is fairly boring. Dialogue choices all tend to lead to the same place making them pointless.  The visual style is bizarre mixing realistic environments with animation and the animation itself is very simplified.  Cutscenes involve minimal character movement or even mouth movement for dialogue.  Anti aliasing appears to do nothing, so everything in the game looks jagged.  Camera movement also feels jittery.  It's an unfortunate experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: This "game" was suggested to me because of other walking sims I have played, I guess. A bit of explanation, I think that while the scenery is kind of well done, the slow story unfolding and the slow movement in general almost made me give up. However I forced myself to continue. At the end it is more like a novel, told through your interaction with some "key object" triggering some interesting, so to speak, dialogue revealing the pieces of a family story. Don't want to spoil it, but the "game" is really short, in two hours and a half you get to learn all you need to learn. and that's it, done. It's indie, I get it, but I have played a few other similar games with at least more "meat to the bone", more suspense, more intrigue, etc. I would say $15 for this is 12 too many.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting a long time for this game to be released and had high expectations based on the sneak peaks we've gotten. While it's not an awful game, it just feels so unfinished. I tried to stretch it out for as long as possible, and only got three hours. The story isn't explored in any depth at all. I also found some of the dialogue unrealistic, and the animations uninteresting. It sort of seems like the developers had to hurry up and finish something, and that this isn't the product that was meant to be. I tried really hard to like this game, and I did feel slightly engaged towards the end. But then it was over before it really began. The worst part is that it's simply boring. I would recommend only getting this game if it's free or very cheap. In that case, it's worth it because there are some enjoyable bits.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: this is an incredibly good addition to the narrative adventure/exploration genre, which pretty much these guys started along with the creators of "dear esther" back in 2013. the story, the surroundings (takes you into believable worlds of 2003 and 1968), the cartoony graphics, the two likeable main characters and all the ones we get to learn about over the course of the game, the music, the professional voicing, humor, everything is ten out of ten here. "tacoma" wasn't a disappointment in any respect, a cool game with different ideas, art style and game play techniques, but this gem here is the real spiritual successor to the classic masterpiece that's called "gone home".
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: This game just feels like another walking simulator and not a particularly interesting one at that. Most of the game is just picking up random stuff and going "hey mom". This game also has an intriguing (at first) art style with a hand drawn aesthetic over a 3d background but the allure wears off quickly once you realize the characters are hardly animated and are little more than 2d sprites that don't actually add all that much. _childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game a lot. A lot of people might find the combination of 3D and 2D graphics a little off putting but I really didn't mind it. The story telling is done well with some amazing voice acting. The game is not particularly long, so you should be able to finish it in one session which I highly recommend doing.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: This visual novel/walking simulator has a nice visual style, good voice acting, and a good enough story to make for a decent diversion if you're a fan of the genre and get the game for a decent price. Probably not worth paying full price though, definitely get it on sale. It's by no means the best you can find in the genre, however. The story is pretty sort, and very linear. There are no branching paths, alternate endings, etc. The dialogue choices don't seem to matter, really. The really good examples of this type of game, like Gone Home, have items and clues off the main story path that give you glimpses into side-plots and other people's pasts, not just the main story. There are a few instances of "extra information" that you don't need to complete the game and paint a bit more of the larger picture, but they're pretty scanty. It may sound like I should have thumbs-downed this game, but as I said, it's a decent enough game for the time it takes to play, so long as you get it at a good price.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a breath of fresh air.  Just like Gone Home and Tacoma before it, this was a nice break to play something else in a sea of games that are too similar to each other.  This game, while it still is great, falls short of what Gone Home was able to achieve. Open Roads does a decent job of keeping the player engaged, but I think the level of interaction with the environment was just so much better in Gone Home.  I also believe that Gone home was superior because there were two storylines to follow. One that is laid out in front of you, and another... that is found if you pay attention to the clues and clippings scattered about the house.  I really loved that approach of a second, hidden story going on under the surface which had an arguably more important story than the one that the audience was supposed to experience. Open Roads still had an  interesting story, but wasn't as impacting to me as Gone Home was.  Gone Home actually was able to have me get all teary eyed, whereas Open Roads just simply kept me entertained.  I'm thankful that Open Roads is at least a step in the right direction again, whereas Tacoma was largely forgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: Was it worth all the wait? All that hype? Probably not. Does it live up to Gone Home and Tacoma? I think in terms of the story it tells, absolutely.It's touching, incredibly well-written and an engaging story about a family, told through the lens of the women of that family. If that's your jam, then you'll love this.Just know there's more than meets the eye to the story. There is SCANDAL and there is INTRIGUE. Prepare ur ahnuzz.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game but not without criticism.It's certainly in tone with Gone Home and Tacoma, and that's a lot to say. The story is pretty good although it plays a subservient role to the main characters (no surprise here), who are excellently written and played (no surprise here either). Voice acting is  praiseworthy. I really like the characters, and I could empathize strongly with them and their motivations since the start. Of course they play on nostalgia and relatability. All this I wanted when purchased the game and all this I got, so I upvote.  The game definitely doesn't feel smooth. The roaming sections are of no splendor but not bad. I couldn't say they are beautiful nor cozy. You can interact with a lot of objects, and most of the time that is simply pointless. It doesn't add to the experience. And controls are weird. I can't really point my finger on what is really bugging me here, but I need to say that there was something inherently annoying in the actual-gameplay. There are at least two art decisions that are very jarring and distracting, and that for some times it kind of ruined the experience for me. The first one is the yuxtaposition of 3D-environment with 2D-characters. I am usually fine with these kind of stylistic choices but this time around it didn't work out. The second one is that characters are mostly not-animated, so they seem like in a comic. What's worse is that ocassionaly they move their mouths even though they are not speaking. Eventually you get used to both things, but they never ceased to be irritating to some extent. Finally, the game is overpriced.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like some of the reviews here are unduly harsh. I liked the game.1. Voice acting is excellent.2. Visuals are a little static, but mostly okay, although the last sequence, which takes place on a houseboat, has extremely static water. It's always difficult to make water look good in a game, but the devs should probably have invested in a third-party solution to provide more visual appeal here.3. It's a walking sim; I like walking sims, if well done, and this is, actually. No real puzzle solving, just environment exploration, but that's a perfectly legitimate way to make a game.4. The story is good. Enough twists to make it interesting.5. The mother/daughter dynamic is entirely believable -- fraught, but not extremely so, and both characters are sympathetic.6. Character animation is a little flat; mostly cuts between different images, VN-style, but with occasional lip animation and such at key moments.7. Play time is a bit short, but I'm tolerant of that, if I like the game in other regards, and I did here.I do not regret either the money I spent on the game (albeit I bought it on sale), nor the time spent with these characters. It was about what I wanted for while away a weekend day.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely beautiful game with a cool mix of 2D and 3D with lovely art and amazing voice acting! The characters really pull you in and the story tugs on your heartstrings so much, it especially hit close to home for me. I adored the journey I took through this along with Tess and Opal! And I am happy that being a menace got me rewarded with so many achievements lol!
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game mostly because I was intrigued with the artwork. And it is pretty interesting overall. With the way I could interact with the objects I had one very funny scene where a vase hung awkwardly suspended in the background that I particularly enjoyed. That said, I would have liked a little more action with the characters, especially Opal. The professional ventriloquist act took a little getting used to. The interaction with some of the objects felt a little weird in spots. My idea of what I should be able to interact with while investigating a family mystery is different than what I could interact with. It was fun picking out some of the items that my parents and grandparents had (I recognize those coasters) Overall the storyline was good and I felt the dialogue choices were plentiful enough to keep me interested. I do agree with some of the other reviews that the story felt a bit short, but I don't feel it was detrimental. I am glad that I could undo automatic dialog in the options (I don't read THAT fast). Overall a relaxing slice of life with a bit of mystery and intrigue.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend the game if you enjoy walking simulators, and I don't mean that as an insult.  This game is a chill time, with great writing, and a pensive, slightly-melancholy, bittersweet tone.Much like Gone Home, a lot of the fun in these sort of games comes from snooping around, and appreciating how a story is told through the environment.  It's not an over-the-top thriller; but a more grounded, very human story.As I said, the writing is great, and it's brought to life by stellar voice acting.  Both the lead actresses are extremely talented, and brought so much nuance to their characters.  It was great listening to Tess and Helen's mother-daughter banter.I was very charmed by the early 2000s nostalgia at the start, as well as the mix of 2d art and animation with 3d environments.  My biggest critique is that I wish there was a little more sense of exploration, like in Gone Home.  Exploration feels more on-rails (ironically) in Open Roads.An honest story, with a major theme of the legacy of family across generations.  If going on a little adventure roadtrip with mom in the year 2003 sounds appealing, then check this out
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: It was a fun little indie game. I got into the story. I would say that they reuse a lot of the same objects so sometimes it feels like they cut corners in some areas. _childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: Game play is curiosity-based, so it can be accomplished in as quickly as 25 minutes or as leisurely as 4 hours. The intrigue to the story is fairly compelling and the unpacking of intergenerational trauma is worthwhile, but the most dynamic character is the newly deceased grandmother. The mother in particular lacks dimension. Still, the story itself is worthwhile. Feels a bit pricey for the play time, so I'd recommend saving this for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: interesting walking sim, great voice acting, looks great, interesting environments to walk around. And a story to discover about a mother and her daughter, trying to bond over a journey into her mother's past (and grandmother's)Unfortunately the use of cartoons in a 3d environment is very bold. Also the "need" to keep calling your mother (as you play as the daughter) to start the conversation and getting to see the same animations over and over again is very lazy and boring. And not that it's a good thing, because most items you pick up, have nothing special to check for. But fomo if you don't pick it up and looking for clues you dont need to find. _childDocuments_.review: The story for the game was quite enticing, considering how short the game was.The full price of £15.99 for a rough 2~hour experience I would say is a bit high.The conversations between Tess and Opal were mostly of rinse and repeat facial animations, would've been nice to create more, as the art style initially caught my interest, but in result having a hand full amount of animations really made it lacklustre.The voice acting was of good quality, really enjoyed the VAs.Overall, I enjoyed the experience and would suggest it to anyone in search of a relaxing evening with a simple story about a grandma, a mother, an aunt, and a daughter.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a LONG time in my wish list, waiting to be released. Fortunately i kept it there, because it's really awesome. Fleshes out Mother-Daughter relationship excellently. I warmly recommend this game. It's really great.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: The game is short (shorter then Martin Short), in two hours (dealing with loss, dealing with unknowns ...) all is unraveled.The graphics are great, but the characters (Tess and Opal) look like Scooby Doo (60'ies) extras (so not for everyone's taste).I grew up in the 80ies so a lot of things are familiar and has a great atmosphere of a bygone era.The voice acting is 'cool' and has some fun lines.So overal price/quality I would say okay, I also like this genre of games (gone home, dontnot games ..)
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: A nice, cosy, short storytelling adventure game. Fans of this genre, like Tell Me Why, Gone Home or Life is Strange, will appreciate this.The fact that it's quite a short game and can be completed in one sitting might be an appeal, for some players.To be honest, yes, I did feel some disappointment. The game isn't perfect. It's short and over so soon. Coming from the creativity and novelty of Gone Home and Tacoma, through years of development hell and waiting, this game did feel quite small and over surprisingly soon.The price per hours of gameplay is, arguably, quite high compared to some other games.The juxtaposition of the 3D engine with the 2D cel-shaded scenes (reminiscent of "Scarlet Hollow" or "Detective Ridelle") is interesting and breaks up the 3D scenes a bit, but it does time take away from free-form exploration and nonlinearity in the 3D world.It does feel like there's quite a bit of forced linearity here - whereas, say, Gone Home had a lot more nonlinearity and player freedom to explore many places in any order.I understand the team has been through turmoil and they've worked hard to get the game completed and delivered.Despite minor disappointments, I buy this game and support this game in the hopes that the creators will have more support and resources in the future to make their next game bigger and better, which I absolutely know they're capable of.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: A decent to good story elevated by very good voice work. One of the few games like this with a teen protagonist that actually reads like a teenager. Probably helped by taking place during a time when I was a teenager, so i actually know whether people sounded like that.A very Jamrock Shuffle sort of game, you could probably "speed through" the whole narrative in maybe an hour most of which would be voice clips, but it was worth poking around and seeing what dialogue could fall out, didn't have a bunch of annoying repetition, and it feels like only one single instance of "This dialogue feels like it's not aware of the dialogue we already had"Not a deeply emotional game in the way that a Gone Home or a Tell Me Why is, but the characters felt real, their motivations consistent, conflict when it was warranted, and quality voice work.Definitely worth a play for people who like narrative games.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I have really enjoyed this game, it's a good length, has a fantastic story that has a little bit of everything with good character arcs.  I have had this on my wish list after a trailer was shown at one of the awards shows last year or the year before.  The game leaves me wanting to know more so maybe there will be a follow up store to this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: There was a lot I really loved about this game, but there were also a couple things I didn't like.The mixed art styles are very unique and beautiful to look at, the ambient/background sounds were amazing, and the voice acting was great. It also had a lot of things to interact with.With all of that being said, the story is so... meh. I am not hard to impress at all - I love all kinds of stories. But this was honestly just a bit boring. As I was nearing the end I just kept thinking of all the other ways they could have come up with a more interesting story than this. This is the kind of thing I would give a neutral review if Steam had that option. Overall, I enjoyed it enough and I would recommend it for the chill exploration and scenery. (Only on sale though - I can't recommend a 3 ish hour game with a bland story for $20.) But if you're only interested in the story, skip this. It's very forgettable.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: Rollercoaster of a story. I know this will draw a lot of comparison to Gone Home which is heralded as a feat in storytelling (and it is). But I honestly felt more wrapped up in this game's story and characters which they do an incredible job of capturing the lives and intricacies of. The game takes about 3 hours to complete if you look at everything and also listen to the voice acting instead of skipping through dialogue (and you absolutely should listen to the voice acting, it is very good). Would have loved for it to be longer, but I'm also glad it didn't drag it out or pad in with unnecessary filler and went straight to delivering what it set out to in an effective way. Regardless it is absolutely worth the play.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Gone Home then you may like Open Roads. This title is more linear than Gone Home, but the story and relationship between the two main characters made up for the lack of exploration for me. This game is set in 2003 and hits some fun nostalgia beats from that era (flip phones, soundtrack, easter eggs, etc.) but does not smack you over the head with "the year is 2003, aren't you entertained by that?" like some titles would. You can play through the main story rather quickly, unless like me you are an OCD explorer and pick up everything. However even doing that only adds an hour or so. You are presented with various dialogue options throughout the game, but as of this review I have only played through the game twice so I am unsure if there are multiple endings or not and whether those choices have any real impact. The graphics are nice to look at, and the environments look realistic. The characters are presented in a 2D animation style that contrasts with the world around them though. This is an interesting choice the designers made, and at various times while playing I did not care for it, but at others I did. I do wish there were a few more animations included (especially for Tess) that would help match with the emotion of the dialogue. Sometimes I felt the characters were not emoting enough with the words they were speaking. Oh yes, the voice acting here is top notch! Kaitlyn Dever and Keri Russell voice the two main characters, and I enjoyed both of their performances very much. All-in-all if you enjoy visual novel-style games, are interested in seeing a nuanced mother-daughter dynamic play out, and like unraveling a little mystery check this game out.
_childDocuments_.name: Open Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I've had this one my wishlist for yeaaarss and I was so excited to finally play it! I only wish the playthrough was longer! Open Roads is a cozy story game about exploring around trying to solve a secret family mystery. The 3D graphics are beautiful and while I wish the cut scenes were also in 3D, the 2D scenes grow on you. Dialogue is both cute and extremely realistic for mother and teenage daughter. I love how Theresa wants to keep digging deeper and pushes her mom out of her comfort zone to discover the truth.

_childDocuments_.review:
One fine fall day, Tess Devine and her mother, Opal, discover a cache of old notes and letters carefully stashed away in the attic of their house. Hints of deep-rooted family secrets, decades-old burglaries, a lost treasure somewhere near the Canadian border... What they uncover suggests a much darker mystery, best left well enough alone.

In Open Roads, Tess and Opal embark on a road trip adventure to explore a series of long-abandoned family properties, unearthing the past. They'll search the ruins of these places that hold buried memories, things Opal has tried for years to forget. And in this search, they'll discover not just the truth they've been seeking, but each other.

name: COCOON
detailed_description: From Jeppe Carlsen, the lead gameplay designer of LIMBO and INSIDE — COCOON takes you on an adventure across worlds within worlds. Master world-leaping mechanics to unravel a cosmic mystery. Worlds within Worlds COCOON is a unique take on the puzzle adventure genre, where each world exists within an orb that you can carry on your back. Wrap your head around the core mechanic of leaping between worlds—and combine, manipulate, and rearrange them to solve intricate puzzles. Alien Machinery Interact with alien environments and biomechanical devices left behind by an ancient civilization. Journey through unique and diverse biomes, from industrial structures to massive organic caverns, and discover how they are connected to one another. Orb Abilities Each orb has an ability that can be unlocked, thereby turning the orb into a unique tool for you to utilize within other worlds. Use these abilities to uncover hidden pathways and objects, fire projectiles to trigger switches, and more. Monstrous Guardians Mighty guardians protect every world, and you must face them in fierce battles. Each fight is unique and requires you to master new and satisfying mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Cocoon treats you to a truly alien world. I cannot recall another game world that is so alien and unrelatable to our own. It has its own logic and meaning. The closest other game worlds might be those of Amanita Games, Abzu, or Journey.Cocoon takes a big leaf out of the Half-Life book and subliminally teaches you the mechanics and logic of its world. It is done so masterfully that I didn't even notice that I was learning. When you get stuck in a puzzle, know that the game has already taught you all you need to know to solve it. The game shows you what your brain is capable of. The Ah-ha! Moments are numerous. While I was never stuck on a puzzle too long, the game could get tiring. A brief break always produced the solution.I am sure there is some meaning to all that one sees and experiences. There are themes of cocooning, metamorphosis, and nested worlds and I am sure the internet has gotten together to figure it all out on some wiki. But I am content keeping this alien world as it is - a mystery.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Good puzzle game. Starts off easy, then gets twisty and difficult.It is _absolutely gorgeous_ this is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.The super easy controls (just directions, one action button, and also a pause button) should make it easy to play even by people who aren't used to using game controller or have trouble physically using them. But that's undermined by the many puzzles that require quick execution and good timing, and the boss fights that were surprisingly challenging.It took me 4 hours to play. (This is a good length, I like short games.)
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Cocoon is a great puzzle game that is based on the same type of "platform learning" approach that Portal did so well, and without any hint of dialog to guide you. The novel element, of using orbs of self-contained worlds that you can move through and use for additional world triggers is quick to learn but presents enough of a variety of challenges. It fortunately is a short game but that gives enough time to appreciate the elements without overplaying their welcome. The artwork is great and abstract, interesting enough but without being distracting to identify the key elements. It is definitely one of the better indie games that has been released this year and well worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful and evocative experience.The environments, visual and audio touches, and haunting music all combine to create a mesmerizing world that is easy to understand in the broad strokes (Cocoon = Metamorphosis/Evolution/etc.), but I think deeply personal in what aspects will speak to each individual player.The puzzles are perfectly paced, in my experience, never getting too complex to be frustrating, but gradually ramping up the layers of logic needed to make progress.Overall, an exemplary achievement in gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and kinda fun, but it doesn't really keep my attention. The universe is too well designed, too deliberate. The bosses all feel like puzzles to solve. I don't really feel any danger or motivation to clear them. They're challenging me, not trying to kill me. It's too streamlined and intelligently designed for such an organic and alien environment. There's no narrative elements to the game at all. I don't just mean lack of story in the form of text or storytelling — the boss battles, the pathways, the environment has no narrative. The second boss, for example, buries itself in the ground for no reason other than to expose its vulnerable spot to you. A better designed boss would bury itself in the ground out of fear or pain and *accidentally* reveal its weak spot. But there's no indication of even silent, causal narratives like this in anything that happens in the game. I don't even know where I'm at or why I'm doing what I'm doing. There's no motivation to play except solve another puzzle, and since some of them can be quite frustrating to figure out, I definitely need some sort of motivation to keep at it when it becomes unfun to do so.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Meh.The visual and sound design are captivating, coherently portraying a weird world combining squishy organics with machine-precision transports. There's no story, though there are cut scenes that seem to say something, environmentally, but perhaps it's not intended to be specific. Think of it as an impressionistic or conceptual play or dance. Or maybe I just missed an obvious message.And I must also commend the controls. A lot of work seems to have gone into calibrating them to feel properly responsive and fluid. Leaping between worlds, picking up spheres, and even just pattering around are all good.OK. But this is a puzzle game. Indeed it's  a puzzle game. There are a few boss fights, but they are actually just real-time puzzles. And the puzzles are: meh. If you play puzzle games then you will find 's to be quite easy, with the addition of some optional collectibles, some of which are just a bit hard to find. But the level of difficulty is not, in itself, a problem. The problem is that the solutions become more and more annoying. New mechanics get introduced as the game unfolds (literally!), but they just add more busywork for you. There's no sense of progress or direction. No map, no indication that you're going deeper, farther, or anywhere really. The lack of a story is surely part of the problem, too: it feels like from beginning to end it's just you moving spheres around.The world design wants you to be delighted. But the gameplay, instead, is relentless and even tedious. Especially the late game puzzles involve a lot of back and forth. For a game this short, that's a fatal flaw.Pretty! But there are much more satisfying puzzle games out there. Sorry, but have to give this one a thumbs down.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: A straightforward, fun puzzle game that takes the idea of "worlds within worlds" and really runs with it. It's a masterclass in taking a relatively simple mechanic and exploring all of its ins and outs to the max. It's short and not very difficult -- I would've preferred a longer runtime -- but it's jam-packed with eureka moments, and the unique concept combined with beautiful stylized graphics makes COCOON stand out from the deluge of other puzzle games out there.I can get not wanting to pay the full price for a ~5-10 hour game, but would definitely recommend buying it if it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: its the way my jaw was on the floor CONSTANTLY while playing through this. the art, the music, the puzzles are all top tier. it had a special way to make me uncomfortable even in the most pretty environment - the lack of exposition lends itself to the creepy aspect of the game. overall it is nothing short of gorgeous and stimulatingi will say, it is more in line with a really robust walking simulator than it is with a standard form 'puzzle' game. so if you are looking for a brain melter, you'll likely find faults in this game.one of those games i will play again just to look at it again, and that should speak for itself. the fact that they offered this ON SALE - wild to me buy it while its $20 cause that is a great and fair price for it
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: I love the puzzle game genre. Portal was the game that really brought me into the PC platform originally, and some of my absolute favourite games I've played over the years are brilliant puzzle games like Braid and Manifold Garden. Cocoon is yet another brilliant addition to the upper echelon of gaming puzzlers, and it may actually be my favourite since the original Portal 16 years ago now.The core concept in and of itself is interesting. Dimensions contained within orbs you can carry, manipulate, and nest within other orbs. Like most puzzle games it starts simple, giving the player enough time to understand the basics and fundamental rules. Each central mechanic is given enough time and space to be fully understood before moving on to the next big thing. By the end though the challenges go crazy recursive and creative while avoiding becoming so complex that things become unmanageable. It never felt as though any particular obstacle was too hard to find my way through and I was often surprised and delighted by the solutions the developers trusted me to figure out on my own.Also another part of the gameplay I thought was worthy of note are the boss fights. There aren't too many in the game, but I enjoyed each encounter so much I found myself looking forward to them. Each of them integrate a fun new gimmick so they all feel unique and memorable in their own right. The fights flow very well, feature good music and fun visual flourishes and spectacle, and are brief enough to be fun breaks in the game's pacing without ever feeling like distractions from the main puzzle solving game loop. It's rare that I find I enjoy a game's boss encounters much period, let alone to the degree I do here.The visuals and music combine to fill this entire adventure with atmosphere. The visuals are clean, and nice looking. The game offers landscapes, architectures and technologies that are recognizable mixed perfectly alongside worlds and designs that are altogether completely alien. As for the soundtrack, from beauty, to loneliness, discovery, grandeur and awe, as well as anticipation for upcoming danger, the music effortlessly conveys or complements every given mood all throughout.Reached the end with all achievements in just under 5 hours. Didn't feel short, felt just right to me. Like it had a ton of amazing ideas and used all of them, ending long before it could run out of cool new things to show or overstay it's welcome. Considering how loaded with time wasting filler many games these days can feel, I think a leaner product like this is far preferable to some 20+ hour behemoth, but your mileage may vary on this regard.Overall Cocoon is an incredible release. Clever puzzles with near perfect pacing and difficulty matched with well put together bosses adding variety and excitement, and all of it backed by fantastic visuals and music. Couldn't recommend enough.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: COCOON takes you on an adventure across worlds within worlds.  This tagline is absolutely true.  This game is overflowing with creativity.  The puzzle design is ingenious, always entertaining, never annoying, and always nudging you forward in these beautiful words untarnished by any form of a UI or dialogue.  It’s fantastic.  Plays great on the Steam Deck too.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal.  The atmosphere and aesthetic are beautiful.  As a fan of puzzle games, I put this one up there in the list of all-time greats.  Some really unique twists to the world-within-world mechanic that you might have seen before.  Boss battles are actually pretty awesome, too.  All in all a great game.  10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: The core mechanics revolve around different colors of orbs (worlds), each with specific powers. At various points in the game you have them interact, either directly by world hopping or indirectly by nesting them and introducing outside elements into nested worlds and having their powers combine. The first half of the game is pretty breezy, but the difficulty ramps up later.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic puzzle game - feels very rewarding to figure out the puzzles; many of them will give you that 'eureka' moment. Would be ideal if your character could move a little faster. Conceptually it feels really rather unique, though it is mostly cosmetic. Progression/puzzle complexity is really thought out and balanced. If you're a fan of puzzle games then this a must buy!
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Cocoon is one of the most interesting puzzle games I've played. I hold it up with the greats like baba is you and tunic (for how much it counts). Every new puzzle adds an interesting twist to what you've already learned and it keeps iterating in an insanely fun and creative way. I never had to look up any of the puzzles which is honestly rare for me, I could manage to intuit every puzzle even if it took me a bit. And like all great puzzle games, it has that jaw dropping moment where the mechanics are turned on their head, except this game manages to do it 3 or so times! It managed to answer almost every "I wonder what would happen if..." that I came up with and I was never disappointed. Easy recommendation.I should note there is an alternate end and after seeing requirements I don't plan on going for it, though it doesn't seem to be required (at least not for achievements).
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: This game has amazing puzzles. I found them very enjoyable. I will say though, there were 2 puzzles I had to look online for. I don't think I would have figured them out, as they involved some recursive behavior. I love these kinds of games. I probably should've spent more time figuring out the recursive mechanic, but I think it was better to just get the assistance and move on. The game flows very well, and the time passed without me noticing. This is the second game I've 100%'d on Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Phew what a Game.A very interesting Puzzle/dexterity game.I loved every Minute of it. The atmosphere, the Music, the Visuals all are beautiful.As a Cherry on top all Achievements were (at least for me) gettable in a single playthrough.(with some careful exploring and only a singe, lucky, reload)All-in-all would recommend for People who like logistical Puzzels an don't dislike some skill-based Challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: What's there is a very well made game, but it's too thin for the $25 asking price. Wait for it to go down to $15 or so.Cocoon is a very smooth experience. It plays smooth, it looks good, the environments are neat, the bosses are fun, and your progress is never halted by a real stumper of a puzzle. However, that's also its biggest weakness. It's only a few hours long and lacks any real meat to justify its price point at that length. Its main puzzle mechanic is interesting, but only at the very end does it start getting in-depth enough to make solving puzzles satisfying on its own. Before then the solutions are always obvious at a moment's consideration. The puzzles aren't boring at any point, but they can't carry the experience alone. The bosses share this problem of being fun to play, but that's all. That's fine for a game like Limbo or Inside, where the puzzles serve as a medium to experience an atmospheric and intriguing world, but Cocoon doesn't have that. It looks nice and there are a few cool moments, but nothing that makes these environments feel like more than neat set-dressing.6/10, an enjoyable way to spend a few hours, wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Great game - long enough to get its point across and short enough not overstay its welcome.  All of the puzzles are very clever and do a great job of making you feel smart, even though many situations involve doing the only thing you can followed by the next only thing you can do, until finally the pieces click together and you understand what has to happen so you can proceed.  It's not super difficult and tries really hard not to frustrate you, so in the end it's a very satisfying experience.  However, this isn't really a game you buy for the replay value - like most puzzle games, once you know the solutions there's really no point in playing it again (at least, not until it's been so long that you forget everything and can go in "fresh" once more).Graphically, the game has a very interesting art style and the graphics look and feel great without requiring a supercomputer to run.  My 3080 Ti barely broke a sweat and didn't even upclock most of the time when running a flawless 1440p @ 144 FPS, so just about anything should be able to make this look good.I can't recommend this game enough.  It's one of those games that I feel like everyone should experience at least once.  Get some good headphones, try to curtail any distractions, and get lost jumping between orb worlds for about 6 hours or so.  You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to say how much I F*%$&*(ING HAAAAAAATTEEEE these bosses. WHY did they ruin such an otherwise pretty and intelligent game by having STUPID EXCELLENT TIMING PLATFORMING BOSSES that make no damn sense.  HATE these bosses SO BAD. And don't say 'git gud' - I play the kind of games that I like (which is Puzzle games NOT platforming) and I don't want this sort of stupid game mix that makes it impossible to proceed if you're good at thinking up solutions to problems (like the Cyan series and Kings Quest, etc) but seriously suck at platforming games that require exact timing and aiming WITH A KEYBOARD.  Maaaaaybe if there was a mouse controller it would be better, but this enforced platform bosses just SUCK.  I don't know if I can stand to continue the game which is really sad as it is an otherwise wonderful game.  Just some easy mode that would allow really simple boss fights with really slow bosses - making it a PUZZLE -  would be better.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: A very well designed puzzle platformer.It's short (it took me 4.5 hours to 100%, ), but fits a lot of content into that time without feeling at all cramped. Very good level design, with puzzles that make you think about what to do without leaving you with a headache - generally I found most puzzles to be a bit on the easy side, with a few exceptions dotted around, but they were still enjoyable nonetheless. Very balanced, and some very unique concepts that I haven't seen in other games before.There is no HUD, and yet it still managed to teach you every game mechanic easily. Very nice visuals, completely deserves it's Steam Awards 2023 nomination (which is where I found it).Being a puzzle platformer, there is very little replay value.There are also some collectibles (Moon Ancestors). None of them are too hard to find, and the game adds decoration as you get close to one of them to let you know. I only missed 4 going through it originally, and 2 of those were in very obvious places that I just didn't notice. There aren't too many of them, so there's no pressure to spend ages searching, and with there only being a few that aren't hidden in extremely difficult locations, they don't subtract anything from the experience and only add an extra few things to look out for, which I found fun.Overall, great game, but could do with the puzzles being a bit harder.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: For someone that has never really played a proper puzzle game before, Cocoon was a satisfying experience. With it often making my brain feel too beeg for my skull. I can't find fault in the design and many of the puzzles / boss fights were really clever. Despite this, I'm not sure if this type of game is for me. I played it all through once and found it pretty easy as the game guided me to the correct conclusions but never told me what the answers were. I don't see myself coming back to it, and I also don't know how long I'll remember it for. So I'm not sure how much the purchase was worth it for me.That being said, I can't fault anything about the games' quality. A fascinating world, amazing sound design, a unique and eerie aesthetic using very geometric shapes and organic bug-like designs, and lovely animations and visuals. It is a very neat 3-4 hour experience and if you are a fan of this genre, I can't see you going wrong.The narrative is very obtuse and quite disregardable, but I have no doubt that if one wanted to look into it more they could find a well planned and connected world as there are many visual clues spread that spread throughout your playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzle connoisseur review- Unique designs, - Ok mechanics- not difficult.- Most of time straight forward.- No options of abusing, brute forcing, or cheese. Everything has to be in certain order.Regardless is really good game, where i had great time.  And can recommend it.Similar mechanics : Patrick's Parabox
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: I highly enjoyed this game. This is a great puzzle game with a very relaxing atmosphere. The art style and the vibes I got from it were something between Journey and Monument Valley. The level design is well thought out for a puzzle game, and you really feel like you're in an alien world...within a world...within another world. The boss fights were fun and the puzzles are rewarding yet workable enough where you shouldn't need a guide. The music and sound effects are crisp and well harmonized to the gameplay. The only gripe I have, if any, is that its rather short. It took about five hours for one playthrough. Still, if you can get this game on sale (or even full price), this is a fantastic game.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what I'm looking at half the time, but ♥♥♥♥ if it ain't pretty. In all seriousness, this is a mind-bending indie gem that feels like a cool mix between Death's Door and Shadow of the Colossus.You don't know what you're doing half the time or why you're doing it but figuring out the way the orb worlds meld together to get you where you need to be is a hell of a mechanic.I hope this game gets a sequel and fully fleshes out these ideas, cause in a wholly positive way, Cocoon left me wanting much more.Overall, another win for AnnaPurna. Keep up the good work!10/10
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: A very minimalistic puzzle game.  Feels like the devs were challenging themselves to make a game where you only used one button.  The controls are simple.  You can move around and you can press the interact key.  Interacting with an orb picks it up or puts it down.  If you're not standing in front of an orb, it buzzes your insect wings, which can flip switch panels or press buttons.  And that's it.  With the minimalist controls, most of the puzzles revolve around moving orbs around.  Each of the colored orbs has a special "power" to manipulate the environment.  Like for example the red orb creates bridges if you're carrying it over certain areas.  Simply making it through a puzzle is usually not the complete package, you usually have to find a way to bring your orb (or eventually orbs) with you.  There are some very inventive solutions that require recursive thinking that I quite enjoyed and I didn't have to look anything up, but this is because you rarely can get distracted from the current problem since you're always only solving the current problem.  The game is also super linear - you have to input exactly the solution they want so there's very little freeform thinking and absolutely zero backtracking allowed (gates routinely shut behind you when you finish puzzles).The one real flaw is the optional "collectables" that must be found and collected in very very small time windows or you miss them permanently, since as said there is no backtracking allowed.The game is super short but it's an enjoyable time.  If you can get the game on a sale it should be worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't a big fan of Limbo or Inside besides their art styles, but this game is really good. The puzzles are interesting without requiring an IQ higher than my weight in pounds or constant trial and error (in fact I never felt the need to use trial and error as the solutions felt very intuitive), the art/graphics are great, the soundtrack is relaxing and fitting for the entire game. Story is borderline non-existent in the Dark Souls style of figuring it out through context and imagination and that works really well here. It's a little on the short side but frankly I'd rather have a short amazing game than a long mid one. Perfect game for a relaxing weekend.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Inside and Limbo were both cool games that felt like they came a bit short of living up to their full potential. While they were both engaging and had fun puzzles, they both also felt like they stretched their run time a bit and large swaths of the game were spent simply walking in one direction waiting for the next puzzle to emerge.Cocoon has some similar problems as its predecessors but it's world is so much more vibrant and immersive to me that I never found myself bored in the stretches between puzzles, I think that the flashy navigation mechanics that each of the worlds you were collecting gain after beating their respective bosses adds a lot to this part of the game. Over time the puzzles and the navigation merge together more and more which helps keep the game from feeling like it's dragging on at the end.I wasn't really sure what to expect from the worlds within worlds mechanic that the game is designed around but the team at Geometric created a lot of depth in puzzle design and there are a lot of creative and fun solutions that left me extremely satisfied. It's not quite as ground breaking of an experience as the first time you shoot two portals at the wall and walk through them, but it's pretty dang close.My only real complaint is that some of the orb juggling you have to do to complete the puzzles can become a bit tedious especially in cases where you have to reset the whole thing after realizing a mistake. That being said I still really enjoyed the process of figuring out the puzzles, it was just the execution of the solutions which could be tiresome.I'm a gamer who typically likes to get a long time out of my games to feel like I got my money's worth and while Cocoon isn't a game that you're going to spend years playing, I still found it worth my time and my money and would recommend it to pretty much anyone who likes puzzle games
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very enjoyable experience. Great sound effects, graphics, animations and smooth gameplay. The puzzles are never too hard but well thought out.My only nitpick would be the lack of a soundtrack. While the sound effects are lovely, the game only has ambient songs playing in the background which is fine on its own, but lacks the extra oomph that a fitting song would otherwise give.Easy 9/10 for me. I would recommend buying this on sale though.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game. The visuals are weird and gorgeous. The world-hopping mechanic can be mind-bending (in a good way). The puzzles are super intuitive. There were a few timing-based puzzles later in the games that I found frustrating (skill issue on my part). Beyond that, I found myself cruising through the environments without thinking too much. In my mind, it feels more like an adventure game than puzzler. If you're looking for a challenging puzzle game, this won't scratch that itch.Cocoon gets a thumbs up from me. However, it was 5 hours long. Well worth the full $25 for me, but your mileage may vary. My only complaint about Cocoon is that I wish there was more of it.
_childDocuments_.name: COCOON

_childDocuments_.review: During my time playing, did I ever fully understand why the little protagonist was in the worlds they were in or the meaning of their short journey they took? Not really, but that probably didn't matter.What mattered though, was how this game wasted absolutely no time in taking you on its mesmerising and beautifully haunting journey, with nothing but its very simple controls (just move and interact) and its audio/visual experience to guide you. And as other reviews will agree, each puzzle element feels so fresh and cleverly crafted, and never to the point of frustration.What also surprised me was how fairly easy it was in obtaining all achievements. No need to do a repeat playthrough either.This could very well be the game behind the definition 'short but most definitely sweet'.And please play this game blind, like I did. You won't regret it.
