_childDocuments_.review: COCOON is a great puzzle game created by the developers behind LIMBO and INSIDE, and you can complete it in about 4-5 hours.While it's a solid puzzle game on its own, it didn't impact or impress me as much as the previous games from the same creators. It had its ups and downs for sure.I had to give credit and purchase this game after enjoying both of Playdead's titles for free on the Epic Games Store. The first problem  with COCOON lies in the lack of narrative, as there is virtually none. I didn't even know what to call the protagonist or what species they are. Most of the time, I had to come up with my own story to keep things interesting. You play as this bug-like character that carries balls around, and within these balls are entire dimensions that look uniquely distinct from each other. The main mechanic in this game is plotting the way to the next area by unlocking paths with these balls.To be honest, the game starts off relatively weak and feels somewhat repetitive as you start noticing a pattern where you keep doing the same things multiple times. You acquire a ball, get inside the ball, solve a symbol puzzle, get a drone, take the drone to the boss, and beat the boss. However, things don't get stale toward the end as the game adds more layers to the puzzles using these balls and dimension travel. That's where I found the most enjoyment, particularly from the fourth boss onward until the credits.The bosses are a mixed bag. They are relatively simple, and you can defeat most of them in 2-3 attempts or sometimes even on your first try. Despite being piss easy, they look stunning and intimidating, fitting well within the dimensions they come from.The graphics in COCOON are absolutely stunning for a small project. Not only does the game look good, but it also runs smoothly on mid-tier PCs, the Nintendo Switch, or, in my case, a Steam Deck. So, I can't deny that the optimization of this title is up to standard.I played through the entire game in one sitting on my Steam Deck, and I can't say I didn't enjoy it. While it might not be as much of a standout as LIMBO or INSIDE, it's still a cool and unique puzzle game in its own right, and it won't take long to complete.

_childDocuments_.review: COCOON is a beautiful puzzle game, with a unique puzzle mechanic of having different areas contained in spheres. The different spheres also have their own powers when held, and spheres can be placed within spheres, which amounts to some fairly complicated puzzles towards the end. It took me over 5 hours to complete the game, and I will be playing through it again to 100% the achievements. I picked up this game because INSIDE is one of my favorite games of all time. While this game has a completely different feel in how it plays and it's visual style, I felt it had a similar pace and professional quality in level design, getting the most out of a little. With striking visuals, concepts, and atmospheric soundscapes, COCOON (and INSIDE) unfurls your curiosity to drive you forward. A big difference between the two games comes down to story: the story of INSIDE was profound and continues to resonate with me years after playing; whereas COCOON is much lighter in story, with more of a focus on game mechanics instead. Whatever strands of story exist in COCOON are simply to advance the game mechanics, which works for what it is; there is a benefit to not having an overbearing story, if that isn't the focus of the game. I got this game on sale for $20 and it was definitely worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty short indie puzzle game, but I enjoyed my time with it. Will I ever play it again? Eh, probably not. While I didn't find the puzzles in the game all that difficult, I can imagine that if you don't play through the entire thing in one sitting, it could get pretty frustrating trying to remember things, since for the most part, you are on your own. But the puzzle mechanic of worlds within worlds, and being able to finish the boss of each of these worlds to unlock a new puzzle solving mechanic, is a really neat idea. The game does a pretty good job though of making sure you don't get too lost, as it actively locks off areas that are no longer needed to progress anymore, once you have done everything you needed to there. _childDocuments_.review: If Playdead’s Limbo was the first slice and Inside is the whole cake, then Cocoon is a pie made by a pâtissier who only specializes in pies. Inside its crust is a level of intricacy and refinement not seen in the industry since Portal. Like an artisan pie, Cocoon is simplicity done right. Jeppe Carlsen has mastered easy to approach puzzles with just the right amount of satisfying depth. Perhaps this is due to the game’s strong audiovisual cues, providing clear explanations on how its systems interact without a single line of dialogue or text. Carlsen also eliminated erroneous backtracking, an issue that plagues titles such as the Myst series, all while beguiling players with the game’s esotericism and themes of metamorphosis. With plenty of surprises, Cocoon is a well-paced evolution of the genre, but a simpler description would be if Franz Kafka remembered to go to therapy and became a developer instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for a chill puzzle game, and this is from the lead designer who made Limbo and Inside (both games I loved). Unlike those games, it’s colorful and less depressing. When you press start, the game immediately drops you unceremoniously onto a desert like area. The main character is an unnamed little bug-like alien. The only controls are move around and pick things up and put them down. This is an environmental puzzle game, and the main goal is to progress from area to area. The only thing you directly manipulate are colored orbs that power different mechanisms and esoteric machines. These orbs are in actuality self contained planets! Eventually, alien dude gains the ability to warp inside the orb worlds and each one is a different universe. Each orb also has a special ability when you are carrying it. The puzzles take advantage of the recursive nature of the orbs and you can take orbs *inside* other orbs and it feels super high concept. It’s not a long game so it doesn’t overstay its welcome. _childDocuments_.review: I tumbled through COCOON in most of an evening and the early hours of the next morning, finishing the game in just under the 6 hour mark, compelled forwards by one of the most intriguing videogame worlds I've explored in a while. Before we get started: if I see a single complaint about this game being 'too short for the price', I'm going to explode; COCOON, like few other games, maximises every minute to show you something new, and reminds us what games can be when we take the risk to pursue the original.COCOON reminds me of a number of games: the wide-eyed wonder and revelations of Outer Wilds, the pick-up-and-put-down trial-and-error puzzling of Wind Waker's later dungeons, the alien environment of... well, it's hard to pick just one, as COCOON journeys you through the macro and the micro, stretching your mind like taffy to comprehend where and when you might be. Without the strong environmental and art design holding it together, you'd get whiplash, but as it stands, worlds which begin novel become familiar over time - which, as it turns out, is key to the gameplay.The puzzling premise, here, is diving in and out of glass orbs, each of which contains a world. To keep it as spoiler-free as possible, you soon discover these glass orbs are the core of your puzzling power, as well as the road your journey takes place on. Just as you feel you've discovered the limit of how they can be used, COCOON nudges you a little further, encouraging you to take that mental leap of faith to find a new path forwards.And it really is that - a polite nudge. At no point did I feel like I was headbutting a brick wall in my puzzle-solving. I'm an impatient puzzler, and struggle to get my head around layered puzzles, but COCOON is kind, ensuring I understood the bounds of each puzzle by limiting my area of play, and nearly all frustration is allayed by the feeling that the game wouldn't play tricks on me, or bait me with red herrings. I dislike puzzles of this sort, so if you do, too, you'll hopefully find COCOON is a good balance of puzzle versus progress.There are some brief moments of true frustration, though. For instance, one series of solutions relied heavily on timing, which felt mildly incongruous with the puzzles up until that point. But it wasn't by any means enough to shatter my immersion: and what a world to be immersed in. COCOON is minimalist. A 5-key control system has you absorbed within moments, the need to learn complex key-binds eliminated. COCOON toys with scale, colour, flora and fauna, perspective, shape, so on and so forth, to communicate lore in what is otherwise a wordless, speechless game, and it's at its best for it. COCOON knows exactly what it is, does that extremely well, and leaves you as a player wondering what on earth - or not, as the case may be - you just experienced as you surface for air at its completion.It's very good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game somehow felt like it dragged on forever, but wasn't long enough. $20 on sale for 3.5 hours of play time doesn't feel that great. I thought since it won the indie game of the year, I'd give it a shot. If I had paid $5-10, I think I would feel more satisfied with my purchase.I will admit some of the puzzles were very cleverly designed, but between the ease of 90% of the puzzles, and the tediousness of a lot of the puzzles (especially toward the end), it left me frustrated that I knew how to solve the puzzles, but had to run back and forth multiple times to get everything where it needed to be.This game does an excellent job at making sure you are confident you have everything you need to solve a puzzle without going out of your way only to realize you had everything needed the first time. They block off areas once you enter a new puzzle so you know where to stay confined to.The boss fights were interesting at first but became predictable.Overall, if I were to describe this game in one word, it would be "forgettable". _childDocuments_.review: the most boring game i've played in my lifeThe puzzle gameplay is like taking a walk, but every 20 seconds, you walk a mile backwards to pick up a shiny rock you remembered and then walk back to where you were to throw it back to its original location. There's too much backtracking and the puzzles are not creative at all. The atmosphere is the only thing this game has going for it, and it does not save this game. not by a long shot. I originally played this game after it won at TGA over Pizza Tower, trying to give it a fair chance, and I now have 2.8 hours and 25 dollars of my life that i'll never get back. The puzzles are tedious to complete and are either easy to the point where you're losing braincells, or difficult because the game hasn't shown you every mechanic you need to progress or makes you backtrack somewhere you have to look up to remember how to get to. According to positive reviews, this game has a story, but it's implied in the background, and "shown, not told." After playing for nearly 3 hours, I had no idea what was going on, where I was, why there were different worlds, or why I was solving puzzles. "Show, not tell" can work if you do it right. This game does not do it right. I came to play a game, not to do English class in video games. By the end of the session, I was in shambles, and when I stopped playing, I felt like a weight had been lifted from my shoulders. This game fails so badly in nearly every aspect, you would think it's an illumination movie. I feel like it could have had potential, but it barely does anything with the game mechanics, where it gets repetitive. These puzzles will not make you a puzzle master.

_childDocuments_.review: I am torn... this feels like a weak recommend.The art is an incredible showcase of creativity. Top tier eye candy without a doubt.The puzzles are... solid. They get pretty neat toward the end.But overall, it doesn't tie together. Limbo and INSIDE both generated a lot of tension by injecting disquieting elements into an otherwise familiar world... and by making you responsible for safeguarding a relatable and extremely vulnerable protagonist. The art in Cocoon feels too arbitrary and abstract to create any kind of tension or emotional connection. Seemingly anything goes in this bizarre world, and so nothing seems worth seeking or avoiding on an emotional level. Everything is so inexplicable, it just ends up feeling like neutral (if extremely pretty) set dressing, waiting for you to hit your next checkpoint so another canned animation can trigger... it certainly doesn't give the sense of a real lived-in world that exists independent of the player (again unlike Limbo and INSIDE).  And the protagonist might as well be a robot for all the personality he exhibits.The 3D world also really doesn't integrate with the content of the puzzles, it just adds visual ambiguity and slows down the execution of your solutions... in my experience, 2D is almost always the better choice for puzzle games. 3D usually just obfuscates the visual representation and control scheme, which limits how complex you can make the puzzles. If Portal were ported verbatim to 2D, you would find the puzzles much too simple. To me, Patrick's Parabox (2D and cartoony) was a much more interesting exploration of similar puzzle concepts.Overall however, it really is a super polished experience, from beginning to end. While the puzzle design was not super interesting to me, it has all clearly been very carefully playtested and refined. There were tons of times I saw the game subtly steering me away from potential dead ends and confusion, and deliberately leaving me staring at exactly and only those things I needed to consider to have that A-HA moment. This was very skillful work. Given the complex topology of the game, that must have required a great deal of effort and attention to detail.I also did like the boss battles, for the most part. They broke up the game with some completely different concepts, so the primary puzzle mechanics didn't get too stale.Ach, I think I just set my expectations too high and I feel bad for being so critical... it is in most regards an exceptionally well made game.

_childDocuments_.review:
From Jeppe Carlsen, the lead gameplay designer of LIMBO and INSIDE - COCOON takes you on an adventure across worlds within worlds. Master world-leaping mechanics to unravel a cosmic mystery.

COCOON is a unique take on the puzzle adventure genre, where each world exists within an orb that you can carry on your back. Wrap your head around the core mechanic of leaping between worlds - and combine, manipulate, and rearrange them to solve intricate puzzles

Interact with alien environments and biomechanical devices left behind by an ancient civilization. Journey through unique and diverse biomes, from industrial structures to massive organic caverns, and discover how they are connected to one another.

name: A Memoir Blue
detailed_description: From Cloisters Interactive, A Memoir Blue is an interactive poem about a superstar athlete and the all-encompassing love between mother and daughter. A unique aesthetic combining hand-drawn and 3D art brings Miriam's magical-realist journey to life, as she swims into the depths of her memories. A series of gameplay vignettes blends sacrifice and heartbreak with victory and pride as she reconnects with her inner child and deepens the love she shares with her mother.
about_the_game: From Cloisters Interactive, A Memoir Blue is an interactive poem about a superstar athlete and the all-encompassing love between mother and daughter. A unique aesthetic combining hand-drawn and 3D art brings Miriam's magical-realist journey to life, as she swims into the depths of her memories. A series of gameplay vignettes blends sacrifice and heartbreak with victory and pride as she reconnects with her inner child and deepens the love she shares with her mother.
short_description: A song from years ago triggers a flood of memories for champion swimmer Miriam. Embark on an evocative journey through her turbulent childhood and the complicated relationship she shared with her devoted mother.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed in about 75 minutes.  If you read this review...  don't be one of those jerkfaces who beats a short game and then refunds it.  That is incredibly NOT cool!A Memoir Blue is another really great interactive story from Annapurna and Cloisters.  It reminds me a lot of Florence.  Good visuals, great soundtrack.  It is very light on gameplay, so be warned.  However, you're not playing games like this for the gameplay...  you're playing for the story and experience. _childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I'm probably going to be in the minority on this, but while the game is beautiful, it's also REALLY boring. I played it twice through and both times I almost fell asleep. Simply put, there's almost no actual gameplay. It's almost entirely cutscenes. The only real extent of your gameplay is recreating set pieces/memories. There are no challenging puzzles and the achievements are really easy to unlock. You don't even get to WALK. I don't understand why this is a game when this easily could've been a short film. Now I don't mind games with simplistic gameplay as long as the story and characters are interesting, deep, or charming enough to carry it. This...doesn't quite cut it. Spoilers:The game is pretty cheap and it wouldn't hurt to buy it to support the developers (especially since the game employs gorgeous hand drawn animation), but don't go in expecting anything super deep or engaging. Otherwise, I'd probably go pick up games like Florence or Gris. They're short with simpler gameplay but the emotional stakes feel much more real and are actually engaging to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Though it is not without artistic value,  just failed to captivate me and the persisting feeling of boredom sadly comprises much of my memory of the experience, compelling me to give it a negative review. •	Nice music.•	Mostly pleasant graphics. •	Some impressive visual storytelling. •	Conceptually, not a bad story. •	Achievements* •	Some unpleasant graphics.•	Storytelling was entirely visual and so bored me. •	Controls with mouse a little awkward. •	Achievements* •	Slow. Conceptually, using the graphics of the game as the sole means of telling the story was quite clever. In another game, I think I could have got into this. The whole narrative is a memory, and plays like a vivid dream through thematic environments that are perhaps best described as ‘absurd’. Or perhaps ‘surreal’. Water is, expectedly, a recurring theme (there is a narrative reason for this) and the water effects were, I thought, very impressive. I’ve seen more costly games do far worse. Not every scene is that photogenic though – some seem lacking in colour and fidelity, making the graphics in aggregate merely good, not outstanding. But good is enough, and I nevertheless mostly liked the visual presentation of .The narrative is actually quite touching and there are some scenes that did pull at my heartstrings, as we’re taken on a journey of  introspection,  into the character’s past, exploring memories of familial relations – for better and for worse – and the pursuit of success (and the weight of it) as we try to find our footing in early life as a swimmer.The majority of the game playing out as memories means it is, in this way, rather dreamy, which the visual style really exemplifies too. However, it played out too slowly for me and I often found myself wishing it would move on. I didn’t go into this expecting a fast-paced game, of course, but it was like there wasn’t enough story for the time the game took to tell it to me, contributing to an almost perpetual wish on my part that it would hurry up. At least in other slow narrative-driven games – take Life is Strange – there is a satisfying degree of interaction on our part as the player, that (with the story) keeps us interested in playing on.  didn’t excel here, and so whatever merits there were to its narrative ultimately fell flat due to its rather tedious presentation, and lack of interactivity (see ‘Gameplay’ below).The reason we were going through these dreams in the first place is because of audio. The character hears a song that brings all these memories  back – something I’m sure most of us have experienced in our lives.The game sounds were fine, but nothing felt remarkable to me. Music tracks were nice, thematically consistent with the dreamy feeling the game had. Atmospheric noises were functional, but they were not visceral in the same way as, say,  which I recently reviewed. It did nothing to bridge the gap of disconnection I felt practically throughout.And principally this is, I think, why I felt so disconnected.  merely has the illusion of interaction – or if not an illusion, certainly among the shallowest implementations of it. You play the entire game with the left mouse button (and unlike  [NSFW] it doesn’t give you anything to do with your other hand), just clicking objects in scenes for no real reason. Dragging ice cubes to the bottom of a glass, or pulling fish around floating photographs, etc. Some of these interactions form puzzles but they’re not engaging paired with the rest of the game, and I just felt like they slowed me down in reaching the end. They were really little more than transitions, after which you lose control again as the game plays a cutscene.It's those same interactions that often yield achievements too, and while they're easy enough to 100%, the requirements are somewhat absurd. Several of them are unintuitive, even involving things you might not know you can do in the game, which I don't like as a design philosophy.I have to give  a negative recommendation just because it bored me, even despite its redeeming features and the fact that I’ve listed as many positives as negatives. This is very much the sort of game that I think will heavily divide audiences. Sometimes, doing something uniquely artistic adds a flare to a production that conventional means lack, and the result is something special. But sometimes it doesn’t land, and the quality of the end product is harmed. Unfortunately, I have to fall on the side of the latter – even if only softly. I didn’t enjoy , but I cannot honestly say that it is a bad game, either.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game when it was nominated at The Game Awards 2022 for the Games for Impact category, so I decided to give it a try. Its sort of hard to review this game. Gameplay wise, its feels like a point and click with very light puzzle elements. Overall it reminds me a lot of its fellow Annapurna-published game If Found in terms of the light gameplay and the way the game transitions between scenes, except unlike If Found there is no dialogue. As a child of a single mom myself, I kinda expected it to explore the dynamics of the relationship more than it did. I don't really feel like it communicated more than the pain and separation that is experienced. But really, there's a broad range of experiences that single-mom children have, so I can't really expect it to match my own. But if I compare it to other games with similar concepts - short, artistic, emotional-narrative focused 1-2 hour experiences like Virginia, Before Your Eyes, Dear Esther, Her Lie I Tried to Believe, Her Story, and Gone Home - then its hard to not feel like A Memoir Blue kinda fails to live up to other games in this space - the only one I'd rank it above is Dear Esther. While the artistry is high, this reminds me of something my college creative writing teacher told me - you can't be so obtuse that you fail to communicate most of your point. And that's kinda what I feel the failing of A Memoir Blue is. It failed to communicate its point to me.I will say that, at $8, it feels much more reasonably priced than most games with this short of a run time.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I'll preface this by saying that if you're the child of a single parent, or a single parent yourself, this game might have far more impact on you than it did me.That being said, I can't really recommend this... experience. I have very little bad to say about it, but almost nothing good to say about it either. It's a decent if not basic story about a girl reflecting on her relationship with her mother, but it's not exactly in-depth or anything. The story is broken into basic interactive segments, like clicking on lights to play an animation showing where the relationship is at in the given time. There's not really any merit to this being an interactive experience rather than just like, a short YouTube video.  For example, at one point the girl and her mother take a train ride, and the gameplay for the segment is inserting the coins into the machine, hitting the ticket buttons, dragging the tickets over to stamp them, then putting them in the slot. That's it. There's no real benefit to that being interactive beyond the simple entertainment of being able to fling the coins around the screen. The story is not particularly interesting either, as it kind of just is a very simple life story. I can even sum up the story in a single sentence if I tried. The biggest compliment I can give this game is that it's told very well visually even if there's little to no point in it being interactive. If you're interested in seeing this story, go watch a YouTube playthrough that's over in like 45 minutes, then play it yourself if you think the experience is worth giving your money towards. Otherwise, there's no point.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me 71 minutes to beat the "game." It's a mostly abstract narrative-driven experience with simple gameplay elements. There are some negative reviews mentioning how the interactions are obtuse, but I don't agree. Any casual gamer should be easily able to complete the game. I only see non-gamers (those truly new to gaming where this is maybe there first or second or third game they have ever played) maybe having trouble with some of the gameplay elements as they may not seem intuitive if you've never played a game like this. I found the game to be straightforward. It has a simple message about a mother-daughter relationship. It's abstract enough that you can read into it what you want though. Unfortunately, the game didn't really speak to me. I thought the artwork, music & animations were done well enough given the small budget price.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game and a pretty nice story but also not very engaging.The gameplay is essentially point and click, there are some very minor puzzles but they are extremely easy and not interesting or thought out. The game is only about an hour-long (the other 40 minutes were to get all the achievements) so it is short. There isn’t much more to say you click things to advance the story.The story follows a woman going through her childhood memories. It tells the story through no dialogue and uses 2d vs 3d animation for either memories or the present day. It tells a story of a difficult time for an athlete and how she developed as she got older focusing on her relationship with her mother. It is well done and tells the story in a unique way, it also feels very personal.The art style is gorgeous. The style is incredibly well done and matches the sadder vibe of the story well, each of the images is compelling to look at. The difference in the brightness of the 2d animation from childhood to the darker gloomier 3d animation of present-day works contrasts the two very well.  The soundtrack is fine, the songs fit well I don’t really have anything to say about it. A Memoir Blue has a compelling story and a great art style but the lack of interesting gameplay drags it down heavily for me.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: While A Memoir Blue was a short but interesting experience overall, the lack of more context in certain instances really hurts the game's story and my engagement in it. I may be at wrong here, but just because a couple of lackluster scenes, the whole story felt a bit childish and forced. Like it seems the game doesn't want to dig deeper into the more mature stuff cos its afraid to show something that may be inappropriate for some of the audience or sth!? idk. In short, the game needed more time to tell its story.But hopefully it has some really good scenes and messages to wash off its problems. I also really liked the hand drawn animation to tell the past events.Overall, it was a relaxing experience which could've been a lot better if the game had taken its time to give some parts of the story their reasonable context they needed.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: This one was strange.  It tells the story of an Olympian dealing with moments from her childhood.  The gameplay involves doing a series of simple things like stamping a ticket or adjusting a radio.   The story progresses as soon as you do one of these incredibly mundane tasks.  Not that the story isn't heartwarming or artistic in its own right; the story is done entirely without dialogue and it is a good story.  It's just an odd choice to make it a game.  On the flip side, some of the achievements are very difficult.  The only way to get a couple of them is to use a controller, which it doesn't tell you is essential to the gameplay on a PC.  Overall, not horrible, but I don't see the point as much in this one.  4/10.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A Memoir Blue is a game developed by Cloisters Interactive and published by Annapurna InteractiveThe game offers some nice graphics and a really beautiful aesthetic, especially with its incorporation of both 3D and 2D graphics which blend incredibly well, it is pleasant all the sameThe game does suffer with it being incredibly short and not offering much in terms of gameplay and more of a short, touching story. For me personally, it didn't bug me at all but if you're expecting a really deep, intricate game with some clever gameplay mechanics and such, A Memoir Blue isn't the game for you.A Memoir Blue overall, however, is a short, beautiful game to play, it is a good interactive adventure game to play in short bursts!
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful and interesting game. Well, not exactly a game. _childDocuments_.review: I just finished A Memoir Blue and I have to GUSH about the quality of this game and how overlooked it is in the indie space. _childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more of an interactive narrative but, unfortunately, it feels lacking.The soundtrack is good, and the 2D art that tells you the story is beautiful, but it doesn't really match with the 3D art. It'd be a more powerful experience if the whole game was visually as the small 2D interludes. They create a sense of connection much bigger than the generic 3D.Aside from one of the interactions where the main character , the other interactions don't drive nor add much to the plot. One interaction has you simply feeding coins to a train ticket vending machine, stamping them and feeding them to another machine. It was clunky and doesn't make you connect with the main character and her mother, as most of the other interactions.I was a third into the game and I actually felt bored. Usually stories like this get me emotional, but I felt nothing beyond boredness. I was dreading still having to play the rest of the game. I hoped it improved, but the story never gets any deep or makes you connect with the characters. I forced myself to finish it, but it was not an enjoyed experience.

_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I decided that my vote would have depended solely on the overall score given by other users, as it doesn't deserve an 'extremely positive review', but not even a 'negative' one.The game is nice, is short, is sweet and has a very good soundtrack. As always Annapurna has some creative ideas, but as always it never delivers fully. Like other games of theirs, the game is just... there... Nice, sweet, short, but never really taking off. Luckily it is only 45/60 minutes long, otherwise it would have become too boring in my opinion.Won't recommend, but also won't stop anyone who wants to try it, as even if they don't like it it is easy to finish.The price is too high in my opinion, I suggest buying it when discounted.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: The storyline is the main selling point of this game, but unfortunately, it failed to hold my attention. Despite being visually creative, I found the plot to be lacking in originality. It seemed to be a carbon copy of other stories, rather than something fresh and unique. If you enjoy short and linear experiences, this game may still be what you're looking for. The emotional themes center around the relationship between a parent and child, so if you're looking for a story that explores the bonds of family and the complexities of parenthood, this game may be worth checking out. However, if you're looking for a more diverse and open-ended gaming experience, it may not meet your expectations.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: This game should come with a free box of tissues. You might need them ... I did.It's really more of an emotional journey than a game. You have to take actions to make the story progress and to pick up the achievements, but it's more about the experience than gameplay.It's pretty short, so I'd recommend picking it up on sale. But if you're in the mood for a charming easy game, it's definitely worth grabbing this one.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game with almost no gameplay. It looks beautiful, but all you do is klicking on not even hidden objects to reveal the next series of short movie scenes. This would have been so much more satisfying if it would only be a short film, because it already feels like one. No one ever speaks, there's mostly just the bubbling sounds of the deep sea. Really got onto my nerves after a while. After an hour you'll be through with the game and I don't think it's worth its money.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A Memoir Blue feels influenced by film and animation more than anything else. This quality is a notable strength when it comes to game’s use of music, mixture of art styles, and the layouts of scenes. However, this quality also plays a major part in the game’s biggest shortcoming. A Memoir Blue disappoints in its ability to be an interactive story. The playable segments never feels satisfying or essential to the overall story being told. That’s not to say that I didn’t appreciate what the game was trying to say. As I’ve gotten older I recognize the love and sacrifice my parents made for me, that I was previously oblivious to. As the main character grows and discovers her mother’s humanity, there were aspects I definitely found relatable. However, I don’t think  that was enough to make A Memoir Blue feel anything other than “just fine” in my mind.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know... I wanted to like it, but I constantly kept feeling like I was still in the intro to a game that would begin any moment now. The gameplay is very limited, and most times that you actually have some interaction, as soon as you begin to move an element, it gets taken out of your hand again to auto-complete on its own. Jeez, let me at least do something on my own before another cutscene starts.The protagonist annoyed me from the first moment. She's unbearably slow, timid and sullen. I kept playing because I thought that was going to change any time now and she'd actually DO something besides flinching at everything under the sun and hanging her head. The cartoony mom/daughter story could've been developed in more depth, used more time to actually explain what those weird mood swings they both got were really about. I never got beyond being a passive watcher of two strangers that don't really mean anything to me. I feel like this tries very hard to be deep and meaningful, and maybe it'd feel more so if the player could actually achieve some sort immersion at some point in the game. But I can't built any sort of immersion if I constantly get pulled out of whatever I do and forced to watch another sloooow cutscene before I'm allowed a few clicks again. As a game, this isn't for me. As an interactive movie, it might have been only if the characters weren't so annoying (but I suppose that's rather subjective).
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Few interactive scenes and lots of cutscenes at times feel more like watching than playing. Beautiful mix of traditional 2D animation and 3D environments, with a soothing palette, create some truly magnificent shots. Instead of moving a character, you touch and control objects to relive memories, make things happen and move on.Scenes felt a bit random sometimes and were not always immediately relatable. I could not initially comprehend exactly what this young woman was going through, until the story finally took shape. Parental abandonment, teen boredom, training and performance at what cost, a young woman wanting to feel proud of herself through her mother's eyes. It is quite uneven but definitely ends on an emotional note.As a parent, I felt more attached to seeing the story from the parent's point of view, with an undeniable love for their child but perhaps not always able to give them the full attention and recognition they need or deserve.For a game that spends so much time in high humidity or directly underwater, I was surprised to see no underwater hair physics. Nice cloth physics in a few scenes, but used sparingly.Exactly 1 hour in length is a bit short but suitable for what it is.Recommended at half price for people who enjoy the art style and are looking for an undemanding short story.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I would say that this is more along the lines of an interactive novel as opposed to an interactive puzzle exploration game.However, despite that technicality, the entire design of this game and everything within it moved me to tremendous tears. I am not going to spoil it in this review but let's just say there is a lot of room for personal interpretation within the non-verbal narrative story that these creators developed. Such a lovely and relaxing, deep in thoughtful reflection kind of game. It will hit you in the feels. Tears were pouring down my face at the end of the game. I saved the soundtrack as a playlist because it is so beautiful. Everything about this game is beautiful with all technicalities aside. It is a very short game with very little clicking so if you are looking for something short and simple to get in your feels, this one is for you. 8/10 beautifully created, just wish there were more interactive elements but still, great feels.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Now, for everyone who want an interactive story, do not be fooled by the short lenght, as for this game category I think this is one of the best examples of quality above quantity, and for someone who doesn't generally like these kind of games because generally they are mostly both uselessly long with pointless time wasting activities and at the core not so deep as they seems (the exact opposite very often), let me tell you this isn't like them at all.The concept of the inner search to decide about reconnecting with your loved ones is very straightforward and does that through both stunning and simple scenarios and also simple but deep images.And this simplicity is what will probably make you cry or at least be moved by what you see, in a way or another.And for those who whine about achievements and lenght... you should probably play other kind of games because this isn't the main point of these kind of games, and it's coming from someone who loves the 100% completion of a game.P.s.: Maybe it would be better if from the second walktrough of the game it was possible to hold a button to skip cinematics to be more at ease to complete achievements, I mean for the first time I agree that would ruin the points of the game, but from the second time onward would make things more simple for others, because even with chapter select is a pain for the heart to emotionally suffer a little again from seeing those, not for me as of now since I have already done all the things you can do in this game, but for other players could be useful.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A silent but emotional rollercoaster interactive movie (with simple puzzles) following up a story between a daughter and her mother. Understanding where a person comes from and to remember the past in a way built up in a creative aquatic journey. The Way a person grows up to be always lies in the past and the people who influenced that past. With shivering music queues that makes the story complete, even no words are spoken at all during the whole game... you can easily make out the final words of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: The best game in narrative things talking about that i have played  this year. It this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ perfect, Soundtrack, visual art, graphics. Character development, all that a game can have, this game have it. It´s shot, like 1 hour, if you wanna have the platinum without know, search on youtube and you can have that in 1 hour and 30 minutes. You have to play it. _childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: The ending broke me. It is that impactful.I think someone (probably the marketers, LOL) described this as a visual poem. Which it is. Without spoiling too much, you play as a champion swimmer who is troubled by her past. She investigates it and by the end is able to reconcile it.That's a pretty basic plot, but Memoir Blue handles every last moment so poignantly that it feels like a gift.With that said, the game play is pretty basic (click around on stuff until you advance). It's almost more like an interactive movie than a game. But wow is it a gorgeous and well done one. It's also very short (I think you could complete it in about an hour.) But that's not a detriment to me. I'd rather have an hour of great game play than four of mediocre. Or heck, an infinite number of mediocre hours. Life is too short for that. I loved this game. I was in tears by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Just a classic case of a story trying to be touching but just isn't. It was a little bit of a struggle trying to figure out what was actually happening as there were no words or speech. It's also very short (about an hour long) and honestly, not really worth playing. The environment graphics are great, but the MC design was rather strange and very plasticy. I also wasn't a fan of the memories being in a cartoon style. The interactive, though unnecessary, elements in the game were cool, as was the music, but that's about it. Wouldn't recommend grabbing this unless it's on sale and very cheap.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: This game was beautifully well made! I LOVED THE MUSIC! This is more like a story telling game! There isn’t much gameplay besides interacting with things around the story but it is well worth the playthrough. It takes maybe an hour to fully complete the game. Its really easy to miss achievements since you are only guaranteed one and the other 14 are missable! Interact with as much as you can!  This story with no words made me cry! Give it a try yourself! Relax and enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A bit like "Last day of June" it's more about a touching story then a game. The game spoke to me without words. Although I sensed that it was meant to be a touching story I needed to go online to figure out what the story was so I needed it a little more dumb down. A game worth playing if you're mature enough to fully understand it.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: a very short game, 94 minutes for me. easy, but very clever game. beautiful but simple graphics, good music. a sad story that ends well. i did have one serious problem.  my computer got extremely hot even playing on LOW graphics. i had to turn the game off and cool down several times. i have a gaming machine with a Geoforce RTX 3080, and i'm surprised how it overheated from this game. this happened to me one other time with a simple little game. so i'm not sure if it's my hardware or what. anyway, the game is novel, with interesting game play, and i'm still recommending it with 4 stars out of 5.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: I think anything from Annapurna is at least worth a look and "A Memoir Blue" was no exception, though a little "thin" at times.I would say this is an occasionally-interactive-story-game, so if you're wanting a lot of push and pull you may be disappointed, instead you'll get a simple but well told story of one woman's path through life focusing on her relationship with her mother.This was exactly what I wanted and I was happy to lose myself in the art and movement, occasionally pulling something or clicking a few times, it's a bit like a comic book, in that respect perhaps.Anyway, I liked it though as mentioned, it might be a little "thin" for some.  You can see it all in one hour quite simply; my play time was affected by achievements.  I played this game the same day as "Lona: Realm of Colours" - if you want a double bill with similar games but slightly different approaches, that one would work.Also this played perfectly on Ubuntu 22.04 with Proton 7 specified.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: An attempt at a quick summary aside, Blue Memoir is one of my faviourite 'tell not me not, show me' type of games with sections of beautiful 2D and 3D style that works well for the narrative of the story. The 2D is used in flashback (for simpler time) and 3D use for the present (where it is more complicated). As for the puzzle, they are really easy enough to solve and help transverse from one narrative point to another. There are a few hidden achievements, thanks to the puzzle being interactive if any achievement hunters are interested.  Lastly, the story is quite easy to understand and leaves enough room for a different interpretation that other players to make up their own context, it is even worth it to replay certain sections of the game once you complete the full story to get the whole meaning. Throughout the journey, I was pleasantly happy with how gorgeous and peaceful my experience was, whilst reliving memories between mother and daughter that I teared up a bit hearing that phone call towards the end.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game! It has a really beautiful atmosphere, i kinda loved it! For those who say it's not a game, but an experience, i disagree. It definitely has playful elements and short riddles. It's also pretty emotional, especially near the end. Easy and smooth gameplay, perfect for a chill pc session. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A Memoir Blue is an interesting game to say the least. This isn't a perfect game by any means, but I enjoyed my time with it overall. Graphically, the game looks fine, nothing amazing but nothing bad either. The soundtrack was really good and probably the best part of this game. I also really liked how the story got incredibly interesting at the end, and how there are multiple interpretations of the ending. To me, my issues with the game were that the puzzles were way too easy, the game was really short, most of the story felt really boring, again because the player really doesn't know what is going on until the end, and even then, it is up to interpretation, and the overall gameplay was rather simplistic. Still, I liked this game overall, and this is a 6/10 game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: Although I feel as if the narrative didn’t quite move me as much as it wanted to, the sublime music and blended 2D animation do make A Memoir Blue an admirable piece of aquatic art. Interactive story art games, namely those also published by Annapurna Interactive, excel at using their limited gameplay as clever allegories for a narrative theme or to reinforce the character’s emotions. Aside from a few clever moments, A Memoir Blue falls short in fully capitalizing on the strengths of the storytelling medium that it’s working within. Most of the game’s interactive screens do little more than remind you that ‘this is a boat’ or ‘this concept is obscured’ or simply get you to initialize the next animation. As a result, the game is still serene and beautiful, just in a more passive and traditional sense.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

_childDocuments_.review: A song from years ago triggers a flood of memories for champion swimmer Miriam. Embark on an evocative journey through her turbulent childhood and the complicated relationship she shared with her devoted mother.
_childDocuments_.name: A Memoir Blue

name: EARTH DEFENSE FORCE: WORLD BROTHERS
detailed_description: -A New Fight on a Square Earth A new EDF adventure begins! Only this time, the action unfolds in a parallel world where the Earth is made of digital blocks. This world has befallen into chaos, as the once peaceful square Earth has been shattered into pieces. Shape aside, it is an Earth nonetheless which needs to be defended. It is now up to the EDF to restore peace to the square planet. -Assemble Your Own Team The Earth has been shattered into pieces. EDF soldiers are fighting desperately on their own in various countries around the world. Rescue these soldiers to have them join you, and assemble your own unique team. Each mission can be attempted with up to 4 teammates. Switch among your teammates as you go, making use of each character's unique traits which shall prove useful in battle at different times. -Recruit Soldiers from Past EDF Games Block versions of characters from every previous EDF release, from EDF1 ('Monster Attack') to 'Earth Defense Force 5,' and even the EDF spinoff releases, appear in the game. Also featured are a wide range of weapons and vehicles from past EDF releases. Series veterans will enjoy seeing these familiar characters and weapons, while those new to the series have the opportunity to be introduced to its rich history for the first time. -Familiar Enemies Enemies that invaded the Earth before make an appearance in this game, this time in block form. -Online Co-Op This game supports up to 4-player online co-op, with each player joining the battle using their own team. -Story In a parallel world where the Earth is made of blocks, evil has befallen the otherwise peaceful planet. Led by Dark Tyrant, several Motherships suddenly attacked the planet, shattering the Earth into pieces. The Earth has been attacked by the Invaders, Ravagers, and Aggressors before...but the brave EDF soldiers have always joined together to defend the planet from these threats. With the Earth shattered, EDF soldiers continue fighting on each of their pieces of the planet. But with no way to reach each other to deliver aid or food supplies, the planet remains in despair. You must assume the role of Commander of the EDF and fight back. Find the EDF soldiers fighting around the planet, and begin a counteroffensive. Only a powerful team assembled by you can save our square Earth.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I have like 150 hours on the JP Switch version. Ignore my PC playtime.tl;dr If you can look past the visuals you get one of the best EDF titles, but it lacks the class depth of the mainlines and unlike the others it's a little too self-aware.I vividly remember thinking this game would suck when it was revealed. "EDF but for kids" sounds like a recipe for disaster and it being headed up by the Iron Rain team (a game I'm not too fond of) made it seem like it was headed for the bargain bin.Fortunately, Yuke's surprised me. WB is not only excellent, it might be my favourite EDF title. The first thing you'll likely notice is how different the format is. Mainline EDF gives you 1-4 classes and has a whole mountain of gear, weaponry and vehicles for you to unlock. World Brothers gives you the EDF5 Ranger with a single weapon and tells you to go recruit more people, who each come with one weapon and maybe an accessory. They have recharging abilities like air strikes, tapioca tea and molotov cocktails, and Special moves that recharge upon killing things which have an equally large variety of effects. Rather than unlocking new weapons for a class, you level up that class so they can use other people's weapons (the level cap is 10, which lets you use anything).It doesn't sound very EDF, does it? But it is. Delightfully so, in fact. If you're familiar with Warriors games, this is to mainline EDF what Warriors Orochi is to Dynasty Warriors. Different framework, but the EDF core of charging into swarms of giant aliens, robots and insects is still intact. The team swapping and build flexibility just give you far more options, and the denseness of the maps (to accommodate the Switch's weaker hardware) honestly makes some later missions MORE chaotic than the mainlines, especially from Hardest onwards. Much like Warriors Orochi, this is also a crossover title, so you get to fight a wide variety of enemies and your favourite class from the other games is guaranteed to be in. There's a bunch of returning maps too, including London, so if you're an abolitionist you can take down Parliament.There's a lot of replayability too. Around 150 characters to acquire and six difficulties with the mission pack (launching Jun 10th), and that's not factoring in higher level versions of weapons and accessories (up to level 5 with the mission pack). The story is a bit short, only 60 missions (71 with the mission pack), but they're good missions and there's not much filler.That all said, the game does have a few issues. Despite the lower amount of weapon levels, some higher level variants are a downgrade. Some world brothers/sisters outright suck, and while you can build a team around them, you likely won't be so generous in higher difficulties. Unlike the mainlines, which are corny because they try to be serious, WB tries to be tongue-in-cheek and self-referential. YMMV, but the humour can get old. There are less maps than in other games, so there's a ton of repetition on that front. Some maps have really bad unit placement, which can make grabbing them a pain in the ass. The music gets repetitive FAST and I genuinely recommend disabling it. At the time of writing, the PC version has mouse smoothing that makes turning around a pain in the ass.Despite these issues though, World Brothers is still my favourite EDF, and I've played all but one of them. The variety and fun on offer is amazing and I don't think we'll ever see anything like it again unless this game shifts millions. Buy it, play it, love it. And hey, if you hate it, you only need an hour to decide if this is for you or not.Don't buy the season pass though, just get the mission pack in a couple weeks. Unless you REALLY want to play as Sarge from EDF5 or whatever.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the EDF games. I had to come give a negative review to try and counter some recent unscrupulous business practices. When this game launched, they sold something called a 'season pass' which was like 25 bucks. Then after two weeks they released the first content update which they want another 15 bucks for and is not included in the season pass. Sure, they're well within their rights to do it probably, but it's shady at best and I recommend keeping your money.

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved the old games, you may, like I did at first, boot this thing up and hate it for the first hour. You have to collect randomly selected characters in every level, meaning you start with just a Ranger and have to wait for luck to give you a Fencer or Air Raider. I didn't get either of those for a long time. Instead, I got a Mexican man that hucked burning Tequila as molotovs and did a Mariachi song as an Ultimate move. Followed by a Dutch woman that threw tulips and set up a turret shaped like a windmill as her Ultimate. The levels were small. The number of enemies were also small. You can only find new weapons when you pick up new characters, and that is all the customizing you can do. Each character has a special and an ultimate, and those cannot be switched out. If you're a fan of airstrikes, you have to wait until you find a character with one.I rolled my eyes at the stereotypes, lamented everything that seemed to be missing, and seriously considered refunding this game and going back to EDF 5.But eventually, it grew on me. As I gathered more characters and the new weapons they carried, I realized that the real fun in this game is in making whatever goofy 4-person team your heart desires and kill ants with them. Want to make a classic combo with the Ranger, Wing Diver, and all the rest? Go for it. You want to make all fliers, with not only the Wing Divers, but the Pale Wings and Jet Armor guys from the old-old games? They have them, and you can do that. Wanna go full anime and have a team of E-girls, Cat Maids, and Pop Idols? Have at it, you freaks. Hell, go full Halloween insano-town like I did and go with Cowboys, Pirates, actual Dracula, and a Canadian Bear Furry with a minigun.When you get your team of people you like, and the EDF fan armor is broken through, you may start to warm up to all the good things about this game. You notice that, for the bazillion and one characters you will pick up, the acting for them is done with heart and energy. You notice that when you switch characters, the stage music changes to match them (like when you switch to Dracula, you hear an organ start up). You may notice that the writing starts to get real laughs out of you. The levels, while short and small compared to the Sandlot games, are consistently fun. You remember those endless underground levels in EDF 4 and 5 where you got lost all the time and Air Raiders became useless and you're just traveling through tunnels where nothing happens until you get killed and you realize there were no checkpoints and you have to start all over again? This game doesn't have those. When you get everything from characters (of which there are only 3 per level), there's no more grinding for weapon and armor pickups.This is the LEGO Star Wars of EDF. It's a simple parody that's missing some of what's good about the old material, and a lot of what's bad. The less you take it seriously, the better it gets and the more it surprises you with its quality. Old fans, give this one a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: EARTH DEFENSE FORCE: WORLD BROTHERS

_childDocuments_.review: In the first level alone, I recruited an English royal guard complete with the bushy hat who fights for the Queen, an "Amigo Brother" wearing a sombrero, and a Hollander woman whose superpower is a small windmill that shoots tornados. They were quickly joined in the next few missions by an American cowboy whose cows were kidnapped by aliens, and a time travelling Japanese Ninja very concerned with eating Miso Soup and Honor. Later, an enterprising Dim Sum Sister named Pao was found and immediately attempted to harvest giant spider webs.All of these character engage in banter and drop random country factoids in the broadest of 90's anime and cartoon ways. The dialog is a perpetual mix of being so stupid it's funny and making me grin like an idiot, and being so painful it makes me mute the voices in second hand embarrassment.As a lover of EDF, cheesy things, and "so bad it's good things" I can only give this game's writing and atmosphere the highest of thumbs up.It’s classic EDF gameplay, and I mean that in the best way. Giant insects and robots attack, and you blast ‘em. Carriers, anthills, and even boss fights are here, done like main EDF games, not IA or IR. No crystals or credits.Respectably large maps, destructible buildings, and the ability to destroy even voxelly clouds makes this a pretty solid and familiar playing EDF installment despite its unusual look. Features music, emblems, characters, and weapons from all previous EDF games, from EDF1 to Iron Rain and the original "brothers" in this game. The "team" mechanic might throw you off, but it basically translates to having 4 weapons, abilities, and lives. Each team member can be equipped with a weapon, has a built-in unswappable ability (dodge roll, sprint, etc...), a rechargeable Special ability (healing, air strikes, buffs) and can have an accessory that boosts stats.It's new but not shockingly new, just gives you a few extra options and can let you avoid the nasty surprise of having only short range weapons for flying Ravager drones, saving you a restart.Regarding the team being 'Lives': Losing all your health on the active soldier knocks that team member out, and it works like classic EDF multiplayer - you need health to revive them. So be careful, it's not consequence free like other TPS games. Switching active teammates swaps your current member with another in the exact same spot you are in. The other teammates are still fighting even when not active, though they do seem to do less damage than when you are controlling them. They can also take damage when inactive, though again, seemingly much reduced than when under your control. Some cases like being completely surrounded by Bosses or being caught in an Air Raider's Special Airstrike will still kill them, and they can still whittle down trash if given heavy damage weapons like the Lysander sniper rifle.Various accessories can be found and equipped to alter active and non-active stats such as speed, reload, damage, health recovery. You can also summon them for apparently no cost to your location, which can help in some situations such as saving inactive team members from area effects or a boss stomping through an area. Usually not necessary but helpful in specific situations like cramped caves or huge bosses stomping through.Rescuing teammates replaces scrounging weapon and armor boxes. There are only so many on a map, and who you rescued is randomized each mission, along with a possible weapon and accessory. Rescuing teammates adds them to an empty slot on your team if you have one, and rescuing a teammate you already have on your team results in Skill Points. Levelling up teammate Skill Points lets them use different classes of weapons. So, Ninja Brother can only use Hanzo Steel at first, but if you repeatedly rescue Ninja Brother from levels, he can eventually use Pig Disgusting Gaijin Guns. Note that this only applies to weapons. You can’t ever swap a Ninja’s Dash ability for a Trooper’s Dodge Roll, or swap speed and armor stats. All characters have their own speed, ability recharge speed, jump, and SP recharge stats, influenced only by accessories. Max HP/Armor points increase simply by completing levels with teammates you assigned from the start of the mission. Maps are notably bigger than what I recall in Iron Rain and Insect Armageddon, quite confident they're as big and as vertical as EDF 4 and 5.Computer performance on an RTX 2060 has been flawless with everything at maximum at 2560 x 1080. Though admittedly I've been mostly doing Solo Story mode, so I can't speak for what happens if everyone has the Genocide Gun at the same time.Uh... No, it's a fun EDF Game but still has some inherent jankiness and flaws, like everyone's favorite bug that has lasted the entire series, "An Ant has disappeared into another dimension while climbing wall geometry in a deep cave mission and no amount of explosions can hit it." Trapped enemies eventually die/disappear so you can't softlock, but you will be very confused if this is your first EDF. Tonewise, if you're expecting this game to have the same tone as EDF 5 where Earth was basically facing genocide at the hands of aliens, you might be in for a mood whiplash. On the other hand, the EDF has yet to confuse giant frogs as creatures that look "Just like us" over ten missions in.Completionists are in for a hard time, as well.First off, Hardest and Inferno are not immediately unlocked. Hard is the max at first, and it doesn't seem to count lower difficulties as completed if you beat a mission on Hard. As the game is notably less murderous at the start than other entries, I would have appreciated the chance to see what Inferno was like. You may be frustrated with having to get to higher difficulties than simply having them at the start. Second, you aren't going to find as many weapons, as weapons are attached to the EDF members you rescue in missions. While you can absolutely switch weapons on characters, what TYPE of weapon is severely limited until you level up your members and you rescue some duplicates, and categories only unlock one at a time. You will have to spend some time if you want to make the ninja equip assault rifles. It's not immediately apparent what weapon type the next Skill Level will unlock either. The upside is that you don't need to purchase weapons, it's all EDF rescued members and drops.Completionist issues aside, the team system and maps also have some flaws.The team system can make multiplayer kind of excessively hectic, though friendly fire is scaled by difficulty. While running all Air Raiders and making everything explode all the time is fun at first, you may want to consult with your teammates on what they want from you in order to progress. Or, you know, not melt your computer.There are some unusual map features in this one, namely being able to fall off the edge of the world. This isn't fatal, and teleports you LOTZ style back to the nearest landmass you were on, but shamefully informs everyone of your humiliation in chat. You can't swim, which frankly isn't much of a loss considering how irritating going swimming for weapon boxes used to be. Still, if you were hoping to retreat into the ocean from a hail of explosions, you can't do that, so be aware.

_childDocuments_.review: An EDF game made for EDF fans, but a far-flung experience from the other games in the series. World Brothers plays like a LEGO game, sounds like a LEGO game, and is voiced like a LEGO game (with the exception of some "Damnits"). -The gameplay is decently fun, but inferior to EDF5, and has some semi-interesting swap mechanics. -Most of the abilities are pretty underwhelming (with the notable exception of Spritefall), but the weapons stay true to the series. -There are some comedy lines that land, but the vast majority of them aren't very good, and they get repeated *way* too often. Like, spiderman game levels of repeated quips.A faithful but kinda mediocre game. This is a $20 game at most.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer, this is a first impression after an hour of playtime.If you didn't like Iron Rain, you aint' gonna like this. It's casual EDF for zoomers with none of that mainline japanese EDF charm. The style they've used has been done to death at this point, the music is beyond overbearing (though it suits the visual style perfectly), the menus are somehow worse for kb/m than they were in Iron Rain and the whole thing reeks of corporate inclusivity.BUTIf you can look past that, there's some fun to be had. The ability to build a team of unique brothers and sisters (siblings?) and switch roles on on the fly, along with the addition of ultimate abilities adds a new layer of depth and management to single player gameplay which, at least from an early impression, adds a a fresh take on killing waves of space bugs, especially considering the inclusion of the classes from other EDF games. It feels like if you're not constantly switching, you're doing it wrong. The style is bright and bouncy, and if you like games that play on nostalgia you'll probably like it a lot. In true EDF fashion, the weapon system is incomprehensible at first glance and the special abilities and ultimates are a complete mystery until you add a guy to your team and test them out, which I imagine is going to be an issue later in the game when stuff might actually kill you. Character handling feels almost identical to Iron Rain to the point where it feels more like a reskin than a new game. Additionally, the maps have that claustrophobic Iron Rain feel to them. If you liked these things about IR, you'll feel right at home here. Also, you're definitely going to walk off the edge of the map and die a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: EARTH DEFENSE FORCE: WORLD BROTHERS

_childDocuments_.review: The game loses you pretty quickly.  While better than Iron Rain, it has several issues.Weapons: So picture this.  Instead of multiple weapon crates to pick up, a mission only spawns 3 no matter what.  That is all you get.  Want to grind for better stuff? 3 max per mission.  If you want any leveling up it applies to one of the hundred of so AI's to get, not the weapons.  To me this is even worse than the purchase system in Iron Rain.Voxels:  While the building destruction is nice, the enemy destruction is lame at best.Enemies just blow up in pre-made block segments no matter how you hit them.  It all starts to feel really samey.AI: Your AI help does very little damage.  I saw an AI hit a simple ant with 8 rockets and it did nothing to it.  It will take awhile for them to kill enemies.  Worst of all when it comes to explosions all they do is push the enemies across the map that you need to chase. While the EDF songs are back, they are just a copy from 4.1Levels:  Tons of repeats. Only 60 missions.  Yes I know previous EDF games repeated levels, but here it is VERY noticeable. It 10 missions in expect to have 3-4 repeats.Sound and quips: Characters repeat their lines WAY to often.  Over the course of a level expect your character to say the same thing around 15 times.  It gets annoying very fast.  Story:  The story is told to you at the start of the game.  None of the missions so far seem to care about it, or proceed with it further.  You already know what you are after from the start.  There are no surprises like in 4.1 or 5.  Also the 4th wall breaking is BAD.  Like cringe levels of bad.  "We need to trigger the bosses escape event" bad.The game is NOT worth the price at all.  This is a $20 title sold for $60.  I will give it more of a chance, but so far the entire thing is lackluster.

_childDocuments_.review: Although it'll look like I'm shouting, I picked up a copy of EARTH DEFENSE FORCE: WORLD BROTHERS (WB) recently. I've played a couple of the EDF games, and until this one was released, Iron Rain seemed to be the biggest deviance from the formula. WB makes significant changes to the tone, visual style, and gameplay, although certain factors seem baked into the series. At least one of these games acknowledges that different parts of the world aren't exactly the same.Most of these games have centered around four classes, which utilize distinct weapons, and emphasize different playstyles. WB expanded the number of classes substantially, focusing on different national figures as inspiration for abilities and super moves. For instance, British guards that set up defensive forts, or guys dressed up as bears slashing giant insects with their claws. With such an expansive roster, you're able to bring a team of four into every mission, and can change who you're controlling on the fly. The AI will control them in the meanwhile, but this allows you to take advantage of reload times, by playing as someone who still has a fully-loaded weapon. I've found this flexibility a huge asset in stages, and imagine I'd feel a bit irked if I went back to another title that lacks this feature.When it comes to avoiding one of EDF's bigger flaws, WB suffers from the same problem of being incredibly grindy. What's changed is the way you go about it. Instead of collecting armor and weapon drops from defeated enemies, who only drop health and special ability energy now, you find prone survivors in each mission. If you rescue them, after finishing the stage, they'll be added to your roster. Those who you've already found provide experience to that character, increasing their level to a max of ten, with each upgrade increasing the weapon types you can equip onto that character. Rescuing people is also how you'll find new weapons and accessories, so it's important to do this as often as possible.I thought the controls were well-designed and responsive. By default, your shots are set to home in on nearby targets, and this doesn't seem out of place to me. Bearing in mind how many of your targets are gigantic, there's not much reason in focusing on pin-point accuracy. You're firing at so many enemies in every mission, and not having to be too precise with every shot is a relief.Quite a few missions revolved around silly things in relation to your brothers and sisters. Saving cattle might not be a joke, but focusing on honey and miso soup seemed less important than trying to piece the world back together. Thankfully, it has the basic structure of building blocks, so there's some hope of restoring the planet. Much of the tone is comedic, with fourth-wall breaks, but it occasionally has more serious moments, which feels a little out of place in a parody spin-off.This is the most striking and obvious difference between WB and any other EDF title, as they made use of voxels. It basically just means they used 3D pixels to compose all the in-game objects. From playing the other games, I've gotten used to seeing giant insects, without freaking out like a scared little boy. Seeing them in this style blunts the theoretical fear factor even more, because even though they move, it has the appearance of a toy made of blocks, more than actual monsters. I don't know what inspired this choice, but I liked this aesthetic, and imagine it might cause less strain on people's gaming systems.One area where this title fits in with the others is the music, as it has the same patriotic, uplifting cadence as always. I think this was a smart choice, as the number of enemies, feeling of being overwhelmed, and sheer difficulty on the hardest missions remains. With this music playing though, it helps spur the players' drive to keep up the good fight. Since they made use of so many figures from around the world, not making use of distinct instruments and musical styles from abroad seems like a wasted opportunity though.🌟 With 60 levels, 5 difficulty levels, and 186 characters to rescue, there's a substantial amount of content available. This game offers good value for the asking price. The fact that the number isn't 180 bothers me more than it should.🌟 When you play online coop, as local isn't available, every player still brings their own team of four into each mission. This opens up interesting possibilities for how weapons could work in tandem with others.🌟 I think the sillier tone helped me lean more into the fun factor, without taking things too seriously.❌ Some bosses have an unreasonable amount of HP. It's bad enough that being hit by them once can wipe you out, but when they just won't die, it gets exhausting, “It's been ten minutes, just die already!”❌ Increasing the strength of classes or weapons is all dependent on RNG, instead of being directly based on skill, or powering up items you use heavily.❌ The grind.🔍 For any team I use, I like having one that's highly mobile, and a tank with lots of armor. Mobility is useful for getting across maps to rescue survivors, and the tank can withstand damage, in order to revive fallen members. With the other two, I look for good weapon choices and abilities.🔍 When you select the deploy option, you can switch to other teams you've made. It's possible to arrange a total of six. I'd make a few combinations meant for handling different situations, such as the more durable robots, nothing but insects, flying enemies, etc.🔍 I'd do a playthrough on Easy first, mainly due to how many classes you'll unlock. If you're like me and keep trying out new classes when you unlock them, trying a team of newbies on a later level can be dicey.It's been a while since I've played a shooter, so I rapidly put in several hours, playing through all the stages on the three starting difficulty levels: easy, normal, and hard. In some ways, finding a new survivor could be annoying, as I'd feel compelled to try them out. However, when I discovered a combination of traits I liked, I'd have to consider whether they should join one of my alternative teams. Ironically, despite having so many options, I wind up playing as more of them than I normally do in the other EDF titles, since I can swap around in the middle of a stage. Despite all the hours I've played in EDF 4.1, I've barely touched the fencer or air raider. Comparing the two titles is interesting, as there's significant parallels, and differences. Either way, I really enjoyed WB, which raises my hope that the upcoming sequel will offer more of this distinct gameplay. Ultimately, that'd apply to both EDF 6 and WB 2, so I have two games to look forward to. Here's hoping I'd have as much reason to recommend them as I do this release.

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT buy this unless you have 1-3 friends to play with since matchmaking is completely dead.
